en: Salutations to that unprecedented physician who destroyed all diseases such as passion— which are constantly persistent, spread throughout the entire body, and leave nothing behind— bestowing [instead] freedom from longing, wisdom, and joy. (1)
By one desiring long life, the highest respect should be accorded to the instructions of Ayurveda, which is the means for achieving virtue, wealth, and happiness. (2)
Brahmā, having remembered the Veda of Longevity, taught it to Prajāpati;
he [taught] it to the two Aśvins, they to the Thousand-eyed One, and he to the sages such as the son of Atri and others. // 3 //
They, however, composed separate treatises beginning with Agniveśa; from those [treatises], which were for the most part excessively dispersed, this collection of the very essence has been made. (4)

The *Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya* is composed, being neither too concise nor too prolix, [dealing with] the body, pediatrics, demonic possession, diseases of the head, surgery, toxicology, gerontology, and aphrodisiacs. (5)
1.5bv It is neither too concise nor too prolix;
they say it has eight branches upon which medical treatment is based.
Briefly stated, there are three humors: wind, bile, and phlegm. (6)
These [doshas], both in their vitiated and non-vitiated states, destroy and sustain the body;
though they are pervasive, they reside respectively below, in the middle, and above the heart and the navel.
1.7b–v. Those [humors], located respectively at the end, middle, and beginning of the day, night, and meals, destroy and increase the digestive fire (agni) in sequence.
By them, the fire becomes irregular, sharp, or dull; when they are in equilibrium, it is balanced.

The constitution (koṣṭha) may be cruel, mild, or moderate; it becomes moderate even by those [humors] being equal, just as the embryo at birth is affected by poison due to the presence of poison and worms in the semen and ovum.
And by these, three types—inferior, middling, and superior—are distinguished separately;
among all of them, one with balanced *dhātus* is best, while those arising from two *doṣas* are censurable. (10)
1.10cv When the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) are in equilibrium, [the qualities] therein are balanced.
Vata (wind) is dry, light, cold, rough, subtle, and mobile;
pitta is slightly unctuous, sharp, hot, light, foul-smelling, flowing, and liquid.

Kapha is unctuous, cold, heavy, slow, smooth, soft, and stable; there are also combinations (saṃsarga) and the triad of humors (saṃnipāta), arising from the depletion or aggravation of two or three of them respectively. 12.
The seven bodily constituents (dhātus) are chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen; the impurities (dūṣyas) are the waste products, such as urine, feces, sweat, and so forth. // 13 //
The increase of all [humors] occurs through similar [tastes], while the opposite occurs through dissimilar ones.
The tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent. (14)

These six substances are dependent [on the body], and as previously stated, they bring about strength; among them, the first three destroy wind (māruta), while the three beginning with bitter (tikta) destroy phlegm (kapha). // 15 //
Astringent, bitter, and sweet substances pacify pitta, while others aggravate it; thus, a substance is of three types: pacifying, provocative, or beneficial for those in good health. (16)
Due to the predominance of the qualities of heat and cold, potency (vīrya) therein is traditionally held to be of two kinds;
the post-digestive transformation (vipāka) of a substance is of three kinds, consisting of sweet, sour, and pungent. // 17 //
Heavy, mild, cold, unctuous, smooth, dense, soft, and stable;
these ten qualities, along with their opposites—subtle and clear—make twenty. (18)
The application of time, objects, and actions—whether deficient, improper, or excessive, as well as correct application—should be understood as the sole cause of disease and health respectively. (19)

Disease is the imbalance of the *doṣas*, while the equilibrium of the *doṣas* is health. In that regard, diseases are traditionally held to be of two kinds, distinguished as endogenous (*nija*) and exogenous (*āgantu*). // 20 //
Due to the distinction between body and mind, their basis is also twofold;
passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) are declared to be the two defects of the mind. (21)
1.21cd–22ab: "In this regard, two types of faults have been described.

Furthermore, one should examine the patient through questions concerning [his] vision and touch, and [one should examine] the disease by means of its etiology, premonitory symptoms, clinical signs, therapeutic suitability, and the final outcome."
One should thoroughly examine the patient. Now, regarding the examination of the patient, they say that "place" (deśa) is twofold here, distinguished by the earth and the body.
The arid (jāṅgala) region is predominantly windy, while the marshy (anūpa) region is characterized by an excess of phlegm.

One should designate the common ground as being of three types, characterized by equal impurities; time consists of moments and so forth, as well as the stages of disease, which determines the application of medicine. (24)
Medicine is, in brief, of two kinds: purification and pacification;
these are, respectively, the supreme remedies for the bodily humors (doṣas). (25)

Enema, purgation, and emesis, as well as oil, clarified butter, and honey—along with the discernment of wisdom, fortitude, the self, and so forth—are the supreme medicines for the defects of the mind. (26)
The physician, the medicinal substances, the attendant, and the patient constitute the four pillars of medical treatment; each of these is specified as possessing four qualities. (27)

A physician who is skillful, who has grasped the meaning of the scriptures from authoritative sources, who has observed clinical practice, and who is pure, [should prescribe] medicine that is prepared with many methods, possesses many qualities, is effective, and is appropriate. (28)
One who is devoted, pure, skillful, intelligent, a capable attendant, wealthy, yet free from disease, obedient to the physician, communicative, and endowed with fortitude—[such a person is fit]. (29)
Disease is of two kinds: curable and incurable; these two are further divided into four types: easily curable, curable with difficulty, palliable, and untreatable. (29+1)

In the body of a young man who has conquered his self and whose constitution can withstand all medicinal herbs, [a disease] that does not strike a vital organ (marman), which has minor causes and mild symptoms, and which is free from complications, [is easily cured]. (30)

When the patient, location, season, and constitution are dissimilar [to the disease], and the feet [of the physician] are complete, and the planets are favorable, a new disease following a single path is easily cured. (31)
The means of treatment involve weapons and the like, and it is difficult; furthermore, there is disease resulting from the confusion [of humors].
Because of the remainder of one's lifespan, it is palliable through the practice of wholesome regimens, but otherwise, it is incurable. (32)
If it were established in an absolute reversal [of its nature], it would be beyond all remedy;
it would produce longing, delusion, and aversion, manifest as a fatal omen, and bring about the destruction of the senses. (33)

A physician should abandon one who is afflicted by disease, one who is hated by physicians or kings, one who hates them, one who is hateful, one who lacks necessary equipment, one who is distracted, one who is uncontrollable, and one whose life has reached its end. (34)
Furthermore, for one who is fierce, afflicted by grief, timid, ungrateful, or who merely fancies himself a physician, the summary of the chapters of this treatise will hereafter be declared. (35)

The objects of desire for life-span, wealth, pleasure, and the seasons; the causes of the arising of diseases; food, knowledge, protection from food, proper measure, substances, and tastes—these are the bases [of medical inquiry]. // 36 //
Knowledge of the humors and so forth, their classifications, and their treatment; the two types of therapeutic procedures;
purification and the rest; oleation, sudation, emesis, non-unctuous enema, and nasal medication. (37)
Fumigation, gargling, eye-washes, nourishment, instruments, and surgical tools;
the procedure for venesection, the procedure for foreign bodies, and the applications of surgery, caustic alkali, and fire. (38)
1.38c–v: Venesection, the procedure for foreign bodies, and the section on technical terminology—these thirty chapters are called the *Śārīra-sthāna*.
[The following] consists of the chapters on conception, its abnormalities, and the classification of limbs and vital points (*marman*). 1.39.

The sixth etiological factor (nidāna) is morbid alteration (vikṛti), which pertains to all diseases, including fever, hemorrhage, dyspnea, consumption, intoxication, hemorrhoids, diarrhea, and so forth. (40)

There are sixteen [formulations] for urinary obstruction and prameha, for abscesses and abdominal enlargements, and for those afflicted by anemia, skin diseases, and vāta disorders, as well as for vātarakta. 41.
The treatment for fever, blood disorders, cough, asthma, consumption, vomiting, alcoholism, hemorrhoids, poisoning, and urinary disorders—two [chapters] each are provided for these. (42)
The treatment for abscesses, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, anemia, edema, erysipelas, leprosy, vitiligo, wind diseases, and gout is [described here]. // 43 //

These twenty-two chapters constitute the *Kalpasiddhi*; beyond this are the *Kalpa* on emetics (*vamana*) and purgatives (*vireka*), their successful application (*siddhi*), and the preparation of enemas (*vasti-kalpanā*). 44.
The successful management of complications arising from enemas; thereafter, the sixth section is the chapter on pharmaceutical preparations.
Furthermore, there are two chapters each on the nursing of infants, their diseases, and seizures caused by spirits. (45)

In cases of insanity and loss of memory, [the physician should apply] two [pastes] each on the channels and the joints; in cases of blindness, darkness before the eyes, and loss of vision, three [pastes]; and in systemic diseases, two [pastes] each. (46)

In cases of wounds to the ears, nose, mouth, or head; in fractures; in fistula-in-ano; in glandular swellings (granthi) and other minor diseases (kṣudraroga); and in diseases of the private parts—two [applications] are used separately for each. (47)
Regarding poisons, serpents, insects, mice, and elixirs—this is the fortieth chapter, on the nourishment of the seed for those who are childless. 48.
Chapter 1.48, titled "The Nourishment of the Seed," concludes this twentieth century of chapters, which has been proclaimed as consisting of six sections (sthāna). 1.48u.
In the Sūtrasthāna:
A healthy person should rise during the Brāhma-muhūrta for the sake of preserving life; then, having attended to the needs of the body, he should perform the prescribed rites of purification. (1)
Having eaten in the morning the tender tips of *arka*, *nyagrodha*, *khadira*, *karañja*, *kakubha*, and other such plants, which are astringent, pungent, and bitter; // 2 //
One should chew a tooth-cleansing twig that is twelve finger-breadths long, straight, and as thick as the tip of the little finger, without injuring the gums of the teeth. (3)

2.3cv One should chew the tooth-stick; however, one suffering from indigestion, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, fever, or facial paralysis, as well as those afflicted with thirst, inflammation of the mouth, or diseases of the heart, eyes, head, or ears, should not consume it. 4.
Therefore, one should constantly apply *sauvīra* collyrium, which is beneficial for the eyes;
for the eye consists of light (*tejas*), and it is especially susceptible to harm from phlegm (*śleṣman*).
One who has eaten, one who has bathed his head, one who is fatigued, one who has undergone emesis or nasal medication,
one who has stayed awake at night, and one who is afflicted with fever— these individuals, especially those with a predominance of phlegm, should not apply collyrium to their eyes.
For seven nights from this [time], one should apply *rasāñjana* for the purpose of inducing secretion;
thereafter, one should partake of nasal drops (*nāvana*), gargles (*gaṇḍūṣa*), medicinal smoke (*dhūma*), and betel (*tāmbūla*).
2.6bv For the purpose of inducing lacrimation, *rasāñjana* [is used].
Betel leaf is unwholesome for those whose eyes are afflicted by injury, *pitta*, blood, or dryness;
it is also unwholesome for those suffering from poisoning, fainting, intoxication, and for those with wasting diseases (*śoṣin*).

One should practice oil massage daily; it removes old age, fatigue, and wind-disorders, and it brings about clarity of vision, nourishment, longevity, sound sleep, beautiful skin, and firmness of the body. (8)
One should practice this especially on the head, ears, and feet.

Massage with oil (abhyaṅga) should be avoided by those afflicted by phlegm (kapha), those who have undergone purification therapies (saṃśuddhi), and those suffering from indigestion (ajīrṇin). // 9 //
Lightness, capacity for action, a blazing digestive fire, the reduction of fat, and the development of well-defined, firm limbs arise from physical exercise. (10)

A child, an elderly person, one afflicted by disorders of wind or bile, and one with indigestion should avoid it; however, those who are strong and eat unctuous food may consume it in half the usual dose.
During the cold season and in spring, one should do this only mildly; at other times, having made the body comfortable, one should massage it thoroughly on all sides.
From excessive physical exercise, thirst, consumption of food, fever, internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), fatigue, exhaustion, cough, and vomiting arise. (13)

One who indulges in excessive physical exertion, staying awake at night, travel, women, laughter, idle talk, and other such rash acts, perishes utterly, like one who attempts to drag an elephant as if it were a lion. 14.
2.14dv Since one perishes by using it excessively,
[oil] massage (udvartana) removes phlegm (kapha), dissolves fat (medas),
stabilizes the limbs, and is supreme for clarifying the skin. // 15 //
Bathing is illuminating, aphrodisiac, life-prolonging, and bestows vigor and strength;
it conquers itching, impurities, fatigue, perspiration, drowsiness, thirst, burning sensations, and evil influences. (16)
2.16b–c. Bathing bestows vigor and strength;
sprinkling the lower body with warm water brings strength.
However, using that same [warm water] for the head takes away strength from the hair and the eyes.

And by that same [method], for the head: that very [method] is for the head in cases of facial paralysis (ardita), diseases of the eyes, mouth, and ears, and diarrhea. Bathing [with it] is likewise [indicated].
It is also censured when one suffers from flatulence, catarrh, indigestion, or has just finished eating. // 18 //
When digestion has occurred, one should eat wholesome and moderate food; one should not forcibly suppress natural urges.
One should not attend to other tasks while under the impulse of an urge, nor until the curable disease has been conquered. (19)
All activities of all living beings are considered to have happiness as their goal; yet happiness does not exist without Dharma. Therefore, one should be devoted to Dharma. (20)
One who stays far from the opposite [vices] should serve spiritual friends with devotion;
[one should avoid] violence, theft, as one pleases, slander, and harsh or false speech. (21)
One should abandon the tenfold evil karma—frivolous speech, malice, covetousness, and the perversion of views—through body, speech, and mind. (22)
One should assist those afflicted by lack of livelihood, disease, or grief to the best of one's ability;
one should always regard even insects and ants as one does oneself. (23)
One should honor gods, cows, brahmins, elders, physicians, kings, and guests; one should not turn away those who seek help, nor should one despise or revile them. (24)
One should be intent on doing good even toward an enemy intent on doing harm; one should remain single-minded in both prosperity and adversity, and envy the cause, but not the fruit.
One should speak at the proper time, what is beneficial, measured, non-contradictory, and gentle;
being the first to speak, with a pleasant countenance, virtuous conduct, and soft with compassion. (26)
One is not happy alone, nor is one entirely confident, nor is one entirely apprehensive;
one has no enemy of one's own, nor is one the enemy of anyone else. (27)
One should not reveal the Master’s disregard nor his lack of affection;
rather, having observed the disposition of people, one should act in such a way that each person is satisfied. (28)
One who is skilled in serving others should not manifest contempt for him, but should instead conform to his will in that very same way;
he should neither afflict the senses nor indulge them excessively.
One should not engage in any undertaking that is devoid of the three aims of life (trivarga), provided it does not conflict with them;
rather, one should follow the middle way in all dharmas at every step.

With his hair, nails, and beard kept short, with his pores free from impurity, he should be habituated to bathing, well-scented, elegantly attired, and neither ostentatious nor excessively gaudy. (31)
2.31–32. Habitually bathing and fragrant, he should constantly carry gems, perfected mantras, and great medicinal herbs.
Wearing a sunshade and footwear, he should walk while looking only a yoke’s length ahead.

At night, or in an urgent matter, one who carries a staff, wears a turban, and is accompanied by an assistant may enter; however, he must avoid shrines, objects of worship, banners, weapons, shade, ashes, husks, and impurities. (33)
One should not step on ground containing gravel, clods of earth, offerings, or places used for ritual bathing;
one should not cross a river by swimming with one's arms, nor should one walk over a mass of fire.
One should not board a doubtful boat or climb a tree, just as one would avoid a defective vehicle;
nor should one sneeze, laugh, or yawn without covering the mouth. (35)
One should not suppress a sneeze, laugh, or yawn; one should not pick at the nose, nor scratch the ground without cause;
one should not move the limbs in an improper manner, nor sit for a long time with the thighs crossed.
2.36b–d: One should not dig the earth without a purpose, nor remain for long in a squatting posture.
One should withdraw the activities of body, speech, and mind before they become fatigued;
one should not stand for long with the knees raised, nor should one frequent trees at night.
Likewise, one should not [enter] crossroads, shrines, four-way junctions, or temples, nor slaughterhouses, forests, empty houses, or cremation grounds, even during the day. (38)
One should never look at an unclean mirror, an unadorned woman, or a menstruating woman in the morning, as these are inauspicious. 38+1.
One should never look at the sun, nor carry a burden on one's head;
one should not gaze continuously at anything minute, nor at that which is blazing, impure, or unpleasant. (39)
One should not engage in the sale, brewing, giving, or taking of intoxicants; nor should one expose oneself to the harsh winds, dust, frost, and heat of the east wind. (40)

One who is not upright [should avoid] sneezing, belching, coughing, sleep, food, and sexual intercourse; likewise, the shade of a riverbank, those hostile to the king, and serpents, fanged beasts, and horned animals. 41.
Service to the base, the ignoble, or those who are excessively clever; conflict with superiors; and eating, sexual intercourse, sleep, study, and reflection during the twilight hours. 42.
Eating in a multitude crowded with enemies, sacrificial sessions, and courtesans;
playing musical instruments with one's limbs, face, and nails; and shaking the hands and hair. // 43 //

One should avoid traveling between water, fire, objects of worship, and the center; one should avoid smoke, reliance on corpses, addiction to intoxicants, and excessive intimacy or independence with women. // 44 //
For the wise person, the world alone is the teacher in all activities; therefore, the investigator should follow that very world in matters of worldly affairs.
A moistened mental continuum, renunciation, restraint of body, speech, and mind, and regarding the welfare of others as one's own goal—this is the complete and virtuous vow. (46)
How are my days and nights passing now, such that I am not a partaker of suffering, being thus constantly possessed of mindfulness? (47)
Having thus spent the entire day, when the first watch of the night has passed at home,
one should remember the gods, the sages, and the teachers, and then proceed to sleep.
2.47 When one watch of the night has passed,
this is the summary of the traditional conduct he attains by practicing it:
long life, health, sovereignty, fame, and eternal worlds.
In the Sūtrasthāna, it is taught that the six seasons are reckoned in succession by pairs of months beginning with Māgha:
namely, Śiśira, Vasanta, Grīṣma, Varṣā, Śarad, and Hemanta. (1)
One should know that the three seasons beginning with Śiśira constitute the northern course (uttarāyaṇa);
and during that period, it takes away the strength of men day by day.
For there, by their very nature, the suns and winds—exceedingly sharp, hot, and dry—destroy the gentle qualities of the earth. (3)
In this [season], the tastes—bitter, astringent, and pungent—are progressively more powerful;
therefore, the Ādāna [season] is fiery, as are the seasons of the southern solstice.
The rains and other seasons, as well as the emission [of seed], are that power which this [sun] emits;
because of its gentleness, the moon is indeed powerful here, while the sun wanes.
When the heat on the surface of the earth has been pacified by cool clouds, rain, and breezes,
the juices here become succulent, possessing strength through their sour, salty, and sweet qualities.
In cold weather, strength is at its peak; in rain and heat, it is minimal; but in the remaining two seasons, it is moderate.
Due to the suppression of cold by one who possesses strength, the digestive fire becomes powerful in the winter.
When his digestive fire is weak, he may cook the bodily constituents (dhātus) if impelled by wind;
therefore, during this cold season, one should consume sweet, sour, and salty tastes.
Because nights are now so long, one should, being hungry even at the very break of dawn, attend to the necessary duties and practice accordingly as previously described. 9.
One should perform anointing with Vātaghna oils, apply oil to the head, massage it,
engage in wrestling with those who are skilled, and strike the feet with appropriate force.
Then, having had oil applied to his head for massage, and having had the oil removed with astringent decoctions, he bathed according to the prescribed rite;
he was then anointed with saffron mixed with camphor and perfumed with the smoke of agallochum.

One should consume unctuous juices, nourishing meat, molasses-based preparations, clear *surā* liquor, and *surā*, as well as wholesome preparations derived from wheat flour, black gram, sugarcane, and milk. (12)
New food, fat, oil, and warm water for the act of purification;
a cloak, an antelope skin, silk, a woolen blanket, and a *kaucava* rug as a covering. (13)
Covered with a bed spread with *praveṇī* blankets and *kutha* rugs, he should resort to a bed that is light and naturally warm;
and by means of skillful methods, he should always employ the sun's rays, sudation, and foot-coverings.
Beloved women, full of passion, with plump thighs, breasts, and hips, and limbs warm from incense, saffron, and youth, dispel the cold. (15)
For one who dwells in an inner chamber heated by the glow of burning coals, no affliction ever arises from the harshness of cold. (16)
This very same regimen should be observed during the winter as well, with particular care;
for at that time, the cold is excessive, as is the dryness born of the season of withdrawal.
For the phlegm accumulated in the winter, when heated by the rays of the sun in spring, destroys the digestive fire and produces diseases; therefore, one should eliminate it with haste. (18)
Having conquered the aggravated *śleṣman* by means of strong emetics and nasal drops, light and dry foods, physical exercise, massage, and blows. (19)
Having bathed and anointed himself with camphor, sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron,
he should eat aged barley, wheat, honey, and roasted meat from the forest.
Having tasted those mango-flavored drinks offered by his beloved—perfumed by contact with her mouth and marked by the lotuses of her eyes. // 21 //
For the sake of cheerfulness, he should drink pleasant *āsava*, *ariṣṭa*, *sīdhu*, *mārdvīka*, and *mādhava* liquors, free from acidity, accompanied by his friends.
There were waters of ginger, waters of the heartwood of the sāra tree, honeyed waters, and waters from the clouds,
flowing everywhere, cooled by the southern breeze.

3.23 Or [one should act] with honey-water or rainwater in places where the sun is not seen, where the splendor of jeweled pavements shines, and which resound with the warbling of cuckoos— grounds for the fulfillment of amorous desires.
3.24 In fragrant groves where the sun is never seen to set or rise, and where trees are laden with various flowers,
one may pass the midday happily, engaged in diverse conversations.
One should avoid heavy foods, cold things, sleeping during the day, and substances that are unctuous, sour, or sweet;
for in summer, the sun with its exceedingly sharp rays seems to utterly consume [the body]. (26)
3.26cv The sun, with its exceedingly sharp rays, daily consumes the fat; by this, phlegm diminishes and wind increases.

Therefore, in this [season], one should avoid pungent, bitter, and sour [tastes], physical exercise, and the rays of the sun. 3.27ab/ab 3.27cd/ab 3.28ab/ab 3.28cd/ab 3.29ab/ab 3.29cd/ab 3.30ab/ab One should consume only sweet food that is light, unctuous, cold, and liquid;
having sprinkled one's limbs with very cold water, one should lick parched grain flour mixed with sugar. (28)
Liquor should not be drunk; or if it is to be drunk, it should be in very small quantities and mixed with plenty of water.
Otherwise, it causes emaciation, flaccidity, burning sensations, and delusion. (29)
Otherwise, for the softening of swelling, one should eat *śāli* rice, white as a jasmine flower or a conch shell, with the meat of wild animals;
one should drink broth that is not too thick, as well as *rasālā*, *rāga*, and *khāṇḍava*.
3.30 Rice as white as jasmine or the moon, *rasālā*, *rāgakhāḍava*,
or *rāgaṣāḍava*,
or a *pānaka* made from the five essences, placed in a vessel of fresh clay;
It should be served with pieces of plantain and *coca* fruit, made slightly sour using earthen shells. // 31 //
3.31bv–32. One should drink water that is very cold, scented with *pāṭalā* flowers, mixed with camphor, and kept in a new earthen vessel;
while drinking it at night, one should consume moonbeams as food.
Buffalo’s milk mixed with sugar, cooled by the moon and the stars, [was offered] while the hot rays of the sun were blocked by great *śāla* and *tāla* trees that scraped the very clouds. // 33 //
In groves graced with clusters of grapes entwined by mādhavī vines, where the pavilions were being sprinkled with fragrant, cool water; (34)
The courtyard was adorned with mango sprouts, fruits, and *lumbi* clusters, as well as plantain leaves, white lotuses, lotus stalks, and blue and white water lilies. // 35 //
At midday, afflicted by the heat of the sun, one should sleep on a bed fashioned of soft, laughing flowers and shoots, or else in a fountain-house.

And on the rooftops of palaces during the nights, which are strewn with the rays of the moon and filled with water infused with ushira-roots, flowing from the hands, mouths, and breasts of statues of women. (37)
Seated with a tranquil mind, anointed with moist sandalwood paste, wearing a garland, having turned away from the pursuit of desire, and dressed in very fine, thin garments. (38)
There were palm-leaf fans damp with water, broad lotus-blossom cups,
and gentle breezes that sprinkled water and carried the cold of frost.
Garlands of camphor and jasmine, necklaces together with yellow sandalwood paste, and young mainas and parrots with enchanting, melodious speech; // 40 //
Adorned with bracelets of lotus stalks, radiant with full-blown lotuses,
these beloved women steal away one's fatigue like moving lotus ponds.
Even a fire that has been kindled dies out for those whose bodies are afflicted by fever;
during the rains, when the sky is hung with water, they are further corrupted by the humors (doṣas).
3.42 Their bodies were withered by the sudden onset of frosty winds and chilled by water that was turbid from the earth's vapors and sour from acidic decomposition.
When they are thus mutually disparaging one another due to their dullness of intellect,
he should employ all that is common to them, as well as whatever serves to sharpen their inner heat.

A non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) is indicated for one whose body is purified, who has digested old grain, prepared meat-broths, the flesh of wild animals, vegetable soups, honey, fermented medicinal liquors (ariṣṭa), and aged substances. 45.
On a very cloudy day, one's meal should consist of whey enriched with sauvarcala salt and powdered pañcakola, or rainwater, well water, or boiled water. 46.
3.46 He should consume whey enriched with *sauvarcala* salt, made distinctly sour, salty, and oily; when dried, it is light like honey.
He should not walk on foot, remain fragrant, and always wear perfumed garments.
One should dwell on the roof of a palace, free from the cold spray of mist;
one should avoid river water, sea water, churning, daytime sleep, physical exertion, and exposure to the sun. 48.
In autumn, the accumulated bile of those whose bodies have been accustomed to the cold of the rainy season and are suddenly heated by the rays of the sun becomes aggravated. (49)
To conquer that [fever], one should use bitter ghee, purgation, bloodletting, and, when hungry, light food that is bitter, sweet, and astringent. (50)
Rice, mung beans, sugar, āmalakī, paṭola, honey, and meat from wild animals—[these are] heated by the rays of the hot-rayed sun and cooled by the beams of the cool-rayed moon. (51)
Everywhere, day and night, there is the water known as Haṃsodaka—purified by the rising of the star Agastya, free from poison, stainless, and a cleanser of impurities. (52)
Neither causing secretions nor parching, his drinks and other refreshments were like nectar;
he was radiant with sandalwood, ushira-root, camphor, pearls, garlands, and fine garments. (53)
At the onset of night, they drank moonlight white as a palace from the palaces, and the heat of snow, alkaline salt, satiated curd, oil, and fat. 54.
One should avoid strong liquor, daytime sleep, and the eastern wind; one should consume the first three tastes during the cold season and the rains, and the last three tastes during the spring. (55)
In the summer, one should consume sweet [foods]; in autumn, sweet, bitter, and astringent ones;
in autumn and spring, dry [foods]; and cold [foods] during the periods between the heat and the rains.
In brief, food and drink are the opposite at other times;
there is constant practice of all tastes, each in its own excess according to the respective season. (57)
The last seven days and the first seven days of two seasons are known as the junction of the seasons (*ṛtusaṃdhi*).
During that time, the preceding rule should be abandoned and the subsequent one adopted in due order. (58)

For diseases arising from unwholesome [regimens] may occur suddenly due to the abrupt abandonment or practice [of such habits] during the last seven days and the first seven days of the two seasons. (3.58)
In the Section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna),
one should not suppress the urges of flatus, feces, urine, sneezing,
thirst, hunger, sleep, cough, fatigue, dyspnea, yawning, tears, vomiting, or semen. (1)

From the suppression of downward wind (apāna), there arise abdominal tumors, upward movement of wind, pain, exhaustion, retention of flatus, urine, and feces, impairment of vision, loss of digestive fire, and diseases of the heart. // 2 //
In that case, the procedures for oleation and sudation, suppositories, foods, drinks, and enemas—whatever promotes the downward movement of Vata—are recommended. (2.1)

From [the suppression of] feces arise scrotal swelling, constipation, catarrh, and headache; as well as upward-moving wind (ūrdhva-vāyu), cutting pain in the flanks (parīkartas), and oppression of the heart. // 3 //
4.3cv When the wind moves upward, it causes parīkartā (a cutting pain), the passage of feces through the mouth, and the aforementioned diseases;
as well as breaking pains in the limbs, urinary stones, and pain in the bladder, penis, and groin. // 4 //
Most diseases arise from the prior obstruction of urine;
their treatment consists of suppositories, massage, immersion baths, fomentation, and the administration of enemas.
In cases of consumption (yakṣma) arising from the obstruction of feces, ghee mixed with food and drink that breaks up the stool is recommended;
however, in those arising from urinary disorders, ghee is praised when taken as a drink before meals.
4.6cv And in diseases arising from urine, one should employ a drink; 4.6dv and an *avapīḍaka* of clarified butter,
along with *jīrṇāntika*, in the highest dose for two applications.
And this is designated as the *avapīḍaka* because it is held [in the mouth]. // 7 //
In that condition, there is belching, loss of appetite, trembling, obstruction of the heart and chest, flatulence, cough, and hiccups; the treatment for it is the same as for hiccups. (8)

Headache, weakness of the senses, and stiffness of the neck (manyā-stambha) caused by suppressed sneezing should be treated with sharp medicinal smoke, collyrium, snuffs, nasal drops, and gazing at the sun. // 9 //
One should induce a persistent sneeze and practice oleation and sudation;
[these treat] wasting, lassitude of the limbs, deafness, delusion, vertigo, and heart diseases. (10)

Due to the suppression of thirst, every cooling procedure there is beneficial; [suppression of] hunger causes aching of the limbs, loss of appetite, malaise, emaciation, piercing pain, and vertigo. (11)
4.11dv–12. In that case [of excessive sleep], emaciation, colic, fatigue, and vertigo occur; one should employ light, unctuous, warm, and small quantities of food.
From [excessive] sleep arise delusion, heaviness of the head and eyes, lassitude, and yawning.
4.12ab There is discoloration in that state of hunger; 4.12bc unctuous, warm, and light food is recommended there, as are body massage, sleep, and gentle rubbing.

From the suppression of cough, its aggravation occurs, leading to dyspnea, anorexia, and heart disease. 4.13cd [Note: This line appears to be part of the previous verse's commentary or continuation in some editions.]
In this condition, consumption and hiccups may occur; therefore, a treatment that effectively cures cough should be administered.
Furthermore, abdominal tumors (gulma), heart disease, and delusions may arise from suppressed labored breathing (śrama-śvāsa). (14)
4.14dv Due to the suppression of fatigue-induced dyspnea, rest is beneficial there, as is a therapeutic regimen that subdues Vāta.
In cases of yawning, the diseases are similar to those of sneezing, and every procedure that conquers Vāta is indicated.

4.15 Like sneezing, the diseases arising from yawning are catarrh, pain in the eyes, head, and heart, stiffness of the neck, loss of appetite, and vertigo; along with abdominal tumors, tears [arise] therein, as do dreams, wine, and pleasant conversations.
Erysipelas, urticaria, skin diseases, eye disorders, itching, anemia, fever, cough, dyspnea, nausea, freckles, and swelling result from vomiting. (17)
Gargling, smoking, fasting, vomiting after eating dry food, physical exercise, bloodletting, and purgation are recommended in this condition. (18)
4.18a After consuming gargles, medicated smokes,
and food, 4.18b or after eating dry foods, one should vomit that up.
Oil mixed with alkaline salt is recommended for the purpose of massage;
from semen [discharge], there occurs its flow, as well as pain, swelling, and fever in the private parts. (19)
And for the purpose of massage, it is recommended [for those suffering from] heart pain, retention of urine, breaking pain in the limbs, enlargement of the scrotum, urinary stones, and impotence;
[as well as for] the cock, wine, *śāli* rice, enemas, massage, and immersion baths. 4.19bv–20ab.

One should consume milk prepared with substances that cleanse the bladder and enjoy the company of beloved women; however, one who is afflicted by thirst and colic, emaciated, vomiting feces, or suppressing natural urges should be abandoned [as a patient].
All diseases arise from the forceful arousal or the suppression of natural urges; the remedy for those [diseases] has been most extensively prescribed therein.
Therefore, since the wind (vāyu) generally becomes aggravated in many ways, one should administer food, drink, and medicine that are conducive to its downward movement (anulomana). // 23 //

One who desires his own welfare, having conquered the senses, should always restrain the impulses of greed, envy, hatred, stinginess, passion, and so forth, both in this world and for the sake of the life hereafter.
And one should strive, according to the proper time, for the purification of impurities; for if they are accumulated in excess, they become enraged and may even take away one's life. (25)

The doshas, when subdued by fasting and digestive treatments, may sometimes become aggravated again; however, for those who have been purified by means of cleansing therapies (saṃśodhana), there is no recurrence.

4.26cd–27ab. However, for those who have been purified by the cleansing therapies (saṃśodhana), there is no recurrence [of the disease]. Henceforth, the physician who knows the proper time should administer proven rejuvenative formulations (rasāyana) and aphrodisiac preparations (vṛṣya-yoga) according to the sequence and as appropriate.
4.27–28ab. For one whose body has been depleted by [the administration of] medicines, nourishing food should be prescribed in due order and according to what is appropriate,
such as *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, mung beans, meat, ghee, and so forth.

4.28–29. [One should treat with] soups of mung beans and meat, and other such items, combined with heart-pleasing and digestive-stimulating medicines that provide relish and promote digestion; and by means of oil massages, dry rubs, baths, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), and unctuous enemas (sneha-vasti).
Thus he obtains well-being, the power to burn away all impurities, clarity of intellect, complexion, and the senses, virility, and longevity. (30)
Those diseases arising from spirits, poisons, wind, fire, wounds, fractures, and the like, as well as those consisting of passion, hatred, fear, and so forth, are known as adventitious ailments. (31)
4.31cd–32ab: The abandonment of desire, anger, fear, and the like; the relinquishing of errors of judgment; tranquility of the senses; mindfulness;
knowledge of place, time, and the self; and following the conduct of the virtuous.

The pacification rites prescribed in the Atharvaveda, the worship of adverse planets, and the means for warding off the touch of spirits and other malevolent forces have each been specified individually. (33)
In brief, this method has been demonstrated for the non-arising of disorders, both innate and adventitious, as well as for the pacification of those already arisen. (34)
4.34 In brief, by purifying the accumulation of humors arising from cold during the spring when [diseases] have not yet arisen, that from summer at the time of the clouds,
and that from the rainy season at the end of the heavy rains, one will never quickly incur diseases born of the seasons.

One who constantly practices wholesome diet and conduct, acts with circumspection, is unattached to sense objects, is generous, impartial, devoted to truth, patient, and serves those who are trustworthy, remains free from disease. (36)
The water from the Sūtrasthāna is life-sustaining, satiating, pleasing to the heart, refreshing, and an awakener of the intellect;
it has a subtle and unmanifest taste, is pure, cool, light, and like nectar. (1)
The water of the Gaṅgā, having fallen from the sky and been touched by the sun, the moon, and the wind, depends further upon place and time for its wholesomeness or unwholesomeness. // 2 //
Wherever pure rice-gruel has been showered down and remains shining—unsoiled and unchanged in color—that is to be drunk as water from the Ganges; otherwise, it is not so.
5.3bv Rice-gruel placed in a silver vessel 5.3cv Shall be neither moist nor discolored;
5.3cv Or it shall be neither moist nor discolored;
5.3dv That water is like the Ganges, otherwise it is not.
That ocean water should not be drunk except during the month of Āśvayuja;
one should always drink rainwater from Indra that remains in a good vessel and is undeteriorated.
And in the absence of that, one should use [water] situated on the ground that resembles that of the atmosphere,
which has been struck by the sun and wind in a pure place with black or white earth.
5.5ab And in its absence, for the most part, one should drink earth-water (bhauma).

One should not drink water that is turbid with mud, moss, grass, or leaves; nor that which has not been exposed to the sun, moon, or wind; nor that which has been recently rained upon; nor that which is thick and heavy. 6.
That which is frothy, inhabited by living creatures, heated, or so cold that it can only be grasped with the teeth;
that which is not in its proper season yet is divine, or that which is its first seasonal flow—[these are forbidden]. (7)

Water defiled by contact with the threads of spiders and the like, or with feces, urine, or poison, as well as those flowing swiftly toward the western ocean and possessing pure water—[these are not to be used]. (8)
In brief, those rivers are wholesome; however, others are the opposite.
Their waters are distressed by the striking, tossing, and breaking against rocks.

5.9ab In brief, rivers originating from the Himavat and Malaya mountains are wholesome; they are likewise stable [in their flow], yet they cause diseases of the worms, elephantiasis, heart, throat, and head. // 10 //

Those originating from the East, Avantī, and the Western borderlands cause diseases of the neck; those born in Mahendra cause abdominal ailments and elephantiasis; furthermore, those arising in the Sahya and Vindhya mountains cause similar disorders.

5.11b–v Furthermore, waters originating from the Sahya and Vindhya mountains cause leprosy, anemia, and diseases of the head; those born from the Pāriyātra mountains destroy the [vitiated] humors; those from the ocean produce strength and virility, yet they also provoke the three humors.
5.12dv Sea water causes the three *doṣas*;
it is turbid, impure, blue, thick, or even yellow; it is alkaline and slimy—that is described as *sāmudra* (oceanic) water. 12+1.
One should know that water from wells, tanks, and the like comes from arid, marshy, or mountainous regions;
it should not be drunk when one lacks the physical strength, or in small quantities by those with weak digestion or abdominal tumors. (13)
Those suffering from jaundice, abdominal enlargement, diarrhea, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), emaciation, or edema should drink it;
even a healthy person may drink it sparingly, except during the autumn and summer seasons. (14)
Those suffering from disorders of the *grahaṇī*, edema, or those who are of normal, stout, or lean build, drink water respectively during, after, or before a meal.
Cold water causes intoxication, exhaustion, fainting, vomiting, fatigue, and vertigo. (5.14)
Water that is uniform in consistency—neither too thick nor too thin—subdues hunger, thirst, heat, burning sensations, blood disorders, and poisons.
It is digestive, promotes digestion, is beneficial for the throat, light, hot, and cleanses the bladder. (5.16)
5.16 It is recommended for thirst, feverish heat, burning sensations, hemorrhaging from pitta,
hiccups, flatulence, wind-disorders, phlegm, recent purification therapies, and acute fever;
as well as for cough, vomiting, chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and pain in the flanks.

5.17b–c: In acute fever that has been recently purified [by emesis or purgation], water that is light and non-obstructive (anabhiṣyandi)—either boiled and cooled or left overnight—is beneficial when the humor (doṣa) is associated with pitta; however, that same water, if left overnight, produces all three humors (tridoṣakṛt).

5.18 Coconut water is dry, non-slimy, light, and becomes beneficial when boiled and cooled; however, if it remains standing for a long time, it causes the three doṣas. It is unctuous, sweet, aphrodisiac, cold, and light.
It removes thirst, bile, and wind; it stimulates digestion and cleanses the bladder. // 19 //

During the rainy season, when the water from celestial and terrestrial sources is at its best or worst, [the food] is sweet in digestion and taste, unctuous, vitalizing, and increases the bodily constituents. (20)
Milk generally pacifies wind and bile, is aphrodisiac, increases phlegm, and is heavy and cold; however, cow's milk specifically is vitalizing and acts as a rejuvenative elixir. (21)

It is beneficial for those emaciated by injury, promotes intellect, provides strength, increases breast milk, and is laxative; it cures fatigue, vertigo, intoxication, misfortune, dyspnea, cough, exhaustion, thirst, and hunger. (22)

It destroys chronic fever, dysuria, and hemorrhagic disorders (rakta-pitta), as well as afflictions of breathlessness, cough, thirst, and hunger. Buffalo milk is beneficial for those with excessive digestive fire and insomnia, yet it is heavy and cooling.
Light goat’s meat, when consumed with moderate water intake, physical exercise, and pungent or bitter foods, overcomes consumption, fever, dyspnea, hemorrhagic disorders, and diarrhea. (24)

The meat of the camel is slightly dry, hot, and salty; it stimulates digestion, is light, and is recommended for disorders of wind and phlegm, abdominal distension, worms, swelling, abdominal enlargements, and hemorrhoids. (25)
Human [milk] conquers eye diseases caused by wind, bile, blood, trauma, and other disorders;
it is used for saturation, instillation, and nasal drops. However, warm sheep's milk is not beneficial for the heart.

The meat of the female elephant (hastinī) removes wind-disorders (vātavyādhi), while that of the one-hoofed animal (ekaśapha) strongly cures hiccup and asthma, increases pitta and kapha, provides stability, is hot, and is light. (27)
Milk that is sour and salty removes wind from the limbs but causes numbness;
it is heavy and produces secretions when raw, whereas milk boiled with skill has the opposite effect. (28)
But without the breast milk of a woman, that [milk] is indeed beneficial only when raw.
Curd that is over-boiled becomes heavy, while that which is warm as it flows from the vessel is like nectar;
curd that is sour in taste and post-digestive effect (pāka) is astringent, heavy, hot, and subdues vāta. (29)
It increases fat, semen, strength, phlegm, bile, blood, digestive fire, and swelling;
it is appetizing and is recommended for loss of appetite, cold sensations, and irregular fever. (30)

In cases of chronic rhinitis and dysuria, one should eat dry food; however, in disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), one should not eat at night, nor anything hot, during spring, summer, or autumn.
