Buttermilk is light, astringent and sour, digestive, and it conquers phlegm and wind; however, it causes fever, internal hemorrhaging, bile disorders, erysipelas, skin diseases, anemia, and vertigo. (33)

It overcomes swelling, abdominal enlargement, hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract, urinary retention, loss of appetite, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, complications of ghee therapy, poisoning, and jaundice. (34)
Similarly, whey (mastu) is liquid, purifies the channels, alleviates constipation, and is light.
Fresh butter (navanīta) is aphrodisiac, cooling, and promotes complexion, strength, and digestive fire. (35)

That which is produced from milk is astringent and overcomes wind (vāta), bile (pitta), blood disorders, wasting, hemorrhoids, facial paralysis, and cough; it is also astringent and conquers hemorrhagic fever (rakta-pitta) and diseases of the eyes. (36)
It is recommended for those who desire intelligence, mindfulness, wisdom, fire, strength, longevity, semen, and vision;
and for those who seek vigor, youth, progeny, beauty, delicacy, and a beautiful voice. (37)
It removes wounds, emaciation, spreading diseases, exhaustion from weapons or fire, disorders of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), poison, insanity, consumption, misfortune, and fever. 38.

Ghee is the best among unctuous substances, cooling, and supreme for maintaining youth; possessing a thousand potencies, it performs a thousand functions when prepared according to the prescribed methods.

5.39–40. Prepared according to the prescribed method, Sahasravīrya (the "thousand-fold potency" preparation) overcomes ancient diseases such as intoxication, epilepsy, fainting, and those arising from the head, ears, eyes, and female genital tract; it also cleanses and heals wounds.
Balya, kilāṭa, pīyūṣa, kūrcikā, moraṇa, and so forth, increase semen, sleep, and kapha; they cause constipation, are heavy, and aggravate the doṣas. (41)
5.41bv – *Kūcikā*, *moraṇa*, and others are excellent when derived from cow’s milk and ghee, but are censured when produced from a goat.
The juice of sugarcane is heavy, unctuous, nourishing, and increases *kapha* and urine. 42.
The juice of the mango is aphrodisiac, cooling, and subdues blood and bile; it is sweet in both its post-digestive effect and its taste.
When pressed with the teeth at the beginning, it is salty and resembles sugar. (43)
The processed [substance] undergoes transformation due to being bitten by insects from root to tip, due to affliction, due to contamination with impurities, and due to being held for some time. (44)
Because it can be held for only a short time and causes burning, heaviness, and constipation, Pauṇḍraka is inferior in that regard;
however, Vāṃśika is superior to it due to its coolness, clarity, and sweetness.
5.45ab The *śataparvaka*, *kāntāra*, *naipāla*, and others are, in that order, heavy, burning, and constipating;
they contain alkali and astringent properties, are warm, and cause slight burning.
From that [molasses], in succession, come *śātaparvaka*, *kāntāra*, *nepāla*, and so forth.
Phāṇita (unrefined molasses) is heavy, causes secretions to increase, promotes the accumulation of *doṣas*, and cleanses the urine.
Washed guḍa (jaggery) does not excessively increase *kapha* and facilitates the passage of urine and feces. (5.47)
Another [type of rice] contains abundant worms, marrow, blood, fat, flesh, and phlegm;
that which is old is pleasing to the heart and wholesome, whereas the new kind causes the impairment of kapha and the digestive fire.

Matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa, and sitā are aphrodisiacs, beneficial for those emaciated by wasting or injury, and they alleviate raktapitta and vāta; each is progressively more excellent in its qualities than the preceding one. (49)
Its qualities are bitter, sweet, and astringent; sugar-cane sugar (yāsa-śarkarā) and all other types of sugar destroy burning sensations, thirst, vomiting, fainting, and blood-bile disorders. (50)
Among the products of sugar and sugarcane, treacle (phāṇita) is both superior and inferior;
it is beneficial for the eyes, cuts through [obstructions], and alleviates thirst, phlegm, poison, hiccups, blood disorders, and bile. (51)
Honey conquers urinary disorders, skin diseases, worms, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, and diarrhea; it cleanses, heals, and promotes the healing of wounds, and it increases wind (vāta). (52)
It is dry, astringent, and sweet; honey-sugar is similar to it.
When it is heated, when one is afflicted by heat, and when it is consumed with hot things during the heat, it destroys that [fever]. (53)
It destroys consumption, hemorrhoids, facial paralysis, and disorders of bile and blood; it is astringent, digestive, and stimulates the appetite.
In the case of emesis and non-unctuous enema (nirūha), honey mixed with warm substances is not prohibited;
for in those two procedures, [the medicine] is withdrawn immediately before it has reached full digestion.
5.54c–v Oil that has not yet reached its full maturation is, like its source [the plant], primarily sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), pervasive (*vyavāyin*), and hot;
it causes skin disorders, is harmful to the eyes, and does not increase *kapha*. It is subtle and hot. 55.
It is capable of nourishing the emaciated and reducing the corpulent;
it cures constipation and destroys worms; and when properly processed, it conquers all diseases. (56)
5.56d–57 Castor oil (airaṇḍa-taila), which is sweet, laxative, and heavy, overcomes all defects through processing when combined with bitter and pungent substances;
it cures hernia, abdominal tumors, wind-disorders, phlegm, abdominal enlargement, and irregular fever.
One should conquer swelling and pain localized in the waist, genitals, abdomen, and back;
however, that which arises from the castor-oil plant (raktairaṇḍa) is excessively sharp, hot, slimy, and foul-smelling.
Mustard oil is pungent, hot, and sharp; it subdues phlegm, semen, and wind.
It is light, increases bile and blood, and conquers skin eruptions, leprosy, hemorrhoids, wounds, and parasites. (59)
The fruit of the *ākṣa* tree is sweet, cooling, beneficial for the hair, heavy, and it subdues pitta and vāta.
That produced from the *nimba* tree is not very hot, is bitter, and destroys worms, skin diseases, and kapha. (60)
Umā and kusumbha produce heat; they cause skin disorders, kapha, and pitta.
Fat and marrow destroy vāta and provide strength, pitta, and kapha. (61)
The karañja fruit, which is astringent, bitter, and pungent, purifies wounds.
One should know that fat (medas) also possesses the same nature as the two [muscle and marrow] that follow flesh;
it is digestive, appetizing, moderate, sharp, hot, and bestows contentment and nourishment.
It is sweet, bitter, and pungent; it has an acidic post-digestive taste (pāka) and is laxative;
it is slightly astringent and produces clarity of voice, health, eloquence, and complexion, while being light. (63)

It is beneficial for those who have lost sleep or suffer from excessive sleep; it aggravates pitta and blood, is wholesome for the emaciated and the obese, is parching, subtle, and a cleanser of the channels. (64)
When drunk according to the proper method, it removes wind and phlegm; otherwise, it is like poison.
Fresh [grain] is heavy and generates those same defects, whereas old grain is the opposite. (65)
Grapes, sugarcane, dates, rice-flour, and barley—these are the five excellent sources of intoxicants; among them, grapes are distinguished as the best.

A drink made from the flour of *śāli* rice and barley should not be taken with hot applications, nor by those who have been purged, nor by the hungry; it should not be excessively sharp, mild, or deficient in ingredients, nor should it be turbid. (5.65.1+1bv)
Wine destroys Gulma, abdominal enlargements, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and emaciation; it is unctuous and heavy.
It subdues Vata and increases fat, blood, breast milk, urine, and Kapha. (67)
Vāruṇī liquor produced from that [grain] is beneficial to the heart, light, and sharp;
it destroys colic, cough, vomiting, dyspnea, constipation, flatulence, and chronic rhinitis. (68)
Light and wholesome liquor made from vibhītaka nuts, which is not excessively intoxicating, is not overly contraindicated for use in wounds, anemia, and skin diseases. (69)
Barley liquor (yava-surā) is constipating, heavy, dry, and aggravates the three doṣas.
Ariṣṭa possesses the qualities of its constituent ingredients and excels all other types of liquor in its properties. (70)
It destroys malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, edema, wasting, abdominal enlargement, and fever;
it also cures abdominal tumors, worms, and splenic disorders. It is astringent, pungent, and increases vāta. (71)
Wine made from grapes (mārdvīka) is astringent, pungent, and increases vāta; it is scraping, beneficial for the heart, not excessively hot, sweet, and laxative.
It slightly increases pitta and vāta, and destroys anemia, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, and worms. (5.71–72)
Date wine possesses qualities slightly inferior to this [grape wine]; it increases wind, is heavy, and causes intoxication.
Molasses wine is fragrant, sweet, pleasing to the heart, not excessively intoxicating, and light. (73)
5.73c–d Śārkara [wine] is fragrant, sweet, pleasant to the heart, not intoxicating, light, and promotes the passage of urine, feces, and flatus.
5.74 Gauḍa [wine] is nourishing and stimulates the digestive fire;
sīdhu [rum] increases vāta and pitta, while it cures disorders of unctuousness (sneha) and phlegm (śleṣman).
The fermented juice (pakvarasa) is excellent for destroying fat, edema, abdominal enlargements, and hemorrhoids;
the honey-āsava is sharp, acts as a depletive, and conquers urinary disorders, chronic rhinitis, and cough. (75)
Sour gruel (śukta) excites blood, bile, and phlegm; it facilitates the downward movement of wind (vāta).
It is extremely hot, sharp, dry, and sour; it is beneficial for the heart, stimulates the appetite, and is laxative. (76)
5.76dv Heart-pleasing, highly appetizing, digestive-stimulating, and cool to the touch; it destroys anemia, eye diseases, and worms.
Among these—molasses, sugarcane juice, wine, and mārdvīka vinegar—the lighter one comes later in the sequence.

It cures anemia, heart disease, and destroys worms. One should know that molasses, sugarcane, wine, honey-wine (*mādhvīka*), tubers, roots, fruits, and the like, when fermented with those [ingredients], are similar in effect.
*Śāṇḍākī* and other unfermented vinegars that have turned sour over time are appetizing and light.

Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) is a laxative, sharp, hot, and Pitta-generating; it is cooling to the touch, relieves fatigue and exhaustion, improves appetite, stimulates digestion, and alleviates pain in the bladder. (79)
Sauvīraka and tuṣodaka, possessing these very same qualities, are praised for use in enemas; they are beneficial for the heart, light, and alleviate vāta and kapha. (80)
By holding water in the mouth as a gargle, one overcomes oral impurities, foul odors, and dryness.

One should know that these two [medicinal preparations] are for the destruction of worms, heart disease, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and anemia; they are prepared respectively with dehusked and husked barley. (81)

5.81ab For the destruction of worms, heart disease, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and anemia, [the urine of] cows, goats, sheep, buffaloes, elephants, horses, camels, and donkeys [is used].
5.82 It is bilious, dry, sharp, hot, salty in its aftertaste, and pungent.

The light [form of this medicine] conquers worms, swelling, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, colic, anemia, kapha, and vāta; as well as abdominal tumors, loss of appetite, poisoning, vitiligo, skin diseases, and hemorrhoids. (83)

[It cures] colic, anemia, and diseases of phlegm, [using] groups of water, milk, sugarcane juice, oil, and wine respectively. Thus, this single portion of liquids has been described according to their general characteristics. (5.83–84)
In the Section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna):
Rakta, Mahān, Sakalama, Tūrṇaka, Śakunāhṛta, Sārāmukha, Dīrghaśūka, Lodhraśūka, and Sugandhika. (1)
Puṇḍra, pāṇḍu, puṇḍarīka, pramoda, gaura, śārivā, kāñcana, mahiṣa, śūka, dūṣaka, and kusumāṇḍaka. // 2 //
Pāṇḍuka, Puṇḍarīka, Pauṇḍraka, and Puṇḍarīka; Pramoda, Gaura-śālika,
Lāṅgala, those called Lohavāla, Kardama, and Śītabhīruka.
There were golden pataṅga birds and other auspicious śāli rice.
6.3a *jāṅgalā* and those called *lohavāla*; 6.3b *lāṅgala* and *lohavāla*; 6.3c *lāṅgala* is known as *lohavāla*;
6.3d *kardama* and *śītabhīruka*.

They have sweet post-digestive tastes and potencies, are unctuous, aphrodisiac, cause the binding and slight reduction of feces, have an astringent aftertaste, are wholesome, light, diuretic, and cooling. (4)
Among the *śūka* grains, the red variety is the best there; it removes thirst and the three *doṣas*.
The *mahān* follows it, then the *kalama*, and after that the others.
6.5. Mahāśalka, kalamatha, yavaka, hāyana, pāṃśu, bāṣpa, naiṣadhaka, and others are sweet, hot, heavy, unctuous, sour in digestion, and increase phlegm and bile.

6.6bv – [The varieties] beginning with vāpya, naiṣadha, and kādaṃba, having first voided urine and feces, are each censured in the order mentioned. [Rice] that is unctuous, constipating, light, sweet, stabilizing, cold, and destroys the three doṣas [is the best]. // 7 //
Among grains, the *ṣaṣṭika* is the best; among those, the white is superior to the black-white.
Following that in order are the *mahāvrīhi*, the *kṛṣṇavrīhi*, and the *jatūmukha*. (8)
The eggs of the hen, the quail, the pigeon, and the pig; the *varaka*, *koddālaka*, *ujjvāla*, *cīna*, *śārada*, and *dardura* grains. // 9 //
6.9av *kukkuṭāṇḍaka-pālākṣa-* / 6.9av *kukkuṭāṇḍaka-pālākhya-* / 6.9av *kukkuṭāṇḍaka-lāvākṣa-* / 6.9dv *-cīna-śārada-durdarāḥ*
The *gandhana* and *kuruvinda* varieties are considered to differ only slightly in their qualities.
Another type of *vrīhi* rice is sweet with an acidic post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), increases bile (*pitta*), and is heavy.
It causes excessive urine, feces, and heat, and indeed aggravates the three doṣas; however, pāṭala rice, as well as kaṅgu, kodrava, nīvāra, śyāmāka, and similar grains, are cold and light.
Grass and grain are wind-inducing, scraping, and remove phlegm and bile; they promote the healing of fractures. Among them, *priyaṅgu* is nourishing and heavy. (12)
Koradūṣa is highly absorbent, cool to the touch, and removes poison;
barley is dry, cold, heavy, sweet, laxative, and produces feces and wind. (13)

6.13b–d. Cold to the touch, it destroys poison; it is aphrodisiac, promotes stability, and conquers urine disorders, fat, pitta, and kapha. It cures chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, cough, stiffness of the thighs, and diseases of the throat and skin.
The *anuyava* (small barley) is smaller than barley, while barley produced from bamboo is parched and hot;
[ordinary] barley is aphrodisiac, cooling, heavy, unctuous, life-sustaining, and a destroyer of wind and bile. (15)
6.15a–b. Wheat (*godhūma*) is slightly inferior to other grains; it is unifying, sweet, stabilizing, and laxative.
The *nandīmukhī* variety is cooling, astringent-sweet, and light.
They are pithless, wind-aggravating, dry, causing heartburn and flatulence, and laxative. // 16+1 //
Pulse crops such as mung, āḍhakī, masūra, and others cause constipation;
they are astringent, sweet, constipating, pungent in post-digestive effect, cold, and light. (17)
Mudga is excellent for application as a paste or sprinkling over fat, phlegm, blood, and bile;
it is light and not easily digested, whereas kalāya is excessively provocative of wind.
The chickpea is known to remove blood and bile, to be parching, and to increase wind.
Rāja-māṣa increases wind, is dry, causes much feces, and is heavy.
Kulattha is hot; it is sour in its post-digestive effect (pāka) and [cures] seminal disorders, urinary stones, asthma, and chronic catarrh.
They destroy cough, hemorrhoids, phlegm, and wind, but they greatly increase bile and blood.
Niṣpāva is heavy; it produces wind, bile, blood, breast milk, and urine. (20)
6.20c–d Niṣpāva is laxative, increases vāta, pitta, and blood, and causes a burning sensation; it removes defects of vision, semen, kapha, swelling, and poison.
Māṣa is unctuous, produces strength, kapha, waste products, and pitta, and is laxative. 6.21a–b.
Warm, sweet, subduing wind (vāta), increasing semen, and causing purgation;
one should know that the fruits of *kākāṇḍola* and *ātmaguptā* are like those of *māṣa*. (22)
Sesame is warm, beneficial for the skin, cold in touch, good for the hair, strengthening, and heavy;
it produces little urine, is pungent in its post-digestive effect, and increases intelligence, digestive fire, kapha, and pitta. (23)

6.23ab Hot to the skin yet cold to the touch, unctuous, sweet and bitter, and hot; it increases *kapha* and *pitta*, is heavy, impairs vision and semen, and is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*). Likewise is the seed of the safflower (*kusumbha*).
Among all [grains], the masha is the lowest; among those grown from awns, the yavaka is the lowest.
Fresh grain causes secretions (abhiṣyandi); that which has been stored for a year is light.

6.25b–d Even among grains grown on stalks, *yavaka* is light, as is that which has been stored for a year, as well as legumes that grow quickly, are dehusked, and have been roasted by the proper method.
[This describes] the lightness of *maṇḍa*, *peyā*, *vilepī*, and *odana*.
Barley, wheat, mung beans, and fresh sesame seeds are beneficial; however, those that are old, tasteless, or fine are considered not to be so effective.

As before, the *maṇḍa* there is auspicious, promotes the downward movement of wind (*vāta*), destroys thirst, exhaustion, and residual morbid humors (*doṣa*), acts as a digestive stimulant (*pācana*), and restores the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). (27)
It softens the channels, induces perspiration, and kindles the digestive fire;
it removes hunger, thirst, exhaustion, debility, abdominal diseases, and fever. (28)
Emetic peya (thin gruel) made with harītakī is wholesome; it stimulates digestion and promotes digestion.
Vilepī (thicker gruel) is constipating, pleasing to the heart, thirst-quenching, digestive-stimulant, and beneficial. // 29 //
For those suffering from ulcers or eye diseases, those who have undergone purification therapies (saṃśuddhi), the weak, and those who consume fats,
rice that is well-washed, drained, steamed, and served while still warm is light.
Furthermore, rice that has been prepared with a decoction of fiery medicinal herbs and then fried is light;
whereas that which is prepared in the opposite manner, or cooked with milk, meat, and the like, is heavy. (31)

6.31 And that which is prepared with fried rice in a decoction of fiery (āgneya) herbs—thus one should prescribe everything according to the substance, the process, the combination, the measure, and so forth:
it is a nourishing, pleasing, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and a healer of wounds broth. 32.

Maudga (mung bean) is wholesome for those with purified wounds and those suffering from diseases of the throat and eyes; kaulattha (horse gram) facilitates the downward movement of wind and conquers abdominal tumors, colic, and sub-diaphragmatic pain.
One should know that uncooked meat-soup, cooked meat-soup, thin seasoned broth, and soup— whether sour or non-sour— are progressively heavier.
Preparations of sesame oil-cake, dried vegetables, sprouted grains, śāṇḍākī, and vaṭaka are destructive to the eyesight, aggravate the humors, cause exhaustion, and are heavy to digest. (34)
Rasālā is nourishing, aphrodisiac, unctuous, strengthening, and provides a relish for the appetite;
the *pānaka* drink removes fatigue, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion, while being pleasing and heavy. (35)

Parched grain (lāja) is constipating, diuretic, and beneficial for the heart; it possesses the qualities of its constituent ingredients and cuts through thirst, vomiting, diarrhea, urinary disorders, fat, and phlegm. (36)
Puffed rice (pṛthuka) pacifies cough and bile, stimulates digestion, and is light and cooling;
however, it is heavy, strengthening, and causes the obstruction of phlegm. // 37 //
Parched grains (dhānā) are stabilizing, dry, satiating, scraping, and heavy.
Roasted flour (saktu) is light; it cures hunger, thirst, fatigue, eye diseases, and wounds. (38)

6.38–6.39ab— These nourishing drinks, when consumed, immediately destroy fatigue, eye diseases, and throat ailments, and bestow strength; however, they should not be taken with water interspersed between them, nor twice [in one sitting], nor at night, nor alone.
One should not eat groats after having already eaten [other food], nor should one eat them by cutting them up with the teeth, nor in large quantities;
for oil-cake is satiating, parching, dry, causes constipation, and impairs the eyesight.

Because of its dryness, oil-cake causes obstruction in the digestive tract; due to this obstructive quality, it leads to a burning sensation; and from that burning, it produces exhaustion when consumed at night. (40+1)
Vesavāra is heavy, unctuous, and increases strength and corpulence; those prepared from mung beans and other pulses are heavy, following the specific qualities of their constituent ingredients. (41)
One should know that those born from a single womb become progressively lighter, like cakes cooked in a pit of hot ashes, in a frying pan, on a griddle, or over glowing coals. (42)

6.42ab Those baked on heaps of chaff, in frying pans, in ovens, or over pungent embers; 6.42cd cakes [made from the flesh] of the hariṇa, eṇa, kuraṅga, ṛkṣa, gokarṇa, and mṛgamātṛkā deer, each succeeding one being superior to the last.
The deer are known as the śaśa, śambara, cāruṣka, śarabha, and so forth. // 43 //
The common quail, the vārtīka, the vartīra, the raktavartmaka, the wild cock, the kapiñjala, the upacakra, the cakora, and the kurubāhu; // 44 //
6.44b–45: The raktavartmaka, the kukkuṭa, the vartaka,
the vartikā, the tittiri, the krakara, the peacock (śikhin),
the one called tāmracūḍa, the bakara, the gonarda, and the girivartikā.

6.45c–d The wild cock, the crane, the heron, the one called the copper-crested quail, the partridge, the peacock, the francolin, and others such as the varata—these are the scattering-feeders (viṣkira).
Also, the jīvañjīvaka, the gallinule, the bhrṅga, the parrot, and the myna; 46.
6.46bv – *vāraṭā* and others are the *viṣkira* birds; 6.46bv – *vāraṭāś* and others are the *viṣkira* birds; 6.46bv – *varaṭāś* and others are the *viṣkira* birds.
The *laṭvā*, *kokila*, *hārīta*, *kapota*, *caṭaka*, and so forth [are included].
The pratudas include frogs, iguanas, porcupines, and others; those that dwell in holes are the bileśayas. // 47 //
Cows, donkeys, mules, camels, horses, leopards, lions, bears, monkeys, cats, mice, tigers, wolves, brown bears, and hyenas; // 48 //
Jackals, jackals, hawks, blue jays, scavengers, crows, hyenas, vultures, ospreys, eagles, owls, and sparrows; // 49 //
The hawk, the vulture,
the osprey, the mist-crow, and the honey-eater are the predatory birds;
and the boar, the buffalo, the nyanku deer, the ruru deer, the rohita deer, and the elephant are the predatory land animals.
The sṛmara, the camara, the rhinoceros, and the gavaya are great wild animals;
so too are the haṃsa, sārasa, kādamba, baka, kāraṇḍava, and plava birds. // 51 //
The balāka, utkrośa, cakravāka, madgu, krauñca, and others are water-birds;
the rohita, pāṭhīna, tortoise, crocodile, and crab are fish. (52)

The oyster, the conch, the *udra*, the *śambūka*, the *śapharī*, the *varmī*, the moonlight-fish (*candrikā*), the *culūkī*, the crocodile (*nakra*), the *makara*, the *śiśumāra*, and the *timiṅgila*. // 53 //
6.53–54ab. Oysters, conchs, *udru*, *śambūka*, *cullakī*, crocodiles, sea-monsters (*makara*), *rājī*, *cilicima*, and so forth—they say that meat is of eight kinds.
Regarding the species of goat and sheep, because they range over mixed habitats, their classification is not fixed.

Game animals of the forest, those that scratch with their claws, those that peck, and those that dwell in holes; those that seize by force, large game, aquatic creatures, and fish—thus [meat] is of eight kinds. (54.1+1)
The first and last [groups] are known as the Jāṅgala and Ānūpa, while the two middle ones are considered Sādhāraṇa (ordinary).
Among these, the Jāṅgala animals are beneficial because they bind the waste products (feces), are cooling, and are light.

In cases where bile is predominant, wind is moderate, and there is a combination of humors (saṃnipāta) with phlegm as a secondary factor, rabbit meat is digestive-stimulant, pungent in its post-digestive effect, constipating, dry, and cold. (56)
Partridges and similar birds are slightly warm, heavy, unctuous, and nourishing;
among them, the common quail is the best, as it promotes intelligence, digestive fire, strength, and semen. (57)

The peacock is astringent, praiseworthy, and an excellent remedy for disorders caused by an excess of wind (vāta) and for combined humors (saṃnipāta); it is not very wholesome [for digestion], yet it is beneficial for the ears, the voice, vitality, and the eyes. (58)
Like that [the domestic fowl], the wild cock is aphrodisiac; however, the domestic one increases phlegm and is heavy.
The *krakara* and the *upacakraka* are beneficial for the intellect, stimulate the digestive fire, and are pleasing to the heart. (59)
The *guru* (pigeon) with salt is heavy and causes all the *doṣas*;
sparrows increase phlegm (*śleṣman*), are unctuous, destroy wind (*vāta*), and are supreme for increasing semen.
6.60d–61: These groups [of substances] are, in increasing order, subduers of wind (vātaghna), highly productive of semen (śukrala), heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet;
they increase urine and semen, are strengthening, subdue wind, and increase phlegm and bile (kaphapittala).
The *śītā* are large deer; among them, the *kravyāda-prasaha* are cold, have a salty aftertaste, are pungent in digestion, and increase the flesh. (62)
Furthermore, carnivorous animals of the *prasaha* class are highly beneficial for those suffering from chronic hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, and wasting diseases (*śoṣa*).
Goat meat is not excessively cold, heavy, or unctuous, and it does not aggravate the *doṣas*.
6.63 Not too cold, heavy, and unctuous, it is non-obstructive (*an-abhiṣyandi*) and nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*) because it is similar to the bodily constituents (*dhātu*);
the opposite of this should be known [as the case for other woolens], yet that which is made of sheep's wool (*āvika*) is indeed nourishing. 64.
Beef meat cures dry cough, fatigue, impaired digestion, irregular fever, chronic catarrh, emaciation, and disorders caused solely by wind. (65)
The buffalo is hot and heavy; it produces firmness of sleep and bulkiness.
Similarly, the boar removes fatigue and bestows appetite, semen, and strength. (66)
Fish produce excessive phlegm; the cilicima fish aggravates all three doṣas.
Among their respective groups, the common quail, the rohita fish, the godha lizard, and the eṇa deer are the most excellent. (67)
One should prescribe the large eggs of fish and other such birds;
they are unctuous, aphrodisiac, and possess sweet post-digestive tastes and potencies.
Therefore, one should assign heavy eggs to one side and meat to the other;

one should consume meat that is freshly killed, pure, and from an animal in its prime, but one should avoid meat that is dead, emaciated, excessively fatty, or afflicted by disease, water, or poison. (68)
In the case of males and females, the first half and the second half [of the line] are heavy when pregnant; the female is light.
Furthermore, among quadrupeds, the male is light. // 69 //
One should diagnose heaviness of the head, shoulders, thighs, back, waist, and legs, as well as of the stomach and large intestine, in the order mentioned above. (70)

And among the elements beginning with blood, each subsequent one is more significant than the preceding; [the most significant] after the flesh are the testicles, the penis, the kidneys, the liver, and the rectum. (71)
Vegetables produced from pāṭhā, śaṭhī, sūṣā, suniṣaṇṇaka, and satīna, as well as rāja-kṣava and vāstuka, destroy the three doṣas, are light, and are astringent. (72)

6.72 Vegetable greens such as *pāṭhā*, *śaṭhī*, *śūṣā*, *suniṣaṇṇa*, and *agnikṛt* are aphrodisiacs; among these, *rājakṣava* is the best. It cures disorders of the *grahaṇī* and hemorrhoids, while *vāstuka* is a laxative for the feces.

Kākamācī destroys the three doṣas, treats leprosy, is aphrodisiac, hot, and a rejuvenative; it is laxative and beneficial for the voice. Amlā (Citrullus colocynthis) stimulates the digestive fire. // 74 //

6.74b-vṛṣyā soṣṇā rasāyanam grahaṇy-arśo-'nila-śleṣman-hitoṣṇā grāhiṇī laghuḥ / paṭola-saptalāriṣṭa-śārṅgaṣṭāvalgujāmṛtāḥ // 75 // [The group consisting of] paṭola, saptalā, ariṣṭa, śārṅgaṣṭā, valguja, and amṛtā is aphrodisiac, hot, a rejuvenative (rasāyana), beneficial for the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, wind (vāta), and phlegm (kapha), hot in potency, constipating, and light.
6.75–76. Paṭola, saptalā, ariṣṭa,
the tips of vetra, bṛhatī, vāsā, kuṭilī, tilaparṇikā,
maṇḍūkaparṇī, karkoṭa, kāravellaka, and parpaṭa [are used for this purpose].
6.76a Vetragra, bṛhatī, vāsā, kuntalī, tilaparṇikā, 6.76b nāḍī, kalāya, gojihvā, vārtāka, and vanatiktaka.
Karīra, kulaka, nandī, kucailā, and śakulādanī. // 77 //
Kaṭhilla, kembuka, śīta, along with kośātaka and karkaśa, are bitter, pungent in digestion, constipating, increase wind, and conquer phlegm and bile. (78)
Kaṭhillaka and kembuka are cooling and beneficial for the heart; paṭola destroys worms, is sweet in its post-digestive effect, and provides relish.
The two types of bṛhatī increase pitta, stimulate digestion, are laxative, and subdue vāta.
Vṛṣa destroys vomiting and cough, and is supreme in removing raktapitta;
kāravella is pungent, stimulates the digestive fire, and is excellent for conquering kapha. (80)

The eggplant (vārtāka) is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is sweet, conquers kapha and vāta, contains alkali, stimulates the digestive fire, is beneficial for the heart, appetizing, and does not increase pitta. (81)
Karīra causes flatulence; it is astringent, sweet, and bitter.
Kośātaka and Avalguja are laxative and stimulate the digestive fire.
The two types of *bhedana* (cleavers) stimulate the digestive fire (*agni*).
*Taṇḍulīya* is cold, dry, light, and sweet in both its post-digestive effect (*pāka*) and taste (*rasa*);
it destroys intoxication, bile, poison, and blood disorders. *Muñjāta* conquers wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*).
Pālaṅkyā is unctuous, cold, heavy, sweet, nourishing, and highly productive of semen;
upodakā is also heavy and laxative, and it destroys intoxication.
The beak is considered like a palāṅkya; it is of a grasping nature.
Vidārī destroys wind and bile, is diuretic, sweet, and cooling. (85)
Cuccū is considered to be like pālankya. Jīvantī is vitalizing, nourishing, beneficial for the throat, heavy, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative;
it is good for the eyes, destroys all the doṣas, and is sweet and cooling. (86)
Kūṣmāṇḍa, tumba, kāliṅga, karkārū, ervāru, tiṇḍiśa, as well as trapusa, cīnāka, and cirbhaṭa increase kapha and vāta. (87)
Cucumber (kūṣmāṇḍa) is laxative, constipating, and causes secretions; it is heavy, sweet in taste and digestion, the best among vine-fruits, and subdues vāta and pitta. (88)
Trapusa is a cleanser of the bladder, aphrodisiac, and highly diuretic;
tumba is very dry and constipating, as are kāliṅga, ervāru, and cirbhaṭa. (89)
One should know that the unripe fruit is cooling and pacifies pitta; the ripe fruit is the opposite of this.
However, the fruit with withered stalks, when combined with alkali (kṣāra), increases pitta but conquers kapha and vāta. (90)

The tubers of lotus stalks (mṛṇāla), lotus fibers (bisa), lotus roots (śālūka), and the bulbs of the white and blue water lilies (kumuda and utpala) are clarifying, digestive-stimulating, pleasing to the heart, light, and alleviate abdominal tumors and constipation. (91)
Nandīmāṣaka, kelūṭa, śṛṅgāṭaka,
kaseruka, krauñcādana, and kaloḍya are dry, constipating, cold, and heavy.
The kadamba, nālikā, mārṣa, kuṭiñjara, and kutumbaka;
the cillī, laṭvāka, loṇīkā, kurūṭaka, and gavedhuka. // 93 //
6.93a Kalambu, nālikā, and mārṣa; 6.93b kuṭiñjara and kurumbaka;
[or] kuliñjara and kurumbaka; 6.93d kurūḍhaka and gavedhukā; [or] kuraṇṭaka and gavedhukā.
Kuraṇṭaka, gavedhuka,
jīvanta, jhuñjhu, eḍagaja, yava-śāka, suvarcalā, all varieties of tubers (āluka), as well as pulses (sūpya) and lakṣmaṇa. // 94 //
Barley, potherbs, and suvarcala; likewise, pulses and lakṣmaṇā.
[Lakṣmaṇā] is sweet, dry, salty, increases vāta and śleṣman, and is heavy.
Once cooled and after the discharge of feces and urine, it generally digests with flatulence. // 95 //
Cillī that has been steamed, its juice squeezed out, enriched with fats, not excessively doshic, and possessing thin leaves, is considered equal to vāstūka. (96)
Tarkārī and varuṇa are sweet and bitter, overcoming phlegm and wind;
likewise, the two types of varṣābhū and kāla-śāka are alkaline, pungent, and bitter. (97)
6.97 The varana of the tarkari tree is sweet, digestive, and laxative; it destroys artificial poisons, edema, phlegm, and wind.
The sprouts of the chiribilva are digestive, destroy phlegm and wind, and are laxative.
Śālmalī flower is astringent and especially destroys pitta and blood.
The sprouts of śatāvarī are bitter, aphrodisiac, and remove the three doṣas;
however, the pith of bamboo is dry, causes a burning sensation, and increases vāta and pitta. (99)
Pattūra is digestive, pungent, and overcomes splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, kapha, and vāta.
Kāsamarda is laxative and conquers worms, cough, and the excessive secretion of kapha. (100)
Safflower is dry, hot, sour, heavy, increases bile, and is laxative;
mustard is heavy, hot, binds the feces and urine, and aggravates all the humors. (101)
That radish which is young, with an unmanifest flavor, slightly alkaline, and bitter, removes the bodily humors (doṣas), is light, hot in potency, and is curative. (102)

Furthermore, it cures abdominal tumors (gulma), cough, consumption (kṣaya), asthma, ulcers, diseases of the eyes and throat, as well as loss of voice, impaired digestion, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and chronic catarrh (pīnasa). (103)
It is pungent in taste and digestion, hot in potency, and aggravates the three doṣas;
it is heavy, causes secretions, and though prepared with unctuous substances, it nevertheless conquers vāta. (104)
Even when steamed, it conquers vāta;
when dried, it removes both vāta and śleṣman. However, all [types] when raw are harmful to the doṣas.
Piṇḍālu is pungent and hot, subdues vāta and kapha, but increases pitta.
Kuṭhera, śigru, surasa, sumukha, asuri, bhūstṛṇa, phaṇijjaka, arjaka, jambīra, and so forth, are astringent and cause the binding of the channels. (106)
It causes a burning sensation, is pungent, dry, and hot; it is beneficial for the heart, stimulates digestion, and improves the appetite.
It removes defects of vision, cures seminal disorders, and destroys worms; it is sharp, aggravates the humors (doṣas), and is light. (107)

Surasa destroys hiccup, cough, poison, dyspnea, pain in the flanks, and foul odors; it is pleasant to the taste, has a good aroma, is not excessively heating, and cures artificial poisons and swellings. (108)
Ārdrikā relieves hiccup, cough, vomiting, and dyspnea; it is bitter and sweet, promotes urination, and does not increase pitta.
Garlic is extremely sharp and hot, pungent in both its post-digestive effect (vipāka) and taste, and is laxative. (6.108–109)
It is pleasing to the heart, beneficial for the hair, heavy, aphrodisiac, unctuous, appetizing, and digestive;
it promotes the healing of fractures, is strengthening, yet vitiates the blood and bile. // 110 //
6.110b–c It is unctuous, digestive, and carminative;

it destroys vitiligo, skin diseases, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, worms, kapha, and vata, along with hiccups, chronic catarrh, dyspnea, and cough; it is a rejuvenative tonic. 111.
Onions destroy coughs caused by blood and bile; they possess qualities slightly inferior to those [of garlic], increase phlegm, and do not excessively increase bile.
They are wholesome for phlegm, wind, and hemorrhoids, both when used for fomentation and when consumed.
The *gṛñjanaka* is pungent and astringent; it is not beneficial for those with a predominance of *pitta*.
The *sūraṇa* kindles the digestive fire, is appetizing, destroys *kapha*, is clear, and light. (113)
The root-bulb of the *bhū-kaṇḍa* is especially beneficial for hemorrhoids, yet it is highly aggravating to the humors (*doṣa*).
Among its leaf, flower, fruit, stalk, and bulb, heaviness increases in successive order. (114)
6.114c–d Among flowers, leaves, fruits, stalks, and vegetables, *jīvantī* is the best; mustard is inferior.
6.115 Grape is the best of fruits; it is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and promotes the discharge of urine and feces.
6.115b However, mustard seeds (sārṣapa) are even more inferior than that. [Mustard oil] is sweet in its post-digestive effect and taste, unctuous, slightly astringent, cold, and heavy.
It destroys disorders of wind (vāta), blood-bile (pitta), and hemorrhage (asṛj), as well as a bitter mouth, intoxication (madātyaya), and similar conditions. 116.
Sweet pomegranate destroys wind, blood-bile, thirst, cough, fatigue, dyspnea, hoarseness, chest wounds, and wasting; it overcomes the three doshas when pitta is predominant. (6.116–117)
Not excessively hot, it is not antagonistic to pitta, is sour, and removes vāta and kapha;
all [these qualities] are pleasing to the heart, light, unctuous, constipating, appetizing, and digestive-stimulating. (118)
Moca, kharjūra, panasa, nārikela, parūṣaka, āmrātaka, tāla, kāśmarya, rājādana, and that which is born from madhūka. (119)
Sauvīra, badara, aṅkolla, phalgu, and that which arises from śleṣmātaka; vātāma, abhiṣuka, akṣoṭa, mukūlaka, and nikocaka. (120)
Urumāṇa and priyāla are nourishing, heavy, and cooling;
they alleviate burning sensations, wounds, and consumption, and they clarify the blood and pitta. // 121 //

The fruit of the palmyra palm (tāla) is sweet in taste and digestion, unctuous, causes constipation, and increases phlegm and semen; however, the fruit produced from the kāśmarya tree is pitta-increasing, laxative, and cooling.
It increases phlegm, conquers wind and bile,
cures obstructions of feces and urine, is beneficial for the hair, promotes intelligence, and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana). However,
that which is hot in potency (uṣṇa-vīrya) produces phlegm and bile and is laxative, causing disorders such as vātāmā.
The fruit of the priyāla is extremely wind-dispelling, unctuous, and non-heating;
however, the pulp of the priyāla is sweet, aphrodisiac, and removes pitta and vāta. (124)
The pulp of the *kola* fruit possesses similar qualities; it also conquers thirst, vomiting, and cough.
Ripe *bilva* is very difficult to digest, aggravates the humors, and produces putrid wind.
The young fruit is digestive, destroys phlegm and wind, and both types are astringent.
Raw wood-apple (kapittha) is harmful to the throat and aggravates the humors, yet it also subdues those same humors when ripe.
Both types [of jambū fruit] are astringent when unripe;
when ripe, they cure hiccup and vomiting. All [types] are astringent and antidotes to poison.
The *jāmbava* fruit is heavy, causes constipation, is cold, and is excessively wind-increasing. (6.126b–127)
It is astringent for urine and feces, beneficial for the throat, and subdues phlegm and bile.
It generates wind, bile, and blood; it is beneficial for children and, when its fibers are intact, it generates phlegm and bile. (128)
6.128b–c. The mango fruit that is not from the throat region (akaṇṭhya) alleviates phlegm and bile; it is heavy and subdues wind. When ripe, it is sweet and sour, producing phlegm and semen.
6.129. Tamarind (vṛkṣāmla) is constipating, dry, hot, light, and removes wind and phlegm.
The fruit of the amlā is thirst-quenching, hot, increases pitta, and is laxative.
Śamyā is heavy, hot, hair-destroying, and dry; pīlu, however, increases pitta.
[Pilu] removes kapha and vāta, is a purgative, and cures splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, worms, and abdominal tumors. (130)
The pīlu fruit, which is sweet with a bitter taste and not excessively hot, conquers the three doṣas.
The rind of the mātuluṅga is bitter, pungent, unctuous, and subdues vāta. (131)
Meat is nourishing, sweet, heavy, and alleviates vāta and pitta;
its filaments (keśara), however, are light and cure cough, dyspnea, hiccups, and alcoholism.
It destroys dryness of the mouth, disorders of wind and phlegm, constipation, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, hemorrhoids, colic, and weak digestion. (133)
One should know that the fruit produced from the nāraṅga tree is sweet, slightly sour, pleasing to the heart, an appetizer for food, heavy, and a pacifier of vāta. 133+1.
The bark and pulp of bhallātaka are nourishing, sweet, and cooling;
its seeds are like fire, promote intelligence, and are supreme in alleviating kapha and vāta. (134)
Pālevata fruit is sweet, sour, cold, and hot; it is heavy and of two kinds.
It is appetizing and pacifies excessive digestive fire. Āruka is appetizing and sweet. (135)
6.135d–136ab. Ripe āruka is pleasing to the heart, sweet, and quickly undergoes digestion; it is neither excessively hot nor heavy, and does not increase the doṣas.
Fresh drākṣā and parūṣaka are sour and provide pitta and kapha.
6.136b–c The karamardaka is not excessively hot, is heavy, increases the *doṣas*, possesses a heavy and hot potency (*vīrya*), subdues *vāta*, is laxative, and is beneficial for the eyes;
likewise, the sour varieties of *kola*, *karkandhu*, *likuca*, *āmra-taka*, and *āruka* [share these qualities]. 137.
6.137c–d And like that [mango], the *kola*, *karkandhu*, *likuca*, *āmra*, *āmrātaka*, *āruka*, *airāvata*, *dantaśaṭha*, *sūtuda*, and *mṛgaliṇḍika* [fruits] do not produce excessive *pitta*.
Likewise, the ripe and dried *karamardaka* [fruit] does not produce excessive *pitta*.
The dried fruit of the *amlīkā* and *kola* stimulates digestion, breaks up accumulations, and alleviates thirst, fatigue, and exhaustion; it is light and beneficial for *kapha* and *vāta*. (139)
The jujube fruit (kola) is sweet and sour, light, and when dried and aged, it is a digestive stimulant.
Among fruits, the *likuca* is the lowest there, as it produces all defects;
it is corrupted by cold, fire, heat, foul winds, and the saliva of venomous serpents.
6.140c–d Nāraṅga is said to be heavy, difficult to digest, and a producer of *kapha*; it is overcome by cold, wind, and heat, yet it destroys wind (*vāta*).
It alleviates thirst, colic, the excessive secretion of *kapha*, vomiting, and asthma. (140.1+1)
The coconut is heavy, unctuous, pacifies pitta, sweet, and cooling;
it increases strength and flesh, is beneficial for the heart, nourishing, and cleanses the bladder.
That which is infested by living creatures, submerged in water, not grown from the earth, out of season, mixed with other grains, deficient in potency, and moreover, decayed through age; 141.

6.141d–142ab — One should discard grain that has lost its potency due to being old, as well as vegetables prepared with dry ingredients that are not tender, those whose juices have not developed, and likewise those that are dried out, except for radishes.
Generally, even the fruit is like this; likewise, the *āmabilva* is excluded [from being pungent].
They know all salt to be laxative, subtle, and a producer of waste. (143)
6.143d–144: Saindhava salt is subtle, purifies excreted waste, is mild, alleviates Vāta, undergoes digestion, is sharp and hot, appetizing, and increases Kapha and Pitta.
Among these, [Saindhava] is sweet, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the heart, and pacifies all three Doṣas.
Sauvarcala salt is light, not hot, beneficial for the eyes, non-burning, and stimulates the digestive fire; it is pleasant to the heart, fragrant, and cleanses the eructation. (145)

Feces that are pungent in their post-digestive effect (pāka), remove obstructions, stimulate digestion, provide relish, and facilitate the downward and upward movement of kapha and vāta, are appetizing. (146)

Sea salt (sāmudra) is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), relieves constipation, and destroys obstruction, flatulence, distension, colic, and heaviness; it is sweet in its post-digestive effect, heavy, and increases phlegm (śleṣman). // 147 //
The rock salt (audbhida) is pungent, bitter, and alkaline, sharp, and causes secretion;
in black salt (sauvarcala), the qualities of salt are present except for the odor. (148)
Romaka salt is light, while that derived from dust is alkaline, increases phlegm, and is heavy;
however, among the various salts for medicinal use, one should employ rock salt (saindhava) and others. 149.

One should employ the *saindhava* group [of salts] for treating abdominal tumors (*gulma*), cardiac obstruction, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, anemia, splenic enlargement, flatulence, diseases of the throat,
dyspnea, hemorrhoids, phlegm, and cough; likewise, that which is produced from barley awns (*yavaśūka*) pacifies these same conditions.
6.150cd–151ab: Alkali produced from *yavaśūka* (barley awns) pacifies dyspnea, hemorrhoids, *kapha*, and *vāta*.
All [types of] alkali are extremely sharp and hot; they destroy worms, are light, vitiate the blood and *pitta*, cause suppuration, are excising, unpalatable, and tearing.
Asafoetida (hiṅgu) is unwholesome for semen, vitality, hair, and the eyes due to its pungent and salty qualities;
it destroys wind (vāta), phlegm (kapha), flatulence, and colic, but aggravates bile (pitta). 152.
It has a pungent post-digestive taste (pāka) and flavor (rasa), is appetizing, stimulates digestion, promotes digestion, and is light.
It is astringent and sweet in its post-digestive effect, dry, slightly salty, and light. (153)
It is illuminating, digestive, clarifying, and supreme for stabilizing youth;
it is hot in potency, promotes longevity, and bestows strength upon the intellect and the senses. (154)
It cures leprosy, discoloration, hoarseness of voice, chronic and irregular fevers, diseases of the head, eyes, anemia, heart disease, jaundice, and disorders of the duodenum. (155)
It cures consumption, swelling, diarrhea, obesity, delusion, vomiting, worms, asthma, cough, excessive salivation, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, abdominal distension, and poisoning. (156)

6.156b–157. Harītakī conquers urinary disorders, delusion, vomiting, worms, obstruction of the channels, abdominal tumors, stiffness of the thighs, and loss of appetite; it overcomes those various diseases born of kapha and vāta.

Likewise, the āmalaka fruit is cooling, sour, and removes pitta and kapha; it is pungent in its post-digestive transformation (pāka), cold, beneficial for the hair, good for the eyes, and possesses these qualities only slightly. (158)

6.158c–d This [triphala] is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), non-cold (ahima), beneficial for the hair, and the best among rejuvenatives (rasāyana); it removes eye diseases, promotes healing, and conquers skin ailments, moisture, fat, urinary disorders (meha), kapha, and blood disorders. 159.

The four-fold aromatic (catur-jāta), consisting of saffron along with cinnamon, leaf-cinnamon, and cardamom, and the three-fold aromatic (tri-jātaka) are provocative of bile, sharp, hot, dry, appetizing, and digestive-stimulating. (160)
One should employ fragrant perfumes for all drinks, condiments, linctuses, foods to be chewed, cooked dishes, and powders. (160.1+1)
Black pepper is pungent in taste and post-digestive effect, subdues phlegm, and is light.
Long pepper is phlegm-increasing, sweet, cold, moist, heavy, and unctuous. (161)
The dried variety is the opposite of this; it is unctuous, aphrodisiac, pungent in taste, sweet in its post-digestive effect, dispels wind, phlegm, dyspnea, and cough, and is laxative. (162)
One should not consume it excessively except as part of a prescribed regimen for rejuvenation (rasāyana).
Dry ginger (nāgara) is a digestive stimulant, aphrodisiac, astringent, cordial, and a reliever of constipation. (163)
It is palatable, light, sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), unctuous, hot, and subdues kapha and vāta;
likewise, fresh ginger (ārdraka) and these three together as the "three pungents" (trikaṭuka) conquer [these same humors]. 164.
Cavikā and pippalīmūla [cure] obesity, sluggish digestion, dyspnea, cough, elephantiasis, and chronic rhinitis; the latter is slightly inferior in its qualities to marica. (165)
Citraka is equal to fire in its digestion; it destroys swelling, hemorrhoids, worms, and skin diseases.
This is known as *pañcakolaka*, excluding black pepper. (166)
This *pañcakolaka* is an excellent digestive stimulant (*dīpana*) that destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*), splenic enlargement (*plīhodara*), flatulence (*ānāha*), and colic (*śūla*).
[The formulation] "Great" (*mahat*) consists of *bilva*, *kāśmarya*, *tarkārī*, *pāṭalā*, and *ṭuṇṭuka*.
6.167b–168. The *pañcamūla* (five roots), which is astringent, bitter, and hot, destroys colic (*śūla*), stimulates digestion (*dīpana*), is light, and conquers *kapha* and *vāta*.
The "short" (*hrasva*) *pañcamūla* is known to consist of *bṛhatī*, the two types of *aṃśumatī*, and *gokṣura*.
6.168ab It conquers that which is astringent, sharp, and hot; it is sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka) and taste (rasa), neither excessively cold nor hot, and overcomes all the doṣas.
[It is prepared] with balā, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, and the two types of śūrpaparṇī. 169.
6.169c–d With *balā*, *punarnavā*, and *eraṇḍa*, and with the two types of *śūrpaparṇī*. 6.169d With the two types of *śūrpaparṇī*.
6.169d But with the two types of *śūrpaparṇī*.
This [decoction] is considered moderate, subduing kapha and vāta, not excessively increasing pitta, and laxative; it is prepared with abhīru, vīrā, jīvantī, jīvaka, and ṛṣabhaka. (170)
That which is called *jīvana* (life-giving) is beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, and pacifies *pitta* and *vāta*.
That which is called *tṛṇa* (grass-like) conquers *pitta* when prepared with *darbha*, *kāśa*, sugarcane, *śara*, and *śāli* rice. (171)

6.171 This category of food known as *jīvana* (life-sustaining) and *cakṣuṣya* (vision-enhancing), consisting of grains such as *śūka* and *śimbī*, prepared cooked foods, meats, vegetables, fruits, and medicinal herbs—
this group of foods has been described as suitable for daily consumption.
6.172dv Thus has been described that which is for constant use.
[In the] Sūtrasthāna, a king should establish a physician near his royal residence.
Thus, at all times and in all places, he remains ever vigilant. // 1 //

One should protect food and drink from poison, especially that of a lord of the earth; for his security and well-being depend upon them, as do dharma and the other goals, which are bound up with them.
7.2dv The qualities such as taste and so forth are dependent upon that [moisture]; like thick rice-porridge mixed with poison, it reaches a state of being non-exudable.
It is digested slowly, and once cooked, it becomes like something that has turned stale. // 3 //
With a heat equal to that of a peacock's neck, it causes delusion, fainting, and salivation;
its color and fragrance fade, and it becomes moist as if covered in moonlight. (4)
7.4dv It becomes moistened when accompanied by moonlight; 7.4dv it becomes moistened when covered by moonbeams;
7.4dv it becomes moistened when joined with the moon.
Furthermore, the condiments there dry up quickly, and the decoctions turn dark.
A shadow that is deficient, excessive, distorted, or not visible at all [is inauspicious]. // 5 //
7.5dv Shadows may be seen or not; there is the appearance of foam, upward streaks, hairlines, threads, and bubbles.
The flavors are broken and tasteless; the sweets, vegetables, and meats [are likewise]. 6.
7.6cv–dv: The tastes are interrupted and flavorless; the meat is like dry wood. A dark-blue streak is seen in the juice, and a copper-colored one in the milk and curd.
It is dark brown, yellow, or black when in buttermilk; when in ghee, it resembles water. // 7 //
7.7bv It appears in milk and curd; in whey, it is pigeon-colored; in *tuṣodaka* (rice-wash water), it is black;
in wine and water, it is dark; in honey, it is green; and in oil, it resembles the color of dawn.
The ripening of unripe fruits is their maturation; for ripe fruits, it is their decomposition.
For substances, whether moist or dry, there may be withering and discoloration. (9)
There would be a reversal of touch for things that are soft and hard;
the tips of garlands would wither, they would fade, and a different scent would arise. (10)
7.10c The blossoms of garlands have their tips withered; 7.10d there is a fading caused by the emergence of another scent.
7.10d There is a loss of luster and the emergence of another scent; on the garments, there is a darkened circle and the fraying of the threads and fibers.
The state of being stained by impurities exists in elements such as pearls, wood, stones, gems, and so forth. // 11 //
7.11b–c: There is the fraying of threads and eyelashes, a loss of luster, oiliness, and touch; however, in the case of an earthen vessel, there is a loss of its natural brilliance.
7.12: A poison-giver has a dark, parched face and looks about the directions with a startled expression.

Trembling with perspiration and shivering, one who has consumed poisoned food falters, yawns, and becomes terrified; furthermore, the digestive fire, becoming singularly turbulent, bursts forth excessively.

7.13 Even if it has a single curl and bursts open, emitting smoke and flames resembling the color of a peacock’s neck, or being without visible flame yet possessing a fierce odor; flies die upon tasting it, and a crow becomes hoarse-voiced.
Seeing this, the parrots, water-hens, and mainas cry out; the swan falters, and exhaustion comes upon the pheasant. (15)
The cakora bird experiences a loss of luster in its eyes, the krauñca bird suffers an excess of passion,
while the pigeon, the cuckoo, the peacock, and the ruddy goose all give up their lives.
The cat becomes agitated, the monkey voids its excrement, and the peacock rejoices at the sight of that [poison]; thus, the poison loses its potency. (17)
7.17 A cat causes alarm, while a peacock rejoices upon seeing it;
thus, recognizing food to be like poison, one should discard it with great effort, so that even small creatures do not perish because of it. 7.18
7.18ab Knowing food to be thus poisoned, one should indeed discard it with great effort.

[there may also be] the falling out of nails and hair, and swelling. In that condition, medicinal pastes prepared with sevya, candana, padmaka,
somavalka, tālīśapatra, kuṣṭha, amṛtā, and nata are recommended.
Salivation, numbness of the tongue and lips, a burning sensation with tingling, sensitivity of the teeth, loss of the sense of taste, and lockjaw occur within the mouth. (21)
7.21ab Salivation, numbness of the tongue and lips, and a tingling sensation in the mouth [occur];
in that case, gargles with *sevya* and other [medicines], as well as everything beneficial for overcoming poison, should be employed.

When [the poison] has reached the stomach (*āmāśaya*), there is sweating, fainting, flatulence, intoxication, and vertigo. 7.22cd [Note: This line is part of the preceding verse's context in some editions.]
When it has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), there is horripilation, vomiting, a burning sensation, obstruction of the eyes and heart, and a swelling of the limbs due to [excessive] secretions. (23)
One vomits matter of many colors, passes urine, and suffers from diarrhea; there is drowsiness, emaciation, pallor, abdominal enlargement, and loss of strength. (24)
For one who has undergone emesis and purgation, [one should administer] the two types of *haridrā*, *kaṭabhī*, jaggery, *sindhuvārita*, *niṣpāva*, *bāṣpikā*, and *śataparvikā*. (25)
One should employ the roots of *taṇḍulīyaka*, *kukkuṭāṇḍa*, and *avalguja* for nasal drops, collyrium, and internal potions to pacify poison. (26)
And to one who has consumed poison, once purified, one should give fine copper dust mixed with honey at the proper time, both above and below, for the cleansing of the heart. (27)
Then, when the heart is purified, one should apply an abrasive of gold powder;
like water on a lotus leaf, poison does not adhere to the golden limb. (28)
Great longevity is produced; this same procedure is prescribed even for *gara* (slow-acting poison).
One should know that even incompatible food is like *viṣa* (acute poison) and *gara*. // 29 //
7.29dv One should know that marshland meat is like artificial poison (gara-viṣa) when combined with black gram, honey, milk, or sprouted grains;
it is incompatible with lotus stalks, radish, or molasses. 7.30ab
Especially fish with milk; among fish, the cilīcima;
and all sour fruit likewise, when taken with milk, is incompatible. (31)
In the same way, having consumed horse gram, chickpeas, millet, vetch, and black gram, or having eaten green vegetables such as radishes and the like, one should avoid milk. (32)
Likewise, after eating horse-gram (*kulattha*), common millet (*varaka*), green tubers, radishes,
and the like, one should avoid milk;
one should not eat boar-flesh with milk, nor should one eat porcupine or wild cock with curd.
Raw meat with bile, and radish with black gram soup. // 33 //

7.33 One should not eat a boar with the meat of a porcupine, nor a goat with kusumbha greens and lotus stalks, nor a sprouted grain with black gram soup, molasses, milk, curd, or ghee, nor the lakuca fruit.
The fruit of the plantain with buttermilk, or with curd, or with the fruit of the palmyra; or *kākamācī* with black pepper and long pepper, or with honey, or with jaggery. (35)
Whether it was cooked in a fish-processor's kitchen, in the kitchen of a city-dweller, or cooked elsewhere in a vessel—having spent that night according to her desire—she [presented herself]. (36)
7.36b And in the digestion of ginger; 7.36d [one] should not eat her out of desire if she has spent the night [with another]; 7.36d [one] should not eat her if she has spent the night as a *kapotā*;
7.36d [one] should not eat her if she has spent the night [with another]; 7.36d [one] should not eat her out of desire if she has spent the night [with another].

One should discard long pepper (pippalī) that has been kept overnight in a vessel from Kāmācī and cooked in the oil used for frying fish; likewise, one should discard ghee that has been kept for ten days in a bronze vessel, or that which is hot in the case of Aruṣkara.
One should avoid *pippalī* prepared with fish, flattened grains, and oil; likewise, warm ghee prepared with *aruṣkara* is incompatible.
*Bhāsa* roasted on a spit and *kampilla* prepared with buttermilk are mutually contradictory.
One should avoid milk-rice, liquor, and sesame-mash all at once.
Honey, clarified butter, muscle fat, oil, and water—whether taken two by two, three by three, or all together in equal proportions—are mutually incompatible. (39)
Even when honey and ghee are separated, they may be combined by taking divine water as an after-drink;
likewise with honey and lotus seeds, or honey, maireya wine, and sugar-cane juice. 40.
The Manthānu-pāna, Kṣaireya, Hāridra, and Kaṭutailavān [are used];
for diarrhea caused by Upodaka, [the gruel] is prepared with sesame paste.
The crane, when combined with the *vāruṇī* liquor and boiled grains (*kulmāṣa*), is incompatible;
that same crane, if fried in boar fat, immediately destroys life. (42)
In the same way, partridges, richly seasoned with leaves, iguanas, quails, and grey partridges, prepared with castor oil and tempered with that very oil [are likewise effective]. (43)
The flesh of a green partridge, roasted on a spit over a fire of turmeric, instantly destroys life by means of the fire of turmeric. (44)
7.44c–d That very same [substance], when immediately reduced to ashes by the fire of turmeric and mixed with honey and dusted with powder, will,
in brief, expel whatever disorder has been provoked. 7.45ab [This applies] to anything at all.

Purification here is held to be either incompatible with those [defilements], or tranquility through substances that oppose them, or else the prior refinement of the body by means of those very same substances. (46)

For those who engage in physical exercise, whose digestive fire is stimulated by unctuous substances, who are in the prime of youth, and who possess strength, even an incompatible food does not cause affliction; likewise, a small quantity of food is wholesome. (47)

7.47 One who has undergone physical exercise, whose digestive fire is stimulated by unctuous substances, or whose fire is naturally bright, may abandon unwholesome food after every fourth meal, or even after every third meal; likewise, one should consume wholesome food at intervals of one, two, or three meals.
For even that which is unwholesome, when abandoned, or that which is wholesome, when practiced, results in disorders of habituation or non-habituation if changed suddenly. (49)
7.49c–d: Unwholesome things lead to disorder; humors diminished gradually and qualities increased gradually reach a state from which they do not return and become unshakable. 50.
7.50 Those who have attained the state beyond rebirth do so by overcoming the faults that are inherently corrupting due to their extreme proximity.
A wise person ought not to allow himself to be corrupted again by those things that are harmful. 51.
The body is constantly sustained by means of food, sleep, and celibacy, when employed with skill, just as a house is maintained by supports. // 52 //
7.52b–c — Diet has been described in various places with its associated practices when followed according to reason, and it will be discussed further in those respective sections.
Pleasure and pain, nourishment and emaciation, strength and weakness—all depend upon sleep. (7.53)
In various instances, virility, impotence, knowledge, ignorance, and even life itself are observed; likewise,
through excessive indulgence at improper times, sleep is not properly cultivated.
It would destroy one's happiness and lifespan like another night of doom;
waking at night is harsh, while sleeping during the day is soothing.

It is non-rough and non-mucilaginous, characterized by sitting and nodding off; this occurs in summer due to the accumulation of wind (*vāyu*), the onset of dryness, and the short duration of the night. (56)
7.56cv During the summer, sleeping during the day is beneficial for the removal of accumulated vāta; however, in other seasons, it produces kapha and pitta.
One should avoid it, however, after speaking, traveling by vehicle, walking long distances, drinking alcohol, sexual intercourse, carrying loads, or performing physical labor. // 57 //
Those exhausted by anger, grief, and fear; those suffering from dyspnea, hiccups, and diarrhea;
the elderly, children, the weak, the emaciated, and those afflicted by wasting, thirst, and colic. (58)
For those afflicted by hunger, thirst, and pain, those suffering from indigestion, those who are intoxicated, and even those accustomed to sleeping during the day—
this [sleep] restores the equilibrium of their constituent elements (dhātus), and phlegm (śleṣman) nourishes their limbs.

7.59 Those suffering from indigestion, those afflicted by [poison], the insane, those with excessive fat or phlegm, and those who constantly consume unctuous substances should not sleep during the day.
One afflicted by poison and one suffering from throat diseases should never sleep even at night.
From sleeping at improper times arise delusion, fever, numbness, catarrh, headache, swelling, nausea, obstruction of the channels, and dullness of the digestive fire. (61)
In that case of excessive sleep, one should employ fasting, emesis, sudation, nasal medication, and medicine; specifically, strong emetics and collyrium. (62)
Gargling, fasting, anxiety, sexual intercourse, grief, fear, and anger—by these very factors, as well as from the excessive depletion of *śleṣman*, sleep is destroyed. (63)
From the loss of sleep arise body aches, heaviness of the head, yawning, dullness, exhaustion, vertigo, indigestion, drowsiness, and diseases born of Vāta. (64)
7.64cv Dullness, exhaustion, vertigo, and indigestion occur when Kapha, stirred up by Vāyu, obstructs the channels (dhamanīs);
it produces a severe torpor that robs one of consciousness and causes delusion.
There, your eyes were wide open and bulging, with pupils rolled upward and lashes disheveled.
She is to be mastered within two and a half nights; she is not to be mastered beyond that.
Therefore, one should habitually resort to sleep at night according to the proper time;
however, due to the unwholesome practice of staying awake, one may sleep for half the night in the morning while fasting.
One who has difficulty sleeping due to unwholesome habits should practice moderation in sleep and consume milk, wine, meat broth, and curd;
he should also employ oil massage, dry rubbing, bathing, and the filling of the head, ears, and eyes with nourishing substances.
The embrace of the vine-like arms of a beloved woman is bliss; it is the fulfillment of all duties;
its objects are agreeable to the mind, and it surely bestows the happiness of sleep. (67)
For one who delights in the holy life, whose mind is free from longing for sensual pleasures, and who is satisfied with contentment, sleep does not exceed its proper time. (68)

In sexual intercourse, he should avoid a woman who is not lying on her back, one who is menstruating, one who is disliked, one whose conduct is disagreeable, or one whose vulva is diseased or contaminated. (69)

One who is excessively obese or emaciated, one who has recently given birth, a pregnant woman, another's wife, a woman of a different caste, or a woman of a different species, as well as the abode of a teacher, a deity, or a king—[these should be avoided]. (70)
7.70b–c: A pregnant woman, another's wife, a sacred tree, a cemetery, a temple, a crossroads, water, and a place where four roads meet;
the lunar festivals, the bodyless one (the wind), the day [of the sun], and the striking of the head and heart. 7.71.

One who has overeaten, one lacking self-control, one afflicted by hunger, one with disordered limbs, one suffering from thirst, a child, an elderly person, one distressed by other intense urges, and a sick person should abstain from sexual intercourse. (72)

One may indulge in desire according to one's wish when satisfied by aphrodisiacs in the winter; [one may do so] every three days in spring and autumn, and every fortnight during the rainy season and the summer. // 73 //
7.73b–d: Satisfied by aphrodisiacs in the cold season, one may practice after two days in spring and autumn,
and after a fortnight during the rainy season and the heat of summer.

Dizziness, fatigue, weakness in the thighs, loss of strength, depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and the sense faculties, and even untimely death may occur for one who approaches a woman in a manner other than [the prescribed way]. (74)
Dizziness, fatigue, weakness of the thighs, and the depletion of strength, bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and the sense faculties;

[these are avoided by those] who are restrained with women. Through memory, intelligence, longevity, health, nourishment, sensory acuity, fame, and vigor, they become superior and subject to slow aging. (7.74–75)

In women, these [vital essences] become concentrated through bathing, unguents, cold breezes, sweets, cold water, milk, meat broth, vegetable soup, wine, and clear spirits. Furthermore, one should resort to the bed immediately after the cessation of sexual union; in this way, the vital essence of the body quickly returns to its original state.

When a king entrusts the protection of his body to a physician who is rich in learning and conduct, skilled in action, and compassionate, he—free from further entanglements—becomes possessed of vast splendor, health, fame, and power; enjoying the fruits of his own merit, he lives a long life. (77)
One should always eat in the proper measure, for measure is what sets the digestive fire in motion;
substances depend on measure, whether they be heavy or light. (1)
For heavy foods, half-satiation is prescribed; for light foods, a state of not being over-sated.
This is defined as the proper measure of quantity: that which can be digested with ease. // 2 //
8.2dv For food that is digested with ease, when taken in a small measure, does not lead to strength, nourishment, or vigor;
rather, it becomes the cause of all wind-related diseases. // 3 //
Furthermore, an excessive amount quickly provokes all the humors (doṣas). For the wind and the other humors, being thus simultaneously provoked, cause affliction. // 4 //

8.4cv When the [doshas] such as vāta are oppressed by impure food (āma), they enter that very [food] and cause [disease]; causing obstruction, they produce alasaka, and causing displacement, they produce viṣūcikā. // 5 //
For one who has not conquered the self, by means of both the downward and upward paths,
[the vital breath] moves neither upward nor downward, and food is not digested.
Because it has become sluggish in the stomach (āmāśaya), it is known as alasaka; this occurs due to the intense provocation of vāyu and the other doshas, resulting in various piercing pains. // 7 //
It is called *viṣūcikā* because it pierces the limbs as if with needles;
therein, from the wind (*anila*), there arise piercing pain, vertigo, flatulence, trembling, stiffness, and so forth. (8)
From pitta arise fever, diarrhea, internal burning, thirst, prostration, and so forth;
from kapha arise vomiting, heaviness of the limbs, obstruction of speech, spitting, and so forth. // 9 //
Specifically, in one who is weak and has a small digestive fire,
the food— its momentum obstructed— is compressed by the wind (vāyu) and blocked within by phlegm (śleṣman).
When the [vital essence] is sluggish and agitated by the humors (doṣas), it remains as if a thorn and produces intense pains and other symptoms, with the exception of vomiting and diarrhea. (11)

8.11b–c As if established as a foreign body (śalya), that [wind] becomes exceedingly sluggish; however, when the corrupted humors (doṣas) are excessively vitiated and have obstructed channels, they move obliquely through the entire body and, if they cause stiffness like a staff, [it is known as daṇḍaka]. 8.12d.

One should quickly abandon that person known as Daṇḍakālasaka, who acts with haste; he exhibits the symptoms of poison in one who habitually eats incompatible foods, overeats, or eats before the previous meal is digested. (13)

One should avoid the extremely terrible disorder of undigested matter (*āmadoṣa*), which is designated as "poison" (*viṣa*), because it acts rapidly like poison and because its treatment involves contradictory procedures. (14)
Then, one should quickly scarify that ulcer which has become stagnant and non-suppurating;
thereafter, one should have the patient drink warm water mixed with *saurāṣṭra* salt, *paṭu* salt, and *phala* salt. // 15 //
One should apply fomentation and fruit-candles (phalavarti) to facilitate the downward movement of impurities and flatus;
furthermore, one should wrap the limbs that are being bent with substances that have been thoroughly fomented.

Madana, pippalī, kuṣṭha, vacā, and white mustard seeds, combined with jaggery and alkali, are recommended as a medicinal suppository (phala-varti) that facilitates the downward movement of impurities and morbid humors.
When *viṣūcī* has become excessively aggravated, cauterization of the heels is recommended;
on that same day, one should fast the patient and treat him as if he had undergone purgation. (17)
Even if suffering from intense pain, one who has indigestion should not drink medicine that relieves colic;
for the digestive fire, suppressed by undigested matter (āma), is incapable of digesting the humors, the medicine, and the food.
Furthermore, their confusion may suddenly kill one who is already distressed;
however, in the case of a stiff and heavy abdomen caused by indigestion, one should administer medicine.

8.19b–c. A sudden complication arises from the remaining morbid humors (doṣa) seeking to undergo digestion and from the stimulation of the digestive fire (agni).
