Having examined that [dosha] within the three types of doshas, one should apply [treatment] accordingly:
fasting is beneficial for a mild [dosha], while fasting combined with digestive therapy is for a moderate one. (21)
Having observed that,
one should prescribe purification when [the disease] is abundant, for that indeed uproots the impurities from their very source;
in this same way, one should treat other diseases as well by means of the opposite of their own causes.

But when a secondary condition (anubandha) exists, the physician should treat it; having abandoned the [primary] cause, he should apply the appropriate remedy for the disease according to its specific nature. (23)

Or, when the doshas have been ripened and the digestive fire kindled, one should appropriately administer beneficial treatments such as massage, oleation, and enemas according to the proper method. (24)

When the *doṣa* has increased while the digestive fire (*pāvaka*) is weak, there is indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) and *āma* due to *kapha*; in that condition, there is swelling of the eyes and cheeks, eructation like that after a recent meal, excessive salivation, nausea, and heaviness. (8.25)
The *viṣṭabdha* type, caused by vāta, produces colic, constipation, flatulence, and exhaustion;
the *vidagdha* type, caused by pitta, is characterized by thirst, delusion, vertigo, acid eructations, and a burning sensation. (26)

8.26dv–27. When there is undigested matter (āma) causing dizziness, acid eructations, and burning sensations, fasting should be practiced; when it is obstructed (viṣṭabdha), strong sudation is required;
when it is partially digested (vidagdha), emesis is indicated, or whatever is beneficial according to the specific stage of the condition.
8.27dv One should employ beneficial treatments according to the specific condition;
vilambikā arises from excessive āma that has become stagnant.

8.28c–29ab: When there is an aversion to food, pain in the heart, and even after purging, eructations persist due to the presence of residual taste mixed with phlegm and wind, one should lie down for a short while; furthermore, one should remain entirely unfed during the day.
Furthermore, one who has not eaten at all should sleep during the day;

when hunger has arisen due to indigestion, he should eat in moderation and light food. Obstruction of the channels, excessive discharge, exhaustion, or the stupefaction of the vital air (māruta) [result from eating improperly]. 8.29–30ab.

8.30–31. Malaise, wind-induced colic, and indigestion are the general signs [of ama]; likewise, distension, heaviness, and dizziness. However, food that is not excessively large in quantity does not by itself lead to the disorder of undigested matter (āma-doṣa).
Food that is disliked, obstructive, burnt, heavy, dry, cold, impure, burning in digestion, parched, or excessively saturated with water does not digest. (32)
Eating while afflicted by grief, anger, hunger, and the like;
or eating wholesome and unwholesome foods together—this is considered "mixed eating" (samaśana). (33)

One should know that *adhyaśana* (overeating) is eating again after having already eaten, due to grief, anger, hunger, and so forth—or due to anger, grief, fear, and so forth. Eating at an improper time, whether in large or small quantities, is called *viṣamāśana* (irregular eating). (8.34)
All three of these may bring about death, or they may produce terrible diseases;
however, at the proper time, one who is pure, focused on that [regimen], and has a clear mind should consume what is wholesome, beneficial, unctuous, warm, and light.
Consisting of six flavors and predominantly sweet, neither too fast nor too slow;
one who has bathed, is hungry, is in a secluded place, and has washed his feet, hands, and face. (36)
Having gratified the ancestors, the gods, guests, children, and teachers,
he also looked after even the animals that had accepted his protection.

Having properly examined himself, neither reproaching nor speaking hastily, he should eat what is desired together with those who are dear to him, provided it has been brought by people who have eaten pure food. (38)
One should avoid food that is infested with grass, hair, and the like; that has been reheated; that consists mostly of vegetables and inferior grains; and that is excessively hot or salty. (39)
Curdled milk, curd, inspissated milk, alkaline substances, fermented gruel, raw radish, and the flesh of emaciated or dried-out boars, sheep, cows, fish, and buffaloes; 40.

One should not habitually consume alkaline substances, fermented gruel, sour liquids, radishes, black gram, flat beans, lotus roots, lotus stalks, flour products, sprouted grains, dried vegetables, barley-gruel, and molasses. (8.40b–41)
One should habitually consume sprouted sesame flour, along with *śāli* rice, wheat, barley, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice;
meat from wild animals; and *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *jīvantī*, young radish, and *vāstuka*.
Haritaki, amalaka, mṛdvīkā, paṭolī, mudga, and sugar;
ghee, divine water (rainwater), milk, honey, pomegranate, and rock salt. 43.
One should take Triphalā at night with honey and ghee for the strengthening of the eyes;
furthermore, whatever promotes the maintenance of health and whatever effects the eradication of disease [should be employed]. 44.
One should first consume heavy, unctuous, sweet, slow-digesting, and stable substances such as sugar-cane juice, grapes, coconut, mango, sweetmeats, and *utkārikā* cakes. (45)
Conversely, at the end [of the meal], it should be the opposite; in the middle, it should be intensely sour and salty.
One should fill two parts of the stomach with solid food and one part with drink. (46)
One should leave a fourth part remaining as the base for the wind and other humors;
cold water is beneficial as an after-drink for barley and wheat.

In the case of curd, liquor, poison, honey, and food made from flour, [the water should be] lukewarm; however, for preparations of vegetables, mung beans, and the like, it should be whey, buttermilk, sour gruel, or fermented rice-water.
8.48b–c And for those who are emaciated, lukewarm wine mixed with flour-based preparations is for the purpose of nourishment; but for those who are obese, honey-water [is used].
8.49 In cases of wasting (śoṣa), meat broth is used; and when the fire of digestion is very weak, wine is used along with meat.

Honey-water is for those who are corpulent; and milk is as beneficial as nectar for those with weak digestion, for those emaciated by disease, medicine, travel, speaking, women, fasting, exposure to the sun, or physical labor, and for the elderly and the young. (8.49–50)
8.50 An after-drink (anupāna) that is contrary to the disease, the medicine, the journey, the physical load, or women, yet not antagonistic to the qualities of the food—
such a drink is always recommended in brief.
The post-prandial drink (anupāna) produces vigor, satisfaction, pervasiveness, and firmness of the limbs; it also effects the loosening of the massed food, its softening, and its digestion. (52)
It is beneficial for pain above the clavicle, dyspnea, cough, chest injury, and coryza, as well as for those engaged in singing or speaking excessively and for hoarseness of voice. (53)

Those suffering from diseases of the body, urinary disorders, eyes, throat, or wounds should abstain from drinking; furthermore, everyone should avoid excessive talking, traveling, and sleeping [during the day]. (54)
Having drunk [liquor], having eaten, [exposing oneself to] the heat of the sun, fire, [using] a vehicle, or [engaging in] swimming or riding; // 55ab //
When feces and urine have been discharged, when the heart is perfectly pure, and when the humors (doṣas) have returned to their own paths; // 55c //
When the belching is pure, or when hunger has arrived and the wind flows accordingly. // 55d //
Likewise, when the fire element is predominant, the sense organs become clear and the body becomes very light. (55e)
One should consume food regulated by the prescribed rules; for that indeed is considered the proper time.

One should consume food regulated by the prescribed rules, for time is considered the primary factor; indeed, the substance itself is superior to the tastes and other qualities, since they are dependent upon it.
That [body], consisting of the five elements, arises by depending upon the earth. // 1 //

That [body] is produced from the combination of water, the womb, fire, air, and space; its specific differentiation, however, is designated according to the predominance [of one element over another].
9.2dv Furthermore, because it arises from a combination of the elements (*bhūta*), a substance is for the most part not of a single taste;
therefore, diseases do not arise from a single *doṣa*. In that case, the taste is considered to be manifest (*vyakta*). // 3 //
Therefore, a substance produced from more than one element does not have its unmanifest secondary taste (anu-rasa) manifest at first; rather, it is held that it becomes manifest only at the end.
Qualities such as heaviness (guru) reside in substances like earth, which serve as the substrates for tastes.
They are designated by the names of the tastes through metaphorical usage based on association.
Among them, the substance [earth] is heavy, gross, stable, and characterized by a predominance of the quality of odor.
The earthy [taste] brings about gravity, stability, compactness, and growth;
it is characterized by an abundance of the qualities of liquidity, coldness, heaviness, unctuousness, slowness, density, and sapidity.
The watery element (āpya) is characterized by the predominance of the qualities of dullness, density, and viscosity; it produces lubrication, trickling, moisture, refreshment, and cohesion.
[The fiery element] is characterized by the predominance of the qualities of dryness, sharpness, heat, clarity, subtlety, and form.
The fire element consists of burning, existence, color, light, and wind;
the air element is characterized by an abundance of the qualities of roughness, clarity, and lightness of touch.
The aerial element (nābhasa) causes dryness, lightness, clarity, movement, and exhaustion; it is characterized by the predominance of the qualities of subtlety, clarity, lightness, and sound. // 9 //

9.9bv – Nothing in this world exists as a substance that does not possess the nature of reducing [doshas] through its analytical action, nor one that does not produce internal cavities or lightness; thus, there is no drug whatsoever that does not come under the influence of various purposes and applications. (10)
In that context, a substance whose upward movement is predominant generally possesses an excess of the qualities of fire and wind;
whereas one whose downward movement is most prevalent possesses a predominance of the qualities of earth and water. (11)
Thus, the substance [of each rasa] will be explained later through its various classifications; as for potency (vīrya), some authorities describe it as heavy, unctuous, cold, and mild. (12)
9.12ab Thus, substance (dravya) is considered to be of eight kinds according to its variations: taste (rasa), lightness, dryness, heat, and sharpness.
But Caraka says: "Potency (vīrya) is that by which an action is performed. 9.13cd/ab 13 //

9.13cd–14ab Caraka, however, says: "Potency (vīrya) is that by which an action is performed; nothing is done without potency, for everything is produced by potency. Therefore, potency is described as being 'true to its name' (anvartha) specifically with respect to qualities such as heaviness."

Among those things which possess the essence of all qualities and manifest through the excellence of their power, [the term "all"] is used for practical purposes because of its primary status and because it includes many foremost instances. (15)

9.15 Because it possesses the essence of all qualities (guṇas) and because it manifests as the excellence of power (śakti), and because it is the opposite of that [other quality], even though it exists, it is not intended to be expressed among rasa and the other [qualities]; therefore, heaviness (guru) and the rest are [the qualities] of vīrya. 16.
Furthermore, others declare that potency (vīrya) is of two kinds: hot and cold;
yet even a substance of manifold nature possesses the great powers of both Agni and Soma.
The manifest world never transcends the unmanifest;
therein [in the manifest] are found heat, delusion, thirst, exhaustion, perspiration, burning sensations, and rapid digestion. (18)

This world consists of the manifest and the unmanifest; furthermore, the cold [quality] brings about the pacification of wind and phlegm, while it provides refreshment, sustenance, stabilization, and clarity for blood and bile. (9.18–19)
That other taste which arises at the end of the transformation of tastes through conjunction with the digestive fire is known as *vipāka*. // 20 //
The sweet and pungent tastes are digested as sweet; the sour taste is digested as sour;
and the bitter, acrid, and astringent tastes are generally digested as pungent. (21)
In that regard, this [substance] yields results equal to its tastes;
therein, a certain substance performs its function through its taste, while another does so through its post-digestive transformation (pāka).

By means of another quality—namely, potency (vīrya) and even efficacy (prabhāva)—whichever among the qualities such as taste (rasa) and the rest prevails within a substance by virtue of its strength [is the one that determines the action]. // 23 //
Overpowering the others, each respective factor attains the status of being the cause;
for when qualities that are mutually opposed are combined, the lesser is indeed overcome by the greater. (24)
Taste, post-digestive effect, potency, and specific power—these [latter qualities] override the former when they are of equal strength; such is the inherent power of taste and the rest. (25)

9.25b–c. That specific action which occurs when the taste and other factors are equal is produced by *prabhāva* (potency), for *prabhāva* sets them aside. For example, although *dantī* is identical to *citrika* in its taste and other qualities, it acts as a purgative. 9.26. [The verse continues: *Dantī*, despite being equal to *citrika* in its taste and other properties, is a purgative.
Madhuka and mṛdvīkā, along with ghee and milk, are digestive stimulants;
such is the general action of substances and the like, and that [action] is further [detailed as follows]. 27.
A substance is differentiated by the diversity of the causes from which it originates: wheat is sweet and heavy, while barley overcomes wind and produces wind. (28)
Fish are warm, milk is cold; a lion is pungent, not a boar. // 28 //

In the Section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna), the origin of the sweet and other tastes arises from the elements (bhūtas) in their respective order, through the predominance of two elements at a time: earth-water, earth-water-fire, ether-space-air, fire-air-earth, and air-fire. (1)
Among them, one should recognize that pleasant taste which anoints the mouth;
when tasted, it brings delight to the body and clarity to the senses.

10.2b That which is pleasing to ants and other such creatures, yet when sour, washes away the mouth; that which causes the bristling of hair and teeth, and the contraction of the eyes and eyebrows—[this is the sign]. // 3 //
10.3b The sour [taste] causes the mouth to flow; the salty makes the mouth water and produces a burning sensation in the cheeks and throat;
the bitter clarifies the mouth and impairs the sense of taste.
10.4dv The pungent [taste] obstructs the sense of taste and agitates it, causing a tingling sensation at the tip of the tongue;
it causes discharge from the eyes, nose, and mouth, and burns as if scorching the cheeks. // 5 //
Astringent taste numbs the tongue and causes obstruction of the channels of the throat;
such are the forms and functions of tastes, beginning with the sweet taste.
Through lifelong habituation, it produces powerful strength in the bodily constituents (dhātus),
as well as for children, the elderly, those emaciated by injury, those with diminished complexion, hair, and sense organs, and for the vital essence (ojas).
It is praised as nourishing, beneficial for the throat, a promoter of breast milk and tissue repair, heavy, life-prolonging, vitalizing, unctuous, and a remover of pitta, vāta, and poison. (8)
By excessive consumption, it produces diseases born of fat and phlegm, such as obesity, loss of digestive fire, fainting, urinary disorders, goiters, tumors, and the like. (9)
Sour [taste] cures diseases born of fat and phlegm; it stimulates the digestive fire, is unctuous, pleasing to the heart, digestive, and appetizing.
It is hot in potency, cold in touch, nourishing, moistening, and light.

10.10c–d: Hot in its potency yet cold in touch, it is pleasing, digestive, and light; it increases phlegm, bile, and blood, and brings about the downward movement of obstructed wind. When consumed in excess, it causes looseness of the body, blurred vision, and vertigo.
10.11b–c: It restores the downward movement of obstructed vāta and cures itching, pallor, erysipelas, swelling, vesicles, thirst, and fever.
10.11d–12: Salt removes stiffness, rigidity, and constriction, and it stimulates the digestive fire.
It is emollient, sudorific, sharp, appetizing, and causes excision and incision; when used excessively, it indeed causes hemorrhage, wind-disorders, baldness, graying hair, and wrinkles. (13)
The bitter [taste] produces thirst, skin diseases, poison, and erysipelas; it destroys strength.
Being itself unpalatable, it causes loss of appetite, worms, thirst, and poison. (14)
It conquers skin diseases, fainting, fever, nausea, burning sensations, and disorders of pitta and kapha;
it dries up moisture, fat, muscle-fat, marrow, feces, and urine. (15)
It is light, wholesome, cold, dry, and it cleanses the breast milk and the throat;
however, through excessive use, it causes depletion of the bodily tissues (dhātus) and diseases of Vāta. (16)
10.16c–d Astringent [taste] overcomes the depletion of the bodily elements (dhātus), moving diseases, disorders of the throat, urticaria, leprosy, intestinal torpor, and swelling;
it consolidates ulcers and dries up unctuousness, fat, and moisture. 17.
It kindles the digestive fire, promotes digestion, improves the appetite, purifies, and dries up food;
it cuts through obstructions, opens the channels, and removes phlegm. (18)

10.18b–c. This [purgative] is a cleanser of food and a laxative; however, through excessive application, it causes thirst, depletion of semen and strength, fainting, contraction, trembling, and pain in the waist, back, and other regions. 10.19.

This intensely astringent [substance], when applied with great force, destroys pitta and kapha; it is heavy, purifies the blood, causes compression, promotes healing, is cooling, and dries up moisture and fat. // 20 //
It checks undigested matter (āma), is constipating, dry, and excessively clarifies the skin; yet, when consumed in excess, it causes obstruction, flatulence, and pain in the heart. (21)
[It cures] thirst, emaciation, loss of virility, obstruction of the channels, and the retention of waste products;
[and it consists of] ghee, gold, jaggery, almonds, *moca*, *coca*, and *parūṣaka*. (22)
[It cures] obstructions of the channels, throat-constriction, blockage of the channels, and retention of waste. [The following drugs are used]:
Abhīru, Vīrā, Panasa, Rājādana, the three types of Balā, the four types of Medā, the four types of Parṇinī, Jīvantī, Jīvaka, and Ṛṣabha. (10.22–23)
Madhūka, madhuka, bimbī, vidārī, the two types of śrāvaṇī, kṣīraśuklā, tukākṣīrī, the two types of kṣīriṇī, kāśmarī, and the two types of saha. (24)
10.24c–d The sweet group (madhura-gaṇa) consists of kṣīraśuklā, tāvakṣīrī, kṣīrekṣu, gokṣura, honey (kṣaudra), grapes (drākṣā), and so forth.
The sour group (amla) consists of āmalaka (dhātrī), phalāmlīkā, mātuluṅga, and amlavetasa. 10.25ab.
Pomegranate, silver, buttermilk, tamarind, pālevata, curd, mango, āmrātaka, bhavya, wood-apple, and karamardaka. // 26 //
Vṛkṣāmla, kola, likuca, kośāmla, ātaka, dhanvana, whey, fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), wine, jambīra, and tilakaṇṭaka. // 26+1 //
The group of salts (lavaṇa-gaṇa) consists of sauvarcala, kṛṣṇa, viḍa, sāmudra, audbhida, romaka, pāṃsuja, sīsa, and kṣāra.
The group of alkaline and salty substances;
the bitter group consists of *paṭolī*, *trāyantī*, *vālaka*, *uśīra*, *candana*, *bhūnimba*,
*nimba*, *kaṭukā*, *tagara*, *aguru*, and *vatsaka*.
Naktamāla, the two types of dvi-rajanī, musta, mūrvā, āṭarūṣaka, pāṭhā, apāmārga, kāṃsyāya, guḍūcī, and dhanvayāsaka; // 29 //
The five roots, the two types of *vyāghrī*, *viśālā*, *ativiṣā*, *vacā*, *kaṭuka*, asafoetida, black pepper, *kṛmijit*, and the five *kolaka* fruits. (30)
10.30c–d: Asafoetida and black pepper are pungent; the five types of *kolaka* are vermifuge;

the *kuṭhera*-group vegetables and green leafy herbs are bitter; bile, urine, and *aruṣkara* are astringent; the group beginning with *pathyā* (harītakī) and *akṣa* (vibhītaka), as well as *śirīṣa*, *khadira*, and honey, are sweet.
Pitta, urine, and *aruṣkara* constitute the group [of astringents]. The *pathyā-akṣa* group is astringent;
as are *kadamba*, *udumbara*, pearl, coral, collyrium, red ochre, tender *kapittha*, date palm, lotus stalk, *padma*, *utpala*, and so forth. (10.31b–32)
10.32d–10.33ab Lotus stalks, lotuses, and water lilies are generally sweet and increase *śleṣman* (phlegm), except for aged *śāli* rice and barley,
mung beans, wheat, honey, sugar, and the meat of wild animals.
Generally, sour substances generate *pitta*, with the exception of pomegranate and *āmalaka*;
salt is generally unwholesome for the eyes, with the exception of *saindhava* salt. (34)
It is predominantly bitter and pungent, non-aphrodisiac, and aggravates vāta, with the exception of amṛtā, paṭolī, śuṇṭhī, kṛṣṇā, and rasona. (35)
Astringent (kaṣāya) is generally cold and constipating, with the exception of Abhayā;
the tastes—pungent, sour, and salty—are hot in potency, each succeeding one being hotter than the last. (36)
Abhayā and Amṛtā are astringent, bitter, astringent, and sweet, and likewise cool;
they are bitter, pungent, and astringent, dry, and cause the binding of the waste products.
Sour, acidic, and sweet tastes are unctuous and facilitate the passage of feces, urine, and flatus;
among these, the astringent is lighter than the sour, and the sweet is the heaviest of all. (38)
Light, sour, and pungent—after that [comes] bitter;
there are fifty-seven combinations, while the preparations are of sixty-three kinds. (39)
From salt, sour and sweet [tastes] should be prepared in due order for the purpose of pacifying the digestion of wind that has no associated humors. (39.1+1)

10.39.1–2 For the purpose of pacifying the ripening [of the fever], a bitter [decoction] is administered first, followed by a sweet one, and finally an astringent one at the end. By these, the *pitta* is brought to subsidence once it has been ripened, cooled, and solidified.
First pungent, then bitter, and finally astringent is the sequence prescribed;
by these, phlegm (śleṣmā) is pacified when it has been ripened, cooled, and condensed.
Pungent first, then bitter—once matured, it becomes clear and condensed;
thus the tastes are divided according to their combinations, roughly as follows:
when each one is omitted, those tastes become fifteen in the case of dyads (dvika).
10.40cd–41ab. These five tastes proceed by decreasing one at a time in pairs: there are five sweet, five sour, four salty, three bitter, two pungent, and one [astringent]—thus making fifteen.
In combinations of three, the sweet taste occurs ten times, the sour six times, the salty three times, and the bitter once.
In combinations of four, the sweet occurs ten times, the sour four times, and the salty once.
In a group of four, there are ten sweet [tastes];
in groups of five, there is only one sour [taste] which partakes of five sweet ones.
One substance possesses six tastes, and the six tastes exist when uncombined.
There are six groups of five and six distinct tastes; the combinations of four and two are of fifteen kinds;
the varieties of three are twenty; and there is one single substance with six flavors—thus, there are sixty-three.

These variations of tastes, arising from primary and secondary tastes as well as through the conceptualization of degrees of intensity, exceed all calculation; they are to be employed according to the specific faults and the required remedies. (44)

In the Sūtrasthāna, it is stated that the *doṣas*, *dhātus*, and *malas* are always the root of the body; they are mobile through the initiation of enthusiasm, inhalation, exhalation, movement, and the flow of urges. (1)
Through its proper movement and the proficiency of the elements and the sense faculties, the unmodified *pitta* sustains them by means of digestion, heat, and vision. (2)
Phlegm [is characterized] by hunger, thirst, appetite, luster, intelligence, wisdom, valor, and softness of the body;
and by stability, oiliness, firmness of the joints, endurance, and so forth. (3)
Satisfying, sustaining, anointing, lubricating, supporting, filling, and producing the embryo—these are remembered as the preeminent functions of the bodily constituents (dhātus), respectively. (4)
When increased, the wind (vāyu) causes the retention of feces, the obstruction of the flow of urine, and the suppression of perspiration. (5)

11.5c–d: [Excessive] sweating causes the loss of hair; 11.5d: And increased *vāyu* produces emaciation, dark complexion, thirst for heat, trembling, constipation, retention of feces, loss of strength, sleep, and the senses, as well as delirium, vertigo, and dejection.

11.6ab Emaciation, blackish discoloration, heat, desire for cold things, yellowing of the feces, urine, eyes, and skin, hunger, thirst, burning sensations, and little sleep—these are [the signs of] pitta; while the suppression of digestive fire, salivation, lassitude, and heaviness are those of kapha. //7//
Whiteness, coldness, flaccidity of the limbs, labored breathing, coughing, and excessive sleepiness;
the bodily fluids as well as the blood become like phlegm, leading to erysipelas, splenic enlargement, and abscesses.

It [causes] leprosy, disorders of wind and blood, hemorrhagic diseases, abdominal tumors, scrotal enlargement, jaundice, freckles, loss of digestive fire, delusion, and redness of the skin, eyes, and urine. (9)
11.9c–d: It causes loss of limbs, loss of digestive fire, and delusion; it produces fleshy growths, tumors, nodules, goiters, and enlargement of the thighs and abdomen;
likewise, it causes excess flesh in the throat and other areas, as well as fat and exhaustion. 11.10.

Swelling of the cheeks, thighs, and abdomen; labored breathing even with slight exertion; sagging of the buttocks, breasts, and belly; additional bones, additional teeth; marrow [disorder]; and heaviness of the eyes and limbs. 11.10b–d. 11.10e–f.

It causes pricking pain in the bladder, thick-based nodes in the joints, painful urination, ulcers, excessive sexual desire, and even seminal calculi in an elderly man who indulges excessively in women. (11.13cd–12)

Distension of the abdomen, flatulence, heaviness, pain, feces, and urine, as well as a pricking sensation in the bladder and the perception that [the enema] has not been administered even when it has been given. (13)
One should observe perspiration, excessive sweating, foul odor, and itching; likewise, one should recognize the impurities such as eye-secretions by their abundance, heaviness, and so forth. (14)

When the wind (vāyu) has diminished, the signs are a sense of exhaustion in the limbs, little speech or activity, confusion of consciousness, and the arising of diseases described as resulting from an increase of phlegm (śleṣman). // 15 //

When pitta is diminished, there is weak digestion; when kapha is diminished, there is coldness, loss of luster, dizziness, a sense of emptiness in the seats of phlegm, fluidity in the heart, and looseness of the joints. (16)
11.16dv–17: In [the stage of] *hr̥d-gada* (heart disease), there is looseness of the joints, dryness of taste, fatigue, emaciation, lassitude, and intolerance to sound.
In [the stage of] blood [vitiation], there is a craving for sour and cold things, flaccidity of the veins, and dryness.
In the flesh [vitiation], there is exhaustion of the eyes, goiters, swelling of the buttocks, emaciation, and pain in the joints;
in the fat, there is excessive sleep, enlargement of the spleen, and leanness of the body. (18)
In the bone, there is a piercing pain in the bones and a loosening of the teeth, hair, nails, and so forth;
in the marrow of the bones, there is porosity, vertigo, and the appearance of darkness before the eyes. (19)
11.19 In the bone [semen-retaining disorder], there is piercing pain in the bones and a sense of exhaustion; semen is discharged only after a long time, or it may be blood instead.
There is excessive piercing pain in the testicles, and the penis feels as if it is smoking. 20.
In the feces, the wind moves with a sound as if wrapping around the intestines; it wanders in the abdomen, ascends upward, and causes intense pain in the heart and the sides. (21)
11.21c–d The urine wanders in the abdomen, moves upward, and one voids it in small quantities with difficulty; it may be discolored or even bloody.
During sweating, there is loss of body hair, stiffness of the hair, and cracking of the skin. 11.22a–b
One should observe the destruction of extremely subtle impurities, which is difficult to perceive, by means of the drying up of their own seats, pricking sensations, emptiness, and lightness. (23)

The physician should understand the increase and decrease of the doshas and other factors according to their respective natures, through the depletion of opposing qualities and the augmentation of those that are concordant. (24)
From attachment [to food], there is an increase of impurities; from excessive excretion, there is their depletion.
Because the body is accustomed to impurities, their depletion causes suffering, whereas their increase brings nourishment. (25)

In that regard, wind resides in the bones, bile in sweat and blood, and phlegm in the remaining [tissues]; therefore, among these, there is a mutual relationship between the substrates and their contents. (26)
That which is a medicine for the increase or decrease of one [element] is not so for both the bone and the wind; for generally, increase results from satiation. (27)
Therefore, it is accompanied by phlegm; its depletion arises from the opposite of that, and it is accompanied by wind because of the occurrence of increase and decrease. (28)
One should quickly cure disorders other than those arising from Vāyu by means of fasting and nourishing therapies applied in the proper sequence;
however, for disorders born of Vāyu itself, one should employ those same therapies applied in the reverse order.

One should treat diseases arising from an increase of blood specifically with bloodletting and purgation, and those born from an increase of flesh with the application of surgical instruments, caustics, and thermal cautery. // 30 //

Those [diseases] born from fat (medas) should be treated with regimens for obesity or emaciation, while those born from the depletion of bone (asthi-saṃkṣaya) should be treated with milk, ghee, and enemas (vasti) combined with bitter substances. // 31 //
Likewise,
one should treat diseases arising from marrow and semen with enemas combined [with appropriate drugs], as well as with foods that are sweet and bitter;
and for increased semen caused by sexual intercourse and other factors, as well as any other condition characterized by the wasting of semen.

Marrow and semen are beneficial for the increase or decrease of [bodily constituents] when acting as an antidote to their opposites. Diarrhea caused by the increase of feces should be treated with the therapeutic measures for diarrhea;
that arising from the decrease of feces should be treated with mutton, barley-meal, half-cooked grains (*kulmāṣa*), barley, the two types of *māṣa* beans, and so forth.
One should treat conditions arising from the increase or decrease of urine with the therapies used for urinary disorders (meha) and dysuria (kṛcchra);
those arising from perspiration or its depletion should be treated with physical exercise, massage, sudation, and alcohol.

A preceding element, when increased, affects the subsequent one; when diminished, it likewise affects that same subsequent one.
The doshas, when vitiated by the rasas, corrupt the dhatus, and both together corrupt the malas.
There are two apertures below, seven in the head, and those that carry sweat; these are the excretory channels (malāyana), and diseases arise in them according to their respective locations.
Ojas, however, is known as the supreme essence among the elements ending with semen;
though situated in the heart, it is pervasive and the basis for the maintenance of the body. (37)
It is unctuous, of the nature of the moon, pure, and slightly reddish-yellow;
when it perishes, destruction is certain, and as long as it remains, [the body] remains. (38)
From which various bodily states arise, [that] vital essence (*ojas*) is diminished by anger, hunger, anxiety, grief, fatigue, and so forth. (39)
The weak one fears constantly; his senses are distressed and he broods;
he becomes ill-favored, dejected, coarse, and emaciated upon that depletion. (40)
11.40c–d: One becomes lusterless, dejected, parched, and emaciated due to its depletion. 11.40d:
In that case, the medicines are those that promote vitality (*jīvanīya*), milk, meat broth, and so forth;
for when *ojas* increases, there arises satisfaction, nourishment, and strength in the body.
When there is an increase in *ojas* (vital essence) of the body, contentment, nourishment, and the arising of strength occur; moreover,
whatever food one dislikes or desires, provided it is not incompatible [with one's constitution], [should be consumed].
By abandoning each [of those] and experiencing each [of those], one should conquer both increase and decrease.
Whether abandoning or consuming various things, the doshas indeed produce a relish for what is either contrary or similar to themselves;
those that are increased or diminished mostly perceive this, whereas the ignorant do not.

11.43ab Indeed, the humors produce their characteristic signs according to their strength and according to their own nature; when increased, they manifest their symptoms, when diminished they abandon them, and when balanced they perform their own functions. 44.
Those very same humors that are balanced lead to the growth of the body, while those that are unbalanced lead to its destruction;
therefore, they must be protected through wholesome conduct, both from their increase and from their depletion.
11.45dv Due to both depletion and increase, the following must be protected:
the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), the waist, the thighs, the ears, the bones, and the sense of touch. (Sūtrasthāna)
That is the location of wind (vāta), and specifically the receptacle for digested matter (pakvādhāna).
The navel, the stomach, sweat, lymph, blood, and plasma are the seats of pitta; among these, the navel is its particular seat. (2)
The chest, throat, head, kloman, joints, the stomach, lymph-chyle, fat, the nose, and the tongue—of these, the chest is the primary seat of phlegm. (3)
Air, which consists of five aspects through its divisions such as prāṇa and the rest, is here [designated] as prāṇa when it moves to the head;
it moves through the chest and throat, and sustains the intellect, heart, senses, and mind. // 4 //

The region of the chest is the seat of the udāna breath; it moves through the nose, the navel, and the throat, producing spitting, sneezing, belching, and exhalation, as well as the intake of food. (5)
Moving through the nose, navel, and throat,
performing the functions of speech, exertion, vigor, strength, complexion, memory, and action,
the vyāna wind resides in the heart and courses throughout the entire body with great speed. 12.5d–6a.
Movement, throwing downward, lifting upward, closing, opening, and so forth—practically all the actions of embodied beings are dependent upon that [wind]. (7)
The *samāna* [vāyu], situated near the fire, moves everywhere within the abdominal cavity;
it takes up food, digests it, separates its components, and releases the waste.
Apāna moves downward; its range is the hips, bladder, penis, thighs, and groin;
its functions are the emission of semen, menstrual blood, feces, urine, and the fetus. // 9 //
Therein, bile (pitta) consists of five components and is located between the stomach and the small intestine;
although it is composed of the five elements, it arises from the manifestation of the quality of fire. // 10 //

That which has relinquished its state as a material substance, designated as "fire" through the process of cooking and so forth, cooks the food and likewise separates it into its essential nutrients and waste products. (11)
12.11dv Likewise, that which separates the essence and the waste within those very [bile fluids] and also provides support to the remaining types of bile by bestowing strength is known as *pācaka*.
The *rañjaka* bile is located in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), so called because it colors the nutrient essence (*rasa*);
and [the *sādhaka* bile] is so called because it accomplishes desired objects through the functions of intellect, memory, and self-conceit (*abhimāna*). (13)
The Pitta located in the heart is known as the *sādhaka* (the accomplisher) because it perceives forms;
that situated in the eyes is the *ālocaka* (the perceiver); and that situated in the skin is the *bhrājaka* (the illuminator) because it illuminates the skin. (14)

Phlegm (śleṣman), however, resides in five locations: in its own location by virtue of its own power, in the heart by virtue of the power of food, and in those very same locations through its watery action. (15)
12.15ab–16. Phlegm (śleṣman), when located in the five upper parts of the body, provides support for the seats of kapha and the remaining [organs];
therefore, phlegm situated in the stomach (āmāśaya) is called the "supporter" (avalambaka).
12.16d That [bile] which resides in the stomach is the "moistening" (kledaka) bile; it is called "awakening" (bodhaka) because it moistens the mass of food and awakens the sense of taste.
Residing in the tongue, it is the "tasting" bile, and located in the head, it is the "satisfying" bile because it nourishes the sense organs.

It is nourishing because it binds the joints together, and it is called "the binder" (śleṣaka) because it resides in the joints; such, generally, are the locations of the humors when they are in their natural state. (18)
One should know that the *śleṣaka* (the binder) is situated at the joints; even though [the *dhātus*] are pervasive, their functions are each distinct.
Dry substances and others combined with heat cause the accumulation (*saṃcaya*) of *vāyu*. (12.18b–19)
The qualities such as unctuousness and others, when combined with cold, bring about the pacification of anger;
whereas those such as sharpness and others, when joined with cold, produce an accumulation of pitta.
Those qualities beginning with "mild" (mandādi), when combined with heat, bring about the pacification of *kopa* (aggravation);
whereas those beginning with "unctuous" (snigdhādi), when joined with cold, produce the accumulation (*caya*) of *śleṣman*. (21)
By that very heat, the qualities such as roughness and so forth are pacified;
accumulation is increase within its own domain, and aversion toward the causes of increase [is the sign of health]. (22)
A desire for contrary qualities, anger, following the wrong path, seeing one's own [auspicious] marks, ill-health, and the onset of disease. // 23 //
Equilibrium when situated in its own location is the absence of morbid transformation; this is tranquility (*śama*).
The accumulation (*caya*), provocation (*prakopa*), and pacification (*praśama*) of *vāyu* occur during the three seasons beginning with summer. (24)
During the rainy season and so forth, pitta is accumulated; during the cool season and so forth, kapha is accumulated; and vāyu is accumulated by means of light and dry medicinal substances. (25)
12.25 And in the rainy season and other such times, that same type of pitta does not become aggravated in a body of that same type because of the heat of the season;
likewise, [pitta] of that nature [is not aggravated] by waters and medicinal herbs that have an acid post-digestive effect (vipāka).
Pitta undergoes accumulation and provocation, yet not due to the coldness of the season;
likewise, Kapha is accumulated by unctuous and cold waters and medicinal herbs. (27)
Even when time and the body are equal, [the wind] does not become provoked because it has been suppressed;
such is the nature of time, yet it may again arise through the influence of food and other factors. (28)
12.28 Because it has flowed out, it does not cause agitation;
the humors (doṣas) reach [the body] either immediately or after some time, yet it does not suddenly pervade the entire body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. 12.29
But the provoked impurities recede only very slightly, like a flood of water;
the provoked impurities manifest through various and innumerable transformations. (30)
Therefore, because they cause the body to suffer, the means for establishing the cause and the form of that [suffering] cannot be stated individually; hence, it is described in general terms. (31)
Indeed, the humors alone are the single cause of all diseases, just as a bird flying about in every direction throughout the entire day [is the cause of its exhaustion]. (32)
Just as one does not transcend one's own shadow, so too this entire manifold collection of transformations does not transcend the three qualities (guṇas). // 33 //
Likewise, the entire range of disorders is always caused by an imbalance of one's own constituent elements (dhātus);
however, the provocation of those [elements] is due to the three humors (doṣas). (34)
Contact with unsuitable objects, time, and past misdeeds—this [affliction] is further divided into three types by way of deficient, excessive, or perverse application. (35)
Deficiency of the sense organ is its insufficient contact with its object, or no contact at all; excessive application is over-contact with subtle, brilliant, or terrifying objects. (36)
When a form that is too near, too far away, unpleasant, or distorted is perceived by the eye, that is a severe instance of improper contact (mithyā-yoga). (37)

12.37cd–38ab: Thus, one should understand that the improper application [of sense objects] is extremely dreadful, as it pertains to the objects of the senses—such as excessively high or foul odors—and so forth, according to their nature; furthermore, time is considered to be threefold, distinguished by cold, heat, and rain.

12.38–39. According to the difference in years, that [time] is considered to be of three kinds: deficient (hīna) is characterized by an excess of cold and so forth; excessive application (atiyoga) possesses the characteristics of excess;
whereas false application (mithyāyoga) is defined as having the opposite of its own natural characteristics.
One should also divide karma into three types according to the distinctions of body, speech, and mind.
Inferior engagement in actions of the body and so forth is designated as "inferior. (40)

12.40c–d: The deficient engagement of actions such as those of the body is designated as "deficient" (hīna). Excessive application (atiyoga) and excessive engagement (ativṛtti), however, consist of the forceful provocation or suppression of natural urges, the initiation of uneven bodily movements, falling, stumbling, and so forth. 41.
12.41ab Excessive application, transgression, speaking while eating only half-full, passion, hatred, fear, and so forth; and the tenfold action such as the taking of life which is censured.
All this false application, whether performed here or in the next world, is the primary cause of the afflictions; by it, the humors are provoked in manifold ways.
12.43b–d. Whether performed here [in this life] or elsewhere [in a previous one], [karmic actions] produce various diseases in the branches, the cavities, the bones, and the joints.
The "branches" refer to blood and the other [tissues], as well as the skin; for that is the locus of external diseases. 12.44.
12.44d–45ab For she is indeed the abode of external diseases; depending upon her [the body] arise moles, freckles, swellings, carbuncles, tumors, and the like,
as well as external ailments such as hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and edema.
The internal cavity is the great channel (mahā-srotas), which is the site of the stomach (āmāśaya) and the large intestine (pakvāśaya).
Diseases located there include vomiting, diarrhea, cough, dyspnea, abdominal enlargement, and fever. (46)
Internal abscesses, swellings, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, erysipelas, and suppurating ulcers; as well as the vital organs such as the head, heart, and bladder, and the joints of the bones. (47)
12.47–48. The vital points (*marmāṇi*), however, are the joints of the bones; the veins, sinews, tendons, and so forth are bound to them.
This is the middle path of disease, wherein reside those afflicted by consumption (*yakṣma*), paralysis of the wings (*pakṣavadha*), and hemiplegia (*ardita*).

Diseases of the head and so forth, pain and stiffness in the joints, bones, and the sacrum (trika), as well as falling out, spreading, piercing, numbness, exhaustion, aching, pricking, and splitting sensations. (49)
Contraction of the limbs and joints, constriction, whirling, horripilation, and satiation;
trembling, roughness, hollowness, emaciation, throbbing, and twisting. (50)
Stiffness, an astringent taste, and a dark or reddish-brown complexion are the functions of Vāyu; while burning, redness, heat, and suppuration are those of Pitta. (51)
Perspiration, moistening, discharge, putrefaction, lassitude, fainting, and intoxication;
the tastes are pungent and sour; and the color, excluding pale white and reddish-brown. // 52 //
From phlegm (śleṣman) arise unctuousness, hardness, itching, coldness, heaviness of the skin, constriction, coating, numbness, swelling, lack of digestion, and excessive sleepiness. (53)
The color is white, the tastes are sweet and salty, and there is a delayed onset; thus has been described the characteristic of the humor (doṣa) which pervades all diseases without exception. (54)

Being attentive through observation and other means, he should correctly examine [the patient], discerning the distinctions between the stages of the disease as he observes the afflicted at every moment. (55)
Through practice, one attains the vision that reveals the accomplishment of karma;
the knowledge of whether gems and such are genuine or counterfeit does not arise from scripture alone. (56)
From habitual practice, vision arises. From habitual practice alone, vision arises;

some [vision] is born from the transgression of what has been seen, and some is born from a prior offense. Through their combination, another [type of vision] occurs; thus, it is traditionally taught as being threefold. (57)
12.57b–d Thus, disease is considered to be of three kinds: arising from the derangement of the *doṣas*, born of past actions (*karmaja*), or occurring without [apparent] causes.
12.58 A severe affliction that arises from a minor cause is a disease born of both *doṣas* and past actions.
The former [attainment] results from the cultivation of the antidotes; that born of karma [ceases] through the exhaustion of karma;
but that which arises from both [causes] goes to its destruction through the exhaustion of both defects and karma. (59)

Diseases are twofold because they depend on oneself or another; furthermore, the latter are twofold: those born previously are called premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), and those that arise later are complications (*upadrava*). (60)

One should know that the humors (malas) are likewise independent, characterized by clear symptoms, and aggravated by factors similar to those that cause their respective diseases; whereas others are the opposite. 61.
Therefore, one should attentively observe those [fever-inducing factors] as they undergo transformation in each case of fever;
for when their primary cause is pacified, the fever is pacified, and likewise, it remains unappeased if that cause is not.
Or one should treat a powerful secondary affliction (upadrava) immediately;
for it causes even greater pain to a body already afflicted by disease. (63)
12.63–64ab. One who is unskilled in the names of diseases should never feel ashamed whether he treats the condition first or later;
for there is no fixed certainty regarding the names of all diseases.
That very same provoked humor (doṣa), through the particularity of its origin and by reaching different locations, produces many disorders.

Therefore, having understood the modifications and their primary causes, as well as other underlying factors and the specific reasons [for the disease], one should promptly apply the therapeutic treatment. (66)

One must consider the patient, the location, the strength, the time, the digestive fire, the constitution, the age, the mental temperament, as well as suitability, the diet, and the various different conditions. (67)
He who, having scrutinized their most subtle faults, proceeds with medical treatment by determining the appropriate remedy, never falters at any time. (68)

The manifestation of a disease may appear either severe or slight depending on the strength or weakness of the patient's constitution and physical body; since it may even appear otherwise than expected, one should remain vigilant regarding that. (69)
But a pseudo-physician, misjudging a disease as heavy when it is light, errs regarding the wholesome regimen due to his failure to perceive the smallness of the humors.

But a pseudo-physician, calculating or prescribing [the medicine] incorrectly, will certainly cause harm; for a purificatory treatment that is either too small in dose or too weak in potency, when administered in a case of a severe disease due to improper application, will only further aggravate the diseases. (12.70–71)

If purification is performed with excessive application, or if it is reversed when the opposite is required, it would not merely destroy the impurities, but would instead emaciate the body itself. (72)

12.72 Even though the body is exceedingly fragile, one who is diligent should constantly examine everything in every way and administer medicine for the sake of health in such a manner that it is certain [to succeed]. 73.
12.73–74ab. Hereafter, for the sake of health, the doshas will be described according to their distinctions of increase and decrease.
Know that there are three [types] individually; in that regard, know the combinations (saṃsarga) to be threefold, making nine in total.
12.74–75c. Know that there are three distinct [types] of [doubled doshas], three of combined [doshas], six by the increase of one [dosha] over the others,
thirteen when all [three] are increased together, and six by the predominance of two or one [dosha].
12.75dv By means of the six, the two, and the one with a single excellence, and by means of equals and superiors, there are six through the differentiation of degrees; thus,
there are twenty-five [types] for those who have increased [merit], and an equal number for those who have diminished it.
12.76c–d Thus, there are twenty-five [results] through the combinations of increase by one, equality, and decrease; these six, and again those six,
as well as those with the decrease of one and the increase of two, and also their opposites.
Sixty-two varieties have been specified; sixty-three are the cause of health. // 78ab //
Likewise, through contact with their juices, blood, and so forth, [the seeds] of these [plants]. // 78c //
Likewise, through their association with the rasa, blood, and other constituents,
these doshas manifest according to the distinctions of decrease, equilibrium, and increase.
12.78d–e: [The diseases] reach infinity through the distinctions of the decrease, equilibrium, and increase of the humors (doṣas), and through their combinations in varying degrees of intensity.
One should understand them with an attentive mind according to their respective natures. // 78f //
In the Section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna),
the treatment for Vāta consists of oleation (sneha), sudation (sveda), mild purification (saṃśodhana),
foods that are sweet, sour, salty, and hot, as well as massage and rubbing (abhyaṅga-mardana). (1)
Wrapping, inducing fear, sprinkling, liquor made from flour or molasses, unctuous and warm enemas, the regular administration of enemas, and a pleasant lifestyle. (2)
Unctuous substances of many origins—clarified butters that are digestive and carminative—and especially unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) made from fat, meat-broth, or oil [are recommended]. (3)
For pitta, the drinking of ghee, purgation with sweet and cold substances, and foods and medicines that are sweet, bitter, and astringent are recommended. (4)
The enjoyment of fragrances that are sweet-smelling, cool, and pleasing;
and the wearing upon the neck of necklaces and upon the chest of gems possessing excellent qualities. // 5 //
Anointing with camphor, sandalwood, and ushira at every moment;
the evening moon, the moonlit palace, enchanting song, and the cool breeze. (6)

A friend who offers unconditioned happiness, a son whose speech is hesitant and innocent, a wife who follows one's will and is beloved, adorned with virtuous conduct—[these are the true blessings]. (7)
A friend whose face offers no restraint,
houses filled with streams of cool water, and the long ponds of pleasure gardens upon the sandy banks of vast, pure reservoirs at excellent bathing places. (13.7)
On the banks of lotus-pool waters, amidst groves of trees resounding with song, gentle dispositions prevail—specifically water, clarified butter, and purgatives. (9)
In one suffering from excessive phlegm (śleṣman) in a place crowded with trees, strong emesis and purgation should be administered according to the prescribed method;
food should be dry, small in quantity, sharp, and hot, possessing pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes. // 10 //
Wine that has been kept for a long time, sexual pleasure, staying awake, various forms of physical exertion, anxiety, and dry massage; 11.
Specifically, emesis, vegetable broth, honey, and medicines that destroy fat; fumigation, fasting, gargles, and the removal of discomfort—all these lead to well-being. (12)
This therapeutic procedure which has been described by specifying the individual doshas should be applied accordingly in cases of dual or triple dosha involvement. (13)
One should prescribe it accordingly:
for wind and bile, generally that of summer; for phlegm and wind, that of spring; and because wind acts as a vehicle for other humors, for phlegm and bile, that of autumn. (13.13cd–14ab)

One should conquer the humor that has become aggravated by means of its own accumulation, provided it does not conflict with the others; for when all humors are aggravated, one should treat the strongest one without disturbing the remaining humors. (15)
A therapeutic application that pacifies one disorder while provoking another is not pure;
however, that which pacifies without provoking is pure. (16)
13.16 A medical application that pacifies one disease while provoking another should be avoided.

This is because of physical exertion, the sharpness of the bodily heat (*ūṣman*), the practice of unwholesome habits, and because the wind (*māruta*) moves swiftly from the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*) to the peripheral branches, bones, and vital points (*marman*). // 17 //

Likewise, the humors (doṣas) are expelled from them through the cleansing of the channels and orifices, due to their increase, their spreading, their suppuration, and the suppression of the bodily wind (vāyu). // 18 //
Remaining there, they linger further, awaiting their cause;
having acquired the power of time and other factors, they become provoked even toward other substrates. (19)

In that regard, when [the humors] are located in other sites but are weak, one should apply one's own specific treatment; however, when they overcome other [humors] through their strength, one should treat them according to their own nature.
One should pacify an incoming disorder by counteracting the resident one;
for generally, disorders that have spread horizontally cause patients suffering for a long time. (21)
Or one should perform a rite common to both types of practitioners.
One who knows the strength of the body's digestive fire should not perform medical treatment on these [patients] with haste;
rather, one should pacify those [doshas] through appropriate application or bring them comfortably into the gastrointestinal tract.
Having recognized that they have reached the receptacle (koṣṭha), one should expel them as soon as possible;
for [if not], there arise obstruction of the channels, loss of strength, heaviness, and confusion of the vital air (vāyu). (23)
Heaviness, obstruction of wind,

lassitude, indigestion, spitting, retention of waste products, loss of appetite, and exhaustion are the signs of impurities associated with *sāma* (undigested) states; for those that are *nirāma* (free from *āma*), the symptoms are the opposite.

There will be yellowness of the feces, urine, nails, teeth, skin, and eyes; furthermore, there will be redness or blackness [of these], and pain in the spine, bones, and the joints of the hips. (24.1+1)

13.24.1–2. In the case of *pṛṣṭha* (back-bone), intense headache arises in the joints of the back and the waist; there is sleepiness, a bad taste in the mouth, swelling in some part of the body, fever, diarrhea, and horripilation.

Because the digestive heat (ūṣman) is weak, the first tissue-element (dhātu) remains undigested; when this vitiated element reaches the stomach (āmāśaya), it is called "undigested" (āma) rasa. // 25 //
Others say that undigested matter (āma) arises from the extremely corrupted humors (doṣas) themselves, through their mutual fermentation, just as poison arises from *kodrava* grains. (26)
When the humors (doṣas) and the bodily constituents (dūṣyas) are vitiated by that [dosha] in its raw state (āma), they are designated as "sāma"; and so too are the diseases that arise from them. (27)
The Vāyu, accompanied by Sāma, gradually afflicts the limbs with constipation, loss of digestive fire, stiffness, rumbling in the intestines, pain, swelling, and piercing sensations. (27+1)
It may also move about simultaneously and seize [the patient] violently when provoked;
it increases through unctuous substances and the like at night upon the rising of the sun and clouds.
Free from mucus, clear, dry, unobstructed, and with little pain, it finds relief through substances possessing opposite qualities, especially those that are unctuous. // 27+3 //

One should designate bile that is foul-smelling, greenish, dark-brown, sour, thick, and heavy as *sāma* (undigested), noting that it causes burning in the throat and heart, like the taste of tamarind. // 27+4 //
When ripe, it should be known as slightly copper-red or yellow, very hot, pungent in taste, unstable, and foul-smelling; it bestows appetite, digestion, and strength. (27+5)
13.27+5dv The *āvila* type of *balāsa* provides luster, digestive fire, and strength;
it is thick, remains stagnant in the region of the throat, is accompanied by phlegm (*sāma*), is foul-smelling, and causes loss of appetite and suppression of belching. 13.27+6 //
When it is foamy, compacted, pale, sapless, and indeed odorless, that very substance should be known as ripe; when cut, it exudes juice and provides purification for the mouth.
One should not eliminate the *sāma* doshas that have spread throughout the entire body,
as they remain latent within the tissues (*dhātus*) and are not yet provoked, like unripened juices still contained within fruit.
For they would lead to the destruction of the physical basis because they are difficult to remove;
therefore, one should treat them with ripening, stimulating, oleating, and sudation therapies. (29)
One should purify with cleansing agents at the proper time, according to proximity and strength;
a substance administered through the mouth quickly destroys the impurities located in the stomach. (30)

One should expel by means of the nose those [doshas] arising above the clavicle, and by means of the rectum those from the receptacle of digested food (pakvādhāna), whether they have become aggravated and are moving downward or upward; however, one should not expel those that are undigested (āmān) on their own.

One should suppress the humors with medicinal drugs, for once suppressed, they cause disease; therefore, one who eats wholesome food should overlook the humors when they have already begun to manifest.
Those that are obstructed, one should cause to ripen with various digestive (pācana) remedies, or else one should eliminate them;
this should be done respectively during the months of Śrāvaṇa, Kārttika, and Caitra, which are conducive to such treatment.

One should digest and eliminate [the impurities], and likewise purify during these months of the rainy season, autumn, and spring; according to the prescribed method, one should cleanse the accumulated wastes at intervals of three months during the common seasons.
One should quickly remove the accumulation of wind and other humors caused by summer, the rainy season, and winter;
for the arrivals of summer, the rains, and winter are characterized by excessive heat, rain, and cold, respectively. (34)

At the common juncture of these [periods], one should purify the defects of those who are afflicted; however, this should be done with reference to the regimen for health during the absence of disease, whereas during illness, it must be according to the requirements of that specific disease. (35)
Among those, there are three common [divisions], beginning with the rainy season (prāvṛṣ). Of these, Śuci and Nabhas are known as the rainy season; Śarad and Ūrja-Saha are recorded as [the next].
The month of Tapasya, Madhumāsa, and Vasanta are conducive to purification;
having thus distinguished these seasons, the physician should administer purificatory therapy.
Having provided appropriate remedies for cold, heat, and rain as required, one should perform the action that has arrived and not let the time for action pass by. // 36 //

One should employ non-food at the beginning of eating, in the middle, and at the end; between morsels, with every mouthful, repeatedly, along with food, in a balanced manner, and likewise medicinal herbs at night. (37)

In a disease characterized by an excess of phlegm (kapha), fasting is prescribed for both the patient and the physician when they possess strength; however, if the apāna wind is impaired, fasting is desired at the beginning of the meal, and if the samāna wind is impaired, it is desired during the middle of the meal. (38)

When the vital breath (prāṇa) is disturbed at the end of the vyāna [breath], one should perform it in the morning; when it is disturbed after the evening meal, one should do so later; and when it is disturbed between mouthfuls of food, one should do so during the prāṇa [breath]. 39.

In cases of repeated vomiting of poison, hiccups, thirst, dyspnea, and coughing, medicine should be administered with food; and in cases of anorexia, it should be given with various kinds of appetizing foods.
For those eating light food, the *sāmudga* [posture] is recommended during sleep for tremors, convulsions, and hiccups, as well as for disorders above the clavicle.
Since the objects of treatment are twofold, treatment itself is considered to be of two kinds:
one is satiation (saṃtarpaṇa), and the second is desatiation (apatarpaṇa). //1//
"Bṛṃhaṇa" (nourishing) and "laṅghana" (lightening) are cited as its synonyms;
that which leads to bulkiness is nourishing, and that which leads to lightness is lightening.
For your body, which is for the most part composed of earth and water, there are the treatments of oleation and drying, as well as sweating and astringency. (3)
Furthermore, because living beings are of two types, that [treatment] does not exceed two categories:
purification (śodhana) and pacification (śamana); even within those, fasting (laṅghana) is of two kinds.

That which expels the humors (doṣas) from the body externally is the fivefold purification: non-unctuous enema (nirūha), emesis (vamana), oil-enema (kāya-sneha), head-enema (śiro-reka), and bloodletting (asra-visruti). // 5 //
That which does not purify the humors, nor even excites them when they are balanced, but equalizes them when they are disturbed—that pacification is of seven kinds. (6)
Digestion, stimulation of the digestive fire, hunger, thirst, physical exercise, sunlight, and wind [are the means for these];
however, nourishment and pacification are for the wind (vāyu) and for bile-wind (pittānila).

One should nourish those emaciated by disease, medicine, wine, women, or grief; as well as those exhausted by heavy loads or travel, those with chest wounds, those who are wasted, dry, weak, or afflicted by vāta. (8)

In the summer, one should also treat pregnant women, those who have recently given birth, children, and the elderly with meat, milk, sugar, ghee, and other sweet and unctuous substances, as well as with enemas. // 9 //

Those suffering from urinary disorders, excess of the humors (doṣas), excessive unctuousness, fever, stiffness of the thighs, or skin diseases (kuṣṭha) should avoid the pleasures of sleep, beds, massage, bathing, and exhilaration. // 10 //

Those suffering from erysipelas, abscesses, splenic disorders, diseases of the head, throat, or eyes, as well as those who are obese, should always undergo fasting; furthermore, others may do so during the cold season. (11)

In that regard, those who have an excess of obesity, strength, pitta, and kapha should be treated with purificatory therapies [saṃśodhana] for the sake of disorders caused by undigested matter (āma), fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and heart disease. (12)

Those afflicted by constipation, heaviness, eructation, nausea, and similar symptoms, generally characterized by moderate or excessive corpulence, should first be treated with digestive (pācana) and appetizing (dīpana) remedies. (13)

Those afflicted by these very same diseases who are deficient in bulk and strength, and those afflicted by the disorders of hunger and thirst who possess moderate strength and are robust—[these are the ones for whom this treatment is intended]. (14)
Those of middling strength who are afflicted by the defects of suppressing hunger and thirst,
and those of weak strength— how much more so men who are afflicted by wind, heat, and exertion?
One should not administer nourishing therapy to those who require lightening therapy; however, one should apply mild lightening therapy to those who require nourishing therapy.
Or one should treat them by means of reasoning, through the power of place, time, and so forth;
when [the body] is nourished, there will be strength and nourishment, and the destruction of those diseases that can be cured thereby. (16)

The faculties become stainless; there is the casting off of impurities, lightness, and a relish for food; hunger and thirst arise with ease; and there is clarity of heart, as well as purity of the voice and throat. (17)

When fasting is practiced without regard for the proper dosage and other factors, it produces mildness of disease, enthusiasm, and the destruction of drowsiness; however, those same qualities arise when one has undergone the fast. (18)

Excessive obesity, excessive emaciation, and so forth will be described, along with their medicinal treatments; by those very [conditions], one should recognize the state of being excessively nourished or excessively depleted. (19)

14.19c–v Their very form should be recognized as [causing] extreme obesity, apacī, prameha, fever, abdominal enlargement, fistula-in-ano, cough, loss of consciousness, dysuria, asthma, leprosy, and other such most dreadful diseases.
In that case, everything that destroys fat, wind (vāta), and phlegm (kapha) is desired;
namely, horse gram (kulattha), old grain, śyāmāka, barley, mung beans, and honey-water. (21)
One should strike the *ariṣṭa* with the staff of curd-whey, purify oneself from anxiety, and remain awake; one should lick *triphalā*, *guḍūcī*, *abhayā*, and *ghana* with honey. (22)
The application of *rasāñjana*, *mahat-pañcamūla*, and *guggulu*, as well as the use of *śilājatu* with the juice of *agnimantha*, is beneficial. (23)
14.23c–d The application of *śilāhvā* (realgar), along with *viḍaṅga*, ginger, alkali, iron powder, honey,
and the powder of barley and *āmalaka*, is a formulation that overcomes the defect of excessive corpulence. 14.24.
Vyoṣa, kaṭvī, varā, śigru, viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, sthirā, hiṅgu, sauvarcala, ajājī, yavānī, dhānya, and citraka. (25)
Take *niśā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *hapuṣā*, *pāṭhā*, and the root of *kembuka*;
their powder, along with honey, ghee, and oil in equal proportions, [should be used]. (26)
14.26d–27. This oil, mixed with an equal portion of flour and combined with sixteen times its amount of roasted grain flour (saktu), when drunk,
destroys all diseases such as excessive obesity and other ailments of that kind.
It cures heart disease, jaundice, vitiligo, dyspnea, cough, and throat obstructions;
it promotes intelligence, intellect, and memory, and stimulates the digestive fire. (28)
Excessive emaciation, vertigo, cough, excessive thirst, loss of appetite, and the depletion of unctuousness, digestive fire, sleep, vision, hearing, semen, vitality, hunger, and voice [occur]. (29)

Excessive emaciation, vertigo, dyspnea, excessive thirst, anorexia, pain in the bladder, heart, head, calves, thighs, sacrum, and flanks, fever, delirium, upward movement of wind (ūrdhvānila), exhaustion, vomiting, and a splitting sensation in the joints and bones [occur]. (14.29–30)
14.30dv–31ab. From excessive fasting (ativilaṅghana), vomiting, pain in the joints and bones, and retention of feces and urine arise;
emaciation is indeed better than obesity, for there is no medicine for the obese.

14.31ab Retention of feces, urine, and so forth, as well as planetary afflictions (grahas), [occur]. 14.31cd Indeed, neither nourishing therapy (*bṛṃhaṇa*) nor reducing therapy (*laṅghana*) is the remedy for obesity; for excessive fat, digestive fire, and wind are not conquered by these.

Since [obesity] is destroyed through happiness by means of sweet, unctuous, and satiating [regimens], [reducing therapy is not appropriate]. 14.32ab [Omitted in source] 14.32cd [Omitted in source]
