Neither nourishing therapy nor fasting is sufficient [to counteract this], for leanness perishes through the excessive indulgence in sweet, unctuous, and satiating foods— [the very things] diametrically opposed to corpulence— and it is destroyed by [the pursuit of] pleasure.
In that case, one should employ every kind of nourishing drink, food, and medicine.
Through lack of anxiety, through exhilaration, through constant satisfaction,
and through indulgence in sleep, one who was emaciated flourishes like a boar.
14.34ab Through lack of reflection, through excessive joy, and through indulgence in dreams, a man [is led astray].
14.34cd Indeed, there is nothing else that causes the body to grow as much as meat;
for meat-eating consists of meat, especially because it is nourished by meat.
Because it is nourishing, it is superior; due to its nourishing nature, it produces bulk, is heavy, and causes satiation.
For a person who is obese, the opposite is beneficial; for one who is emaciated, [heavy food] is beneficial.
For both types, preparations of barley and wheat are appropriate when administered according to their respective requirements.
14.36dv Thereafter, the formulation of what is suitable and beneficial; 14.36dv and then, the formulation of what has been administered.
These therapeutic measures (upakrama) exceed [in number] the [simple] movement of the humors (doṣagati), due to the distinctions such as those between the "grasping" and "dividing" types.
Although they are distinct from one another, they are not like diseases (gada), which, despite being different, are only two in number.
14.37cv Regarding the therapeutic measures, there are not two [types] because of the following:
Madana, Madhuka, Lambā, Nimba, Bimbī, Viśālā, Trapusa, Kuṭaja, Mūrvā, Devadālī, and Kṛmighna; [these are listed] in the Sūtrasthāna.
Vidula, dahanā, and citrā; the two types of kośavatī; karañja; and kaṇa, lavaṇa, vacā, elā, and sarṣapa—these are emetics. // 1 //
Nikumbha, kumbha, triphalā, gavākṣī, snuh, śaṅkhinī, nīlinī, tilvaka, śamyāka, kampillaka, hemadugdha, milk, and urine are purgatives. // 2 //

Madana, kuṭaja, kuṣṭha, devadālī, madhuka, vacā, the ten roots (daśamūla), dāru, rāsnā, barley, miśi, kṛtavedhana, horse gram (kulattha), honey, salt, and trivṛt are the ingredients for non-unctuous enemas (nirūhaṇa). // 3 //
15.3cv Barley, kṛtavedhana, horse gram, vella, apāmārga, the three pungents (vyoṣa), dārvī, surālā, śirīṣa seed,
bṛhatī, śigru, madhūka heartwood, rock salt, tārkṣyaśaila, the two types of trutī, and pṛthvīkā— these cleanse the head. // 4 //
Bhadradāru, nata, kuṣṭha, daśamūla, and the two types of balā destroy vāta; likewise, the vīratarādi group and the vidāryādi group [subdue it]. // 5 //
15.5b–d: Daśamūla, the three types of balā, and the vidāryādi group [of drugs] should purify [the channels]. 6:
Dūrvā, anantā, nimba, vāsā, ātmaguptā, gundrā, abhīru, śītapākī, and priyaṅgu;
the nyagrodhādi group, the padmakādi group, the two types of sthirā, padma, vanya, and the śārivādi group [purify] pitta.
The groups beginning with Āragvadha,
Arka, Muṣkaka, Asana, Surasa, Musta, and Vatsaka overcome phlegm (balāsa).
Jīvantī and kākolyau, the two types of medā, mudgaparṇī and māṣaparṇī, along with ṛṣabhaka, jīvaka, and madhuka—this group is known as the life-promoting (jīvanīya). // 8 //
Vidārī, pañcāṅgulā, vṛścikālī, vṛścīva, devāhvaya, śūrpaparṇī, kaṇḍūkarī, and the two known as jīvanī and hrasvajīvanī—these are five groups of five; then gopasutā and tripādī. (9)

Vṛścīva, the two types of Devadālī, Śūrpaparṇī, Kaṇḍūkarī, Gopasutā, and Tripādī—this group beginning with Vidārī is pleasing to the heart, nourishing, and it subdues Vāta and Pitta; it cures consumption, abdominal tumors (gulma), body aches, upward breathlessness (ūrdhvaśvāsa), and cough. (15.9b–15.10d)

Śāriva, uśīra, kāśmarya, madhūka, the two types of śiśira, yaṣṭīmadhu, and parūṣaka destroy wasting, abdominal tumors, weakness of the limbs, burning sensations, hemorrhagic disorders, thirst, and fever. (15.10cd–11ab)
Padmaka, puṇḍraka, vṛddhi, tugākṣīrī, śṛṅgī, and amṛtā—these ten are known as the "vitalizers" (jīvana).
They increase breast milk, destroy wind and bile, and are nourishing, vitalizing, bulk-promoting, and aphrodisiac. // 12 //
Parūṣaka, excellent grapes, kaṭphala, the fruit of the kataka tree, rājāhva, pomegranate, and śāka are conquerors of thirst, urinary disorders, diseases, and vāta. (13)
Añjana, phalinī, māṃsī, padma, utpala, rasāñjana, śaila, madhuka, and nāgāhva remove poison, internal burning, and pitta disorders. (14)
Patola, kaṭurohiṇī, candana, madhusrava, guḍūcī, and pāṭhā—this [decoction] conquers poison, internal burning, and pitta;
it removes phlegm, pitta, skin diseases, fever, poison, vomiting, anorexia, and jaundice. (15)
Guduchi, Padmaka-arista, Dhanaka, and red sandalwood destroy fever, vomiting, burning sensations, and thirst caused by pitta and kapha, and they stimulate the digestive fire. (16)
15.16b–d: *dhānyaka*, red sandalwood (*rakta-candana*), *dhanikā*, red sandalwood; *āragvadha*, *indrayava*, *pāṭali*, *kākatiktā*, *nimba*, *amṛtā*, *madhurasa*, *sruva-vṛkṣa*, and *pāṭhā*.
Bhūnimba, sairyaka, paṭola, the two types of karañja, saptacchada, agni, suṣavī, phala, bāṇa, and ghoṇṭā. // 17 //
The group beginning with Āragvadha overcomes vomiting, skin diseases, poisons, and fevers;
it subdues phlegm, itching, and urinary disorders, and serves as a purifier of malignant ulcers. (18)
15.18–19: *Medā*, *udara-viśodhana*,

*asana*, *tiniśa*, *bhūrja*, *śvetavāha*, *prakīryā*, *khadira*, *kadara*, *bhaṇḍī*, *śiṃśipā*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *trihima*, *talapalāśa*, *joṅgaka*, *śāka*, *śāla*, *kramuka*, *dhava*, *kaliṅga*, *chāgakarṇa*, and *aśvakarṇa*.
The *asanādi* [group of drugs] overcomes vitiligo, leprosy, phlegm, and worms;
it cures anemia and urinary disorders, and eliminates defects of adipose tissue. (20)

15.20b–c. Varuṇa, the two types of Sairiyaka, Śatāvarī, Dahana, Moraṭa, Bilva, Viṣāṇikā, the two types of Bṛhatī, the two types of Karañja, the two types of Jayā, Bahala, Pallava, Darbha, and Ruja-karā [are used] for leucoderma, skin diseases, vomiting, and worms. 15.21. [These] are the causes of disease.
The Varuṇādi group— consisting of varaṇa, the two types of sairya, śatāvarī, and others— subdues phlegm, fat, and weak digestion;
it also treats āḍhyavāta, headache, abdominal tumors (gulma), and internal abscesses (vidradhi).

15.22ab *Varaṇa* and others [remove] phlegm and fat; 15.22cd downward wind, headache, *uṣaka*, *tutthaka*, asafoetida, the two types of *kāsīsa*, rock salt, realgar, and lac remove dysuria, urinary stones, abdominal tumors, fat, and phlegm.

15.23–24: Vellantara, araṇika, būka, vṛṣa, aśmabheda, gokaṇṭaka, etkaṭa, sahācara, bāṇa, kāśa, vṛkṣādanī, nala, the two types of kuśa, guṇṭha, gundrā, bhallūka, moraṭa, kuraṇṭa, karambha, and pārtha [are used] to alleviate gulma, urinary disorders (meha), and kapha.
15.24b – *gokaṇṭaka*, *utkaṭa*, *sahācara*, *bāṇa*, and *kāśa*;
15.24c – *vṛkṣādanī*, *nala*, the two kinds of *kuśa*, *guñcha*, and *gundrā*.
15.24c – *vṛkṣādanī*, *nala*, the two kinds of *kuśa*, *guñcha*, and *gundrā*.
This group of drugs beginning with Vīrataru—consisting of Vṛkṣādanī, Nala, the two types of Kuśa, Guccha, and Gundrā—destroys diseases caused by Vāta;
it removes urinary calculi, gravel, dysuria, and the pain of trauma. // 25 //
15.25dv–26. Lodhra, śābaraka-lodhra, palāśa, jiṅginī, sarala, kaṭphala, kutsitāmba, kadalī, gataśoka, sailavālu, paripelava, and mocā remove difficult labor, injury, and pain.

Lodhra, śābara, kadamba, palāśa, jhiñjhiṇī, sarala, and kaṭphala—this group of drugs, known as the lodhrādika, destroys fat and phlegm; it cures disorders of the female reproductive tract, is astringent, improves the complexion, and destroys poison. (15.26–27)
Arka, alarka, nāgadantī, viśalyā, bhārgī, rāsnā, vṛścikālī, prakīryā, pratyakpuṣpī, pītatailodakīryā, the two types of śvetā, and the tree of the ascetics (tāpasavṛkṣa). // 28 //
This group of drugs beginning with arka removes phlegm, fat, and poison;
it pacifies worms and skin diseases, and especially purifies wounds. // 29 //
15.29 This group, known as *arkādika*, consists of *surasā*, the two types of *yavānī*, *phaṇijjaka*, *kālamālā*, *viḍaṅga*, *kharabūṣa*, *vṛṣakarṇī*, *kaṭphala*, *kāsamarda*, *kṣavaka*,
*sarasa*, *bhārgī*, *kārmuka*, *kākamācī*, *kulahala*, *viṣamuṣṭi*, *bhūstṛṇa*, and *bhūtakeśī*.
15.30bv *kharabuka-vṛṣakarṇī-kaṭphalāḥ kāsamardaḥ* 15.30bv *kharabusavṛṣakarṇī-kaṭphalāḥ kāsamardaḥ* 15.30bc *kharamukha-vṛṣakarṇī-kaṭphalaṃ kāsamardaḥ* 15.30cv
Kṣavaka,
surasī, bhārgī, kārmuka, and kākamācī.
The group beginning with surasā destroys phlegm, fat, and worms;
it cures catarrh, loss of appetite, dyspnea, and cough, and it purifies wounds. (31)
Muṣkaka, snuhī, varā, dvīpī, palāśa, dhava, and śiṃśipā conquer gulma, urinary disorders, calculi, anemia, obesity, hemorrhoids, kapha, and seminal defects.
Palāśa, dhava, śiṃśipā, vatsaka, mūrvā, bhārgī, kaṭukā, marīca, ghuṇapriyā, gaṇḍīra, elā, pāṭhā, ajājī, kaṭvaṅga, phala, ajamoda, siddhārtha, and vacā. (15.32b–33)
Cumin, asafoetida, viḍaṅga, paśugandhā, and the five spices (pañcakolaka) destroy unstable phlegm, obesity, chronic catarrh, abdominal tumors, fever, colic, and hemorrhoids. (34)
Paśugandhā, pañcakolaka, vacā, jalada, devāhva, nāgara, ativiṣā, abhayā, the two types of haridrā, yaṣṭyāhva, kalaśī, and kuṭaja destroy [the worms]. 15.35cd–36ab.
The groups beginning with vacā and haridrā destroy acute diarrhea;
they eliminate disorders of fat, phlegm, wind, and defects of breast milk. (36)

Priyaṅgu, the two types of puṣpāñjana, and the pair of lotuses (padma) are digestants for undigested matter (āma) in diarrhea; so too are the pollen of the lotus, yojanavallī, anantā, mānadruma, moca-rasa, samaṅgā, punnāga, śīta, and madanīya. // 15.36b–37 //
Sāradruma, mocarasa, and samaṅgā; those with masculine names, śīta, and madanīya-hetu; ambaṣṭhā, madhuka, namaskarī, nandīvṛkṣa, palāśa, and kacchurā.
Lodhra, dhātakī, bilva-paste, kaṭvaṅga, and lotus pollen. // 38 //
The groups beginning with priyaṅgu and ambaṣṭhā destroy chronic diarrhea (pakvātīsāra);
they are healing for the joining of tissues, beneficial in cases of pitta, and also promote the healing of wounds. (39)

Mustā, vacā, agni, the two niśās, the two tiktās, bhallātaka, pāṭhā, triphalā, viṣā, kuṣṭha, truṭī, and haimavatī destroy diseases of the female reproductive tract and the breasts, and they are purifiers of the bodily wastes. (40)

Nyagrodha, pippala, sadāphala, the pair of lodhras, the two types of jambū, arjuna, kapītana, somavalka, plakṣa, āmra, vañjula, piyāla, palāśa, nandī, kolī, kadamba, viralā, madhuka, and madhūka. (41)
Nyagrodha, pippala, sadāphala, the two types of lodhra,
the two types of jambū, arjuna, kapītana, and somavalka constitute the nyagrodhādi group; it is healing for wounds, astringent, and a remedy for fractures.
It destroys fat, bile, blood, thirst, burning sensations, and diseases of the female reproductive organs. // 42 //
The Nyagrodhādi group [of drugs] should be praised as it destroys disorders of the female reproductive tract (yoni-doṣa). [It consists of:
the two types of Elā, Turuṣka, Kuṣṭha, Phalinī, Māṃsī, Jala, and Dhyāmaka. // 43a //
Spṛkkā, coraka, coca-leaf, tagara, sthauṇeya, and jātī-essence. // 43b //
15.43bv–śpṛkkā, coraka, coca-leaf, tagara, sthauṇeya, jātī-rasa, śukti, vyāghranakha, amarāhvam, aguru, śrīvāsaka, and kuṅkuma.
15.43c–d: *śukti*, *vyāghranakha*, *amarāhvam*, *aguru*, *śrīvāsaka*, *kuṅkuma*, *caṇḍā*, *guggulu*, *devadhūpa*, *khapura*, *punnāga*, and *nāgāhvaya*.
The elādi group subdues vāta, kapha, and poison; it clarifies the complexion and destroys itching, pustules, and urticaria. // 44 //
15.44c–45a: The group of drugs beginning with kaṇḍū, śyāmā, dantī, dravantī, kramuka, kuṭaraṇā, śaṅkhinī, and carmasāhvā is described as clarifying (prasādana).
15.45ab *Śyāmā*, *dantī*, *dravantī*, *kramuka*, *kuṭaraṇī*, *śaṅkhinī*, *carmasāhvā*,
*svarṇakṣīrī*, *gavākṣī*, *śikhari*, *rajanaka*, *chinnarohā*, and *karañja*.
The bastāntrī, vyādhighāta, the thick and highly succulent [plants], and the fruits from the tīkṣṇavṛkṣa; // 45c //
Bastāntrī, vyādhighāta, the fruits of the *bahulabahu-rasa* and *tīkṣṇavṛkṣa*,
and the *śyāmā* group destroy abdominal tumors (*gulma*), irregular appetite, kapha disorders, heart pain, and dysuria.
The groups are said to be thirty-three; among them, one should employ that which is appropriate when others are unavailable, and one should discard any substance that is unsuitable.

These groups [of drugs], when combined with pastes (kalka), decoctions (kvātha), fats (sneha), electuaries (leha), and so forth, in consideration of the humors (doṣa) and the affected tissues (dūṣya), destroy even most difficult diseases through internal or external application, such as by drinking, nasal administration (nasya), oil enemas (anvāsana), plasters (lepa), or massage (abhyaṅga). (47)
15.47ab These groups [of drugs], having considered the *doṣas*, the *dūṣyas*, and other factors, 15.47cd destroy even most difficult diseases through washes and ointments;
15.47cd they destroy even most difficult diseases through sudation and massages.

In the Section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna), medicinal substances that are heavy, cold, liquid, unctuous, slow, subtle, soft, and fluid generally produce oleation (snehana); those with opposite qualities generally produce desiccation (virūkṣaṇa). // 1 //
Among unctuous substances, ghee, marrow, muscle fat, and oil are considered the best;
among these, ghee is the most excellent because it conforms to the requirements of medicinal processing.
Because they are sweet, non-burning, and because one practices them from birth onwards, they subdue bile as listed first; they subdue the others [wind and phlegm] in successive order. (3)
Oil is heavier than ghee; muscle fat is heavier than oil; and marrow is even heavier than that.
A *yamaka* (double) compound is formed by two of these, a *trivṛta* (triple) by three, and a *mahat* (great) by four.

Those who are addicted to sudation, purificatory therapies, wine, women, and physical exercise; those who are constantly anxious; the elderly, children, the weak, and the emaciated; and those who are parched or have diminished blood and semen—[these should not undergo oleation]. // 5 //

Those suffering from wind disorders, ophthalmia, cataracts, or severe insomnia should be treated with oleation; however, those with extremely weak digestion, sharp digestion, obesity, or weakness should not be so treated.
Those afflicted by stiffness of the thighs, diarrhea, consumption, diseases of the throat, and poisons;
and those suffering from fainting, vomiting, loss of appetite, phlegm, thirst, and intoxication. // 7 //

Ghee is recommended for those who have undergone difficult labor, and for those who have received nasal medication, enemas, or purgatives; it is especially praised for those desiring wisdom, memory, intelligence, and other such qualities.

16.8cv In those cases of impaired intellect, memory, or intelligence; in those with weak digestive fire; in those suffering from glandular enlargements, diseases of the channels, worms, phlegm, fat, or wind; and in persons who desire lightness or firmness, or who have a hard bowel, oil [is indicated]. // 9 //
In those whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are depleted by wind, heat, travel, carrying loads, women, or physical exercise;
and in those who are emaciated, afflicted by suffering, excessively hot-natured, or traveling on a path obstructed by wind. (10)
The remaining two [medicines] and muscle-fat (vasā) are used for pain in the joints, bones, vital points (marma), and the abdominal cavity,
as well as for injuries from fire or trauma, and for disorders of the female reproductive tract, ears, and head.
Oil is recommended during the rainy season, ghee at the end of the rains, and the other two types of fat during the month of Mādhava;
in a temperate season, any unctuous substance is praised when administered on a clear day under a bright sun.
Oil should be used in cases of urgency, as well as during cold weather; ghee should be used during hot weather and at night.
Ghee alone is indicated at night for disorders of pitta and vāta, as well as for their combined involvement (saṃsarga) when pitta predominates.
If administered otherwise, diseases arising from wind and phlegm may occur at night, while those from bile may occur during the day;
one should therefore apply oleation skillfully through food such as edibles and by means of enemas.
Through nasal drops, ointments, gargles, and the satiation of the head, ears, and eyes, along with the variations of taste and their unification, there are sixty-four formulations. (15)

Because the unctuous substance is subsequently overcome by other factors and because it becomes diminished, these stages are prescribed in sequence; furthermore, due to the absence of the aforementioned causes, there is no need for the clarification of the liquid nor for the process of straining. (16)
Because the oil is not overwhelmed by food, it should not be drunk clear; this method of preparing oil is considered the best because it accomplishes the action of oleation quickly.
[The three types of oils] are digested in two, four, and eight *yāmas* respectively. (16.16–17)

The measures are short, medium, and superior; one should determine a measure even shorter than those, having first considered the humors and other factors, but indeed from the very beginning, one should employ the shortest measure.
When yesterday's food has already been digested, a copious amount of clear unctuous liquid is recommended for purification;
however, for one who is hungry, a moderate dose of a pacifying agent taken on an empty stomach is praised. (19)
That [emetic] is nourishing when taken with meat broth, wine, and the like; it is beneficial in small doses when accompanied by food.
It is also suitable for children, the elderly, those afflicted by thirst, and those who are fond of fats, purgatives, and wine. (20)

16.20b That [ghee] which contains a small amount of food is beneficial for those who are constantly addicted to women, those with sluggish digestion, those seeking comfort, those afraid of hardship, those with soft bowels, those with few bodily humors, and those who are emaciated, especially during the hot season.

Devoted to the east, the middle, and the north [respectively], one should conquer the diseases arising from the lower, middle, and upper parts of the body, and likewise bestow strength upon the limbs in due order. (22)

One should drink warm water after the oil while it is still clear for easy digestion, and for the sake of cleansing the coating of the mouth; however, this is not the case with *tuvaraka* or *āruṣkara* oils. (23)
Fainting, burning heat, aversion, thirst, yawning, delusion, vertigo, and exhaustion occur while the unctuous substance is being digested; once it has been digested, these symptoms subside. (23.1)
If there is doubt as to whether [the food] has been digested or not, one should drink warm water again;
by that, the cleansing of eructation occurs, and thereafter lightness and a relish for food arise. (24)

One who intends to eat food tomorrow should consume it today in the proper measure; likewise for one who intends to drink tomorrow or has already drunk; the liquid should be warm, non-obstructive to the channels, not excessively unctuous, and free from impurities.
One should use warm water for ritual purposes, remain celibate, and sleep at night;
one should not suppress natural urges, nor should one engage in physical exertion, anger, grief, cold, or heat. (26)

Traveling by vehicle in a strong wind, traveling on a road by vehicle, speaking excessively, remaining in a seated posture for too long, using very low or very high pillows, sleeping during the day, and exposure to smoke and dust. (27)

One should avoid those days on which one has drunk [liquor], as well as an equal number of other days— whether they involve the recitation of scriptures, excessive eating, or remaining in a fixed posture.
This is generally the procedure for all ritual acts, as well as for those whose diseases have been exhausted. // 28 //

The post-procedural regimen for the pacification [of the doshas] should be observed as in the case of oleation after purgation; one should drink clear gruel for three days if the digestive tract is soft, or for seven days if it is hard. (29)
Then, it should be properly unctuous until it becomes thoroughly habituated;
thereafter, there will be downward movement of wind, a stimulated digestive fire, and stool that is unctuous and non-obstructed.
In one properly lubricated, there is an urge to urinate, agitation, and exhaustion; in one that is dry, the opposite occurs.
In one excessively lubricated, however, there is pallor and discharge from the nose, mouth, and anus. (31)
16.31a Softness and oiliness of the limbs, lassitude;

16.31b Aversion to unctuous substances and lightness of the body; 16.31c However, when there is excessive unctuousness, paleness, 16.31d Clarity of the sense organs, and proper discharge from the nose, mouth, and anus—these are the signs of proper oleation.

In a person with a dry constitution, the opposite occurs: when unctuous therapy is administered in improper quantity, at the wrong time, or through incorrect diet and lifestyle, it causes swelling, hemorrhoids, drowsiness, stiffness, and loss of consciousness. (32)
[It cures] itching, skin diseases, fever, nausea, colic, abdominal distension, vertigo, and so forth;
[it provides] remedies for hunger, thirst, emesis, sweating, dryness, drinks, food, and medicine. (33)
[One should treat] colic, constipation, and loss of strength; [the remedies are] hunger, thirst, emesis, sudation,
dry drinks, food, and medicine, as well as buttermilk, *ariṣṭa*, *khala*, *uddāla*, barley, *śyāmāka*, and *kodrava* grains.
Pippalī, triphalā, honey, pathyā, cow’s urine, and guggulu. // 34 //
Buttermilk-ferment (takrāriṣṭa), as well as khalu, uddāla, barley, śyāmāka, and kodrava,
are the remedies for complications of oleation, each according to its specific disease.
Regarding the treatment for desiccation, the signs of excessive and deficient administration are the same as those for fasting (laṅghana).
One who has consumed unctuous, liquid, warm, and fatty meat juices from the desert region should undergo sudation;
having remained thus unctuous for three days, he should then administer purgation and emesis. (36)
16.36bv–37. Consuming [only] liquids while practicing sudation for one day and another day, they aggravate the phlegm by means of its provocative factors;
being fleshy, corpulent, possessing abundant phlegm, and having irregular digestive fires, [they become afflicted].

Those who are accustomed to oleation and require it should first be treated with drying therapies; thereafter, having oleated them, one should purify them. In this way, complications from oleation do not arise. (38)
Affection is sufficient to remove impurities, yet it has become unwholesome in the case of children, the elderly, and others who are unable to endure the abandonment of affection. (39)
One should employ these non-stimulating (anudvega) unctuous formulations that provide immediate oleation;
in them, there should be abundant meat broth, or a gruel (peyā) fried with unctuous substances.
16.40–41. Or, a gruel fried with fats, along with sesame powder mixed with fat and molasses, or likewise *kṛśarā*;
or a milk-gruel rich in ghee and warm, or the liquid from curd mixed with jaggery.

16.41–42. Sesame powder with fat, molasses, *kṛśarā* (rice and pulse porridge), and *peyā* (thin gruel)—these five, each consisting of five *prasṛta*s of grains with fats, are the seven unctuous (*snehana*) preparations. They are immediate unctuous agents (*sadyah-sneha*) when enriched with salt.

And unctuous substances (sneha) that are rich in salt— namely molasses, meat from marshy regions, milk, sesame, black gram, wine, and curd— are indeed obstructive to the channels (abhiṣyandi), non-dry (arūkṣa), subtle (sūkṣma), hot (uṣṇa), and pervasive (vyavāyi). 16.42–43ab.
For that [oil], being liquefying and non-dry,

should not be prescribed for the purpose of oleation in cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), edema (śopha), and urinary disorders (prameha). [One should instead use oils] cooked with triphalā, pippalī, pathyā, guggulu, and so forth.

One should administer these unadulterated fats according to their respective requirements; however, for those whose [digestive] fire and body have been diminished by diseases, one should employ those capable of rekindling the fire and the body. 45.

A man who consumes fats is declared to be one whose internal fire is kindled despite being afflicted by diseases, whose digestive tract is purified, whose bodily tissues are renewed, who possesses strength and a healthy complexion, has firm sense organs, undergoes slow aging, and lives for a hundred years.
In the Sūtrasthāna, sudation (sveda) is of four types, distinguished as dry heat (tāpa), poultice (upanāha), fomentation (uṣman), and liquid (drava).
Dry heat is produced by means of fire-heated clothing, a plowshare, the palms of the hands, and so forth. (1)
Upanāha [plaster] is prepared with vacā, kiṇva, śatāhvā, and devadāru;
or with all the grains, the fragrant substances (gandhas), rāsnā, eraṇḍa, jaṭā, and meat. // 2 //

In the case of isolated vāta, one should use [medicines] with an abundance of salt, saturated with fats, sour gruel, buttermilk, and milk; when associated with kapha, they should be prepared with the surasā group of herbs and so forth. // 3 //
In the case of pitta, however, one should repeatedly apply poultices known as *śālvaṇa*, made with *padmaka* and other such ingredients,
which are mild yet unctuous and hot in potency, using non-putrid leather strips.
In cases of pitta-fever, one should apply [the cooling measures] repeatedly with lotus-root and other such substances, or with those known as *śālvala*.
If these are unavailable, one should use garments made of leaves, silk, or wool to overcome the wind (*vāta*).
One should bind the patient at night and release them during the day; if bound during the day, one should release them at night.
Heat [is produced] by means of heated earth, clods of soil, potsherds, stones, dust, leaf-fragments, grain, dried cow-dung, sand, and husks. // 6 //
One who has been tormented by many means should employ [the remedy] according to place and time, using *śigru*, *vāraṇaka*, *airaṇḍa*, *karañja*, *surasā*, and *arjaka*. (7)
With leaf-patterns made from śirīṣa, vāsā, bamboo, arka, mālatī, and dīrghavṛnta, as well as with vacā and other herbs, and with the flesh of animals from marshy and aquatic habitats.

And with the ten roots—either individually or combined according to the specific impurity—one should prepare [medicinal oils] using fats processed with wine, fermented gruel, water, milk, and so forth. // 9 //
Having filled leaking vessels or channels that are afflicted with pain, one should sprinkle the lubricated body, covered with a cloth, as comfortably as possible. 10.

17.10c–d When wind pervades all the limbs, the patient should remain immersed up to the neck in a vat filled with those same liquids while the body is covered with a cloth; this is also indicated for hemorrhoids, dysuria, and other such pains.

In a windless place, with internal and external unctuousness, having digested his food, one should practice sudation; its intensity—middling, superior, or inferior—should be determined by the nature of the disease, the patient, the location, and the season. (12)

17.12 One afflicted by *kapha* should undergo drying therapy (*rūkṣaṇa*) while staying in a windless place, having been lubricated internally and externally; one who is already dry should be lubricated when *kapha* and *vāyu* are present.
When *vāyu* has entered the stomach (*āmāśaya*), it should be treated with drying; when *kapha* has taken refuge in the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*), it should be treated with lubrication.

In the case of kapha, that [enema] should be administered with drying (rukṣaṇa) agents; it may be preceded by drying measures or preceded by oleation (sneha), according to the specific location [of the disease].
It should be given in small quantity for the groins, very little for the eyes, the scrotum, and the heart, or not at all.

17.14c–d When the sweating in the groins is slight, when the cold and pain have subsided, and when softness has arisen in the limbs after fomentation, one should be gently massaged, bathe, and then follow the regimen for oleation. 17.15a–b.
Aggravation of bile and blood, thirst, fainting, weakness of voice and limbs, vertigo, pain in the joints, fever, and the appearance of dark-red circular patches [on the body]. // 16 //
From excessive application of sudation, vomiting occurs; in that case, a stabilizing (stambhana) medicine is required.
This is also necessary for those suffering from poisoning, alkaline burns, thermal burns, diarrhea, vomiting, or fainting. (17)
Sudation therapy (svedana) is generally heavy, sharp, and hot; conversely, other [therapies] are usually restraining (stambhana).
Medicaments are also characterized as liquid, stable, mobile, unctuous, dry, and subtle. (18)
In brief, [therapies] that are sudorific, astringent, smooth, dry, subtle, mobile, and liquid are generally bitter, astringent, and sweet. (19)

When strength has been regained through the destruction of the aforementioned diseases, there may be a state of rigidity (stambhita) characterized by stiffness of the skin and tendons, contraction, tremors, and obstruction of the heart, speech, and bowels. // 20 //
One should diagnose excessive stiffness by the dark discoloration of the feet, lips, skin, and hands.
One should not apply sudation to those who are excessively obese, dry, weak, or fainting.

Those requiring immobilization, those suffering from wounds, those who are emaciated and wasted, those afflicted by alcoholism, and those with cataracts, abdominal diseases, erysipelas, leprosy, consumption, and other such ailments; // 22 //
17.22–23: Those suffering from diseases characterized by leprosy (kuṣṭha) or swelling (śopha), those who have consumed milk, curd, fats, or honey, those who have undergone purgation (virecana),
and those afflicted by prolapse or burns of the rectum, exhaustion, anger, grief, or fear— [these should not be given enemas].
Those afflicted by anger, grief, or fear; those suffering from blood-loss due to anger;

those with hunger, thirst, jaundice, anemia, or urinary disorders; those oppressed by pitta; a pregnant woman, one experiencing menorrhagia, or one who has recently given birth; and [these] in cases of mild or urgent illness.

17.24d–25. However, mild [treatment] is indicated for urgent diseases, as well as for dyspnea, cough, catarrh, hiccups, flatulence, constipation, hoarseness of voice, disorders of wind (vāta), phlegm (śleṣman), stiffness due to undigested matter (āmastambha), and heaviness.

In cases of aching in the limbs, hips, sides, back, abdomen, and jaw; in enlargement of the scrotum, in the *khalyā* (the space between the shoulder blades), in stretching pains, and in *vātakaṇṭaka* (sciatica). // 26 //

In cases of dysuria, tumors, glandular swellings, seminal obstruction, and disorders characterized by an abundance of Vāta, one should apply sudation (sveda) according to the specific requirements and the classification of the relevant medicinal substances. (27)

Sudation is beneficial even when not of a fiery (pitta) nature, in cases where Vata is occluded by Medas and Kapha; it should be administered in a windless room, accompanied by physical exertion, heavy clothing, and the induction of fear. (28)
Resentment, strife, anger, excessive drinking, hunger, and heat. // 28 //
Heavy footwear, wrestling, anger, excessive drinking, hunger,
and exposure to the sun— these ten cause perspiration in a person, even without the quality of fire.

The doshas—whether moistened by unctuous substances, located in the visceral cavity (koṣṭha), situated in the tissues (dhātus), adhered in the channels (srotas), or residing in the peripheral branches and bones—are liquefied by sudation and, having been brought to the visceral cavity, are properly expelled through purificatory procedures. // 29 //
In the Section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna), one should administer emesis in cases of Kapha, or when there is a combination of humors in which Kapha is predominant;
likewise, one should administer purgation in cases of Pitta, though one should especially induce emesis in those instances. // 1 //
Those suffering from acute fever, diarrhea, downward-moving bile, hemorrhaging, and pulmonary consumption;
those with skin diseases, urinary disorders, scrofula, glandular swellings, elephantiasis, insanity, and cough; (2)

Those suffering from dyspnea, nausea, erysipelas, defects of breast milk, or diseases of the upper body; a pregnant woman, one who is parched, hungry, or constantly afflicted by pain—these should not be subjected to emesis. (3)

Those suffering from diseases of breast milk or upward-moving diseases (ūrdhvaroga), those who cannot be made to vomit, pregnant women, the dry, the hungry, and those who are constantly afflicted; as well as children, the elderly, the emaciated, the obese, those with heart disease, those with chest wounds, and the weak— [these should not be given emetics].
[It is contraindicated] for those suffering from persistent vomiting, splenic enlargement, visual impairment, worms, or intestinal disorders. // 4 //

Those whose voices are impaired by the administration of enemas using upward-moving vāyu-infused blood, as well as those suffering from urinary obstruction, abdominal enlargement, abdominal tumors, difficult vomiting, excessive digestive fire, or hemorrhoids; 5.

18.5 Those suffering from upward-moving wind and blood (ūrdhvapravṛttavātāsra), upward movement of wind (udāvarta), vertigo (bhrama), prostate enlargement (aṣṭhīlā), pain in the flanks (pārśvaruk), or diseases of wind (vātaroga) [may undergo purgation],
except in cases of poisoning (viṣa), artificial poison (gara), indigestion (ajīrṇa), or the consumption of incompatible foods (viruddhābhyavahāra). // 6 //

18.6 Those suffering from upward-moving wind (udāvarta), fatigue, aśṛthilā, persistent vomiting, and those with indigestion-fever (āmajvara) should generally avoid all therapeutic procedures ending with smoking; furthermore, those with undigested food (ajīrṇin) must avoid them entirely.

Abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids (arśas), eruptive rashes (visphoṭa), facial freckles (vyaṅga), jaundice (kāmalā), chronic fever (jīrṇajvara), abdominal diseases (udara), poisoning (gara), vomiting (chardi), splenic enlargement (plīha), and halīmaka are to be treated with purgation (vireka). // 8 //
Chronic fever, abdominal enlargement, vomiting, splenic disorders, flatulence, halīmaka,
splenomegaly, anemia, halīmaka, abscesses, blindness, cataracts, ophthalmia, and pain in the large intestine.
Diseases residing in the female reproductive tract and semen, those located in the visceral cavity, intestinal worms, and ulcers. // 9 //
18.9cv Diseases of the womb and the semen; 18.9cv diseases of the uterus and the seminal receptacle;

upward-moving wind-blood (vātāsra), blood [disorders], urinary obstruction, constipation, vomiting, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (meha), and so forth; however, one suffering from acute fever should not be purged.

18.10 Blood that moves upward due to wind-blood (vātāsṛg) may be treated with bloodletting; however, those suffering from acute fever, weak digestion, downward-moving pitta and blood, hemorrhoids, diarrhea, those with foreign bodies, those who have not undergone oleation therapy, those with hard bowels, excessive unctuousness, or emaciation should not be purged.
18.11 [Those who have undergone] oleation therapy, those with hard bowels, those who are excessively unctuous, and those who are emaciated [should also avoid it].
18.11c–d Then, during a moderate season, having properly oleated and sweated [the patient] who has been struck by a foreign body (śalya) or afflicted by a cruel [disease],
and whose kapha has been excited so that vomiting will occur the next day by means of fish, black gram, sesame seeds, and so forth; 18.12.

Having slept through the night, with his food well-digested, having performed auspicious rites in the forenoon, and being either without solid food or slightly lubricated with unctuous substances, he should drink ghee along with a medicinal gruel (*peyā*) made from fish, meat, sesame seeds, and the like— or meat, mung beans, sesame seeds, and so forth. (18.12–13)

18.13 One should give wine, milk, sugarcane juice, or meat broth to those who have slept through the night, those whose food is digested, the elderly, children, the weak, the impotent, the timid, and those suffering from disease, until they are full to the throat.

18.14c–15. One should have the patient drink wine up to the throat, prepared according to the specific disorder and mixed with honey and rock salt; having divided the body into its constituent elements, one should administer the medicinal dose consecrated with mantras.
May Brahmā, Dakṣa, the Aśvins, Rudra, Indra, the Earth, the Moon, the Sun, Wind, and Fire;
the sages along with the multitude of medicinal herbs and the hosts of spirits—may they all protect you. 16.
May this medicine be for you like an elixir for the seers, like nectar for the immortals, and like fine wine for the noblest of serpents. 17.
Like an elixir for the sages, like the nectar of the gods—
homage to the Blessed One, the Teacher of Medicine, King of Lapis Lazuli Radiance.
To the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha. // 17+2 //
It is as follows: // 17+3 //
In medicine, in medicine, in great medicine, arisen, svāhā! // 17+4 //
"Bhaiṣajye bhaiṣajye mahā-bhaiṣajye bhaiṣajya-samudgate svāhā! Bhaiṣajye mahā-bhaiṣajye samudgate svāhā!
One should have [the patient] drink this facing the east, and once drunk, one should wait for a moment.
With his mind fixed upon that, and with the flow of saliva arising from the thrill of joy, he should then vomit it up.

One should have the patient drink [the medicine] while facing east; once it has been drunk, one should induce vomiting by means of finger-salivation. Then, without exerting force, one should use either a soft tube or fingers.
Without injuring the throat or palate, he set in motion the vital energies that had not yet been activated. // 19 //
One should not cause those who have not yet engaged [in practice] to engage; nor,
while causing them to engage,
should one remain seated on a seat as high as the knees for those who are already engaged.
And one should hold [the breath] as it flows out from both sides and from the forehead. // 20 //
One should likewise press upon the navel and the back in the reverse direction;
[this is done] with sharp, hot, and pungent substances in cases of kapha, and with sweet and cold substances in cases of pitta. // 21 //
One should induce emesis with unctuous, sour, and salty substances when kapha is associated with vāta;
this should continue until signs of pitta appear or until there is a cessation of the phlegm.

If the force [of the vomiting] is weak, one should induce vomiting again and again with water boiled with *kaṇā*, *dhātrī*, *siddhārtha*, and salt; in that case, there will be no further occurrence of the urges.
Whether the application is accompanied by an adjunct or consists of the medicine alone, its improper administration results in spitting, itching, urticaria, fever, and other such conditions. (24)

In the case of correct administration, phlegm, bile, and wind proceed in their proper sequence without obstruction; however, in the case of excessive administration, they emerge like foam, moon-like circles, and blood respectively. (25)

18.25dv Like foam, moonlight, or blood, the clarity of mind, composure, and stability will arise spontaneously; there will be no adverse effects from improper practice, nor will there be excessive suffering. 25.1+(1)
18.25.1+(1)a Tranquility of mind and composure; 18.25.1+(1)b stability shall arise of its own accord.
Vomiting, emaciation, burning sensations, dryness of the throat, darkness of vision, and vertigo occur;
moreover, due to the loss of vital blood, there arise terrible wind-related diseases and death. (26)

When [the patient] has vomited by means of correct yoga, one should have him rest for a moment and then drink one of the three types of medicinal smoke; thereafter, one should prescribe the regimen of unctuous substances. // 27 //
Then, whether in the evening or at dawn, being hungry and having bathed in pleasant water, one who is eating red śāli rice should follow the sequence of the liquid diet (peyā) and so forth. (28)
One should consume food consisting of old red *śāli* rice,
avoiding fats, salt, and pungent spices;
one should follow this sequence of *peyā* and the other stages in due order.

A person who has been purified by superior, middling, or inferior degrees of purification should follow this sequence of liquid foods and so forth— thin gruel, thick gruel, unseasoned soup, seasoned soup, meat broth, and likewise three, two, or one of each— at the meal times in successive order. (29)

Just as a tiny spark of fire, being fanned by grass, cow dung, and other fuels, gradually becomes great, stable, and capable of cooking everything, so too does the internal fire of one who is pure [increase] through the consumption of liquids and other foods.

18.30–31. For one who has been purified by means of emetics and other therapies, the digestive fire (antar-agni) is considered low, middling, or superior; accordingly, four, six, or eight bouts of vomiting are desired.
In purgation, these numbers are doubled or tripled, becoming ten, twenty, or thirty bouts. Likewise, the quantity of the enema fluid should be one, two, or four *prasthas*.
They say that emesis ends with bile, purgation is half [the strength] of emesis, and purgation ends with phlegm;
in purgation, one should measure after discarding two or three urges containing feces, but in emesis, after the [drug] has been drunk.

Then, once the time for phlegm has passed, knowing that the patient has been sufficiently oleated and sweated, one should properly administer a purgative to the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha). // 33 //

One with a predominance of bile has a soft bowel and is purged even by milk; one with a predominance of wind has a hard bowel and is purged only with difficulty, even by strong drugs such as *śyāmā* and others. (34)
In cases of pitta, purgation should be induced with astringent and sweet substances; in kapha, with pungent substances;
and in vāta, with unctuous, hot, and salty substances. However, if there is no movement [of the doshas], one should administer [purgatives] as follows. 35.
One should apply a warm-water fomentation to his abdomen with the heat of the palms;
when he has risen after a short time on that day, he should eat, and on the following day, he should drink again. (36)
However, one whose internal receptacle (koṣṭha) has weak attachment to oleation should drink a purgative again after ten days,
once their body has been further prepared with oleation and sudation.

Having correctly considered the etymological derivation and recollecting the previous transgression, there arises impurity of the heart and stomach, lack of relish, and nausea due to the derangement of phlegm and bile. (38)

18.38b–d. Recalling the previous sequence: itching, burning, pustules, coryza, and retention of flatus and feces are the signs of inadequate administration (ayoga). Proper administration (yoga) consists in the absence of these, as described above. 18.39.

18.39 When feces, bile, phlegm, and wind have sequentially emerged, there is itching and a burning sensation, and pustules appear; subsequently, one should discharge— devoid of phlegm and bile— a white, black, or blood-stained fluid.
The prolapse of the anus resembles the washing away of meat or appears like a fragment of fat; there is thirst, vertigo, and the eyes roll back into their sockets. (41)
Fatigue, the eyes rolling upward, and diseases resulting from excessive vomiting likewise occur in one who has been excessively purged.
One who has been properly purged should be treated with the same measures prescribed for vomiting.
Then, following the procedure excluding the use of smoke, as if one has already vomited, one should gradually eat foods and return to one's natural diet. // 43 //

One who has drunk medicine should undergo fasting (laṅghana) if their digestive fire is weak, if the morbid humors have not been fully purified, if they are not emaciated, if their strength is impaired by the humors, or if the signs of digestion have not yet appeared. (44)

He is not afflicted by the accumulation of unctuous substances, sweat, or the agitation caused by medicinal drugs; nor is he troubled by purificatory therapies, bloodletting, the administration of oleation, or fasting. (45)
Consequently, the digestive fire becomes weak; therefore, one should follow the gradual regimen beginning with thin gruel (peyā).
This applies to those who have undergone purgation, those with diminished bile and phlegm, those who drink alcohol, and those with a predominance of wind and bile. (46)
One should not give them thin gruel; instead, a regimen beginning with *tarpaṇa* (satiating drinks) is beneficial for them.
For those whose doshas are undigested, emesis is indicated; for those whose doshas are being digested, purgation is indicated. (47)

The therapeutic sequence beginning with nourishing (tarpaṇa) is beneficial; this sequence beginning with nourishing is considered [the proper course]. Therefore, one should eliminate [the doshas] by means of emesis and not wait for their digestion.
One who is weak and full of many defects, through the ripening of those very defects; 48.
One should treat that patient with purgative foods;
this applies to a weak man who has already been cleansed, whose humors are slight, and who is emaciated. (49)
One should treat him with suitable foods; moreover, if his digestive tract (koṣṭha) is not yet fully known, he should drink medicine that is mild and in small doses.
It is better for that to be drunk repeatedly than otherwise, as it would bring about danger.
It is better that [the medicine] be drunk repeatedly rather than otherwise, for it brings about uncertainty;
it removes many unstable doshas little by little again and again.
However, in the case of one who is weak, one should pacify those [doshas] which are small in quantity using mild substances.
For those [afflictions] cause suffering for a long time; indeed, if not extracted, they might even kill him.
For one with weak digestion and a harsh bowel, [one should treat them] with ghees containing alkali and salt. (52)
If not extracted, these [impurities] may even kill him;
therefore, one should purify the patient whose fire has been kindled and whose *kapha* and *vāta* have been conquered.
This applies to those who are dry, have excessive *vāta*, possess a cruel digestive tract (*krūra-koṣṭha*), or are habituated to physical exercise. (18.52b–53)
For those with a blazing digestive fire, medicine is digested even without a purgative;
therefore, one should first administer an enema to them, followed by an unctuous purgative. (54)
18.54c–v: To these patients, one should first administer an enema, or, after removing some feces with sharp fruit-poultices (phalavarti),
a lubricated purgative should easily expel the waste that has been mobilized.
One should purify those who are not excessively unctuous and who suffer from poisoning, trauma, pustules, leprosy, swelling, erysipelas, jaundice, anemia, or urinary disorders. (56)
One should administer purgatives that are not too unctuous to all those who have been prepared with unctuous purgatives; however, for those already saturated with oil, one should use dry purgatives.
Furthermore, between the intervals of procedures such as emesis and the rest, [dry treatments should be applied].
18.57b–v: One should apply oleation and sudation even with dry substances to those conditioned by dryness; at the end, one should administer oleation for the sake of strength.
For impurity, once agitated, is removed from the body just as dirt is removed from a garment.

Just as impurity is cleansed by purificatory measures once it has been mobilized by oleation and sudation, so too one who undergoes purification without having practiced oleation and sudation [will suffer]. (59)

18.59ab By means of oleation and sudation, the morbid matter (mala) is first excited and then removed by purificatory therapies; 18.59cd otherwise, his body would break apart like dry wood that has not been softened by moisture.

When properly administered, purification brings clarity of intellect, strength of the sense organs, stability of the bodily constituents, radiance of the digestive fire, and eventually slows the process of aging. (60)
18.60clarity of the intellect, strength of the sense organs, stability of the bodily constituents (dhātus),
and the brilliance of the digestive fire— Sūtrasthāna.
When the humors are dominated by wind, or when wind itself is predominant, enema (vasti) is desired;
it is the foremost of all therapeutic measures, and it is of three types. // 1 //

That foremost [therapy] is threefold: nirūha, anvāsana, and uttara-vasti; by means of these, one should treat abdominal tumors (gulma), distension (ānāha), sciatica (khuḍa), splenic disorders (plīha), diarrhea after purification (śuddhātīsāra), and colic (śūlin). // 2 //
It cures chronic fever, catarrh, disorders of semen and wind, obstructions by impurities, scrotal enlargement, urinary calculi, consumption, and even severe diseases caused by wind (vāta). // 3 //

However, those who are excessively unctuous, those with chest injuries, those who are very emaciated, those suffering from undigested matter (āmātīsāra), those vomiting, those who have undergone purification therapies, and those to whom nasal drops (nāvana) have been administered, should not be subjected to the non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana). // 4 //

Those suffering from dyspnea, cough, excessive salivation, hemorrhoids, hiccups, flatulence, and weak digestive fire; those with an inflamed anus, those who have overeaten, and those suffering from intestinal obstruction, perforation, or ascites—[these should not be treated]. (5)

19.5dv Those suffering from intestinal obstruction, perforation, ascites, skin diseases, and diabetes mellitus, as well as a pregnant woman for seven months, should certainly be treated with non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) and subsequently with unctuous enemas (anvāsa), especially those with excessive digestive fire.

Those who are rough and afflicted solely by vāta should not be given an oil enema (anuvāsana); likewise, those for whom a decoction enema (āsthāpana) is contraindicated, as well as those suffering from anemia (pāṇḍu), jaundice (kāmalā), urinary disorders (meha), and chronic rhinitis (pīnasa). // 7 //

Those suffering from lack of appetite, splenic disorders, constipation, heaviness of the digestive tract, or kaphaja abdominal enlargements; those with excessive secretions, extreme obesity, intestinal worms, or a digestive tract dominated by vāta—[these should avoid it]. // 8 //

One with a heavy abdomen suffers from *kaphodara*. In cases of *abhiṣyanda*, emaciation, obesity, jaundice, artificial poison (*viṣa*), *gara* poisoning, indigestion (*apacī*), elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), and goiter (*galagaṇḍa*), the nozzle (*netra*) for these two [types of enema] should be made of gold and other metals, wood, bone, or bamboo. (19.8b–19.9)
Having the shape of a cow’s tail, without gaps, smooth, straight, and with a rounded tip;
it should be five finger-breadths long when the age is less than five years, and six finger-breadths from the fifth year up to the seventh.
In the seventh year, there are seven; in the eighth, twelve; in the sixteenth, nine; and up to the twentieth, twelve; and likewise in the subsequent years. (11)
One should increase the age, strength, and body according to the proper measure: at the base, it should be equal in thickness to one's own thumb, and at the tip, to the little finger.
When the year is complete, having taken one finger-breadth [as the base], it increases by half of that half;
the maximum opening is three finger-breadths, which flows at the root and at the tip.

Mudga, māṣa, and kalāya [seeds], as well as a moist karkandhu fruit, should be used in sequence; they should be the size of the root-opening, with a carved karṇikā (central boss) at the edge. // 14 //
One should fashion two *karṇikās* on the eye, covered at the tip and separated by two finger-breadths at the base as appropriate; and there, one should apply [the wick]. (15)
One should prepare [the nozzle] at intervals of two finger-breadths according to the respective [patient],
and one should apply it there.
One should use the bladder of a goat, sheep, buffalo, or similar animal, well-softened and firm.
It is dyed with astringent dyes, possesses no holes, its knots, fragrance, and fibers are intact, and it is thin. // 16 //
19.16 For cows, goats, sheep, buffaloes, and the like,
the medicinal substances should be bound well with thread so that they may be easily positioned;
in the absence of a bladder, one should place them on a marked foot or within a thick cloth.
19.17ab Tied securely with thread, the dose for the first year of a Nirūha enema is one *prakuñca*;
thereafter, it increases by one *prakuñca* every year until it reaches six *prasṛtas*. (18)

19.18b–d. After one year, one should increase the dose by one *prakuñca*; beyond that, for those aged twelve to eighteen, it should be increased by one *prasṛta*. This measure [of increasing] continues until age seventy; beyond that, the maximum is ten *prasṛtas*.
19.19b–c: For the twelve- and eighteen-fold enema (*nirūha*), the dose for the oil enema (*anuvāsana*) should be one-fourth, according to each respective case.
[The patient] should be treated with a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpya*), then lubricated, fomented, purified, and once strength has been regained... 20.
Having recognized that a patient is fit for an oil enema, one should administer it beforehand;
during the cold season and spring, one should do so by day, while some say at night, and at other times otherwise.
Some [recommend it] at night, while others say otherwise;
[the patient] should have been anointed and bathed, and should have eaten food that is appropriate, light, deficient by one-quarter [of the usual amount],
non-unctuous, dry, and accompanied by a liquid drink, such as broth and the like.
Having consumed liquids with a post-drink (sānu-pāna), or having finished walking about and voided excrement and urine, he should lie down on a comfortable bed,
neither too high nor with the head raised, resting on his left side.
Having contracted the right thigh and extended the other, he should then introduce the lubricated nozzle into the anus, which has been lubricated as well. (24)
19.24d–25. Having lubricated [the nozzle] when the mouth and anus are lubricated,
having caused [the patient] to breathe out, and having secured the opening of the enema bag, one should insert it toward the spinal column without shaking the hand,
neither too fast nor too slow.
One should squeeze [the nose] neither too forcefully nor too gently, but only once;
one should leave a residue, for the vital air remains in that remainder. (26)
19.26c–d When [the enema] has been administered, one should leave a residue; then, while the patient's body is supine, one should strike his buttocks with the hand.
Likewise, one should lift the bed three times from the foot-end using both heels. 19.27.
Then, having anointed his limbs with oil, one should massage him while he lies with his limbs extended and his head on a pillow; one should strike the heels with the fist and rub the body.

Affection does not cease quickly for one who is afflicted by pain; therefore, another affection should be applied quickly once it has ceased, for affection that does not remain brings about what should not be done. (29)
One should feed [the patient] a light meal in the evening when his digestive fire is kindled and his appetite has returned;
the time for cessation is the final watch, and after that, it is beyond [the need for food].
One should wait for a day and night, or else one should make an effort to eliminate the oleation by means of suppositories containing medicinal fruits or sharp enemas. (31)

If, due to extreme dryness, [the medicine] does not come down and does not cause defects such as dullness of the senses, one should simply ignore it; then, having stayed overnight, one should drink it.
In the morning, one should administer an enema consisting of warm water with powdered ginger, or even water alone,
on the third or fifth day, and repeat it again.

Or, just as there might be a cooking of oil, [this applies] daily for those with excessively aggravated wind (vāta), those who constantly engage in physical exercise, those with a keen digestive fire, and those who are dry. 34.
Distension, constriction, constipation, impairment of the sense organs, loss of appetite, breaking pain, lameness,
and fractures of the limbs or joints caused by vāta are indeed curable by means of unctuous enema (anuvāsana).

19.34+1dv — For wind disorders and Sādhya conditions are indeed treated with an oil enema (anuvāsana). When the channels have been purified by three or four applications of unctuous substances (sneha), one should administer a purifying decoction enema (nirūha) for the sake of cleansing the channels; however, if the body has not been lubricated, one should employ an enema that provides oleation to the body.
Then, on the fifth or third day, when the practitioner is auspicious, at midday having slightly passed, when the offerings and auspicious rites have been performed. (36)

Having carefully observed the person—whose impurities have been removed by massage and sudation, who is not excessively hungry—as well as the humors (doṣas), the medicines, and other relevant factors; 37.
19.37c–v Having ascertained the person and the nature of the disorder, the physician, together with many experts in that science, should prepare a decoction enema (basti).
He should boil twenty palas of the medicinal substance along with eight fruits. 19.38 //
19.38bv Together with many who know that [decoction] and many who are skilled in it; 19.38bv Then one should prepare the oil as a fourth part of the decoction for Vāta;
for Pitta and in a healthy person, as a sixth part; and when Kapha is predominant, as an eighth part. 39.
One should prescribe unctuous substances (sneha) in cases of Vāta; indeed, one should prescribe unctuous substances in all [formulations].

Furthermore, the paste (kalka) should constitute one-eighth part [of the total], or as may be appropriate so that the enema (vasti) is neither too thin nor too thick. Additionally, one *pala* of jaggery (guḍa) should be added.
And all the remaining substances, such as honey and pungent spices, are combined together by this method; they are heated by the steam from a pot of hot water and stirred with a churning stick. (41)
Having inserted it into the rectum, one should administer it—neither too hot nor too cold, neither too oily nor too dry, and neither too sharp nor too mild. (42)
Those who know [the subject] recite that it should not be too clear, nor too thick, nor too mild, nor too salty, and likewise not too sour. (43)
19.43d–44. However, other experts in that matter say that one should prepare three palas each of the fat and honey;
half a karṣa of maṇimantha, and two palas of paste for a healthy person.
For all other substances, one should prescribe ten palas each, in the following order: honey, salt, oil, paste, and decoction.
This is the procedure for the administration of non-unctuous enemas (nirūha): one should pour [the medicine] into the rectum;
as soon as the nirūha has been administered, the patient should lie on his back and focus his mind on that. 46.
Having prepared his cushion and with vital energy aroused, he should assume the utkaṭaka posture;
when [the breath] has arrived, this is the supreme moment for death. 47.

19.47b–d: And one who voids with force while sitting in a squatting posture (utkuṭaka) for even a moment faces death; in that case, an enema prepared with unctuous substances (sneha), alkali (kṣāra), urine, and sour liquids (amla) is appropriate.
One should quickly administer another enema that is unctuous, sharp, and hot. // 48 //

In that case, one should administer an unctuous enema (sneha) that is concordant with the patient's constitution, or a medicinal suppository (phalavarti), as well as sudation (sveda) and frightening (uttrāsana) therapies. However, when the [first] enema has been spontaneously expelled, a second enema is desired.
19.49b–d Whether it be sudation, fright, and so forth—

whether for the third, the fourth, or until it is well-established— one should understand the application of yoga and other measures to be like that of one who has undergone purgation; however, during the state of yoga, one should provide nourishment.

Or rather, one should know [the proper time] as long as the state of being well-purged by the enema persists; then, once the patient has bathed with lukewarm water, one should administer a meal of rice with thin meat broth in that regimen.
As for those disorders that arise in one who has been purged due to the movement of the impurities (mala): [19.51]
19.51ab Bathing with lukewarm water; 19.51cd Those disorders which arise from a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) subside when the patient has been sprinkled with pleasantly warm water and has eaten.
Then, if the patient is again afflicted by Vāta, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) immediately. 52.
And for him, there would arise correct understanding and the practice of yoga, like one who has drunk oil;
and that which remains for a short time and then returns along with the feces. (53)
When the oil remains for a short time with the downward-moving wind (anulomānila), that enema is considered successful. However,
in cases of phlegm (balāsa), one should administer one or three oil enemas (sneha-vasti).
One should administer five or seven unctuous enemas (sneha-vasti) in cases of pitta, or nine or eleven in cases of vāta;
thereafter, one should again apply an odd number [of unctuous enemas], followed by a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana).
In cases of Kapha, Pitta, and Vāta, food should be taken respectively with vegetable broth, milk, and meat juice;
combined with a decoction of Vāta-alleviating herbs, Trivṛtā, and rock salt. (56)
In the case of vāta, a single unctuous enema (vasti) should be administered, combined with sweet, sour, and hot tastes;
it should contain a decoction of the nyagrodhādi group of drugs along with padmakādi, sugar, and other ingredients. (57)

19.57b–c: [The three types of *pācana*] combined with sweet, sour, and hot tastes are indicated for *pitta*; those combined with sweet and cold tastes, along with ghee, milk, sugarcane juice, and honey;
and the three [decoctions] consisting of the *āragvadhādi* group, the *vatsakādi* group, and [the *mustādi* group]. 19.58.

In cases of *kapha*, [the three emetics] are dry, mixed with honey and cow’s urine, and are sharp, hot, and pungent; these three also destroy the humors in cases of *saṃnipāta* because they act in successive order. (59)
19.59c–v: In the case of a combination of all three [doshas] (saṃnipāta), some physicians do not desire more than three enemas;
for there is no fourth dosha toward which a further one might be administered.
Therefore, according to the teacher Caraka, an enema is not intended for more than three [applications].
Others also declare that one should prepare the enema in exactly three ways: as a provoker, as a purifier, and as a pacifier of the humors (doṣas) respectively.
19.61c–62. One should thus administer the enema in three ways, according to the strength of the doshas, the medicine, and so forth; one should take all of this into account.
However, once the signs of a properly administered nirūha have appeared, one should not withdraw it as long as they are still possible to observe.
First there is one oil enema, followed at the end by twelve non-unctuous enemas along with their post-procedural massages;
thus, thirty enema procedures are prescribed.
In this [treatment], there is one application of oil at fifteen [muhūrtas] intervals; likewise, three applications at the end;
six applications separated by five bladder-washes (vasti); and here, however, eight bladder-washes constitute the regimen.
There are three types of non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) and three types of unctuous enemas (sneha); both the first and the last are unctuous.
One should not habitually employ either the unctuous enema (snehavasti) or the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) exclusively.

Because of the fear of [rekindling] the fire of the secondary afflictions (*utkleśa*) through oleation, and because of the danger [to the patient] from *nirūha* enemas due to *vāta*, one who has undergone a *nirūha* should be treated with oleation, and one who has undergone an *anuvāsana* should be treated with a *nirūha*. (66)
Thus, the enema procedure (vasti-karma), which conquers the three doṣas through the very method of purifying the unctuous element (sneha-śodhana),
is balanced when administered with a small dose of unctuous substance for drinking.

This oil enema (mātrā-vasti) is prescribed as a therapeutic unctuous treatment that should always be practiced by children, the elderly, those exhausted by travel, those burdened by heavy loads, women, those engaged in physical exercise, and those lost in anxious thought. (68)
19.68c–d For children, the elderly, those exhausted by travel, those speaking much, women,

those afflicted by wind (vāta), the weak, those with low digestive fire, kings, lords, and those who value comfort, [this regimen] destroys the humors (doṣas) without the need for restrictive avoidance; it is strengthening, promotes the elimination of waste, and is easy to endure.

19.69b–70. For those who have attained the happiness of royal sovereignty, and for women suffering from diseases of the vagina and the uterus, one should administer the *uttara-vasti* (urethral/vaginal enema) after they have been purified by two or three *āsthāpana* (non-unctuous enemas).

That eye should be twelve finger-breadths in measure according to the measurement of a patient's own fingers; it should be circular like a cow’s tail, with a karṇikā (a raised rim) formed at its base and its tip.

The best for entry is the *siddhārthaka* (white mustard seed), which is smooth, made of gold or other precious materials, firm, and resembles the stalks of jasmine, *aśvamāra*, or *sumanaḥ* flowers. // 72 //

For him, an enema (vasti) that is mild and light, or one with a dose of one śukti, should be prepared; then, after he has bathed and become cool, it should be administered according to the procedure for an oil enema (sneha-vasti). // 73 //
The dose should be measured as one *śukti* (two karṣas), having determined it accordingly; or, having prepared the dose as a *śukti*, [the procedure follows]:

for one seated comfortably on a soft seat with the legs straight and knees level, while the penis is erect and remains steady, [the enema] should be administered slowly for the purification of the channels. (74)

One should insert a fine probe; once it is cleared by that, one should follow with the [medicated] thread. Then, like the rectum, the nozzle should be held steady until it reaches the end of the urethra.
When the rectum has been purified by that [enema] and the oil has entered and the perineal raphe (anu-sevanī) is pressed, the procedure for an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) is beneficial.
One should administer three or even four enemas according to this method.
19.76 When the oil has been administered and has entered [the rectum],
one should consider all the remaining points for this procedure exactly as prescribed for an *anuvāsana* enema.
However, during a woman's menstrual period, the vagina receives [the oil] because it is open.

Therefore, one should administer it even outside the proper season or during times of distress, in cases of displacement of the womb, colic pains, disorders of the female genital tract, and menorrhagia. (78)
The nozzle should be ten finger-breadths long with an opening for a mung bean four finger-breadths wide;
it should be applied to the birth canal, while the one for the urinary passage should be two finger-breadths wide. (79)
In disorders of dysuria, the dose for children is one finger-breadth;
a *prakuñca* is the medium dose, while for children it is indeed only a *śukti*. 80.
With the woman lying on her back, having properly drawn together her thighs and with her knees raised, one should join [the penis] for three or four days and nights. (81)
In this manner, one should administer enemas for three nights while gradually increasing the quantity of oil;
then, after resting for exactly three days, one should again administer them for three days.

19.82b–c: One should increase the dose of oleation for a fortnight; thereafter, after being treated with emesis, one should undergo purgation for a fortnight. After being given a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), one may receive an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) immediately; after being purged, one may receive an unctuous enema after seven nights.
Just as a cloth removes the dye from water mixed with safflower and other pigments, so does enema extract impurities from the body once it has been softened. (84)

Whether diseases reside in the peripheral channels (śākhā), in the visceral cavities (koṣṭha), or are born in the vital points (marman), the upper body, or all the limbs and members—among all those that exist, there is no other cause for their arising than Vāyu. (85)

19.85cv Among those who exist, there is indeed no other agent for the dispersal or collection of the accumulated impurities such as wind, phlegm, and bile; therefore, for the pacification of that which has become excessively increased, there is no remedy whatsoever other than enema therapy. 86.
For wind (vāyu) is that which effects the dispersal and withdrawal of the accumulations of waste products such as feces, phlegm,
and bile; since there is no medicine equal to the bladder (vasti).
Therefore, it is declared that the enema (vasti) alone constitutes half of medical treatment, yet the entire treatment is contained within the enema;
likewise, venesection (sirā-vyadha) is also included because it serves as a blood-purifying medicine for both endogenous and exogenous disorders. (87)
Therefore, it is declared that "treatment is for the sake of healing," and some maintain that even the entirety of medical treatment is the enema (*vasti*).
In the *Sūtrasthāna*,
nasal medication (*nasya*) is specifically prescribed for disorders above the clavicle.
For the nose is the gateway to the head; therefore, having pervaded it, he destroys those [senses]. // 1 //
It is of three types: purgative, nourishing, and palliative.
The purgative type is used for headache, heaviness of the head, ophthalmia, and diseases of the throat.
Palliative treatment is of three kinds, consisting of what are called *marśa*, *dhmāna*, and *avapīḍaka*; furthermore, that [treatment] is traditionally held to be of six types.
From [the application of] rubbing, blowing, and pressing, [benefit is seen] in cases of swelling, goitre, worms, tumors, skin diseases, epilepsy, and chronic rhinitis;
it is nourishing in wind-born colic, solar vertigo, and loss of voice. (3)
That [oleation] is prepared with unctuous substances along with sharp [medicinal] pastes, decoctions, and so forth.
It is used for the drying of the nose, impediment of speech, difficulty in awakening, and drooping of the arms;
it is a pacifier for the defects of dark spots, freckles, hair, and the streaks in the eyes.

[This applies] to those with defects of the hair and diseases of the eyes. [It is] the conqueror of defects of the hair and eye diseases, using appropriate unctuous substances (snehas) prepared according to their respective indications, as well as pastes (kalka), decoctions (kvātha), and so forth, and even honey, salt, and fermented liquors (āsava). // 5 //
One should employ nourishing therapy using meat juices from arid lands, blood, and honey; for palliative therapy, one should use the aforementioned substances with milk or water.
20.6d–20.7ab: With milk and water, or with milk and water, there are two types of oleation here according to their dosage: *marśa* and *pratimarśa*.
However, *avapīḍa* consists of a paste and other substances; it is a sharp head-purgative.
For sharp [doshas], one should employ head-purgation (mūrdhavirecana),
blowing, or powder-purgation (virecanacūrṇa) using the breath from the mouth; this should be done through a tube six finger-breadths long with two openings, containing the medicinal drug within.

20.8ab Blowing [into the rectum] with powders for purgation [is performed] through a tube containing medicinal substances within. 20.8cd For that [tube] extracts a much greater amount of morbid humor (doṣa) because it is in the form of powder;
[the powder is taken] from what has been submerged and withdrawn from two joints of the index finger. // 9 //
As long as that drop falls— whether ten, eight, or six times in succession—
those very measures are, respectively, the superior, middling, and inferior durations of the *marśa*.

One should administer the paste (kalka) and other preparations minus two drops, but one must not apply it as nasal drops (nāvana) to those who have drunk water, wine, poison, or oil, nor to those desiring to drink.

[It is forbidden] for those who have just eaten, those who have just bathed their heads, those desiring to bathe, those who have just shed blood, those afflicted by the onset of a new catarrh, women who have recently given birth, and those suffering from asthma or coughing. (12)

20.12 One should administer nasal therapy (nasya) to those who have eaten, been anointed, bathed, and purified, and to whom enemas (vasti) have been given, provided it is not during the menstrual period or on an unfavorable day; except in cases of urgent illness. 13.
In the case of phlegm, [one should eat] in the morning; in the case of bile, at midday; and in the case of wind, in the evening or at night.
However, for one who maintains a healthy regimen during the autumn and spring seasons, [one may eat] in the forenoon. // 14 //
In cold weather, at midday in summer, in the evening during the rains, when the head is overcome by wind, in cases of hiccups, and in apatanaka (epilepsy). // 15 //
In cases of stiffness of the neck and loss of voice, one should perform this [treatment] every morning and evening daily;
otherwise, one should practice it once every day for seven days.
After the head has been lubricated and fomented, and after the patient has first performed his necessary duties,
one should again apply sudation above the clavicle while he is lying in a windless place.
Then, with the body lying supine and straight, the hands and feet extended, the feet slightly raised, and the head slightly bent; (18)
Having closed one nostril, one should pour [the medicine] into it by turns;
the medicinal substance, heated with warm water, should be administered either through a tube or with a cotton swab. (19)
Then, using a tube or a cotton swab, one should massage the soles of the feet, the shoulders, the hands, the ears, and so forth;
having slowly extracted [the phlegm], one should then spit it out from both sides.
20.20c–v: Having slowly drawn it out, one should spit it out;
thus one should administer the nasal medication two or three times until the medicine is exhausted.
In the event of fainting, one should sprinkle [the patient] with cold water, avoiding the head. 21.
One should administer unctuous substances at the conclusion of a purgative therapy, taking into account the nature of the humors and other factors;
after a nasal medication (nasya), one should remain lying on one's back for a hundred recitations of the Veda, and thereafter maintain the posture.
20.22 After inhaling oil as a purgative or nasal therapy, one should drink lukewarm water and mouthfuls [of it] for the cleansing of the throat.
When properly lubricated, there is easy respiration, sleep, awakening, and clarity of the eyes. (23)

In the case of excessive dryness (rūkṣa), there is stiffness of the eyes, dryness of the nose and mouth, and a sense of emptiness in the head; in the case of excessive unctuousness (snigdha), there is excessive itching, heaviness, salivation, loss of appetite, and catarrh. // 24 //

When well-purged, there is lightness of the eyes and purification of the mouth and voice. When poorly purged, there is an increase in disease; when over-purged, there is extreme emaciation. 25b–c.
