Pratimarśa should be administered for those suffering from wounds, emaciation, children, the elderly, or those seeking personal comfort; it may also be used during unseasonable rain, but it is not desired in cases of malignant coryza.

For when one has drunk liquor, when the channels of the senses are weakened, when the head is infested with worms, and when the humors are excessively provoked, [the medicine] is indeed [ineffective] because it is administered in an insufficient dose. // 27 //
20.27d–28. For, due to his lack of pride, he [regarded] as equal to the food of night-prowlers, to what has been vomited, to the day's sleep, to fatigue from travel, and to semen;
and to head-anointing, mouth-rinsing, urine, collyrium, and excrement.
This [practice] ending with two drops should be applied at the conclusion of using the tooth-stick and laughing.
Through these five, there is purification of the channels; through three, there is the gradual destruction of fatigue. (29)
The strength of vision [is restored] in five [days]; thereafter, there is firmness of the teeth and the pacification of wind.
Nasal medication (nasya) should not be administered to one under seven years of age, nor to one over eighty years. 30.
There is no smoke until the eighteenth; no solid food until the fifth; there is no purity until the tenth; and none once seventy has been exceeded. (31)

20.31b–c: A bolus dose is recommended for those less than five years old from birth until death; however, the *pratimarśa* (repeated enema) is like a *vasti* (enema), and it produces the same benefits as a *marśa* (medicated enema) when used regularly. 32.
In this case, there is no restriction, nor is there fear of complications as in the case of marrow;
indeed, oil alone is recommended for nasal administration through constant practice. (33)
20.33–34. Furthermore, oil alone is for the purpose of nasal therapy (nasya), because the head is the seat of phlegm (śleṣman); these oleaginous substances are for the healthy person, and no others.
[The distinction between] acting quickly or slowly, and the excellence or inferiority of their qualities, [is as follows].
If there were no distinction between *marśa* and *pratimarśa* regarding the excellence or deficiency of qualities (*guṇotkarṣāpakarṣatā*), [then they would be identical].
Therefore, who would resort to deliberation that involves risk and is fraught with calamity? // 35 //
Then one should prescribe *sāpada*;

likewise, one should specify those known as *acchapāna* and *vicāra*, as well as staying in a hut (*kuṭī*), exposure to wind and sun (*vātātapa-sthiti*), *anuvāsana*, *mātrāvasti*, and *āsthāpanavasti*. // 36 //
In the same manner,

one should prescribe *śāli* rice and barley with the juices of *paṭola*, *mudga*, *vārtāka*, small radish, and meat from wild animals during the sixfold administration of nasal therapy (*nasya-karman*).
The person who has received nasal medication should avoid loud speaking, physical exertion, eating indigestible or unwholesome food, anger, and traveling by vehicle or similar means. (36+2)
Jīvantī, water, devadāru, jalada, tvak, sevya, gopī, and hima. // 37a //
Dārvī-bark, madhuka, plava, aguru, varī, puṇḍrāhva, bilva, and utpala. // 37b //
Dhāvanyau, surabhi, sthire, kṛmihara, pattra, truṭī, and reṇukā. // 37c //
One should boil the filaments of the lotus and balā in a hundredfold measure of divine water. 37d.
Having extracted oil from the marrow with ten times as much water and boiled it down until ten parts remain, one should cook that oil with water for ten more turns;
during the tenth cooking, one should add an equal amount of goat's milk. They declare this highly efficacious *aṇu-taila* to be an excellent nasal medication (*nasya*). (38)
One should cook the oil with water ten times; those who habitually use this as a nasal drop will have thick,
elevated, clear skin on their shoulders, neck, face, and chest,
and they will possess firm senses and be free from gray hair.
20.39cv Those with firm sense organs and free from graying hair [attain] the non-arising of disorders caused by kapha and vāta above the clavicle. (Sūtrasthāna)
And for the destruction of those who have been born, the self-possessed one should always drink smoke.
21.1ab Above the collarbone, [the procedure] arising from kapha and vāta is unctuous; it is moderate for vāta, sharp for vāta and kapha, and [sharp] for kapha.
It should not be employed in cases of blood-bile affliction, those who have undergone purgation, abdominal enlargements, or urinary disorders. // 2 //

It should not be administered in cases of affliction by *pitta* and blood, in blindness (*timira*), upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvānila*), flatulence (*ādhmāna*), or *rohiṇī*; nor in those who have received an enema (*vasti*), nor in those who have consumed fish, wine, curd, milk, honey, fats, or poison. (3)
When it strikes the head, it causes anemia (pāṇḍu-roga), insomnia at night, and produces blood-bile disorders, blindness, deafness, thirst, fainting, intoxication, and delusion. // 4 //

If there is smoke or an excessively yellow color [in the urine], or if it is cold, a cooling regimen is beneficial there; as is the case following sneezing, yawning, voiding feces or urine, sexual intercourse, or surgical procedures. (5)
21.5dv–For those engaged in sexual intercourse, the use of weapons, or manual labor,
one should inhale mild smoke at the end of laughing or using a tooth-stick. At these times, as well as after eating at night or after nasal medication, one should inhale moderate smoke.
21.6 After laughing, using a tooth-stick, sleeping, applying nasal drops or collyrium, bathing, or vomiting, one should undergo purgation.
One should have a rectal enema nozzle made of suitable materials, straight, and consisting of three chambers.
The smoke-tube (dhūmanetra) should have its base and tip respectively the thickness of a thumb and a jujube seed;
for sharp, oily, and moderate [treatments], it should be three, four, or five [finger-breadths] in length.
21.8 At the base and the tip, there are eight [units] respectively measuring the thumb, the *kola*-berry, and the finger;
one who is seated upright, with mind focused on that and mouth open, [should perform this] three times.
Seated upright with the mind focused on that [object], and closing each opening one by one, one should inhale smoke through the nose.
One should first inhale through the nose when the humors (doṣa) have become aggravated and have reached the nostrils and the head. // 10 //

21.10 When the disorder has reached the nose or the head, one should inhale [the smoke] through the mouth for the purpose of inducing nausea; however, when it has reached the throat, one should do the reverse.
One should expel the smoke through the mouth alone; [expelling it] through the nose causes injury to the eyes.
The smoke should be inhaled through three rounds of drawing in and releasing;
one should drink it once a day when it is unctuous, and twice for maximum purification. (12)

21.12b–c. The smoke [is applied] three times with each of the three [substances], or three times with four; in that mild [application], the substances are aguru, guggulu, musta, sthauṇeya, śaileya, nalada, uśīra, and vālaka.
21.13–14. There, for three or four applications, one should use soft substances:
*varāṅga*, *kauntī*, *madhuka*, the marrow of *bilva*, *elavāluka*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, resin of the *sarja* tree, *dhyāmaka*, *madana*, and *plava*.
Śallakī, saffron, mung beans, barley, kunduruka, sesame seeds, the oil of fruits, the essences of heartwoods, fat, marrow, muscle fat, and ghee. (15)
For pacification: śallakī, lac, pṛthvīkā, lotus, blue water-lily, and the bark of nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, and lodhra, along with sugar. (16)
Yaṣṭīmadhu, Suvarṇatvak, Padmaka, Raktayaṣṭikā, Gandha, Akuṣṭha, Tagara, Jyotiṣmatī, and Niśā are used in the Tīkṣṇa [oil]. (17)
The ten roots, realgar, lac, white [mustard], the three fruits,
pungent aromatic substances, and sharp drugs constitute the group that induces head-purgation (mūrdhavirecana).
Having soaked the ten roots, realgar, lac, white [musta],
and the three fruits in water for a day and night, one should then coat a twelve-finger-long reed stalk five times with these same ground medicinal substances used for fumigation.
21.19c–d A wick made from the ground medicinal ingredients for fumigation should be as thick as a thumb and taper in the middle like a barley grain;
it should be dried in the shade, its core removed, and then smeared with oil as appropriate. 21.20a–b [It should be inserted] according to the specific requirements.
One should apply a wick, as thick as a thumb, which has been scorched by fire, to be consumed while placed in a smoke-tube;
having inserted a tube ten finger-breadths long through a hole in a pair of joined earthen saucers. // 21 //
Or, one suffering from cough should inhale smoke through the mouth using a pipe eight finger-breadths long. // 21½ //

Cough, dyspnea, catarrh, hoarseness of voice, foul odor, pallor, defects of the hair, discharge from the ears, mouth, and eyes, itching, pain, numbness, drowsiness, and hiccups do not affect one who inhales smoke. (22)
Purification of the heart, throat, and sense organs, lightness of the head, and tranquility are the signs of one who has properly drunk [the medicine] regarding the aforementioned defects. (22)
In the Sūtrasthāna, there are four types of gargle (gaṇḍūṣa): the unctuous, the pacifying, the purifying, and the healing.
Among these, three should be employed for the three conditions beginning with "unstable" (cala). // 1 //

The last [type] is a wound-healer that is unctuous; here, pacification is achieved with unctuous substances prepared from sweet, sour, and salty [tastes], along with bitter, astringent, and sweet medicinal herbs. // 2 //

Purification is achieved by bitter, pungent, sour, and salty [tastes] along with heat; healing, moreover, is achieved by astringent and bitter [tastes]. In these cases, the application of oil, milk, honey, and water [is recommended]. // 3 //

One should employ fermented liquids (śukta), wine (madya), meat broth (rasa), urine, and sour gruel (dhānyāmla) as appropriate, either combined with medicinal pastes (kalka) or boiled together, according to their specific tactile properties.
In cases of sensitivity of the teeth, looseness of the teeth, and wind-related diseases of the mouth, lukewarm or cold water mixed with a paste of sesame seeds is beneficial. (5)
Oil or meat broth should always be used for gargling in cases of suppuration accompanied by heat and burning, as well as in traumatic wounds.
22.6dv In cases of wounds, exogenous poison, or burns from alkali or fire, clarified butter or milk should be held in the mouth;
it quickly produces clarity and heals ulcers in the oral cavity.
22.7 When burned by poison, alkali, or fire, holding a mouthful of honey produces clarity in the mouth and heals wounds of the oral cavity; it also pacifies burning sensations and thirst.
Fermented grain water (dhānyāmla) destroys bad taste in the mouth, impurities, and foul odors. // 8 //
That same [water], when cooled and without salt, is the supreme remedy for dryness of the mouth;
moreover, a gargle of alkaline water quickly breaks up the accumulation of phlegm. (9)
By rinsing the mouth with lukewarm water, lightness of the face arises; and by being fomented and massaged in a windless place with sunlight, the shoulders and neck become supple. // 10 //
Without swallowing the gargle, one should hold it with the mouth slightly raised until the mouth is filled with phlegm or until there is discharge from the nose and eyes. (11)
A mouthful (*gaṇḍūṣa*) is that which cannot be moved when the mouth is full; otherwise, it is a morsel (*kavaḍa*). (11u)
22.11 When the nozzle is not inserted properly into the mouth, diseases of the neck, head, ears, mouth, and eyes arise, as well as salivation, throat ailments, and dryness of the mouth;
furthermore, nausea, drowsiness, loss of appetite, and coryza occur. These conditions are especially curable by means of kavala-graha (gargling).
Poultice (kalka), liquid extract (rasakriyā), and powder (cūrṇa)—these are the three types of topical applications (pratisāraṇa). // 13ab //

One should employ paste (kalka), liquid extract (rasakriyā), and powder (cūrṇa) with drugs prescribed for gargles in diseases caused by phlegm (kapha). This facial application (mukhālepa) is of three types; it destroys the humors (doṣas) and poisons, and it improves the complexion.

22.14c–d The signs of purity regarding mouth-washes (*mukha-lepa*) are the threefold reduction of the humors (*doṣa*) and diseases, nourishment, clarity, lightness of the mouth, and the lucidity of the sense organs; this is the characteristic of purity in gargles (*kavaḍa*). 14.1+1.
From deficient application [of the tongue], there arises dullness, an aggravation of kapha, and indeed a lack of the sense of taste;
from excessive application, there is inflammation of the mouth, dryness, thirst, loss of appetite, and exhaustion. (14.1+2)
22.14.1–2ab: For those suffering from emaciation, phlegm, or pitta, a warm [instrument] is recommended when vāta and kapha are involved; for the remaining [doshas], it should be excessively cold.
It should have three measurements [in length] and a height of one-fourth, one-third, or half a finger-breadth.
The retention of a non-dry [foreign body] causes the dry [tissue] to corrupt the complexion;
one should remove it after moistening it, and at the conclusion of that procedure, one should perform an oil massage.
One should avoid sleeping during the day, excessive talking, exposure to fire, sunlight, sexual intercourse, and anger.
It should not be administered in cases of chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), indigestion (ajīrṇa), when nasal drops have already been given, or in cases of lockjaw (hanugraha). // 17 //
When administered as a nasal drop (nasya) for lockjaw,
loss of appetite, or insomnia, it— when properly applied—
destroys premature graying of the hair, facial freckles, wrinkles, cataracts, and dark spots on the eyes.
And when well-prepared, it kills [the worms];
likewise, the pulp of the jujube (*kola*), the root of *śābara*, white mustard seeds, the root of *siṃhī*, black sesame, the bark of *dārvī*, and dehusked barley. (22.18b–19)
Darbha roots, hima, uśīra, śirīṣa, miśi, and rice grains;
kumuda, utpala, kalhāra, dūrvā, madhuka, and sandalwood. // 20 //
Kālīyaka, tila, uśīra, māṃsī, tagara, padmaka, tālīśa, gundrā, puṇḍrāhva, yaṣṭī, kāśa, nata, and aguru. (21)
Thus, six ointments are prescribed for the winter and other seasons, increasing by half a portion at each stage;
for those who habitually apply these facial ointments, their vision becomes firm.
The face is unblemished, smooth, and resembles a red lotus;
and there are four types [of treatment]: massage, affusion, poultices, and enemas. (23)
One should know that head oil possesses many qualities, each succeeding one being superior to the last;
among these, massage with oil should be applied in cases of dryness, itching, impurities, and the like. (24)
22.24 In cases of dryness, itching, impurities, and the like;
in *arūṃṣikā*, headache, burning, suppuration, and ulcers; as well as for hair-falling, cracking, and fumigation, a *pariṣeka* (pouring) or a *picu* (medicated cotton pad) should be applied. 25.

22.25bv – It is used for burning sensations, suppuration, and ulcers, as well as for the stiffening of the eyes; furthermore, it is indicated for numbness, facial paralysis, insomnia, dryness of the nose and mouth, blindness, and severe diseases of the head. // 26 //
The procedure for him, seated upon a soft seat level with his knees,
his body purified, anointed, and sweated, at the end of the day, [involves] the products of the cow and the buffalo.
A leather strap twelve finger-breadths wide, level with the head, should be fastened as far as the ears at the place of binding on the forehead, which has been wrapped in cloth. (28)
Having bound it with a cloth-strip, one should smear it with a paste of black gram (māṣa).
Then, one should pour lukewarm oil that has been boiled according to the specific disease. // 29 //
One should wear it above the hairline for one finger-width;
[the duration] until moisture appears on the face and nose is ten, eight, or six [days] for those who are unstable and so forth.

22.30cv Until the moisture [of the oil] has dried from the face and nose, one may massage the shoulders and other parts for thousands of measures; however, once the oil has been released, its maximum application is for seven days. 31.
One should maintain the pouring [of oil] into his ear for seven days, massaging the root of the ear while filling it;
this should continue until the pain becomes mild after one hundred measures, at which point there will be no further sensation.

22.32b–c One should massage the root of the ear until the tip of the right hand reaches the circle of the knee; that duration, equal to the time of one closing and opening of the eyes, is known as a *mātrā*. 22.33d–22.34a [The text continues: "In this manner, one should perform the massage for the left side as well. This procedure is prescribed for those suffering from stiffness of the neck, facial paralysis, and similar conditions. 22.34b–22.35a "One should apply oil to the head and face, and likewise to the ears, nose, and eyes. Having massaged the body with oil, one should then proceed to perform the *svedana* (fomentation) treatment. 22.35b–22.36a "The *sveda* (fomentation) is of four types: *nastaḥsveda*, *dhūmasveda*, *upakrama-sveda*, and *jalasveda*. Among these, *nastaḥsveda* is considered the best for curing diseases of the head. 22.36b–22.37a "One should inhale the medicinal smoke through the nose according to the prescribed method. By this, diseases of the head, mouth, and throat are quickly pacified. 22.37b–22.38a "The *upakrama-sveda* is performed by means of heated stones, iron, or earth, or by using heated water, milk, or oil. It is beneficial for stiffness, swelling, and pain. 22.38b–22.39a "The *jalasveda* is performed by immersing the body in hot water or by pouring it over the body. It is effective for removing coldness and for alleviating wind-related disorders. 22.39b–22.40a "One should avoid *sveda* in cases of fever, thirst, hemorrhaging, and in those who are emaciated. It is also contraindicated for those afflicted by *pitta* and *rakta* disorders, as well as for those who are very old or very young. 22.40b–22.41a "After performing *sveda*, one should immediately apply *abhyaṅga* (oil massage). Then, having fanned the patient with a fan, one should provide them with a light diet. 22.41b–22.42a "By this method, all diseases arising from the vitiation of *vāta* are quickly subdued. Therefore, one should always diligently employ *sveda* for the relief of *vāta*. 22.42b–22.43a "Now, the procedure for *jalasveda*: having prepared a vessel filled with hot water, one should place the patient inside it. It also removes stiffness and provides great comfort to the body. 22.44b–22.45a "One should not perform *sveda* on a person who has just eaten a heavy meal, nor on one who is exhausted from travel. The tip should be shaped like a lotus bud to prevent injury to the nasal passages. 22.49b–22.50a "The medicinal substances for the smoke include *śallakī*, *sarjarasa*, *guggulu*, *mustā*, and *tagara*. These should be ground into a paste and mixed with honey and ghee. 22.50b–22.51a "Having lit the mixture, one should inhale the smoke slowly and steadily through the nose. This cures diseases of the head, eyes, and throat, as well as nasal catarrh. 22.51b–22.52a "One should avoid *dhūma-pāna* during the rainy season, in those with *pitta* disorders, and in those suffering from *raktapitta*. It is also contraindicated for those who are very thirsty or who have just consumed alcohol. 22.52b–22.53a "After smoking, one should rinse the mouth with water and eat sweet foods. This practice maintains the clarity of the voice and the health of the senses. 22.53b–22.54a "Thus, the wise physician, understanding the proper times and dosages, should employ *dhūma-pāna* to alleviate various diseases. 22.54b–22.55a "Now, the procedure for *nasya* (nasal medication): it is of two types, *śirovirecana* (head-purgative) and *snaihika* (oleaginous). 22.55b–22.56a "The *śirovirecana* is indicated for phlegm disorders, headaches, and sinusitis. The *snaihika* is used for those suffering from wind disorders and those who are emaciated. 22.56b–22.57a "The substances for *nasya* include *brāhmī*, *rasāñjana*, *kṣudrā*, and *madhu*. These should be combined with honey and applied as drops into the nostrils. 22.57b–22.58a "One should administer *nasya* in the morning or evening, after the patient has rested. It clears the head, improves memory, and strengthens the eyes. 22.58b–22.59a "One should avoid *nasya* in cases of fever, thirst, and hemorrhaging. It is also forbidden for those who are very young, very old, or suffering from *pitta*. 22.59b–22.60a "By this systematic administration of *nasya*, the physician shall remove the impurities of the head and restore the patient's vigor. 22.60b–22.61a "Now, the description of *vamana* (emesis): it is the foremost among purificatory therapies for clearing the channels and removing phlegm. 22.61b–22.62a "The emetic drugs include *mustā*, *pippalī*, *viḍaṅga*, and *śuṇṭhī*. These should be mixed with honey and ginger and given to the patient to drink. 22.62b–22.63a "The patient should be made to vomit until the appearance of clear bile. After vomiting, they should be given a light diet and rest. 22.63b–22.64a "One should avoid *vamana* in those who are weak, dehydrated, or suffering from *pitta* disorders. It is also contraindicated for pregnant women and those with heart disease. 22.64b–22.65a "By this method, the physician shall expel the accumulated phlegm and restore the balance of the humors. 22.65b–22.66a "Now, the description of *virecana* (purgation): it is the best therapy for removing toxins from the lower part of the body. 22.66b–22.67a "The purgative drugs include *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *citraka*, and *harītakī*. These should be taken with warm water or buttermilk. 22.67b–22.68a "The patient should continue to purge until the appearance of healthy stool. After purging, they should be given a diet of rice and milk. 22.68b–22.69a "One should avoid *virecana* in those who are weak, dehydrated, or suffering from *pitta* disorders. It is also forbidden for those who have recently undergone surgery or bloodletting. 22.69
In merely the time of a blink or an opening of the eyes,
head oil conquers grayness, whiteness, and tawny discoloration of the hair, as well as the cracking of the head and wind-diseases;
it produces clarity of the senses and strength for the voice, jaw, and head.
22.34a The falling out of the hair, its whiteness, and its tawny color;
22.34a The falling out of the hair, its whiteness, and its tawny color; 22.34a The falling out of the hair, its whiteness, and its tawny color.
In the Section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna):
At the outset, eye-drops (āścyotana) are beneficial for all eye diseases; they eliminate pain, pricking, itching, friction, tearing, burning, and redness. (1)
It destroys diseases caused by burning sensations; it is warm for wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha), lukewarm for those conditions, and cold for blood and bile (rakta-pitta).
For one staying in a windless place, having opened the eye with the left hand— // 2 //
With another applicator made of cotton wick, one should pour ten or twelve drops onto the two pupils from a distance of two finger-breadths, while holding it suspended over a conch shell.
Then, having wiped [the area] with a soft cloth, one should apply mild fomentation using another cloth soaked in lukewarm water to alleviate phlegm and wind.
An eye-wash that is excessively hot and sharp causes the destruction of pain, redness, and vision;
however, one that is excessively cold produces pricking, stiffness, and aching sensations. (5)
Astringent discharge from the eyelids, rubbing, difficulty in opening the eyes, excessive increase of the disorder, very slight inflammation, and lack of suppuration. // 6 //
Having reached the joints, the head, the nose, and the channels of the mouth,
the medicine applied to the eyes draws out the impurities that move upward.
23.7 Having undergone bloodletting, cauterization, and nasal therapy, one whose body is purified should apply collyrium when the impurity resides solely in the eyes,
provided the signs of suppuration are present and characterized by slight swelling, excessive itching, and sliminess.

23.8cv When the signs of suppuration are present— characterized by slight swelling, pain, mild friction, tearing, and redness— and when there is thick discharge (dūṣikā) in the eye afflicted by pitta, kapha, blood, and especially by vāta, [this treatment] should be applied. // 9 //
Collyrium is of three types: scraping, healing, and clarifying the vision.
Among these, the scraping collyrium is prepared with astringents, acids, salts, and pungents. (10)
Irritation [of the eyes] is treated with bitter substances, while clarity is restored with sweet and cold ones;
when the eyes are inflamed by strong collyrium, that [latter treatment] brings about clarity. (11)
When applied, it is known by the name *pratyañjana*;
its rod is ten finger-breadths in length at the middle and has a bud-like tip. (12)
A copper needle is recommended for incision, one made of black iron for suturing, one made of gold for probing, and one made of silver for soothing. (13)

The preparation of collyrium is of three kinds: a bolus (piṇḍa), a medicinal paste (rasakriyā), and a powder (cūrṇa); one should employ them respectively for heavy, medium, and light degrees of the disorder. // 14 //
23.14c–d: When the humors (doṣas) are heavy, moderate, or light, one should administer those [medicines] in that order—those made from sharp substances and those made from mild substances.
They also state that the dosage for a pill made of sharp substances is the size of a *hareṇu* bean, while for one made of mild substances, it is double that measure.
In the preparation of medicinal pastes (rasakriyā), one should likewise use a measure equal to the fruit of the *viḍaṅga*;
for sharp powders, double that amount; and for mild powders, triple that amount. (14+2)

The dose of the bolus is the size of a hare's dust-particle (hareṇu), while the dose of the liquid extract (rasakriyā) is the size of a vella fruit; for a sharp (tīkṣṇa) medicine, that dose is doubled, as it is for a mild (mṛdu) medicine when administered as a powder.
The bolus should be the size of a *hareṇu* seed;
the medicinal preparation of the juice should be the size of a *valla*; and the same applies to the powder and the collyrium of the clay.
Two sticks are for the sharp [poison], and three for the other;
[the test is performed] at night during sleep, not at midday when they have withered under the hot rays of the sun.

In the other [eye], there may be three [types of causes]: at night by sleep, at midday by drink and food, and by the hot rays [of the sun]. When the humors (doṣas) are increased, provoked, or liquefied, they lead to eye disease.
For the sake of its pacification, one should always apply collyrium to the eyes at dawn and at dusk when the sun is free from clouds.
Others, however, say that sharp collyrium should not be applied during the day;
for the eye, weakened by purgation, suffers when it encounters the sun. (18)
Satiated by sleep at night and by the gentleness of time, the fiery vision, which is accustomed to cold, regains its stability once more. (19)

However, when the disease is characterized by excessive phlegm (balāsa) and requires scraping, one may certainly apply a sharp instrument to the eye even during the day, provided it is not excessively hot. (20)
The birth of stone and iron occurs from that very same source, as does their sharpness; likewise, injury to the eye arises from its own brilliance. (21)

Even at night, during cold weather, sharp medicinal collyrium is not beneficial for the eyes; it causes the discharge of morbid humors (doṣa) and induces stiffness, itching, numbness, and other such conditions. // 22 //
If it does not drain the morbid humor (doṣa) and causes stiffness,
itching, numbness, and so forth, one should not apply it;
nor should one apply it to those who are frightened, have vomited, have been purged, have eaten, or are under the impulse of natural urges.
In cases of anger, fever, exhaustion of the eyes, headache, grief, and staying awake at night; // 23 //

When the sun has not yet risen, when one has bathed the head, when smoke or wine have been consumed, when food is undigested, when one is scorched by fire or the sun, when one has slept during the day, or when one is thirsty; (24)
23.24 One should not apply collyrium during the daytime, when thirsty, or when the eye is excessively sharp, soft, small, large, clear, thick, rough, extremely cold, or hot. 25.

23.25c–d If [the eye] is excessively cold or hot, one should close the eyes and slowly move the gaze inward; when the eyelids have been anointed, one should slightly move them, and thus apply the collyrium. 23.26.
One should not suddenly apply a sharp [instrument], nor perform opening and closing of the eyes, nor exert pressure on the eyelids, nor wash them. (27)

When the eye has ceased its inflammation from the application of medicinal drugs and has become tranquil, one should then wash it with water appropriate for the disease, the bodily humors, and the season. (28)
Then, using the right thumb and a cloth, one should hold the upper eyelid of the left eye;
if it is the other [eye], it should be cleaned with the left hand.
If the morbid humor (doṣa) reaches the eyelid due to the application of collyrium, it will produce other diseases;
therefore, in cases of itching and numbness, one should again apply a sharp collyrium or administer medicinal smoke. 30.
If the medicinal collyrium reaches the eyelids, it causes disorders; otherwise, it acts differently.
When the eyes are scorched by a sharp collyrium, a cooling counter-collyrium in powder form should be applied.
23.30 When there is excessive application of sharp collyrium or when it has been heated, the application of a counter-collyrium (pratyañjana) powder is beneficial. Sūtrasthāna.
The eyes are fatigued, fixed, dry, rough, or injured; they are afflicted by wind and bile, distorted, with decayed eyelashes, and clouded vision. (1)
[The eye diseases] include Kṛcchronmīla, Sirāharṣa, Sirautpāta, Tamas, Arjuna, Syanda, Manthānya, Atovāta, Vātaparyāya, and Śukra. (2)

For a patient whose passion has been pacified, who is afflicted by tears and the agitation of pain, and who is free from wind, one should administer a satiation treatment after the head and body have been purified. (3)
At the common time of morning or evening, while lying on one's back,
one should place a level line made of barley and mung beans outside the eyelid-fold.

24.4b–d. In the evening, while the patient lies on his back, one should prepare a firm [plug] two finger-breadths high and insert it as prescribed. Once the eyes have closed, one should apply ghee that has been melted by hot water.

24.5dv For one suffering from night-blindness, wind-disorders, darkness of vision, difficulty in opening the eyes, and so forth, [the physician] should apply fat (vasā) that has been dissolved in hot water;
then, while the patient slowly opens the eyes as far as the tips of the eyelashes, [the oil should be applied]. // 6 //
In that case, one should calculate the measures for the eyelid, the junction, the white part,
the black part, and the pupil, respectively, as one hundred, three, and five [mātrās] according to the disease.

24.7ab One should calculate the dosage therein as seven hundred, eight hundred, or ten hundred [drops]; in the case of wind (vāta), one should maintain ten [drops] in a churned drink (mantha); in bile (pitta), six; and in one of healthy constitution or in phlegm (balāsa), five. // 8 //
24.8bv Ten times for wind in the *mantha* [region], ten times at the outer corner of the eye;
then, having caused the oil to flow out through the opening into a vessel, one should drink it and inhale smoke, and one should not look at the sky or bright forms. 9.
24.9dv One should administer [the medicine] daily when the wind (vāyu) is predominant;

when bile (pitta), every other day; and when phlegm (kapha), every second day. However, when the humors are in equilibrium (svastha), one should give it every third day, continuing until satiety is reached. Thus should one apply it. // 10 //
The eyes become capable of perceiving light, healthy, clear, and light; this occurs when one is satisfied.
In the case of insufficient satisfaction, the opposite occurs; and with over-satiation, diseases born of phlegm arise. (11)
When [the patient] is satiated, pains born of excessive phlegm arise;
the vision fails, becoming weary like a body that has consumed oil. Therefore, immediately after the satiation, one should administer a treatment that provides strength to the sight.
One should employ the method of *puṭapāka* for the very same types of consumption (*yakṣman*) mentioned previously;
it is beneficial as an emollient when [the disease] is associated with wind (*vāta*), and as a depleting agent when associated with phlegm (*śleṣman*). (13)
24.13 In these aforementioned types of consumption (yakṣman),

when there is weakness of vision and when vāta and pitta are present while blood is healthy, a clarifying treatment should be administered using the fat, marrow, muscle-fat, and flesh of land-dwelling, predatory, and marshy animals. 24.14.
One should prepare an unctuous enema (snehana) with milk and pastes of the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs,
as well as with the liver and flesh of wild animals and birds, pearl, iron, copper, and rock salt.
An ointment for scarifying consists of conch shells, sea foam, and *srotoñjana* ground into a paste with whey;
or [an ointment] made from the liver, marrow, fat, intestines, heart, and flesh of wild animals and birds. (16)
Clarification [of the milk] is achieved with sweet substances mixed with ghee and ground with breast milk;
a bolus the size of a bilva fruit should be made separately from the pastes of meat and medicinal drugs. (17)

Having wrapped [the vessel] in turn with leaves of the urubūka, vaṭa, and ambhoja plants, and having smeared it with clay mixed with the resin (sneha) and other substances, as well as with the ashes of dhava, dhanvana, and cow dung; // 18 //

One should cook [the drug] with its leaves in substances such as oils and the like, in sequence, until it reaches the appearance of fire; having squeezed out the juice of that which is cooked, one should apply it to the eye like a *tarpaṇa* (eye-satiation), and one should maintain it for one hundred, two, or three [units of time]. // 19 //

In the final stages of scraping (lekhaṇa) and oleation (snehana), the first two [procedures] should be lukewarm, while the other [the final one] should be cold; at the end of those two, inhalation (dhūmapāna) should be administered, and their applications there are like those for saturation (tṛpti).

One should not administer saturation therapy (tarpaṇa) or cupping (puṭapāka) to those unfit for nasal therapy (nasya); for as many days as one employs these treatments, for twice that duration thereafter, the patient will partake of well-being. // 21 //
Having bound his eyes with *mālatī* and *mallikā* flowers, he should dwell there through the night. (21½)

24.21 One should dwell at night with eyes bound, exerting oneself with one's whole being for the strength of the eyes through treatments such as nasal drops, collyrium, and eye-ointments; otherwise, vision is lost and the manifold world becomes a uniform mass of darkness. 24.22.
That which is the means for extracting various types of foreign bodies (śalya) lodged in various locations, and that which is used for visualization, is called a surgical instrument (yantra). (1)

25.1b In the application of surgical instruments, alkali, and cautery for hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, and other ailments that afflict various regions of the body; in the protection of the remaining parts of the body; and likewise in procedures such as enemas (vasti) and others—// 2 //

From this [wood], various mechanical devices (yantras) of manifold forms and functions are made, such as water-clocks (ghaṭikā), gourds (alābu), horns (śṛṅga), and those with mouths like a *jāmbava* fruit. // 3 //
Having conceptualized it through the intellect, it will be described according to its gross form:
[the measurements] of the heron, lion, bear, crow, and other such beasts and birds are equal. (4)
One should fashion many iron faces for the mechanical devices, each bearing the same name as the device itself, and measuring eighteen finger-breadths in length.
One should know that the svastika-machines have ends shaped like lentils, are bound at the neck with pegs, and are curved like hooks at their base.
At the base, they resemble hooks;
with these firm instruments, the extraction of splinters embedded in the bone is desired.
There are two types of forceps (saṃdaṃśa) with tips bound by pins or released from them, measuring sixteen finger-breadths in length. // 7 //
One [probe] six fingers long is for extracting splinters lodged in the skin, veins, tendons, or flesh; another is for removing fine splinters and eyelashes.
Mucuṇḍī has fine teeth and is bent at the root; she is adorned with a torque (rucaka) and is the destroyer of deep-seated ulcers, fleshy growths, and remaining cataracts. // 9 //
The *mucūṭī* has fine teeth and a straight tip;
it is twelve finger-breadths long and shaped like a fish or a palm. These two types of *tāla* instruments are prescribed for extracting foreign bodies from the ear canals.

25.10b–d: Like the palate, there are two types of palate-instruments; they are prescribed for extracting foreign bodies from the ear and for removing [foreign bodies] from channels. 25.10d: The tube-instruments (nāḍī-yantra) are hollow, having one or multiple openings, and are used for extracting foreign bodies from channels.
And for the purpose of seeing arrows and diseases that have entered the channels. // 11 //
25.11b–d. However, one should provide instruments with single or multiple openings for the sake of ease of operation and for suction;
their width, circumference, and length should conform to the dimensions of the channels.
A tube five fingers long, with its circumference half that length, having five openings and four ears, is used for extracting foreign bodies from the throat. (13)
25.13b–d: For examining a foreign body in the throat, there should be a probe with two ears and three openings;
its dimensions should correspond to the size of the probe's ears, as well as the circumference and length of the swelling.
One should have surgical instruments made to see such channels and others;
one should be like a lotus pericarp at the head, twelve finger-breadths long. (15)
The fourth tube, with four apertures, is considered suitable for extracting foreign bodies; for hemorrhoids, the instrument should be four finger-breadths long and shaped like a cow's teat. // 16 //
For men, it should not be less than five finger-breadths, and for women, six finger-breadths;
it should have two openings for the diagnosis of disease, but only one opening for therapeutic procedures. (17)
In its center, there is a hole three finger-breadths wide, as broad as the belly of a thumb;
above that, there is a raised and protruding pericarp (karṇikā) half a finger-breadth in height.
Above that, however, is the instrument called *śamyā*, which has a central pin (*karṇika*) and is similarly without perforations; it is used for pressing out hemorrhoids.
In the case of fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇdarā*), one should in every way withdraw the lip [of the wound] above the opening.
For nasal polyps and hemorrhoids, there should be a tube with a single opening, two finger-breadths in length, and a circumference equal to that of the index finger,
similar to the instrument used for fistula-in-ano.
A finger-guard made of ivory or wood, four fingers long, with two holes in the shape of a cow’s teat, is comfortable when the mouth [of the nozzle] is opened. (21)
The examination of the vulvar wound consists of a hollow space sixteen finger-breadths deep in the center;
it is bound with a seal, has four walls, and its opening is like a lotus bud. // 22 //
25.22cv A [tube] bound with a seal (mudrā), divided into four, quadrangular, with four ribs, and compressed at the base—this expands at the opening;
it is six finger-breadths long for the purpose of lubricating and washing wounds of the channels (nāḍīvraṇa) in a mechanical device (yantra). // 23 //
The two enema-syringes (vasti-yantra) are shaped like a gourd; at the base and the mouth they are the size of a thumb and a pea respectively;
they have no valve at the tip, and soft leather is fastened to their base. (24)
In the abdomen, double-mouthed tubes or feather-tubes [are used], and instruments such as the smoke-enema (dhūmavasti) and others are prescribed according to their respective requirements. // 25 //
The horn for sucking should have a mouth three finger-breadths wide and be eighteen finger-breadths long;
it should have a hole at the tip the size of a mustard seed, be well-fastened, and shaped like a nipple.

The alābu gourd should be twelve finger-breadths in height and eighteen finger-breadths in circumference; its mouth should be circular with four or three finger-breadths, it should be glowing, and it removes phlegm and blood from within. (27)
In the same way, the *ghaṭī* is beneficial for the dissolution and elevation of *gulma*;
and there are instruments called *śalākā*, which come in various shapes for various functions. (28)

25.28dv However, those [instruments] which have various shapes according to their respective functions and dimensions have two types of actions: seeking [the foreign body] and extracting the foreign body; both are used at the mouth of an ant-hole and through the channels. // 29 //
25.29 For the act of probing them, there should be two probes with mouths like lentil seeds, measuring eight or nine finger-breadths;
there are six śaṅkus, each measuring sixteen and twelve finger-breadths respectively.
For the purpose of expansion, the two [fingers] have the faces of a snake's hood and measure ten and twelve finger-breadths respectively;
for moving [the object], they have the faces of an arrow and its nock; and for drawing it out, they are shaped like a fishhook. (31)
The fetal pin (garbha-śaṅku) is known to be equal in length to the pin at the tip [of the instrument];
with that, eight finger-breadths long, one should extract the fetus from the woman's womb. (32)
The stone-extractor has a curved tip at the front like a cobra’s hood;
its shaft-end is like the nock of an arrow, four finger-breadths in length, and is used for extracting teeth.
In the extraction of stones (aśmarī), the opening at the front [of the instrument] should be like the hood of a serpent;
there are six probes for cleansing, provided with cotton turbans (uṣṇīṣa).
For the purpose of reaching near or distant parts of the rectum (pāyu), there are two types measuring ten and twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) respectively.
The two nostrils are six and seven finger-breadths [in length]; the two ears are eight and nine finger-breadths.
The ear-cleaner has the tip of an *aśvattha* leaf and the mouth of a *sruva* ladle. (35)
One should employ the three types of probes—the *śalākā*, *jāmbavauṣṭha*, and *kṣāra*—separately for thick, thin, and long [fistulas], as well as for those with anal stenosis (*antravardhana*). (36)
A probe with a rounded shaft that is thick in the middle and resembles a half-moon at its base, with a tip like the blade of a jujube seed, is used for cauterizing nasal polyps and tumors. (37)

In the procedure for alkaline medicines, there are three [vessels] eight finger-breadths deep with downward-facing openings, their mouths equal in size to the nails of the little, middle, and ring fingers respectively. (38)
25.38c–d The little finger, the middle finger, and the ring finger are said by me to be the respective instruments for cleansing the penis, applying collyrium, and so forth.
25.39 The secondary instruments are the magnet, cords, cloth, stones, and hammers.
25.39c–d Minute instruments include the magnet, leather, the intestine, the tongue, and hair; as well as the branches [of the body], nails, mouth, and teeth.
Time, digestion, the hand, the foot, fear, and joy are their functions. 40.

One who knows the means [of treatment] should, after careful examination with a discerning intellect, distinguish between those whose intestines, tongue, and hair are like leather straps (*vadhry-antṛ*), and those whose branches, nails, mouth, and teeth are like leather straps (*vardhra*). (25.40)
Expelling, uprooting, filling, purifying the channels, arranging, drawing out, binding, and pressing;
suction, elevating, depressing, moving, breaking, turning away, and straightening—these are the functions of the instruments. 41.67.

Because it revolves well, plunges in, seizes the object to be grasped, and extracts it, the heron-beak is therefore the foremost among machines; and because it is effective in all positions, it is the most authoritative. (42)
25.42 That which is well-fitted, sinks down, and rises up; that which is unchanging in all positions—
these twenty-six [instruments] of the Sūtrasthāna have been fashioned according to rule by skilled smiths.
Surgical instruments that remove hair are generally six finger-breadths in length. // 1 //
One should have [the needles] made beautiful in form, with excellent edges, and easy to grasp; they should not be jagged, but well-forged and very sharp, fashioned from tempered iron. (2)
With their tips focused in meditative concentration and possessing the hue of blue lotuses, they are forms that correspond to their names and are always present. (3)
One should generally employ one, two, or three fruits each, corresponding to half, a quarter, or a third of its own measure, according to the specific location.
The tip of the mandala is one-fourth of half its own measurement; the growth-leaf is [shaped like] an utpala flower;
the two supports are half-measures; the snake-searching [brush], the reed-named [brush], the arrow-head-mouthed [brush], and the three-fold tufted [brush]. 4+(1)

The *kuśāsya* (grass-mouth), the *sāṭa-vadana* (cloth-face), the *antar-vaktra* (inner-mouth), the *ardha-candraka* (half-moon), the *vrīhi-mukha* (rice-grain-mouth), the *kuṭhārī* (axe), the *śalākā* (probe), and the *aṅguli-śastraka* (finger-sword). 4+(2)
26.4+(2) av: [The face] with its mouth closed; 26.4+(2) bv: [The face] with a half-moon within the mouth; 26.4+(2) bv:
[The face] with a half-moon concealed within the mouth.
The curved-mouthed crescent-shaped hook, the barb known as the leaf-hand, the scissors, the claw-instrument,
the tooth-scaler, the needles, the brush, and that called the ladle (khaja). 4+(3).
The *ārā* is of four types, and likewise there is the *karṇavedhanī*.

26.4+(4)bv Likewise, there should be ear-piercing; the *maṇḍalāgra* is for fruits, and that which has the shape of the nail of the ring finger is for writing and cutting, to be applied to conditions such as *pothakī* and *śuṇḍikā*. // 5 //
26.5a Their tip is like a mandala; their leaf is like a razor for cutting, splitting, and lancing.
When the swelling is elevated, its point is straight; when it is deep, it is otherwise.

26.6dv But in the case of the *gambhīra* [incision], it is otherwise: the tip is bent backward, and it is long, short, or wide according to the underlying structure; this applies likewise to the incisions known as *utpala*, *adhyardha*, and *dhārā*, as well as to excisions. // 7 //
26.7bv – A short-mouthed [instrument] according to the site; 26.7bv – A short-mouthed [instrument] according to the sequence;
26.7bv – A short-mouthed [instrument] as appropriate; 26.7bv – On the short-mouthed [instrument], as appropriate.
For cutting hemorrhoids of the nose or ears, the snake-mouthed [instrument] has a blade of half a finger-breadth.
For the search for the path, there is the smooth probe with the mouth of an earthworm. // 8 //
Another, with a needle-like tip and its base fixed in the root, is for the purpose of incision;
for piercing and draining, one should use the *śarāryāsya* and the *trikūrcaka* [instruments]. // 9 //
In the mouth of the *kuśāṭā* strainer, there should be two finger-breadths [of space]; that is the result for those two.
Likewise, the interior of its mouth should be one and a half finger-breadths; that is its result.
26.10 A *kuśāṭā* should be applied to the mouth for drainage;
this same instrument has a crescent-moon-shaped tip and measures one and a half finger-breadths in width.
Having employed a *vrīhi-vaktra* (rice-grain-mouthed) instrument, it is used for piercing the head and the abdomen.
The *pṛthu* and *kuṭhārī* [needles] have mouths resembling a cow’s tusk and measure half a finger-breadth;
with their shafts directed upwards, one should pierce the vein situated above the bones.
A copper probe with two openings, shaped like a *kurubaka* flower at its mouth, should be used to pierce the *liṅganāśa*; one may also fashion a surgical instrument for the fingers. (13)
26.13 A copper probe with two openings, its tip emerging from a ring; on the blade, it is half a finger-breadth in length,
equal [in width] to the growth-leaf through its application, or like a crescent-headed lancet.

That [mudrā], which has the measure of the tip of the first phalanx of the index finger as its offering, when bound with thread, serves for cutting and piercing diseases of the throat and the channels. (15)
For catching [animals] such as pigs and rhinoceroses, there is a hook with a well-rounded tip;
for cutting bones, however, there is a saw with a sharp edge ten fingers long.
The *baḍiśa* has a well-rounded face;
it is two finger-breadths in width, with fine teeth and a well-fastened handle.
For cutting tendons, sutures, and hair, there is the *kartarī*, which resembles a pair of scissors. (26.16–17)
The nail-sword (nakha-śastra) is nine finger-breadths long, with two faces and a curved or straight edge;
it is used for extracting fine splinters, excision, incision, scarification, and scraping. (18)

26.18–19: For scraping the interdental spaces, one should use a tooth-scaler that has a single edge, is four-cornered, and is shaped like a tied knot on one side; with it, one should cleanse dental tartar.
26.19b–20. Furthermore, there are three types of needles for suturing here: those that are large in form, circular on one side, and have hidden, firm loops;
and those for fleshy regions, which are triangular and three finger-breadths in length.

For wounds located in small muscles, bones, or joints, the probe should be two finger-breadths long, with a mouth like a grain of rice and curved like a bow; for those in the marmas of the mature and immature digestive tracts, it should be shaped accordingly.

Each of those [vessels] is two and a half finger-breadths wide and entirely circular; they are four finger-breadths [in height], and the *kūrca* (grass mat) rests upon a single circular base, with seven or eight well-fastened [strands]. // 22 //
Each of these [pestles] is two and a half finger-breadths thick and four finger-breadths in circumference;
they are to be used for grinding in cases of dark spots, freckles, and hair loss.
A churning-stick (*khaja*) consists of eight circular spikes, each with a mouth of half a finger-breadth.
26.23b–24. By rubbing the hair-shedding [root] with the hands and squeezing it through the nose, one may draw out blood;
the piercing of the earlobes is performed with the face of a *yūthikā* bud.
26.24c–d For the piercing of the earlobes:
[the instrument] has a face like a *yūthikā* bud, with a circumference of half a finger-breadth at its tip; it enters [the lobe] in that manner and is likewise directed upwards.
It is four-cornered; with it, one should pierce the swelling when there is doubt as to whether it is suppurated or raw. 25.
A thick earlobe is recommended for a thick [needle];
the ear-piercing needle should be three finger-widths long, with a hole one-third its diameter. (26)

And for that very [purpose], leeches, alkali, cauterization, glass, stone, the fingernail, and so forth are recommended as secondary instruments made of materials other than iron; one should employ them in this manner. (26.26bv–27)
Furthermore, there are other instruments and the like, as well as their medicinal applications:
excision, incision, suturing, extraction, scarification, cauterization, and pulverization. (28)
26.28c–d: Uprooting, tearing, sewing, drawing out, scraping, covering, and cutting; excision, splitting, piercing, churning, extraction, and cauterization—these are the surgical procedures.
[The qualities of the instruments are: blunt, jagged, thin, thick, short, long, and curved. (29)
The sharpness of the edges of surgical instruments is proclaimed as their eight defects;
for the purposes of excision, incision, and scraping, the instrument is held between the handle and the tip of the blade.
With the index, middle, and thumb fingers, one who is well-composed should grasp the [stalks];
and the draining [of the sap] from the tips of the stalks should be done with the index finger and the thumb.
The tip of the stalk, concealed by its sheath, should be grasped at the mouth like the opening of a grain;
for the purpose of extraction, it may be held at the base, or otherwise, according to the ease of the action.
26.32cv For the purpose of extraction from the roots, [the probe] should be nine finger-breadths in width, well-solidified, twelve finger-breadths in length,
and made of linen, leaves, wool, silk, dukūla cloth, or soft leather. // 33 //
With the noose properly arranged, well-sewn, containing a blade within its inner lining,
with its opening covered by a probe, and well-stocked with instruments, it is a well-arranged sheath for surgical tools.

One should employ leeches for the extraction of blood from those who are otherwise healthy; however, one must avoid those born in foul water, or those originating from fish, frogs, snakes, corpses, putrefying matter, or filth. (35)
26.35–36. Those [eruptions] caused by corrupted water, fish, frogs, and the like are red, white, or very black; they are unstable, thick, and slimy;
they possess variegated upward stripes like a rainbow and are hairy.
One should avoid those [lotuses] that are poisonous, for they cause itching, suppuration, fever, and dizziness;
in such cases, one should employ water-born [lotuses] that are free of poison and which alleviate poison, bile, and blood disorders. 37.

26.37c–d: To conquer poison, bile, and blood, [the following] should be prepared: 26.37d: Therein, those produced in pure water which are free from poison, dark-green like algae, circular, with vertical blue stripes on their backs, thin-bodied, and slightly yellow-bellied; these are the ones to be used.
Because they do not vomit properly and because they fall down continuously, they sink even upon reaching water; one should therefore abandon those who are intoxicated with blood. (39)
26.39cv Having reached water, they sink; however, others, when immersed in water mixed with the paste of *niśā*,
survive in *avantisoma* or buttermilk (*takra*), and are further revived by being placed in water.
26.40c–d One should cause them to soak [the wound] in sour gruel (kāñjika) or kālaśeya; [one should treat] wounds caused by ghee, earth, breast milk, blood, or the application of a blade.

One should cover with a soft cloth those [women] who are drinking [the liquid] and whose shoulders are raised. 26.41a–b [One should cover] those who are drinking with a soft cloth, while their shoulders are held high.

26.41–42. One should apply leeches to a wound from which corrupted or pure blood flows, mixed with meat, earth, or breast milk; the leech draws out the corrupted blood first, just as a swan takes the milk from a mixture of milk and water.
Leeches pacify abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, abscesses, skin diseases, gout, throat ailments, eye diseases, poisons, and erysipelas arising from vitiated or pure blood that has become mixed.
In the event of a sting by a gadfly, or when there is itching, one should release her [from the bite] and cause her to vomit;
her face should be smeared with pungent oil and rubbed with a fine abrasive powder. (43)
26.43b Or one should release or cause them to vomit; 26.43c Their faces smeared with pungent oil,
26.43d Coated with a fine powder of ground grain.

Protecting [the patient] from the intoxication of blood, one should not let those leeches remain for more than seven days; as before, there will be vigor and firmness when the leeches have properly disgorged.
Excessive exertion leads to fatigue or even death; if vomited poorly, there is stiffness and intoxication.
These [complications] should be treated elsewhere, while the clay and water inside the jar should be set aside. (45)
For the purpose of destroying the pustules caused by saliva and other secretions, they should be treated with poisons according to that lineage;
if purification has not occurred, one should drain the bites with turmeric, jaggery, and honey.
Then, with plasters cooled by being saturated a hundred times with clarified butter, there is an immediate alleviation of redness and pain due to the removal of the vitiated blood. (47)
If the blood is impure, moving from its place, stagnant, or located in a wound-bed, it becomes excessively sour if left overnight; therefore, one should drain it again.
If the blood is vitiated by pitta, one should employ a gourd vessel (alābughaṭikā) that has become sour after standing overnight; however,
if it is vitiated by kapha and vāyu, one should employ those [vessels] through their contact with fire.
26.49d One should treat blood vitiated by phlegm and wind with [purgatives], but one should not extract it with a horn;
however, blood vitiated by wind and bile should be extracted with a horn because of its thickened consistency. 50.

One should not extract [the foreign body] with a horn; rather, having firmly secured the limb above with a rope or a bandage evenly, one should perform the incision while avoiding the tendons, joints, bones, and vital points (marmans). 26.51ab–cd.
He did not place one foot upon another, nor did he stride with steps that were too deep, too heavy, or directed sideways, but rather with steps extended downward and rising upward.
One should not move the foot upon the foot;
[one should remove] that which is hidden, situated in one part, and knotted by lotuses;
one should extract the stagnant blood with horns and the like, and the pervasive [blood] by venesection.
26.53b–c: When [the blood] is knotted together with lotus-fibers, it should be extracted by means of a sponge; or, when it is clotted and deep-seated, leeches should be used.
When the blood is located in the skin, a gourd, a tube, or a horn should be used; when the blood is widespread, a vein should be opened.

Or, if the blood has flowed out due to the locations of wind and the other humors, one should apply horn, leeches, or gourd respectively; then, once the blood has drained, cooling plasters and other treatments should be used for the provocation of the wind.
If there is swelling accompanied by pricking pain and itching, one should sprinkle it with warm clarified butter.
26.55 That [wound] which is accompanied by pricking pain, itching, and swelling is described in the *Sūtrasthāna*;
it is sweet, slightly salty, neither cold nor hot, and not thick.
It is like a lotus, an indragopa insect, molten gold, the moon, and vermilion. // 1 //
Blood is pure by origin and remains so within the body;
however, it is generally vitiated by bile and phlegm, and consequently, it produces [diseases]. // 2 //
Pure red blood indicates erysipelas, abscesses, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, loss of digestive fire, and fever;
it also portends diseases of the mouth, eyes, and head, as well as intoxication, thirst, and a salty taste in the mouth. (27.2)

Those diseases such as skin disorders (kuṣṭha), disorders of wind (vāta), blood (asra), and bile (pitta), vomiting of pungent or sour substances, and vertigo, which persist despite being treated with cold, hot, unctuous, dry, and other such remedies; // 4 //
When diseases that ought to be properly cured do not subside, they arise from the provocation of blood (rakta-prakopa);
in such cases, one should venesect to drain the excessive blood. // 5 //

But not for those who have passed seventy years of age, nor for those whose blood flows from a wound less than sixteen days old, nor for those who are dry, nor for those who have not been fomented, nor for those excessively fomented, nor for those afflicted by wind (vāta).

27.6ab Not for those less than sixteen years of age, nor for women past childbearing, nor for those who have recently given birth, nor for those suffering from chronic bile-blood disorders, dyspnea, or cough;
nor for those with diarrhea, abdominal enlargement, vomiting, anemia, or swelling of the entire body. // 7 //
When the five therapeutic procedures have been administered after the patient has drunk oleaginous substances,
one should not pierce a vein that is unrestrained, nor one that is oblique, nor one that has not been raised.
27.8dv One should not [apply it] horizontally nor on a non-elevated area, except in cases of emergencies or disease caused by excessive cold, heat, wind, or clouds;
in disorders of the head and eyes, one should release the vein at the forehead. // 9 //
One should venesect the lālāṭyā vein;
or, in cases of ear diseases, one should venesect the apāṅgyā or upanāsyā veins, or those located in the ear (karṇajā).
In diseases of the nose, one should place [the mind] at the tip of the nose or between the nose and the forehead. // 10 //

27.10 Those located in the outer corners of the eyes or near the nose are for nasal diseases; those affecting the tongue, lips, jaw, or palate are for diseases of the mouth; and those situated in the glands above the collarbone, or in the neck, ears, temples, and head, are for diseases of those regions.

In cases of abscess (vidradhi), pain in the sides (pārśva-śūla), and pain between the sides, the armpits, and the breasts, one should apply [medicines] located on the chest, the outer corners of the eyes, and the forehead, with vessels leading to the middle of the eyebrows.
In tertian fever (tṛtīyaka), one should apply them between the shoulders; in quartan fever (caturthaka), below the shoulder-blade.
In cases of dysentery accompanied by colic, it should be applied two finger-breadths from the pelvis;
in diseases of the semen and the penis, on the penis; and in goiters and glandular swellings, on the thighs. (14)
In the *gṛdhra-sī* [fever], one should apply [the treatment] four finger-breadths below or above the knees;
in *apacī*, two finger-breadths below the *indra-vasti*; and in *catur-aṅgula*, four finger-breadths [below]. // 15 //
Above the ankle are the two *sakthi* (thigh) joints, as well as the *kroṣṭuka-śīrṣaka* (hip joint);
[these are the locations for] *pāda-dāha* (burning of the feet), *khuḍa*, *harṣa*, *vipādī*, and *vāta-kaṇṭaka*. (16)
27.16ab Two finger-breadths above the ankle joint, in cases of arthritis or sciatica, one should pierce above the *kṣipra* marman,
as in the case of *gṛdhrasī*, when the [specific] *viśvācī* symptoms described are not observed.

In a region devoid of vital points (marman) and as close as possible, one should pierce another vein; then, the patient—having been lubricated, become lean, equipped with all necessary instruments, and possessing strength—[should be prepared]. (18)
Having performed the rites for auspiciousness, having been served a meal of savory juices,
and having sweated from the heat of fire and the sun, he sits upon a seat with his knees raised.

With the ends of his hair gathered in soft silk, and his elbows resting upon his knees, I think he would press [the opponent] firmly with both fists, which are clenched around the folds of his garment. (20)
27.20d I think it would cause intense pain; it may lead to clenching of the teeth, labored breathing, and swelling of the cheeks.
Therefore, a person should restrain him from behind by wrapping a cloth around him. 21.
A person should wrap a cloth around the neck and insert the left index finger inside;
this is the procedure for restraining veins other than those located within the mouth.

27.22b–c: [The physician] should place his left index finger inside her [vagina]. Then, once he knows it has risen, the physician should strike it with the middle finger, released from the thumb, except for those [positions] where the mouth is internal; or [he may do so] by pressing with the thumb based on the sensation of touch. 27.23.

27.23–24. One should identify a vein at the base of the thumb by pressing with the fingers while holding a small axe (*kuṭhārī*) in the middle with the left hand; once the vein is clearly perceived as being perfectly motionless at the site of the incision, one should release it in that same manner.
Striking and pressing her, one should pierce her with the "grain-mouth" [instrument], having raised the tip of the nose toward the sub-nasal region with the thumb. (25)
Striking or pressing her [the patient], one should strike or press her;
for a vein located at the base of the tongue when its tip is raised and bitten, one should restrain her above the breasts;
and for a vein situated in the neck, one should restrain her from above the breasts. (26)

When the hand containing a stone is placed on the knee with the forearm extended, and [the area] starting from the flank is massaged, one should pierce [the fetus] while a tight upper bandage is applied. (27)
One should lance the vein in the forearm of a patient seated comfortably, having bound his fist with the thumb tucked inside, while the elbow remains unbent. (28)

27.28dv Forming a fist with the thumb tucked inside, one should pierce the vein on both sides while the patient is supported by his two arms, at a distance of four finger-breadths above the site to be pierced and secured with a bandage. 29.
When the penis is erect, one should press upon the vein of the calf at the knee while the knee is slightly bent;
the foot should be well-positioned below, pressing against the joint of the knee. // 30 //

27.30cv When one foot is placed on the ground, [the practitioner] should firmly grasp it with both hands from the ankle upward; then, having slightly ascended upon that second foot which is bent, he should proceed as with the hands. // 31 //
Having bound [the limb], one should thus pierce the vein; even in cases not explicitly mentioned, the expert in means should apply the appropriate instrument to those various locations.
One should insert the *vrīhyāsya* [needle] into a fleshy part to the size of a grain of rice;
for piercing a vein over a bone, one should use the *kuṭhārikā* [knife], measuring half a barleycorn.
When piercing a vein with a *kuṭhārikā* (scalpel),
it should be pierced correctly so that a stream of blood flows once the instrument is released; however, it should not flow once the instrument has been withdrawn.
If pierced poorly, it flows for a short time and only a small amount [of blood], due to the application of oil and powders. // 34 //

27.34 When properly pierced, a stream [of blood] flows; when the instrument is released, it does not flow. If poorly pierced, it flows with a sound due to being smeared with oil and powder; if excessively pierced, however, it flows with pain and is difficult to hold steady.
Fear, fainting, loosening of the machine, blunted weapons, and excessive satiety. // 35 //
Emaciation, rapid pulse, and perspiration are the causes for the improper flow of blood;
when the blood flows inadequately, [it is treated] with vellā, vyoṣa, niśā, and nata.
One should apply a plaster of salt, oil, and smoke from a house (sāgāra-dhūma) to the opening of the vein;
once the flow is properly established, one should apply lukewarm oil and salt.

27.37 If vitiated blood flows out first with oil or salt like yellow pigment from a safflower, it will stop on its own once it has flowed properly; being thus purified, one should not extract it further.
Having released the magical device (*yantra*) while he is in a state of unconsciousness, and fanning him with fans, one should cause [the poison] to flow out;
if he faints again, it may take another day or even three days.
From vāta, the urine is dark reddish-brown, rough, discharged with force, and clear and frothy;
from pitta, it is yellowish-black, has a fishy odor, does not coagulate, and due to its heat, contains glistening particles.
Blood that is not clotted, hot, accompanied by *candraka* (spots), and quickly absorbed by the earth when covered is due to *vāta*.
Blood that is unattractive to flies is due to *pitta*. (40+1)
That which is caused by phlegm is infested with flies; it dries up and does not move.
From kapha, the blood is unctuous, pale, stringy, slimy, and thick;
from the combination [of two doṣas], it possesses mixed characteristics; and from the three doṣas, it is dirty and turbid. (41)
If there is no purification, even a strong person should not cause excessive blood to flow from the incision;
for if there is excessive bleeding, death may occur, or severe and shifting disorders may arise.
Even if blood does not flow despite the application of force,
the remedies there are massage, meat broth, milk, and blood-transfusion.
Once the blood has flowed, the bandage should be slowly removed and the area washed with cold water.
Having washed the opening of the vein and applied a cotton pad soaked in oil, it should be bound;
if it is not purified, one should cause it to bleed again in the evening, on the following day, or even later.
