Therefore, even if there is a remainder, it should be retained; one should not allow it to flow out excessively.
One should remove the remainder with horns or similar means, or else take it as a consecrated gift (prasāda). // 46 //
One should thus purify vitiated blood that is not excessively increased by means of cooling treatments, therapies for pitta and blood disorders, purification, and drying agents. (47)
If, however, the blood does not stop, one should quickly perform a hemostatic treatment using *lodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, *pattaṅga*, *māṣa*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, and *gairika*. (48)

One should powder the opening of the ulcer with powdered earthen potsherds, collyrium, linen cloth, soot, the bark of milk-exuding trees, and sprouts; one should drink the cooling decoction of the padmakādi group.
Or one should pierce that very same vein immediately after the incision; otherwise, one should quickly cauterize the opening of the vessel with a heated probe. (50)

27.50–51. Until the openings of the vessels, which have quickly gone astray due to the pressure of the instrument, return to their natural state, one should consume wholesome food and maintain a wholesome regimen so that the vitiated humors (doṣas) that have entered the blood do not further corrupt it.
When the blood has been removed, food and drink that are neither too hot nor too cold, light, and digestive-stimulating are beneficial;
for at that time the body's blood is unstable, and the digestive fire must be protected with particular care. (52)
At that time, since the blood in the body is unstable, the digestive fire (agni) must be protected with special care; indeed,
the fire must be guarded especially by one who desires clear complexion and the functioning of the senses, and whose digestive impulse remains unimpeded.
They say that such a person is endowed with happiness, possessed of nourishment and strength, and has pure blood. // 53 //

Skin discolorations, leprosy, and other such ailments arising from blood, as well as diseases of the throat, mouth, eyes, and head, along with afflictions such as premature graying of hair and scaly eruptions—these are all pacified by venesection. (53+1)

By venesection on the forehead, one will obtain eyes like the petals of a disease-free blue lotus, hair that is clearly black at the roots and well-bound, a face resembling the moon, and a fragrance as sweet as a lotus. // 53+2 //
In the Sūtrasthāna: the movement of foreign bodies (śalya) is fivefold—curved, straight, transverse, upward, and downward.
[The site of entry] appears dark, is accompanied by swelling and pain, and frequently discharges blood. (1)
One should know that a swelling which rises up like a bubble, is covered with pustules, and is a soft-fleshed ulcer, briefly indicates an internal foreign body. // 2 //

One should recognize that when the foreign body (śalya) has reached the skin, there is a swelling that is elevated like a bubble, soft to the touch, and specifically discolored, hard, and elongated; when it is situated in the muscle (māṃsa), there is a burning sensation, and the swelling increases in size. (28.2–3)

Inability to endure pressure, suppuration, and the non-healing of the wound tract occur when [the foreign body] has entered between the muscles; it is like a case where [the object] has reached the flesh, being without swelling. // 4 //
28.4ab Intolerance to pressure is the sign of suppuration (pāka). 28.4cd–5ab [In the case of swelling] without convulsions, there is a throbbing, stiffness, and pain in the network of ligaments;
this is difficult to cure when located in the ligaments, and there is distension of the vessels when it has reached the veins (sirā). 5.
28.5c–v. When [the vāyu] resides in the channels (srotas), this [condition] is difficult to cure; it causes the loss of one's own natural functions and qualities.
When the vāyu resides in the arteries (dhamanī), it brings forth blood mixed with foam.

When [the fetus] emerges mixed with froth, there is a sound and a sense of nausea; when it reaches the joints of the bones, there is intense friction and a sensation of the body being filled with bones. // 7 //
When located in the bones, there is intense pain of various forms; when situated in the joints, there is swelling similar to that [of the bones];
and when residing in the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha), there is cessation of movement and flatulence (āṭopa). //8//

One should recognize that a foreign body has reached a vital organ (marman) by the presence of constipation, as well as the appearance of food, feces, and urine at the opening of the wound, through the characteristic signs of a pierced vital organ. // 9 //
One should discern [the humors] in the skin and other tissues according to their respective secretions;
however, in those of pure bodies, that [humor] remains in its natural downward direction and heals.
28.10 Just as [the disease] may again cause affliction through the discharge of fluids due to the agitation caused by the provocation of the humors (doṣas), trauma, and so forth,
wherever the skin has been destroyed, there one should apply oil massage (abhyaṅga), fomentation (sveda), and rubbing (mardana).
That place where there is redness, swelling, burning, and throbbing, and where the clarified butter melts away,
or where an ointment dries up quickly, one should declare it to be like a thorn.
28.12b Where the clarified butter melts away, or where an ointment dries up quickly, [that is a sign of a lost muscle].

28.12c–d One should recognize a foreign body (śalya) by its agitation through redness and other symptoms; and likewise, when a muscle has been destroyed, it becomes flaccid due to purification and emaciation.
28.13b–14. One should recognize that an [impacted] bone which has become loose due to traction and is lost within the muscle,
bone, joint, or abdominal cavity can be recovered by means of oiling, fomentation, bandaging, compression, and massage of the bones.

A dislocation of a joint occurs through extension or contraction, like a bone [out of place]; likewise, when the tendons, veins, channels, and arteries are displaced onto an uneven path, [the limb becomes dysfunctional]. (15)

Having placed the patient upon a chariot yoked with horses that has a broken wheel, one should carry him away quickly; then, from his agitation, the physician should indicate the location of the arrow.

The loss of vital points (marman) is not mentioned separately because they are included within the categories of flesh and so forth; however, when accompanied by a foreign body (sa-śalya), it is generally characterized by pain due to provocative treatment. 17.
Briefly stated, one should discern the shape of an invisible foreign body by its wound's appearance as being round, broad, quadrangular, or having three layers. (18)
The two means for their extraction are the reverse and the direct orders;
one should extract them by reversing that [sequence] into the downward and upward directions. (19)
28.19c–d. Whether directed downward or upward, once the [flesh] has been easily removed from that side, one should extract the foreign body by moving transversely;
however, a foreign body located in the chest, the armpit, the groin, or the flank must not be forcibly extracted.

One should not extract a foreign body that is embedded in reverse, one that lacks a point, one that is to be cut out, one with a broad opening, one that destroys the vital organs, one that has disappeared, or one that is harmless. (21)
Then, one should retrieve what is reachable by hand with the hand itself;
furthermore, that which is visible [should be retrieved] from the mouths of lions, snakes, crocodiles, porcupines, and crabs.
Since that which is invisible can be apprehended by its wound-shape through the beaks of the *kaṅka*, *bhṛṅga*, *kurara*, *śarāri*, and the crow; (23)

One should extract [the poison] located in the skin and other tissues with forceps; that situated in the hollows with spatulas; that in the cavities with reed-tubes; and the remainder with the remaining [instruments], as appropriate. (24)
Alternatively, having first incised [the area] with a surgical instrument and then made the wound bloodless,
one should foment it with ghee, bandage it, and prescribe the regimen for the patient.

28.25dv One should perform the treatment with a bandage; however, if it is lodged in a vein or a tendon, one should move it with a probe. A foreign body situated in the heart [should be removed] after frightening the patient with cold water.
28.26ab And if it is caught in the vessels or the tendons, then once it has reached another location, one should extract it according to the circumstances.
If it is difficult to pull out along its natural path, one should likewise extract it from another direction. // 27 //
In the case of one bitten by a bone-crusher, one should extract [the fang] after pressing the man with the feet;
thus it is said, when [extraction] is impossible, [the victim] should be firmly seized by very strong servants.
If the bone is visible, one should remove the man from his feet; if the bone is lost, one should remove the man from his feet;
if the bone is stuck, one should remove the man from his feet; and if the bone is lodged within, one should remove the man from his feet.
Nevertheless, if it cannot be extracted, one should bend the shaft and [remove it] with the bowstring.
One who is well-composed should bind it firmly at the neck-ring. // 29 //
Then, as if raising his head with force, he should strike that well-restrained steed on the crown of its head with the whip of his fivefold [limbs]. (30)

28.30 One should raise it up with force, just as one would extract a splinter; or, in the case of a tree branch, one should arrange it so that, having bound the weak handle with kusha grass, one may extract the splinter. 31.
Having pressed the swelling on the affected limb according to the proper method,
one should extract the protruding portion by striking it with a mallet through a tube.

And by those very [means], one should lead him along the path; however, for one who is stubborn regarding the wrong path, one should subdue him by crushing the ear with a barbed arrow or by seizing him with a tube-mouthed shaft. (33)

Alternatively, one should extract the foreign body by that same method, even if it has entered off-course; a foreign body located in the colon— which lacks ears, has its opening wide open, stands straight, and is situated in the *pakvāśaya*— should be removed by means of purgation (*vireka*).
When a foreign body has entered the passage of the throat due to the sucking of foul wind, poison, breast milk, blood, water, or similar substances, one should insert a thread into the throat. (35)
Then, once the lotus stalk has been cut, one should extract the lotus fiber along with its thread;
having inserted a probe heated by fire and stabilized in water into the channel, one should draw it out. (36)

One should bring out a non-wax object smeared with wax, or a wax object smeared with non-wax from the throat; one should extract a thorn by means of a hair-whorl (keśonduka) that has been soaked in liquids.
28.37b–c: smeared with lac, yet not made of lac; drunk by a "hair-ball" (keśāṇḍaka/keśoṇḍuka).
If, while vomiting, something else is suddenly obstructed by a thread tied [to the nose],
and it cannot be drawn out through the mouth or nostrils, one should push it out from the other side.

One should introduce the foreign body of a morsel through the destruction of the mass of food and drink; one should remove foreign bodies from the eyes, wounds, and minute openings with linen, hair, and water. (39)
One should cause the man to shake himself while submerged in water, with his head hanging down and his body extended;
or one should make him vomit, or bury him face-down in a heap of ashes.
One should blow ash into the mouth until it flows out;
or, when the ear is filled with water, one should churn it with the hand using oil and water.
One should thrust the ear downward, strike it, or suck it. // 41 //

If the insect has entered the ear canal, one should strike it or suck it out; or else, one should fill the ear with salt water, sour gruel (*śukta*), or lukewarm water. Once the insect is dead, the procedure for removing moisture should be applied.
An arrow-head made of lac, or produced from elements such as gold and silver, generally melts away through the heat generated by the body, even if it has remained for a long time. (43)
Not clay, bamboo, wood, horn, bone, ivory, hair, or stone;
nor even after a long time, a horn, bamboo, iron, palm-wood, or a wooden splinter. 44.

28.44b–d. Teeth, hair, stones, and the like are generally not extracted by bending them back, for they quickly cook the flesh and blood; this is especially true if the foreign body is deeply embedded in the flesh and that region does not become inflamed.
28.45c–d. When a foreign body (śalya) is deeply embedded in the flesh, one should then treat it with massage, sudation, purification, depletion, and nourishment;
and with sharp poultices, drinks, food, thick applications, and branding with instruments or the foot.

28.46bv–47. Having brought the area to suppuration through purification, emaciation, or nourishing therapies, one should extract the foreign body by means of incision, probing, or excision, after considering the various forms of the foreign body, its location, and the instruments required.
By various means, the wise man should recognize the thorn and extract it accordingly.
28.47 One should recognize the underlying foreign body (śalya) and then extract it;
for a wound generally arises from suppuration preceded by swelling.
Therefore, one should attend to that very [element], protecting the immature [mind] with great effort.

Through the application of very cold ointments and sprinklings, bloodletting, purification therapies, and so forth, the swelling becomes slight, with low heat and pain, immature (sāma), matching the color of the surrounding skin, hard, and stable. // 2 //

When well-cooled applications and sprinklings [are applied], the swelling is slight, with little heat and pain; it is immature (āma) when it is of a normal color, but as it ripens, it becomes discolored and reddish like a distended bladder. It feels as if it is bursting, accompanied by pricking pain, body aches, and yawning. // 3 //
Accompanied by agitation, aversion, burning sensations, distress, thirst, fever, and loss of sleep,
it liquefies the solidified fat (ājya) and, like a wound, is intolerant to touch.

In its mature stage, there is diminished intensity, flaccidity, pallor, the appearance of wrinkles, elevation at the edges with depression in the center, and softness accompanied by itching, swelling, and other such symptoms. (5)
29.5av When [the fever] has ripened, there is diminished intensity; when it has ripened, there is lassitude; when it has ripened, there is slight pain;
when it has ripened, there is slight pain and exhaustion.
Upon contact, the pus spreads like water within a bladder;
there is piercing pain from wind (vāyu), burning from bile (pitta), and swelling from the increase of phlegm (kapha).
From the redness comes inflammation, and from that, suppuration arises due to the humors (doṣas) together with the blood.
When the suppuration has progressed excessively, the cavity is consumed by the humors and the thin skin.
Covered with folds, dark-brown in color, and with its hair falling out,
the blood in swellings born of phlegm undergoes deep suppuration.

29.8a-c. Covered with folds, dark-colored, and with the signs of ripening indistinct; where there is coldness, swelling, and numbness, along with a color of the skin similar [to the surrounding tissue], slight pain, and a hardness like a stone—[these are the characteristics]. 9.

A wise person, free from doubt, should call that "blood-inflammation" (rakta-pāka) when it occurs in one who has little vitality, is weak, or is a child; or when, due to inflammation, it is excessively aggravated.
29.10 When the suppuration is excessively elevated, or when it is located in the joints of the vital organs (marmas) and so forth, there is tearing; otherwise, there is incision.
In the excision of undigested matter (āma), there is injury to the vessels (sirās) and ligaments (snāyus), as well as excessive hemorrhaging. // 11 //
Excessive pain, cracking, or erysipelas arising from a wound occurs;
furthermore, the pus remaining inside may affect the vessels, ligaments, blood, and flesh. (12)
He who cuts down what is raw out of ignorance, and he who neglects what is ripe—both, once grown large, quickly consume [the person] like fire consumes grass and weeds. (13)
Like fire to a blade of grass,
or like fire to a heap of straw, those two who act without certainty should be known as being like dog-cookers (outcastes).
Before the surgical procedure, one should feed the patient the desired food.
One should know that two who act without certainty are like dog-cookers (outcastes). Before the surgical procedure,
one who is capable of enduring pain should be made to drink the best liquor, which is sharp and intoxicating.
It does not swoon from contact with food, nor does a weapon fail to strike one who is intoxicated by it. 15.
Except in the case of those suffering from fainting, pregnancy, stones, facial diseases,
or abdominal dropsy, the physician, having gathered the necessary instruments, should have the patient face the east.

29.16cv Then, having brought the instruments and positioned himself face-to-face, he should quickly insert [the instrument], avoiding the vital points (*marman*) and other such areas; he should apply the well-sharpened blade in the direction of the hair until the pus is visible. // 17 //

Having quickly secured it facing [the opening], one should extract it all at once; even if the inflammation is very great, one should properly incise it to a depth of two fingers, with an interval of two or three fingers [between incisions]. // 18 //
Having searched thoroughly with the "seeker" [the mind] and having examined it well on all sides—
with the stalks of the fingers and the hairs— according to the location and according to the disposition, (19)
One should make an incision well-divided and free of internal cavities at that very place where one knows the path has gone and where the swelling is located. (20)

29.20b Wherever the lap [of the patient] is extended and broad, so that no defect remains; where there is valor, quick action, a sharp instrument, and an absence of perspiration and trembling. // 21 //
29.21c–d Courage, quickness of action, a sharp instrument, absence of perspiration and trembling, and lack of confusion are praised in a physician during surgical procedures.
29.22 One should make oblique incisions on the forehead, the eyebrows, the gums, and the collarbones.

In the abdomen, the armpits, the eyes, the temples, the lips, the cheeks, the throat, and the groins—other than by means of excision—one commits the offense of severing veins or tendons by cutting transversely. (23)
After the surgical instrument has been applied, one should comfort the patient with soothing words and cold water;
then, having pressed around the wound with the fingers, [one should proceed]. (24)
Having washed it with a decoction and removed the water with a cloth,
[he should fumigate it] with guggulu, agaru, siddhārtha, hiṅgu, and sarjarasa.
One should fumigate with long pepper, vacha, and nimba leaves soaked in ghee,
or with sesame paste, clarified butter, and honey, using the appropriate medicinal substances for each case.
Then one should apply a poisoned wick and cover it with those very [substances];
thereafter, one should place a thick pad of roasted grain flour (saktu) smeared with clarified butter (ghṛta).

29.27b–d. One should cover that [wound] with those very [leaves], place it skillfully, and bind it securely with a cloth bandage; either on the left side or the right, but neither below nor above. 28.

29.28bv With a cloth, being well-composed; cloths that are clean, fine, and firm, along with cotton-wool (kavalya) and hair-filters (vikeśika); fumigated, soft, smooth, and free of folds—these are beneficial for the wound. // 29 //

29.29b–c. One should have the cavities well-cleansed; immediately thereafter, one should perform protection for him to ward off the *rakṣas* spirits. 30. One should always offer oblations (*bali*) to them and wear [the protective substances] upon the head.

Immediately thereafter, one should properly perform protection for the sake of warding off demons; one should always bear upon one's head Lakṣmī, who dwells in the cave, the secret cave, who has matted hair, and who observes celibacy.
Vacā, chattrā, aticchattrā, dūrvā grass, and also white mustard seeds.
Then, on the day after the application of oil, one should prescribe his regimen;
sleeping during the day causes itching, redness, pain, swelling, and suppuration in the ulcer. (32)

[If it is discharged] by means of a dream, one should drink a decoction of the three myrobalans (tri-phalā) mixed with honey; otherwise, one should drink ghee. One should also avoid women who have not bathed after their period, as well as those who are ill, distressed, or whose menstrual flow has ceased. 29.34. Swelling in a wound arises from exertion, and that [swelling] and redness arise from staying awake;
those two and pain arise from sleeping by day, and those [three] as well as death arise from sexual intercourse. 33+(1)
And as for food, it should be according to one's constitution: barley, wheat, and ṣaṣṭika rice;
lentils, mung beans, tuvarī, jīvantī, and suniṣaṇṇaka. (34)
29.34ab As for food that is wholesome according to one's constitution:
young radish, eggplant, *taṇḍulīyaka*, *vāstuka*, *kāravellaka*, *karkoṭa*, *paṭola*, and the fruit of *kaṭukā*. 35.
Rock salt, pomegranate, emblic myrobalan, ghee, and water that has been boiled and then cooled;
well-cooked old śāli rice, unctuous, in small quantity, followed by an abundance of warm water. (36)

29.36 One who eats food that is small in quantity, warm, and predominantly liquid, along with the meat of wild animals, quickly heals a wound. Food that is wholesome, eaten in the proper measure at the right time, undergoes digestion easily.
From indigestion, however, a powerful derangement of the wind and other humors arises;
from that, one may suffer swelling, pain, suppuration, burning sensations, and flatulence. (38)

29.38–39ab. However, when food is undigested, one should avoid new grain, sesame, black gram, liquor, meat that is not from the arid regions, preparations of milk and sugarcane, sour substances, salt, and pungent foods, as these aggravate the wind and other humors.
29.39b–d. Alcohol, non-forest meat, and whatever else is constipating, burning, heavy, or cold—
this group beginning with "new grain" (navadhānyādi) produces all the [three] doṣas in one suffering from a wound.
29.40 For those with ulcers, liquor— which aggravates all the *doṣas* and is sharp, hot, dry, and sour— will quickly destroy the ulcer.
One should fan the patient with *vālaka* and *uśīra*, and one must not shake him about.
He should be fanned with young *uśīra* grass;
he should not prick himself nor scratch, and while moving about,
he should protect himself by listening to pleasing stories told by elderly, virtuous brahmins.
Lying down, he should protect [the wound]. Full of hope for liberation from disease, he removes the ulcer quickly by means of perfected, aged, and twice-born [practitioners].
On the third day, one should again perform the wound-treatment as before. (29.42–43)
One should not perform washing and so forth on the second day;
thus, a wound that is intensely painful and knotted heals slowly. // 44 //
One should not apply a paste (kalka) to a wound that is oily, dry, loose, tight, or poorly applied, nor when there is loose hair; for due to oiliness, moisture will increase. (45)
Excessive cutting of the flesh leads to intense pain and dryness, tearing, and hemorrhage;
whereas loose, overly tight, or improper placement [of the instrument] causes friction against the edges of the wound. (46)

29.46cv A wound that has putrefying flesh, a sinus tract, or a cavity filled with pus— whether caused by bandages that are too loose, too tight, or improperly applied— should be cleansed quickly, for the hair-like parasites (vikeśikās) reside within it. 47 //
One should treat an ulcer that has burst and become excessively inflamed with digestive (pācana) therapies, as well as with diets and poultices that do not excessively aggravate the wound. 48.
29.48–49. One should immediately suture fresh wounds that have opened due to trauma, provided they have not been excessively cleansed;
likewise, one should suture glandular swellings arising from fat that have been scraped, as well as short earlobes.
In the head, eyes, forehead, nose, lips, cheeks, ears, thighs, and arms;
in the neck, forehead, testicles, buttocks, penis, anus, belly, and so forth. (50)
One should apply wounds to deep, fleshy, and stable areas, but not to the groin, the armpits, or other such places that have little flesh or are unstable. (51)
One should suture wounds that have little flesh, are unstable, allow air to pass through, contain a foreign body, or are caused by alkali, poison, or fire; however,
one must first remove loose bone fragments, dried blood, grass, and hair.
Having removed the hair and the hanging flesh, and having severed and set it back in its own place,
he [stitched] the joint-bone while blood remained with sinews, thread, and bark-fibers.
When the blood has subsided and remains within the bone, one should suture it with a thread made of sinew or bark-fibers,
neither too far nor too close, taking care not to pull too little nor too much;
then, having consoled the suffering patient, one should apply honey and ghee melted together to the wound.

29.54 Having pacified the pain, one should apply [the ointment] to the ulcer with *añjana*, linen-soot, *phalinī*, and the fruit of *śallakī*, saturated with honey and ghee, taking either a very small amount or not too much.
Having then pacified the afflicted [wound],
one should apply a plaster made of *lodhra* and *madhuka*, and proceed with the binding and other treatments as before.
A wound whose lips are bloodless should be lightly scratched until blood appears; one should then suture it, for its healing depends upon blood. (56)

One should apply the binding materials after considering the location and other factors; among them, one should scrape a small amount [of the substance] onto a sheepskin, a goat-skin, or silk for warmth, but onto linen for coolness. (29.56–57)
Cold and hot substances—namely cotton, silk-cotton, sinew, and bark;
as well as copper, iron, tin, and lead—are used for wounds where fat and phlegm predominate. (58)
29.58b–c: One should employ a splint made of cotton, sinew, or bark, as well as leather, bark, *kuśa* grass, and so forth, when there is a fracture.
Furthermore, there are fifteen types of bandages, each named according to its specific form. 29.59d: [End of verse]
The treasury, the svastika, the muttolī, the Chinese chain, the entwined [pattern], the bedstead, the crossbar, the box, the canopy, the lap, and the cow’s hood. // 60 //
One should employ the *vitāna*, the *utsaṅga*, the *go*, the *phaṇā*, the *yamaka*, that which is called *maṇḍala*, and the *pañcāṅgī*.
The wise person should apply whichever of these is most appropriately situated in each particular case.
Wherever a vein may be situated, one should apply the probe (kośa) precisely to those respective finger-joints;
the *svastika* [bandage] is prescribed for the ears, armpits, breasts, and joints.

One should apply a cloth-band (muttolī) around the penis, the neck, and so forth; a Chinese-style band (cīna) at the outer corners of the eyes; a cord (dāma) on a constricted part of the body; and likewise, a winding band (anuvellita) upon the limbs.
One should apply the *khaṭvā* bandage to the cheeks, jaws, temples, and the obstruction in the back or abdomen;
the *sthagikā* bandage to the tips of the thumbs, fingers, and penis; and [the same] for inguinal hernias (*antravṛddhi*).
One should employ the *vitāna* (canopy) mudrā on the broad shoulders and so forth, as well as on the head;
likewise, the *vilambinī* (hanging) and *utsaṅga* (lap) mudrās are used on the nose, lips, chin, and other such parts.
A *goṣphaṇa* [scar] occurs at the joints; likewise, a *yamaka* occurs on a double-jointed wound. A scar called *maṇḍala* occurs on a rounded limb, and a *pañcāṅgī* occurs above the collarbone.
One should bind [the patient] firmly on the thighs, buttocks, armpits, groins, and head; likewise on the limbs, face, ears, chest, back, sides, neck, and abdomen. (62)
In cases arising from Vāta and Śleṣman, one should apply a bandage evenly around the penis, scrotum, eyes, and joints; or, if the area is lax, one should apply it so that it is even.

In the case of a balanced [dosha], they should be applied very firmly; in the case of that [dosha] located in its seat, they should be applied very intensely. Furthermore, in the cold season and during spring, those two [poultices] should be removed every three days.

29.64b–d: In that location, [the bandage] should be very tight; likewise during the cold season and in spring, one should release those two every three days. A bandage applied to a site where a tight one is indicated for disorders arising from pitta and blood should be considered moderate, and it should be released every three days.
In a state of equanimity, there is no laxity; likewise, there is no slackness in the underlying intention.
Their release is intended for evening and morning, during the summer and autumn;
[the practitioner] remains unbound, though afflicted by gadflies, mosquitoes, cold, wind, and other such things. (66)
In this case, the medicinal paste may become putrid and will not remain for long; it attains purification or healing only with great difficulty, and once healed, it leaves a discolored mark. (67)
Whether it be bound, powdered, fractured, dislocated, or even split,
and even if the tendons and vessels are severed, the wound heals quickly and easily.
In all activities such as rising and lying down, he is not afflicted;
[the tongue] has upturned lips, is elevated, uneven, hard, and extremely painful. 69.
29.69b–c: One should not cause pain during any of the procedures. When the lip has been elevated, the wound—being even, raised, soft, and painless—quickly becomes purified and heals.
For firm wounds with little flesh that do not heal due to dryness, [the following is prescribed]: 70.
The medicinal preparation should be covered with leaves— according to the specific disorder and the season—
using fresh, unblemished leaves that are well-secured all around with small gaps.

29.71–72. For those suffering from leprosy (kuṣṭha), for those with burns caused by fire, and for those with honey-like diabetes (madhumeha), [the application of] vesicles produced from the milky trees, birch (bhūrja), arjuna, and kadamba— [vesicles] which are not immature, have no holes, are washed clean, and are not rough— is recommended.

In cases of *conduru* poison, the *karṇikā* (eschar) should be cauterized with alkali and treated with anti-poisonous measures; however, it should not be bound [with a ligature] in cases of gangrenous ulceration or severe anal fistula. (73)
One should not apply [bandages] in cases of meat-decay (māṃsapāka), nor when the flesh is sloughing away,
accompanied by pain and burning, spreading through the stages of swelling;
for if these are left unprotected, flies will deposit worms into the ulcer.
While consuming these [worms], they cause pain, swelling, and the discharge of blood;
in such cases, one should employ the *surasādi* group for washing and filling [the wound]. (75)

29.75b–c. A plaster made from the barks of *saptaparṇa*, *karañja*, *arka*, *nimba*, and *rājādana*, ground with cow’s urine, is beneficial for pain, swelling, and the discharge of blood; irrigation with alkaline water is also recommended. 76.

29.76c–d A plaster made from the paste of cow’s urine, or by covering the ulcer with a piece of flesh, shall quickly expel them; however, one should not, out of haste, allow it to heal while the morbid humors (doṣas) remain inside. 77.
Because even with a slight lapse he becomes greatly disturbed, one should avoid indigestion, physical exercise, sexual intercourse, and the like, even when [the wound] has healed. (78)
This procedure, characterized by joy, anger, and even fear, should be followed with diligence for six or seven months until stability arises. (79)

29.79 When those various [emotions] such as joy, anger, or fear arise amidst various reports, one who is diligent should treat them according to the strength of the [underlying] humors (doṣas) and so forth, employing the respective means described in detail in the subsequent [section].
In the Section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna),
among all primary and secondary surgical instruments, caustic alkali (kṣāra) is the best, for it performs many procedures such as excision and incision even in difficult locations. // 1 //

In treatises concerning the administration of emetics, as well as in those that have established its efficacy in cases of extremely severe diseases, it is also prescribed for use in the form of a drink. (2)

If it does not achieve success through that [method], it should be drunk in cases of hemorrhoids, loss of digestive fire, urinary stones, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and artificial poisons;
it should be applied directly for freckles, vitiligo, external hemorrhoids, skin diseases, and numbness. // 3 //

In cases of fistula-in-ano, tumors, glandular swellings, malignant sinus tracts, ulcers, and the like, neither of the two [therapies] should be employed when pitta, rakta, and vāyu are aggravated or when the patient's strength is diminished. (4)
In cases of fistula-in-ano, apacī (scrofula), and glandular swellings; when pitta or blood is aggravated, whether strength is present or absent;
in fever, diarrhea, diseases of the heart and head, anemia, and loss of appetite;
in cases of cataract after purification has been performed, and in swelling affecting all parts of the body—[these are the indications for this treatment]. // 5 //
30.5dv In cases of swelling occurring in all limbs;

in those who are timid, pregnant women, or women in their fertile period; in those with displaced uteri; when food is undigested; in children, the elderly; or when it occurs in the vessels, joints, or vital spots (marmas). // 6 //

In young persons, [bloodletting is contraindicated] in the bones, veins, tendons, suture-lines, throat, navel, in regions with little flesh, and in the testicles, penis, urinary channels, and between the nails. (7)

In a region with little meat, on the penis, the testicles, the glans, between the foreskin and the nail, and except for diseases of the eyelids and the eyes, during cold weather, rain, heat, or foul days,
one should [use] *kālamuṣkaka*, *śamyāka*, *kadala*, and *pāribhadraka*. (30.7–8)
The great tree Aśvakarṇa, Palāśa, Āsphoṭa, Indravṛkṣa, Arka, Pūtīka, Naktamāla, and Aśvamāraka trees. // 9 //
Kākajaṅghā, apāmārga, agnimantha, agni, and tilvaka— these,
fresh with their roots and branches, should be prepared in pieces.
Having gathered four *kośātakī* plants and the awn of barley stalks separately upon a stone slab in a windless place, [he should prepare them]. (11)
Having added the awns of barley and pieces of sudhā-stone to a heap of muṣkaka, one should set them on fire;
then, once the fire has subsided, one should separately burn sesame seeds with *kutala* grass.

Then, having taken one *droṇa* of the ash of lime-stones (*sudhāśman*) made from bundles of sesame stalks, and more than one *muṣkaka* of the other ash, [one should place] each separately in water and urine. (13)
One should strain one *droṇa* of the other ashes with a large cloth using half a *bhāra* [of liquid]; when it has become sharp, clear, and slimy-red, then one should take it. (30.14)
Having taken the alkaline liquid, one should cook it in an iron vessel while stirring; then, as it is being cooked, those sugar-like particles of lime-ash [are added]. 15.
Having placed oyster shells, conch shells, and *śaṅkhanābhi* in an iron vessel,
one should repeatedly heat them until they are fire-colored within a *kuḍava* measure of alkaline solution.

30.16b–c: Having poured [the powder] into an iron vessel containing one *kuḍava* of alkaline water, one should grind it and then add the following as an additive (*pratīvāpa*) using that very same liquid:
finely ground dung from a peacock, a cock, a vulture, a heron, and a pigeon. (17)
Having thoroughly mixed around the four-footed bird, bitumen, realgar, orpiment, and salts, one should then stir it with a ladle.
And when it rises with bubbles like tears and becomes as thick as a linctus, one should then remove it and cool it upon a heap of iron filings. (19)
When it remains with tears [of moisture],
then, having removed it, once it has become cool, this medium alkali should be placed there; however, one should not throw it in after grinding it when it is mild.
Having extinguished it, one should remove it; for a sharp [fever], the counter-potioning is as previously described. // 20 //
Likewise, lāṅgalikā, dantī, citraka, ativiṣā, vacā, svarjikā, kanakakṣīrī, hiṅgu, and the leaves of pūtika; // 21 //
Tālapattrī and viḍa—after seven nights have passed, this sharp [preparation] should be applied for tumors and other ailments arising from vāta, kapha, and fat. (22)
Tālapattrī and viḍaṅga are for these same intermediate [doshas]; another intermediate [remedy] is for the arising of pitta-blood disorders and hemorrhoids.
To provide strength when the water is diminished, one should again add alkaline water. // 23 //
And among those that are moderate, there is another variety which is moderate,
occurring in cases arising from bile, blood, or the rectum.
It is neither too sharp nor too mild, smooth, slimy, swift-moving, white, peaked, easy to extinguish, not prone to dripping, and not excessively painful. (24)
30.24 Not too sharp, mild, and smooth, the alkali possesses tenfold qualities; it performs the work of both the surgical instrument and fire.
As if sucking [the blood] out of excitement, it presses upon the body as if squeezing it. // 25 //
Tracing faults from every side, he uproots them from their very foundation;
having performed his task, he becomes free from affliction and subsides by himself. (26)
When a disease is to be treated with caustic (kṣāra), after it has been incised, scraped, or bled, one should apply the caustic with a probe while the patient's body is covered with a cloth. (27)
30.27dv–28. With the body drenched in a cloth, one should wait for a hundred measures [of blood] while the opening is obstructed in cases of hemorrhoids;
in diseases of the eyelids, one should form a nozzle with the hand over the two eyelids.
Having rolled it up and covered it with a cotton swab, one should apply it to the black portion;
for nasal polyps, an application of alkaline paste as thin as a lotus petal should be used.

30.29–30. For nasal polyps (*ghrāṇārbuda*), however, one should sit facing the sun, elevate the tip of the nose, and hold the medicinal paste for fifty measures (*mātrā*). The same applies to ear polyps (*karṇaja-arśas*).

30.30b–d: Having raised the tip of the nose, one should hold [the breath] for fifty measures; after having applied the alkali with cleansing and having understood [its effect], it should be wiped away.
It should be well-burnt, smeared with ghee and honey, and [washed] with milk, whey, and sour gruel. // 31 //
One should quickly extinguish the caustic by wiping it away; thereafter, one should apply a plaster of sweet and cold substances mixed with ghee.
Furthermore, foods that cause secretions should be eaten to induce moistening.

And if, because its roots are firm, it does not wither even when cauterized with alkali, one should then apply a plaster made of fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), seeds, liquorice (yaṣṭyāhva), and sesame. // 33 //

A paste of sesame seeds mixed with madhuka and smeared with ghee promotes the healing of wounds. A properly cauterized area resembles a ripe jambu fruit in color; if it is black, it is under-cauterized; if it is sunken, it is over-cauterized. (34)

30.34c–d. A burn that resembles a ripe jambū fruit, is depressed, and is characterized by redness, heat, pricking pain, itching, and so forth, is called *durdagdha* (imperfectly cauterized); one should cauterize it again.
In the case of *atidagdha* (over-cauterized), blood flows out, and fainting, burning sensations, fever, and other such symptoms occur. (35)

30.35b–c. That which is over-burnt should be cauterized again, especially in the anal region; for from the cutting away of the anus, there will certainly result obstruction of feces and urine, excessive discharge, loss of virility, or death.
30.36. [The same applies to] the penis. From the cutting away of the penis, there will certainly result obstruction of feces and urine, excessive discharge, loss of virility, or death.

30.36dv There is certain tearing of the anus; 30.36dv there is certain sinking of the anus; 30.36dv there is certain prolapse of the anus. In the nose, it arises from the splitting and contraction of the nasal bridge.
And there would be cognition of objects even in the case of the auditory organ and the others, just like that. // 37 //

Specifically in this case, irrigation with acidic substances, anointing with honey, ghee, and sesame seeds, as well as every action that alleviates Vāta and Pitta and is cooling in nature, are recommended. (38)
For sour [substances] are cold to the touch, whereas alkali is hot; when combined with the former, it quickly attains sweetness. Therefore, one should especially quench it with sour substances. (39)
If administered in excess, even a small amount may become like poison, fire, a weapon, a thunderbolt, or death;
yet, when properly administered by a wise person, it destroys even terrible diseases without delay. (39+1)
Fire is superior even to alkali because those burnt by it do not [re]emerge;
furthermore, it does not require treatment with medicines, alkalis, or surgical instruments once it has been accomplished.
It is joined to the skin, flesh, vessels, tendons, joints, and bones; and to moles, body parts, exhaustion, headache, itching, warts, black spots, and so forth. (41)

30.41b–42. That [cauterization] is to be applied to the joints and bones; skin-burning [cauterization] is performed with a wick, cow-tusk, sun-crystal, arrow, and so forth, for hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, tumors, sinus tracts, malignant ulcers, and the like.

Burning of the flesh occurs due to the application of honey, fats, jambu-fruit, guḍa, and similar substances; it also arises from the obstruction of the eyelid margins, blood loss, the presence of nīlī pigment, or improper incision and other such procedures.

30.43c–d: One should not cauterize with those same [cautery instruments] in cases of obstructed canals, hemorrhaging, improper application of *nīlī* dye, or improper venesection; nor should one cauterize those who have been treated with alkali, those with internal foreign bodies, those with internal hemorrhage, those with perforated viscera, or those suffering from extensive wounds.
One should not cauterize those [wounds] that exclude the use of alkali (kṣāra).

When well-cauterized, one should apply an ointment of ghee and honey, followed by cooling and unctuous plasters. Its symptom, while the blood remains, is characterized by a sound-like discharge accompanied by lymph (lasikā).
When it resembles a ripe palmyra fruit or a pigeon in color, is well-healed, and not excessively painful, it is like a wound properly cauterized;
this applies to all cases, as opposed to those that are poorly cauterized or over-cauterized. (46)
That [characteristic] is fourfold; it is the characteristic of the void together with the void:
the skin becomes excessively discolored, and there is no occurrence of eruptions. // 47 //
30.47ab That [is] fourfold with *tuccha*; 30.47ab that indeed is fourfold with *tuttha*; 30.47ab there, with *tuccha*, 30.47b it is the definition of *tuttha*.

Due to excessive burning, there is a severe burning sensation accompanied by cracking and inflammation; the flesh becomes charred, hangs down, and contracts, while one suffers from the pain of burning and fuming. (48)
The destruction of the vessels (sirā) and so forth, thirst, fainting, deep ulcers, and death [result from excessive depletion];
for that which is depleted, the application of fire, heating, and warm medicine should be administered. (49)

30.49ab Destruction of the vessels and so forth, thirst, and fainting; 30.49cd For *tuttha* [applied] to clotted blood, heating with fire causes excessive pain; when it has dissolved, the pain becomes mild.
In the case of over-burning, one should apply cold and heat at first, and then cold. 50.

Once it has been properly cauterized, one should apply a plaster of *tavakṣīrī*, *plakṣa*, sandalwood, and red ochre mixed with ghee and honey; thereafter, the treatment should be like that for a pitta-type abscess.

When properly cauterized, the treatment for *tukākṣīrī* is like that for a pitta-type abscess (*pitta-vidradhi*). If it is over-cauterized, one should quickly apply all the treatments used for pitta-type erysipelas (*pitta-visarpa*).
However, if it is excessively burnt by oily substances, one should apply a very dry remedy there.
Since surgical instruments, caustics, and fire are the supreme weapons of Death, the physician should therefore apply them correctly and with vigilance. 52+(1)
30.52+(1) One should apply oneself correctly to this; this section on the heart concludes as something like a secret teaching.
Herein, subtle meanings have been indicated in brief, and they shall indeed be expanded upon in every respect. // 53 //
30.53cv Here, the subtle meanings have been indicated: "When the body, its locations, the semen, and the menses are pure, the *sattva*, impelled by its own karma and afflictions..."
The embryo comes into being through the power of causal conditions, like fire from the fire-drill wood. // 1 //

1.1b–c. Impelled by the fruits of its own karma, it gradually grows in the womb through the subtle great elements (mahābhūta) which exist in the form of seeds and are accompanied by the sentient being (sattva), as well as by those produced from the essence of the mother’s food. 2.
Just as the heat of the sun's rays, when refracted through a crystal, does not appear to reach the fuel, so too a sentient being is not seen while proceeding to the womb. // 3 //
Because effects conform to their causes, they possess that very nature;
therefore, a sentient being assumes various forms of birth and appearance, like molten metal. (4)
For this very reason, from the predominance of semen a male is born;
from that of blood, a female; when the two are equal, a eunuch; and furthermore, from the semen and the menses [in equal measure], [the same occurs].

When repeatedly split by the wind (*vāyu*), they produce many offspring according to their respective natures; however, due to the morbid humors (*mala*), they are born from improper wombs (*vi-yoni*) with deformed shapes.
Every month, for three days, a flow of menstrual blood produced from the vital essence (rasa) issues from women;
after the twelfth year, it continues until it reaches its cessation at age fifty.
A woman who has reached the full sixteen years of age unites with a man who has reached twenty;
when the womb, the channels, the blood, the semen, the vital wind, and the heart are pure, [conception occurs]. (8)
She gives birth to a son endowed with vigor; however, if the [parents'] ages are less than that, the fetus will be diseased, short-lived, unfortunate, or may not even come to term.

One should declare semen or blood produced by the humors (doṣas) to be characterized by their respective symptoms as being called "windy," "corpse-like," "knotted," "pus-like," "wasted," or "impure," and as being incapable of producing offspring. // 10 //
1.10c–d: Semen capable of producing offspring is [normal]; that which is discharged with blood is a *kuṇapa*; that which resembles a tumor due to phlegm and wind;
that which resembles pus due to blood and bile; and that which is diminished due to wind and bile.
These [conditions] are difficult to treat; however, that which is incurable has the appearance of urine or feces and arises from the vitiation of all three doṣas.
Furthermore, when the *kuṇapa* (corpselike discharge) is corrupted by vāta and the other doṣas, one should apply its own specific remedies.
One should cause [the patient] to drink ghee prepared with dhātakī flowers, khadira, dāḍima, and arjuna, or else ghee cooked with the asanādi group of drugs. // 13 //

When there is an appearance like a tumor, or when pus and semen are present, or when [the semen] is diminished due to *palāśa* ash, *aśmabhida*, *parūṣaka*, *vaṭa*, and so forth, one should perform the treatment that restores the semen. (14)
One who has undergone oleation, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enema, and unctuous enema should be properly treated with urethral/vaginal enemas (uttara-vasti) when afflicted by disorders of semen.
Once thoroughly purified, one should drink ghee prepared with *hiṅgu*, *sevya*, and other ingredients over a cow-dung fire;
for glandular swellings (*granthi*) and menstrual disorders, one should drink water boiled with *pāṭhā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and *vṛkṣaka*.

1.15b–c. That which is prepared with *hiṅgu*, *sevyā*, and *agni* should be drunk when there is a corpse-like odor, pus, or blood; however, regarding what will be stated concerning *candana* for diseases of the private parts, all of that should be administered as a urethral enema (*sottara-vasti*). 16.
Furthermore, the menstrual blood (ārtava) of a woman with a healthy womb is white, bright, heavy, unctuous, sweet, thick, and abundant; it resembles clarified butter, honey, or oil. (17)

Pure semen is heavy, unctuous, resembling the color of lac juice or rabbit blood, and it becomes free of discoloration when washed; pure semen and menses belong to one who is healthy, and such a couple, being mutually impassioned, [attain union]. 1.18.

The man should be made unctuous with oleaginous substances that promote the birth of a male child, purified [by emesis and purgation], and especially treated with enemas prepared with milk, ghee, and sweet medicinal herbs. (19)

One should treat the woman with oil prepared from sweet medicinal herbs and with *māṣa* beans that increase *pitta*, until her face becomes radiant and slender, and her hips and breasts begin to throb with life. (1.19–20)

One should recognize a woman who has reached her fertile period (ṛtumati) by her emaciated appearance, a serene face, drooping eyes and belly, and a longing for a man; just as a lotus closes its petals when the day has passed. // 21 //
When the fertile period has passed, that womb does not receive the semen;
rather, the blood accumulated over a month [is received] through the two channels during the fertile period. (22)

The wind may expel from the opening of the womb a semen that is slightly dark and odorless, which does not remain within; therefore, for three days following the appearance of the menses, she should contemplate only auspicious things. (1.22) (1.23)
Devoid of cleansing and ornaments, lying upon a bed of darbha grass, she subsists on a small amount of milk-rice or barley-gruel, which serves to cleanse and emaciate her body. (24)
1.24d–25. She who observes the vow of celibacy (brahmacāriṇī) should eat from a leaf, a shallow bowl, or her hand, which cleanses the internal organs and causes emaciation.
Then, on the fourth day, having bathed, pure and wearing white garlands and garments, [she should proceed].
Desiring a son who resembles her husband, she should look upon her husband as if he were before her;
for the fertile period consists of twelve nights, of which the first three are censured. (26)
The first three [lunar days] are censured, as is the eleventh; among the even-numbered days, a son is born, while on the others, a daughter is born.
Then, the teacher should perform the rite for obtaining a son according to the prescribed rule.
In other cases, a son shall be born;
however, for a Śūdra woman who is devoted to salutation, [the rite] is performed without mantras.
In this way, the union shall not be fruitless, and offspring may be obtained according to one's desire.
For the virtuous have said that the secret union of a husband and wife is for the sake of offspring;
yet even in a great lineage, a bad child born is like charcoal to the family. (29)
1.29b The couple should meet in private. 1.29c–d They should desire a son who is not a wick for the family; they should consider what kind of son they wish for, as well as his appearance and conduct.
30. They should consider the people [of the country], their customs, and their possessions.
And at the conclusion of the ritual, the man, having eaten ghee, milk, and boiled rice,
should lie down upon the bed with his right foot first, according to the instruction of the astrologer.
A woman, however, should mount him from his left side on his right flank;
with a diet consisting primarily of oil and black gram, she should there employ the mantra.
And the woman should mount [the chariot] with her left side, [reciting]:
"Thou art a serpent; thou art life; thou art a support on every side."
1.32+1ab You are a serpent; you are the foundation on all sides.
May Dhātṛ establish you; may Vidhātṛ establish you. 32+1b
"May you be endowed with spiritual luster," [he says]. // 32+1c //
"May he be endowed with Brahman-splendor.
Thus [it is said]: "May Brahmā, Bṛhaspati, Viṣṇu, Soma, Sūrya, as well as the two Aśvins, Bhaga, and Mitra-Varuṇa grant me a heroic son. (1.32+1cv) (33)
Having thus comforted one another, they should lie down together, filled with joy;
the woman, her mind fixed on him, should remain lying on her back with her limbs well-positioned.
1.34 Having thus pacified each other, they should dwell together filled with joy;
for in this way, the seed is received when the humors (doṣas) are established in their own locations. However, the sign of immediate conception is the retention of the seed by the womb. 1.35

1.35bv By the humors (doṣas) residing in their own locations; 1.35dv there is retention of the seed in the womb. Satiety, heaviness, throbbing, obstruction of semen and blood, palpitations of the heart, drowsiness, thirst, exhaustion, and horripilation [occur]. // 36 //
In the first month, while still unmanifest, the embryo becomes a *kalala* after seven days; one should perform the *puṃsavana* rites here before it becomes manifest. (37)
For a powerful man-made effort indeed overcomes even fate;
under the asterism Puṣya, one should fashion a human figure made of gold, silver, or even iron.
Having made [the powder] the color of fire and extinguished it in milk, one should drink an añjali of it;
likewise, [one should drink an añjali of] gauradaṇḍa, apāmārga, jīvaka, ṛṣabha, and sairyaka. (39)

One should drink the roots of white bṛhatī ground in water under the Puṣya asterism—either singly, in pairs, in threes, or all together—and one should personally apply them with milk into the nostrils. (40)

One should sprinkle the root of the Lakṣmaṇā plant with milk on the right side for the sake of a son, and on the left side with the desire for a daughter; this bestows the birth and stability of a son.
Likewise, one should drink eight *vaṭa* sprouts through the nose or the mouth,
and one should apply life-sustaining herbs both externally and internally.
Likewise, she who bears the embryo should be attended with eight *vaṭa* buds and served by her husband and servants with things that are pleasant and beneficial;
and one should always attend to her with fresh butter, ghee, and milk.
Excessive sexual indulgence, physical exertion, heavy loads, heavy clothing, staying awake or sleeping at improper times, and sitting on hard or uneven seats. // 44 //
1.44ab Excessive sexual intercourse and physical exertion; 1.44cd waking and sleeping at improper times;
1.44d sitting in a rigid, difficult, or squatting posture.
The suppression of grief, anger, fear, agitation, and intense faith; fasting; travel; and the consumption of pungent, hot, heavy, or constipating food. (45)

1.45c–d She should avoid fasting and other such practices, pungent or hot foods, blood, red clothing, looking into pits or wells, liquor, meat, sleeping on one's back, and whatever else women do not desire. 46.

1.46–47ab. If there is blood, nakedness, a cavity, or likewise a discharge of blood, the bladder remains pure until the eighth month; by these [signs], the fetus may be discharged as immature, or it may wither or die within the womb.
1.47–48. Thus, the fetus may be miscarried while still unformed (*āma*);

or, through *vāta*-provoking factors, the fetus may become humpbacked, blind, dull-witted, or dwarfed; through *pitta*-provoking factors, it may become bald, tawny, afflicted with vitiligo, or pale; and through those characterized by *kapha*, it may likewise be deformed.
One should overcome her diseases with medicines that are mild, pleasant, and not sharp.
In the second month, from the *kalala*, there arises either the *ghana*, the *peśī*, or the *arbuda*. (49)

From these [humors], male, female, and neuter [fetuses] arise respectively; therein, the characteristic of the manifest [fetus] consists of emaciation, heaviness of the abdomen, fainting, vomiting, and loss of appetite. (50)

1.50–51. Emaciation, heaviness in the abdomen, yawning, salivation, lassitude, the appearance of the line of hair (roma-rājī), a craving for sour things, full breasts with milk and dark nipples—[these are the signs]. 51.
Swelling of the feet, burning sensations, and various other cravings arise;
for his heart is born from the mother, and it is joined with the mother's heart. (52)
1.52–53ab. Swelling of the feet, a burning sensation during digestion, and consequently a loss of appetite for food occur; therefore, the neglect of her cravings is undesirable for a pregnant woman.
Even if it is unwholesome, it should be given to her in small quantities, combined with something wholesome.
The obstruction of faith is not desired, nor is the disparagement of faith;
for through the destruction of faith, there occurs either a deformity or even the miscarriage of the fetus.
In its third month, the five limbs of this [fetus] become manifest. (1.54)
1.54ab Due to the obstruction of faith, there arise the head, the two thighs, the two arms, and the birth of all subtle limbs;
for knowledge regarding pleasure and pain occurs simultaneously with the head and the other [limbs]. (55)

But the birth of all its subtle limbs and the consciousness of pleasure and pain [occur]. A cord is attached at the navel of the embryo to the heart of the mother; by means of this, it attains nourishment, just as a field is irrigated by a canal. (1.56)
By this [food], he attains nourishment;
in the fourth month, the limbs become manifest, and in the fifth, consciousness;
in the sixth, the sinews, vessels, hair, strength, complexion, nails, and skin [are formed].
In the seventh [month], he is nourished by all states of being, with all his limbs fully complete. (58ab)
The humors, compressed by the fetus, take refuge in that heart. // 58cd //
They cause itching, a burning sensation, and eruptions in pregnant women. 58ef.

In that case, fresh butter is beneficial; likewise, food that has been prepared with jujube fruits, water, and sweet medicinal herbs—being light, sweet, containing little salt or oil, and easy to digest—is wholesome. (59)
One should smear the thighs, breasts, and abdomen with a paste of sandalwood and uśīra, combined with the best blood of a bamboo-horned deer, a common deer, or a rabbit. (60)
Having anointed [the wound] with oil prepared from *aśvaghna* leaves, one should massage it;
then one should sprinkle it again with the juices of *paṭola*, *nimba*, and *mañjiṣṭhā*.
One should practice cleansing with a decoction of dārvī and madhuka;
for at the eighth [month], the *ojas* circulates repeatedly and alternately between mother and child. (62)

Because of that, the two become respectively withered and joyful; an infant born there does not survive due to the instability of its vital energy (*ojas*), while a woman becomes subject to doubt regarding her life.
In these two cases, the child may not survive; or, having been born, it does not live.

In this situation, milk-gruel (kṣīrapeyā) mixed with ghee should be administered as a drink, followed by an oil enema (anuvāsana) prepared with ghee and drugs of the sweet group (madhura). Likewise, for the sake of purification, a purgative made from old cow dung should be given.
An oil enema (anuvāsana) with ghee is beneficial;
it is recommended as a decoction enema (basti) prepared with a decoction of dried radish and sour jujube,
along with a paste of dill (śatāhvā), oil, ghee, and rock salt.

But even if one day has passed since that [conception], the time for birth will not occur beyond that; however, if it is retained in the womb by the wind (vāta), it may undergo transformation after a year.
1.66 Even when that [period] has passed by only one day,
in the ninth month, it is recommended that he eat rice with meat broth and fat, or thick gruel (yavāgū) with abundant oil, or the previously mentioned unctuous enema (anuvāsana). 1.67.

She should eat rice with unctuous meat broth, and from that very same [mixture], one should constantly insert a tampon (picu) into her vagina. For daily bathing, cold water infused with the decoction of leaves of Vāta-alleviating plants is beneficial.
With limbs free from oiliness, she should not remain [in bed] for more than nine months;
previously, she was one whose breast milk flowed from the right breast and who moved primarily on her right side.

She who delights in inquiries concerning the pregnancy-longings for a male child, who sees dreams of males, and whose right side of the belly is elevated while the fetus is well-rounded [is pregnant with a son]. (70)
She who desires union with a man gives birth to a son, otherwise she gives birth to a daughter;
she is fond of dancing, instrumental music, song, perfumes, and garlands. (71)
That [prognosis] is impotent when there is a mixture [of signs]; in that case, it is middling if the abdomen is elevated.
Twins result from elevation on both sides, as if situated in two hollows within the abdomen.
And before the ninth month, she should take up residence in the birth-chamber in an auspicious location, well-provided with all necessary materials on a favorable day. (73)
1.73b–74 She should take refuge in the maternity chamber and await the birth there, surrounded by female attendants.
On the day of delivery or the following day, there occurs exhaustion, looseness of the abdomen and eyes, and fatigue.
1.74c–d When delivery is near, there is exhaustion, heaviness in the lower body, loss of appetite, salivation, and frequent urination;
there is also pain in the thighs, abdomen, waist, back, heart, bladder, and groin. 75.
There is pain from the dilation of the birth canal, piercing sensations, throbbing, and discharge;
following the emergence of the afterbirth (āvi), there is then the flow of the amniotic fluid.

Then, when she had conceived and performed the auspicious rites of protection, holding a fruit with a male name in her hand and having been sprinkled with warm water mixed with fragrant unguents, (77)

One should repeatedly have her drink lukewarm gruel (peyā) mixed with ghee, which has been smeared [with oil] and sprinkled with warm water; she should be lying on the ground on her back with her legs slightly flexed and her limbs anointed.
One should massage below the navel and induce yawning and walking; thus the fetus moves downward, for that is its sign upon release from the heart. (79)
Having entered the womb, the fetus stays above the bladder;
then, as labor pains hasten her, one should cause her to ascend the bed.
When labor comes at 1.80 cv (cubits), they urge her on; then, when the fetus has descended, one should dilate her birth canal.
She should first push gently, and then more firmly until delivery.
One should treat her birth canal and repeatedly gladden her with the sounds and water of the words "a son is born.
In this way, the vital breaths, which have been exhausted by the pains of labor, return.
If there is obstruction of the fetus, one should fumigate the birth canal with the sloughs of black snakes and hold the root of *hiraṇyapuṣpī* in the hands and feet.
In the case of *suvarcalā* or *viśalyā*, even when the placenta has not fallen, this [procedure] should be performed; likewise, having lifted her up by the arms, one should cause her to tremble.
This is the procedure: having thus raised her up, one should cause her hips to tremble by [shaking] her arms; one should strike with the heel and firmly press the buttocks.
One should touch the palate and throat with the braid and apply the milk of the *snuhī* plant to the head. (85)
An application and fumigation for the vagina should be performed using *bhūrja*, *lāṅgalikī*, *tumbī*, snake skin, *kuṣṭha*, and *sarṣapa*, either individually, in pairs, or all together. (86)
One should administer vaginal fumigation and anointment;
or one should cause [the patient] to drink a paste of *kuṣṭha* and *tālīśa* with the scum of wine (*surā-maṇḍa*),
or with the broth of *kulattha* beans, or with *bālbaja* liquor.
Or [one may use] an asava prepared from bilva;
or mustard oil with *śatāhvā*, mustard seeds, cumin, drumstick, long pepper, and *citraka*;
or mustard oil with asafoetida, costus, and *madana*—[these should be taken] with urine and milk.
Oil prepared with these is beneficial for administration into the rectum or as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) into the vagina;
it is made from a paste of śatapuṣpā, vacā, kuṣṭha, kaṇā, and sarṣapa. (89)
Or, if [the fetus] is in the birth canal, an oil enema (anuvāsana) or a decoction enema (nirūha) containing unctuous substances and salt quickly causes the other [uterus] to descend;
for wind (vāyu) is the cause of their entanglement, and that [fetus] emerges quickly upon its conquest.

A skilled woman should remove [the fetus] with her hand, which has been smeared with oil and has well-trimmed nails; she should then massage the woman's body and the vaginal canal, once the fetus has been released, with oil.
In cases of the disease called makkalla, as well as in headache and abdominal pain, one should administer well-powdered yavakṣāra with ghee or warm water. // 92 //

Or she may give rice-water mixed with the powders of jaggery, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and the three aromatics (trijātaka); then, a woman should attend to the child according to the customary care for infants.
A woman who has recently given birth and suffers from hunger should drink a large dose of either oil or ghee containing the five spices (pañcakola), followed by warm jaggery water.
Or, by means of water containing wind-subduing herbs, the wind is likewise not provoked; furthermore, the vitiated blood is purified. This procedure should be followed for two or three nights. (95)
Or, so that the wind (vāyu) does not become aggravated, one who is unfit for oleation (sneha) should follow this very procedure without oleation.
And once she has drunk [the medicine], one should wrap her abdomen with a cloth soaked in a mixture of the two [substances].
When it has been digested, she should bathe and drink a gruel prepared with the aforementioned medicinal herbs;
after three days have passed, she should drink one prepared with a decoction of the Vidārī group of drugs.
A beneficial gruel enriched with fats, or milk according to suitability, is wholesome; after seven nights, nourishing therapy administered gradually is beneficial for her. (98)

After seven nights have passed, or even if twelve days have not yet elapsed, one should not consume meat. One should attend to the woman who has recently given birth with great care, for her illness is difficult to cure. (1.98–99)

1.99bv One should certainly not administer meat [at this stage], due to the pain of fetal growth, labor, discharge, bleeding, and distress; likewise, for one and a half months, there should be restraint regarding pearl necklaces and other such luxuries. 100.
She is designated as *gatasūtā* (one who has given birth) again upon the appearance of her menses. // 100½ //
"Due to the improper maintenance of the body, the consumption of things to be avoided by a pregnant woman, or due to disease;
or when menses are seen, or when there is pain—[one should apply] external and internal unctuous and cooling [treatments]. (1)
2.1bv Or, due to disease, one may apply, through service [of massage],

cotton-pads or woolen cloths that have been repeatedly moistened and smeared with a paste of lotus stalks, *śītala* (a cooling substance), milky trees, and bark, along with clarified butter; these should be held in the vagina or the bladder.

2.2cv One should insert [a tampon] smeared with hundred-times-washed ghee into the vagina and the womb; one should then immerse the woman in that water [containing] sugar, honey, and the filaments of kumuda, kamala, and utpala lotuses. // 3 //
One should lick milk mixed with ghee, or eat śṛṅgāṭaka and kaseruka;
one should drink milk together with kāntā, lotus root, śālūka, and the fibers of the udumbara fruit.
One should eat red *śāli* rice with milk boiled with *kākolī*, the two types of *balā*, *madhuka*, and sugarcane,
along with honey and sugar.
Or, omitting the purification, one may perform what is prescribed for blood using the meat of wild animals;
for a woman whose three months are not yet complete, one should treat her after having rejected [the blood]. // 6 //
One should follow the regimen prescribed for wind (vāta), with the exception of [heavy] food; and when there is an excess of undigested matter (āma), cold and dry treatments are desired.
Fasting, as well as thick grass, ushira, guduchi, aralu, and coriander [are beneficial].
Durālabhā, parpaṭaka, candana, ativiṣā, and balā, boiled in water, should be drunk; and grasses and grains should be used as food. (8)

2.8dv When raw matter (*āma*) has been conquered, one should eat grass, grains, and the like with soups of mung beans and so forth; [once that is digested], one should follow the previous regimen starting with unctuous foods.
If a miscarriage occurs, one should drink strong liquor according to one's capacity. // 9 //
For the sake of purifying the womb and for the forgetting of pain, she should then drink a dry gruel prepared with the five light roots (pañcamūla). // 10 //

One who does not drink intoxicants should drink a gruel prepared as a paste in the *pañcakaulika* decoction, using the five [herbs] beginning with *bilva*, along with sesame, *uddālaka*, and rice. (11)
In this manner, for as many days as there are months [of the period], the sequence of gruel and so forth is prescribed when [the limb] has fallen;
it should be light, without fat or salt, and combined with digestive stimulants. (12)

2.12d–13ab For this regimen, combined with digestive stimulants (dīpanīya), is intended for the purpose of moistening and drying the humors (doṣas) and tissues (dhātus). Subsequently, unctuous substances, food, enemas, and those that are strengthening, digestive, and life-sustaining [should be administered].
When the great embryo has attained its essential substance, yet fails to achieve further growth due to an obstruction of the birth canal, it remains within the womb, throbbing with life. (14)
They call that "sitting" (upaviṣṭaka); by it the abdomen does not increase, due to grief, fasting, emaciation from dry foods, and so forth, or else from excessive discharge from the womb. // 15 //
When the wind (vāta) is provoked, the fetus becomes emaciated and withers; this condition is called nāgodara.
In this state, even though the abdomen is enlarged, it diminishes and throbbing occurs only after a long time.
2.16bv That [condition] is *nāgodara* (elephant-belly) due to the fetus;

for those two, one should provide satiety with ghee, milk, and meat broths prepared with nourishing, wind-alleviating, and sweet substances, and one should cause them to eat raw flesh containing fetuses. // 17 //
And by means of those very vehicles for travel, there is the agitation of Subhikṣā;
in the [region] called Līna, which is motionless, there are born hawks, cattle, fish, cranes, and peacocks. (18)
And for one who has been well-satiated by those very [drugs], juices made from mung beans and radishes mixed with plenty of ghee should be given;
she should also drink young *bilva* fruits, sesame seeds, mung beans, and roasted grain flour (*saktu*) with milk. (19)
She should habitually consume ghee, meat, or honey, and apply oil massages to her waist;
she should also constantly gladden her [the husband]. In this way, the fetus develops. (20)
Otherwise, even after many years of nourishment, the fetus may be born with great difficulty or not at all;
however, one should quickly overcome the upward movement of wind (udāvarta) in a pregnant woman by means of unctuous substances (sneha).

For he may kill a pregnant woman along with her fetus by means of enemas that are unsuitable, due to the excessive accumulation of morbid humors in the fetus caused by unwholesome things or even by fate. (22)
When the fetus has died, the abdomen becomes cold, rigid, distended, and intensely painful; there is a cessation of fetal movement, vertigo, thirst, labored breathing, and exhaustion. (23)
2.23ab If [the fetus] dies within, the abdomen becomes cold, rigid, distended, and extremely painful; there is restlessness, drooping of the eyes, and the failure of the birth-pains (āvī) to arise.
Having sprinkled her with lukewarm water, one should grind [the following] and smear it upon the vagina: 2.24cd [The text continues with the medicinal paste.]
One should repeatedly fill it with jaggery, fermenting agent, and salt, as well as with ghee and a paste made from the resin of *śālmali* and *atasī*. (25)
If the fetus with its membranes does not fall due to mantras and yogic applications, then the physician, having sought permission from the Lord, should extract it quickly and with great effort. (26)
2.26cd–27ab Then, having asked the lord for permission, the physician,
having anointed his hand and the vulva with a brush made of *śālmali* fibers mixed with clarified butter,
should [insert] the hand itself; by that same means, he may also correct a limb that is positioned unevenly.

2.27d–28. And if the body is positioned unevenly, one should bring it back to its natural state through stretching, pressing, squeezing, shifting, lifting, and so forth; then, having brought it straight toward the birth canal, one should draw it out in accordance with the natural direction.

2.28c–d He who, being bent, enters the womb head-first in the natural order, one should pull him out by means of the hands, feet, and head; likewise, he who is bent and enters with one foot into the womb and the other into the anus.
Those two fools named Viṣkambha deserve the cutting of weapons;
in that case, the ritual action is recommended with the maṇḍala-finger weapon.
One should not insert a sharp-pointed incision blade into the vagina;
rather, having first opened the cranial bones, one should clear the passage. // 31 //
Then, having firmly grasped either the armpit, the chest, the palate, or the chin, the skilled [practitioner] should pull [the fetus] out with the "fetal hook" (garbha-śaṅku).

Then, having cut off the arm of one whose abdomen is distended with wind (vātādhmātodara) and which is attached to the shoulder—provided the head is not severed—at any one of these locations: the armpit, the chest, the palate, or the chin; or even at the eye-sockets or the cheeks. (2.32–33)
Having torn open the abdominal cavity and drawn the intestines outward,
or likewise for one whose [bowel] is stuck in the pelvis, one should split open the pelvic bones.
Whichever part of the fetus should become stuck due to the force of the wind, one should cut that very part into pieces and extract it properly, while protecting the woman with great effort. (35)
2.35–36. Cutting those various parts and extracting them improperly, the vitiated *vāyu* indeed causes manifold movements within the fetus;
therefore, one who is not of small intellect should act with due regard for the specific stage [of development].
One should cut out the fetus while it is still alive, for it would kill the mother;
once its life has departed, it should not be neglected even for a moment, lest it [kill] oneself as well. (37)

One should abandon a woman who is afflicted by discharge from the womb, loss of restraint, exhaustion, or labored breathing; one who has foul-smelling eructations, whose limbs are cold, or whose fetus is dead. // 38 //
Then, the physician should cause another [arrow] that is not falling to fall as previously described;
once the shaft has been thus extracted, he should sprinkle the wound with warm water. (39)
Then, one should insert an oil-soaked tampon into the vagina of the woman whose body has been anointed;
by this, the vagina becomes soft and her pain is alleviated. (40)
Then, one should administer a powder, a paste with a fatty medium, or a decoction made from *dīpyaka*, *ativiṣā*, *rāsnā*, *hiṅgu*, *elā*, and the five types of *kolaka*. (41)
Then one should have her drink that decoction;
likewise, for the purpose of discharging the morbid humors and for the alleviation of pain, [one should give] kaṭukā, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, śāka, tvak, hiṅgu, and tejinī.
For three nights one should take *śāka*, bark, *hiṅgu*, and *tejanī*; likewise for seven days, one should drink only oil.
In the evening, one should drink *ariṣṭa* as well as well-prepared *āsava*.
One should insert tampons of a decoction of śirīṣa and kakubha into the vagina;
furthermore, whatever other complications may arise, one should treat them according to their respective [specific remedies]. (44)

Milk prepared with wind-alleviating (vāta-hara) herbs is beneficial for ten days in one's diet; likewise, meat broth is beneficial for ten days, provided that the food is light, wholesome, and taken in small quantities. 45.
Devoted to sudation and massage, she should employ oleaginous substances such as *balā*-oil and others; after four months have passed, she should gradually partake of pleasant things. (46)
Six parts of the decoction of *balā* roots, as well as six parts of milk, and ten parts each of barley, jujube, horse gram, and the ten roots combined; (47)
One part of the decoction and fourteen parts of oil [should be combined], along with two types of medā, dāru, mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of kākolī, and candana. (48)
And fourteen parts of oil [should be added] along with śārivā, kuṣṭha, tagara, jīvaka, ṛṣabha, saindhava,
kālānusāryā, śaileya, vacā, aguru, and punarnavā. // 49 //
With the juices of kālānusārī, śaileya, aśvagandhā, varī, kṣīraśuklā, yaṣṭī, varā,
śatāhvā, śūrpaparṇī, elā, tvak, and pattraka, finely ground into a paste; (2.49–50)
Oil cooked over a mild fire conquers all disorders caused by Vāta;
