it is highly esteemed for women after childbirth, for children, and for those afflicted in their vital organs (marmans), bones, or who are emaciated. 51.

2.51–52. It is highly esteemed for those suffering from wasting due to injury; it conquers fever, abdominal tumors (gulma), seizure disorders (graha), insanity, urinary obstruction, and hernia (antra-vṛddhi).
It is favored by Dhanvantari and removes diseases of the female reproductive tract and consumption (kṣaya).
If the abdomen of a woman who has passed away at the birth canal throbs,
then one should quickly cut her open and extract the infant at the time of birth.
Madhuka, śākabīja, payasyā, and suradāru; aśmantaka, black sesame seeds, tāmravallī, and śatāvarī. // 54 //
2.54b–c: Payasyā and devadāru;
vṛkṣādanī, payasyā, and the creeper utpala-śārivā;
anantā, śārivā, rāsnā, padmā, and madhuyaṣṭikā.
2.55b latā and utpala-śārivā; 2.55d padmā or madhuyaṣṭikā; 2.55d padmāhvā or madhuyaṣṭikā; 2.55d padmaka or madhuyaṣṭikā.

Ghee prepared with the two types of *bṛhatī*, *kāśmarya*, the bark of the sprouts of milky trees (*kṣīrin*), *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *śigru*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *madhuparṇikā* [is used for this purpose]. (56)
Ghee prepared with the two types of *bṛhatī*, *kāśmarya*,
the shoots and bark of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīrin*),
*śṛṅgāṭaka*, lotus stalks (*bisa*), grapes (*drākṣā*), *kaseru*, *madhuka*, and sugar [is beneficial].
These seven formulations with milk are completed by half-verses each. // 57 //
If the fetus miscarries during the seventh month, one should administer [a decoction] prepared from wood-apple, bilva, bṛhatī, paṭola, sugarcane, and nidigdhikā. (58)
In the eighth month, one should administer milk boiled with the roots of *paṭola*, *ikṣu*, and *nidigdhikā*;
likewise, in the ninth month, [milk] with *śārivā*, *anantā*, *payasyā*, and *madhuyaṣṭi*.
In the tenth month, one should administer prepared milk with *payasyā*,
or alternatively, with *yaṣṭimadhuka*, *nāgara*, and *amaradāru*.
Those lacking in knowledge declare that the retained menstrual blood of a woman is the embryo;
however, because it possesses the form of an embryo, when it is discharged by pungent, hot, and sharp substances, there remains only the blood itself.

The dull-witted say that the fetus is carried off by the *bhūtas*, because they have not seen the carrying away of a physical form; or else, because the *bhūtas* feed on vital energy (*ojas*), the mother of the fetus would not be neglected by those unstable beings.
"The body consists, in brief, of six parts: the trunk, the head, the two arms, and the two thighs; its minor limbs (pratyaṅga) include the eyes, the heart, and so forth. (1)
3.2c–d: In ether, air, fire, water, and earth, there is a successive increase of one quality each;
The tongue, the moisture of taste, and the nose are watery; the bone is earthy.
Here, the soft parts—blood, flesh, marrow, the rectum, and so forth—are born of the mother.
That which is inherited from the father consists of the stable elements: semen, the channels, bones, hair, and so forth;
while the conscious consists of the mind, the sense organs, and birth in various wombs. (5)

The mind is born of the self; the senses are born of habituation; while longevity, health, lack of lethargy, luster, strength, the birth of the body, its maintenance, growth, and steadiness are born of the nutrient essence (rasa). // 6 //
3.6av Longevity, health, and well-being arise from suitability;
[likewise] purity, faith in the hereafter, and an inclination toward virtuous conduct constitute the quality of *sattva*.
Excessive talkativeness, pride, anger, hypocrisy, and envy constitute the quality of *rajas*. (7)
Pride, anger, hypocrisy, and envy;
fear, ignorance, sleep, laziness, and despondency—these constitute the body composed of the elements (bhūtamaya). Within it, there are seven layers of skin produced from blood.
Just as cream arises from milk being heated, so too the moisture within the elements and the internal cavities, when matured by its own respective heat, is produced. (9)
Covered by phlegm and sinews, the one called *kalā* is like the heartwood of wood;
these seven [tissues] have seven supports each, beginning with blood, in successive order. (10)

3.10–11. Covered by phlegm and ligaments, [the receptacles] are situated below the blood; in order, the others are known to be those of phlegm, undigested food, bile, digested food, wind, and urine. The womb is the eighth [receptacle], found in women between the receptacles of bile and digested food.

The components of the visceral cavities situated therein are the heart, the kloman, the lungs, the liver, the spleen, the omentum, the two kidneys, the navel, the bladder, the intestines, and the urinary bladder. (12)
The heart, the kloman, and the lungs—these ten are the seats of life: the head, the tongue-attachment, the throat, the blood, the heart, the navel, the bladder, semen, ojas, and the anus. (3.12–13)
3.13d–14: One should specify sixteen distinct structures in the body: the bladder, the semen, the ojas, the anus, the webs, and the tendons (kaṇḍarāḥ).
There are six tufts (kūrcāḥ) and seven sutures (sīvanyaḥ), located in the penis, the tongue, and the head.

3.14cv There are six *kūrca*s and seven *sevanī*s; one should avoid these with the surgical instrument. There are four muscular cords (*māṃsa-rajjū*), fourteen bony unions (*asthi-saṃghāta*s), and eighteen *sīmanta*s. 15.
3.15 One should avoid these with the surgical instrument:
three hundred and sixty bones, together with the teeth and nails;
however, Dhanvantari has stated that there are two hundred joints.
3.16ab The son of Atri declared that there are two thousand one hundred and sixty bones;
for men, there are nine hundred ligaments and five hundred muscles.

3.17c–d There are nine hundred ligaments (snāyu); 3.17d–18a there are five hundred muscles (peśī), twenty more in women, which are located in the genital tract and the breasts. Ten root-vessels (mūla-sirā) reside in the heart; they [pervade] the entire body from all sides. 18b–d.

3.18b–d. Originating from the womb and the breasts, these channels, which consist of rasa, carry the *ojas*; for all physical activity is bound to it. They have thick roots and extremely subtle tips, like the spreading lines on a leaf.
They are further divided, and thus there are seven hundred of them;
however, one should not pierce even a single one among those hundreds within each branch.
3.20c–v There, in each individual branch, there is one vessel named Jālandharā and three that are situated internally.
In the pelvis there are sixteen times two [of these], and of those, two are in each groin. 21.
One should touch with the instrument eight [points], two each on the two young hip-bones (kaṭīka-taruṇa), but one should avoid the single upward-pointing [point] in each of those two sides. 22.
3.22dv One should avoid the upward-moving veins;
there are twenty-four on the back along both sides of the spinal column.
Among them, one should not touch with the surgical instrument the two upward-moving veins located there. // 23 //

3.23b–d. When they are located on the sides of the spinal column, they are like those on the back; when they are situated in the abdomen above the urethra, one should not touch the two [veins] on either side of the line of hair with a surgical instrument.
There are forty [veins] in the chest; one should not pierce fourteen of them:
two each in the breasts, the *rohitaka*, their roots, and the heart. (25)
One each on the two [bones] called *apastambha*, as well as on the two *apālāpa*s; likewise, there are the *nīla*s, the *manye*s, and the *kṛkāṭikā*s on the neck, just as on the back. (26)
In the case of a fracture, one should avoid the eight and sixteen *mātṛkā* bones;
among those sixteen at the jaws, two are for the function of binding the joints.

3.27b–c. One should abandon these sixteen [channels] on the tongue, as they are like those on the jaw; below them are two for the perception of taste, two for the production of speech, and fourteen in the nose. 3.28.
There are twenty [muscles] that perceive smell, one of which goes to the palate; and there are fifty-six for the functions of closing and opening the eyes. (29)
One should avoid two on each of the outer corners of the eyes, making six for those;
sixty are located on the nose and eyes, and one is situated on the forehead. // 30 //
In that regard, one should avoid one, two, likewise two curls, four at the ends of the hair, and seven; thus, among those [lines], there are sixteen here on the ears.

Two [channels] are for perceiving sound, and the [other] channels are supported by those very [bones]; two are located at the junction of the temples, and there are twelve of them on the crown of the head. // 32 //
Each one is described individually as being situated separately above the parting of the hair; thus, the veins have been described for each limb in order to show that they are not to be pierced. (33)
In that regard, there are ninety-eight points in the body that are not to be pierced in their entirety;
they are mixed, knotted, minute, curved, and situated at the joints. (34)
Of those seven hundred [channels], one quarter flows separately as blood;
thus the impurities remain, being either afflicted by wind, bile, and phlegm, or pure. (35)
They sustain the body, or otherwise, they afflict it;
in that state, the veins become dusky-red, subtle, and alternately full and empty in an instant. (36)

Those that are pulsating carry wind (vāta) and blood; those that are warm to the touch and flow rapidly carry bile and blood; furthermore, those that are blue-yellow in color carry phlegm (kapha). (37)
White, unctuous, firm, and cool [veins indicate] a combination of doshas when their signs are mixed; hidden, level-positioned, and unctuous [veins indicate] Rohiṇī, which is pure blood. 38.
Twenty-four vessels are connected to the navel; the navel is surrounded by them, just as the hub of a wheel is surrounded by its spokes. (39)
3.39c–v Enveloped by these [channels], this body is sustained by them above, below, and across;
[these include] the channels, the two nostrils, the two ears, the two eyes, the anus, the mouth, and the urethra. 40.
The two breasts and the menstrual flow—these three are the additional [vital points] of women;
they say there are thirteen internal channels that are the abodes of life. 41.

The channels carrying vital breath, the bodily constituents, waste products, water, and food become corrupted by the indulgence in unwholesome things, leading to disease; when purified, they lead to well-being. (42)
The channels are the same color as their own elements; they are circular, thick, and minute, and in shape they are long and resemble spreading tendrils.
Whatever food or lifestyle is balanced in its defects and qualities, yet discordant with the bodily constituents (dhātus), that is a corrupter of the channels (srotas). // 44 //
Excessive flow, stagnation, or even the formation of knots in the vessels, or their movement along an abnormal path—these are the signs of the vitiation of the channels (srotas). // 45 //

3.45cd–46ab: The characteristic signs of the vitiation of the channels (*srotas*) are as follows: the openings of the channels in the body are minute like lotus fibers (*bisāni*) and extend far; it is through these that the nutrient essence (*rasa*) is accumulated.

In the case of piercing the channels (srotas), however, there occur delusion, trembling, flatulence, vomiting, and fever; along with delirium, colic, and the obstruction of feces and urine, or even death itself. (47)
Therefore, the physician, having rejected [the case of] a wound pierced by a stream, should treat it after carefully extracting the foreign body according to the procedure for fresh wounds. 48.

The bile that digests food is called *pācaka* (the digestive), as previously mentioned; it is the heat (*ūṣmā*) of the humors (*doṣa*), tissues (*dhātu*), wastes (*mala*), and so forth—this is the teaching of Ātreya. (49)
Slightly to the left of the navel is the orb of the sun;
in its center is a gentle orb, and in the center of that, fire is situated. 49+1.
Merely concealed by the fetal membrane, like a lamp within a glass vessel. // 49+2ab //
The *grahaṇī* is considered so because it seizes (*grahaṇa*) food by means of that [pitta] as its substrate;
in the opinion of Dhanvantari, it is the very same thing as the organ called the "receptacle of bile" (*pittadhara-kalā*). (50)

For the nourishment of life-span, health, vigor, vitality, the elements, and the digestive fire, she stands at the gate of the receptacle of digested food like a bolt on the path of what has been eaten. (51)
3.51d–52ab Like a bolt on the path of food, it blocks what has been eaten in the stomach and, having digested it, leads it downward;
when strong, however, it releases the food only as undigested matter.
For the strength of the *grahaṇī* is indeed the digestive fire (*agni*), and that fire is also dependent on the strength of the *grahaṇī*;
therefore, when the fire is vitiated, the *grahaṇī* becomes corrupted and causes disease. (53)

That food which nourishes the body, the tissues, the vital essence (*ojas*), strength, complexion, and so forth—in that regard, fire is the cause; for from food that is not digested, the nutrient fluids (*rasa*) and other constituents do not arise. (54)
Food consumed at the proper time, brought into the stomach by the vital breath (prāṇa), has its mass broken up by liquids and rendered soft by unctuous substances. (55)
3.55b–c. The digestive fire within the belly, brought into the abdominal cavity by the *prāṇa* wind and kindled by the *samāna* wind, digests what resides in the stomach,
just as the external fire cooks the water and rice contained in a cooking pot.
At first, even food possessing all six tastes becomes sweet;
then, having turned into froth, it reaches the state of phlegm (kapha); and thereafter, through burning heat (vidāha), it attains acidity.

3.57 When the phlegm has become frothy and the bile has moved from the stomach, the wind (vāyu), as it is being expelled or has already been expelled, dries it with its heat; thus matured, it becomes condensed, pungent, and windy. 3.58
The five types of heat—those of earth, water, fire, wind, and ether—successively digest their respective fivefold qualities of food, such as the earthy and the rest. (59)
And when matured, those elements nourish their own respective qualities separately:
the earthly [elements] nourish only the earthly ones, and the remaining [elements] nourish the remaining qualities residing in the body.
3.60 And these [elements] nourish their respective waste products (*kiṭṭa*) and essences (*sāra*). That digested food arises in two ways:
therein, one should know that the clear waste product of food is urine, while the thick is feces. 61.
3.61–62ab. The waste product (*kiṭṭa*) and the essence (*sāra*) are likewise matured; the essence, moreover, is further cooked by its own respective seven fires.
From the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) comes blood, from that flesh, from flesh fat (*medas*), and from that bone.
3.62d–63. From flesh comes fat, from fat bone, from bone marrow, and from that, semen; from semen the embryo is produced.
Phlegm, bile, the excretions in the channels, sweat, nails, and hair [arise from the food].
3.63c–d Kapha, pitta, feces, unctuousness in the channels, the eyes, the skin, and poison are the impurities (mala) of the tissues (dhātu) in their respective order.
Thus, through the transformation (pāka) of the tissues, they proceed in two ways as essence (prasāda) and waste (kiṭṭa). 3.64ab.
Due to their mutual support, there is a continuous succession of the moisture of the elements;
some say [it lasts] for a day and night, others for six days, and still others [for longer]. 65.
Through the process of digestion and so forth, food attains the state of semen within a month;
indeed, the continuous transformation of the constituent elements of what is consumed proceeds like a wheel.
Substances that increase virility and so forth produce semen and other effects immediately through their potency;
however, most other medicinal substances produce their effects within a day and night. (67)
3.67b–c: Indeed, by means of the *vyāna*—which has the function of distributing the nutrient essence (*rasa-dhātu*)—semen is immediately produced;
for it is constantly and perpetually distributed everywhere throughout the body simultaneously.
Wherever that rasa, being cast forth due to a deficiency in the ether (kha), becomes attached, there it produces a transformation, just as a cloud produces rain in the sky. // 69 //

In this same way, there may also be a localized provocation of the humors (doṣas); this process is defined as the action of food, the elements, the tissues (dhātus), and the digestive fire (agni). // 70 //
The cooker of food is considered superior to all other cooks;
for they are rooted in him, and their increase or decrease is characterized by his own increase or decrease. (71)

Therefore, one should carefully protect that [fire] with wholesome food, drink, and fuel, according to the prescribed rules; for its maintenance depends upon the maintenance of life-force and strength. (72)
The digestive fire is balanced when situated in its normal location; it becomes irregular when it has deviated from its path;
it is sharp when overwhelmed by pitta; and it is weak when afflicted by kapha. (73)
Fire is of four kinds: even, uneven, sharp, and dull.
That which digests food properly when it has been eaten properly is the even fire. (74)

3.74d–75ab. When food is eaten properly, that [digestive fire] is balanced; when eaten improperly, it is unbalanced. Even if eaten properly, an unbalanced fire may digest quickly, or even if eaten properly, it may digest slowly. A sharp fire, however, digests food rapidly even if it is eaten improperly.
3.75ab A *viṣama* [agni] digests food improperly and quickly; 3.75b a *sama* [agni] digests it properly but slowly.
However, a *manda* [agni], even when food is consumed properly, digests it only after a long time, causing dryness of the mouth, flatulence, rumbling in the intestines, distension, and heaviness.
3.76bv That which has been consumed will digest slowly when the digestive fire is diminished; it causes death when the fire is balanced, and one lives long and free from disease when it is increased.
When the fire is deranged, one becomes diseased; therefore, the root [of health] is said to be the stabilization of the digestive fire. 76+1.
3.76+1dv The suppression of fire is now described.
Bodily strength is threefold: innate (*sahaja*), time-born (*kāla-ja*), and produced by means (*yukti-kṛta*).
Among these, innate strength is that which arises from the *sattva* and the body, being natural (*prākṛta*). // 77 //
It is produced by age, by the seasons, and by time; furthermore, it is produced by application, by conduct and diet, and likewise by the practice of strengthening regimens.
A region with few waters and trees is known as *jāṅgala*, which causes very little disease;
*ānūpa* is the opposite of this; that which is intermediate between these two is considered *sādhāraṇa*. // 79 //
In this body, marrow, fat, muscle-fat, urine, bile, phlegm, feces, blood, lymph, and water each increase by one añjali [handful] respectively. (80)
The individual natural secretions of ojas, the brain, and semen are said to be one handful each;
however, the milk of a woman is two añjalis, and her menstrual blood is four. 81.
One should know that this pride arises from the notion of an equal realm; from it, there follow increase and decrease. (82ab)

The constitution (prakṛti) is declared to be of seven types according to whichever humor (doṣa) is predominant during the periods of semen, blood, pregnancy, food, activity, the womb, and the menstrual season. (83)

3.83–84 The nature of the [three] humors is traditionally held to be sevenfold: due to its pervasiveness, its rapid action, its strength, its provocation of the others, its independence, and its association with many diseases, wind (anila) is the most powerful among the humors.

For this very reason, humans dwelling in windy regions are generally of a bilious temperament; their hair and limbs are cracked and grey, they loathe the cold, and their fortitude, memory, intellect, physical exertion, kindness, vision, and gait are unstable; they are excessively talkative. (85)

They possess little wealth, strength, lifespan, or sleep; their speech is faltering, attached, unstable, and broken; they are nihilists, gluttonous, and full of coquetry; they are addicted to song, laughter, hunting, and strife. // 86 //

Those with little bile, phlegm, vitality, and sleep; those for whom sweet, sour, salty, hot, and pungent tastes are wholesome and desired; those who are thin and tall in stature; and those who move with a sound—[these are the characteristics of the Vata constitution].
They are neither firm, nor have they conquered their senses; they are neither noble, nor beloved by their husbands, nor do they have many offspring. // 87 //
3.87 Their forms are emaciated and tall; they travel with a rattling sound.
Their eyes are rough and greyish, round, unattractive, and like those of the dead.
When they sleep, these mountains, trees, and the sky appear as if they were open-eyed. // 88 //
Their eyes are indeed harsh and grey;
these unfortunate ones, puffed up with envy, are thieves with protruding calves.
They resemble dogs, jackals, camels, vultures, rats, and crows, and they are driven by wind-like impulses.
Thieves have prominent calves;

bile (pitta) is fire, or that which is born from fire; therefore, one in whom bile is predominant has intense thirst and hunger, fair and warm limbs, copper-colored hands, feet, and face, is brave, proud, has reddish-brown hair, and sparse body hair.
One with a predominance of bile (pitta) has intense thirst and hunger;
he is fond of garlands, ointments, and ornaments; he is well-conducted, pure, and affectionate toward those who depend on him;
endowed with wealth, daring intellect, and strength, he becomes a refuge even for his enemies in times of fear.
Intelligent, with loose-jointed muscles and little flesh, he is unloved by women and has scant semen and desire;
he is a dwelling place for gray hairs, wrinkles, and dark spots, and he eats food that is sweet, astringent, bitter, and cold. (92)
One who hates the heat, perspires excessively, has a foul odor, and possesses frequent excrement, anger, drinking, eating, and envy;
while asleep, such a person sees *karṇikāra* and *palāśa* trees, as well as conflagrations of the quarters, meteors, lightning, the sun, and fire. (93)
Their eyes are thin, tawny, and tremulous; with sparse lashes, they are fond of cold, yet through anger, intoxication, and the glare of the sun, they quickly turn red.
Those with Pitta-dominant constitutions have thin, tawny, and restless hair;
they possess medium lifespans and moderate strength, are compact in build, and are fearful of hardship.
They resemble tigers, bears, monkeys, cats, and yakṣas.
Those with a predominance of *pitta* resemble wolves;
*śleṣman* is Soma, and therefore one with a *śleṣman* constitution is *saumya*. Such a person has joints, bones, and flesh that are hidden, smooth, and closely knit.
Not tormented by hunger, thirst, suffering, affliction, or heat, he is endowed with intelligence, is of a *sāttvika* nature, and is true to his word.
With a complexion like the color of priyaṅgu, dūrvā grass, the stalk of a reed, a sword, yellow orpiment, and a lotus;
with long arms, a broad and full chest, a large forehead, and thick, dark hair. // 97 //
With soft limbs and a body that is well-proportioned, beautiful, and symmetrical, he possesses great vigor, pleasure, passion, semen, sons, and servants;
being righteous in nature, he never speaks harshly, and he harbors a firm enmity secretly for a long time. (98)
With soft limbs and a body that is well-proportioned, beautiful, and symmetrical;

with a gait equal to that of a rutting lord of elephants; with a voice like the roar of clouds, the ocean, a drum, or a lion; possessing mindfulness and diligence, he is disciplined, and even in childhood he does not weep excessively nor is he fickle.

3.99b–c His voice resounds like the sound of water, the ocean, a drum, or a conch; he eats little that is bitter, astringent, pungent, hot, and dry, yet he remains strong. Furthermore, his eyes have reddish corners, are very glossy, wide and long, with clearly defined white and black parts and thick lashes. 3.100d–3.101a [He possesses] a broad forehead, high eyebrows, and a straight nose. His lips are red, his teeth are white, even, and closely set. His tongue is long, thin, and red. His neck is like that of a conch shell. His shoulders are broad and his chest is well-developed. His arms are long and his hands are large. His fingers are long and his nails are copper-colored. His gait is like that of a lion or an elephant. His body is well-proportioned and his skin is golden-hued. He is endowed with all these marks of greatness. 3.102–3.103 [The Blessed One] is free from all afflictions and has overcome all fears. He is the refuge for all beings, the teacher of the world, and the one who has attained the state of omniscience. Having realized the ultimate truth, he teaches the Dharma out of compassion for all living beings. Through his wisdom and power, he leads them across the ocean of suffering to the island of nirvana. Thus, the Buddha is the supreme among men, the peerless one, and the one who has reached the end of all existence. 3.104–3.105 [The Blessed One] is the king of dharma, the lord of the three worlds, and the master of all dharmas. He is the one who has extinguished the fires of passion, hatred, and delusion. He is the one who has attained the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses. He is the one who has realized the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor marks. He is the one who has perfected the six perfections and the four immeasurables. He is the one who has transcended birth and death and attained the eternal bliss of nirvana. Thus, the Buddha is the most excellent of all beings, the one who is worthy of offerings, and the one who is the field of merit for the world. 3.106–3.107 [The Blessed One] is the one who has opened the gate to the Dharma and shown the path to liberation. He is the one who has destroyed the darkness of ignorance and brought light to the world. He is the one who has turned the wheel of the Dharma and established the community of disciples. He is the one who has taught the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. He is the one who has revealed the nature of dependent origination and the emptiness of all phenomena. He is the one who has shown the way to the cessation of suffering and the attainment of peace. Thus, the Buddha is the true refuge, the protector of the helpless, and the guide for those wandering in the cycle of rebirth. 3.108–3.109 [The Blessed One] is the one who has conquered Mara and his hosts. He is the one who has subdued the passions and the defilements. He is the one who has attained the state of a Victor and is known as the Tathagata. He is the one who has realized the Dharma-body and is the embodiment of wisdom and compassion. He is the one who has manifested the form-body for the sake of sentient beings. He is the one who has appeared in the world for the benefit of all. Thus, the Buddha is the source of all blessings, the root of all virtues, and the ultimate goal of all spiritual practice. 3.110–3.111 [The Blessed One] is the one who has spoken the words of truth and the one who acts in accordance with his word. He is the one who has abandoned all attachments and the one who is free from all conceptualizations. He is the one who has realized the non-arising of all phenomena and the one who has attained the state of non-duality. He is the one who has transcended all extremes and the one who dwells in the middle way. He is the one who has realized the equality of all things and the one who is impartial toward all beings. He is the one who has attained the state of a Buddha and is the teacher of gods and men. Thus, the Buddha is the incomparable one, the one who is beyond compare, and the one who is the jewel of the world. 3.112–3.113 [The Blessed One] is the one who has manifested the great compassion and the one who is filled with great love. He is the one who has extended the great joy and the one who is established in great equanimity. He is the one who has realized the four immeasurables and the one who has perfected the six paramitas. He is the one who has attained the ten stages and the one who has fulfilled the five paths. He is the one who has crossed over the river of samsara and the one who has reached the shore of nirvana. He is the one who has liberated himself and the one who liberates others. He is the one who has attained enlightenment and the one who leads others to enlightenment. Thus, the Buddha is the supreme being, the one who is worthy of worship, and the one who is the refuge for the entire universe. 3.114–3.115 [The Blessed One] is the one who has turned the wheel of the Dharma and the one who has established the three vehicles. He is the one who has revealed the secret treasury of the Dharma and the one who has entrusted the teachings to his disciples. He is the one who has prophesied the future buddhahood of his followers and the one who has shown the way to the ultimate fruit. He is the one who has manifested the various forms of skillful means and the one who has adapted his teachings to the capacities of beings. He is the one who has realized the ultimate reality and the one who is the source of all manifestations. He is the one who has attained the state of a Buddha and is the teacher of the three times. Thus, the Buddha is the one who is eternally present, the one who is omnipresent, and the one who is the embodiment of all Buddhas. 3.116–3.117 [The Blessed One] is the one who has manifested the pure land and the one who has adorned it with jewels. He is the one who has invited the assembly of bodhisattvas and the one who has led them to the realm of dharma. He is the one who has manifested the various transformations and the one who has displayed the inconceivable powers. He is the one who has realized the nature of the mind and the one who has shown the way to the transformation of consciousness. He is the one who has transcended all dualities and the one who dwells in the state of non-conceptualization. He is the one who has attained the state of a Buddha and is the teacher of the dharma-realm. Thus, the Buddha is the one who is beyond thought, the one who is ineffable, and the one who is the ultimate reality itself. 3.118–3.119 [The Blessed One] is the one who has manifested the great mandala and the one who has presided over the great assembly. He is the one who has bestowed the empowerment of the dharma and the one who has transmitted the seal of the lineage. He is the one who has realized the samadhi of the vajra and the one who has attained the state of the vajra-holder. He is the one who has manifested the various mudras and the one who has shown the way to the union of method and wisdom. He is the one who has transcended all worldly phenomena and the one who dwells in the state of the absolute. He is the one who has attained the state of a Buddha and is the teacher of the secret mantra. Thus, the Buddha is the one who is the source of all mantras, the one who is the essence of all deities, and the one who is the ultimate goal of all practitioners. 3.120–3.121 [The Blessed One] is the one who has manifested the great yoga and the one who has entered the state of great bliss. He is the one who has realized the union of the two truths and the one who has attained the state of the great seal. He is the one who has manifested the various forms of emanation and the one who has shown the way to the transformation of appearances. He is the one who has transcended all conceptual constructs and the one who dwells in the state of the great emptiness. He is the one who has attained the state of a Buddha and is the teacher of the mahayana. Thus, the Buddha is the one who is the embodiment of all yanas, the one who is the source of all teachings, and the one who is the ultimate refuge for all beings. 3.122–3.123 [The Blessed One] is the one who has manifested the great mandala of the dharma and the one who has presided over the great feast offering. He is the one who has realized the samadhi of the dharma-realm and the one who has attained the state of the great samadhi. He is the one who has manifested the various offerings and the one who has shown the way to the transformation of all
One who has little speech, anger, drinking, and desire for food; who possesses long life and wealth, is far-sighted, and generous;
who is faithful, profound, liberal, and patient; who is noble, sleep-prone, slow to act, and grateful. (101)

3.101ab One who speaks little, is free from anger, abstains from intoxicants, and is devoid of envy; 3.101bc one who possesses abundant life-span and conduct, is far-sighted, and is generous; 3.101cd one who is faithful, profound, liberal, and patient; 3.101d one who is noble yet prone to sleep.
He is prolix in speech, grateful, upright, wise, fortunate, modest, devoted to his teachers, and firm in friendship;
in dreams, he sees reservoirs of water filled with lotuses and rows of birds, as well as clouds pouring forth rain. (102)

3.102 Those of a phlegmatic constitution (śleṣma-prakṛti) are upright, wise, fortunate, and modest; they are equal to Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Varuṇa, Tārkṣya, the swan, and the lordly elephant, as well as to the lion, the horse, the cow, and the bull.

One should describe the *prakṛtis*—which arise from all pairs and consist of the qualities—as being composed of qualities through such attributes as purity, faith, and so forth, during the emergence of all dualistic qualities. (104)
Up to the age of sixteen, one is a child; therein occurs the increase of the elements, the faculties, and the vital essence.
Up to seventy, it is middle age; therein occurs non-increase, and beyond that, decline. (105)
Each person’s own body of three and a half cubits is a vessel for happiness and long life, provided it is not joined with the eight excessive and censured personal traits. (106)
Hair that is not hairy, not white, not coarse, and not long—possessing these qualities along with their opposites [of being smooth, soft, fine, having many roots, and firm]—is excellent. (107)
The forehead is prominent, with well-knit temples resembling the half-moon; the ears are neither too high nor too low, large at the back, and joined by fleshy tissue. 108.
The eyes are clearly distinguished as black and white, with thick eyelashes well-set;
the nose is prominent at the tip, high in its breath-space, plump, straight, and symmetrical. 109.
3.109b–110a: His eyelashes are thick and well-set;
his lips are red, not protruding, and large; his jaws are neither too prominent nor too small; his mouth is large; and his teeth are thick, glossy, smooth, white, and even.
The tongue is red, long, thin, and fleshy; the chin is large;
the neck is short, thick, and rounded; and the shoulders are elevated and robust. (111)
The abdomen is elevated with a rightward-turning, concealed navel;
the nails are thin, reddish, raised, glossy, slightly copper-colored, and fleshy. 112.
His fingers are long and without gaps; his hands and feet are large and well-placed; his ankles are concealed, his back is broad, and his joints are hidden and firm. // 113 //
3.113c–d His back is large with well-concealed vertebrae;
his voice is steady and resonant; his complexion is glossy and possesses a stable luster.
3.114 His innate courage is firm and remains unchanging even in times of calamity.
The body, an increasingly excellent field, free from disease from the time of conception, gradually increases in auspiciousness through its growth in stature, knowledge, and discernment. // 115 //
Thus, in a body endowed with all these qualities, a lifespan of a hundred autumns, sovereignty, and all desired states are firmly established.

The eight [elements], beginning with skin and blood and ending with consciousness (sat-tva), are said to be the progressively superior essences of embodied beings, for the purpose of determining their strength, measure, and knowledge. 117.

The eight [qualities] are superior in succession; he should be endowed with all of them in their highest degree, possessed of supreme dignity, hopeful in all undertakings, patient, wise, and steadfast. (3.118)
3.118d–119ab Enduring, well-disposed, and steadfast, he experiences both happiness and sorrow without arrogance or dejection;
being possessed of *sattva*, though undergoing suffering, he is neither *rājasa* nor *tāmasa*.

3.119c–120ab: One endowed with *sattva*, even when being provoked, possesses the group of qualities consisting of generosity, ethical conduct, compassion, truthfulness, celibacy, gratitude, elixirs (*rasāyana*), and friendliness; this group increases merit and lifespan.

“There are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas) located in the body; of these, one should designate eleven for each of the two thighs and likewise for the two arms, three in the trunk, and nine in the chest. (1)
On the back, fourteen [finger-breadths] above the *jatrū* [collarbone], and thirty-seven [finger-breadths] from the middle of the sole of the foot,
they say [the heart is located] on both sides of the middle finger.
The one called *talahṛd* (palm-heart) is located there; one pierced there meets death within five days.
Situated between the thumb and the fingers is *kṣipra*, which causes death by convulsions. // 3 //
Two finger-breadths above that is the *kūrca* [vessel], which causes the foot to turn and tremble;
below the ankle joint is the head of the *kūrca*, which causes swelling and pain.
The ankle (gulpha), located at the junction of the shank and the foot, causes pain, stiffness, and weakness;
however, the Indra-vasti, situated in the middle of the shank, kills by means of the depletion of blood.

The ankle causes pain, stiffness, and impotence; [it may also cause] pain, stiffness, and lameness. The knee is located at the junction of the shanks and thighs; while one lives, lameness occurs there.
[If it is] three finger-breadths above the knee, it causes swelling of the thigh and the calf.
Urvi occurs between the thighs due to piercing them; it causes emaciation of the legs through the depletion of blood.
Lohitākṣa, located at the root of the thighs, destroys [the patient] within a fortnight through the loss of blood.
4.7cv At the base of the thigh is the vessel called *lohita*, and between the scrotum and the groin is the *viṭapa*, which causes impotence; thus it is for the legs.
Likewise, for the arms, the *maṇibandha* is like the *gulpha* [ankle]. 8.
4.8bv If the *viṭapa* [vessel] is injured, it causes impotence; if the *kūrpara* [vessel] is injured like the *jānu*, it causes lameness (*kauṇya*).
Furthermore, if the *viṭapa* [vessel] is injured again, lameness occurs there between the armpit and the eye, supporting the armpit.
The rectum, bound by the large intestine, is immediately fatal; it expels feces and flatus.
The bladder, the reservoir of urine, is curved like a bow and contains little blood or flesh. (10)
A wound with its opening facing downward at the middle of the waist immediately destroys life;
the same applies to a wound on both sides, except in the case of a wound from a stone (aśmarī).

4.11cd–12ab. Even among those, one that discharges urine from both sides, or one that is perforated on one side and heals with effort, located between the trunk, the abdomen, and the sites of undigested food (āmāśaya) and digested food (pakvāśaya), and supported by all the vessels— [these are incurable].
The navel is also the immediate destroyer [of the body] and the gateway to the stomach;
the heart, which is the abode of the *sattva* and other qualities, is situated between the breasts and the center of the chest.
One should state that two finger-breadths (dvy-aṅgula) above and below the roots of the breasts are called the *stana-rohita*;
if blood and phlegm fill the abdominal cavity (*koṣṭha*) in those two [locations], one will perish in due order. 14.
4.14cv When the upper and lower channels carrying wind (anila) in the chest and flanks are obstructed by blood and phlegm,
the patient dies here from dyspnea and cough due to the abdominal cavity being filled with blood.

4.15cv–16. One should know that the two vital points called *apālāpa* are located where the chest and the spinal column meet, on both sides of them, and below the shoulder-blades; these are filled with blood.
If the two cavities are filled with blood that has turned into pus, death occurs;
[the disease] is situated on both sides of the spinal column, extending toward the hips and ears. (17)

4.17dv–18. The two *śroṇikarṇa* [joints] are situated at the hips; they are supported by the spinal column and are known as the *kaṭīkataruṇa* (kidney-bones) located above the buttocks (*sphij*). Due to the loss of blood there, one becomes pale, loses one's physical form, and perishes.
The two joints on both sides of the spinal column at the level of the hips and flanks, located on the outer part of the buttocks, are the *kukundara* vital points (marmans). (19)
4.19ab–20. On both sides of the spinal column, injury to these [veins] causes loss of movement in the lower body and lack of sensation to touch.
Those two which are bound to the other side, extending upward from the hips to the ears [are the next].
Those two buttocks, which conceal the internal disposition and are composed of young bones, when afflicted by swelling in the lower body, lead first to weakness and then to death. (21)

Those two [bones], the āśaya and the chādana, are attached to the other sides; they are indicated as being oblique and upward in the middle of the sides of the pelvis. One should perform the incision at their side-joints.
4.22b–d: Those two, located in the middle of the sides of the pelvis, are designated as the side-joints (pārśva-saṃdhī). One should pierce them obliquely or upward;
for one whose internal cavities are filled with blood, the production of another body occurs.
The two vessels located at the level of the base of the breasts, resting upon the spinal column, are the *pṛṣṭhavaṃśāśraya-sire*. // 23 //
In those two *bṛhatī* [points], death occurs for one who is pierced due to the loss of blood;
they are located on both sides of the spinal column, connected to the base of the arms. (24)
He pierced the two shoulder-blades, which cause the numbness and wasting of the arms;
and he pierced the two tendons on both sides of the neck, located between the neck, the arms, and the head. (25)

4.25bv – numbness or wasting from piercing them; 4.25bv – numbness or swelling from piercing them; 4.25bv – numbness or swelling from piercing them. The shoulders (*aṃsau*) are the junctions between the shoulder-blades and the shoulder-tops; they cause the loss of arm function.
On both sides of the windpipe, there are veins situated at the jaw. // 26 //

The two [vessels] bound to the seat of the shoulder-blade for the purpose of supporting the shoulders, and the two bound to the shoulder-socket— among those four, two are known as the *nīla* and two as the *manya* vital points (*marman*).
There is a loss and distortion of the voice, as well as a lack of perception of tastes, when that [vein] is pierced. // 27 //
4.27cv–dv: Loss of voice, abnormality of the voice, and loss of the sense of taste occur from piercing that [vein]; the veins leading to the tongue and nose are on both sides of the throat-passage.
These four, called by the name of Mātṛkā, separately and instantly destroy the vital breaths.
The *kṛkāṭika* is the joint of the head and neck; there the head moves.
Below the ears, at the depressions, are the *vidhura*, which cause loss of hearing. (29)
4.29bv–30. There, at the joints, the head is mobile; on both sides are the two hoods (phaṇau) which follow the path of the nostrils and the path of the ears.
Situated within the throat, they carry away the perception of smell through piercing.
The outer corners of the eyes are at the ends of the eyebrows;
below those are the two hollows, and likewise above the eyebrows are the two depressions; blindness occurs when these [marks] are present.
The two *śaṅkha* [sutures] at the end of the ears and the edge of the forehead cause immediate destruction;
the two *utkṣepa* [sutures] are above the *śaṅkha*s at the hairline, and then again the *sthapanī*. 32.
If there is a splinter (śalya) here between the eyebrows, even in these three cases, one may live if it is not extracted;
however, if it falls out spontaneously through suppuration or is extracted [by force], one perishes immediately.
At the junction of the tongue, eyes, nose, ears, and the four openings, there are four palates; these are the apertures, and within them lie the vital points (*marmans*). (34)
One pierced in the places called *śṛṅgāṭaka* immediately gives up life;
in the *kapāla* there are five joints, including the *sīmanta*s that run obliquely and upwards. (35)
4.35cv There are five skull-joints;
when these are pierced, one perishes through vertigo, insanity, or loss of mind.
Above the head is the internal junction where the vessels and joints meet. 36 //
4.36c–v: Between the head and above it, there is a whirl of hair called *adhipa*, a vital point (*marman*) that instantly takes away life;
where there is irregular throbbing and pain upon pressure, that is a vital point.
The convergence of flesh, bone, sinew, vessels, veins, and joints is called a *marman*; therefore, life is established there all the more firmly. (38)
However, the teaching is generally given as sixfold; thus is the conceptualization of the vital points (marmas).
Alternatively, the unity of the vital points is held to be due to their commonality as bases of the life-faculties (prāṇāyatana). // 39 //
4.39d–40ab. Or, the unity of the vital points (marmans) is recorded [as follows]:

those born of the flesh are ten, namely: the one called Indra, the two palms (tala), the heart, the two breasts, the two Rohitas, the two temples (śaṅkha), the two Kaṭīkaruṇas, the two hips (nitamba), and the two fleshy parts of the shoulders (aṃsaphala).
There are eight bone-marmas, twenty-three ligament-marmas, and [the following] channel-marmas:
the kūrcas, the kūrcasiras, the apāṅgas, the kṣipras, the utkṣepas, the aṃsas, and the vastis. (41)
4.41ab One should designate eight marma-sites located in the bones, nine in the tendons— namely the gudā, apastambha, vidhura, and śṛṅgāṭa—
and thirty-seven situated in the vessels (dhamanī) that reside within the veins (sirā).
4.42ab The rectum, the posterior pillar, the two large [muscles] devoid of support,
the *mātṛkā*, the two blue [spots], the two jaws, the two armpits,
the two shoulders, the two branches, the heart, the navel, the two side-joints, and the two breasts; 43.
4.43dv At the side-joints, between the breasts, there are two apālāpas; there are four sthapanīs and four ūrvīs, as well as the red [channels].
At the joint, there are twenty āvartas; at the wrist-joints are the two kukundaras.

The sīmantas, the two elbows, the two ankles, the two nape-of-the-neck regions, the two knees, the patis, the flesh-marmas, the anus, and for others, the two armpits and the two supports of the armpits are likewise [flesh-marmas]. (45)
4.45cd–46ab: The two tendons at the armpits, the two *viṭapa* [shoulder regions], and the two called *vidhura*; the *śṛṅgāṭas*, however, are located in the veins (*sirās*).
The two *apastambhas* and the two *apāṅgas* are situated in the arteries (*dhamanīs*); they are not recorded as being among those [veins].
When pierced, there is constant bleeding and the flesh flows out like wash-water;
the body becomes pale, the senses fail, and death occurs swiftly in the case of a wound in the muscle. (47)
In a wound arising from muscle tissue, there is either death or rapid discharge; in one involving the marrow, it is clear, interrupted, and accompanied by discharge and pain.
In a wound to a bone or vital point (*marman*), there is extension, convulsions, and stiffness; in one arising from the tendons (*snāyu*), the pain is especially intense.
In a tumor arising from the sinews (snāyu-ja),
there is excessive pain; there is an inability to walk, stand, or sit, or else deformity, or even death.
When located in the vessels (dhamanī), the blood is red, accompanied by sound and froth, hot, and causes loss of consciousness.
When a vein or a vital point (marma) is pierced, thick blood flows out copiously and incessantly;
from that depletion, death occurs through thirst, vertigo, dyspnea, fainting, and hiccups. (50)

When it arises in the solid tissues (vastu), the body is as if strewn with thorns; when it has become chronic, there is clubbed fingers, lameness, loss of strength and activity, emaciation, and swelling of the joints. (51)
The navel, the conch, the head of the penis, the heart, the śṛṅgāṭaka, and the bladder—these eight vital points (mātṛkā), together with the [other] nineteen, cause instantaneous death. (52)
Nineteen [vital points] strike [the body];
their maximum duration for drawing forth death is seven days.
There are thirty-three joints at the supports of the waters, the soles, the heart, and the sides.
4.53ab For them, the maximum duration is seven days: the waist, the soft palate, the hairline, the root of the breasts, and the bladder;
the *kṣipra*, *apālāpa*, *bṛhatī*, the buttocks, the breasts, and the *rohitā*.

Those that take away life after a lapse of time, those whose vitality lasts for a month or half a month, the utkṣepa, and the sthāpanī—these three are indeed the destroyers of the arrow-head (viśalyaghna). // 55 //
4.55dv Among those [conditions] that destroy the arrow-head (viśalyaghna), the wind (vāyu) dries up the flesh, fat, marrow, and brain matter;
upon the removal of the arrow-head, as it exits, it destroys the vital breaths through dyspnea and coughing. 56.

I consider the two temples, the two outer corners of the eyes, the two dark [spots] on the forehead, the two hollows at the back of the neck, the two shoulder-blades, the two whirlpools on the shoulders, the two depressions on the chest, and the two hollows of the hips to be the [eight] auspicious marks. 57.
4.57ab The two hoods, the two outer corners of the eyes, the two eyebrows, the two knees, the two red eyes, the two armpits, the beard, and the two elbows— these forty-four [parts] produce deformity.
4.58ab Those [vessels] known as the *sajānu* and *lohitākhyā* also take away life, sometimes due to injury;
the eight [vessels], namely the *kūrca*, *śiras*, *gulpha*, and *maṇibandha*, cause pain. 4.59cd/58ab.
Their thighs, held within the armpits of the branches, and their tufted heads measure twelve finger-breadths, while the jeweled bands are two finger-breadths wide.
4.60b–61. The *urvī*, *kūrca*, and *śiras* veins, as well as the two ankles, the two roots of the breasts, the knees, and the elbows— each measuring three finger-breadths [in length]—
as well as the *apāna*, *vasti*, *hṛd*, *nābhi*, *nīla*, *sīmanta*, and *mātṛkā* veins.
The two knees and the two elbows are three finger-breadths [in length]; the nīla, sīmanta, mātṛkā, beard (kūrca), śṛṅgāṭa, and manyā are thirty minus one (twenty-nine);
those measured by the span of one's own hand are as stated; for the remaining parts, one should say they are half a finger-breadth.

There are fifty-six vital points (marmas), even those as small as sesame or rice grains; others maintain that these vital points are desired to be fourfold, as are the vessels (sirās) that have been described. 63.

Then, having resorted to the vital points (marmas), they nourish the entire body; from the injury to those [vital points], blood is produced, and through the resulting depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus), [the body wastes away]. // 64 //
Due to that injury, for the purpose of producing blood from the wound, there is an activity [of the wind] when the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are depleted.
The increased and mobile wind, as it stirs, spreads intense pains;
that extracted heat (*tejas*) produces thirst, emaciation, intoxication, and vertigo. (4.64–65)
Then Antaka (Death) carries him away, whose body has become withered, collapsed, and limp;
yet, if a vital organ (*marman*) is struck, he quickly joins the limb back together and causes it to swell.
Because the site of the incision is constricted, the veins indeed contract; therefore, the life of living beings remains as long as the blood remains there. (67)
Therefore, even if severely wounded, one may survive if the injury is not in a vital organ, but not if it is in a vital organ;
however, someone might survive even a life-threatening wound through the skill of a physician. (68)
And because of an uneven impact, that [wind] also suffers from deficiency;
therefore, one should carefully avoid alkaline substances, poisons, fire, and the like at the vital points (marmans). // 69 //
Even a very slight injury to a vital point (marman) generally causes much greater suffering;
likewise, diseases that have taken refuge in the vital points persist even when treated with great effort. (70)
4.70cv Diseases located in the vital points (marmas) are likewise [fatal].
"The flower on the tree is the precursor of fruit; smoke is the sign of fire; and the appearance of clouds is the precursor of rain."
Just as there are signs of what is to come, so too are the fatal omens (riṣṭa) of death certain. // 1 //
O long-lived one, all medical treatments administered by physicians become fruitful for the well-being of the patient, just as they are toward a grateful king. (1+(1))
An action performed when one's lifespan has been exhausted is as futile as a deed done for a base person;
it brings ill repute, danger to the body, and the loss of one's own welfare. (1+2)
5.1+(2)cv: From this exertion, there arises a doubt regarding the body; therefore, the characteristics of those whose life-force has departed are now being proclaimed.
A transformation of the natural state (prakṛti) is designated by the wise under the name of *riṣṭa* (a fatal sign). 1+(3) //
5.1+(3) Furthermore, there is no such thing as death for those whose life-force has departed, nor is there life for one whose signs of death have been seen.
Through lack of skill, one perceives signs of death where there are none, and fails to perceive them even when they are present.
Some, however, say that it is of two kinds, distinguished by being stable or unstable; due to the multiplicity of defects, a semblance of a fatal sign may arise. (3)
He may be pacified by the pacification of the [three] humors, but if he remains stable, he will inevitably face death;
this is discerned through the form, the sense organs, the voice, the shadow, the reflection, movements, and so forth. // 4 //

5.4 When those [humors] are pacified, it should be pacified; furthermore, among other natural states, one should recognize that any abnormality occurring without a cause is, in brief, a fatal sign (*ariṣṭa*). // 5 //
One whose hair and body hair appear as if smeared with oil even though no oil has been applied, and whose eyes are excessively restless, fixed, or withdrawn within; (6)
The eyes are squinting, wide and then narrowed, or narrowed and drooping; the gaze is wandering or dull, resembling that of a mongoose. (7)
The eyes are pigeon-colored or like glowing embers, watery, and with disheveled eyelashes;
the nostrils are excessively dilated or constricted, and covered with pustules. (8)
If one's upper lip is swollen, cracked, or withered, and the lower lip droops, or if both should become like the color of a ripe jambū fruit; (9)
The teeth become covered with tartar, darkened, copper-colored, and appear as if flowering or stained;
or they may suddenly fall out, while the tongue becomes crooked or tremulous.
Swollen, dry, heavy, dark-brown, smeared, numb, and covered with thorns—the head, the neck, or the back [of such a person] is unable to bear its own weight. (11)
Furthermore, one who is unable to move a morsel of food situated in the mouth, or whose limbs become unnaturally heavy or light without any apparent cause; 12.
If blood flows from one's orifices without the presence of toxic disorders (viṣa-doṣa), and if the penis is swollen and the testicles are excessively protruded; 13.
Or otherwise, whoever possesses these [marks], they are all impelled by Time;
likewise for one who has unprecedented lines on the palms, even if they are shaped like the crescent moon. (14)
5.14b–c All these [signs] are impelled by Time;
he does not live for six months if they appear on the forehead or at the top of the bladder.
5.15 If water on the body of that embodied being spreads like a drop on a lotus leaf, [he will not survive].
The life of one whose veins appear greenish-yellow and whose hair follicles are closed remains for six months as he floats upon the water. (16)
His life lasts for six months. That man who craves sour things meets his death through pitta.
He whose powder on the head or even on the face resembles cow-dung powder. (17)
If there is oily smoke on the head for up to a month, his life remains;
or if new whorls and curls appear on the head or between the eyebrows. (18)

5.18 If eruptions should appear on the head or between the eyebrows, death occurs within six nights for one who is healthy, but within three nights for one who is ill; likewise, if the tongue is dark-brown, the mouth is foul-smelling, and the left eye sinks in.
5.19 One should avoid that patient upon whom birds alight on the head after three nights; likewise,
one whose chest dries up excessively first, even when he has bathed and been anointed with unguents.
When all his limbs are moist, he does not live for half a month; if, without cause, two colors—natural and abnormal—appear simultaneously on his body, [he will die]. (21)
Likewise, for one whose fingers crack even when not pulled— whether due to growth, exhaustion, dryness, or oiliness— that person does not survive.

Likewise, in cases of sneezing, coughing, and so forth, for whomsoever there should be an unprecedented sound—a breath that is short or long, or one that is foul-smelling or fragrant—[that person is to be known as one whose death is near]. (23)
If one’s body, whether bathed or unbathed, possesses a superhuman fragrance, or if there is such a scent on the filth, clothing, or wounds, his life will last until the end of the year. // 24 //

5.24c–d Or, if lice, flies, and the like frequent his body because of its extreme fragrance— whether due to dirty clothes, wounds, or other causes— and then abandon it because of its extreme foul odor, he too shall not live out the year.
When coolness is perceived in limbs that are constantly warm, or excessive heat in those that are cold, or when there is perspiration and rigidity without cause; 26.

5.26dv Sweating and stiffness without apparent cause, the appearance of cold eruptions, or having cold limbs while burning with internal heat; one who hates warmth yet suffers from cold is within the domain of the Lord of the Pretas. // 27 //
5.27b–c Or one whose limbs are cold may yet burn intensely; 5.27d Or even one whose limbs are cold experiences a burning sensation.
He in whom there is heat in the chest and extreme cold in the abdomen, who has broken stools and thirst—he is just like a deceased person. 5.28 //
5.28b–c. Excessive coldness in the abdomen, or urine, feces, spittle, or semen that sinks in water; or whose spittle is of many colors—for such a person, death occurs within a month.
5.29. Or whose spittle is of many colors—for such a person, death occurs within a month.
He who is like space that has become solidified, yet is like space though dense;
who is as if formless yet possessed of form, and who, though possessing form, exists as if formless. (30)
He is radiant and yet devoid of radiance, white and black, both non-existent and existent;
he is free from eye disease, the moon, and possesses many forms without a mark.

5.31 Just as lightless [forms] appear within light, so too [does one see them] therein; likewise, one who is not afflicted by eye disease sees the moon while awake, as well as *rakṣasas*, *gandharvas*, *pretas*, and others of that kind.
He who perceives such forms and various transformations perishes.
5.32–33. He who does not perceive the form and appearance of the Seven Sages, nor Arundhatī situated near them,
nor the Pole Star (dhruva), nor the celestial Gaṅgā— he does not see that [true] equality.
He hears the sounds of the roar of rain-clouds and torrents of water, as well as lutes, drums, and flutes, and other sounds, whether they be non-existent or existent. (34)
Just as one who, pressing his ears, does not hear the *dhukadhuka* sound [of the wind], so too one who perceives odors, tastes, and tactile sensations erroneously [is considered insane]. (35)
5.35b-v He who does not hear the *dhukadhuka* sound at all, or he who does not smell the scent of a lamp;
for whom tastes lead to disorder through improper application, but to health through proper application.
He whose limbs are covered as if with dust, or who does not feel pain in his body—without intense austerity or yoga performed according to the prescribed rules—[does not attain this]. (37)
5.37 One whose limbs appear as if strewn with ashes, and one who can predict their death through extrasensory perception;
or one whose voice is diminished, wretched, indistinct, or even stammering.
He who suddenly becomes bewildered when wishing to speak, or suffers from a weakening of his voice and a loss of strength and complexion, does not live. (39)
And seeing the increase of the disease through improper treatment, one should predict death;
for he who speaks with a discordant voice has reached his own end. (40)
And one should avoid from afar the hearer of this sound, whether by its shape, its size, its color, or even its radiance. (41)
The reflection of that sound, or of its hearer, appears to him even in a dream; he is indeed a *preta*.
[That which appears] in sunlight, a mirror, water, and so forth, according to its shape and size— // 42 //
It is said that a reflection arises from the body as its counterpart;
however, that which is based on color and luster is simply the shadow residing upon the body.
If one's reflection appears cut, broken, distorted, or agitated; headless, double-headed, crooked, deformed, or otherwise altered; (then it is inauspicious). 44.
One should know that his life is at its end if no reflection arising from a visible object appears, nor if a maiden is not seen in his eyes. (45)
The shadows of the five types of cotton cloth possess various characteristics:
that which belongs to the sky is stainless, blue, glossy, and as if radiant. (46)
From wind, it is reddish-brown, dark, rough as ashes, and lusterless;
whereas that from fire is pure red, radiant in appearance, and pleasing to behold. (47)
The water-born [earth] is pure like stainless beryl, very smooth, and pleasant;
the terrestrial [earth] is stable, smooth, dense, pure, dark, and white. // 48 //
5.48b–c: For that [earth-born] is very smooth; the water-born is also [smooth]; the wind-born leads to disease, death, and affliction, while the others result in the arising of happiness.
The fire-born is the consumer of all, and it is traditionally held to be of seven kinds.
5.49–50ab. The Vāyavyā [lines] are associated with disease and death; they may be red, yellow, white, dark-brown, green, pale-yellow, or black.
Among these, those that are expanding, glossy, and clear are auspicious.
5.50ab Those that are red, yellow, white, or dark are auspicious; those that are soiled, rough, or contracted portend inauspicious results.
A *chāyā* (shadow) overlays the *varṇa* (color), whereas a *prabhā* (luster) illuminates the *varṇa*.
5.51b–d: They are contracted and do not result in happiness. Radiance (*prabhā*) is the manifestation of color;
it is perceived when [an object] is near, while shadow (*chāyā*) shines forth when it is distant.

Nothing is without shadow or without radiance; rather, specific qualities serve as their distinguishing marks. 5.52: [The text continues: ... [no entity is devoid of shadow or luster; however, particular characteristics indeed mark them out].
He who, as if testing the auspicious and inauspicious fate of men arising in due time, creeps along with drooping shoulders while resting his feet upon shadows.

5.53b–d Those who constantly lose strength while relying on shade at the proper time; he who, though eating much wholesome food, wastes away; he who eats little yet has excessive feces and urine, or eats much yet has scanty feces and urine; [these are signs of approaching death]. 5.54ab–cd.
5.54d–55. He who eats much yet has little urine and feces, or he who eats little but is afflicted by phlegm, breathes deeply and exerts himself;
he who, having breathed out long, breathes in short and becomes exhausted.
He who breathes out short breaths, whose body trembles violently, and who with great difficulty turns his head while bending his hands forward; 56.
He whose sweat flows from the forehead, whose joints and ligaments are loose, and who becomes bewildered when being raised up—whether he be strong or weak—is one who will die. (57)
He who sleeps on his back, he who moves his feet about, and he who desires to grasp at non-existent things such as beds, seats, or walls—[these are signs of one possessed by a spirit]. // 58 //
5.58 He who always desires to seize beds, seats, walls, and so forth; he who laughs when there is no cause for laughter, being utterly deluded; he who licks his lips;
he who repeatedly laps at his upper lip and makes blowing sounds. 5.59
5.59 One who does not belch, one whose shadow pursues him— whether it be black, yellow, or reddish—
and those who hate physicians, medicines, drinks, food, elders, and friends; [these are signs of approaching death].
5.60b–c Whether black, yellow, or reddish, all these are to be known as submissive and moving in equal measure.
61. He whose neck, forehead, and heart perspire and become cool [is likewise to be understood].
Another region is hot, and the deities are his refuge—he who has but a tiny light, whose attention is scattered, and who is always shadowed by misfortune and dejected in mind. (62)
When all the premonitory symptoms enter a person in excessive measure during fevers and other ailments, death follows him, preceded by the fever. (62.1+(1))
He whose offerings, when presented by those who bring tribute, he does not consume;
and he who, being without external cause, [bestows] wisdom, splendor, prosperity, and glory.
5.63ab He whose offering the consumer of offerings receives, or from whom he suffers a loss, goes to the abode of Yama;
for such a person—whether healthy or diseased—the [medicine] consists of both virtues and defects. 64.
5.64 He whose nature, consisting of both virtues and vices, undergoes change within six months does not live;
[his] devotion, character, memory, renunciation, intellect, and strength become causeless.
These six [signs] revert for one who will die within six months;
gait, speech, trembling, and delusion like those of an intoxicated person indicate death within a month. (66)

One who is unaware [of the practice] perishes after six days from the pain of plucking out the hair; likewise, one whose food does not even reach the throat suffers from a disease of the throat itself. (67)
Servants act with hostility, a ghostly appearance arises, and if one's sleep is constant or non-existent, he does not live. (68)

5.68–69. For one who is about to go to the realm of King Yama, sleep will be constant, the mouth will be filled with tears, the feet will perspire excessively, and the eyes will fall into a state of agitation.
5.69 For one who is about to go to the realm of Yama, that for which he formerly took delight brings him no pleasure;
and in him, a transformation characterized by all [the signs of death] suddenly arises. (70)
Or it may suddenly recede, yet it may also suddenly perish; a fever that is powerful, deep-seated, and chronic destroys one's strength. (71)

Accompanied by delirious speech, confusion, and labored breathing; emaciated yet swollen, with impaired digestive fire; not excessively thin, with obstructed speech, bloodshot eyes, and pain in the heart. (72)
That cough which is dry and occurs either in the forenoon or in the afternoon,
accompanied by phlegm, in one who is devoid of strength and flesh— // 73 //
In the dry cough, there is blood-pitta (rakta-pitta) in the forenoon; it may be intensely red, black, or the color of a rainbow,
and it manifests as coppery, yellow, or greenish in appearance.
Spreading from the pores of the skin, it clings to the throat, mouth, and heart;
like the discharge of a foul-smelling disease, it is excessively copious and acts as a stain upon clothing. (75)
[The patient] who has dyed clothing that is foul-smelling and aged [is afflicted by] jaundice, fever, vomiting, cough, and swelling;
likewise one suffering from cough, dyspnea, fever, vomiting, thirst, diarrhea, and swelling. (5.76)
Consumption (yakṣmā) is characterized by pain in the sides, abdominal distension, vomiting of blood, and heat in the shoulders;
the vomiting is forceful, has the odor of urine and feces, and contains specks of light (candrikā). (77)
5.77–78ab — [Vomiting] accompanied by blood, feces, pus, pain, cough, and dyspnea, occurring in one who suffers from thirst, vomiting of blood, and fever in the limbs;
or [thirst] that persists in one emaciated by other diseases, whose tongue has protruded, and who is unconscious.
5.78–79. One with protruding tongue, unconscious, with a protruding tongue and impaired intellect, afflicted by extreme cold, emaciated, with a face having the luster of oil;
one suffering from hemorrhoids, and with swelling of the hands, feet, navel, anus, scrotum, and mouth—[these are signs of alcoholism].

5.79–80: [One should avoid treating] a patient suffering from swelling of the anus, scrotum, and so forth, or afflicted by pain in the heart, flanks, and limbs, vomiting, inflammation of the rectum, and fever;
likewise, one should avoid treating diarrhea characterized by stools that resemble the liver, a lump of flesh, meat-washings, or are as black as ink.
It is equal to oil, ghee, milk, curd, marrow, fat, and liquor;
to brain matter, soot, pus, vesavāra, water, and honey. (81)
It is excessively red, black, glossy, putrid, clear, thick, and painful;
it is variegated, discharging the bodily constituents (dhātus), and either devoid of feces or containing excessive stool. (82)
Covered with cobwebs, infested by flies, streaked with veins, and marked by spots like the moon;
with the folds of his anus decayed, his rectal canal prolapsed, and suffering from pain in his joint-bones. (83)
With his anal sphincter prolapsed, suffering from pain in the joints and bones, with strength diminished, he passes only undigested food;
accompanied by thirst, dyspnea, fever, vomiting, burning sensations, abdominal distension, and dysentery. (84)

One should indeed prescribe a diet for a patient suffering from urinary calculi (aśmarī), characterized by swollen testicles, suppressed urine, and intense pain; as well as for one afflicted by urinary disorders (meha), thirst, burning sensations, pustules, sloughing of the flesh, and diarrhea. (5.84–85)

Pustules appearing on the vital points (marmas), the heart, the back, the breasts, the shoulders, the anus, or the head, or those located on the joints, feet, or hands, cause a lack of energy in a patient suffering from urinary disorders (pramehin). (86)

5.86bv–87. [These diseases] arise on the breasts, shoulders, anus, and head; they are located in the joints, feet, and hands. Furthermore, [the patient suffers from] putrefaction of all the flesh, burning sensations, thirst, intoxication, and fever;
erysipelas (visarpa), obstruction of the vital organs (marma), hiccups, dyspnea, vertigo, and exhaustion.
Furthermore, the *māṃsa-saṃkoca-gulma* (fleshy contraction tumor) is broad in circumference, dense, elevated like the shell of a tortoise,
bound with visible veins, and accompanied by fever, vomiting, hiccups, flatulence, and pain. // 88 //
One suffering from cough, catarrh, nausea, dyspnea, diarrhea, swelling, retention of feces and urine, asthma, edema, hiccups, fever, and vertigo; // 89 //
Accompanied by fainting, vomiting, and diarrhea, it destroys the weak abdominal region; it causes swelling of the eyes, curvature of the genitals, and moistness of the body and skin. (90)
For one whose abdominal distension has been removed by purgation but recurs again and again, there occurs jaundice accompanied by swelling, with yellowing of the eyes, nails, and vision. (91)
5.91–92a. Afflicted by exhaustion from purgation,
accompanied by drowsiness, burning sensations, anorexia, vomiting, fainting, flatulence, and diarrhea,
and beset by many complications, [the disease] spreads through both feet to the man.
In a woman, swelling from the mouth kills; from the abdomen and the private parts, it kills both.
When covered with streaks and discharging fluid, it kills one suffering from vomiting, fever, dyspnea, and diarrhea.
Fever and diarrhea occurring at the end of swelling, or swelling occurring when those two have subsided—especially in a weak person—arise for the destruction of the embodied being. (94)
The physician should avoid that patient whose swelling is located in the feet, whose two calves are sagging, and whose two thighs feel as if they are sinking. (95)
If the face and hands and feet of one who is wasting away become especially swollen,
or if they swell even without [swelling of] the rest of the body, he goes to the state of the five elements within a month.
5.96b–97 Specifically, that [type of] visarpa in which the patient suffers from cough, discoloration, fever, fainting, and breaking pain in the limbs,
as well as vertigo, swelling of the face, nausea, exhaustion of the body, and diarrhea, dries up.

5.97–98. It causes vertigo, dryness of the mouth, nausea, leprosy, and the wasting away of the limbs; it destroys one who has bloodshot eyes, a lost voice, weak digestion, is infested with parasites, and suffers from thirst and diarrhea.
Vāta-rakta (gout) causes the skin to become numb, the body to be bent, and affliction with tremors, swelling, and pain;
it is accompanied by delusion, fainting, intoxication, sleepiness, and fever. (99)

Vāyu [produces] a broken skin that feels numb, accompanied by headache, anorexia, dyspnea, contraction, eruptions, and suppuration; [it is characterized] by diseases of the head, anorexia, dyspnea, fainting, diarrhea, thirst, and vertigo. (5.99–100)
All diseases strike those whose voice, bodily constituents, strength, and digestive fire have been depleted:
those with wind-disorders, epilepsy, leprosy, blood-disorders, abdominal dropsy, and consumption. (101)
One should avoid those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) or urinary disorders (meha), even if their other symptoms are slight, should they be emaciated;
for there will be severe loss of strength and flesh, an increase in the disease, and loss of appetite. (102)
That patient in whom three hard, painful, and greatly enlarged wind-tumors (vātāṣṭhīlā) remain in the heart for three fortnights does not live.
In one overwhelmed by thirst, death snatches away life instantly;
the wind, having brought laxity to the calves and crookedness to the nose, [departs]. (104)
But for one who is overwhelmed by thirst and emaciated, I consider that this [disease] immediately robs him of life;
having reached the space between the navel and the anus, or taking refuge in the groins.
5.105 Or, I believe, a strong [vata] wind, having seized the rectum and heart of one whose life-force (āyus) is exhausted or whose body is emaciated,
obstructs the excretions at the bladder-head and the navel, producing pain. 106.
The Vāyu, having seized the anus and the groins, produces pain in the groins, thirst, diarrhea, or dyspnea. (107)
Having seized the anus and the groins,
having stretched out the tips of the ribs and the chest, the wind instantly robs of life one who is paralyzed and whose eyes are fixed.
5.108 When death is imminent, the feverish heat, thirst, fainting, loss of strength, and the loosening of the joints suddenly arise as the sides of the body are stretched out. 109.
If, upon the release of a cow, sweat flows profusely from one's mouth,
then for such a person afflicted by the Lepajvara fever, life is difficult to maintain.
He on whose body eruptions resembling coral beads appear and vanish quickly will perish before long. (111)
Resembling split lentils and likewise similar to coral, with inward-facing openings and appearing like calluses, these eruptions destroy the body. (112)
One should avoid that person whose eyes are reddish-yellow, whose face is sunken, whose temples are devoid of flesh, and who suffers from terror and heat in the limbs. (113)
And that which arises from Vāta due to running about suddenly and rubbing against the skin, which results neither in pain like that born of Vāta nor in burning like that born of Pitta; (114)
They possess the scents of sandalwood, uśīra-root, wine, and a corpse, as well as crows;
they have the luster of moss, a cock's crest, saffron, and soot.
Wounds that have the luster of *naktamāla* soot,
or the luster of jasmine and rice,
which burn internally while lacking external heat, cause the destruction of life.

That which is not born of phlegm nor does it turn into pus, which is not born of a vital spot (marman) nor causes pain, which is not powdery yet resembles scattered powder, and where it appears suddenly—[that is a sign of death]. // 115 //
One should avoid all those wounds that have the appearance of a spear, a banner, and so forth;
as well as fistula-in-ano (bhagandara), which discharges feces, urine, and wind, and is infested with worms. 116.
He who, being afflicted, repeatedly strikes knee against knee, lifts up his feet and lets them fall, and casts his face about, does not live.
Biting his fingernails with his teeth, and with them [biting] his hair and grass;
scratching the ground with a piece of wood, or striking a clod of earth with another clod. (118)

5.118b–119 And he whose hair or body hair stands on end, who has thick urine, who suffers from dry cough and fever; who laughs repeatedly, who shrieks repeatedly, and who strikes the bed with his foot— [these are signs of death].
5.119d And he who repeatedly strikes his bed with his foot while searching for vulnerabilities is a sick man who does not survive;
a sudden disappearance of a birthmark or mole on the body of one who is afflicted portends death.
Flowers in the mouth, teeth, and nails; various veins in the abdomen;
labored upward breathing; loss of body heat; and groins afflicted with piercing pain. (121)
A wise person should avoid one who finds no peace, whose transformations increase while his fundamental nature declines. (122)
While he is suddenly attaining relief, death suddenly carries away his life—
the patient for whose sake the physician has prepared the medicine.
Even one who exerts himself cannot attain life, which is so difficult to obtain, unless it has been recognized many times, perfected, and practiced according to the prescribed rules. 124.
