For one for whom there is no medicine, no treatment can be accomplished;
likewise, for one for whom a reversal occurs when medicine or food is being prepared. (125)

If, despite being healthy, his complexion, scent, and other qualities suddenly vanish, and if his fire-like vitality is extinguished even when there is fuel and he is in a windless place, he does not live. (126)
In whose house the vessels of a sick person break or fall excessively, for him life is difficult to obtain. (127)
When a disease suddenly releases a weak man,
Ātreya considers his life to have entered a state of uncertainty.

5.128–129. A physician, even when questioned, should not speak of a doubtful prognosis nor of a death that is painful to hear; nor should he desire to treat one whose life has departed, for the sake of his kinsmen and friends.

One should not speak even when questioned by the messengers of Yama, piśācas, and others, for he who is being attended by them is already deprived of life; since they destroy the potency of medicines, one should therefore avoid such a person.
Since the entire fruit of Ayurveda is established in the one who knows life, a physician should always be intent upon the knowledge of fatal signs (riṣṭa). 131.

Death is observed for living beings due to the exhaustion of both lifespan and merit; it is also observed even when those two have not yet exhausted, as in the case of those who fail to avoid dangers. (132)

"For those belonging to the Ārya regions, heretical sects, stages of life, or castes, messengers of the same class [as the patient] lead to the success of the rite; those who are the opposite lead to the failure of the rite. (1)
One who is wretched, frightened, fleeing, or terrified; one who speaks harsh or inauspicious words;
one bearing a weapon or a staff; one who is a eunuch; or one who wears a shaven head, a beard, or matted locks. (2)
One who bears a sword or a staff, one with a severed limb, one with a shaven head or beard, or one wearing matted locks;
one who is shaven-headed, bearded, or has matted hair;
one with an inauspicious name, one of cruel deeds, one who is filthy, or a woman.
Many who are diseased and deformed, adorned with red garlands and unguents. // 3 //
Marked with oil and mud, wearing a single old, discolored, and wet garment, mounted upon a donkey, camel, or buffalo, and crushing wood, clods of earth, and the like. // 4 //

6.4dv A physician should not follow a messenger who carries wood, iron, or similar items; nor one who calls from afar; nor one whose thoughts or speech are inauspicious; nor one who is naked; nor one who is cutting or breaking [anything]. // 5 //
While offering oblations into the fire, he may also offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors even when [the recipient] is asleep,
has disheveled hair, is anointed with oil, is weeping, or is otherwise impure.

Furthermore, messengers of men who are about to die arrive while the physician is weeping or perhaps when he is not prepared; or else, they come at a time and place that share the same qualities as the disease. // 7 //
Upon seeing a messenger who has arrived, one should not treat him as if he were ill;
rather, one should touch his navel, nose, mouth, hair, body hair, nails, and teeth.
6.8c–d Touching the navel, nose, eyes, private parts, back, breasts, neck, and belly with the ring finger;
[or touching] cotton, chaff, lead, bone, a skull, a pestle, or a stone. 9.
6.9bv – A stomach, the ring finger, a broom, a winnowing basket, the hem of a garment, ashes, charcoal, a wick, husks,
a rope, sandals, a scale, a noose, or anything else that is broken or fallen away.
Furthermore, messengers who report seeing lightning that has broken or occurred previously [in such a manner] declare that those persons will die;
likewise when it occurs at midnight, at midday, during the two twilights, or on a festival day.
On the sixth, fourth, and ninth lunar days; during the rising of Rāhu and Ketu; and under the asterisms of Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Āśleṣā, Pūrvā, Ārdrā, Maghā, and Mūla. (12)
Furthermore, while the messenger is delivering words concerning a patient, if the physician should perceive an inauspicious omen, he should not follow after him. (13)
For example: "a mutilated preta," or "the very ornament of a preta," or words such as "cut," "burnt," or "destroyed. (14)
6.14b And there may be the ornament of a ghost (pretālaṅkāra), or a pungent and intense flavor, or a great cadaverous odor, or a vast and cruel touch, or whatever else is of that nature. // 15 //

The cry of "Alas! Alas!", loud wailing, reviling, stumbling, sneezing, the mishap of one's garment, parasol, or footwear, and the sight of someone in distress. (17)
The submerging of shrines, banners, and full vessels;
the destruction of beloved proclamations; and defilement with ashes and dust. (18)
An interruption of the path by a snake, a cat, a monitor lizard, a chameleon, or a monkey;
or the cries of cruel beasts and birds directed toward the blazing quarter [of the sky]. (19)
Of black grain, molasses, sour gruel, salt, fermented liquors, hides, mustard seeds, fat, oil, grass, mud, and fuel; 20.
[One should avoid] the impotent, the cruel, and dog-cookers; as well as nets and snares, vomited food, excrement, and that which is foul-smelling or loathsome to behold. (21)
One sees even enemies—such as cotton and other materials used for bedding, seating, and vehicles—that are devoid of essence and spread out flat. (22)

6.22cd–23ab Furthermore, seeing vessels and other objects turned face up is auspicious, while seeing them turned face down is inauspicious. Male-named birds on the left side are favorable, whereas female-named birds on the right side are auspicious.
Birds and deer moving clockwise are auspicious, whereas dogs and jackals are not; furthermore, odd-numbered deer are praised, as is their constant appearance.
The blue jay, the bhāsa, the bharadvāja crane, the mongoose, the goat, and the peacock [are auspicious];
however, seeing an owl, a cat, or a lizard at all times is inauspicious. (25)

The boar, the monitor lizard, the snake, the hare, and the chameleon are auspicious when their names are mentioned; however, the monkey and the bear are not so, whether by sight or by sound, except in the case of the latter.
The bow of Indra and that which is on the forehead are inauspicious, while others are auspicious;
vessels full of fire, those that are broken, and those without handles [are also inauspicious].
The physician, upon entering the house of those about to die, sees auspicious items such as curd, unbroken grains, and so forth, as well as other auspicious things that will be described hereafter.

Having thus observed that the messenger and others are improper, one should abandon such a distressed person; otherwise, with a mental continuum purified by compassion, one should diligently attend to him. (29)
6.29 One should diligently employ curd, unbroken rice, sugarcane, flat beans, *priyaṅgu*, honey, and ghee;
likewise, barley-gruel, collyrium, the *bhṛṅgāra* plant, a bell, a lamp, and lotuses.
Of fresh durvā grass, fish, meat, parched grain, and the eating of fruit;
of jewels, an elephant, a full water-jar, a maiden, and a chariot. (31)
As the man grew, so did the prosperity of the deities and the king;
likewise, there were white *sumana* flowers, yak-tail whisks, garments, and horses.
Of a conch shell, a virtuous person, two, a turban, an archway, and a svastika;
of the earth being uplifted, and of a blazing fire. // 33 //
Of a pleasing cart filled with food and drink, of a cow with its calf, of a mare, and also of a woman [carried] by men. 34.
Of the jīvañjīvaka, the sāraṅga, the sārasa, and the sweet-voiced birds; of the swans, the hundred-petalled lotuses, and likewise of the bound sacrificial animal—35.
There is the sight of the rucaka jewel, a mirror, white mustard seeds, and yellow orpiment; the fragrance is most fragrant, the color is very white, and the taste is sweet. // 36 //
The lowing of the cattle was favorable to their owner; likewise, the voices of the cows, as well as those of the beautiful deer, birds, and men, were auspicious.

6.37 The raising of umbrellas, banners, and flags; the chanting of praises for the Lord of Cows (Indra); and the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and conchs—these are the proclamations of an auspicious day.
The sound of Vedic study, pleasant wind blowing from the right, and [auspicious omens] at the entrance of the house on the road—these one should know as the signs of good health. (39)
Thus has been described the omen of messengers; hereafter, they explain dreams:
he who, in a dream, is dragged by a dog while drinking liquor together with ghosts (pretas), [is foretold to die]. 40.

6.40b After [discussing] dreams, [the following] will be explained: That mortal who, laughing, is carried away by a woman whose body and garments are red with garlands, is swiftly led away by Death in the form of fever. 41.

That mortal who departs toward the southern direction quickly meets death by consumption (yakṣman), as well as by blood-bile (asrapitta), or by [the forms of] buffalo, dog, boar, camel, and donkey. // 42 //
In whose heart a thorny creeper, a bamboo, or a palmyra tree grows,
he will quickly be afflicted by gulma or by a fire that emits no flames.
A lotus grows upon the chest of one who, naked and smeared with ghee, performs oblations; he who drinks [the water] along with Caṇḍālas shall perish from leprosy.
In his dreams, he loses various kinds of oily substances due to prameha;
and he who sinks into water while dancing with rakshasas suffers from unmada.
The mortal who, possessed by epilepsy, is led away dancing by a *preta* [ghost], travels in a vehicle drawn by donkeys, camels, cats, monkeys, tigers, and boars. (46)
He who, having eaten cakes and fried pastries, wakes up and vomits them up like that, stands in the mouth of death, surrounded by ghosts or jackals.
Beholding the eclipses of the sun and moon does not lead to eye disease while one is alive;
however, witnessing their conjunction (pāta) results in the destruction of vision.
Likewise, there is the growth of bamboo creepers and the like upon his head, as well as the nesting of birds; there is baldness and being surrounded by crows, vultures, and other such creatures. (49)
Likewise, there is contact with pretas, piśācas, women, Dravidians, Āndhras, and cow-eaters, as well as entanglement in cane-vines, bamboo, grass, and thorns. (50)
Lying in pits or in cremation grounds, falling into dust or ashes, sinking in water or mud, and being carried away by a swift current. // 51 //
Dancing, instrumental music, and singing; wearing red garlands and garments;
the growth of age and limbs; anointing with oil; marriage; and the grooming of the beard. (52)
The consumption of cooked food, fats, and wine; emesis and purgation;
the acquisition of gold and iron; and strife, imprisonment, and defeat. (53)

6.53b–c. Vomiting and purging, the destruction of a pair of shoes, falling down, and the peeling away of the skin from the feet; 6.54a. intense horripilation and being severely threatened by the ancestors when they are greatly provoked.
The falling or destruction of lamps, planets, stars, teeth, deities, or eyes, as well as the shattering of a mountain; 55.
6.55d–56: Or the splitting of a mountain in a forest of red flowers, the site of sinful deeds;
entering a funeral pyre crowded with the darkness of smoke, and entering into one's mother.

6.56 For those who wear the saffron robe but lack gentleness— those who are blinded by the darkness of anxiety, who fall from palaces, mountains, and the like, or who are swallowed by fish, as well as those who go naked or carry staffs [of punishment]— [there is this fate].
The sight of those with red eyes or black [complexion] is never desired;
nor one who is black, of sinful conduct, and has long hair, nails, and breasts. (58)
In a dream, the dark night of death is considered to be adorned with garlands and garments of passionlessness, because the channels carrying the mind are filled with powerful impurities. (59)
Terrible dreams are seen by which a sick person goes to his death;
one who is not ill, having fallen into danger, is perhaps released.
Dream is considered to be of seven kinds: that which is seen, heard, experienced, desired, imagined, real, and born of a defect. // 61 //
6.61–62. Dreaming is said to be of seven kinds. Among these, the first five are fruitless; they correspond to one's own [bodily] constitution and occur during the day.
A dream forgotten [upon waking], one that is long or short, or one occurring in the early part of the night, bears fruit only after a long time.

6.62b–c: According to its own nature during the day, even if long or short [vowels] are forgotten, or whether they are seen as long or short, on that day at the time of releasing the cattle (gosarga), they produce a trifling result or a great one.
Or, being unassailed by sleep, [he should be addressed] with such counter-arguments.

A wicked person who has seen [an inauspicious dream] produces a trivial result, or if unafflicted by sleep, the evil dream reaches a state of diminished fruit through acts such as giving, fire-offerings, and recitation.
Furthermore, he who, having seen even an inauspicious dream, [performs these] right there [in that same place]... (64)
Even a sinner reaches a state of fruitlessness;
if one beholds a gentle person, auspiciousness shall surely be his auspicious fruit.
[One should avoid looking at] gods, the twice-born, bulls, living beings, friends, and kings.
One sees virtuous people, illustrious men, a kindled fire, clear reservoirs of water, maidens, young boys, fair-complexioned individuals, those dressed in white garments, and those of great splendor.
6.66cv He who sees a maiden, young boys, fair men, a man-eater with a blazing body smeared all over with blood, or he who obtains an umbrella, a mirror, poison, or meat; 67 //
6.67a One with a radiant body [sees] a man-eater; 6.67b [one who is] drenched in blood on all sides [sees] white flowers, beautiful garments, unclean ointments, and fruit.
[One sees] mountains, palaces, trees bearing fruit, lions, men, and elephants. 68.
One may mount a bull, a horse, or a vehicle; one may cross rivers, lakes, and oceans.
Traveling toward the northeast constitutes approaching the unapproachable, which results in death.
6.69bv He shall cross rivers and great oceans; there is release from narrow straits and the acclaim of gods and ancestors.
There is weeping, rising from a fall, and the crushing of enemies. 70.

6.70 He who possesses longevity, health, and great wealth shall experience deliverance from distress along with the gods, as well as the crushing of his enemies; likewise, his retinue, endowed with auspicious conduct, will be free from affliction. 6.71
6.71b–72 He who is faithful and compliant enjoys abundant wealth many times over, possessing a great accumulation of goods;
he is endowed with the characteristics of a virtuous being and has devotion toward physicians and the twice-born.
"Non-despair in medical treatment is the characteristic of health"—in this regard, birth and death have been correctly illustrated [by this]. (73)
Therefore, this [section] concerning the location of the body is called the "Śārīra" (The Body). // 73½ //
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna), the following terms are synonyms for disease: *roga*, *pāpmā*, *jvara*, *vyādhi*, *vikāra*, *duḥkha*, *āmaya*, *yakṣmā*, *ātaṅka*, *gada*, and *bādhā*. (1)
The etiology, the premonitory signs, the clinical forms, the aggravating factors, and the pathogenesis—these are known as the fivefold knowledge of diseases. (2)

They say that the "source" (nidāna) is designated by various synonyms—such as sign (nimitta), cause (hetu), sphere (āyatana), condition (pratyaya), arising (utthāna), and reason (kāraṇa)—by which the prior form (pūrvarūpa) is characterized. // 3 //
A disease about to arise, not yet governed by a specific imbalance of the humors (doṣas), has unmanifest signs due to the smallness of the diseases; this is according to their respective natures.
That very [subtle essence], having attained manifestation, is designated as "form" (rūpa);
it is also called configuration (saṃsthāna), articulation (vyañjana), mark (liṅga), characteristic (lakṣaṇa), sign (cihna), and shape (ākṛti). // 5 //

The application of medicines, foods, and regimens brings happiness to those whose diseases are caused by [past] actions, by [present] humors, or by the perversion of objects, and who act in a perverted manner. (6)

One should recognize the alleviation of a disease as *sātmya* (wholesome); it is traditionally known by that name. Its opposite is *an-upaśaya*, which is designated as *asātmya* (unwholesome) for the disease. // 7 //
Just as the disease is produced by a specific humor and as it spreads accordingly, so too is its manifestation termed *saṃprāpti*, *jāti*, and *āgati*.
It is differentiated according to number, conceptual variation, predominance, strength, and specific time; as it will be stated right here: "there are eight types of fever. (9)
The differentiation of the combined humors is the conceptualization of their respective proportions;
one should determine the predominance of a disease based on whether the factors are independent or dependent. (10)

The specific strength or weakness [of the planets] is determined by the entirety of their causal factors and other components, as well as by the portions of night, day, and season occupied, according to the nature of the disease and the time. (11)
Thus has the meaning of the etiology been stated; he will explain it in detail:
the etiology of all diseases indeed consists of the provoked humors (malās).
Thus has the meaning of the diagnosis been declared; it will be taught in detail [by him]. It is being taught in detail [by him].
He will teach it in detail. It will be taught by him in detail. He [will teach it] in detail.
That [which causes their provocation] is taught by Vyāsa;
indeed, the service of various unwholesome things is said to provoke them.
Unwholesomeness consists of a threefold application, as previously described for the three [humors]. (13)

1.13c–d Harmful [regimen] consists of three types of improper application (ayoga): through bitter, pungent, and astringent foods, as well as those that are scanty, dry, or eaten in insufficient quantity; and through the suppression of natural urges, excessive exertion, staying awake at night, and speaking in an excessively loud voice.

The wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated by excessive physical activity, sexual union, fear, grief, anxiety, exertion, and intercourse; also at the end of summer, during the day, at night, and after eating. (15)

Pitta [is aggravated] by pungent, sour, sharp, hot, salty, and acrid substances, by anger, and by burning sensations; and it increases during autumn, at midday, at midnight, and during the period of internal heat. // 16 //

And during the summer seasons, [the body is afflicted] by things that are sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, heavy, obstructive, and cold; by pleasant sitting and sleeping; by indigestion; by sleeping during the day; and by excessive nourishing foods.

Due to excessive sleep, indulgence in pleasure, indigestion, or improper administration of emetics and other therapies; or immediately after eating, during the spring season, in the forenoon, or in the first part of the night—phlegm (śleṣman) increases; however, due to the combination of factors, two humors may increase together.

Furthermore, there is the combination (saṃnipāta) of all [humors] due to their becoming mixed, as well as through eating food that is contaminated, undigested, irregular, incompatible, or consumed in excess, and so forth. // 19 //
With spoiled liquor, drinking water, dried vegetables, raw radishes, oil-cake, clay, barley, wine, putrid matter, dried meat, and lean flesh; // 20 //

Due to various factors that aggravate the three *doṣas*, through changes in diet, from the corruption of the seasons, from easterly winds, from possession by malevolent spirits, and from poison or artificial toxins; // 21 //
Likewise, from the transformation of food,

from the consumption of corrupted food, from contact with mountains, from the affliction of the natal star by planets, from various improper associations, and from the practice of sinful deeds. (1.21–22)

Due to the affliction by wicked mothers, from the pressure of mountains, from the complications of women's childbirth, and likewise from improper medical treatment— thus, provoked according to each specific disease, they [the humors] move toward the seats of the diseases. (1.22–23)
The humors quickly reach the rejuvenating channels and undergo transformation within the body.
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna):
Fever is the lord of diseases, a malevolent force, death, the consumer of vitality, and the end-maker;
it is wrath itself, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and that which arose from the upper eye of Rudra. (1)
2.1b Mṛtyu, Tejo’śana, Antaka, Mohamaya, Saṃtāpātman, and Apacāraja— this cruel one exists under various names throughout diverse wombs. (2)

It arises in eight ways through the humors (doṣas)—individually, in combination, or all together—and there is also the exogenous type; in these cases, the impurities (malās) are corrupted by their respective specific causes of vitiation.
Having entered the stomach, followed after the undigested matter (āma), and blocked the channels,
it casts the digestive fire outward from its place of digestion.
Moving along with that [wind], scorching the entire body and making the limbs excessively hot, they bring about fever (jvara). //5//
2.5. Those who exercise their bodies excessively quickly dry them out due to the obstruction of the bodily channels; consequently, perspiration generally does not arise.
Its premonitory symptoms are laziness, lack of interest, and heaviness of the limbs. (6)
A bad taste in the mouth, loss of appetite, yawning, eyes clouded with tears, aching of the limbs, indigestion, diminished vitality, and excessive sleepiness; // 7 //
2.7bv – yawning, eyes clouded with tears, horripilation, stooping, cramps in the calves, fatigue,
intolerance toward wholesome advice, and a fondness for sour, salty, and pungent tastes. // 8 //
There is hatred toward delicious foods, as well as intense thirst for children; and there is an uncaused aversion toward sound, fire, cold, wind, water, shade, and heat. (9)
Following that, desire and aversion arise, and the manifestation of fever occurs through the coming and going, agitation, mildness, pain, and heat. (10)
In various parts of the body, there arise various shifting pains;
in the feet, numbness, stiffness, cramps in the calves, and loss of sensation.
2.11dv There is a twisting pain in the calves, exhaustion, a sensation as if the joints were coming apart, weakness in the thighs, and stiffness in the waist.
The back feels as if it is being crushed, and the abdomen feels as if it is being squeezed. 12.
The bones of the ribs, especially those on the sides, felt as if they were being cut; there was a seizing and piercing pain in the heart, as if the chest were being prodded with a goad.
There is churning of the shoulders, a splitting sensation in the arms, and pressure on the shoulder blades;
there is an inability to chew with the jaws, yawning, and a ringing sound in the ears. (14)
Piercing pain in the temples, headache, a distaste for food, or a bitter taste in the mouth, as well as the non-excretion of waste products; // 15 //

Roughness and reddish discoloration of the skin, mouth, eyes, nails, urine, and feces; excessive salivation, loss of appetite, lack of faith [in food], indigestion, perspiration, and sleeplessness. (16)
Dryness of the throat and lips, thirst, parched vomiting and cough, a sense of poisoning, horripilation on the body and teeth, trembling, and suppression of sneezing; // 17 //
2.17–18. In fever caused by Vāta (anila-jvara), there is swelling, sneezing, seizure, vertigo, delirium, a desire for heat, and bending of the body;
furthermore, there is simultaneous pervasion of the limbs, incoherent speech, and a bitter taste in the mouth.
There is inflammation of the nose, desire for cold things, vertigo, fainting, intoxication, aversion, discharge of feces, vomiting of bile, spitting of blood, and acid eructations. (19)
In the Pitta-born [fever], there is the eruption of red boils, a yellowish or greenish discoloration of the skin and other parts, perspiration, foul-smelling breath, and excessive thirst. (20)

Specifically, there is loss of appetite, dullness, obstruction of the channels, diminished force [of the breath], excessive salivation, sweetness in the mouth, coating of the heart, dyspnea, and chronic rhinitis. // 21 //

In the case of a disorder arising from phlegm (kapha), there is a sense of horripilation, vomiting, coughing, stiffness, whiteness of the skin and other parts, cold eruptions on the limbs, lassitude, and urticaria. (22)
At the proper time, the activity or even the increase of all things occurs according to their own nature. // 23ab //
The alleviation of symptoms as described in the etiology is the state of being relieved by the opposite [of the cause]. // 23cd //
And fever arising from a combination [of doshas] also occurs according to the respective combination of their symptoms. (23ef)

Headache, fainting, vomiting, burning sensations, delusion, dryness of the throat and mouth, restlessness, pain in the joints, insomnia, thirst, giddiness, horripilation, yawning, and excessive talkativeness—these arise from a mobile (vāta) humor combined with pitta. (24)

Fever born of phlegm and wind has as its symptoms: a lack of heat, loss of appetite, pain in the joints, headache, catarrh, dyspnea, cough, constipation, coldness, numbness, blurred vision, vertigo, and drowsiness. (25)
Coldness, stiffness, perspiration, and burning sensations occurring irregularly; thirst, cough, and the discharge of phlegm and bile;
delusion, drowsiness, and a sense that the mouth is smeared with or bitter—these should be known as the symptoms of fever arising from phlegm and bile (śleṣma-pitta-jvara). // 26 //
2.26b–c: Thirst, cough, and the discharge of phlegm and bile; the fever born from all [three] humors possesses all these symptoms, as well as burning sensations that recur again and again.
Likewise, there is coldness, excessive sleep during the day, and wakefulness at night. 2.27a–b.
Constant sleep or its total absence, excessive perspiration or its total absence, and the engagement in distorted desires such as singing, dancing, laughter, and the like. (28)
2.28b–c There is either excessive sweating or none at all;
the eyes are tearful, turbid, red, and sunken, with disheveled eyelashes.
2.29 There is pain in the calves, the sides of the body, the head, the joints, and the bones, as well as vertigo.
The ears are accompanied by ringing sounds and pain; the throat is as if covered with bristles;
the tongue is scorched and rough; and the limbs and joints are heavy and drooping.
2.30–31. A heavy head, drooping of the limbs and joints, expectoration of blood, bile, and phlegm, tossing of the head, excessive pain,
and the appearance of dark-red eruptions (koṭhas) and circular patches (maṇḍalas) [are the symptoms].
2.31b–c. Excessive thirst, pain in the heart, and the retention or excessive discharge of waste matter; a greasy mouth, loss of strength, hoarseness of voice, and delirious talk; 32.
2.32ab Pain in the heart, association with impurities, delayed maturation of the humors (doṣas), drowsiness, and constant gurgling in the throat—
these one should call *saṃnipāta*, *abhinyāsa*, and "deprived of vitality" (*hṛtaujas*).
And one should tell him that his vital energy has been destroyed by wind obstructed by phlegm, while the pitta is intensely compressed within;
due to its pervasive nature and subtlety, it moves toward the external pathways. (33+1)
Therefore, there is yellowness of the eyes in a fever arising from the combination of the humors (saṃnipāta). // 33+2ab //

When the humors are obstructed and the digestive fire is destroyed, it exhibits all the complete symptoms and is incurable; otherwise, it may be difficult to treat or even result in physical impairment.

Furthermore, that which arises from a combination [of humors], where the bile (pitta) is situated separately, produces a burning sensation either on the skin or within the visceral cavity (koṣṭha), either before or after [the fever]. (35)

2.35 And there is another type arising from the combination [of all three humors] (saṃnipāta), which is like that; in the cases of Vāta and Kapha, coldness and burning sensations respectively are difficult to overcome.
In that [saṃnipāta fever], when coldness occurs first, it is due to Pitta having liquefied and dried up the Kapha.
When the fever has subsided, coldness, sour eructation, fainting, intoxication, and thirst arise;
furthermore, at the end of the burning sensation and other stages, drowsiness, spitting, vomiting, and exhaustion occur. (37)
Exogenous [fever] arises from injury, contagion, curses, and malevolent spells; among these, that born of injury is fourfold, caused by wounds, incisions, burns, and so forth. (38)
Furthermore, due to physical exertion, the wind (vāyu) generally vitiates the blood in that [person], producing a fever accompanied by pain, swelling, discoloration, and distress. (39)
Possession by spirits arises from medicinal herbs, poison, anger, fear, grief, or desire;
and due to such affliction, there is sudden laughing or weeping in this person as if seized by a spirit.
From the scent of medicinal herbs, fainting, headache, vomiting, and sneezing arise;
from poison, fainting, diarrhea, a dark discoloration of the face, burning sensations, and heart disease occur. (41)
Headache, swelling, and sneezing; headache, trembling, and sneezing;
a darkish complexion, burning sensation, and cardiac oppression—these arise from anger; while trembling, headache, and delirium arise from fear and grief.
From desire arise delusion, lack of appetite, burning fever, and the destruction of shame, sleep, wisdom, and fortitude. // 42 //

2.42d–43ab: In possession by spirits (*graha*) and the like, there is a destruction of fear, sleep, intellect, and fortitude; in cases of fear and the like, it is the wind (*marut*); in the triad [of afflictions], it is the provocation of bile (*pitta*); and in cases of provocation, it is also bile—except for those two [types of affliction] born of curses and malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).
In anger, there is an aggravation of pitta; however, in rage, there is an aggravation of both wind and pitta. Those two—sannipāta fever and rage—are considered terrible and most unbearable.
In that state, one suffers as if being offered into the fire by means of malevolent mantras.
2.44bv Those two are considered the most difficult to cure:
first the mind, then the body; thereafter, for one seized by eruptions, thirst, giddiness, burning sensations, and fainting, the fever increases day by day.
Thus, fever is seen to be of eight types in brief; however, it is manifold:
bodily and mental, mild and sharp, and based internally or externally. (46)

In the *śārīra* [type of suffering], there are the natural (*prākṛta*), the modified (*vaikṛta*), the curable (*sādhya*), the incurable (*asādhya*), that with phlegm (*sāma*), and that without phlegm (*nirāma*).
First, in the body there is bodily heat (*tāpa*), and in the mind there is mental heat (*mānasa*). (47)
In the wind [element], due to its nature as a carrier of yoga, there would be cold when it is joined with phlegm;
burning when joined with bile; and a mixed sensation when joined with both; furthermore, when it resides internally, there is internal heat.
In fever, disorders are more numerous when the impulse is internal, characterized by internal agitation and the retention of waste products;
whereas when the impulse is external, there is heat only on the surface, and the condition is easily curable.
In the rainy season, autumn, and spring, the natural (prākṛta) fever arises respectively from wind and the other [doshas];
the other is the unnatural (vaikṛta). That [unnatural fever] is difficult to cure, and the natural fever is generally caused by wind (anila).
During the rainy season, the vitiated wind (vāyu), combined with bile (pitta) and phlegm (kapha), produces fever;
and in autumn, it is the bile that causes it, with phlegm acting as its secondary strength.

2.51d–52. And its secondary humor is phlegm (kapha), due to its innate nature and because it is released [at that time]; therefore, there is no danger from fasting there. In spring, phlegm [increases], and wind and bile (vāta-pitta) follow after it.
2.52ab Due to its own nature, fever caused by the discharge [of doshas] when they are strong and the complications are few is curable; however,
if there is any sign of morbid transformation (vikṛti) at all, it is declared from the outset to be incurable.

Intense complications of fever, lack of exhaustion, copious urination, absence of bowel movements, undigested feces, and lack of hunger—these are the characteristics of *sāmajvara* (fever with undigested humors). // 54 //

Excessive force of fever, thirst, delirium, labored breathing, confusion, the discharge of waste products, and nausea are the signs of the fever being in the process of maturation (pacyamāna). // 55 //
The intensity of the fever increases, as does thirst, due to the non-digestion of the [febrile] matter and because of fasting for seven nights.
Fever is said to be of five types, according to the strength or weakness of the morbid humors (mala) and the time (kāla). // 56 //
It is generally taught that [fevers] mostly arise from the combination [of all three humors];
they are classified as continuous (saṃtata), constant (satata), quotidian (anyedyuṣka), tertian (tṛtīyaka), and quartan (caturthaka). (57)

2.57 Generally, those impurities, increased by the simultaneous corruption of the [vitiated] elements (dūṣya) and other factors, pervade the channels that carry the bodily constituents (dhātu), urine, and feces; spreading through the entire body, they cause a burning sensation.
Strong, heavy, and rigid, especially when dependent on the rasa-dhātu,
and being constantly without any opposing factors, they produce a fever that is extremely difficult to endure.
That fever-heat may quickly exhaust the impurities of the tissues (dhātus), or it may do so in every way through the sequential purification or non-purification of the rasa and other elements. (60)

The heat of fever pursues the impurities or the bodily constituents (dhātus) through the actions of wind, bile, and phlegm for seven, ten, or twelve days; generally, this serves as the boundary for both recovery and death.
2.61d–62ab: "For liberation or for destruction"—this is the opinion of Agniveśa; however, the traditional teaching of Hārīta is as follows:
the seventh [day] is doubled, and likewise the ninth and the eleventh.
This is the boundary of the three humors (doṣas), leading both to liberation and to death;
whether in a state of purity or impurity, fever persists for even a long time.
2.63–64. In those who are emaciated, whether they have been purified or not, or in those who have recovered from disease but indulge in improper diet and other habits,
even a slight derangement of the *doṣas* gains strength from any one of the *dūṣyas* (tissues) and other factors over time, resulting in fever.

Accompanied by its opposing factors, the dosha produces an irregular fever characterized by fluctuation between decrease and increase; becoming powerful, it manifests at its own specific time, causing the fever.

2.65dv At its own time, the powerful fever returns again, according to the strength or weakness of its opposing forces; when the *doṣa* has been diminished, the subtle fever dissolves into the *rasa* and other tissues.
Because it is constricted, it produces emaciation, discoloration, dullness, and so forth, due to the proximity of its opening to the channels that carry the nutrient fluid (rasa). (67)
A continuous and constant pervasion of the entire body by the *doṣa* occurs; because of that, the opposite [condition] arises from its reversal. (68)
The irregular type, characterized by an irregular onset, activity, and duration, and associated with the blood as its primary seat, generally causes fever continuously. (69)
He should take [the medicine] twice during the day and night, and once on the following day; in that tertian fever, the channels carrying flesh and the channels of fat are affected. (70)

In this [fever], the vessels carrying the flesh are seized by pitta and vāyu; it arises from kapha and pitta in the head and the *trika* (the sacral region), and from vāyu and kapha in the back. It is known to have an interval of one day (*ekāhāntara*).

That [fever] is remembered as occurring with a single-day interval (vaikāhāntara) when it resides in the fat, marrow, or bone; others say it resides specifically in the marrow. It, however, manifests its power on the fourth day.
Due to phlegm, it first manifests in the calves, and due to wind, in the head;
when it has entered both the bone and the marrow, there occurs the fourth-day irregular fever (caturthaka-viparyaya).

2.73d–74. The reversal of the quartan fever is threefold: it causes fever for two days and then releases [the patient] for one day, depending on the relative strength or weakness of the *doṣas* arising from food, physical activity, and other factors.
For three days it causes fever for two days, and on the first day the fever releases;
the fever occurs at various times due to the mind and likewise due to karma.
The fever arises from the strength of the humors (doṣa), the affected tissues (dūṣya), the seasons, the day and night, and so forth. // 75 //
The affliction, agitating the elements, encounters its respective time regarding the mind and the sense objects; it dissolves at the time of liberation.
Then the man, gasping, perspiring, moaning, and struggling, trembles and raves, his limbs becoming hot and cold while his luster is destroyed. (77)

Deprived of consciousness and afflicted by the force of the fever, he looks about as if filled with rage; and with great intensity, he voids liquid feces accompanied by the sound of the morbid humors.

The body becomes light, free from fatigue, delusion, and fever; there is a sense of ripening in the mouth, excellence of the senses, and absence of pain; there is perspiration, sneezing, a natural desire for food, and itching on the head—these are the signs of one whose fever has departed.
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna):
Through the excessive consumption of very hot, sharp, pungent, sour, salty, and burning substances, as well as *kodrava* and *uddālaka* grains, along with foods prepared with them [1].
When pitta is provoked by pitta-increasing factors, it becomes liquefied along with the blood;
having attained a state of mutual similarity, these two pervade the body. (2)
Pitta is designated as "blood" (rakta) because of its transformation into blood, its association with it, its corruption by it, and its conformity to the smell and color of blood. // 3 //

3.3ab Pitta, which is a morbid transformation of blood, arises from its own site, namely the spleen and the liver. It causes heaviness of the head, loss of appetite, a desire for cold things, a sensation of fuming, and acid eructations. (4)
Vomiting, disgust for food, cough, dyspnea, giddiness, exhaustion, a metallic or bloody fish-like odor in the mouth, and loss of voice; // 5 //
The appearance of red, yellow, and green colors in the eyes and other [faculties], and the failure to distinguish between the colors blue, red, and yellow; (6)
In this [state], there occurs the seeing of those colors in a dream;
[the winds] move upward through the nose, eyes, ears, and mouth, and downward through the penis, vagina, and anus. // 7 //
When provoked, it flows out through all the hair follicles;
since it arises from kapha and moves upward, it is curable by means of purgation. // 8 //
There are many medicines for pitta, for purgation is indeed the best medicine; and as for the persistent kapha that remains there, it too is cleansed by that [purgation].
Even sweet astringents are beneficial for one whose phlegm is purified;
how much more so those astringents that are bitter, which by their very nature dispel phlegm? (10)

Since that which is unstable must be expelled downward, emesis is the means for its discharge; moreover, because it requires only a small amount of medicine, emesis is not the superior treatment for pitta.
That which is continuous and unstable does not lead to his peace;
for him, even the astringent tastes are beneficial, while the sweet ones are merely so.
The *ubhayāyana* type, which is a combination of *kapha* and *māruta*, is incurable because it is impossible to reverse [the doshas] and because there is no medicine for it. (13)
Indeed, there is no purificatory treatment for this that proceeds in the reverse direction;
for in cases of raktapitta, the physician’s mastery consists of purification and [treatment] in the reverse direction. (14)
3.14bv There exists for this a reverse-order [treatment]; 3.14bv there exists for this a counter-measure (pratilomaka).
In this very way, a pacifying treatment that is effective in every respect is not found for it.
For when the doshas are combined, a pacifying treatment that conquers all is beneficial. // 15 //

In that regard, one should observe the progression of the doshas as being like [the flow of] blood in the vessels, and the complications through the knowledge of their morbid transformations, which are predominant therein. (16)
Since cough is a condition that requires prompt treatment, he will therefore describe it now.
Five types of cough are recognized: those caused by vāta, pitta, śleṣman, injury (kṣata), and wasting (kṣaya). (17)
Therefore, they will now describe that very [condition]: when all these [doshas] are neglected, they lead to wasting (kṣaya), each becoming progressively more powerful.
The premonitory symptom (pūrvarūpa) of their impending manifestation is itching in the throat and loss of appetite.
3.18bv And in these [conditions], they become increasingly severe;
there is a sensation as if the throat were filled with bristles. In that state, the wind (vāyu), struck below, moves upward;
reaching the chest and becoming obstructed within that throat— 19.
Having filled the channels of the head, it then seems to lift up the limbs, as if casting the eyes back, and presses upon the back, the chest, and the sides. (20)
That [sound], with a resonance like that of cracked bell-metal, proceeds from the mouth;
it is due to the difference in causes that there is a difference in the obstruction of the impetuous wind. (21)
From that, a discordance of pain and sound arises in the coughs;
then, the Vata aggravated by Vata-aggravating factors causes dryness of the chest, throat, and mouth.
3.22cv When the wind (vāyu) is provoked by vāta-aggravating factors,
it causes pain in the heart, flanks, chest, and head, as well as delusion, agitation, loss of voice, dry cough, and a sound accompanied by great force and pain. // 23 //
3.23cd–24ab: It causes a dry cough, a sense of horripilation in the limbs, and the expectoration of dry phlegm with difficulty, after which it subsides slightly.
From pitta, there is yellowness of the eyes and phlegm, a bitter taste in the mouth, fever, and vertigo.

There is vomiting of bile and blood, thirst, hoarseness of voice, a sensation of fumes, and sour eructations; there is constant coughing with forceful paroxysms, and a vision of lights as if from celestial bodies. (25)

From kapha arise hoarseness, a sensation of fumes, and intoxication; there is slight pain in the chest, the head and heart feel numb and heavy, there is a coating in the throat, lassitude, coryza, vomiting, and anorexia. // 26 //

When there is an internal injury to the chest, the powerful Vayu, accompanied by Pitta and becoming aggravated, produces a cough that expels phlegm along with blood. (28)
One spits out phlegm that is yellow, dark-brown, dry, knotted, and copious;
with a throat that is painful and as if the chest were being torn apart. (29)
3.29–30ab: [The patient] has yellowish or dark urine that is parched;
he suffers from piercing pain as if by sharp needles, accompanied by colic, fever, dyspnea, thirst, loss of voice, and tremors. He experiences splitting pain in the joints. 30ab.
Then, moaning like a pigeon, he suffers from pain in his sides;
and gradually his vitality, appetite, digestive power, strength, and complexion decline. (31)

In one whose [bodily constituents] are depleted, there occurs the presence of blood and urine [in the stool], as well as stiffness in the back and waist; the bodily tissues (dhātus) of the patient suffering from royal consumption (rājayakṣman) become aggravated, with vāyu being predominant. // 32 //
Through the seats of consumption (yakṣma), they produce cough; thereafter, one spits out phlegm that is foul-smelling, resembling pus, yellow, putrid, greenish, or reddish. // 33 //
The sides feel as if they are burning, and the heart feels as if it is falling; suddenly there is a desire for both heat and cold, excessive appetite, and a loss of strength. (34)

His two sides appear as if they are wasting away, his face becomes glossy and serene, and his eyes possess a majestic appearance; thereafter, all the symptoms of its decline manifest in him. (3.34–35)

3.35bv–36. This cough arising from wasting (kṣayaja), characterized by beautiful teeth and eyes, destroys the bodies of those who are already emaciated; however, it may be palliable in those who are strong.
Likewise, the cough arising from injury (kṣataja) is fatal in the weak, while both of these types are curable when they are recent.
The three types of curable [diseases] may be cured through supportive treatment, even when they are individually afflicted by complications;
those that are mixed [with complications] are palliable; and all types become incurable due to old age or in the case of an elderly person.

3.37 Even diseases such as cough, dyspnea, consumption, vomiting, and loss of voice may be cured through [the treatment of] that [kapha] alone by virtue of its capacity; however, since they arise from neglecting it, one should therefore conquer that [kapha] with haste. 38.
Dyspnea (śvāsa) may arise from an increase in cough, or from the provocation of the humors (doṣas) by the aforementioned factors,
or even from undigested matter (āma), diarrhea, vomiting, poisoning, anemia, and fever. (1)
Through dust, smoke, wind, injury to the vital points (marmans), and extremely cold water, there arise five types of asthma:
the minor (kṣudraka), the obstructive (tamaka), the interrupted (chinna), the great (mahān), and the fifth, the upward-moving (ūrdhva).
The wind (vāyu), its movement obstructed by phlegm (kapha) and situated throughout the body, becomes vitiated and corrupts the channels that carry the vital breath, water, and food. // 3 //
Located in the chest, it produces dyspnea arising from the stomach (āmāśaya);
its premonitory symptoms are pain in the heart and the flanks, and the upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa).
In that condition, constipation and splitting pain in the temples occur; the wind (marut), impelled by exertion and excessive eating, should itself expel the minor [doshas] through self-pacification.
Moving in a retrograde direction through the vessels, the wind excites the phlegm;
having seized it, it afflicts the head, neck, chest, and sides.
It causes coughing, wheezing, delusion, loss of appetite, nasal catarrh, and thirst, as well as a violent onset of labored breathing that afflicts the vital breaths. // 7 //
He faints from its force; at the end of the spitting, he is momentarily relieved; lying down with difficulty, he pants, and when seated, he attains some composure. (8)
With eyes bulging, forehead profusely perspiring, and suffering great pain, his mouth parched, breathing repeatedly, and trembling, he longs for warmth. (9)
It increases due to clouds, rainwater, cool eastern winds, and phlegm-inducing factors; that Tamaka asthma is palliable, though it may be curable if it is recent or occurs in a strong person. (10)
Accompanied by fever and fainting, that condition is *pratamaka*; it is pacified by cold treatments.
Afflicted by the pain of a cutting sensation in the vital organs (*marman*), the patient breathes with gasps that are broken and interrupted.
He is covered in sweat and fainting, bound by his girdle, and suffers from burning and obstruction in the bladder;
he looks downward with rolling eyes, becomes delirious, and one of his eyes turns bloodshot. (12)
With a parched mouth, speaking incoherently, dejected, his luster vanished and consciousness lost,
he gasps and chokes with a great, agonizing sound.
4.13cd–14ab: Oppressed by the great [suffering], the wretched man, agitated and frantic like a rutting bull, is incessantly tossed about;
his knowledge and discernment are lost, and his eyes and face are bewildered.
Withdrawing his chest, with suppressed urine and feces, his speech faltering, his throat parched, fainting repeatedly, and suffering extreme pain in the ears, temples, and head. (15)
He breathes out long and upward, and does not draw [the breath] back down;
his channels of the mouth are obstructed by phlegm, and he is afflicted by the enraged wind (vāyu). (16)
With his vision failing, he gazes upward while casting his eyes about in confusion;
as his vital organs are being cut away, he laments with his speech choked.
These [afflictions], whether unmanifest or manifest, certainly bring about the loss of life;
they are based on the number, nature, and primary cause of the breath, as well as its preceding symptoms. // 18 //
Hiccup (hidhmā) arises from number, constitution, and its location;

it is classified as *bhaktodbhavā*, *kṣudrā*, *yamalā*, *mahatī*, and *gambhīrā*. Among these, in the case of *marut* [hiccup], [the condition] should be treated with prompt application of appropriate measures.
Afflicted by food and drink that is dry, sharp, rough, and unwholesome, one produces hiccup that is painless, of low volume, and followed by sneezing. (20)
That which subsides through wholesome food and drink is born of food;
however, the minor wind (pavana), due to exertion, brings about the minor hiccup (kṣudrā hidhmā).
4.21c–d Due to physical exertion, the wind (pavana) becomes aggravated; it spreads to the base of the collarbones, becoming slow-moving and mild.
It increases as the person is about to eat, and returns to its mild state immediately after eating.
That which proceeds toward food with slow and steady impulses increases when it is directed toward digestion and reaches its full development once digestion has occurred. (23)
Shaking the head and neck, [the patient] suffers from flatulence and extreme thirst, as well as delirium, vomiting, diarrhea, impairment of the eyes, and yawning. (24)
4.24 That hiccup which causes the head and neck to tremble, which is twin-folded, rapid, and occurs as a complication of a chronic disease,
belongs to one whose pair of eyebrows and temples are stiffened and whose eyes are flooded with tears.

Bending backward, with emaciation, the great hiccup (mahā-hidhmā) sets in;
it has deep roots, a loud sound, great velocity, and great strength. // 27 //

Whether it proceeds from the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) or from the navel, as described previously, that [wind], taking on such a form, repeatedly causes yawning and the stretching out of the limbs. (28)
One should employ those [women] who are deep in their resonance;
one should avoid the first two types, but may employ the last two, as well as those who possess all the [auspicious] marks and those who are vigorous. (29)
And all the accumulated merit of this elder, who was diligent in practice, whose body has been worn away by diseases, or who has been weakened by the cessation of food; (30)
Although all diseases lead to destruction, none act with such speed as hiccup and asthma; for these two indeed take up their abode at the time of death.
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna),

the royal consumption (rājayakṣma)— also known as wasting (kṣaya), emaciation (śoṣa), and the king of diseases— is traditionally recorded as being followed by many diseases and preceding many others. // 1 //
Because he was formerly the king of the stars and the twice-born, and because he is both a king and a consumption (yakṣman), he is therefore considered the "King-Consumption" (rājayakṣman). // 2 //

It is called *kṣaya* (decay) because it causes the depletion of the body and the medicinal substances; it is called *saṃbhava* (arising) because it originates from them; it is called *śoṣa* (wasting) because it dries up the bodily fluids such as plasma; and it is the "king of diseases" (*roga-rāj*) because it rules over them. (3)

5.3dv Because it is the king of diseases, the suppression of natural urges constitutes violence. The depletion of semen, ojas, and unctuousness, and the abandonment of the proper regimen for food and drink—these four are its causes. (4)
The wind (anila), aggravated by those [factors], having provoked the bile (pitta) and phlegm (kapha) throughout the body, enters the joints of the body and afflicts the channels (sirā). // 5 //
By obstructing the openings of the channels, or likewise by excessively dilating them, [the vāyu] moving upwards,
downwards, or transversely produces diseases according to its respective location.
For one who will become [a fetus] in the form of male, there will be severe catarrh, frequent sneezing, salivation, sweetness in the mouth, and a languor of both the digestive fire and the body. (7)
Even when vessels, food, drink, and the like are clean, there is often the sight of impurity, and the falling of flies, grass, hair, and so forth, upon the food and drink. (8)
Heartburn, vomiting, loss of appetite even when eating, loss of strength, a preoccupation with the hands, swelling of the feet and face, and excessive whiteness of the eyes; // 9 //
Inquiry regarding the measurement of the arms, a sense of disgust toward the body, a fondness for women, wine, and meat, loathsomeness, and veiling the head. (10)
There will be excessive growth of nails and hair, and in dreams, there will be an encounter with defeat by means of moths, lizards, snakes, monkeys, beasts of prey, and birds. (11)
5.11dv–12. Ascending onto heaps of hair, bones, chaff, ashes, and the like;
seeing empty villages and regions; and seeing water drying up.
There is light from mountains falling and trees burning;
there is catarrh, labored breathing, coughing, pain in the shoulders and head, hoarseness of voice, and loss of appetite. (13)
When located in the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha), it causes upward expulsion of feces, dehydration, and vomiting;
when situated obliquely, it causes pain in the flanks; and when located in the joints, it produces fever. (14)
5.14ab When located in the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha), there arise these eleven symptoms in one afflicted by rājayakṣman: upward discharge of feces and dryness, and downward vomiting.
5.14cd One should recognize their complications as hoarseness of the throat and pain in the chest.
Yawning, aching of the limbs, spitting, loss of digestive fire, a bad taste in the mouth, and fetid breath occur therein;
among these, from Vāta arise pain in the head and sides, and aching of the shoulders and limbs. (16)
Destruction of the throat, loss of voice, burning sensation in the feet, shoulders, and hands, diarrhea, vomiting of blood, foul odor from the mouth, fever, and intoxication [arise] from pitta. (17)
From kapha arise loss of appetite, vomiting, cough, heaviness of the head and limbs, excessive salivation, rhinitis, dyspnea, hoarseness of voice, and diminished digestive fire. (18)

5.18–19. A change in voice tone and diminished digestive fire occur due to the humors (doṣas), specifically when they are dominated by phlegm (kapha) and cause internal obstructions; as the openings of the channels become blocked and the heat of the bodily tissues (dhātu-ūṣman) becomes feeble, the digestive fire (anala) becomes sluggish.
Burning in its own location, the rasa produces various complications;
failing to reach the muscle tissue and other elements, it flows upward into the blood.
Food is digested only within the stomach; and that which is digested by his digestive fire mostly turns into waste, being no longer capable of nourishing the bodily constituents.
Even its essence does not turn into blood, much less into flesh;
supported only by excrement, it exists in a state of decay.

5.22–23. If the patient is obstructed by feces and has diminished strength—being unable to withstand the force of the disease or the medicine—even if the piles are small, one should desist from treatment; otherwise, if the condition is different from this, one should certainly treat him even if the piles are large.

5.23cd–24ab One should avoid [treating] such a case, yet one should treat it if the patient’s flesh and strength have not diminished; however, one should abandon a patient afflicted by the aforementioned premonitory signs.
Having declined to treat a man who is destitute, one should quickly attend to one who possesses the necessary resources. 23+1.

Hoarseness of voice (svarabheda) occurs due to the individual doshas, all of them combined, from wasting (kshaya), and sixthly, from fat (medas). In that condition, the voice becomes weak, dry, and unstable.

As if smearing the throat with phlegm, the voice becomes weak and makes a "khura-khura" sound; when obstructed by all [doshas], it rasps with all the symptoms due to wasting (kṣaya).
One characterized by phlegm (kapha) smokes excessively due to an abundance of fat;
in this case, the syllables are difficult to discern, and one should avoid all [such patients], as well as those with the final [sign]. (27)
Anorexia may arise from humors localized in the tongue and heart, from the combination of all three humors (saṃnipāta), and fifthly, from mental distress. (28)

5.28b–c. Depending on whether [the humors] are located in the tongue or the heart, the mouth becomes astringent, bitter, or sweet respectively in cases of Vāta and the other [humors]. When all three are provoked, it is tasteless; and in cases of grief, anger, and so forth, it is according to the specific impurity [involved].
Vomiting occurs due to the humors individually, all together, or by disagreeable objects as the fifth cause;
when the udāna wind is deranged, it ejects the humors upward in all these cases.
In those [women], nausea, salivation, loss of luster, and lack of appetite are the foremost symptoms;
furthermore, the wind (vāyu), afflicting the navel and the back, may cause vomiting of food from the sides.
Then one should vomit bile that is intermittent, very small in quantity, frothy, accompanied by sound and eructation, black, clear, and expelled with great force and difficulty. (32)
Accompanied by cough, dryness of the mouth, pain in the heart, head, and voice, and exhaustion, [the patient] vomits from pitta a substance resembling alkaline water, smoky, green, or yellow. (33)
That which is mixed with blood is sour, pungent, and hot, accompanied by thirst, fainting, fever, and a burning sensation;
that which arises from phlegm (kapha) is unctuous, thick, cold, and covered with phlegmatic threads.
Accompanied by thirst, fainting, heat, and burning sensations,
it is characterized by excessive and persistent sweetness and salinity,
horripilation, swelling of the face, sweetness in the mouth, drowsiness, nausea, and cough. (5.34–35)
One should abandon that woman who exhibits all the signs of impending death mentioned in the section on fatal omens (ariṣṭa), as well as those indicated by foul odors,
impurities, filth, or by sights and sounds that are loathsome.
When the mind is heated and the heart is afflicted, vomiting arises from contact with loathsome objects;
in cases of worms, grass-like parasites, or pregnancy-cravings (daurhṛda), one should examine the humors such as wind (vāta) and the rest.
One should specifically identify that caused by parasites (kṛmija) by means of piercing pain, trembling, and nausea;
heart diseases are known to be of five types, including those characterized by the symptoms of parasitic heart disease (kṛmi-hṛd-roga). // 38 //
Their manifestation occurs through the same etiological factors and origins as those described for gulma.
In the case of the vāta type, it is excessively painful with piercing sensations, pricking, and a feeling as if it were bursting. (39)
Its manifestation differs according to its origins:
the heart becomes parched, rigid, and empty; there is a sense of fluidity, sudden dejection, grief, fear, and intolerance of sound. (5.39b–40)
5.40b–c Due to pitta, there is a sense of emptiness in the heart, a feeling of melting, trembling, convulsions, delusion, suppression of breath, and scant sleep;
41. as well as thirst, vertigo, fainting, burning heat, perspiration, acid eructation, and exhaustion.
Vomiting of sour bile, a sensation of fumes, yellowness, and fever [arise from pitta]; while by kapha, the heart feels stiff, heavy as if filled with stones, and distended. (42)

5.42b–d: Tamaka fever, jaundice, cough, loss of digestive fire, expectoration, sleepiness, lassitude, and anorexia; when caused by all three doshas, it exhibits all symptoms, while with worms, there is a dark-brown discoloration of the eyes.
5.43c–d When all three doshas are involved, there is entry into darkness (fainting), nausea, emaciation, itching, and discharge of phlegm;
furthermore, in this condition, the heart feels as if it is being sawn apart by a saw.

One should treat that terrible disease quickly, for it acts with rapidity; [it arises] from vāta, pitta, kapha, their combination (saṃnipāta), or from the depletion of the bodily fluids (rasakṣaya). 45.

The genitive case may also be used after a prefix; moreover, wind (vāta) and bile (pitta) are the causes [of this condition], for their aggravation occurs in all [humors] due to the drying up of the somatic elements (saumya-dhātu). 46.
The vessels carrying water to the tongue-root, throat, kloma, and palate cause trembling, heat, thirst, burning sensations, and delusion throughout the entire body. (47)
When thirst has been dried up, [other disorders] arise; their general characteristics are dryness of the mouth, lack of satiety from water, aversion to food, and loss of voice. (48)

Roughness of the throat, lips, and tongue; protrusion of the tongue; exhaustion; delirium; and mental derangement—these, as well as diseases such as thirst and possession by spirits, [are the symptoms]. (49)
From [excess of] Vāta arise emaciation, dejection, piercing pain in the temples, vertigo, loss of the sense of smell, bad taste in the mouth, deafness, sleepiness, and loss of strength. (50)
5.50cd–dv: Loss of smell, knowledge, and taste; loss of hearing, sleep, and strength. 5.50dv:
[Loss of] hearing, sleep, and strength.
From drinking cold water, there is an increase [of pitta], as well as fainting and a bitter taste in the mouth due to pitta.
Redness of the eyes, constant emaciation, burning sensations, and excessive belching; // 51 //
When the phlegm (kapha) becomes aggravated, it obstructs the wind (vāyu) within the water-carrying channels; consequently, that phlegm is dried up like mud by that [wind]. (52)
The throat is as if covered with bristles; there is sleepiness, sweetness in the mouth, flatulence, heaviness of the head, numbness, a sense of being drenched, vomiting, and loss of appetite. (53)
Lassitude and indigestion may arise from all [causes], and it may possess all the symptoms; furthermore, it arises from the suppression of food and is produced by vāta and pitta. (54)

When one who is exhausted by heat suddenly resorts to cold water while thirsty, the internal heat becomes obstructed and enters the digestive tract; the condition it produces is born of bile (pitta). 55.

That [fever] which arises from the consumption of intoxicants is characterized by a sharp internal heat; that born from unctuous substances arises from the intake of oily, heavy, sour, and salty foods; and that produced by phlegm arises from similar dietary habits. (56)

5.56b–c. That thirst which arises from a sharp digestive fire (tīkṣṇāgni) or from oleation (sneha) is of the nature of depletion (kṣayātmikā), characterized by the symptoms described for the depletion of rasa (rasakṣaya).
[It also occurs] due to complications from other chronic diseases such as consumption (śoṣa), urinary disorders (meha), fever (jvara), and so forth. 5.57.
5.57cv When a severe thirst arises from other conditions such as consumption (śoṣa), delusion (moha), or fever (jvara), it is known as being characterized by complications (sopasargātmikā). // 57 //
Wine is sharp, hot, dry, subtle, sour, diffusive, quick-acting, light, expansive, and clear; its properties are the opposite of those of *ojas*. (1)
6.1a-pungent, hot, dry, subtle, sour, pervasive, quick-acting, light,
6.1c-expansive, and clear— these are the qualities of wine; pungency and the other [qualities] are also said to exist in poison, causing the agitation of the mind.
They arise for the end of life when poison is administered in an excessive dose. // 2 //

Intoxicating liquor, through its qualities such as sharpness and others, agitates the ten qualities of vitality (ojas) beginning with dullness; having thus disturbed them, it brings the mind to a state of transformation.
Abiding in the first intoxication and in the second, the abode of negligence, the fool, struck down by evil conceptualizations, is convinced that this is happiness. (4)
In the first intoxication and in the second, one is deluded by the notion that "this is happiness"; one conceives of it as happiness,
and one regards it as happiness.
Having reached the junction between the middling and the superior states, the dull-witted person of rajasic and tamasic nature might do anything at all, like an unrestrained, venomous beast. (5)
What indeed would a fool not do?
This is the ground of blameless faults; this is the abode of immorality.
He alone is the supreme guide for the many paths leading to miserable rebirths. // 6 //
This stage belongs to those possessed by ignorance; remaining in the third intoxication, he lies motionless like a corpse.
Yet this evil-souled one has fallen into a state even more wretched than death itself. // 7 //
How could a wise person practice that [conduct] by which, when attached, one does not recognize dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, gain and loss, or benefit and harm? (8)
In liquor reside delusion, fear, grief, anger, and death; along with insanity, intoxication, fainting, epilepsy, and paralysis. (9)
Where there is a single lapse of mindfulness, everything therein becomes improper;
for food that is not prepared according to reason leads either to disease or to death. (10)
Alcohol destroys the three aims of life, as well as intelligence, fortitude, and shame;
yet those who are strong, having eaten their fill, do not become excessively intoxicated.

Those of their lineage are unctuous, endowed with strength and youth, constantly addicted to wine, characterized by an excess of fat and phlegm, with diminished wind and bile, and possess strong digestive fires. // 12 //

Those who are excessively intoxicated, those who are overconfident, and those who are angry, as well as those who drink liquor that is sour or dry, or who drink too much when food is undigested—[these suffer] in the opposite case. (13)
6.13d–14. When [the wine] has not been digested, there may be four types of alcoholism (madātyaya) caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, or all [three doshas] together, even with large quantities.
Although all [types] arise from all [doshas], they are designated according to whichever [dosha] predominates.
Their general characteristics are profound delusion, pain in the heart, frequent diarrhea, thirst, fever characterized by both cold and heat sensations, and loss of appetite. (15)

6.15b–c. Confusion, pain in the heart, headache, pain in the sides, bones, and joints, trembling, piercing pain in the vital organs (marmans), stiffness in the sacral region (trika), obstruction of the chest, darkness before the eyes, cough, dyspnea, and insomnia [arise]. 6.16.
6.16ab Pain and stiffness in the head, sides, and bones; excessive sweating; constipation; swelling; mental confusion; delirium; vomiting; nausea; giddiness; and the seeing of bad dreams. // 17 //
Due to the specific [imbalance] of wind (anila), there arise wakefulness, labored breathing, trembling, and pain in the head;
in dreams, one wanders, feels as if flying, and converses with ghosts (preta). (18)
From pitta arise burning sensations, fever, perspiration, delusion, diarrhea, thirst, and vertigo;
the body becomes greenish or yellowish, and the eyes and cheeks become red. (19)

From phlegm (kapha), there is vomiting, nausea, excessive sleep, urticaria, and heaviness of the limbs; in the case of fever born from all three doshas, all symptoms appear together. Furthermore, one who drinks liquor [when afflicted] should be treated as follows. (20)
From the destruction or depletion of phlegm (kapha), vomiting, nausea, and loss of appetite occur; or other [symptoms] may arise.
For a weak person, these two conditions—destruction and depletion—become particularly difficult when caused by wind (vāta).

6.21 Furthermore, there is another [condition] that arises suddenly and is unsuitable [for treatment]. In the case of *dhvaṃsaka*, there is the wasting away of the patient and of parasites; in *śleṣman* (phlegm-type), there is spitting of phlegm, dryness of the throat, excessive sleepiness, intolerance to sound, and drowsiness. In *vikṣaya*, there is extreme pain in the limbs and head.
In the case of the destruction of the Viṭ humor, there is excessive pain in the limbs and head,

diseases of the heart and throat, delusion, cough, thirst, vomiting, and fever. However, he who has desisted from intoxicating drinks, who has conquered his self, and acts with conscious deliberation [is not afflicted by these].

he is free from all physical and mental afflictions. 6.49ab He is never afflicted by the three diseases born of wind, bile, and phlegm, which arise from passion, delusion, and unwholesome food. 6.49cd For him, there is no obstruction of the heart or throat
Intoxication, fainting, and coma arise from the obstruction of the channels that carry rasa, blood, and consciousness; each subsequent state is more severe than the preceding one. (25)

In this state of intoxication, caused by all the [usual] defects as well as blood, wine, or poison, he is attached to things, speaks little and rapidly, is unsteady, and his movements are faltering. (26)
In intoxication arising from wind (vāta), the body becomes rough, dark-brown, and reddish;
through bile (pitta), one is prone to anger, has a red-yellowish complexion, and is fond of quarreling. // 27 //
In the case of [madness] caused by Vāta, there is very little coherent speech; from Kapha, one is pale, lost in thought, and indolent;
from the combination of all [humors], it is of a mixed nature; and from blood, there is stiffness of the limbs and the eyes.
6.28–29ab. In poisoning by liquor, there is scanty and incoherent speech, pallor, the symptoms of bile (pitta), and a distorted voice and limbs.
In [poisoning by] venom, there is trembling and excessive sleep; however, it is more severe than all [the others].
From poison (viṣa), there is trembling and excessive sleep, and it is more intense than all [the other doshas].
One should recognize vāta and the others in the blood and other tissues by the predominance of their respective symptoms;
seeing the sky as reddish, black, or blue, one enters into darkness.
In a fainting fit caused by Vāta, one awakens quickly, and there is pain in the heart, trembling, vertigo, emaciation, a dusky-red complexion, and fainting itself.
6.31c–d. One who suffers from emaciation and perceives the sky as having a dark-brown or reddish-brown hue, or as red or yellow due to the action of bile (pitta), will enter into darkness;
and upon awakening, he is afflicted by perspiration and tormented by burning sensations, thirst, and heat.
When the wind is deranged, one sees blue and yellow hues; when by bile, red and yellow; and when by phlegm, seeing the sky as resembling a cloud, one should enter [the treatment]. // 33 //
After a long time, he awakens from that state with a sense of heart-failure and excessive salivation, his limbs heavy and motionless like those encased in moist leather. (34)
Possessing every form, like another seizure caused by the three humors, it quickly casts one down motionless, even without loathsome movements. (35)

6.35–36. Among the afflictions of embodied beings, when intoxication and fainting have reached their full intensity, they subside by themselves without loathsome treatments; likewise, renunciation [of the body] occurs without the aid of medicines.
The extremely powerful impurities, having gathered together and taken refuge in the seat of the vital breaths, forcibly arrest the activity of speech, body, and mind, resulting in total paralysis.
By that [disease], a person becomes like a piece of wood, resembling one who is dead;
he would die quickly if medical treatment is not applied swiftly. (38)
6.38 Like wood, like one who is dead, as if sinking in a bottomless flood of water teeming with crocodiles,
one should quickly turn back a man who is immersed in renunciation. 6.39
And in the state of *abhinyāsa*,

he sinks while being embraced by his own enemies— intoxication, pride, anger, joy, and the like— as well as by liquor, which, though devoid of reason, treats the appropriate and the inappropriate as equal.
If one drinks [the medicine] after having analyzed the strength, time, place, suitability, constitution, assistants, disease, and age, and acts accordingly, then one drinks nectar.
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna),
because they pierce like enemies and are like stakes of flesh,
and because they obstruct the path of the rectum, they are called hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi). // 1 //

The humors (doṣas), having vitiated the skin, flesh, and fat, produce various types of fleshy sprouts in the region of the descending wind (apāna) and elsewhere; these they have called hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi). // 2 //

Briefly stated, the anus, which is situated in the thick intestine, is of two types based on the distinction between congenital and acquired; it is further divided into the dry and the exuding varieties. (3)
In that [space] measuring four and a half finger-breadths, three channels remain, each measuring one and a half finger-breadths:
the *balyā*, the *pravāhiṇī*, and between them in the middle, the *visarjanī*.
The external covering of that [vagina] is one finger-breadth wide at the lip of the anus;
it measures one and a half barley-corns in size, and beyond that point, there are hairs.
7.5ab The external [hemorrhoids] are to be concealed; in that regard, [the internal ones are] by a measure of one and a half barley-corns.
The cause therein is the scorching of the seeds of the folds that arise simultaneously.
But the scorching of the seeds of hemorrhoids is due to the misconduct of the mother and father. // 6 //

7.6bv The aggravation of the folds (valī) and the seeds (bīja), and by fate, from those two arises the provocation of the *saṃnipāta*; therefore, all diseases arising from [hereditary] lineage are declared to be thus incurable. // 7 //
They are especially congenital, rough, and difficult to look upon; they are inward-facing, pale, and accompanied by terrible complications. // 8 //
The other six types arise separately from the vitiation of the *doṣas*—from their combination (*saṃsarga*) or their accumulation (*nicaya*).
Those that are dry are caused by *vāta* and *śleṣman*, while those that are moist are caused by blood (*asra*) and *pitta*.

The causes for the provocation of the humors (doṣa) have been stated previously; when the digestive fire has been impaired by them and the waste matter (mala) has accumulated excessively, it is further aggravated by excessive sexual indulgence. (10)
From sitting on uneven, hard, or rough seats that cause agitation of the vehicle, and from being struck by the bladder, the nozzle, stones, clods of earth, the ground, clothing, and so forth; (11)
From contact with very cold water, from excessive straining, from suppressing the urges of flatus, urine, and feces, and from forcibly inducing them; // 12 //

Furthermore, in women, [the menstrual flow is obstructed] by fever, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, consumption, malabsorption syndrome, edema, and anemia, as well as by emaciation and irregular physical exertions. (13)
Due to the falling of the immature fetus, due to the pressure from the growth of the fetus,
and by other such causes, the downward-moving wind (apānavāyu) becomes agitated and [disturbs] the waste matter.
It deposits that [fecal matter] within the folds of the rectum;
when those folds become congested, hemorrhoids arise, and their premonitory symptom is a sluggish digestive fire. (15)

It localizes in the folds of the anus; it causes constipation, weakness in the thighs, cramps in the calves, vertigo, exhaustion in the limbs, swelling of the eyes, diarrhea, or alternatively, constipation. (7.16)
When the wind is predominant and obstructed, it generally moves below the navel;
accompanied by pain and a cutting sensation, it emerges with difficulty and a sound. (17)
Gurgling in the intestines, flatulence, emaciation, frequent belching, excessive urination, scanty feces, lack of appetite, a sensation of fumes, and acid reflux. (18)

7.18c–d There is excessive urination, pain in the feces, head, back, and chest, lethargy, and discoloration; 7.19 there is drowsiness, weakness of the sense organs, anger, and difficulty in maintaining one's health.

Diseases such as anxiety, disorders of the digestive tract, anemia, abdominal tumors, and abdominal enlargements increase further when these [malignant] growths have arisen and their names have been struck down. (20)

Likewise, it crushes the urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and the bodily tissues along with their receptacles; consequently, almost everyone becomes afflicted with hemorrhoids. (22)
Extremely emaciated, his vigor utterly destroyed, dejected, wasted away, and utterly lusterless; devoid of substance and shorn of splendor, he was like a tree inhabited by living creatures. // 23 //
He is seized by all the aforementioned complications that afflict the vital organs,
as well as by cough, thirst, bad taste in the mouth, dyspnea, and chronic rhinitis.
Those afflicted by exhaustion, bodily aches, vomiting, sneezing, swelling, and fever;
those suffering from impotence, deafness, blindness, gravel, and urinary stones. // 25 //
With a wasted body and a broken voice, he broods, frequently spitting, and suffers from anorexia; he experiences pain in all his joints, bones, heart, navel, anus, and groins. (26)
From the anus, there flows a slimy discharge resembling water mixed with broken grains of rice;
it is alternately obstructed and discharged, dry and moist, and ripe and unripe. (27)
