One passes stools that are pale, yellow, green, or red, and slimy; the anal papillae are characterized by an excess of wind (vāyu), being dry and accompanied by a tingling sensation. (28)
They are withered, dark-brownish red, stiff, uneven, rough, and harsh; they are dissimilar to one another, crooked, sharp, and have cracked openings.
Some resemble the fruits of the bimba, the karkandhu, the date palm, and the cotton plant;
some have the appearance of kadamba flowers, and some are like mustard seeds. // 30 //
They cause excessive pain in the head, sides, shoulders, hips, thighs, and groins, and they produce sneezing, eructation, constipation, cardiac oppression, and loss of appetite. (31)
7.31–32. They cause pain in the heart, loss of appetite, cough, dyspnea, irregularity of the digestive fire, ringing in the ears, and vertigo.
Afflicted by these, [the patient] voids stool that is knotted, scanty, with sound, and accompanied by tenesmus.
One passes stool that is mixed with mucus, foam, and shreds of membrane;
furthermore, the skin, nails, feces, urine, eyes, and face become blackish. // 33 //
From that very [cause] arise gulma, splenic enlargement (plīhodara), and aśmari;
they are dominated by pitta, have blue mouths, and exhibit red, yellow, or black luster. // 34 //
Their bodies were thin, oozing with secretions, foul-smelling, soft, and flaccid;
they resembled the tongues of parrots, pieces of liver, or the mouths of leeches. (35)
They cause burning, suppuration, fever, perspiration, thirst, fainting, loss of appetite, and delusion;
they are hot, and their stool is liquid, blue, hot, yellow, red, or dark-colored. (36)

Those with a barley-shaped center, and whose skin, nails, and other parts are greenish-yellow or turmeric-colored, are dominated by phlegm (śleṣman); they have deep roots, are thick, cause little pain, and are white. (37)
7.37 Their middles are like those of barley; they are greenish-yellow, with turmeric-colored skin, nails, and so forth.
They are swollen, thickened, unctuous, stiff, round, heavy, and firm; they are slimy, motionless, smooth, abundant with itching, and fond of touch.
Resembling the fruit of the *karīra* or the kernel of the *panasa*, and likewise resembling a cow's teat;
they cause distension of the groins and cut through the anus, bladder, and navel. (39)
They cause cough, dyspnea, nausea, excessive salivation, loss of appetite, and catarrh;
they also produce urinary disorders, difficulty in urination, heaviness of the head, and fever with a cold sensation. // 40 //

They cause impotence, mildness of the digestive fire, vomiting, and disorders characterized by undigested matter (āma); they produce stool resembling fat, accompanied by abundant phlegm, and are associated with dysentery (pravāhikā). // 41 //
7.41c–d Those [tumors] resembling fat, accompanied by abundant phlegm, do not suppurate nor do they burst; the skin and other parts become pale and oily.
Those with combined symptoms arise from the combination [of two doshas], and those with all characteristics arise from the accumulation [of all three doshas]. 7.42 //
Hemorrhoid tumors (kīla) dominated by blood, accompanied by the characteristics of pitta,
resemble the shoots of the banyan tree and are similar in color to the gunja berry or coral.
Being excessively afflicted by foul and hot feces, they suddenly discharge blood; and because of that excessive flow, [the patient suffers]. (44)

Resembling a frog, he is afflicted by sufferings arising from the loss of blood; his complexion, strength, and enthusiasm are diminished, his vitality is destroyed, and his sense faculties are clouded. (45)
Through dry and constipating foods such as mudga, kodrava, jūrṇāhva, karīra, caṇaka, and others,
the wind (vāyu), provoked in its own seat, becomes powerful.
7.46d–47ab. When provoked and powerful in its own seat,
[the wind] obstructs the downward-carrying channels and, drying them out from below,
causes a severe retention of feces, flatus, stool, and urine.
By that [vitiation], there occurs intense pain in the abdomen, back, heart, and sides; flatulence, distension of the belly, nausea, and cutting pain [in the stomach]. (48)
There is also intense pain in the abdomen, the occurrence of swellings and glandular enlargements, upward movement of the wind (vāyu), and consequently, vomiting, loss of appetite, and fever. (49)
Heart disease, disorders of the duodenum, retention of urine, dysentery, deafness, blindness, asthma, headache, cough, and chronic catarrh; // 50 //
Mental disturbances, thirst, blood-bile disorders, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and so forth—those various diseases born of wind arise with extreme severity. (51)
This condition known as *udāvarta* is the most severe among those with difficult names;
it arises even without those [other factors] in those whose digestive tracts (*koṣṭha*) are overwhelmed by wind (*vāta*). (52)

Those congenital (sahaja) disorders of the three humors (tridoṣa), as well as those situated within the inner layer of the skin (valī), are incurable; they can only be palliated by means of digestive power (agni-bala) and other such factors. // 53 //
Those [diseases] born from pairs of humors, those located in the second layer [of the skin],
and those that have persisted for a full year, they say are curable only with great difficulty.
Hemorrhoids that have arisen on the outer fold, those in which a single doṣa is predominant, and those that have not protruded are easily curable. (55)

Those located on the penis and other such parts will be described according to their respective locations; however, those born from the navel are shaped like the mouth of a *gaṇḍūpada* worm, slimy, and soft. (56)
The Vyāna wind, having seized the phlegm, produces a hemorrhoid on the exterior of the skin that is like a wedge, firm, and rough; they know that as Carma-kīla. // 57 //
From Vāta there is pricking pain and roughness; from Pitta, a blackish-red coloration;
and from Śleṣman, oiliness, a knotted consistency, and a color matching that of the surrounding skin. (58)
A wise person should quickly exert effort toward the pacification of hemorrhoids; for if left unchecked, they may soon obstruct the rectum and cause the condition known as *baddhagudodara*. (59)
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna), diarrhea is of six types: caused by the doshas individually or combined, as well as by fear and grief;
it arises most excessively from the drinking of excessive water. (1)

[The causes are] lean and dried meat, unwholesome sesame flour, sprouted grains, liquor, dry food, and excessive eating; [furthermore, it arises] from hemorrhoids and the improper administration of oleation therapy. // 2 //
Due to worms and the suppression of natural urges, the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated by those same factors;
it causes the watery element (ab-dhātu) to flow downward and, by that very means, destroys the digestive fire (agni).
When, due to malice, the digestive fire repeatedly brings the fecal matter in the stomach to a liquid state, it prepares for diarrhea; such is the sign of its impending occurrence. (4)
When [the doshas] are located in the heart, rectum, and abdomen, there is prostration of the limbs, retention of waste products, flatulence, and indigestion;
therein, due to vāta, both feces and urine are affected. (5)
One voids stool that is very scanty, abounding in pain and sound,
obstructed, dry, frothy, clear, or knotted, repeatedly.
Likewise, [the patient] has the appearance of burnt molasses, suffers from slimy discharge and cutting pain, has a dry mouth, a prolapsed anus, bristling body hair, and groans. (7)

With hair standing on end and speech impaired by bile, [the patient voids urine] that is yellow, black, turmeric-colored, or greenish like young grass; it is mixed with blood, extremely foul-smelling, and accompanied by thirst, fainting, perspiration, and a burning sensation. (8)
Accompanied by thirst, fainting, perspiration, and burning sensations, and characterized by pain, heat, and suppuration in the anus, the stool is thick with phlegm (kapha),
slimy, stringy, white, unctuous, undigested (āma), and associated with kapha. // 9 //
Due to phlegm (śleṣman), there is frequent discharge that is thick, heavy, foul-smelling, obstructed, and accompanied by persistent pain;
the patient is drowsy, lethargic, averse to food, passes very small amounts of stool with straining (pravāhikā). // 10 //

Accompanied by horripilation and nausea, with heaviness in the bladder, rectum, and abdomen, one perceives even what has been done as not done; such is the "universal self" possessing all characteristics. (11)
8.11b–c. When the mind is agitated by fear, the heavy bladder and heavy abdomen—accompanied by pitta—liquefy the feces;
then the vāyu causes diarrhea of material that is hot, liquid, and floating. 8.12d. [End of verse]
They say that diarrhea caused by grief has symptoms identical to those of [diarrhea] caused by vāta and pitta;
in brief, diarrhea is of two types: with undigested matter (sāma) and without undigested matter (nirāma). // 13 //
8.13–14. That [blood] is of two kinds: with blood (*sāsṛk*) and without blood (*nir-asrak*). Among these, the first [type with blood] sinks in water due to its heaviness.
The second [type without blood] is foul-smelling like excrement and is accompanied by flatulence, constipation, pain, and salivation.
The opposite case, however, is when it is devoid of oiliness; even if digested, it sinks due to *kapha*.
This condition of the *grahaṇī* occurs in cases of diarrhea where one has not applied sufficient effort [in treatment]. (15)

For him, there may be diarrhea—either with or without undigested matter (āmadoṣa)—caused by substances consumed by another that destroy the digestive fire, once those substances have been digested. (16)

That diarrhea, because it passes through excessively, is by its very nature swift-acting; it occurs spontaneously either when food has not yet been digested, or when it is already digested, or even when there is no food at all. (17)

The disorder of the *grahaṇī* causes one to defecate after a long time; it may be suddenly constricted or suddenly relaxed at intervals, and it discharges due to the accumulation of morbid humors. (18)
It arises in four ways: from the individual doshas, and from their combination (sannipata).
Its premonitory symptoms are lassitude, delayed digestion, and acidity. (19)
Excessive salivation, distaste in the mouth, loss of appetite, thirst, fatigue, giddiness, abdominal distension, vomiting, ringing in the ears, and rumbling in the intestines. // 20 //
The general symptoms are emaciation, cough, catarrh, fever, fainting, headache, constipation, and swelling of the hands and feet. (21)
Therein, from wind (vāta), there arise dryness of the palate, darkness before the eyes, ringing in the ears,
frequent pain in the sides, thighs, groins, and neck, and choleraic colic (viṣūcikā).
There is greed for all flavors; hunger and thirst are like a saw;
when digested, there is flatulence, and once eaten, one attains a sense of well-being. (23)

One who suspects wind-disease of the heart, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, or anemia, after a long time voids stool that is painful, liquid, dry, thin, undigested, and accompanied by sound and froth. (24)
One afflicted by pitta voids feces repeatedly, suffering from pain in the anus, dyspnea, and cough;
being yellowish in appearance, he voids liquid that has a blue or yellow hue. (25)

8.25c–d Due to pitta, [the stool] is blue or yellowish; due to pitta, it has a yellow-blue appearance. Afflicted by foul and sour eructations, burning in the heart and throat, loss of appetite, and thirst, one suffers. Due to kapha, food is digested with difficulty; there is vomiting and anorexia. 8.26ab [The stool is] white, cold, heavy, oily, sweet, and associated with a sense of fullness. It is accompanied by nausea, a feeling of being stuffed, and a lack of hunger. 8.26cd Due to all three doshas, the stool is variegated, like the color of a peacock's neck, and resembles the hue of a pigeon. It is characterized by a burning sensation and a cold sensation, and is associated with all the aforementioned symptoms. 8.27ab When the digestive fire is weak, the food remains undigested within the stomach and is expelled as it was consumed. This condition is called āma-vibandha (obstruction by undigested matter). 8.27cd–28ab When the digestive fire is extremely weak, the food is not digested even after a long time. It moves slowly, causing pain in the flanks, and is difficult to digest. This is known as alasaka (intestinal torpor). 8.28cd–29ab When the digestive fire is weak and obstructed by wind, the food is not digested. It causes distension of the abdomen and is expelled with great difficulty. This is called viṣūcī (cholera-like syndrome). 8.29cd–30ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a piercing pain in the sides. It moves upward and downward, and is accompanied by vomiting and diarrhea. This is known as pratyādhmāna (repeated distension). 8.30cd–31ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a burning sensation in the chest and throat. It is accompanied by thirst and fainting, and is known as udāvarta (upward movement of gases). 8.31cd–32ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of heaviness in the abdomen. It is accompanied by a lack of hunger and is known as ānāha (abdominal distension). 8.32cd–33ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a piercing pain in the rectum. It is accompanied by a discharge of mucus and is known as parikartika (cutting pain). 8.33cd–34ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a burning sensation in the anus. It is accompanied by a discharge of blood and is known as parighāta (striking pain). 8.34cd–35ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of coldness in the abdomen. It is accompanied by a lack of hunger and is known as śleṣmavibandha (obstruction by phlegm). 8.35cd–36ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of heat in the abdomen. It is accompanied by thirst and is known as pittavibandha (obstruction by bile). 8.36cd–37ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of heaviness in the head. It is accompanied by drowsiness and is known as śirobhitāpa (headache). 8.37cd–38ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of tightness in the chest. It is accompanied by a lack of breath and is known as uraḥstambha (chest constriction). 8.38cd–39ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of numbness in the limbs. It is accompanied by weakness and is known as aṅgasāda (prostration). 8.39cd–40ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of burning in the eyes. It is accompanied by blurred vision and is known as netrapāka (inflammation of the eyes). 8.40cd–41ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of itching in the skin. It is accompanied by eruptions and is known as kaṇḍū (itching). 8.41cd–42ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of swelling in the abdomen. It is accompanied by a discharge of fluid and is known as udara (ascites). 8.42cd–43ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of pain in the joints. It is accompanied by stiffness and is known as sandhipīḍā (joint pain). 8.43cd–44ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of burning in the stomach. It is accompanied by thirst and is known as kukṣiśūla (stomach ache). 8.44cd–45ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of heaviness in the throat. It is accompanied by a lack of appetite and is known as kaṇṭhagaurava (heaviness of the throat). 8.45cd–46ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of coldness in the hands and feet. It is accompanied by numbness and is known as hastapādastambha (numbness of hands and feet). 8.46cd–47ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of burning in the ears. It is accompanied by ringing in the ears and is known as karṇaśūla (earache). 8.47cd–48ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of pain in the nose. It is accompanied by nasal discharge and is known as nāsāpīḍā (nasal pain). 8.48cd–49ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of burning in the mouth. It is accompanied by a bad taste and is known as mukhapāka (mouth inflammation). 8.49cd–50ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of heaviness in the tongue. It is accompanied by a lack of taste and is known as jihvāgaurava (heaviness of the tongue). 8.50cd–51ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of pain in the teeth. It is accompanied by sensitivity and is known as dantaśūla (toothache). 8.51cd–52ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of burning in the lips. It is accompanied by cracking and is known as oṣṭhapāka (lip inflammation). 8.52cd–53ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of pain in the palate. It is accompanied by swelling and is known as tāluśūla (palate pain). 8.53cd–54ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of burning in the throat. It is accompanied by a hoarse voice and is known as kaṇṭhapāka (throat inflammation). 8.54cd–55ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of pain in the chest. It is accompanied by a cough and is known as uraḥśūla (chest pain). 8.55cd–56ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of burning in the back. It is accompanied by stiffness and is known as pṛṣṭhapāka (back inflammation). 8.56cd–57ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of pain in the shoulders. It is accompanied by heaviness and is known as aṃsaśūla (shoulder pain). 8.57cd–58ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of burning in the arms. It is accompanied by weakness and is known as bāhuśūla (arm pain). 8.58cd–59ab When the digestive fire is weak and the food is not digested, it causes a sensation of pain in the hands. It
There is coating of the mouth, spitting, coughing, nausea, and catarrh; one feels the heart to be numb, and the abdomen to be rigid and heavy. (27)
8.27–28ab. There is a coating in the mouth and sweetness [in the mouth], cough, spitting, and rhinitis;
eructation that is foul and sweet, lassitude, lack of desire for women, and the passage of heavy stools mixed with undigested matter (āmadoṣa) and phlegm.
Even for one who is not emaciated, there is weakness; when [the fever] arises from all [three doshas], there is a total confusion of symptoms.
Furthermore, regarding the classification of the bodily constituents, there are the three types of fire mentioned, beginning with the irregular (viṣama) fire. // 29 //
These too would be disorders of the *grahaṇī*, whereas equilibrium is the cause of health. (30ab)
Wind-diseases, urinary stones, leprosy, urinary disorders, abdominal enlargements, and fistula-in-ano; // 30cd //
Hemorrhoids and dysentery—these eight are the great diseases that are very difficult to overcome. (30ef)
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna),
it is stated that the bladder, the neck of the bladder, the penis, the waist, the testicles,
and the anus are connected as one, being situated within the cavity of the pelvic bone. // 1 //
For even when positioned face down, the bladder is filled from its sides by the minute openings of the urine-carrying channels, which flow into it incessantly.

By those very same [factors], having entered this [body], the doshas produce twenty types of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta), prameha disorders, and difficult urinations (kṛcchra) localized in the vital organs (marman). // 3 //
In the vāta-type of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), one voids urine in very small quantities repeatedly, accompanied by pain in the bladder, groin, and penis;
in the pitta-type, the urine is yellow and characterized by burning and pain.

In the case of a kaphaja (phlegm-born) hemorrhoid, the discharge is blood-streaked, accompanied by heaviness and swelling of the bladder and penis; it is also associated with slimy mucus and constipation.
When caused by all three humors, it possesses the characteristics of all of them.
When the wind, having obstructed the opening of the bladder, dries up the urine—whether it be accompanied by bile, phlegm, or semen—then [the following occurs] in succession: // 6 //

A terrible stone (aśmarī) is produced from bile, like the gallstone of a cow; moreover, it should be understood that all [types] have phlegm as their substrate. Now, its premonitory symptoms are as follows: // 7 //
Distension of the bladder, intense pain all around its neighboring regions, a goat-like odor in the urine, dysuria, fever, and anorexia [are the symptoms]. // 8 //
9.8cv When there is a smell of goat's urine in the urine, it is a general symptom; pain occurs in the navel, the perineal raphe, the bladder, and the pubic region.
The urine may be discharged in a broken stream due to the obstruction of the urinary passage by that [stone]. // 9 //
9.9dv Likewise, by obstructing the passage, due to its displacement, one may void clear urine resembling a *gomedaka* gem;
however, from its agitation, there may be blood in the case of injury, and from the exertion, there would be extreme pain. // 10 //
Therein, one afflicted by intense pain from wind gnaws at the teeth, trembles, rubs the penis, and presses upon the navel, moaning incessantly. (11)
He passes stool accompanied by wind and urinates repeatedly drop by drop;
his urinary stone becomes dark and rough, as if covered with thorns. (12)
Due to pitta, the bladder is burned as if being cooked and becomes hot;
the stone (aśmarī) is shaped like the kernel of a bhallātaka fruit and is red, yellow, or black. (13)
9.13–14. In the case of blood, bile, and phlegm, the stone is red, yellow, and black respectively;
the bladder feels as if it is being pricked by needles, is cold, and heavy.
The stone is large, smooth, honey-colored, or white.
These [foods] are easy for fools to grasp and carry because their physical bodies are small and their capacity for accumulation is slight. // 15 //

Semen-stone (śukrāśmarī), however, arises from the retention of semen in those who are large-bodied; for when the wind (anila) [is provoked], it causes the semen—which has moved from its place but is not discharged—to collect between the testicles.
Having seized the semen, it dries it up; that dried [semen] becomes a stone (aśmarī), which causes pain in the bladder, difficulty in urination, and swelling of the scrotum. // 17 //
As soon as that [urine] has arisen, the semen enters and dissolves;
moreover, when this space is compressed, it becomes gravel and urinary calculi.
Divided into minute particles by the wind, it flows out along with the urine when that [wind] moves in its natural direction; when it moves in the reverse direction, it becomes obstructed. (19)
In one who suppresses the urge to urinate, the wind (vāyu), having obstructed the opening of the bladder,
may cause retention of urine, pain, itching, and occasionally [discharge] from its own seat.
Having displaced the prolapsed bladder—which resembles a fetus, is swollen, and is distended—it causes pain, burning, throbbing, and a twisting sensation in that region. (21)
If a drop of urine is emitted when the bladder is pressed, or if it flows in a stream, this is known as the two-fold *vāta-vasti*. // 22 //
The second [type of] *dustara* is *dustaratara*, characterized by powerful wind;
this wind has taken refuge in the space between the rectum and the bladder. (23)
It forms a firm, immovable, elevated knot with the consistency of a stone;
this is called *vātāṣṭhīlā*, which causes flatulence and the obstruction of feces, urine, and flatus. (24)
When the Vāyu, deprived of its qualities and coiled within the bladder, causes intense pain, it churns the urine, resulting in rigidity, twisting sensations, and heaviness. (25)
9.25c–d Having entered the urine, it wanders through it, or else it voids the urine in very small quantities while passing feces;
this is called *vātakuṇḍalikā*, occurring when the urine has been suppressed for a long time. 9.26ab //
When urine is obstructed by its suppression, it does not flow out or is passed with little pain;
this occurs when it is struck back and driven upward by Vāta.
If one fills the abdomen below the navel with urine, it will cause intense pain, flatulence, indigestion, and the retention of feces. (28)

That urine-born abdominal swelling (mūtrajaṭhara) occurs when, due to a defect in the urinary channels or by the action of Vāyu, a small amount of urine is forced into the bladder, the urethra, or the glans penis. (29)
9.29c–d When a small amount of urine that has been drawn up remains and then flows out slowly after a delay— either with pain or without pain— that is *mūtrotsaṅga*.
It is characterized by an interrupted stream, residual urine, and heaviness of the penis.
9.30b Or it may be painful, or even painless; 9.30c This obstruction of urine is intermittent;
9.30d It leaves a residue, and the penis feels heavy.
A round, firm, and small mass that suddenly forms at the opening of the bladder, causing pain similar to that of a urinary stone, is called *mūtra-granthi* (urinary gland). // 31 //
When one who has urinated approaches a woman, the semen, being stirred up by the vital wind (vāyu), is displaced from its place; it flows either before or after the act of urinating. (32)
When the urine and semen resemble ashes or water due to wind (vāta) in those who are dry and weak, it is called udāvarta of the feces. 33.
9.33 When the upward-moving feces enters the urinary tract and becomes mixed with it,
the urine then acquires a smell identical to that of feces; one should designate this condition as *viḍvighāta* (obstruction by feces).
Pitta, increased by physical exercise, pungent and hot foods, walking, exposure to the sun, and so forth, and driven by Vāyu, causes pain and a burning sensation in the bladder and the perineum. (35)
When one passes urine that is hot, repeatedly with difficulty, and either mixed with blood or purely red after drinking [the aforementioned substances], they call that *uṣṇavāta*. (36)

In one who is dehydrated and whose body is exhausted, the pitta and vāta located in the bladder produce a deficiency of urine accompanied by pain and burning; that condition is so named [mūtrātisāra].
If both pitta and kapha, or even both together, are congealed by vāyu, then one shall void urine that is yellow, red, white, or thick with great difficulty. (38)
If it becomes accompanied by a burning sensation and has the color of powdered gorocanā or conch-shell, or if it is dried up and possesses all colors, they call that *mūtrasāda*. (39)

Thus have the diseases arising from the non-discharge of urine been described in detail according to their etiology and symptoms; hereafter, those arising from excessive discharge will be explained. (40)
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna), there are twenty types of urinary disorders (prameha); among them, ten arise from phlegm (śleṣman), six from bile (pitta), and four from wind (anila).
Of these, [the first] group brings about fat, urine, and phlegm. (1)
That which generally consists of the activity of food and drink—namely, that which is sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, heavy, slimy, and cold—is the initiator [of the disease]. (2)
New grain, liquor, meat from marshy lands, sugarcane, molasses, and cow's milk;
delighting in staying and sitting in one place, and sleeping while disregarding the prescribed rules. // 3 //
Corrupted *kapha*, having vitiated the moisture of the body, sweat, fat, plasma, and flesh, produces urinary disorders (*prameha*) by taking refuge in the bladder. (4)
When phlegm and the other humors are depleted, the wind (vāta) draws sweat, fat, muscle-fat, flesh, bile, and even blood toward the bladder, taking refuge in the urine;
and even when those [other] tissues are exhausted, the wind continues its course. // 5 //

Urinary disorders arising from that same [wind] are to be treated, palliated, or abandoned, respectively, due to their being equal [in severity], their lack of response to treatment, and their great danger. // 6 //

Their general characteristic is the abundance and turbidity of urine; even though there is no distinction between the humors (doṣas) and the affected tissues (dūṣyas), it arises from the specific nature of their combination. // 7 //
10.7b–v. Abundance and turbidity of urine—differences in the color and other qualities of the urine—are used to distinguish the various types of *meha*.
[In *udakameha*: it is clear, copious, white, cold, odorless, and resembles water. (8)
In *mehatī* (urinary disorder), the urine is slightly turbid and slimy;
in *ikṣumeha*, it is extremely sweet like the juice of sugarcane. (9)
If it becomes thick after standing overnight, one urinates with *sāndrameha*.
One suffering from *surāmeha* urinates what resembles liquor—clear on top and thick at the bottom. (10)
With his hair standing on end, the one suffering from *śukrameha* passes urine that is thick and white like flour ground with flour, resembling semen or mixed with semen. (11)
In *sikatāmeha*, one voids copious amounts of solidified particles like flour, appearing as fine sand;
in *śītamēha*, one voids a very large quantity of sweet and extremely cold urine. (10.11b–12)

10.12a–b. The patient with *sikatā-meha* passes minute particles like sand in the urine. 10.12c–d. The patient with *śanair-meha* voids urine very slowly and gradually. In *lālā-meha*, the urine is slimy and mixed with threads of saliva.
Through its odor, color, taste, and touch, it is like an alkaline solution or alkaline water;
in *nīla-meha* it has a blue luster, while in *kāla-meha* it resembles ink.
In *hāridrameha*, one voids urine that is pungent, resembling turmeric, and burning;
in *mañjiṣṭhameha*, it is foul-smelling and resembles the water of madder.
In one suffering from *rakta-meha*, the urine is foul-smelling, warm, salty, and blood-red;
in one with *vasā-meha*, the patient frequently voids urine mixed with fat or fat itself. (16)
One who suffers from marrow-urine (majjamehī) frequently passes urine mixed with marrow,
like an elephant in rut, incessantly and without any sense of urgency.

The patient suffering from *hastimeha* passes urine resembling marrow, mixed with marrow, accompanied by *lasīkā*, and obstructed; the patient suffering from *madhumeha* passes urine like honey, and that [condition] is said to be of two types. (10.17–18)
10.18c–d When Vāyu is provoked by the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus) in Madhumeha, or when its path is obstructed by the doshas,
it manifests the symptoms of the obstructing dosha even without an apparent cause. 10.19.
10.19b Or, even when the channels are obstructed by the *doṣas*, [the patient] becomes depleted and then in an instant is restored; thus, he undergoes a state of being difficult to cure.
All [types of *prameha*], if neglected over time, turn into *madhumeha*.

And because one who passes urine that is sweet in all respects, mostly like honey, is called a "madhumehin" (one with honey-urine); and because of the sweetness of the body, they are all thus designated. (21)
Lack of digestion, aversion to food, vomiting, sleepiness, cough accompanied by nasal catarrh—these complications arise from urinary disorders born of phlegm (kapha). // 22 //
Pain in the bladder and penis, tearing of the scrotum, fever, burning sensation, thirst, acidity, fainting, and diarrhea are the symptoms arising from Pitta. (23)
In those afflicted by vāta, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), trembling, cardiac oppression, instability, colic, insomnia, emaciation, cough, and dyspnea arise. (24)
10.24b–25. Śarāvikā, kacchapikā, jālinī, vinatā, alajī, masūrikā, sarṣapikā, putriṇī, and vidārikā cause a seizing of the throat and heart, as well as restlessness.
10.25d–26. Furthermore, the putriṇī, the vidārikā, and the vidradhi—these ten types of carbuncles arise from the neglect of urinary disorders (prameha).
They develop in the joints, vital points (marmas), and fleshy parts of the body.
A *piṭikā* that is elevated at the edges, depressed in the center, dark-colored, accompanied by discharge and pain, and shaped like a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) is called *śarāvikā*. (27)
A pustule that is deeply painful and pricking, characterized by the grasping of a large substance, smooth, and resembling the back of a tortoise, is considered a *kacchapī*. (28)
The Jālinī ulcer is stiff, covered with a network of veins, exudes a fatty discharge, has a large base, is characterized by intense pricking pain, and possesses minute pores. (29)

10.29b–d. A large, blue, depressed pustule that discharges a slimy secretion, has a broad base, and is characterized by deep-seated pain and moisture on either the back or the abdomen, is known as Vinatā.
Visarpiṇī, which arises with extreme pain, burns the skin upon its emergence;
it is accompanied by red and black discoloration, excessive thirst, eruptions, burning sensations, delusion, fever, and alajī.
The *masūrikā* is equal to a lentil (*masūra*) in size and shape;
it is the size and shape of a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), ripens quickly, and is accompanied by great pain. (32)
The *sarṣapī* is surrounded by eruptions equal in size to mustard seeds;
the *putriṇī* is large and covered with many very fine eruptions. (33)
10.33ab–d: Vidārikā is shaped like a mustard seed, covered with very fine pustules, or accompanied by very fine pustules; it is round and hard, like the tuber of the vidārī plant.
Abscesses will be described elsewhere; among them, the first three are types of pustules (piṭikā).
Putriṇī, vidārī, and duḥsahā arise from an abundance of fat;
however, the others arise with a predominance of pitta and occur with little fat.
And among them, there may be an increase of defects according to their respective nature due to the influence of passion. (36ab)
Even without urinary disorders (prameha), these [afflictions] arise in one whose fat (medas) is corrupted. // 36cd //
And they are not perceived as long as there is no grasping of an object. // 36ef //
If one voids urine that is turmeric-colored or red, yet is devoid of the premonitory symptoms of meha, they know that this is not meha, but rather rakta-pitta. // 37 //
They know that [condition] as raktapitta.
Perspiration, body odor, flaccidity of the limbs, excessive attachment to the comfort of beds, seats, and sleep;
a coating on the heart, eyes, tongue, and ears; heaviness of the body, and the overgrowth of hair and nails—[these are its signs]. (38)
10.38b–c Desire for comfort in beds, seats, and dwellings;

a fondness for cold; dryness of the throat and palate; sweetness in the mouth; and a burning sensation in the hands and feet—these are the signs of the impending group of urinary disorders (meha). Furthermore, ants swarm toward the urine.
Upon seeing that the prameha is sweet, slimy, and resembles honey, there may be various considerations:
it may arise from kapha due to over-nutrition, or it may be of the nature of vāta when the other doshas have been depleted. (40)

10.40c–d Those urinary disorders (mehas) arising from excessive nourishment (saṃtarpaṇa) due to the production of kapha, those with their premonitory symptoms (sapūrvarūpa), those caused by kapha and pitta, and those caused by vāta in sequence—these are curable.

However, those caused by pitta are palliable (yāpya), provided that the fat (medas) is not excessively vitiated; otherwise, they are curable. 10.41ab [Note: The verse number 41 is included here as per the source text's numbering system, though it contains no Sanskrit.]
10.41dv And [the patient] should be treated if the fat (medas) is not excessively vitiated.
[The causes are: from eating stale, very hot, dry, parched, or burning foods; [from the Section on Diagnosis].
By means of lying on uneven beds, various movements, and those various factors that vitiate the blood; // 1 //

That swelling, whether external or internal, which rests upon the skin, flesh, fat, bone, sinews, blood, and tendons, and which has deep roots and causes great pain, is called a duṣṭa-śopha (malignant swelling). // 2 //
11.2ab That which is malignant, occurring in the skin, flesh, fat, or bone, or that which is known to be elongated—this abscess (vidradhi) is said to be of six types:
caused by the humors (doṣa) individually, by them combined, by blood, and by trauma. // 3 //
In this case, the external [swelling] occurs here and there on the limb, being harsh, knotted, and elevated;
the internal [swelling] is even more harsh, deep-seated, and dense like a *gulma* tumor. // 4 //
Rising like an anthill, it is quickly fatal like fire or a weapon;
[it occurs] in the navel, bladder, liver, spleen, kloma, heart, abdomen, or groin. (5)
It may occur in the kidneys and the rectum due to Vata; there, the pain is extremely intense, dark-red in color, slow to arise and to suppurate, and irregular in its localization. (6)
11.6av In the kidneys or in the *apāna*, [the wound] may be characterized by piercing, cutting, whirling, distension, throbbing, crawling, and sound;
due to *pitta*, it is blood-red, copper-colored, or black, and is accompanied by thirst, delusion, fever, and burning sensations. // 7 //
Due to kapha, the swelling arises quickly and suppurates slowly; it is pale, accompanied by itching, nausea, coldness, stiffness, yawning, anorexia, and heaviness. // 8 //
The maturation [of karma] arises after a long time and is mixed due to the combination [of humors];
one should distinguish here, by implication, the external and internal characteristics. (9)

11.9a–b. That which arises after a long time, suppurates slowly, is covered with black vesicles, is dark-brown, and is accompanied by intense burning, pain, and fever, possesses the characteristics of Pitta; it occurs through blood, both externally and likewise internally in women. 10.
In one who has sustained an injury from weapons or the like, or who consumes unwholesome food, the heat of the wound is dispersed by the Vāyu, which then agitates the Pitta along with blood. (11)
When pitta, together with blood, is provoked, it produces a suppurative abscess (vidradhi) characterized by both pitta and blood, accompanied by many complications.
Furthermore, the specific variations in these complications are understood to arise from the differences in their locations. // 12 //
Hiccup occurs in the umbilical region; urine is emitted with difficulty and with a foul odor in the bladder;
dyspnea occurs in the liver; obstruction occurs in the spleen; and furthermore, thirst occurs in the respiratory tract.
There would be a seizing of the throat in the *kloman*, a gripping of all the limbs in the heart, delusion, asthma, coughing, a throbbing sensation in the heart, and pain. (14)

There is pain in the abdomen, the sides, and between the shoulders; a rumbling distension arises in the belly; and there is a seizing pain in the thighs, the groins, the kidneys, the hips, and the back. (15)

There is pain in the sides and in the anus, as well as the obstruction of flatus; one should diagnose their states of being undigested (āma), partially digested (pakva), or over-digested (vidagdha) according to the same criteria used for swellings. 16.

One should know that in a suppurated abscess (vidradhi), the pus flows from the mouth if it is above the navel, from the anus if it is below; and one should identify the location as being from the anus to the mouth or from the navel based on the discharge of morbid humors (doṣa) and moisture.

11.17c–v One should know that the [fever] born from both [wind and bile] arises from the navel; among these, the one born from the combination of all three humors (saṃnipāta) should be avoided, like a [severe] wound.
When it has ripened and is located in the heart, navel, or bladder, whether it has burst internally or externally, [it is fatal].
Just as a wound that is suppurated internally, oozing from the mouth, and accompanied by complications in an emaciated person, so too do the breast-veins of women become dilated. (19)
In women who have given birth or those who are pregnant, a dense swelling may arise in the breast—
whether it contains milk or not— characterized by the symptoms of an external abscess.
Because the openings of the channels are narrow, that [wind] does not arise in young women;
however, moving with its path obstructed, the enraged wind causes swelling and pain. (21)

11.21b However, it does not arise in virgins. 11.21c When the enraged *vāyu*, its movement no longer upward, reaches the scrotum from the groin, it compresses the vessels that carry [blood] to the testicles and causes enlargement of the two testicles. 11.22d [This is] *vṛddhi*.
That disease, Vṛddhi, is of seven types: [caused by] the humors (doṣa), blood, fat, urine, and intestines;
although the two arising from urine and the intestines are also due to wind (anila), the difference lies solely in their specific causes. 23.
From wind (vāta), there is a sensation like touching a leather bag filled with air, it is rough, and pain arises without an apparent cause;
from bile (pitta), it resembles a ripe udumbara fruit and is characterized by burning, heat, and suppuration. // 24 //
From kapha, it is cold, heavy, unctuous, itchy, hard, and slightly painful;
from blood, it is covered with black vesicles and exhibits the symptoms of increased pitta. // 25 //
11.25c–v: A black eruption covered with pustules arises from pitta and kapha; its increase is due to fat, being soft and resembling a palmyra fruit.
That which is born of urine occurs in one who habitually suppresses the urge to urinate, and it moves as he walks.
Like a leather bag filled with water, it becomes agitated and painful;
there is difficulty in urination, and a ring-like swelling occurs below the scrotum.

By foods that aggravate the wind (vāta), by immersion in cold water, by the retention [of breath], by combat, by carrying heavy loads, by travel on roads, and by moving the limbs in uneven ways; // 28 //
When the wind is agitated by other disturbing factors and renders the components of the small intestines disordered, it leads them downward from their own location. (29)
11.29c–11.30ab: Then the Vāyu, having doubled its force and being located at the groin joint (vaṅkṣaṇa-saṃdhi), produces a swelling that resembles a tumor (granthy-ābha).
And in one who neglects it, that same vāyu causes enlargement of the scrotum accompanied by distension, pain, and stiffness. (30cd)
When pressed within, it moves with a sound; when released, it returns, causing a swelling. 30ef.
This intestinal hernia (antra-vṛddhi), which has a clinical appearance similar to that of a hernia caused by Vāta, is incurable. // 31 //
Thus ends the diagnosis of swelling (vṛddhi); now follows the diagnosis of abdominal tumors (gulma). // 31+1 //

The gulma, characterized by a lattice-work of rough, blackish-red veins acting like windows, is of eight types: arising from the individual doṣas, from their combinations, and from their collective accumulation. (32)
The eighth [type] arises in women due to a disorder of the menstrual blood (ārtava), as well as through treatments such as emetics and by means of fevers, vomiting, diarrhea, and so forth. (33)
One who is emaciated eats wind-increasing foods, or being hungry drinks cold water; or one who, after eating meals, engages in fasting, swimming, and similar activities. (34)
11.34b–c. When hungry, one who consumes cold water experiences agitation of the body or induces vomiting;
furthermore, such a person does not eliminate the humors—whether they have been provoked or not—from the wind (vāta) and the others.
If one undergoes purification therapy without having practiced oleation and sudation, or if, after being purified, one quickly indulges in burning foods or laxatives, [the disease will persist]. (36)
His humors (malas), aggravated by an excess of wind (vāta), become disturbed either separately, in pairs, or all together;
they may also be associated with blood and reside within the great channels (mahāsrotas). // 37 //

Obstructing the upward and downward paths, they produce what is known as *gulma*, which is preceded by piercing pain (*śūla*), is perceptible to touch, is characterized by swelling, and takes the form of a knot (*granthi*). (38)

11.38–39. Due to emaciation, or by the obstruction of the passage caused by phlegm, feces, and bile, the wind (vāyu) takes up residence in the abdominal cavity; through dryness, it becomes hardened into a raised, knot-like mass.
Independent [consciousness] is defiled within its own basis; dependent [consciousness] is defiled within the basis of another.
Because it is condensed, although it is formless, it assumes, as it were, the state of being possessed of form. (40)
That which resides in the bladder, navel, heart, and sides is called gulma;
from vāta arise pain in the neck and head, fever, splenic enlargement, and rumbling in the intestines. (41)

Association with the wicked is like a thorn piercing with a needle; there is labored breathing repeatedly, stiffness in the limbs, dryness of the mouth, emaciation, and irregularity of the digestive fire. (42)
The state of having rough and dark skin and so forth arises from the mobility of the wind (anila), which has an unascertainable configuration, location, increase, decrease, and pain. // 43 //
Like a bush infested by ants, it throbs and pricks;
from pitta arise burning sensations, acid eructation, fainting, diarrhea, perspiration, thirst, and fever. (44)
There is a yellowish discoloration in the skin and other [tissues], as well as abdominal tumors (gulma) that cannot endure touch;
it feels painful and burning, is hot, and seems to consume its own location with fire.
From kapha arise numbness, loss of appetite, lassitude, fever with a cold sensation, chronic rhinitis, lethargy, nausea, cough, and whiteness of the skin and other parts. (46)
A Gulma that is deeply seated, hard, heavy, numb, stable, and slightly painful, located in its own site and abode, causes pain at its respective times. (47)
Generally, however, three types of gulma arise from the combination of two [humors] and exhibit mixed characteristics;
that born from all [three humors] is characterized by intense pain and burning, rapid suppuration, and is thick and elevated. 48.
This incurable blood-born gulma arises only in women—either during menstruation, or after a recent childbirth, or in one suffering from a disease of the womb. (49)
If a woman consumes wind-increasing foods while her husband is angry, his aggravated wind obstructs the menstrual blood that has accumulated in the womb every month. (50)
She develops a distended abdomen and manifests the signs of pregnancy, such as nausea, pregnancy-longing, the appearance of breast milk, emaciation, and so forth. (51)
Gradually, through contact with the wind (vāyu) and by virtue of its origin in bile (pitta),
that blood produces for her the symptoms arising from a gulma born of vāta and pitta.
It causes complications such as pain in the arms, stiffness, burning sensations, diarrhea, thirst, and fever;
and when the vitiated blood is localized in the uterus, it produces especially severe colic there. (53)
Furthermore, there is discharge from the womb, foul odor, pricking, throbbing, and pain;
unlike a fetus, a *gulma* does not move with the limbs, but rather is characterized by sharp colic. (54)
11.54bv–55. There are sensations of pricking and throbbing, or sensations of moisture and perspiration; that very [mass] of hers, having become a solid lump, sometimes throbbs after a long time.
Her abdomen does not enlarge, but the *gulma* itself increases in size.
Every gulma is based upon its own specific doṣa;
therefore, it undergoes suppuration only after a long time, whereas a vidradhi (abscess) does not do so at all.
It suppurates very rapidly because it is based upon corrupted blood;
therefore, due to its quick inflammation, it is designated as a *vidradhi* (abscess). // 57 //
When the Gulma has taken internal refuge, there is pain in the bladder, abdomen, heart, and spleen;
a loss of digestive fire, complexion, and strength, and the non-emergence of natural urges. (58)
11.58b–59: [In the internal type, there are] pains in the abdomen, heart, and flanks;
the opposite of this occurs in the external abdominal organs, though there is not excessive pain.
There is discoloration of the space [within], and the external protrusion is more pronounced.
A distension of the abdomen accompanied by swelling and extremely severe pain,
caused by the obstruction of flatus moving upward and downward, is designated as ānāha.

A dense, knotted mass resembling a bone (aṣṭhīla) that is elevated above it is called aṣṭhīlā; one with the same shape but situated transversely and possessing the symptoms of intestinal obstruction is called pratyaṣṭhīlā. // 61 //
11.61c–d When the vāyu moves obliquely from the colon toward the anus or the perineum with intense pain, it is characterized by constipation;
when this same [movement] occurs in the reverse direction, it is called tūṇī or pratūṇī.
Excessive belching, constipation, inability to feel satiated, rumbling in the intestines,
flatulence, abdominal distension, and lack of digestive power are said to be the symptoms of imminent gulma.

11.63cv Distension, flatulence, and the inability to digest; all diseases described in the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna) arise when the digestive fire is weak, but abdominal enlargements (udarāṇi) especially so.
They arise from the accumulation of impurities due to undigested food and filthy meals. // 1 //

Having obstructed the upward and downward channels that carry water, and having vitiated the prāṇa, agni, and apāna, [the doṣas], having reached the skin, flesh, and joints, produce [these diseases]. // 2 //

Having distended the abdomen, it ruptures into eight types: those caused by the individual humors (doṣas), by all three combined, by splenic enlargement (plīha), by intestinal obstruction (baddha), by perforation (kṣata), and by ascites (udaka). // 3 //
Afflicted by that, their palates and lips become parched; their feet, hands, and bellies swell;
their movement, strength, and appetite are lost; they become emaciated, yet their bellies remain distended. (4)
Men may appear like ghosts; these are the signs of what is to come:
the destruction of hunger, food being digested only after a long time, and everything being cooked with a burning sensation.
It is digested with a burning sensation;
one does not know whether it is digested or undigested, nor can one tolerate satiety.
Strength constantly diminishes, and one pants even when performing slight exertion. (6)

There is swelling, the non-activation of poison, and some edema in the feet; furthermore, there is pain at the bladder joints and a sense of tightness, even when eating light and small amounts of food. (7)
In cases of poisoning, there is swelling or a lack of movement;

in cases of abdominal enlargements (*jaṭhara*), however, there is the appearance of streaks, the disappearance of skin folds, lassitude, exhaustion, retention of waste products, and weak digestion in all such instances. (8)
Burning sensation, swelling, distension, and finally the appearance of fluid;
however, that which is without fluid is reddish, without swelling, and not excessively heavy. (9)
Covered with networks of veins like a lattice window, it constantly makes a gurgling sound;
having distended the umbilical region and the intestines and produced a forceful urge, it then subsides. (10)
The wind causes pain in the heart, waist, navel, anus, and groin; it issues forth with sound, while the feces are bound and urine is scant. (11)
12.11b–d — There is pain in the anus and the groin; the digestive fire is not excessively weak; there is no excessive greed, nor is the mouth tasteless.
In that case of vātodara (wind-belly), there is swelling in the hands, feet, scrotum, and abdomen.
Pain in the flanks, sides, abdomen, waist, and back; a splitting sensation in the joints; dry cough; aching of the limbs; heaviness in the lower body; and the retention of waste products. (13)
The abdomen becomes dark brownish-red in complexion and the like, with sudden fluctuations in size; it is accompanied by pricking and splitting pains, and is covered with thin, black veins. (14)
12.14d–15. It is thin, covered with dark veins, and when struck, it makes a sound like an inflated leather bag;
furthermore, the wind moves through it in all directions, accompanied by pain and sound.

In Pitta-type abdominal enlargement (pittodara), there is fever, fainting, burning sensation, thirst, a bitter taste in the mouth, giddiness, diarrhea, yellowness of the skin and other parts, and the abdomen appears greenish-yellow. (16)
Covered with yellowish-brown veins, accompanied by perspiration and heat, it burns;
it emits smoke, is tender to the touch, suppurates quickly, and is intensely inflamed. (17)

In Śleṣmodara (abdominal enlargement due to phlegm), there is a sensation of fuming, softness to the touch, lassitude of the limbs, sleepiness, swelling, heaviness, excessive drowsiness, nausea, loss of appetite, dyspnea, cough, and whiteness of the skin and other parts. 12.17c–d, 18.
12.18b–d. There is drowsiness, swelling, and heaviness; the abdomen is distended, motionless, smooth, covered with white streaks, and large;
it increases slowly, is hard, cold to the touch, heavy, and stable. 12.19.

12.19ab The abdomen becomes rigid and glossy due to those various factors that aggravate the three *doṣas*, as well as by the impurities of menstrual blood administered by women, and by artificial poisons (*gara*), latent poisons (*dūṣīviṣa*), and the like; thus the humors (*malas*) accumulate along with blood.

Having reached the abdominal cavity and undergoing transformation, they produce a most dreadful abdominal enlargement (udara) characterized by three symptoms, accompanied by emaciation, fainting, and vertigo, which suppurates quickly. (21)
And that [disease] is especially aggravated by the sight of cold winds and clouds, by overeating, and by agitating activities such as traveling in vehicles or on foot. (22)
12.22b–c Due to the sight of cold winds and clouds, excessive sexual indulgence, physical labor, travel, emesis, and emaciation from disease,
the spleen situated on the left side is displaced from its location and increases in size. 23.
Or, when blood has increased from the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) and other elements, it causes that [condition] to increase;
it becomes extremely hard like a stone-nodule (*aṣṭhīlā*), and thereafter resembles the back of a tortoise. (24)
12.24dv A common [fetus] develops gradually like the back of a tortoise and brings about the enlargement of the abdomen in the womb;
[it is accompanied] by dyspnea, cough, thirst, a bad taste in the mouth, flatulence, pain, and fever. 12.25ab
Accompanied by pallor, fainting, vomiting, burning sensations, and delusions, it appears reddish, discolored, or marked with blue and yellow streaks. (26)

One should recognize the morbid humors (malas) therein by their respective symptoms: pallor, fainting, excessive vomiting, burning sensation, and delusion; upward movement of wind (udāvarta), pain, and abdominal distension; delusion, thirst, internal heat, and fever; heaviness, loss of appetite, and hardness. (12.26–27)
Due to upward movement of wind (udāvarta), pain, or intestinal obstruction (ānāha),
the liver, like the spleen, may become displaced from the right side; furthermore,
when eyelashes or hair are swallowed with food, they may cause a constriction in the rectum.

When provoked, the wind (vāyu), having obstructed feces, bile, and phlegm by means of the "bad-name" (dur-nāman) upward-reversing disorders or other intestinal obstructions, produces [the disease]. (29)

12.29bv By means of foods that cause intestinal coating, the apāna vāyu becomes obstructed; consequently, there may arise burning sensations, fever, thirst, and sneezing, as well as cough, dyspnea, weakness in the thighs, and pain in the head, heart, navel, and anus. (30)
12.30b–c. There may be burning sensations, fever, thirst, and hunger; 12.31.
retention of waste products, anorexia, vomiting, abdominal enlargement with obstructed flatus, which is either firm and covered with blue or reddish venous streaks, or devoid of such streaks.
And above the navel, it generally takes on the shape of a cow's tail when one has eaten food containing bone or other such foreign matter, or due to overeating. (32)

12.32c–d The intestine is pierced or cooked by bone and other foreign objects along with food; through those perforations, undigested matter (āma) flows out, emerging from the anus in small quantities mixed with the essence of feces. 12.33 //
The intestines are torn apart and cooked; the stool and the rasa are discharged in very small quantities, smelling like a corpse, slimy, and yellowish-red.
The remaining [fluid] fills the abdomen and brings about a terrible abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara).
One should increase that [fluid] below the navel; it quickly attains the nature of water, and its form becomes one of aggravated doṣas, pervaded by dyspnea, thirst, and vertigo. (35)

That [fluid] increases below the navel, and the patient is afflicted by dyspnea, thirst, and fever; this is called *chidrodara*, though others call it *parisrāvī*. It occurs in one who has suddenly drunk water after having undergone the administration of unctuous substances and other treatments. (12.35–36)
In one who drinks excessive water, whose digestive fire is weak, or who is emaciated or extremely thin,
the wind (vāyu) and phlegm (kapha), having obstructed the pathways of the water and being saturated with fluid, [cause edema].
Those two, having taken refuge in the abdomen, cause that very water to increase from its original location;
from this, there arises abdominal enlargement (udara) accompanied by thirst, discharge from the anus, and pain. (38)
Accompanied by anal discharge and pain, associated with cough, dyspnea, and loss of appetite, covered with veins of various colors,
it feels like a water-filled leather bag to the touch, making a sound when shaken and trembling.
12.39bv Endowed with veins of various colors; 12.39bv Covered with veins of various colors; 12.39bv Enveloped by veins of various colors:
that great ascites (dakodara) is oily, firm, and has a protruding umbilicus.
And through equanimity, all faults fall away from their own place. // 40 //

Due to the digestive process (pāka), the fluids (drava) liquefy even the openings of the joints and channels; furthermore, external sweating is obstructed when it is directed obliquely into the side-channels. (41)
12.41ab Through cooking, they would liquefy the liquid;

having replenished that very water, one should make it into a thick mucilage (picchā). Then it would become a heavy abdomen (gurūdara), stable, round, and when struck, it would not produce a sound. 12.42ab/12.41cd (as per the numbering above)
It is soft, free of lines, touched at the navel, and spreads across it; born without water, it causes an even greater enlargement of the belly.
The disappearance of the veins and the symptoms described for *udaka-jaṭhara* (water-belly) [are present];
these include *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, *plīha* (splenic), and *saṃnipāta-udakodara* (combined humors with water-belly). 44.
The difficulty increases progressively; after a fortnight, for the most part, others are destroyed.
Furthermore, all [such cases] where water has appeared, accompanied by the complications mentioned regarding fatal signs (riṣṭa), [are incurable].
Generally, all types of abdominal enlargement (udara) are considered most difficult to treat from the very moment of their birth;
however, that which is strong, has not yet accumulated fluid, and has recently arisen can be managed with effort.
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna):
When the humors (malas) are aggravated by the aforementioned provocative factors, with pitta being predominant, the pitta situated in the heart is then driven [further] by the powerful vāyu. (1)
Having reached the ten vessels (dhamanīs) and pervading the entire body,
it vitiates the phlegm, skin, blood, and flesh, taking refuge within.
It acts upon the skin and the flesh, producing various kinds of colors in the skin—
such as pale yellow, turmeric-yellow, and green— and among these, paleness is predominant.
For this reason, that disease is called "pāṇḍu" (pallor); by it, there occurs heaviness of the bodily constituents (dhātus), laxity, and the depletion of the qualities of ojas.
Then, with little blood and fat, he becomes essence-less, his faculties slack;
his limbs feel as if they are being crushed, and there is no firmness in his heart.
13.5b–d: He is devoid of essence, with lax sensory faculties, or with a sense of fluidity in his heart; his eye-sockets are swollen, he is languid, irritable, spitting, and speaks little;
he has an aversion to food, a hatred for cold, his body hair is withered, and his digestive fire is extinguished.
13.6a One with swollen eyes, temples, and face; 13.6b irritable, perspiring, and speaking little;
13.6c irritable, dejected, and speaking little; with sinking thighs, feverish, dyspneic, having ringing in the ears, dizzy, and fatigued.
It is of five kinds, distinguished by the individual humors, by all of them combined, and from eating clay. // 7 //

13.7 With weak thighs, fever, and dyspnea— these are its premonitory symptoms: palpitations of the heart, dryness of the skin, loss of appetite, yellowish urine, absence of perspiration, and diminished digestive fire.
Exhaustion from wind (vāta) consists of fatigue, aching in the limbs, piercing pain, and trembling;
it is characterized by blackness, dryness, and a reddish hue of the veins, nails, feces, urine, and eyes. (9)

From pitta arise swelling, flatulence, bad taste in the mouth, dryness of the stool, pain in the sides and head, a greenish or yellowish appearance of the veins and other parts, fever, and darkness of vision. (10)

Thirst, perspiration, fainting, desire for cold, foul odor, a pungent taste in the mouth, diarrhea, acid eructation, burning sensation, and whiteness of the veins and other parts result from Kapha. (11)
Drowsiness, a salty taste in the mouth, horripilation, loss of voice, coughing, and vomiting—these are the combined symptoms of the [three] humors, which are exceedingly difficult to endure. (12)
Horripilation, loss of voice, and a parched throat;
wind (vāyu) becomes bitter and astringent, bile (pitta) becomes alkaline and sweet, and phlegm (kapha) is corrupted;
having vitiated the rasa and other tissues, it dries up the food consumed due to its own dryness. // 13 //
Having filled the channels with undigested matter and obstructed them as before, one then develops jaundice (pāṇḍu-roga), characterized by swelling of the navel, feet, face, and genitals. (14)

A person suffering from jaundice who consumes pitta-aggravating substances may discharge feces containing worms, or pass broken stools mixed with blood and phlegm; such a patient develops kāmalā (icteric jaundice). 15.
Pitta, having burnt the blood and flesh located in the visceral cavities and the peripheral tissues, brings about yellowness of the eyes, urine, skin, nails, face, and feces. (16)

13.16 When pitta is located in the visceral cavities (koṣṭha) and the peripheral branches (śākhā), the patient experiences burning sensations, indigestion, and thirst; he has a complexion like that of a frog and his sense organs are weak.
This condition occurs even without the disease of jaundice (pāṇḍu-roga) in one whose pitta is predominant.
When that [jaundice] is characterized by swelling due to neglect, it becomes the difficult-to-cure Kumbhakāmalā;
furthermore, when a greenish, dark-brown, or yellowish tint occurs in a case of Pāṇḍuroga, [it indicates a grave condition]. // 18 //

Dizziness and thirst arising from wind and bile, lack of sexual desire for women, mild fever, drowsiness, and loss of strength and digestive fire—this condition, characterized by a coating [of the tongue], is called Halīmaka. (19)
They declare that lassitude is also among them, preceded by afflictions characterized primarily by swelling; therefore, that very [condition] is now described. (20)

The vitiated wind (vāyu), having led the corrupted bile (pitta), blood (rakta), and phlegm (kapha) into the external vessels, its movement obstructed by them, produces [the disease] localized in the skin and flesh. // 21 //
They call that swelling (śopha) which is elevated and compact "nicaya" because of its accumulation;
yet, due to the distinctions among their causes, it is of nine types according to the differences in its symptoms.

It arises from the humors (doṣas) individually, in pairs, or from all three together, as well as from injury or poison; it is of two types—endogenous (nija) and exogenous (āgantuka)—and it may affect the whole body or a single limb.
They know that swellings are of three types according to the distinctions of being broad, elevated, or knotted;
however, the general cause of all swellings arising from the humors (doṣas) is specifically [the same]. (24)

For one who is emaciated by disease, labor, fasting, and so forth, [heavy food is beneficial]; for another, however, it is quickly harmful when consumed in excess, being heavy, sour, unctuous, and cold. (25)

13.25b–c — For one who is emaciated, consuming liquids in excess, or eating food that is excessively salty, alkaline, pungent, or hot; or [consuming] vegetables, water, sleep, or staying awake; or [eating] clay, domestic meat, or dried meat; or indulging in sexual intercourse during indigestion or after physical exertion.
Traveling on foot along the road, or by means of a jolting vehicle;
and [diseases such as] dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargement, menorrhagia, and fever. (27)

Visūcī, alasaka, vomiting, internal hemorrhage (garbha-visarpa), anemia (pāṇḍu), and other conditions resulting from improper treatment—by these [factors], the doshas become localized in the chest. // 28 //

13.28bv–29. Those [doṣas] located in the middle [of the body] produce edema in the abdomen, jaundice, and swelling in the upper part, while those in the lower part produce it in the bladder; those located in the middle [part] produce it in the middle; those moving through the whole body produce it everywhere; and those residing in the various limbs produce it in those specific parts.
Its premonitory symptoms are distress, stretching of the vessels, and heaviness of the limbs; due to Vāta, the swelling is mobile, dry, rough-haired, and reddish-black. (30)
It is characterized by contraction, throbbing, horripilation, pain, piercing, splitting, and numbness;
it rises quickly when pressed, subsides rapidly, and the body part elevates swiftly when squeezed. (31)
It may be relieved by applications that are unctuous, warm, and massaging; it is slight at night and great during the day;
and the skin feels as if smeared with mustard seeds, experiencing a tingling sensation.
Having a yellow, red, or blackish luster, it arises from bile (*pitta*); it makes the hair copper-colored;
it is quickly followed by subsidence; in its middle stage it first becomes thin. (33)
Accompanied by thirst, burning sensations, fever, perspiration, emaciation, moisture, intoxication, and vertigo;
desiring cold things, having loose stools, foul-smelling, unable to bear touch, and soft. // 34 //
It is characterized by itching, pale hair and skin, and is hard, cold, heavy, unctuous, smooth, stable, and thick; it causes drowsiness, vomiting, and impairment of the digestive fire. // 35 //

When attacked, the night-strength [blood] arising from the subsiding of distress should not rise up; wounded by the *kuśa*-grass instrument or other tools, it flows after a long time as a slimy discharge rather than blood. (36)

One who desires contact with warmth due to phlegm, and likewise the three types arising from combinations of two humors according to their respective natures; and that which is composed of a collection [of all three] due to the combination of causes and symptoms—[these are the various types]. // 37 //

By trauma such as cutting, piercing, and wounding from weapons and the like; and by cold, wind, water, curd, and air; and by [contact with] marking-nut (*bhallātaka*) and the *kapikacchū* plant. // 38 //
13.38c–d Due to contact with snow, fire, water, ghee, wind, vegetable juices, or thorns, there occurs an edema accompanied by spreading (visarpa),
characterized by intense heat, a reddish appearance, and generally the symptoms of pitta. 13.39.
Poison arises from the crawling over or urination by venomous creatures, and even among non-venomous creatures, it arises from the falling of their fangs, teeth, or claws. (40)
13.40c–d From the bite of fangs, teeth, or claws; from contact with clothing defiled by feces, urine, semen, or impurities;
from the touch of the wind from poisonous trees; and from being dusted with artificial poisons (gara-yoga). 13.41 From [these causes], [the poison spreads].

13.41b–42a — A swelling that resembles a cloth stained with dirt, which is soft, mobile, pendulous, rapid in onset, and causes burning and pain; when it is recent and free from complications, it is curable, whereas those previously mentioned are incurable.
Visarpa may arise from the doshas and dushyas through trauma and other causes, similar to swelling (shotha).
They say it has three bases, depending on whether it is external, internal, or both. (43)
And among them, the doshas are increasingly difficult to treat as one proceeds;
they become especially aggravated by provocative factors, particularly those that cause a burning sensation.
One should know that those [humors] situated within quickly spread from the interior to the exterior;

those situated outside spread from the exterior to both; and those situated in both [interior and exterior] spread in both directions. Among these, one should recognize the internal as the primary refuge.

Due to the affliction of the vital points (marmans), due to delusion, due to the obstruction of the channels, due to excessive attachment to craving, and due to the irregular movement of the bodily urges. // 46 //

13.46ab Due to injury to the vital spots (marmans), delusion, and irregular onset, 13.46cd and due to the rapid loss of digestive fire and strength, [the disease] is external; the opposite of this constitutes the internal type.
Among these, that caused by Vāta is Parīsarpa, characterized by pain equal to that of Vāta-fever.
Accompanied by swelling, throbbing, piercing pain, tearing sensations, distress, and horripilation;
moving rapidly due to pitta, characterized by the symptoms of pitta-fever, and being very red—[this is the fever caused by pitta]. (48)

From kapha, [the carbuncle] is accompanied by itching, is unctuous, and has a pain similar to that of kapha-fever; if neglected, all of them become covered with eruptions (sphoṭa) characterized by the symptoms of their respective doṣas. // 49 //
When these have suppurated and burst open, they each bear the characteristic marks of a wound;
due to [an excess of] wind and bile, they are accompanied by fever, vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, thirst, and giddiness.
Accompanied by splitting pains in the bones, a sinking sensation, fainting, and loss of appetite, it makes the entire body feel as if it were strewn with glowing embers. (51)
Whichever region the spreading [disease] spreads to, that place quickly becomes covered with ash-colored, black, blue, or red [eruptions], which are then pacified. (52)
Due to its rapid movement, that visarpa spreads quickly like burns from fire with eruptions;
it follows the vital points (marmas), and consequently, the vāta becomes exceedingly powerful. (53)
It causes the limbs to tremble, takes away consciousness and sleep, and stirs up the breath; it brings on hiccups—such a state as this no man ever attains. (54)
In some places, seized by a craving for flesh, he moves about upon the ground, beds, seats, and so forth;
thereafter, afflicted, he experiences the suffering arising from mental and physical exhaustion.
One who finds it difficult to awaken from sleep suffers from what is called agni-visarpa;
this occurs when the wind (pavana), obstructed by phlegm (kapha), breaks that phlegm into many parts.
Or blood, in one with increased blood, having vitiated the skin, vessels, ligaments, and flesh, [produces] long, thin, round, thick, and rough-natured [lesions]. (57)
It produces a garland of red nodules accompanied by intense pain and fever, along with dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, dryness of the mouth, hiccups, vomiting, and vertigo. (58)
Accompanied by delusion, discoloration, fainting, breaking pain in the limbs, and a sensation of coldness, this is the granthi-visarpa born from the provocation of kapha and vāta. (59)
From the combination of kapha and pitta arise fever, stiffness, drowsiness, lethargy, headache, exhaustion of the limbs, tossing about, delirium, anorexia, and vertigo. (60)

Fainting, loss of digestive fire, cracking of the bones, thirst, heaviness of the sense organs, the passage of undigested stools (āmopaveśana), and a coating of the channels—this [dosha] spreads throughout the body. (61)
Generally seizing a portion of the stomach (āmāśaya) without excessive pain,
it is covered with pustules that are excessively yellow, red, or pale.
It has a variegated luster, is black, glossy, and dirty; it is swollen, heavy, and undergoes deep suppuration; it is intensely hot to the touch, becomes moist, and breaks open. (63)
13.63–64ab. That which has a dark-blue luster, is black and glossy, with its flesh sloughed off like mud, and where the network of tendons and veins is clearly visible,
and which smells like a corpse— they call that *vīsarpa* "Kardama" (the muddy one).
Arising from all [causes] and possessing all characteristics, it spreads throughout all the bodily constituents (dhātus);
provoked by an injury from an external cause, it impels the bile along with blood. (65)

13.65b–66. When the Vāta spreads through all the bodily tissues (dhātus), it produces Visarpa (erysipelas), which is covered with eruptions resembling Kulattha beans, and is characterized by swelling, fever, pain, and burning, appearing dark-red in color.
The three types caused by individual doshas, as well as those arising from two doshas when they are without complications, are curable.
Those arising from injury (kshata) and those originating from all three doshas together are incurable, as are all cases where the vital points (marmas) have been affected.
With their sinews, veins, and flesh decayed, they are moist and reek with the stench of corpses.
In the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna):
Primarily through improper diet and lifestyle that are specifically antagonistic, and by practicing such acts as censuring the virtuous, killing, and seizing one's own property; // 1 //
The impurities, driven forth immediately by past sinful actions,
enter the obliquely coursing vessels and reach the skin, lymph, blood, and flesh.

14.2bv Impurities, impelled by past actions, corrupt [the tissues], and having loosened them, they emerge from within; causing discoloration of the skin, these vitiated humors are called *kuṣṭha* (leprosy). // 3 //

14.3 Because it corrupts [the body] once it has been neglected over time and weakened, it consumes that entire physique; having entered and pervaded all the internal elements (dhātus), it causes them to become excessively moistened and brings about [their destruction]. // 4 //
[They produce] worms that are minute and extremely cruel, which cause sweating, moistening, and putrefaction,
and which successively destroy the hair, skin, sinews, vessels, and cartilage.
One should consume this for white leprosy (śvitra), which is declared to be external to [the major types of] kuṣṭha.
There are seven kinds of kuṣṭhas, arising from the humors (doṣas) individually, in combination, or when they have all come together. (6)
14.6dv In all cases of the three *doṣas*, whether occurring individually or combined in pairs, the designation is according to whichever is predominant:
from *vāta* comes *kāpāla-kuṣṭha*, from *pitta* comes *audumbara*, and from *kapha* [comes *maṇḍala*]. // 7 //
Maṇḍala, vicarcī, and ṛkṣaja arise from vāta and pitta; as do carma, eka-kuṣṭha, kiṭibha, sidhma, alasa, and vipādikā. (8)
14.8b-v *Ṛkṣākṣa* arises from *vāta* and *pitta*; from *vāta* and *śleṣman* arise *dadrū*, *śatāruṣī*,
*puṇḍarīka* along with *visphoṭa*, *pāmā*, and likewise *carma-dala*.
By all [these] together, there is the *kākaṇa* first; with the three, *dadru* along with *kākaṇa*;
and *puṇḍarīka*, *arkṣa*, and *jihvā*—these are the seven great leprosies (*mahā-kuṣṭha*). 10.
14.10b–c: Trika, ringworm (dadrū), and kākaṇā; as well as puṇḍarīka and arśas-jiḥvā.

14.11: Excessive smoothness, roughness to the touch, exhaustion, lack of perspiration, discoloration, burning sensation, itching, numbness of the skin, pricking pain, elevation of eruptions (koṭha), and fatigue [are the symptoms].
In these cases, there is excessive pain in the ulcers, rapid onset, and long duration;
even when healed, they remain dry and become aggravated by even a slight cause. (12)
Horripilation, blackness of the blood, and the primary symptoms of leprosy arise first:
it has the appearance of a blackish-red skull, is dry, numb, rough, and thin.
The *kāpāla* type is extensive with even margins, covered with bristling hair, characterized by intense pricking sensations and slight itching, and it spreads rapidly. (14)

14.14b–d. It is covered with discolored hairs, resembling the copper-colored bark of a ripe udumbara fruit; it is filled with pale veins, thick, moist with abundant exudation and blood, and characterized by excessive burning and pain. // 15 //
One should recognize Udumbara as being covered with hair and pale veins, thick, with abundant discharge, characterized by rapid onset, bursting, and the presence of worms;
it is firm, dense, heavy, unctuous, white-red in color, and does not spread quickly. (14.15b–16)
A circular patch, mutually adherent, extensive, with much itching, discharge, and parasites, having smooth and yellowish margins. (17)
14.17 When [the skin] is swollen and adheres to one another, with itchy pustules, dark-brown, and abounding in serous discharge, it is called *vicarcikā*.
When it is rough, thin, red at the edges, dark-brown within, and elevated—[this is *dadrū*]. 18.
Accompanied by pricking, burning, pain, and discharge, and covered with rough pustules, that which has the shape of a bear’s tongue is called Ṛkṣajihva; it contains many worms. (19)
