14.19c–d: That which has the shape of a deer’s tongue is called *ṛśyajihva*; it is full of worms and has the touch of elephant skin or a donkey. 14.20: The single-skin disease (*carmaikākhya*) is a great refuge for parasites;
it is without perspiration and resembles the scales of a fish. Furthermore, *kiṭibha* is likewise.
Sidhma is dry, characterized by a rough sensation like a scar, itchy, and coarse-black;
it is dry on the surface yet oily within, and when rubbed, it sheds dust.
It has a smooth touch, is thin, and is whitish-copper in color like the *dugdhika* flower;
it generally occurs on the upper part of the body and is covered with itchy eruptions. (22)
Due to blood, there is alasaka (intestinal stasis), cracking of the hands and feet, and vipādikā (cracking of the soles);
these are accompanied by intense pain, slight itching, and are covered with reddish pustules.
Dadru is characterized by long-extended patches resembling durvā grass, having the hue of linseed flowers,
with raised circular areas, accompanied by itching, and prone to spreading.
Śatāru has thick roots, is accompanied by burning pain, is reddish-brown, contains many ulcers, is rich in discharge and parasites, and generally arises at the joints. (25)
With reddish margins and pale in the center, accompanied by itching, burning, and pain, it is raised and covered with red [spots] like the rays of a lotus petal. // 26 //
Puṇḍarīka consists primarily of thick, abundant lymph and blood, is quickly suppurating, and is covered with thin skin and white or reddish pustules. (27)
Eruptions, pustules, scabies, and itching, accompanied by excessive moisture and pain—numerous, minute, and dark-red in color—occur mostly on the buttocks, hands, and elbows. (28)
Accompanied by cracking, intolerable to touch, and characterized by itching, piercing pain, and burning;
red, with bursting skin, it is called *kākaṇa*, marked by intense burning and pain. (29)
First it becomes red and black, resembling the fruit of the kākaṇantī;
then, endowed with all the symptoms of leprosy (kuṣṭha), it becomes multicolored. // 30 //

One should determine the predominance of the doshas in skin diseases by means of the signs and actions prescribed for the classification of the doshas; one should avoid treating those cases where all the doshas are excessively aggravated.
That which is described as occurring in the *riṣṭa* (fatal signs), as well as that which resides in the bone, marrow, and semen, is palliable;
that which has reached the fat is difficult to cure, while that which reaches the pitta, the two combinations (of doṣas), the blood, or the flesh is incurable.
That which is not difficult to treat is characterized by an abundance of kapha and vāta, and is located in the skin with only a single doṣa.
When kuṣṭha is situated in the skin, there is pricking pain, discoloration, and roughness. (33)
In the blood and the flesh, there is perspiration, sleepiness, and swelling; furthermore, there are eruptions localized in the hands and feet, and excessive moisture in the joints. (34)
When [the wind] resides in the fat (medas), there is lameness, loss of movement, and the crushing of the limbs;
when it resides in the bone and marrow (asthi-majjas), there is the collapse of the nose, redness of the eyes, and loss of voice. // 35 //
When the semen is afflicted by worms, there is injury to one's own wife and offspring;
and all the symptoms previously described for blood and the other humors likewise occur.

14.36b–c. Washing one's own wife or children [with the patient] is the sole cause of *kuṣṭha*. That which is *śvitra*, *kilāsa*, and *dāruṇa* is designated as non-exuding (*aparisrāvi*) and arises from the involvement of all three *dhātus*.

14.37b–v: That [disease] is kilāsa and aruṇa. From vāta it is dry and reddish; from pitta it is copper-colored like a lotus petal, accompanied by burning, and causes the destruction of body hair; from kapha it is white, thick, and heavy.
One should recognize itching as occurring successively in the blood, flesh, and fat;
by its color alone, both [types] are thus identified, and each subsequent one is more difficult to cure. (39)

Vitiligo that has hair which is not white, is thick, not confluent with one another, and is newly arisen, and which is produced without being burnt by fire, is curable; otherwise, it is to be rejected as incurable. (40)

14.40ab Diseases generally arise from contact with one who has not white hair, who is not excessively aged, who is not defiled, and who is moreover new [to the practice], even if the transmission occurs through the private parts, the palms of the hands, or the lips, and though it may have occurred recently; this is due to the use of the same touch, food, bed, and so forth.
14.41cd [Diseases] generally arise from such service as sharing touch, food, and bedding.
All disorders of the eyes and skin are mobile; specifically, worms are said to be of two kinds, distinguished as external and internal. 42.

The external [defilements] are of four types according to their origin from external filth, phlegm, blood, and excrement; by name, they are of twenty kinds, among which those arising from lack of cleanliness are [the first]. (43)
Among them, the external [parasites] arise from filth; others there arise from blood. They are the size, shape, and color of sesame seeds, and they reside in the hair and clothing.
Known by the names *yūka* (lice) and *likṣā* (nits), they have many legs and are minute.
These two types produce eruptions, pustules, itching, and swellings;
they arise internally from the same causes as *kuṣṭha*, and among them, phlegm (*śleṣman*) is predominant. (45)
[The worms] born from feces [are nourished] by sweet foods, molasses, milk, curd, parched grain flour, fresh rice, various beans, grains, leafy vegetables, meat, and the like. // 46 //
Due to kapha, [these worms] arise in the stomach through the consumption of sweet, sour, molasses, milk, leafy vegetables, sesame oil-cakes, and similar foods; having grown, they spread everywhere.
Some resemble broad soles, while others are like earthworms. // 47 //
Having the appearance of sprouted grains, they are slender, long, and minute;
white and with a coppery luster—thus, by name, they are of seven kinds.
The Antrādās, Udarāveṣṭas, Hṛdayādās, Mahākuhas, Kuravas, Darbhakusumas, and Sugandhas—they too cause [these afflictions]. (49)
The *antrādā* worms enter the abdomen; the *mahā-ruhā* worms devour the heart; the *curuva* worms resemble *darbha* flowers.
[Their symptoms include] a sense of fluttering in the heart (*hṛllāsa*), salivation, indigestion, and loss of appetite.
Fainting, vomiting, fever, abdominal distension, emaciation, sneezing, and chronic rhinitis.
Minute creatures born of blood arise from the emergence of blood-carrying vessels; they are legless, circular, and copper-colored, and some are invisible due to their extreme subtlety. (51)
Located in the region of the blood-carrying vessels,
the Keśādā, Roma-vidhvaṃsā, Roma-dvīpā, and Udumbarā— these six, along with Saurasa and Mātara, share the same function as Kuṣṭha. // 52 //
14.52–53. Congenital hemorrhoids arise from the feces in the colon and spread downward; when they have increased in size, they may turn upward toward the stomach.
14.53c–d Those [worms] would be large; and then his eructations and breaths would follow the odor of feces.
They are broad, round, thin, or thick, and dark-brown, yellow, white, or black.
These five types of worms— namely the *kakerukas*, *makerukas*, *sausurādās*, those called *sulūnas*, and the *lelihās*— cause [the disease] to arise.

14.55–56ab. From its discharge, there arise sausurādā, the condition known as śalūna, dysuria (viḍbheda), colic (śūla), constipation (viṣṭambha), emaciation (kārśya), roughness (pāruṣya), pallor (pāṇḍutā), horripilation (roma-harṣa), loss of digestive fire (agni-sadana), and itching of the anus (guda-kaṇḍū).
14.56dv—Anus-itching; those that have emerged; 14.56dv—Anus-itching; those that go by wrong paths. In the Section on Pathology (Nidānasthāna):
The sole cause for all that is beneficial and harmful in this universe.
The wind, though not inherently corrupt, becomes corrupted specifically with respect to the body. // 1 //
He is Viśvakarman, the soul of all, the universal form, and Prajāpati; he is the creator, the sustainer, the omnipresent Viṣṇu, the destroyer, death, and the ender. // 2 //
Therefore, one should always strive with effort to avoid that [defect];
for once its defect has been recognized, the prescribed treatment—both natural and modified—has already been stated. (3)

In this [treatise], the classification of defects according to their names and locations is presented both in brief and in detail; furthermore, the movement and function of each [defect] are fivefold, as is their morbid alteration.
Its classification is now explained, along with its causes and characteristics:
the wind becomes provoked by the excessive indulgence in things that cause the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus). (5)
Even that which is beyond number, having been calculated and previously stated as eighty [times], 5.1+(1)ab.
15.5.1+(1) Just as a powerful person, while moving along channels that have been emptied by another, fills them completely;
or, having encountered an obstruction from those [channels] filled with other defects, remains strong. // 6 //

When provoked in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), it causes colic, abdominal distension, rumbling in the intestines, obstruction of waste, urinary stones, scrotal enlargement, hemorrhoids, and stiffness in the sacrum, back, and waist. (7)
And it produces various painful afflictions in the lower part of the body,
while in the stomach it causes thirst, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, and choleraic pain.
15.8 It causes obstruction of the throat, belching, and diseases above the navel in the lower parts of the body;
it brings about the destruction of the sense organs in the ears and other [senses], and cracking and roughness in the skin. 9.
When [the blood is] vitiated, there is intense pain, numbness, burning, discoloration, ulcers, constipation, loss of appetite, emaciation, and vertigo. (10)

15.10c–e: Ulcers on the limbs, stiffness, nodules located in the flesh and fat that are intensely pruritic and hard, exhaustion, heaviness of the limbs, and extreme pain with rigidity as if struck by a fist or a staff; // 11 //

[The vāta] residing in the bones causes intense pain in the thighs and the joints of the bones, accompanied by piercing sensations and severe exhaustion; residing in the marrow, it causes hollowness in the bones, insomnia, and constant pain. (15.12)
15.12cd–13ab: [The physician should recognize] sleeplessness, stiffness, pain, rapid emission of semen, or its obstruction and even its morbid alteration;
likewise, when located in the vessels, it causes distension and depletion of the fetus.

When the *vāyu* is located in that [tendon], situated within the sinews, it causes torticollis (*gṛdhrasī*), stretching, and hunchback; when the *anila* has reached the joints, it produces swelling with the sensation of a wind-filled leather bag.
15.14b–d: It causes torticollis and kyphosis like a vulture, as well as painful movement in extension and flexion;
when localized in the entire body, it produces pricking, splitting, throbbing, and breaking sensations.
When the enraged [wind] repeatedly enters all the channels, it causes paralysis, convulsions, sleep, joint-bending, contraction, and trembling. (16)
Then this disease, known as ākṣepaka, seizes the limbs;
the wind, moving upward after being obstructed below, takes refuge in the heart. (17)
15.17 Moving upward, it enters the channels based in the heart, and by afflicting the heart, the head, and the temples,
it convulses the limbs all over and bends the body like a bow.
15.18 Then, it afflicts the head and the temples; one breathes with difficulty, with eyes that are fixed, drooping, or closed;
and like a dove, one coos while unconscious—this is apatantraka.
That very same [wind], when it has descended and is released into the heart, would experience well-being again and again; but when it is obstructed, it experiences ill-being again and again.

15.20c–d That [fever] arising from miscarriage, that produced by excessive hemorrhage, and that arising from injury may seem as though it were returning to health; however, it is indeed the most difficult to treat. 15.21a–b [It is] most difficult to cure.
I think that when the wind, having become obstructed within and constricting the vessels,
pervades the entire body, then the collarbone is stretched.
When [the wind], entering the channels within, makes the body like a drawn bow, causes stiffness of the eyes, yawning, gnashing of the teeth, and the spitting out of phlegm; 15.22b–23a.
Pain in the sides, as well as stiffness of the speech, jaw, back, and head—this is known as internal āyāma; external āyāma is of the same nature.
The head is drawn backward from the outward extension of the body;
there, the chest is lifted up and the neck is pressed down.
The head is drawn backward, there is discoloration of the teeth and the mouth, perspiration, and drooping of the limbs; they call this *bāhyāyāma*, *dhanuḥ-skambha*, and *vegina*. (15.25–26)
15.26c–d Upon reaching external extension, a stiffening of the bow,
or a wound located at a vital point (marman), the humors (doṣas), impelled by the wind (samīraṇa), cause the entire body from head to foot to undergo convulsive movements. 15.27.

15.27 When a wound reaches a vital point (marman) in one who is thirsty and has pale limbs, that extension of the ulcer is fatal. Once the paroxysm has subsided, there may be recovery in all cases of convulsions (ākṣepaka).

15.28dv–29. However, in all cases of displacement (ākṣepaka), the Vāyu located at the root of the jaw becomes aggravated by scraping the tongue, eating dry food, or trauma; having displaced the two jaws, it causes them to droop.
It causes the mouth to remain open or, alternatively, to remain closed;
by that [condition], there occurs a drooping of the jaw, making chewing and speaking difficult. (30)
The Vata wind, located in the speech-carrying channels, causes the tongue to become stiff;
this is jihvā-stambha (tongue-stiffness), by which one loses control over eating, drinking, and speaking.
Because of carrying a burden on his head, speaking with excessive laughter, [experiencing] terror, sneezing from the mouth, and drawing a stiff bow; // 32 //
From labored breathing, distorted sneezing, and terror; from drawing a stiff bow, from an uneven pillow, and from chewing hard things; (15.32cd–15.32dv)
And the wind, increased by those various wind-aggravating factors, has ascended upwards. // 33 //
He distorts half of his face; what was said becomes laughter or a glance; then his head trembles, his speech falters, and his eyes become fixed. (34)

15.34dv–35. Stuttering of speech, fixedness of the eyes, looseness of the teeth, loss of voice, impairment of hearing, suppression of sneezing, loss of the sense of smell, confusion of memory, and terror arise in one who is asleep.
Salivation, wandering to one side, closing of one eye, and intense pain above the collarbone or even in one half of the body—these are the symptoms. (36)
Regarding this, some call it *ardita*, while others call it *ekāyāma*;
the wind, having taken hold of the blood, causes the vessels of the head to become rigid. (37)
Rough, painful, and black, that constriction of the vessels (sirā-graha) would be incurable;
having seized half the body and dried up the vessels and tendons, the wind (vāyu) [causes this]. (38)
It destroys one side [of the body] by loosening the joints of the ligaments;
the entire half-body becomes incapacitated and devoid of sensation. (39)

Some know that [disease] as ekāṅga-roga (monoplegia), while others call it pakṣa-vadha (hemiplegia); likewise, when the vāyu resides throughout the entire body, it is known as sarvāṅga-roga (general paralysis).
A hemiplegia caused by pure wind is considered most difficult to cure;
that which is associated with another [dosha] is difficult to treat, while that caused by wasting (kṣaya) should be rejected as incurable. // 41 //

The wind (vāyu), conjoined with phlegm (kapha) and obstructing the channels, causes the limbs to become rigid; when all its functions are destroyed, it renders the condition incurable, producing a "staff-like" stiffness (daṇḍaka).
The wind situated at the base of the shoulder, contracting the vessels located there,
produces avabāhuka, which causes the loss of movement in the arm.
The tendon that runs from the back of the arm to the fingers at the palm, which robs the arm of its movement, is known as Viśvācī. (44)
When the vāyu situated in the waist, which causes the exhaustion of action in the arms, seizes the tendons (kaṇḍarā) of the thighs,
then the person becomes lame; if it seizes both thighs, he becomes a cripple.
One who trembles at the start of movement and walks as if limping should be known as a *kalāya-khañja*, whose joints and ligaments have become loose.
Through the consumption of cold, hot, liquid, dry, heavy, and unctuous substances;
likewise through exertion, agitation, sleep, and wakefulness, whether during digestion or indigestion; // 47 //
When undigested matter (āma), excessively accumulated along with phlegm, fat, and wind, overcomes the other doshas and reaches the thighs, [it causes ūrustambha]. // 48 //
When the bones of the thighs are filled internally with stiffened phlegm, it then causes a blockage; consequently, the two thighs become rigid, cold, and insensate. (49)

15.49cd–50ab. Then, because of that [semen], the thighs overflow as if they were those of another person; they become extremely painful and heavy, accompanied by a crushing sensation in the limbs of the body during meditation, numbness, drowsiness, vomiting, loss of appetite, and fever.
Accompanied by difficulty in moving the feet and sitting, as well as numbness, they call that *ūrustambha*; others, however, call it *āḍhyavāta*.

15.51–52. A swelling arising from the vitiation of vāta and blood, accompanied by great pain, occurring between the knees and involving both legs, is known as *kroṣṭuka-śīrṣa* (jackal’s head); it is large and resembles the head of a jackal.
When a swelling as large as a jackal's head arises on the foot due to uneven weight-bearing or from fatigue,
and it occurs because the wind has taken hold of the ankle, that is called Vātakaṇṭaka.
The tendon at the back of the fingers that is afflicted by the wind (vāta) and which causes the upward displacement of the thigh is called gṛdhrasī. // 54 //
Viśvācī and gṛdhrasī are said to be characterized by severe pain in the ankles; likewise, one whose feet become numb as if asleep [suffers from the same]. (55)
When there is intense pain in the ankles, that should be known as *pāda-harṣa* (cramp of the feet), arising from the provocation of *kapha* and *vāta*.
When *vāyu*, accompanied by *pitta* and blood, causes a burning sensation in the two feet, [that is another form]. 15.56b–c.
And specifically, one should diagnose that as a burning of the feet occurring while walking. // 56½ //
15.56 Furthermore, especially for one who is walking about,
food that causes a burning sensation and is incompatible [with the constitution] leads to the vitiation of the blood.
And for those who indulge in sexual intercourse during sleep or wakefulness in a manner devoid of scriptural injunctions. // 1 //
16.1b That corruption of the blood occurs generally among those who are very delicate and habituated to not walking about;
it arises from injury or impurity when the blood of men has become vitiated.
Vata, increased by cold, windy substances, becomes aggravated and moves along an improper path;
obstructed by blood of a similar nature, it first vitiates that very blood. (3)
Obstructed by such blood, it causes āḍhyaroga, khuḍa, vātabalāsa, or vātaśoṇita;
these are the names by which it is known, and it first attacks the feet. (16.3cd–4)

16.4bv – Vāta-śoṇita (blood-wind disorder) is characterized by a redness like that of a Palāśa leaf; it occurs especially from traveling in vehicles, and its symptoms include the hanging down of the limbs, a condition similar to leprosy, as well as exhaustion and looseness of the joints. // 5 //
In the knees, shanks, thighs, hips, shoulders, hands, feet, and the joints of the limbs,
there occur itching, throbbing, piercing pain, splitting pain, heaviness, and numbness.
Having come into being again and again, they perish; and repeatedly they manifest, sometimes at the base of the feet and sometimes even at the hands. (7)
Like the enraged poison of a serpent, it spreads throughout the entire body; first, it arises superficially, taking refuge in the skin and flesh. (8)
Over time, it spreads deeply into all the tissues;
when associated with itching and other symptoms, the skin becomes elevated, copper-colored, and dark reddish-brown.
In the evening, there is intense burning pain; in the deep [seats], the previous pain increases; the swelling is knotted and suppurates; and the Vāyu [afflicts] the joints, bones, and marrow. (10)
Moving with great speed, it wanders within as if cutting through [the body], and by twisting it, it causes lameness or paralysis as it moves everywhere throughout the body. (11)

When there is an excess of Vāta, it moves as if cutting within, and there is excessive piercing pain, throbbing, and pricking; furthermore, there is dryness, blackness, or a dark-brown discoloration of the swelling, along with its fluctuating increase and decrease. (16.11–12)
Contraction of the vessels, fingers, and joints, stiffness of the limbs, and excessive pain;
aversion to cold and lack of relief from it; as well as rigidity, trembling, and numbness [are the symptoms]. (13)

In the blood-type [ulcer], there is swelling, excessive pain, pricking, and a coppery discoloration; it feels as if it is tingling, and it does not subside with either unctuous or dry treatments, being accompanied by itching and discharge. // 14 //
In the case of pitta, there is a burning sensation, confusion, perspiration, fainting, intoxication, thirst, intolerance to touch, pain, redness, swelling, suppuration, and intense heat. (15)
In cases of kapha, there is a sense of stiffness, heaviness, numbness, oiliness, and coldness;
itching and mild pain occur, and when there is a combination [of two or all three doshas], the symptoms of two or all three appear together.

A case following from a single doṣa is curable; one born from two doṣas is palliable; one born from three doṣas should be abandoned, as well as that which is discharging, rigid, or forms tumors (arbuda). 17.

One should abandon that [condition] involving all three doṣas which discharges blood from the channels; for the wind (māruta), having quickly destroyed [the channels] in the branches and joints, settles there, obstructs one another, and takes away the vital breaths with its pains. (16.17c–18)

It quickly destroys the blood-path when the fivefold wind is [disturbed] by dryness, physical exertion, and fasting; or by overeating, injury, travel, the arousal of natural urges, and suppression [of those urges]. (16.18–19)
Aggravated by dryness, physical exercise, and fasting, it brings about impairment of the eyes and other senses,
as well as many diseases such as chronic rhinitis, affliction with thirst, cough, and dyspnea. (16.19–20)

The *udāna* wind, when disturbed by the suppression of sneezing, belching, eructation, vomiting, and sleep, as well as by heavy loads, excessive weeping, loud laughter, and the like, produces diseases. (21)
By suppressing vomiting and sleep,
one may cause constriction of the throat, mental confusion, vomiting, anorexia, chronic rhinitis, goiter,
and various other diseases localized in the region above the clavicles.

The vyāna [vital air], when vitiated by excessive walking, meditation, play, or irregular movements, as well as by opposing factors such as dryness, fear, joy, and despondency, [causes disease]. // 23 //
16.23–24ab. Vyāna [vāyu] causes excessive movement, inability to remain stationary, loss of virility, enthusiasm, and strength, as well as swelling, mental agitation, fever,
diseases of the entire body, piercing pain, horripilation, and numbness of the limbs.

16.24d–25. Due to irregular, undigested, cold, or mixed foods, the *samāna* [vāyu], causing horripilation and numbness of the limbs, produces skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), and other ailments affecting the entire body.

And when vitiated by sleeping or staying awake at improper times and other such factors, it produces diseases arising in the stomach and the colon, such as colic, abdominal tumors, and malabsorption syndrome. (26)
The *apāna* [vāyu] is provoked by dry and heavy food, suppression of natural urges, excessive riding, and the over-indulgence in traveling, sitting, standing, and walking. (27)
16.27b–28. Aggravated by the suppression of natural urges or excessive riding, [the vāyu] produces difficult-to-cure diseases localized in the colon (pakvāśaya),
including many disorders such as defects of urine and semen, hemorrhoids, and prolapse of the rectum.
And all [diseases] caused by the wind (māruta) are characterized by drowsiness, numbness, heaviness, unctuousness, anorexia, lethargy, coldness, swelling, and loss of digestive fire. // 29 //

One should recognize that the āma has been eliminated when there is a desire for pungent and dry things and when such [pungent and dry] palliatives provide relief; this is known by the reversal of symptoms such as drowsiness.
The obstruction of vāyu will now be described in its many varieties.
The symptoms of vāyu obstructed by pitta are burning sensation, thirst, colic pain, giddiness, and darkness before the eyes.
16.31b–c It is described as having many varieties;

burning (vidāha) caused by pungent, hot, sour, and salty [substances], a desire for cold things, coldness, heaviness, and colic are present, and there is greater relief from pungent and similar [remedies]. 16.32ab–c [The symptoms] are more pronounced.
When [the heart] is obstructed by phlegm (kapha), there is a desire for jumping, exertion, dryness, and heat;
when obstructed by blood (rakta), there is intense burning pain located between the skin and the flesh. (33)
There may be passion (rāga), swelling occurs, and circular patches (maṇḍala) arise; furthermore, there is a hard swelling (śopha) due to the flesh, discoloration, and pustules (piṭikā). // 34 //
A sensation of horripilation arises like the movement of ants;
there is a swelling in the limbs that is mobile, glossy, soft, and cold, accompanied by loss of appetite. (35)
The itching of ants and similar insects is to be known as *āḍhyavāta*; it is difficult to cure when covered by fat (*medas*).
When covered by bone (*asthi*), the patient welcomes touch that is extremely hot and pressure.

When the marrow is obstructed, the limb feels as if it were being pierced by a needle; it becomes excessively weary, suffers from piercing pain, bends, yawns, and experiences a sensation of being constricted.
When [the semen] is obstructed by pain, one finds relief by pressing it with both hands;
or else there is excessive force, or it may even be fruitless. (38)
When the wind is obstructed by food, there is colic and pain during digestion; yet there is no lack of results from eating,
and the pain in the abdomen subsides once the food has been digested.
When the bladder is obstructed by urine, there occurs non-emission of urine and distension of the bladder. // 39 //

When the bladder is obstructed by urine, there is retention; when obstructed by feces, there is a cutting pain in its own location (the rectum). The unctuous substance (sneha) quickly undergoes digestion, and the person suffers from abdominal distension after eating. (16.39–40)
When obstructed by feces (viḍ), there is excessive suppression of the urge;
the stool cuts into its own place,
and being pressed down by food, it is expelled with difficulty, dry, and after a long time.
When the wind obstructs all the bodily constituents (dhātus), there is pain in the hips, the groins, and the back. (41)
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is obstructed by bile (pitta), the wind becomes contrary, the heart is distressed, and there is vertigo, fainting, pain, and a burning sensation. (42)

When the *udāna* wind is deranged, there is contrary movement of the breath, physical unwellness, vertigo, fainting, pain, and distension; when food is undigested, there is vomiting, as well as vertigo and other such symptoms.
When the *vyāna* wind is deranged, there is an internal burning sensation, loss of vigor, and a burning sensation that is pervasive throughout the entire body.
In the case of Vyāna, however, there is a burning sensation that spreads throughout the entire body, along with exhaustion, impairment of physical movement, and a sense of heat accompanied by pain.
In the case of Samāna, there is a loss of bodily warmth, excessive perspiration, restlessness, and thirst.

16.44 When the *apāna* wind is obstructed by *mala*, there occurs exhaustion, impairment of limb movement, and a burning sensation; furthermore, the feces become yellowish in color, and there is excessive discharge of *rajas* (menstrual blood) along with a feverish heat in the vagina, penis, and anus.

When the *prāṇa* is obstructed by *śleṣman*, there is an excessive increase of *rajas*, heat, lassitude, drowsiness, loss of appetite, vomiting, spitting, sneezing, eructation, and obstruction of exhalation and inhalation. (16.45–46)
In the udāna [vāyu], there is heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, and suppression of speech and voice;
in the vyāna, there is the destruction of strength and complexion, as well as stiffness in the joints, bones, and speech. (47)
16.47dv–48. When *vyāna* is obstructed, there is pain in the ribs, loss of speech, heaviness in all limbs, and extreme faltering in gait.
When *samāna* is obstructed, the body becomes excessively cold, there is absence of perspiration, and the digestive fire is sluggish.
In the case of the *apāna* [vāyu], there is the discharge of urine and feces along with *kapha*.
Thus, they know the obstruction of *vāyu* to be of twenty-two kinds. (49)
In the case of the *apāna* [vital air], urine mixed with phlegm may be discharged along with feces. Likewise, the *prāṇa* and the other vital airs obstruct one another in their respective order;
one should know that all these constitute twenty types of obstruction (*āvaraṇa*).
When udāna is obstructed by prāṇa, there occurs obstruction of exhalation and inhalation according to their respective functions, as well as catarrh, stiffness of the head,
heart disease, and dryness of the mouth (16.50b–51).
16.51 When the prāṇa is obstructed by udāna, there is heart disease and mouth disease, as well as the depletion of complexion, vitality, and strength.
Following this method, the physician should distinguish all forms of obstruction. 52.
Having observed the locations of the winds, the increase and decrease of their functions, and the mutual mixed obstruction of the five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa; (53)
Through the twelve [factors] beginning with bile (pitta) mixed together, and through those same factors being combined in various ways, there are manifold mixtures of bile and the others. (54)
And due to the variations in degrees of intensity, the obscuration reaches an incalculable state;
one who is attentive should perceive that according to its own specific characteristics as they arise. (55)
And because it gradually and repeatedly withdraws [the breath] even when it is hidden, it is especially called *jīva*; *prāṇa* is said to be life, while *udāna* is said to be strength. (56)
From the oppression of those two, there may be the loss of both lifespan and strength;
or the winds, whether unrecognized or recognized, remain obstructed for a year.
Even with great effort, abscesses, splenic disorders, heart disease, abdominal tumors, loss of digestive fire, and other such ailments may become difficult to cure or incurable. (58)
Calamities befall those [beings] because of the neglect of those who are thus obstructed. // 58 //
In order to eliminate doubt regarding diseases, that wise person who is vigilant toward others must constantly contemplate their etiology. 58½+1.
In the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna):

Because the dosha, residing in the stomach (āmāśaya), destroys the digestive fire (agni) and obstructs the channels (mārga) when accompanied by undigested matter (sāma), it produces fever; therefore, one should perform fasting (laṅghana). //1//
Whether during the premonitory symptoms or at the onset of fever and other ailments, one should protect one's strength with great effort;
for health is founded upon strength, and the sequence of medical treatment is for the sake of health. (2)
1.2dv Regarding the therapeutic procedure for the sake of health:

When the *doṣas* have been diminished by fasting (*laṅghana*), when the digestive fire (*agni*) is kindled, and when lightness has been attained, well-being, hunger, thirst, relish, digestion, strength, and vitality arise. (3)

In that case, when the morbid matter is aggravated to an extreme degree, predominantly composed of phlegm (kapha), and mobile, it is accompanied by nausea, excessive salivation, aversion to food, cough, and choleraic symptoms (viṣūcikā). // 4 //

When fever has arisen immediately after eating, especially when it is accompanied by undigested matter (āmadoṣa), emesis is recommended for one who is fit for emetics; otherwise, one should perform [treatment] differently.
One should administer ghee combined with long pepper (pippalī) for dyspnea, diarrhea, delusion, heart disease, and irregular fever; or with *kaliṅga* fruits and licorice (*madhuka*).
One should drink it with warm water mixed with honey or salt, or else with the decoction of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *karkoṭa*, *vetra*, and *pattrā*. // 7 //
One who understands the distinctions of strength and time should administer emetics using sugarcane juice, wine, or liquors prepared according to the prescribed methods.
Whether emesis has been performed or not, the patient suffering from fever should undergo depleting therapy (viśoṣaṇa) for the purpose of digesting and pacifying the provoked doshas. (9)
When the digestive fire is covered by the *doṣa* as if by ashes, food is not digested;
therefore, one should fast those suffering from fever until the *doṣa* has been digested. (10)
In a fever born of Vāta and Kapha, one who suffers from thirst should drink very small amounts of warm water, like ashes poured upon a fire that is still damp;
this will dissolve the Kapha and quickly alleviate the thirst.
One who is thirsty should drink warm water in small quantities; this kindles the digestive fire, softens the channels, and purifies them,
while promoting the downward movement of stagnant pitta, vāta, sweat, feces, and urine.
Cold [food] removes drowsiness, lethargy, and loss of appetite, and serves as a support for the vital breaths; the opposite of this increases the accumulation of the bodily humors. (13)
Although it possesses such qualities, one should not employ the hot [remedy] in cases of purely bilious disorders;
rather, it is for those with aggravated bile who suffer from burning sensations, feverish heat, delusion, and diarrhea. (14)

In cases arising from poison or alcohol, during the summer season, or for those who are emaciated by ulcers or afflicted with blood-bile (raktapitta), water boiled with thickened paste (ghanasāra), sandalwood, ginger, parpata, and ushira should be administered. // 15 //
Cold water is beneficial for them; it is digestive and removes thirst and fever.
There is no heat without bile (pitta), and there is no fever without heat.

Therefore, one should avoid substances antagonistic to pitta, especially when pitta is predominant; furthermore, one should avoid bathing, oil massage, external applications, and the remaining measures such as fasting. 17.
One should not take medicine during an acute, painful fever accompanied by undigested matter (āma), as if suffering from indigestion, for that would only further increase the state of āma. 18.

For one whose digestive tract is overcome by undigested matter (āmā), milk is like the venom of a snake; likewise for one suffering from urticaria, catarrh, and dyspnea, or from pain in the calves, joints, and bones. (19)
In cases where there is pain in the calves and the bones of the sides caused by vāta and śleṣman, sudation (sveda) is recommended;
it promotes the flow of sweat, urine, feces, and flatus, and produces sharpness of the digestive fire.
One should observe at all times the rules of conduct prescribed for those treated with oleation therapy;
fasting, sudation, time, gruel, and bitter tastes [are also required]. (21)
Barley gruel and bitter tastes serve as digestives for the impurities (malas), either according to the specific condition or in a sequential manner.
Fasting (laṅghana) is indicated for those suffering from pure vāta disorders, wasting (kṣaya), exogenous fevers (āgantujvara), and chronic fevers (jīrṇajvara).
For among those [fevers], that which is beneficial is pacification rather than emaciation;
one should recognize that as "non-drying" (aviśoṣita) by its similarity to the symptoms of *sāmajvara*. (23)
1.23 One should observe the knowledge of the two types of therapeutic measures: that which is palliative (*śamana*) and not depleting (*akarṣaṇa*).
When [the patient] is properly endowed with the signs of having undergone fasting (*laṅghana*), one should treat him with thin gruels (*peyā*).
One should administer [the medicine] from the beginning for six days, starting with the scum (maṇḍa) of one's own specific medicinal preparation, until the fever attains mildness.
His digestive fire blazes up by means of those [drinks], like a purifier with fuel-sticks;
first, one should consume well-cooked *lāja-peyā* (barley gruel) with ginger, coriander, and long pepper. (26)
One who desires sourness should drink that [gruel] with rock salt and pomegranate;
or, one who has passed stool and has excessive bile should drink it cold with ginger and honey. (27)
One suffering from pain in the bladder, the flanks, or the head should drink [a decoction] prepared with vyāghrī and gokṣura, along with pṛśniparṇī, balā, bilva, nāgara, utpala, and dhānyaka. (28)
One suffering from fever and diarrhea should drink a sour *peyā* (gruel), which is digestive and carminative;
one suffering from hiccups, pain, dyspnea, or cough should take it prepared with the small *pañcamūla*.

One afflicted by phlegm with obstructed stools should drink a large decoction prepared with the five roots (pañcamūla) and barley, along with barley, long pepper (pippalī), and emblic myrobalan (āmalaka).
1.30dv A gruel boiled with long pepper (pippalī) and emblic myrobalan (āmalaka), and fried in ghee, facilitates the downward movement of waste products and morbid humors;
[it may also be prepared] with chaba pepper (cavikā), long pepper root (pippalī-mūla), grapes (drākṣā), emblic myrobalan (āmalaka), and ginger (nāgara). // 31 //
When the bowels are obstructed and painful, or when there is cutting pain (parikartika), one should drink a decoction prepared with jujube (kola),
vṛkṣāmla, kalaśī, dhāvanī, and śrīphala.

One who suffers from thirst due to lack of perspiration and sleep should take a decoction prepared with dhāvanī, śrī, and balā; or one afflicted by thirst should take a preparation made with sugar, āmalaka, and nāgara;
or [a preparation] with sugar, badara, mṛdvīkā, śārivā, musta, and candana.

One afflicted by lack of perspiration, sleeplessness, and thirst should take [the remedy] combined with honey. One should prepare drinks consisting of medicinal decoctions, as well as meat broths, vegetable soups, and the like, which destroy thirst, vomiting, burning sensations, and fever.

In intoxication arising from liquor, when the kapha has moved into the seat of pitta in one who is constantly drinking, or when both [pitta and kapha] are predominant in summer, the patient suffers from thirst, vomiting, and burning sensations as accompaniments. (1.34–35)
1.35dv For those afflicted by thirst, vomiting, and burning sensations, and when blood is flowing upwards, they do not desire a gruel (peyā).
Instead, for such cases, one should provide a satiation with parched grain (lāja-tarpaṇa) using fruit juices or water that alleviate fever.
Or one may drink a satiation of parched grain with water, mixed with sugar and honey; then, once that satiation has been digested,
the hungry person should eat either gruel or boiled rice made from fried grains.
Then, once that satiation has been digested, one who is hungry should drink gruel mixed with sugar and honey;
or, when hungry, one may eat boiled rice with gruel, along with soups seasoned with water and salt, or with the broths of mung beans and common quail.
Thus, this six-day period should be observed by one who guards against both strength and the humors.
Then, once the humors have been ripened by fasting and other such measures, a decoction is recommended to either digest the remaining humors or to pacify them. (39)
Bitter [taste] should be employed especially in cases of pitta, and pungent [taste] in cases of kapha;
although astringent [taste] also removes both pitta and kapha, it is not recommended for that purpose. (40)

1.40d–41a. However, a decoction (kaṣāya) is not recommended in acute fever because it causes the stagnation of impurities; furthermore, a decoction may produce irregular fever (viṣama-jvara), as well as anorexia, nausea, hiccups, flatulence, and other such symptoms.
Some say the medicine should be administered after seven days, others after ten; some say it should be given to one who has eaten light food, but not when the *āmadoṣa* is predominant. (42)
And others say that [the fever] occurs after ten days,
because when one is overwhelmed by a severe fever, there is an onset of the force of the *doṣas*; or else,
when the *doṣa* has become excessively accumulated, it produces drowsiness and a sense of stiffness.
Medicine that is not being digested further inflames the fever;
however, when the fever has become mild, the body light, and the impurities have been mobilized, [the medicine will act]. 44.
Even for one who has recently suffered from fever, one should then administer medicine combined with *mustā*, *parpaṭa*, *śuṇṭhī*, or *duḥsparśā*. (45)
One should drink either a decoction or a cold infusion of pāṭhā, uśīra, and vālaka;
and likewise, one should drink [a decoction of] bhūnimba, guḍūcī, musta, and nāgara.
These decoctions, as appropriate, should be administered to digest the humors (doṣas) and to destroy fever, anorexia, thirst, bad taste in the mouth, and indigestion. (47)
Kaliṅgaka, the leaf of paṭola, and kaṭukarohiṇī. // 48ab //
Paṭola, śārivā, mustā, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, and rohiṇī;
paṭola, nimba, triphalā, mṛdvīkā, mustā, and vatsaka. // 49 //
Kirātatikta, amṛtā, candana, and viśvabheṣaja;
dhātrī, mustā, amṛtā, and kṣaudra—these are the formulations completed by half-verses. (50)
These five are considered the pacifiers for the five [types of] fevers beginning with *saṃtata*; in fever born of *vāta*, *durālabhā*, *amṛtā*, *mustā*, and *nāgara* are used. (51)
Alternatively, long pepper root, guduchi, ginger, and the minor pentad of roots (kanīya-pañcamūla) [are used]; and in cases of pitta, śakrayava and musta [are used]. 52.

In cases of pitta, [the drugs] combined with honey and kaṭukā are used; likewise, mustā and parpaṭaka with honey, as well as dhanvayāsa and bhūnimba; and the vatsakādi group is used in cases of kapha.
Alternatively, kaliṅga, musta, and kaṭukā— or else vṛṣa, gāṅgeyī, śṛṅgavera, and durālabhā—
act as digestive stimulants and carminatives for conditions associated with pain, constipation, wind, and phlegm.
Abhayā, pippalīmūla, śamyāka, kaṭukā, and ghana;
drākṣā, madhūka, madhuka, lodhra, kāśmarya, and sārivā. // 55 //
Mustā, āmalaka, hrīvera, padmakeśara, padmaka, mṛṇāla, candana, uśīra, nīlotpala, and parūṣaka. // 56 //
A decoction or a cold infusion of grapes and other such ingredients, scented with jasmine flowers and combined with honey, sugar, and parched grain, conquers diseases born of wind and bile. (57)
It cures fever, alcoholism, vomiting, fainting, burning sensations, exhaustion, vertigo, upward-moving hemorrhaging (raktapitta), thirst, and jaundice as well. (58)

One should cook *kaṭukā* after grinding it in a clean, new earthenware pot; its juice, squeezed out and mixed with ghee, overcomes fever and burning sensations caused by intoxication (*madātyaya*) and vomiting. (1.58–59)
In cases of Kapha-Vāta, a decoction of Vacā, Tiktā, Pāṭhā, Āragvadha, and Vatsaka,
combined with the powder of Pippalī, or a decoction of Chinnodbhava (Guḍūcī) is recommended.
A decoction of vyāghrī, śuṇṭhī, and amṛtā, combined with the powder of pippalī, conquers fever caused by vāta and śleṣman, as well as dyspnea, cough, coryza, and colic. (61)
Pathyā, kustumburī, mustā, śuṇṭhī, kaṭtṛṇa, parpaṭa, along with kaṭphala, vacā, bhārgī, devāhva, honey, and hiṅgu. (62)
It subdues disorders of phlegm and wind, fever, spitting, pain in the abdomen, heart, and flanks, as well as diseases of the throat, swelling of the mouth, cough, and dyspnea. (63)
In fever caused by *kapha* and *vāta*, the *āragvadhādi* group taken with honey overcomes fever characterized by *kapha* and *pitta*.
Likewise, *tiktā*, *vṛṣa*, *uśīra*, *trāyantī*, *triphalā*, and *amṛtā* [have this effect]. (1.63–64)
Paṭola, ativiṣā, nimba, mūrvā, and dhanvayavāsaka;
for fever caused by the combination of all three doṣas (saṃnipātajvara), [one should use] vyāghrī, devadāru, niśā, and ghana.
Patola leaves, nimba bark, triphalā, kaṭukā, ginger, puṣkaramūla, guḍūcī, and kaṇṭakārikā; // 66 //
In a fever characterized by excessive wind and phlegm, accompanied by cough, dyspnea, and pain in the sides, [one should administer] Madhūka flowers, Mṛdvīkā, Trāyamāṇā, and Parūṣaka. (67)
One should prepare a cooling decoction of uśīra, tiktā, triphalā, and kāśmarya;
by drinking this at the proper time, one dispels all fevers. (68)
It dispels all fevers:
*jāti*, *āmalaka*, and *mustā*, as well as *dhanvayavāsaka*;
for one with constipated stools, *kaṭukā*, *drākṣā*, *trāyantī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and jaggery [are used]. 1.68–69.
When the medicine has been digested, one who has excess phlegm (śleṣman) should consume food such as thin gruel (peyā), but not with treacle (guḍa) mixed with trāyantī and triphalā;
for gruel increases kapha, just as rain increases mud among the dust.

Therefore, even before that, for those whose bodies are afflicted by an excess of phlegm, one should administer light soups prepared with horse gram (*kulattha*), chickpeas (*caṇaka*), peas (*kalāya*), and similar pulses. (71)

For those whose bodies are characterized by the accumulation or the movement of phlegm, aged *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice— dried, endowed with a bitter taste, pleasing to the heart, appetizing, and sharp— are beneficial in fever. (72)

In cases where phlegm predominates, barley grains from which the husks have been removed and made into groats should be used; rice cooked with them, strained twice or thrice, should be administered as appropriate.

Soups prepared with light ingredients such as mung beans or horse gram (kulattha), and cooked with decoctions that alleviate fever according to the strength of the doshas and dushyas, destroy fever. (74)
With *kāravellaka*, *karkoṭa*, young radish, and *parpaṭa*; with eggplant, nimba flowers, *paṭola* fruit, and shoots. // 75 //
Broths made from extremely tender meat of wild animals are beneficial,
as are those prepared with vyāghrī, parūṣa, tarkārī, grapes, āmalaka, and pomegranate.
They may be prepared with black pepper, ginger, coriander, cumin, and rock salt;
generally, they are combined with sugar and honey, whether processed or unprocessed.
One should also employ appetizing side dishes prepared with non-sour buttermilk, which are clear and stimulate the digestive fire, even as a post-drink (anupāna). 78.

At the end of the day, one should feed the patient— whether suffering from fever or recently recovered from it— a light meal along with boiled water cooled down, or wine, according to what is suitable for them.
Then, the digestive fire (analas), strengthened by the depletion of phlegm (śleṣma) and increased heat (ūṣman), becomes powerful;
this occurs either at the appropriate time or in accordance with the suitability of the region (deśa-sātmya). // 80 //
Previously, when one with a weak digestive fire eats, one is not afflicted by indigestion;
for ten days, one should fast while consuming astringent decoctions and wholesome food. (81)
One should administer ghee when kapha is diminished and vāta and pitta predominate in the fever;
it is like nectar when the doshas have ripened, but otherwise it is like poison. (82)

Even if ten days have passed, if there is an increase in the complications of fever, one should employ the sequence of treatments beginning with fasting (laṅghana) until the depletion of phlegm (kapha). 83.
Furthermore, because the body's tissues and strength have been depleted, the chronic fever persists;
for the heat that causes fever is parched, and it belongs to one who has already been parched by that very heat. (84)
Through emesis, sudation, cold water, decoctions, and light meals, that bodily constituent (dhātu) which is exceedingly strong, mobile, and constantly moving [is subdued]. (85)
Clarified butter is the pacifier for that [fever], like water for a burning house;
it is the foremost among those that conquer Vāta and Pitta, provided it is prepared according to the proper processing.
One should follow the specific treatment even more closely, for it should be administered as prepared with the appropriate medicinal drugs;
thus, by means of coldness, it overcomes the feverish heat and the bile which are of the opposite nature. // 87 //
Ghee, when prepared with appropriate medicinal processing, pacifies Vāta through its oily quality and Kapha through its astringent quality;
all the aforementioned decoctions should be used with ghee according to the specific Dosha involved. 88.
A decoction of triphalā, the bark of picumanda, madhuka, the two types of bṛhatī, and the leaf of masūra, combined with ghee, cures fever and cough. (89)
With pippalī, indrayava, dhāvani, tiktā, śārivā, āmalaka, and tāmalakī; with bilva, musta, hima, pālani, sevya, drākṣā, ativiṣā, and sthirā. // 90 //
Ghee prepared with these [herbs] quickly destroys fever, irregular digestion, halīmaka, loss of appetite, intense heat in the shoulders, vomiting, pain in the sides and head, and consumption. (91)
In the case of a fever born of Vāta, one should employ the Tailvaka ghee— devoid of Trivṛt— for severe and irregular fevers as well as Halīmaka.
For Pittaja fever, one should use Tiktaka ghee, Vṛṣa ghee, or the clarified butter cooked with Pālanikā.

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *pala* each of viḍaṅga, sauvarcala salt, cavya, pāṭhā, vyoṣa, agni (citraka), rock salt, and yavaśūka, along with an equal amount of milk; this destroys chronic fever caused by kapha. (93)
1.93c–d. Ghṛta prepared with one part each of the juice and paste of guḍūcī, or of triphalā, or of vṛṣa, or of mṛdvīkā, or of balā, along with an equal amount of milk, are curative of fever. 94.
When the ghee has been digested, one should eat soft rice with meat broth; for that is sufficient to remove the humors, is highly strengthening, and bestows great strength. (95)
1.95bv–96. Foods consisting of soft meat and juices, as well as juices derived from mudga, kāravella, and similar substances, generally pacify kapha and pitta;
therefore, they are usually not beneficial when fever is chronic or when vāta is predominant.
If, despite this, the fever is not pacified—causing piercing pain, upward movement of wind, constipation, and aggravating the fever—one should perform purification therapy (śodhana). // 97 //

For one who is fit for purification, one should administer emesis as previously described, when the morbid humor (doṣa) has reached the stomach (āmāśaya), while preserving the strength of a strong patient. (98)
When the morbid humors (doṣas) have been ripened and become softened, or in cases of fever caused by poison or alcohol,
one should administer a bolus (modaka) composed of triphalā, śyāmā, trivṛt, pippalī, and keśara.
One should administer a purgative such as *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) along with sugar and honey; or likewise, the juice of *drākṣā* and *dhātrī*, or *harītakī* together with *drākṣā*.
Or one should lick the powder of the three sweets (traivṛta) combined with honey and clarified butter.
A person suffering from fever should drink either *āragvadha* with milk or with the juice of *mṛdvīkā*, or *triphalā* or *trāyamāṇā* with milk. (101)
For those who have been purged, a restorative diet beginning with thin gruel (*maṇḍa*) should be administered in the proper sequence;
furthermore, one should always allow the morbid humor (*mala*), when agitated by fever and about to be expelled, to pass naturally. 102.

For even a matured disorder, having established its seat in the digestive tract, may undergo transformation; or, if it flows excessively, it may lead to a state of depletion while being processed. (103)
The complications arising from the retention of *āma* and the treatment for those complications have been described;
yet, he who out of delusion administers purgatives to remove the *doṣas* during *āmajvara* [commits an error]. (104)
Because it involves the accumulation of undigested matter (āma), this is declared to be the management of the humors (doṣas).
One might as well touch a black snake while it is dormant with the tip of one's hand;
likewise, emesis or purgation is not beneficial for one who is emaciated by fever.
However, for one accustomed to milk, whose phlegm has been diminished, and who suffers from burning sensations, thirst, and wind, one may remove the impurities with milk or with decoctions. 106.
Although milk is wholesome even for one suffering from bile and wind, or for one with diarrhea,
it is like a forest scorched by fire for a body already heated by fasting.
Divine water (divyāmbu) restores life and quickly subdues his fever; whether it is prepared cold or warm, or even simply "warm from the stream" (dhāroṣṇa), it serves this purpose. // 108 //
In the same way, one should administer milk that is merely warm after dividing it at the appropriate time; otherwise, it kills the patient suffering from fever.
[Milk] with ginger, dates, raisins, sugar, and ghee—109.
Boiled and cooled, mixed with honey, it destroys thirst, burning sensations, and fever;
likewise [is the decoction] made from grapes, balā, yaṣṭīmadhu, śārivā, pippalī, and sandalwood. (110)

One should drink [the decoction] boiled with water four times the quantity of the drug, or with long pepper (pippalī), for the sake of cough, dyspnea, headache, pain in the flanks, and chronic fever. (111)
One suffering from fever is liberated from it by drinking milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), or with the root of the castor plant (eraṇḍa), or with young bilva fruit. 112.
Or, having drunk milk that is warm from the cow, for one whose flatus and feces are obstructed, who suffers from bloody and slimy diarrhea accompanied by thirst, colic, and tenesmus; (113)
Milk prepared with dried ginger, balā, vyāghrī, gokaṇṭaka, and jaggery is an effective remedy that conquers swelling, urinary retention, constipation, fever, and cough. (114)
Milk prepared with *vṛścīva*, *bilva*, and *varṣābhū* removes fever and swelling; likewise, milk boiled with the heartwood of *śiṃśipā* quickly dispels fever. 115.
Alternatively, a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) prepared with the heartwood of *śiṃśipā*,
when administered when the doshas have matured and reached the colon, quickly restores strength, digestive fire, freedom from fever, joy, and appetite.
The laxative enema (sraṃsana-vasti) removes pitta or kapha-pitta located in the colon (pakvāśaya), as well as all three types of morbid humors (malas) residing in the colon. 117.

One should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) to a patient whose kapha and pitta have been depleted, who suffers from stiffness in the sacrum, back, and waist, who has a stimulated digestive fire, and whose stool is bound, provided the enema is applied to the colon (pakvāśaya). 1.117–118.
With *paṭola*, *nimba* leaves, *kaṭukā*, and *caturaṅgula*;
with *sthirā*, *balā*, *gokṣuraka*, *madana*, *uśīra*, and *vālaka*. (119)
One should prepare a decoction by boiling milk with half its quantity of water until only the milk remains,
and then mix it with the paste (kalka) of musta, madana, kṛṣṇā, madhuka, and vatsaka.
One should administer an enema with honey and ghee to destroy fever, using the four *parṇinīs*, liquorice, *phala*, *uśīra*, and *nṛpadruma*. (121)
One should boil and form a paste of licorice (yaṣṭī), dill (śatāhvā), phalinī fruit, and musta;
this enema, combined with jaggery, honey, and ghee, is a destroyer of fever.
Jīvantī, madana, medā, pippalī, madhuka, vacā, ṛddhi, rāsnā, balā, bilva, śatapuṣpā, and śatāvarī; (123)

Having ground [the drugs] together with milk, water, ghee, and oil, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) for fever, according to the nature of the unctuous substance and the state of the patient's humors. 124.
In fever, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana), providing oil according to the nature of the impurity, the specific humor (doṣa), and the patient's strength; furthermore,
those enemas that destroy fever which will be described in the Siddhisthāna [should be used].
It removes headache and heaviness, subdues phlegm, and awakens the senses. // 125 //
In chronic fever, one should administer nasal medication (nasya) that stimulates appetite or a purgative;
for one with an empty head, an oleaginous treatment is given, and for those suffering from burning sensations, a pitta-alleviating remedy is prescribed.
One should prepare medicinal smokes, gargles, and mouthfuls according to the specific dosha to alleviate diseases of the nose, mouth, loss of taste, head, and throat. (127)
If there is a lack of relish, one should hold in the mouth the filaments of a citron with ghee and rock salt, or a paste of emblic myrobalan, grapes, and sugar. (128)
Just as one employs tactile applications consisting of cold or hot substances—such as massages, ointments, and affusions—when fever has subsided and is localized in the skin. (129)
One should likewise apply collyriums and medicinal smokes even in cases of exogenous (āgantuja) [inflammation];
in the event of burning pain, one should perform an oil massage with ghee that has been washed a thousand times.

And with those various groups mentioned in the Sūtras—such as sweet, sour, and astringent substances; or with Dūrvā and others that subdue Pitta, as declared in the group of purificatory (śodhana) and other remedies. // 131 //

One should cook oil with milk using [drugs] that are cooling in potency and cold to the touch, prepared as a decoction and paste; when used for massage, it immediately alleviates burning sensations and fever. (132)
One should apply a plaster of those same [herbs], not ground too finely, to the head and limbs;
one should also employ affusion and immersion with their decoction. (133)
Likewise, with water from an Arana tree, milk, sour gruel, clarified butter, and so forth;
and with wood-apple, citron, sour vidārī, lodhra, and pomegranate. (134)
When the body is smeared with the foam produced from *badarī* leaves or from *ariṣṭaka*, burning sensations, pain, delusion, vomiting, and thirst are pacified. (135)
Whether by means of the foam of *ariṣṭaka* or the foam produced from *ariṣṭa*, that regimen for subduing the *doṣas* which was described as removing *pitta*—
for one who practices that, the fever accompanied by burning sensation is quickly destroyed. (1.136)
With the heat of vigorous substances, with hot tactile sensations, and with tagara, agallochum, and saffron;
with kuṣṭha, sthauṇeya, śaileya, sarala, and amaradāru. // 137 //
With *nakha*, *rāsnā*, *pura*, *vacā*, the two types of *caṇḍailā*, *coraka*, *pṛthvīkā*, *śigru*, *surasā*, *hiṃsrā*, *dhyāmaka*, and *sarṣapa* [one should prepare the oil]. (138)
1.138 With *nakha*, *rāsnā*, *mukhavacā*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *amṛta*, the two types of *eraṇḍa*, *pattūra*, and *rohiṣa*;
with *tamālapattra*, *bhūtīka*, *śallakī*, *dhānyaka*, and *dīpyaka*— 1.139 [With these]... [the oil should be prepared].

1.139–140. One should cook oil for cold-fever (śītajvara) with *tamālapattra*, *pūtīka*, *miśī*, black gram (*māṣa*), horse gram (*kulattha*), *agni*, *prakīryā*, the two types of *nākulī*, and other substances of a similar nature.

One should massage with these substances—boiled, made into a paste, and combined with wine, sour gruel, and so forth—and when well-ground, one should apply them as a thick ointment while they are comfortably warm. (141)
Having anointed [the patient] with that [oil] while it is comfortably warm,
one should administer affusion (parīṣeka) and immersion (avagāha) with those same decoctions while they are lukewarm; or likewise, with only vinegar, cow's urine, and whey.
One should employ the group of drugs beginning with *āragvadha* for drinking, massage, and external application;
and those incenses derived from *aguru* which will be described [later] for irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*). (143)
Incenses produced from *aguru*, as well as sudations performed with or without fire, sudorific medicines, and foods;
the womb, the earth, houses, and beds; and rugs, blankets, and *rallaka* woolens.
Laughing with smokeless, glowing embers, they [serve] wine mixed with the three pungents, buttermilk, horse gram, rice, and kodrava grain. (145)
One who suffers from trembling and other bilious conditions should cultivate the company of beloved women, endowed with full breasts, voluptuous, and adorned with amorous grace. 146.
Afflicted by cold, he should partake [of wine] according to reason, and women intoxicated by youth-elixirs should embrace him;
and perceiving that the cold has departed, he should then have them removed once more.

1.147 Once the fever has subsided, one should conquer the humors of equal strength either by increasing that which is deficient, by suppressing that which is elevated, or by following the sequence of the seats of *kapha*. 148.
In cases of combined fevers (*samavāyi-jvara*), one should first pacify the *pitta* that has been aggravated by fasting;
for that [pitta] is indeed more difficult to restrain, especially in those afflicted by fever.
However, vomiting, fainting, thirst, and so forth, which are not incompatible with fever, [should be treated]. 148+2ab.
At the end of a fever caused by the combination of all three humors, a most terrible swelling arises at the root of the ear, by which only a rare few are liberated.
By that [cause], swelling arises; only some are liberated from it.

One should conquer it quickly by bloodletting and by drinking ghee, as well as with external applications (pradeha) that subdue kapha and pitta, and with nasal drops (nāvana) and gargles (kavaḍagraha). // 150 //

If a fever, which spreads through the limbs and does not subside despite the application of plasters that pacify *kapha* and *vāta*, or through treatments that are cold, hot, unctuous, or dry, one should quickly venesect the veins in the arms in successive order. 1.151.

This very same procedure should be applied to the discordant [fevers] as well, according to the circumstances; having distinguished the fever as being due to Vāta and the other [humors], that which is stated immediately thereafter [should be followed]. 152.

And for irregular fevers (viṣamajvara), decoctions prepared from paṭola, kaṭukā, mustā, prāṇadā, and madhuka— taken in combinations of three, four, or five ingredients as appropriate— are destroyers of irregular fever. (1.152b–153)
One should administer Triphalā, Pathyā, Guḍūcī, and Pippalī separately; or likewise, one may take Bhallātaka with jaggery according to various prescribed methods. (154)

On the day the fever first arrives, one should employ either fasting or nourishing therapy; or else, garlic with oil, or likewise clarified butter, should be taken in the morning before the meal. (155)
1.155ab Either lightening therapy (laṅghana) or nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa), as well as [medicines] for the digestion of that [poison], curd, milk, buttermilk, and the six-pala ghee;
the Kalyāṇaka, Pañcagavya, Tikta-nāma, and that prepared with Vṛṣa. 156.

Ghee boiled with the decoction of triphalā, kola, and tarkārī, along with curd, and with the addition of the bark of tilvaka as a post-decoction ingredient, is supreme for conquering irregular fevers (viṣama-jvara). 157.

One should not consume, to one's heart's content, liquor, strong spirits, and intoxicants derived from peacock, partridge, or cock, nor meat that is fatty and hot in potency, together with food. (158)
Having consumed the meat of peacock, partridge, or cock— which is of moderate and hot potency— one should sleep on that very day, or else one should purge.
Or, having drunk a large dose of ghee, one should induce vomiting again.
When a fever is about to arrive, one who has been prepared with oleation and sudation should drink nīlinī, ajagandhā, trivṛtā, and kaṭurohiṇī. (160)
Realgar, rock salt, and long pepper should be used as an ointment for the eyes with oil;
likewise, a nasal medication (nasya) consisting of asafoetida, equal parts of *vyāghrī* fat, and rock salt should be employed. 161.
Old ghee, lion fat, and likewise rock salt;
*palankaṣā*, neem leaves, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *harītakī*. (162)
Mustard seeds with barley, clarified butter, or cat-feces incense; or [incense made] from *pura*, soot, *vacā*, *sarja*, nimba, arka, aguru, and *dāru*. (163)
This invincible incense should be employed in all cases of fever; as well as the incense, nasal drops, collyrium, and frightening [therapies] that have been prescribed for mental derangement. (164)
The *aparājita* [mixture] should be employed; fumigation, nasal drops, collyrium, and frightening [the patient], as well as medicine based on divine power, dispel all fevers.
They especially remove irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*), for those are generally born from the persistence of exogenous factors (*āgantvanubandha*).

In cases of irregular fever (viṣamajvara) that does not subside, one should pierce the appropriate vein; likewise in cases of fever caused by spreading erysipelas (vīsarpa), boils (visphoṭa), or trauma, when they are purely of the nature of wind (kevalānila).
In cases of unsubsided irregular fever (viṣama-jvara) or fever accompanied by eruptive boils (visphoṭa),
one should administer the drinking of ghee, cold applications, affusions, and the consumption of meat broth; furthermore,
one should perform the appropriate therapeutic measures such as bloodletting, as previously described.

In cases arising from seizure spirits (graha), one should employ the drinking of ghee, cold applications and sprinklings, the consumption of meat broth, and the treatments prescribed in the science of exorcism (bhūtavidyā), such as offerings and mantras.
In cases born of medicinal herbs or fragrances, one should apply pitta-alleviating measures; in cases of poison, one should use anti-toxic remedies.

One should conquer fever born of anger and other emotions by means of medicinal fragrances, agreeable and pleasing objects, the pacification of the specific doshas, and the discernment between what is beneficial and what is harmful. (1.168–169)
That which arises from anger is pacified by desire, and that which arises from desire by anger; those born of fear and grief are likewise pacified by the opposite of fear and grief.
The treatment for fevers arising from curses or Atharvaṇa mantras is reliance on divine means;
those fevers first manifest alone and are subsequently pervaded by the humors (malas).
Therefore, one should prescribe food and other treatments for them according to the specific doshas;
for fever does not persist when it is produced without the involvement of vāta and the other humors. (172)
One should remove his memory of the time of the fever by means of captivating sense-objects;
a mind that is pure and moistened with compassion destroys all fevers. (173)
This brings liberation from all fevers.
Until strength is regained, one should avoid physical exercise, bathing, sexual intercourse, heavy, unwholesome, or burning foods, and whatever else is a cause of fever. (1.174)
Likewise, even one who is free from fever should not suddenly consume all kinds of food;
for a fever that has recently subsided can quickly kill a weak person. (175)

1.175b At that time, he may eat all kinds of food; 1.175c for once the fever has subsided, it quickly becomes life-threatening. Therefore, in that specific case, the physician should especially apply the appropriate medical treatment for each respective stage. 176.
One should apply the respective medical treatments, medicinal herbs, gems, and effective mantras; the worship of virtuous teachers, Brahmins, and deities;
and objects that bring pleasure to the mind—even these can destroy a severe fever caused by Viṣṇu.
Medicinal herbs, gems, and effective mantras [are the means]. In the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna):
An upward-moving [dosha] that is strong, without complication, associated with a single dosha, and recent [is easily cured].
One should treat rakta-pitta when it is free from complications and during a favorable season. // 1 //
One should cause the blood that flows downward, as well as that which follows the two [other] humors, to be expelled;
for even when pacified again and again, it may become aggravated and move from one channel to another. (2)
One should avoid administering [purgatives] to those with excessively active digestion, those with weak digestive fire, those with all three doṣas aggravated, or those on the two paths;
having understood the etiology, the course, the impurities, the strength of the doshas, and the patient's own strength. // 3 //

In cases of raktapitta, one should apply lightening therapy (laṅghana), nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa), purification (śodhana), or pacification (śamana) at the outset, according to the specific condition of the place, time, and other factors. // 4 //

2.4cv Regarding depletion (laṅghana) and nourishment (bṛṃhaṇa): first, one should treat a strong patient with abundant morbid humors (doṣa) who has developed [disease] from over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa). That which has moved upward should be treated with purgation, while that which has gone downward should be treated with emesis. // 5 //

2.5dv By means of emesis, [the doshas] move downward; by pacifying and nourishing therapies, as well as by considering those requiring lightening or nourishing treatments, [they are managed]. When [the doshas] have moved upward, bitter and astringent tastes serve as pacifiers. (6)
2.6bv Regarding those requiring lightening therapy and those requiring nourishing therapy, fasting is prescribed for one who drinks water prepared with *ṣaḍ-aṅga* [herbs] minus *śuṇṭhī*.
However, in cases of downward-moving (*adho-ga*) *rakta-pitta*, a sweet taste that is nourishing is indicated. // 7 //
If the disorder moves upward, a satiation therapy (tarpaṇa) should be employed; if it has moved downward, thin gruel (peyā) should be drunk first.
For one who is eating and possesses strength, an impure [dosha] should not be retained, for that indeed causes disease.

2.8bv When [the doshas] have moved downward, gruel (peyā) should be given first; 2.8bv or, when there is downward movement, gruel should be given beforehand. Otherwise, it would quickly act like fire and cause rapid [harm].
[This should be taken] with the decoction and paste of *trivṛt* and *śyāmāka*, along with sugar.
It causes seizing of the throat, putrid nasal discharge, fainting, loss of appetite, fever, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, constipation, vitiligo, and difficulty in urination. (9.1+1)
If it is constricted from the beginning, it may cause leprosy, hemorrhoids, erysipelas, loss of complexion, fistula-in-ano, and impairment of the intellect and the sense organs. (9.1+2)
One should prepare the electuary according to the prescribed method and then lick it from the palm of the hand;
it consists of trivṛtā, triphalā, śyāmā, pippalī, sugar, and honey. (10)
This modaka cures disorders of the humors combined (saṃnipāta), upward hemorrhaging, swelling, and fever.
Similarly, trivṛt mixed with an equal amount of sugar and one-quarter part of pippalī has the same effect.
2.11bv–12. Emesis combined with fruits cures raktapitta, fever, and thirst;
likewise, a nourishing drink (tarpaṇa) with sugar and honey, or water with sugar, or water infused with madhuka mixed with honey [is effective].

Whether it be milk or the juice of sugarcane, the internal regimen for the pure [element] consists of appropriate churned drinks, gruels, and so forth, to be employed while protecting the vital strength. (13)
A churned drink (mantha) prepared with grapes and other Pitta-alleviating fruits as prescribed for fever, or with honey, dates, raisins, parūṣaka, and sugar-water, [is beneficial]. // 14 //
Or a churned drink (mantha) made with the five essences, parched rice flour mixed with ghee, and sour with pomegranate and āmalaka, is for those with weak digestion who desire sourness. (15)
2.15dv For those with weak digestion who crave sour things,
[the following are recommended]: the filaments of the lotus and water-lily, *pṛśniparṇī*, *priyaṅgukā*,
*uśīra*, *śabara*, *lodhra*, *śṛṅgavera*, and red sandalwood.
Hrīvera, dhātakī flowers, the pulp of bilva, and durālabhā—these are prescribed in descending half-doses; those formulated in quarter-doses will now be described. (17)
2.17cv Peys prepared with half-verses (ardharca): 2.17cv Peys prepared with half-halves (ardhārdha):
bhūnimba, sevya, jalada, masūra, and also pṛśniparṇī;
vidārigandhā, mudga, balā, ghee, and hareṇukā. // 18 //
2.18dv One should prepare balā-ghee, priyaṅgukā, and the meats of wild animals that are cold in potency;
having boiled each of these separately in water, one should prepare gruel (yavāgū) using their respective decoctions.
Likewise, meat broths should be served cold with sugar and honey;
they may be slightly sour or unsour, and should be fried in ghee and mixed with sugar.

Grains produced from the *śūka* and *śimbī* pods are recommended as vegetables when blood is [disordered]; that which was described as light and cooling is intended for the proper understanding of the nature of food itself. (21)
The previously mentioned water may be boiled with the five roots (pañcamūla), or it may be boiled with the light [pañcamūla] and then cooled, or it may be honey-water, or fruit-water. // 22 //
A rabbit with vāstuka is recommended for constipation;
furthermore, a partridge prepared with a decoction of udumbara is beneficial when wind (vāta) is predominant.
One should avoid the fruit of the Plakṣa tree as much as that of the Barhiṇa, and the fruit of the Nyagrodha tree like that of the Kukkuṭa;
furthermore, one should avoid whatever constitutes the etiological factors for raktapitta. (24)
Phalinī, earth, lodhra, añjana, and mākṣika, drunk with the juice of vāsā, pacify pitta and blood; or likewise, the exudate of vāṭarūṣaka. (25)
Vṛṣa, whether combined with sugar and honey, or taken alone, or even boiled, immediately conquers hemorrhage; for it is indeed its supreme medicine.
Paṭola, mālatī, nimba, the two types of candana, padmaka, lodhra, vṛṣa, taṇḍulīya, kṛṣṇā, clay, and madayantikā. // 27 //
2.27 Three decoctions—of *paṭola*, *āmalakī*, and *nimba*; of *śatāvarī*, *gopakanyā*, and the two *kākolyau*; and of *madhuyaṣṭikā*—taken with honey and sugar, remove *rakta-pitta*.
Alternatively, one should drink a well-cooled decoction of *palāśa* bark mixed with sugar, or lick the juice of cow and horse dung with honey and clarified butter. (29)
Or one should drink [the powder] with honey and ghee;
when the blood is clotted, one should lick the excrement of a pigeon mixed with honey.
And one whose blood has flowed excessively should drink blood with honey.
2.30b–c One should lick the dung of a pigeon;
2.30c–d or one whose blood has been excessively discharged should eat the raw liver of a wild animal mixed with bile.
With sandalwood, uśīra, water-lily, parched grain, mung beans, long pepper, and barley. // 31 //
A decoction made from bala leaves soaked overnight in water destroys raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
A clear infusion produced by heating a clod of earth in water containing sandalwood, lotuses, and usira root is likewise beneficial.
Very cold and mixed with sugar and honey, it overcomes excessive hemorrhaging;
or, having crushed stalks of sugarcane, one should soak them in a new jar. (33)
That [nectar] remained hidden in the sky; the water that flowed forth at dawn was as sweet as honey, and it possessed the quality of being used as a crest-ornament by blooming lotuses.
And one should also employ those decoctions which have been prescribed for bile-fever (pitta-jvara);
when the digestive fire has been kindled and the phlegm (kapha) has been conquered by these various decoctions.
If the rakta-pitta is not pacified, then in a case where vāta is predominant, one should administer boiled goat's milk; likewise, cow's milk boiled in five times its quantity of water may be used.
Or [a decoction] boiled with the five roots in their light form, mixed with sugar and honey, along with jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, drākṣā, balā, gokṣura, and nāgara. (37)
Milk boiled separately with each [of these], or with ghee and sugar; likewise, milk boiled with gokantaka, abhīru, and the parṇinīs.

It quickly destroys blood accompanied by pain, especially when it is located in the urinary tract; however, it is particularly beneficial when located in the anal tract when combined with the juice of the *moca* plant. (39)
One should also prescribe here the treatment for blood dysentery and hemorrhoids using banyan tree shoots or sprouts, as well as ginger, Udīcya, and blue lotus.
Having drunk decoctions made from the shoots of the *vaṭa* tree or from *śṛṅga*, one should eat with milk;
or one should have [the patient] drink ghee cooked with these same decoction-formulations along with milk.
Having boiled a bull, crushed together with its head and roots, in eight times the amount of water until one-eighth remains, one should cook ghee with that decoction.

That [milk], containing the flowers of that [plant], cooled and mixed with honey, [cures] bile-blood disorders, bile-born abdominal tumors (gulma), fever, asthma, cough, heart disease, and jaundice. // 43 //
One should cook ghee with the juice of the Palāśa stalks and its inner pulp; this destroys cataracts (timira), vertigo (bhrama), erysipelas (vīsarpa), and hoarseness of voice (svarasāda). // 44 //
That [milk] mixed with honey is a destroyer of blood; likewise, when combined with *trāyamāṇā*, it is used for blood that is slimy, phlegmy, and knotted within the passage of the throat. (45)
One should lick the alkali produced from lotus stalks with honey and ghee;
likewise, one should separately lick those produced from lotus pollen, śyāmā, and madhūka flowers.
In the case of hemorrhage specifically from the anus, an enema is desired;
