when blood flows from the nose, once it has been purified, one should administer nasal drops and irrigation.
The previously mentioned decoction formulations, saturated with the juices of milk, sugarcane, and so forth;
milk and other liquids mixed with sugar; water alone; or plain water—these are beneficial. (48)

2.48b–c: One should prepare a juice from pomegranate flowers, mango stones, or green grass, saturated with milk, sugarcane juice, and so forth; one should also employ the group of cooling substances (śītavarga) in applications such as poultices and ointments. 49.
A very fine paste made from mango stone, green grass, and black gram flour fried in ghee, along with *śiva* (asafoetida),
when applied as an ointment to the head, stops nasal bleeding without a doubt.

Whatever medicine has been prescribed for both internal and external use in bilious fever (pitta-jvara) is beneficial in blood-bile (rakta-pitta), as well as whatever is beneficial in cases of wasting due to injury (kṣata-kṣīṇa). 50.
In the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna),
one should first treat cough caused solely by Vāta with unctuous substances, such as gruels (peyā),
soups (yūṣa), meat broths (rasa), and the like, prepared with Vāta-alleviating drugs and made unctuous. // 1 //

One should treat obstructed feces and flatus with linctuses, fumigations, as well as massages, sudation, affusions, and immersions; if pitta is also present, one should treat it with enemas and post-prandial [medicinal] meals. // 2 //

One should conquer [fever] associated with pitta by means of ghees taken before meals, and that associated with kapha by means of ghee-enemas and milk-purgatives. [This is done] in a decoction made from thirty palas each of guḍūcī and kaṇṭakārī.
One *prastha* of this preparation, when cooked with ghee, cures vāta-type cough and stimulates the digestive fire,
containing *kṣāra*, *rāsnā*, *vacā*, *hiṅgu*, *pāṭhā*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, and *dhānyaka*.

One should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter with two *śāṇas* each of the five spices (*pañcakola*) in a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*); this should be drunk while following the regimen of taking gruel as an after-drink.
It cures cough, dyspnea, cardiac and flank pain, disorders of the digestive tract, and abdominal tumors.
One should cook rāsnā, daśamūla, and śatāvarī in one droṇa of water.
Two *kuḍavas* each of *kulattha* beans, jujube fruits, and barley,
along with half a *tulā* of goat meat— these should be cooked in one *āḍhaka* of ghee.

Having considered it appropriate, that [milk] mixed with an equal amount of milk and one-pala portions of the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs should be administered for disorders of Vāta by means of drinking, nasal drops (nasya), and enemas (vasti). // 8 //

It overcomes the five types of cough, trembling of the head, pain in the female reproductive organs and groins, diseases of the entire body or of individual limbs, as well as splenic disorders and upward-moving wind (ūrdhvānila). // 9 //
A preparation prepared with the decoction and paste of the *vidārī* group of drugs conquers cough;
likewise, [a preparation] with *aśoka* seeds, *kṣavaka*, *jantughna*, *añjana*, and *padmaka*. (10)
One afflicted by cough and asthma should lick ghee prepared with viḍa salt, or that same powder saturated with ghee, and subsequently drink goat's milk.

One afflicted by cough and other such ailments should drink goat's ghee; or one may drink the powder of viḍaṅga, nāgara, rāsnā, pippalī, hiṅgu, saindhava, bhārgī, and kṣāra, mixed with a measured amount of ghee. (3.11–12)
In coughs arising from Vāta accompanied by phlegm, and in cases of dyspnea, hiccups, and impaired digestive fire, one should use *durālabhā*, ginger, *śaṭhī*, grapes, and white sugar. (13)
3.13d–14. In cough caused by Vāta, one should lick a paste of ginger (śuṇṭhī), grapes (drākṣā), sugar candy (sitopalā), and karkaṭaśṛṅgī with oil;
or [one may take] duḥsparśā, long pepper (pippalī), mustā, bhārgī, karkaṭakī, and śaṭhī.
One should lick the powdered [drugs] with old jaggery and oil;
likewise, one should take long pepper (kṛṣṇā) with ginger (śuṇṭhī), and similarly, that same [mixture] with bhārgī. 15.
And one should drink black pepper with lukewarm water and rock salt; or ginger with curdled milk and sugar; or *kaṇā* and *reṇukā* with curd. (16)
3.16dv Or one should drink *kaṇa* and *reṇuka* with curd, or the pulp of the *badara* fruit with wine, curd-whey, and buttermilk;
or else, a paste of long pepper fried in ghee with rock salt.

One suffering from cough accompanied by nasal catarrh should drink the marrow of the jujube fruit, or inhale an unctuous smoke according to the prescribed method; furthermore, while subsisting on milk and meat broth, one should also inhale the smokes mentioned in the treatment for hiccup and dyspnea. (3.18)

One should feed [the patient] wholesome meals consisting of village-grown rice, barley, wheat, and ṣaṣṭika rice, along with the juices of mung beans and masha beans, or with soups made from those same legumes. (19)
3.19 With village-grown and marshy products— śāli rice, yavānī, pippalī, the pulp of bilva, nāgara, citraka, rāsnā, jājī, pṛthakparṇī, palāśa, śaṭhī, and pauṣkara— [one should prepare a decoction].

In a disease born of Vāta, one should drink a prepared, unctuous, sour, and salty *peyā* (thin gruel), which destroys pain in the waist, heart, flanks, and abdomen, as well as dyspnea and hiccups. (21)
Similarly, one should drink gruel prepared with the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) combined with pañcakola and jaggery;
or one may drink milk-rice (kṣaireyī) mixed with sesame seeds and rock salt.
Vāstuka, vāyasī-śāka, kāsaghna, and suniṣaṇṇaka may be prepared with the meat of fish, chicken, or boar, along with ghee and rock salt. (23)
The fruit and young leaves of *kaṇṭakārī*, fresh and dried radish, unctuous substances such as oils and the like, and foods consisting of milk, sugarcane juice, and molasses. (24)
One should drink curd-whey, fermented rice-gruel, sour fruit-water, or wine;
however, in the case of pitta-type cough with phlegm, emesis induced with ghee is beneficial. (25)
Likewise, [one may bathe] with water boiled with madana, kāśmarya, and madhuka, or with a paste of madanaphala and yaṣṭimadhu, saturated with the juices of vidārī and sugarcane. // 26 //
In cases of pitta-type cough with thin phlegm, one should administer *trivṛt* combined with sweet substances for purgation;
however, when the phlegm is thick, it should be combined with bitter substances. (27)
Once the morbid humors have been removed, one whose condition has improved should partake of a restorative diet that is cooling, sweet, and unctuous;
however, if the kapha is still thick, it should be cool, dry, and combined with bitter substances.

In Pitta-type [fever], a linctus made of sugar, āmalakī, honey, grapes, and white water-lily is beneficial; with Vāta, it should be prepared with ghee; and with Kapha, it should include cardamom and black pepper. (29)
3.29–30. In the case of pitta [fever], one should lick a linctus consisting of fifty palas of sugar, fifty palas of āmalaka, fifty palas of raisins, thirty pippalīs, and one pala of sugar.
Alternatively, one may lick the juice of cow dung from a cow that subsists on milk, mixed with honey.
With cinnamon-bark, cardamom, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), raisins, the root of long pepper, and lotus seeds;
with parched grain, musta, śaṭhī, rāsnā, emblic myrobalan fruit, and bibhitaka fruit. // 31 //
A linctus made of sugar, honey, and ghee cures heart disease and cough;
barley, śyāmāka, and kodrava grains should be consumed with sweet meat broths from wild animals.

Soups made from mung beans and other pulses, along with bitter vegetables, are beneficial in appropriate doses; furthermore, when phlegm is thickened, bitter electuaries mixed with honey are recommended. (33)
For those with diminished kapha, śāli rice and ṣaṣṭika rice should be used along with meat soups and other broths;
sugar-water, the natural juices of grapes and sugarcane, and milk should be used as after-drinks (anupāna).
In cases of Pittaja cough, one should prepare meat broth, milk, gruel, and vegetable soup with Kākoli, the two types of Bṛhatī, the two types of Medā, Vṛṣa, and Nāgara. // 35 //
One should boil grapes, long pepper, the five roots, and the grass-root group (tṛṇākhya) in water;
with that decoction, one should drink milk that has been boiled and cooled, mixed with honey and sugar. (36)
Or he may drink the gruel prepared by him, well-cooled and mixed with honey, along with *śaṭhī*, *hrīvera*, *bṛhatī*, sugar, and *viśvabheṣaja* (ginger). // 37 //
Having ground these, one should drink the juice strained through a cloth and mixed with clarified butter:
medā, vidārī, kākolī, the fruit of svayaṅguptā, and balā. (38)
Having made a paste of sugar, jīvaka, mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, and durālabhā, one should cook ghee with eight times its quantity of milk. (39)
Used in drinks, foods, or electuaries, it overcomes pitta-type cough;
one should either lick the powder of these [drugs] or drink their decoction. (40)
One suffering from cough due to kapha should first drink the oil extracted from burning pine wood (surakāṣṭha),
strained and sprinkled with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and barley-alkali (yavakṣāra).
3.41 In cases of cough caused by *kapha*, one should first administer unctuous therapy; then, according to the proper method, one should purge the patient from above, from below, and from the head.
For a strong patient, one should employ sharp purgatives and also administer *saṃsarga* (combined) treatments.
[One should eat] with barley, mung beans, and horse gram, along with hot, dry, and intensely pungent foods, combined with kasamarda, eggplant, vyāghrī, alkali, and long pepper. // 43 //
One should drink the decoctions of *dhānvana* and *baila*, or unctuous substances derived from sesame, mustard, and *nimba*,
or water boiled with *daśamūla*, or hot water, or wine, or honey-water.

One should drink water that has been infused overnight with the decoctions of *dhānvana* and *baila*, or with the roots of sesame, mustard, and *bilva*, along with *pauṣkara*, *śamyāka*, and *paṭola*, mixed with honey; this may be taken at the three periods of the meal.
3.45b–46: Long pepper, long pepper root, ginger, and *vibhītaka* combined with *paṭola* and turmeric;
soot from the feathers of peacock and cock, and alkaline ash derived from barley.
Viśālā, pippalī root, and trivṛt, with honey as the liquid—these three electuaries (lehās), each composed of half a verse, cure cough caused by kapha. // 47 //
One should lick black pepper with honey, and likewise long pepper with honey;
and separately, one should take the juices of *vyāghrī*, eggplant, and *bhṛṅga* with honey.
Kāsaghnā, horse dung, surasa, and asita; and devadāru, śaṭhī, rāsnā, karkaṭākhyā, and durālabhā. (49)
3.49b–50. [A preparation] of *surasā* or black [iron], or *pippalī*, *nāgara*, *musta*, *pathyā*, *dhātrī*, and sugar;
or parched grain (*lāja*), sugar, ghee, *śṛṅgī*, and [juice] derived from *dhātrī* fruit.
3.50dv A powder of *śṛṅgī* and *dhātrī*-fruit, combined with honey and oil, constitutes three electuaries for *kapha* associated with *vāta*.
[In another formulation: two *pala* of pomegranate, eight *pala* of jaggery, and three *pala* of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*). 51.
It is clarifying, digestive-stimulant, beneficial for the voice, and overcomes chronic catarrh, dyspnea, and cough.
Molasses, alkali, long pepper, black pepper, and pomegranate overcome dyspnea and cough. (52)
3.52d–53. From pomegranate (*dāḍima*), one should drink [the juice] in successive doses of two palas, half a pala, one akṣa, half a karṣa, and one pala, which conquers dyspnea and cough.
One should also drink the digestive (*pācana*) preparation beginning with *pathyā* mentioned for fevers, along with *śṛṅgī*.

3.53b–54a. Or else, one suffering from cough due to phlegm should take a decoction of *dīpyaka*, *trivṛt*, *viśālā*, *ghana*, and *pauṣkara*, measured at one *karṣa*, half an *akṣa*, or one *pala*, boiled with *kaṇā* (ginger) in urine or even in water.

One should cause [the patient] to drink [this], fried in oil, with a *kārṣika* portion of the paste of *vaidehī*, along with sugar-candy, and saturated with the decoction of *kulattha*; it destroys cough caused by *kapha*. (55)
One *prastha* of ghee should be cooked with one *āḍhaka* of the ten roots and [the following] in quantities equal to one *akṣa*:
*puṣkaramūla*, *śaṭhī*, *bilva*, *surasā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and *hiṅgu*. (56)
3.56c–d A gruel prepared with *puṣkaramūla*, *śaṭī*, and *bilva*, taken as a post-drink (*anupāna*), removes all diseases caused by *vāta* and *śleṣman*.
3.57 Clarified butter (*ghṛta*) processed with the expressed juice of *nirguṇḍī* leaves is a conqueror of cough.
Ghee prepared with the juice of viḍaṅgas and containing vyoṣa as an internal ingredient [is also beneficial]. // 57 //
Punarnavā, śivātikā, sarala, kāsamarda, and amṛtā. // 58a //
With the juices of *paṭola*, *bṛhatī*, and *phaṇijjaka*, combined with milk. // 58b //
By consuming ghee prepared with the three pungents (trikaṭu), [the desired result] is produced. // 58c //
There is no fear of cough, irregular fever, consumption, or hemorrhoids. // 58d //
In one āḍhaka of the juice of kaṇṭakārī, together with its roots, fruits, and leaves, [59ab]
3.59–60. From the roots, fruits, and branches [of the banyan tree],
one *prastha* of ghee should be prepared with *balā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *viḍaṅga*, *śaṭhī*, pomegranate,
black salt (*sauvarcala*), barley-alkali (*yava-kṣāra*), *mūlāmalaka*, and *pauṣkara*.
With vṛścīva, bṛhatī, pathyā, yavānī, citraka, ṛddhi, mṛdvīkā, cavya, varṣābhū, durālabhā, amlavetasa, and [other] sour substances. // 61 //
One should cook [a decoction] with the pastes (kalkas) of śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, bhārgī, rāsnā, and gokṣuraka; this is recommended for all types of cough, as well as for dyspnea and hiccups. (62)
This Kaṇṭakārī-ghṛta is a destroyer of diseases caused by phlegm (kapha). One should cook one tulā of crushed vyāghrī in a fire, using one āḍhaka of water.
Once purified, one should add the powder of vyoṣa, rāsnā, amṛtā, agnikā, śṛṅgī,
bhārgī, ghana, granthi, and dhanvayāsa, each weighing half a pala.
3.64ab Once it has been purified, one should add the powdered ingredients and sixteen palas of ghee along with forty palas of refined sugar; then one should place it back on the fire.
When it has cooled and is no longer sticky enough to smear on a ladle, one should add separately two kuḍavas each of long pepper,
bamboo manna, honey, and fresh butter.
This linctus made from long pepper (pippalī) and *tukākṣīrī* conquers abdominal tumors (gulma), heart disease, hemorrhoids, dyspnea, and cough.
One should inhale pacifying smoke when [the condition] is mild, and purificatory smoke when there is an abundance of phlegm (kapha).

3.67 When phlegm is excessive, one should drink a purifying smoke made of realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *ālā*, licorice (*madhuka*), spikenard (*māṃsī*), nut-grass (*mustā*), and the bark of *iṅgudī* according to the procedure for curing cough, and afterwards drink milk.
At the end of spitting, this lukewarm smoke mixed with jaggery destroys coughs dominated by wind and phlegm, whether they are recent or long-standing, in a short time. (69)
If tamaka cough occurs in the context of kaphaja cough due to the involvement of pitta, one should apply the treatments for pitta-type cough according to the specific stage of the condition. // 70 //
When wind is associated with phlegm, one should perform treatments that alleviate phlegm;
when wind and phlegm are associated with bile, one should perform treatments that destroy bile. (71)

In a dry cough caused by vāta and śleṣman, oleation therapy is prescribed; in a moist one, drying therapy. In a cough born of kapha accompanied by pitta, however, the treatment should be combined with bitter substances. (72)
3.72b–c: When there is internal injury to the chest, one should immediately drink resinous *lākṣā* mixed with honey; this is moistening for what is dry and drying for what is moist.
Once it has been digested, one should eat *śāli* rice with milk, and when that is digested, one should eat *śāli* rice with milk and sugar.

If there is pain in the sides and bladder, with diminished pitta and digestive fire, one should take that [milk] mixed with *surā* liquor, along with *mustā*, *ativiṣā*, *pāṭhā*, and *vatsaka*, for one suffering from loose stools. (74)
One with a stimulated digestive fire should drink lac, ghee, beeswax, the group of vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs, sugar, and bamboo manna,
boiled together with milk.

One suffering from chest wounds (kṣata) should drink milk boiled with *tvakkṣīrī* in equal measure, along with *ikṣvārikā*, lotus stalks (*bisa*), lotus nodes (*granthi*), lotus filaments (*padmakesara*), and sandalwood, mixed with honey, for the purpose of healing the wound.

One should drink the powder of raw barley prepared in milk and mixed with ghee for fever and burning sensations; or alternatively, one may drink sugar, honey, and parched grain flour with milk. // 77 //
One suffering from cough and vomiting should drink ghee prepared with milk and mixed with sweet medicinal herbs;
alternatively, boiled jaggery-water with honey and black pepper is beneficial.
One suffering from cough should drink ghee,
or ghee cooked with *āmalaka* powder and milk mixed with clarified butter;
or one should employ *pippalī* according to the procedure for *rasāyana*.

One suffering from cough, pain in the joints, or bone pain should lick these [drugs]— madhūka, madhuka, drākṣā, tvakkṣīrī, pippalī, and balā— cooked in milk, mixed with ghee, and combined with ghee and honey. (3.79–80)

One should lick [this mixture] with ghee and honey: cinnamon-bark (*tvakkṣīrī*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and *balā*, each in the amount of half a *karṣa*; three spices (*trijāta*) in the same amount; half a *pala* of long pepper; and sugar, grapes (*drākṣā*), *madhūka*, dates (*kharjūra*), and *palāśa*, all finely powdered. (3.80b–81)
These pills, taken with honey, are aphrodisiacs that destroy pitta and blood disorders, as well as cough, dyspnea, anorexia, vomiting, fainting, hiccups, intoxication, and vertigo. (82)
[It cures] fainting, hiccups, vomiting, vertigo,
as well as wasting from injury, loss of voice, splenic disorders, consumption, and disorders of wind;
it also treats the spitting of blood, pain in the heart and flanks, thirst, and fever.

One who spits blood, suffering from spleen enlargement, edema, and aggravated vāta, should drink the powder made from *varṣābhū*, sugar, and red *śāli* rice, processed with grape juice, milk, and ghee. (3.83)
Or one may use *taṇḍulīyaka* prepared with *madhūka*, *madhuka*, and milk;
furthermore, one should administer appropriate medicine once the blood has been released through its respective channels. (85)
One suffering from delusive wind (mūḍhavāta) should take goat's fat fried in wine with rock salt;
such a person becomes lean, emaciated, with a weakened chest, yet possesses little sleep and a stimulated digestive fire.
One should eat the essence of boiled milk with ghee, honey, and sugar;
likewise, sugar, barley, wheat, *jīvaka*, and *ṛṣabhaka* mixed with honey. (87)
3.87c–d: One who is emaciated, wounded, or wasted away should lick sugar mixed with barley and wheat, followed by the drinking of boiled milk;
he should also drink the broth of meat from a carnivorous animal fried in ghee. 3.88.
Combined with long pepper and honey, this increases flesh and blood;
[it is prepared] with the [barks of] Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Śāla, and Priyaṅgu. // 89 //
One should eat [the patient] with the ghee produced from milk boiled with *tālamastaka*, *jambū* bark, *priyāla*, *padmaka*, and *aśvakarṇa*.

For one with a chest wound, diminished semen, strength, and sensory faculties, or for one afflicted by wind and bile, massage with ghee is prescribed when there is a splitting sensation in the limbs. (91)
When one is afflicted by wind-diseases caused by oils,
or suffers from pain in the heart and flanks, there should be a drink of *jīvanīya* ghee.

In cases of pain in the sides caused by hemorrhage (hṛtapārśvārtau), one should administer a drink, or perform a treatment that cures diseases of Vāta without contradicting the requirements for Pitta and blood;
[this involves] ghee cooked with a decoction of Yaṣṭyāhvā and Nāgabalā mixed with an equal amount of milk.
An oil prepared with the pastes of *payasyā*, *pippalī*, and *vāṃśī* is beneficial for wounds.
The *jīvanīya* group [of herbs], along with *śuṇṭhī*, *varī*, *vīrā*, and *punarnavā*, [are also beneficial]. (94)
Balā, bhārgī, svaguptā, ṛddhi, śaṭhī, tāmalakī, kaṇā, śṛṅgāṭaka, payasyā, and the light pañcamūla. (95)
Fruits such as grapes and walnuts are sweet, unctuous, and nourishing;
with these, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee using [the fruits] in portions of one *karṣa*, finely ground into a paste. (96)
When cooled, one-half prastha of honey and half a tulā of powdered sugar should be added, along with milk, vidārī, sugarcane juice, and goat meat broth. 97.
Having dissolved half a pala each of black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, cinnamon leaves, and nāgakeśara in that [mixture], one should lick a dose of it according to one's strength. (98)
One should lick the dose according to one's digestive fire;
this consumption of ghee is like the tasting of nectar. Ghee is the nectar for men;
it should be consumed as a substance with the essence of ambrosia by one who subsists on milk and meat broth.

One should nourish those whose semen is depleted, those suffering from wounds or emaciation, the weak, those afflicted by disease, those addicted to women, the thin, and those deficient in complexion and voice. (100)
3.100b–c: It cures cough, hiccups, fever, dyspnea, burning sensations, thirst, and hemorrhagic disorders caused by weak strength and disease;
it bestows sons and removes vomiting, fainting, and diseases of the heart, female reproductive organs, and urine. 101.
Śvadaṃṣṭrā, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, balā, kāśmarya, kaṭtṛṇa, darbhamūla, pṛthakparṇī, palāśa, ṛṣabhaka, and sthirā—[these should be used]. (102)
One should cook these in earthen vessels with their juice and four times the amount of milk, along with the pastes of *svaguptā*, *jīvantī*, *medā*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and *jīvaka*. (103)
One *prastha* of ghee prepared with *śatāvarī*, *ṛddhi*, *mṛdvīkā*, sugar, *śrāvaṇī*, and lotus stalks (*bisas*) cures wind and bile disorders, heart disease, and colic. (104)

It alleviates pitta, heart disease, looseness of the bowels, and colic; it cures dysuria, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, cough, emaciation, and consumption; and it bestows strength and flesh upon those exhausted by archery, women, wine, heavy loads, or travel on foot. (3.104–105)
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee in a decoction of one *pala* of *madhuka* wood and one *prastha* of *drākṣā*;
when it is prepared, eight *palas* of *pippalī* should be added as a paste once the mixture has cooled. (106)

One should mix eight palas each of honey and sugar separately; this, combined with an equal amount of parched grain flour (saktu), is beneficial for those suffering from chest wounds, emaciation, hemorrhaging, and uterine tumors (raktagulma). (107)
One should cook one *prastha* each of the juice of *dhātrī* fruit, *vidārī*, sugarcane, and *jīvanīya* herbs, along with one *prastha* each of cow's ghee and goat's milk. (108)
Once it has been proven efficacious and cooled, one should then add two prasthas of sugar and honey;
this cures consumption, epilepsy, hemorrhagic disorders, cough, urinary disorders, and wasting. (109)

3.109ab–d: When prepared and purified, this [medicated ghee] contains sugar and honey; it removes cough, urinary disorders, and fever. It stabilizes youth, promotes longevity, and bestows muscle mass, semen, and strength. One should lick this ghee when pitta is predominant, but drink it when vāta is predominant. 3.110: [The physician] should administer it according to the specific dosha involved. Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of chronic fever. Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Chronic Fever," in the Section on Therapeutics of the *Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā*, composed by Śrīmad Vāgbhaṭa. Chapter Four: The Treatment of Consumption (Rājayakṣman) 4.1: Now, therefore, the treatment for consumption will be explained. Consumption is caused by the three doshas, as well as by grief, hunger, and sexual excess. Its symptoms are: dryness of the mouth, thirst, weakness, fever, cough, loss of appetite, vomiting, and pain in the sides. 4.2: The treatment for consumption consists of the following: ghee, meat broth, milk, and gruels; as well as various types of soups, meat preparations, and roasted grains. 4.3: One should prescribe ghee prepared with drugs that pacify the doshas, or meat broth from animals of the marshy (*ānūpa*) or aquatic (*audaka*) classes, or milk processed with medicinal herbs. 4.4: For one suffering from consumption, one should prescribe a diet consisting of *śāli* rice, *mudga* beans, and *māṣa* beans, along with meat juices and various soups. 4.5: One should prescribe the meat of peacock, partridge, quail, and the *tittiri* bird, as well as the meat of the *lāva* and *vartīka* birds, prepared with ghee. 4.6: One should prescribe the meat of the *kapiñjala* partridge, the *cakora*, the *krauñca* crane, the *baka* heron, and the *śatapatra* woodpecker, all prepared with ghee. 4.7: One should prescribe the meat of the *mayūra* peacock, the *kukkuta* rooster, the *tāmracūḍa* red-rooster, the *vartaka*, the *lāvaka*, and the *kapiñjala*. 4.8: One should prescribe In cases where Vāta is predominant, one should lick [the medicine]; if drunk, it would pacify Pitta. Because [the quantity] is small, it does not destroy the digestive fire (anal). When drunk, it overcomes Vāyu and obstructs the internal heat (ūṣman). // 111 //
For those whose limbs are emaciated, wasted, and thin, these very same ghees should be prepared thickened with the powders of *tvakkṣīrī*, sugar, and parched grain (*lāja*). 112.

3.112 One should administer drinks with the powders of *tvakkṣīrī*, *pippalī*, and parched rice (*lāja*); having prepared boluses of ghee and jaggery with an equal portion of honey, one should give them followed by milk.
Through these, one shall very quickly attain semen, virility, strength, and nourishment. // 113 //
One should cook again a *tulā* measure of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin) from which the skin and seeds have been removed, after it has been steamed;
while stirring it in a *prastha* measure of clarified butter that has acquired the color of honey, one should add [the following ingredients] into it. (114)
3.114d–115. But into the honey-colored [syrup], one should add one hundred palas of sugar-candy, two palas each of long pepper and dry ginger, as well as cumin;
and one should add half a pala each of the three aromatics (trijāta), coriander, and black pepper.
Once it has been cooled, one should add honey equal to half the amount of ghee, stir it with a churning stick, and set it aside; when administered, this destroys [the disease]. 116.
It cures cough, hiccup, fever, dyspnea, hemorrhagic disorders (rakta-pitta), chest wounds, and consumption; it promotes the healing of the chest and bestows intelligence, memory, and strength. (117)
One should drink the heart-pleasing *kūṣmāṇḍaka* elixir prescribed by the Aśvins, increasing the dose by half a *karṣa* at a time starting from the root of *nāgabalā*. 118.

Increasing by half a *karṣa* and so forth, up to one *pala*, this preparation— taken with milk for a month while subsisting on milk alone and abstaining from other food— is supreme for producing nourishment, longevity, strength, and a healthy complexion. (3.118–119)
This is the procedure for maṇḍūkaparṇī, yaṣṭī, and viśvauṣadha; one should boil a *tulā* of nāgabalā in a *droṇa* of water until one-quarter remains.
One should prepare ghee and milk in equal proportions with that decoction, along with half-a-pala each of atibalā, balā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and punarnavā. (121)
With *prapauṇḍarīka*, *kāśmarya*, *priyāla*, and *kapikacchu*; with *aśvagandhā*, white *abhīru*, the two types of *medā*, and the three types of *trikaṇṭaka* [122].
With *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *kṣīraśuklā*, the two types of *jīraka*, lotus stalk (*mṛṇāla*), lotus fiber (*bisa*), dates (*kharjūra*), *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and *kaseruka* // 123 //

This Nāgabalā ghee, prepared with milk, śuklā, the two types of jīvaka, and nāgabalā, overcomes pitta-blood disorders, wounds, and consumption; it also conquers thirst, vertigo, and burning sensations, and is supreme for bestowing strength and nourishment. (3.123–124)
It improves the complexion, promotes longevity, bestows vigor, and destroys wrinkles and graying hair; by using it for six months, even an old man becomes like a youth. (125)
Having used this for six months, when the digestive fire has been kindled, this regimen serves as a stimulant and digestive aid for those with weak digestion.
It is recommended for those suffering from wasting (yakṣman) and chest injuries; furthermore, it is astringent when the stool is loose.
The ten roots: *svayaṅguptā*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *śaṭhī*, *balā*, elephant-ginger (*hastipippalī*), *apāmārga*, long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), and *citraka*. (127)
One should boil two palas each of bhārgī and puṣkaramūla, one āḍhaka of barley, and one hundred harītakī fruits in five āḍhakas of water. (128)

One should boil two palas each [of the aforementioned drugs] with one āḍhaka of barley in five āḍhakas of water. When the barley is softened, that strained decoction and one hundred abhayā fruits should be boiled together with one tulā of jaggery (guḍa), adding one kuḍava each of ghee and [the other specified ingredients].
When the barley has been steamed, one should prepare a decoction from it; once this is cooked with oil and pippalī powder and has cooled, one should add honey.
From this, one should daily consume two *abhayā* fruits as a medicinal elixir (*rasāyana*).
These two, taken daily as an unctuous enema (abhyaṅga), destroy wrinkles and graying hair, and increase complexion, longevity, and strength;
they also cure the five types of cough, consumption, asthma, hiccups, and irregular fever.

This auspicious and excellent elixir (rasāyana), prescribed by Agastya, cures urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, heart disease, anorexia, and chronic rhinitis. (132)
The ten roots, balā, mūrvā, the two types of haridrā, the two types of pippalī, pāṭhā, aśvagandhā, apāmārga, svaguptā, ativiṣā, and amṛtā. // 133 //
3.133b–d: Turmeric, the two types of long pepper, *svaguptā*, ativiṣā, amṛtā, young *bilva* fruit, the roots of *trivṛt* and *dantī*, the leaf of *citraka*,
*payasyā*, *kuṭaja*, *hiṃsrā*, the flower of *sāra*, and the seed of *bījaka*.
Boṭa, sthavira, bhallāta, vikaṅkata, śatāvarī, pūtikarañja, śamyāka, candralekhā, and sahācara. (135)
3.135d–3.136: One pala each of *śaubhāñjanaka*, the bark of *nimba*, and *ikṣura*, along with one thousand *pathyā* fruits and two *āḍhakas* of barley mixed with one hundred [of the former]. 136.

One should boil it in water possessing eight qualities until it reaches the consistency of barley-steeping liquid; once strained, one should add long pepper and Pathyā, and into that, a *tulā* of aged jaggery.
Once purified, one should add harītakī (pathyā) along with one *prastha* each of oil, clarified butter (*ājya*), and the juice of *dhātrī*. Then,
one should place it over a gentle fire, and having removed it from the heat once it reaches the "darvī-lepa" consistency, [one should proceed].
When cold, one should add two *prasthas* of honey and a *kuḍava* of *pippalī*, and then mix in three *palas* of powdered *trijātaka*. (139)
One should eat for a month, as before, [the substance] kept in an old grain-jar;
this elixir (rasāyana) spoken by Vasiṣṭha possesses even greater qualities than the previous one. // 140 //
For those in good health, this is recommended for all seasons without exception:
one pala each of rock salt (saindhava) and dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and two palas of black salt (sauvarcala).
One *kuḍava* each of *vṛkṣāmla*, pomegranate, and the leaves of *ārjaka*; one *caturthika* each of black pepper and *ajājī*; and two *caturthikas* of coriander. (142)
3.142b–143. One should provide pomegranate, *ārjaka* leaves, and twelve palas of sugar;
having made these into a powder, one should then administer a dose with food and drinks.
This [mixture] is palatable, digestive-stimulant, strengthening, and it overcomes pain in the flanks, dyspnea, and cough.
Take one part of *ṣoḍaśikā*, two parts of coriander (*dhānya*), and two parts each of cumin (*ajāji*) and bishop’s weed (*dīpyaka*). (144)

3.144b–145 This [preparation] cures pain in the flanks, dyspnea, and cough. To those two [liquids], one should add twice and twice again [the juices of] pomegranate and *vṛkṣāmla*, one *pala* of *sauvarcala* salt,
one *karṣa* of ginger, and five *palas* of the pulp of the *dadhittha* fruit.
3.145c–v: One *karṣa* of ginger and the same amount of *kapittha* should be powdered and mixed with sixteen *palas* of sugar.
This *ṣāḍava* should be administered as before with food and drinks. 146.
The therapeutic procedure prescribed for consumption (yakṣman) is beneficial for chest wounds according to their specific stage;
however, once the morbidity of the wound has subsided, if phlegm (kapha) has increased, [the treatment for] the chest and head [should be applied]. 147.
The person whose chest is being torn apart by coughing should inhale these smokes from a cloth well-saturated with the pastes of the two types of medā, the two types of balā, and yaṣṭī.
If the two [nostrils] of a patient suffering from cough are torn [by discharge], he should not inhale these [standard] medicinal smokes; instead,

having prepared a wick (*varti*) from realgar (*manaḥśilā*), palāśa, *ajagandhā*, the bark of milky trees (*tvakṣīrin*), and ginger (*nāgara*), he should smoke it while following the treatment with *jīvanīya* ghee.
The after-drink should likewise be sugar-cane juice, sugarcane juice, or molasses-water;
or, having ground realgar in equal parts with fresh banyan shoots, [it should be taken]. 150.
One should drink medicated smoke mixed with ghee, followed by a meal of partridge meat;
in cases arising from wasting (kṣaya), one should first administer nourishing therapy and stimulate the digestive fire.
3.151b–152. For one who has been fed partridge, one should administer a mild purgative with unctuous substances to eliminate the many morbid humors (doṣas),
using *śamyāka* or *trivṛt* combined with the juice of *mṛdvīkā*.
One whose body is emaciated should drink ghee prepared with a decoction of *tilvaka* and the fresh juice of *vidārī*, according to the proper method, as a means of purification. (153)

One suffering from wasting cough (kṣayakāsa) due to the depletion of bile, phlegm, and the bodily tissues (dhātus) should drink ghee prepared with karkaṭakī, milk, and the two types of balā. // 154 //
Ghee and milk prepared with vidārī, kadamba, and the grains of the palmyra palm are used for discoloration of the urine and for difficult urination. (155)
When the penis and the anus are empty yet painful, along with the hips and groins,
one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using light ghee-scum or a mixed formulation.

For one who has been treated with the *jāṅgala* meats, birds such as the quail (*vartaka*) and others that dwell in burrows should be administered in succession; likewise, meat-eating birds of prey (*prasaha*) should be employed in the same manner. (157)

Due to their heat and their disruptive nature, they cause the *kapha* to fall away from the channels; and when these channels are purified, the nutrient essence (*rasa*) flows properly and brings about nourishment. (158)
In water, [one should boil] cavya, triphalā, bhārgī, daśamūla, citraka, kulattha, pippalīmūla, pāṭhā, kola, and yava. (159)
One should cook ghee with equal parts of ginger, durālabhā, long pepper, śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, and ground karkaṭaśṛṅgī, all boiled together. (160)
Once this is prepared, one afflicted by wasting cough (kṣayakāsa) should drink an appropriate dose after adding two types of alkali and five salts, according to the proper method. (161)
3.161b–162. Two [parts each] of the five salts, along with *kāsamarda*, *abhayā*, *mustā*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭphala*, *nāgara*, *pippalī*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *kāśmarya*, and *surasā*...
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *akṣa* each [of the medicinal ingredients] in one *āḍhaka* of milk and grape juice;
this auspicious preparation cures consumption, fever, splenic disorders, and all types of cough. (163)
Ghee cooked with the juice and paste derived from the leaves, roots, fruits, and sprouts of vṛṣa, vyāghrī, and guḍūcī destroys cough, fever, and loss of appetite. (164)
Or a person should drink [this], prepared with twice the amount of pomegranate juice and combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa), along with barley alkali, after having eaten. 165.
After a meal, a person should drink ghee mixed with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra);
or ghee prepared with long pepper (pippalī) and jaggery; or ghee combined with goat’s milk.
These ghees are for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire in those suffering from wasting and cough. (166)
For the purification of the channels of the throat and chest constricted by morbid humors, one should boil twenty *vijayā* fruits in a *prastha* measure of barley decoction. (167)

Having massaged those [roots] while they are steaming, one should add six palas of old jaggery, two palas of long pepper (pippalī), one karṣa of realgar (manohvā), and one karṣa of rasāñjana to that [mixture]. (168)
Having added half a measure of *akṣa*, one should cook it again; that linctus conquers dyspnea and cough.
Porcupine quills, burnt and combined with ghee, honey, and sugar, [are likewise effective]. (169)
This linctus cures dyspnea and cough; or else, the two "peacock-feet" (barhipāda) with honey and ghee;
or the alkali of castor leaves combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa), oil, and jaggery.
Or one should have him lick an alkaline preparation made from the leaves of *surasā* and *eraṇḍa*;
or he should lick the powder of the three pungents (*try-ūṣaṇa*) with old jaggery and ghee. (171)
Padmaka, the three fruits (triphalā), the three pungents (vyoṣa), viḍaṅga, devadāru, balā, and rāsnā—this entire powder should be mixed with an equal amount of sugar. (172)
One should eat this entire mixture with equal parts of sugar, or lick it with honey and ghee; it is a supreme remedy for cough.
Likewise, one may take powdered black pepper with ghee, honey, and sugar.
Similarly, one should hold in the mouth a bolus made of powdered black pepper (*marica*) with *pathyā*, ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and *ghana* (cinnamon) mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*).
This is for all types of dyspnea and cough; alternatively, one may use *vibhītaka* alone.
The paste of *tilvaka* leaves fried in ghee, taken with sugar, or as a gruel (*peyā*) or a bolus (*utkārikā*), conquers vomiting, thirst, cough, and diarrhea. (175)

3.175c–d. Gruel and *cotkārikā* prepared with the decoction of *kaṇṭakārī* cure vomiting, thirst, cough, and diarrhea. 3.175e–f. Milk, soups, and meat broths prepared with *gaura-āmalaka* and sour agents are the physician’s remedy for all types of cough.

To one suffering from wasting cough, one should administer milk, soups, and meat broths—prepared from the meat of gallinaceous birds, pecker birds, and burrowing animals—in a decoction of wind-alleviating herbs. (177)

The medicated smokes along with their adjunct drinks that have been prescribed for cough due to chest injury (kṣatakāsa) should also be employed in cough due to wasting (kṣayakāsa), as well as those which will be described in the treatment of pulmonary consumption (yakṣman). 178.
3.178d–179ab: Furthermore, those [remedies] which will be described in the section on consumption (yakṣman)—
namely, those that are nourishing, digestive-stimulating for the fire, and purifying of the channels—
are all praised when administered alternately to those suffering from wasting and cough as being strengthening.

Since this terrible wasting cough arises from the combination [of all three humors], its treatment should be beneficial for that combination, administered according to the strength of the respective doshas. (180)
In the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna), since asthma (śvāsa) and hiccups (hidhmā) have identical causes and other factors, their treatment is likewise the same; therefore,
one should first treat the patient afflicted by these with sudation therapies (sveda).

When these [drugs] are mixed with unctuous substances, salt, and oil, the kapha bound within the channels, even if it is deeply embedded, becomes dissolved; once it reaches the digestive tract (koṣṭha), it is easily eliminated. // 2 //
There shall be softness of the channels and a downward movement of the wind;
once fomented, one should feed the patient food that is unctuous along with the juices of marshy animals. // 3 //
Or, for the sake of restoring the downward movement of the wind (māruta), one may give him curd-whey (dadhy-uttara); thereafter, a mild emetic should be administered to him,
especially for those suffering from cough, vomiting, cardiac oppression, and loss of voice.

When the vitiated bodily constituents have been removed, he who has combined long pepper, rock salt, and honey— provided it does not aggravate the wind— attains comfort even when his body is afflicted by phlegm.
When the channels have been purified, the wind moves unimpeded;
in cases of flatulence, upward-moving wind, and tamaka cough, one should use mātuluṅga, sour substances, and vetasa.

Food combined with asafoetida (hiṅgu), pīlu, and viḍa salt acts as a carminative; or one should administer a mild purgative that is slightly warm, containing rock salt (saindhava) and sour fruits (phalāmla). // 7 //
For these [diseases] arise from the provocation of the vital breath (prāṇa) whose movement is obstructed by phlegm (kapha);
therefore, purification through the upper and lower [routes] is beneficial for the purpose of clearing those channels. // 8 //
Just as water flowing [downhill] surges with great force when its path is obstructed, so too should one clear its passage by means of the wind. (9)
If [the fire] is not pacified, one who has performed the purification should remove the adhered impurity with smoke, using turmeric leaf, castor root, lac, and realgar. (10)
Having ground the roots of *ala* and *māṃsī*, along with grapes (*drākṣā*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), and *devadāru*, one should prepare a wick (*varti*).
One should inhale that smoke while it is smeared with ghee, or alternatively, consume barley grains mixed with ghee.
Beeswax, resin of the Sarja tree, or ghee;
or agallochum, sandalwood, or likewise the horn, hair, or sinew of cows. 12.
4.12d–13ab: Or [one may use] the hair or sinews of cows; or the skins, horns, and hooves of bears, monitor lizards, antelopes, and deer;
or bdellium, or realgar, or even the resin of the *śāla* tree.

4.13ab The skins, horns, and hooves of the *ṛśya*, *godhā*, *kuraṅga*, and *eṇa* deer, as well as *śallakī*, *guggulu*, iron, or *padmaka* wood soaked in clarified butter—these should certainly be applied for a moment even to those who are not otherwise fit for sudation. 4.13cd–14ab [Note: The verse numbering follows the source text's convention.]
Alternatively, one should foment the *padmaka* [herb] soaked in ghee with lukewarm applications of oil mixed with sugar and milk;
furthermore, one should apply poultices (*utkārikā*) and compresses (*upanāha*) using medicinal substances prescribed in the chapter on fomentation (*sveda*).
One should soothe the chest and throat with mild [emetics]; however, if there is *āmadoṣa*, one should follow the regimen for *āma*.
Having observed that the *vāta* has become aggravated by excessive [emetic] application, one should treat it with *vāta*-destroying measures. (16)

One should bring it under control with unctuous substances such as meat broths that are not excessively hot, and with oil massages; for in those whose kapha is not aggravated, who have not undergone sudation, or who are weak, purification [by emesis] leads to harm. // 17 //
When the wind has gained a foothold in the vital points (marmans), it quickly dries them up and takes away the life-breaths;
therefore, one should pacify those [doshas] with astringents, electuaries, unctuous substances, and so forth. (18)
One should treat hiccup and dyspnea arising from the complications of emaciation, injury, diarrhea, hemorrhage, or pitta-type burning sensations with sweet, unctuous, and cold remedies. (19)

Meat broths of wild animals should be prepared in a decoction of *kulattha* and the ten roots (*daśamūla*), as well as vegetable soups made from drumstick (*śigru*), eggplant (*vārtāka*), *kāsaghna*, vetchling (*vṛṣa*), and radish (*mūlaka*). (20)
With the sprouts of *nimba*, *kulaka*, *bṛhatī*, and *mātuluṅga*;
and with *vyāghrī*, *durālabhā*, *śṛṅgī*, the fruit-pulp of *bilva*, and *trikaṇṭaka*. // 21 //
A soup should be prepared by boiling kulattha beans with amṛtāgni in water;
likewise, one may be made from rāsnā, the bṛhaty-ādi group, balā, mudga beans, and citraka.
4.22b–c. A broth (yūṣa) should be prepared with water boiled [with the following], and a gruel (peyā) made from citraka, ajājī, śṛṅgī, and sauvarcala;
or one made with daśamūla, which removes cough, dyspnea, hiccups, and pain.
With the ten roots, śaṭī, rāsnā, bhārgī, bilva, ṛddhi, pauṣkara, kulīraśṛṅgī, capalā, tāmalakī, and amṛtā; // 24 //
When this has been digested, one should drink a decoction, followed by gruel prepared with those same ingredients;
then one should eat *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, and horse gram. (25)
For the pacification of cough, cardiac oppression, pain in the flanks, hiccups, and dyspnea,
one should take roasted grain flour (saktu) soaked in the sprouts of *arka* and milk, mixed with honey.

One should drink barley grains stirred with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) and other ingredients; furthermore, one should add alkali, asafoetida, ghee, viḍa salt, and pomegranate to the food.
One should administer a decoction of pauṣkara, śaṭī, vyoṣa, mātuluṅga, amlavetasa, or the ten roots (daśamūla), or else of devadāru.
One suffering from hiccup and dyspnea who is thirsty should drink a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) or the scum of vāruṇī wine;
[or one should take a preparation] with pippalī, pippalīmūla, pathyā, jantughna, and citraka.
When the wound has been smeared with these powdered ingredients and has healed, one should place it in a vessel of ghee;
that [ghee], having remained for a month in buttermilk, is indeed an appetizer and a conqueror of asthma and cough.
One should drink one *prasṛta* measure each of *pāṭhā*, *madhurasā*, *dāru*, and *sarala*, kept overnight in the scum of wine (*surā-maṇḍa*) with a small amount of salt. (31)
One should drink one *prasṛta* measure of *sarala* resin that has been kept overnight,
or an alkaline preparation (*kṣāra*) combined with *bhārgī*, ginger, and black pepper, taken with lukewarm water;
or alternatively, one should cause the patient to drink *bāṣpikā* (a medicinal smoke) that has been stirred and ground with its own decoction.
The natural juice of *saptaparṇa* or of *śirīṣa* flowers, combined with honey and *kaṇā*, is used when hiccups and dyspnea are accompanied by *pitta* and *kapha*. (33)

A poultice (utkārikā) made of tugākṣīrī, kṛṣṇā, madhūlī, ghee, and nāgara should be applied when there is an association with pitta; however, it should be used when vāyu is the associated secondary factor.

Milk combined with the flesh of the porcupine and rabbit, grains of rice, clarified butter, the blood of the hedgehog, the juice of *suvarcalā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and clarified butter [is used for this purpose]. (35)

In cases where vāta and pitta are the secondary factors, a drink prepared with rice gruel (śāly-odana) or goat's milk boiled with four parts water, along with jaggery and ginger, should be administered.
One should lick the juices of pippalī root, madhuka, jaggery, cow dung, and horse dung, combined with honey and ghee; these destroy hiccup, ophthalmia, and cough. (37)
One who has an excess of phlegm should lick the juice of cow dung mixed with honey, one part at a time—using that of the cow, elephant, horse, boar, camel, donkey, ram, or goat—or else drink it. 38.
Likewise, one suffering from asthma with an excess of phlegm should lick soot produced from the skin, hair, bones, hooves, and horns of four-hoofed animals, as well as that of *vājigandhā*. (39)
Or one may take śaṭhī, pauṣkara, and dhātrī; or pauṣkara combined with kaṇā;
or gairika, añjana, and kṛṣṇā; or the fresh juice derived from kapittha.
Or, with the juice of *kapittha*, one may take *dhātrī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *pippalī*;
or, with ghee and honey, one may take *pathyā*, *viḍaṅga*, long pepper (*uṣaṇa*), and *pippalī*. // 41 //
Either jujube, parched grain, myrobalan, grapes, long pepper, and ginger; or jaggery, oil, turmeric, grapes, long pepper, rāsnā, and black pepper. (42)
One should drink the medicinal powders as a linctus with meat broth, water, wine, or sour liquids; or [one may take] jīvantī, musta, surasa, the two types of tvak and elā, and pauṣkara.
Caṇḍā, tāmalakī, loha, bhārgī, nāgara, vālaka, karkaṭākhya, śaṭhī, kṛṣṇā, nāgakesara, and coraka. // 44 //
This powder, when used as desired with double the amount of sugar, is an excellent remedy for curing pain in the sides, fever, and cough, and it effectively removes hiccups and asthma. (45)
A powder made from śaṭhī, tāmalakī, bhārgī, caṇḍā, vālaka, and pauṣkara, mixed with eight times its weight of sugar, is an excellent remedy for hiccup and asthma. (46)
One should eat equal parts of jaggery and ginger, or one should drink [an infusion of] the root of garlic, onion, or leek. (47)
One should administer the juice of sandalwood as a nasal drop with woman’s milk;
or one may use the excrement of a fly with breast milk, or with the juice of lac. (48)
One should drink ghee prepared with rock salt and milk, or ghee processed with milk and the pastes of sweet substances; or one should apply it as an ointment.
Once warm and once cold, alternately mixed with sugar and honey;
likewise, milk prepared in the same manner, as well as ghee processed with the drugs belonging to the purgative group. (50)

One should cook ghee with *kaṇā*, *sauvarcala* salt, alkali (*kṣāra*), *vayaḥsthā*, *hiṅgu*, *coraka*, and *kāyasthā*, along with curd-whey (*mastu*) and a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*). (51)
One should drink that [milk] with the *jīvanīya* drugs, or lick it after it has been prepared with honey;
[the decoction should contain] *tejovatī*, *abhayā*, *kuṣṭha*, *pippalī*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*. (52)
Bhūtīka, the root of puṣkara, palāśa, citraka, śaṭhī, the two types of salt (paṭu-dvaya), tāmalakī, jīvantī, and the pulp of bilva. // 53 //
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *karṣa* each of *vacā*, leaf (*pattra*), and *tālīśa*, along with a quarter-part of *hiṅgu*; when drunk, it quickly destroys [the disease]. (54)
One should drink ghee with half the quantity of vacā, tālīśapatra, and śākhā,
for the cure of vāta-type hemorrhoids, grahaṇī, hiccups, and pain in the heart and flanks;
or alternatively, with alkali and salt.
One should administer *dhānvantara*, bull’s ghee, *dādhika* ghee, or the *hapuṣādi* group of drugs;
furthermore, sudden sprinkling with cold water, as well as inducing terror, distraction, fear, and grief, [are beneficial].
Joy, envy, holding one's breath, being bitten by insects, and whatever else subdues phlegm and wind, is heating and promotes the downward movement of wind. (57)
4.57ab Joy, envy, and the suppression of breath—these should generally be employed, as well as that which is most effective at subduing vāta.

Excessive pacification leads to harm, while excessive depletion is both severe and difficult to manage;
therefore, one should treat them primarily with both pacifying and nourishing therapies. (59)
It is extremely difficult to emaciate,
and cough, dyspnea, consumption, vomiting, and hiccups [arise] through the mutual administration of their respective remedies.

In the section on therapeutics, one should administer purification— both upward and downward— to a strong patient with abundant doshas who has undergone oleation and sudation; for the patient suffering from consumption (yakṣman), this purification should be combined with unctuous substances and must not be emaciating.
5.1dv That which is emesis accompanied by unctuousness—
using milk mixed with fruits, or with a sweet taste,
or with gruel (yavāgū) containing ghee prepared with emetic substances— is [the mild form]. // 2 //
One should administer a purgative for vomiting using *trivṛt*, *śyāmā*, and *nṛpadruma*, combined with sugar, honey, and ghee, or with milk and a nourishing drink (*tarpaṇa*). // 3 //
Or, for one whose bowels have been purified, one should administer a regimen that is nourishing and digestive-stimulant, combined with the juices of grapes, vidārī, kāśmarya, and meat.
Or [the diet] may be combined with the juices of meats, or consist of pleasant foods and drinks that subdue Vāta and are light;
likewise, Śāli rice, Ṣaṣṭika rice, wheat, barley, and Mudga beans should be well-cooked. // 5 //
That which is light, of unflagging potency, easily digested, and strength-giving; (5+1ab)
Goat’s milk, ghee, meat, and the flesh of carnivorous animals, when combined with *avākpuṣpī*, *laghu*, *acyutavīrya*, and *adbhutavīrya*, conquer consumption (*śoṣa*).
Crows, owls, wolves, leopards, cows, horses, mongooses, and serpents; // 6 //
Food consisting of vultures, hawks, donkeys, and camels, even if beneficial, is harmful when accompanied by deception;
for such food, once recognized, is loathsome and leads to vomiting, not to strength or vigor.
Vultures, blue jays, donkeys, camels, deer, and the like are beneficial for bile and phlegm; those of the "prasaha" group and others are beneficial for wind.
When prepared as *vesavāra* and formulated with meat broths and other liquids, they are wholesome.
Fried in mustard oil or ghee as appropriate, they should be flavorful, tender, unctuous, and seasoned with pungent substances. (9)
Roots of radish and horse gram are beneficial, as are soups prepared from them; likewise, [soups] containing long pepper, barley, horse gram, and ginger are wholesome. (10)
One should drink the unctuous goat meat broth together with pomegranate and āmalaka;
by that, the six disorders beginning with chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) are eliminated. // 11 //
5.11b–d One should drink unctuous goat meat broth,
and one should drink especially well-aged wine that cleanses the channels;
in cases of pitta and other [doshas], honey-wine (madhv-ariṣṭa), clear wine (accha), and vāruṇī are particularly recommended.
5.12d–13. Or one may take honey-ariṣṭa, or vāruṇī liquor, or water prepared with the five roots (pañcamūla), or with tāmalakī,
or with the four parṇinīs, or with coriander and ginger.
Being favorable toward him, one should diligently prepare pure food for him, prepared with milk or meat broth along with the roots of the ten [herbs]. (14)
Ghee containing *balā* should be administered with the meat-broth of carnivorous animals;
or ghee prepared with milk and honey, using ten times as much milk. (15)
Jīvantī, madhuka, drākṣā, the fruits of kuṭaja, puṣkaramūla, śaṭhī, kṛṣṇā, vyāghrī, gokṣuraka, and balā. (16)
Having made a paste of vyāghrī, gokṣuraka, balā, nīlotpala, tāmalakī, trāyamāṇā, and durālabhā,
ghee is cooked; this is the supreme remedy for the king of diseases (fever).
Ghee prepared with dates, raisins, madhuka, parūṣaka,
and pippalī cures hoarseness of voice, cough, dyspnea, and fever.
Fresh ghee that arises from milk boiled with the ten roots, taken together with long pepper and honey, is the supreme awakener of the voice. (19)
Clarified butter prepared from the decoction of the five groups of five roots (pañcamūlas) destroys pain in the head, sides, and shoulders, and removes cough, dyspnea, and fever. (20)
Ghee prepared with the juice of the five roots and four times its quantity of milk conquers the sevenfold strength of pulmonary consumption (yakṣman). // 21 //

5.21cd–22ab: For one suffering from consumption, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with an equal amount of milk, along with the seven-fold strength [of the patient] and a *ṣaṭpala* preparation consisting of *pañcakola*, barley-alkali, and the six salts; this purifies the channels.
It conquers gulma, fever, abdominal enlargement, splenic disorders, malabsorption syndrome, anemia, chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, cough, loss of digestive fire, edema, and upward-moving wind. (23)

Ghee prepared with rāsnā, balā, gokṣuraka, sthirā, and varṣābhū in water, containing jīvantī and pippalī as an internal ingredient, along with milk, is a conqueror of wasting diseases (śoṣa). // 24 //
One should boil milk that has been decocted with *aśvagandhā* along with ghee, sugar, and water; then one should cook a *tulā* of common meat in two *droṇas* of water. (25)

With that decoction reduced to one-eighth, one should prepare one *prastha* of ghee along with one *pala* each of the life-promoting (*jīvanīya*) drugs; this cures diseases caused by *vāta* and *pitta*. (26)
This meat and ghee, when drunk either with meat broth or combined with it, conquers cough, dyspnea, loss of voice, wasting, and pain in the heart and flanks. (27)
Or one may add cardamom, *ajamodā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *saurāṣṭrī*, the three acridities (*vyoṣa*), and *citraka* to meat broths;
or the heartwoods (*sāra*) derived from *ariṣṭa*, *gāyatrī*, *śāla*, and *bījaka*.
One should boil eight palas each of bhallātaka and viḍaṅga separately in sixteen times their quantity of water until reduced to one-sixteenth part. (29)
Furthermore, when this has been prepared, one should add a prastha of ghee, six palas of tāvakṣīrī,
thirty palas of sugar, and twice as much honey.

Three palas of this [mixture] made from ghee and the three aromatics (trijātaka), stirred with a churning-stick and licked, followed by a draught of milk in the forenoon, is said to be a rejuvenative (rasāyana) that requires no restrictive regimen.

It is pure, beneficial for the eyes, promotes longevity, stimulates digestion, and quickly destroys urinary disorders (meha), abdominal tumors (gulma), consumption (kṣaya), jaundice (pāṇḍu-roga), and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara). // 32 //
And those ghee-and-jaggery preparations which have been prescribed for chest wounds (kṣata) should also be employed in cases of wasting (kṣaya);
[the ingredients] are cinnamon, cardamom, long pepper, and milk-tree resin, with sugar added in double the quantity of each in successive order. 33.
When powdered, eaten with honey and ghee, or licked as a linctus, they are beneficial for the voice and destroy cough, consumption, dyspnea, pain in the flanks, and phlegm. (34)
And these [medicines] should be licked with ghee, especially in cases of hoarseness of voice; furthermore, one should employ nasal drops, medicated smoke, and other such treatments.
In that case as well, if the condition is born of Vāta, one should drink the medicine lukewarm after a meal.
5.35–36. One should drink ghee prepared with the fresh juices of *kāsamardaka*, *vārtākī*, and *mārkava* as an after-meal potion;
this conquers cough and improves the voice. Alternatively, it may be prepared with *ārtagala*.
Or a paste of *badarī* leaves fried in ghee with rock salt;
or oil prepared with *madhuka*, grapes, long pepper, and the fruits of *kṛminut*. (37)

5.37–38. One should administer an enema (nastaḥ) prepared with long pepper (*pippalī*), fruits that destroy worms (*kṛmihṛtphala*), and the root of *haṃsapadī*. This should be followed by a drink of lukewarm water, along with rice cooked in jaggery and mixed with clarified butter (*sarpis*).
In this manner, one should eat milk-rice (pāyasa) and employ unctuous sudation;
when arising from Pitta, one should drink ghee followed by boiled, cooled milk.

One should eat milk-rice prepared with milk-porridge (pāyasa), along with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka), honey, and ghee, which has been cooked with a decoction and paste of the sprouts of milky trees (kṣīrivṛkṣa). 40.
Ghee prepared with balā, vidārigandhā, vidārī, and madhuka, along with salt, is an unsurpassed nasal medication (nasya) that restores the voice. (41)
Prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, pippalī, bṛhatī, and balā, prepared with milk and ghee, constitute an excellent nasal medication (nāvana) for the voice. (42)
One should lick the powder of sweet substances soaked in honey and ghee;
or, when the disease is born of phlegm, one should drink pungent drugs with urine while following a dry diet.
One should lick a paste of *kaṭphala*, *āmalaka*, and *vyoṣa* saturated with oil and honey;
or alternatively, *vyoṣa*, the alkalis, *agni*, *cavikā*, *bhārgī*, *pathyā*, and honey. (44)
One should drink barley gruel prepared with two parts of barley and one part each of long pepper and emblic myrobalan;
after eating, one should consume long pepper and dry ginger, or undergo a strong emetic treatment. // 45 //
One whose voice is impaired while speaking loudly should drink boiled milk mixed with sugar, honey, and sweet [medicinal] substances.
Delicious food, prepared with wholesome ingredients for one who has lost their appetite;
external and internal purification; and the extinction of the mind—these are the heart-pleasing medicines. (47)
Twice a day one should chew a tooth-stick and rinse the mouth with cleansing agents;
one should wash the mouth with astringent decoctions and inhale medicinal smoke. 48.
Pills made from powdered tālīśa mixed with camphor and sugar, as well as those called śaśāṅkaraśmi, are excellent edible foods that stimulate the appetite. (49)

5.49d–50. Edible foods that are highly appetizing should be given for loss of appetite caused by vāta. In that case, one should drink a powder made from hareṇu, kṛṣṇā, kṛmijit, drākṣā, saindhava, and nāgara with *prasannā* wine.
Or one may induce vomiting with ghee mixed with cardamom, bhārgī, alkali of barley, and asafoetida; or with water decocted with *vacā*; or, due to pitta, with jaggery-water. (51)
Or one should lick a mixture of sugar, ghee, the best salt, and honey;
if vomiting occurs due to phlegm, one should induce it with neem water or water infused with *dīpyaka* and *āragvadha*.
One should drink wine with honey and *ariṣṭa*, as well as sharp liquors with honey and *mādhava*;
and one should drink the previously mentioned powder of *hareṇu* and other ingredients with warm water. (53)

A powder made from cardamom, cinnamon, nagakesara, long pepper, black pepper, and ginger, with each subsequent ingredient increased by one part in sequence, destroys [the disease] when combined with an equal amount of sugar. (54)
[This formulation] cures excessive salivation, loss of appetite, heart disease, pain in the flanks, cough, dyspnea, and throat disorders;
it consists of *yavānī*, *tintiḍīka*, sour *vetasa*, medicinal herbs, and pomegranate. (55)
Having taken one karṣa of kola and four palas of sugar, along with half a karṣa each of dhānyaka, sauvarcala salt, ajājī, and varāṅga; // 56 //
One hundred pippalīs and two hundred maricas—this powder is supremely appetizing, beneficial for the heart, constipating, and it destroys [diseases]. (57)
This powder stimulates digestion,
improves the appetite, and removes obstructions, cough, heart disease, pain in the flanks, splenic disorders, hemorrhoids,
and diseases of the *grahaṇī*. It consists of *tālīśapattra*, black pepper, ginger, and auspicious long pepper.
With each subsequent ingredient increasing by one part, and cinnamon and cardamom each being half a part, this powder—containing eight times as much sugar—is appetizing and digestive. (59)

5.59ab Those [drugs] increase in proportion by each successive part. 5.59cd That powder is a digestive stimulant (dīpana) and cures cough, dyspnea, anorexia, vomiting, splenic disorders, and pain in the heart and flanks;
it destroys anemia, fever, and diarrhea, and facilitates the downward movement of obstructed wind (mūḍhavāta).

One should eat groats prepared with barley that has been soaked overnight in water containing the alkaline juice of *arka* and *amṛtā*, along with other suitable foods; by this, a strong person will vomit. (61)
5.61–62ab. One should consume meat from wild animals that has been roasted on a spit over a decoction of *arka*, *amṛtā*, milk, and water, along with pungent and bitter substances.
One should also eat dry foods that are very light, followed by a drink of the broth of chickpeas and similar legumes.
When there is excessive secretion of phlegm, the wind (vāyu) expels that phlegm;
the wise man should overcome that discharge of kapha by means of unctuous and warm remedies alone. (63)
One should overcome chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) with treatments that are specifically unctuous and warm; one should also employ this same regimen for vomiting (vamatha).
In particular, for chronic rhinitis, one should habitually practice oil massages, oleation, and sudation.

5.64ab In cases of chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), one should follow this regimen: apply unctuous poultices (utkārikā) and boluses to the head, sides of the chest, neck, and other areas, and administer meat broths that are salty, sour, pungent, and hot, combined with unctuous substances (sneha).
In cases of pain in the head, shoulders, and sides, one should apply treatments according to the specific dosha involved;
well-prepared poultices made from the flesh of aquatic and marshy animals may also be used. (66)

In that case, when there is a combination of doshas, the desired treatment consists of the four unctuous substances (catuḥ-sneha) along with a paste made of tagara, yaṣṭimadhu, śatapuṣpā, kuṣṭha, and candana. (67)
Likewise, [a decoction] with balā, rāsnā, and sesame seeds, along with ghee, madhuka, and utpala; or with punarnavā, kṛṣṇagandhā, balā, vīrā, and vidārī. // 68 //
Nasal drops, inhalations of medicated smoke, unctuous substances taken after meals, oils for massage, and likewise the administration of enemas; 69.
Or, according to the specific humor involved, one should remove their vitiated blood using horn and other instruments;
an external application (pradeha) with lotus, ushira, and sandalwood mixed with ghee is excellent.
Or [one may apply] dūrvā, madhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, and kesar soaked in ghee;
or with oil prepared from vaṭa and other trees, or with clarified butter washed a hundred times.
Anointing with milk and sprinkling with a decoction of madhuka are recommended;
because the digestive fire is generally impaired, one suffers from diarrhea accompanied by mucus. (72)

For that patient suffering from consumption (rājayakṣman), the beneficial medicines prescribed for diarrhea and disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) should be administered; one must take great care to preserve the feces of the emaciated patient. (73)

For one afflicted by the exhaustion of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), his strength indeed comes from excrement; provided he eats meat according to the proper method and subsequently drinks *mārdvīka* wine. (74)
Consumption finds no opportunity against one whose vigor is not diminished;
[one should consume] wine with its scum, Mārdvīka, Ariṣṭas, Sīdhu, and Mādhava.
While eating meat, one should drink non-intoxicating *sīdhu* or *mādhvika* wines as appropriate for the purpose of a post-prandial drink;
this is for the sake of releasing obstructions in the channels and for the nourishment of strength and vitality.
One should cause the patient, who has been well-anointed with oil, to immerse themselves in vats filled with oil, milk, or water;
having emerged, they should be anointed again with various unctuous substances and comforted with gentle hands. (77)

Aśvagandhā, apāmārga, tarkārī, madhuka, balā, vidārī, mustard seeds, kuṣṭha, rice grains, and the fruit of atasī; (79)
One should grind together all of these—black gram, sesame seeds, and fermenting agent—and then add three times as much barley flour, mixed with curd and honey. (80)
This massage should be performed with a paste of white mustard seeds and bathing herbs; it bestows nourishment, complexion, and strength. (81)
This cleansing should be performed with baths and medicinal herbs.
He should bathe in waters that are pleasant for the season and prepared with life-promoting (*jīvanīya*) substances.
He should employ ornaments such as perfumes and garlands, which destroy misfortune (*alakṣmī*). 82.
5.82–83: Adornment with perfumes, garlands, and the like;
the sight of friends; listening to songs, instrumental music, and festive celebrations; medicinal enemas; milk and clarified butter; and the moderate consumption of wine and meat.
Alcohol, meat, virtuous conduct,
and various forms of divine refuge as prescribed in the Atharva Veda are likewise honored.

In the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna), since vomiting generally arises from the provocation of the stomach (āmāśaya), fasting is beneficial at first, except in cases involving Vāyu; in those instances, one should employ emesis. // 1 //
6.1b Generally, emesis is considered beneficial for a strong person with abundant morbid humors who vomits continuously and profusely;
thereafter, a heart-tonic purgative should be administered gradually along with wines or fruit juices. // 2 //
For indeed, [the emetic] taken with milk leads the humor that has moved upward back downward;
moreover, for one who is dry and weak, that very same medicine serves as a pacifier. // 3 //
Food that is dried, agreeable, wholesome, and light is recommended;
likewise, fasting, vegetable soups, meat broths, *kāmbalika* preparations, and *khala* pastes are advised.
Vegetables, linctuses, foods, savory soups, sweet syrups, drinks, various kinds of dry snacks, fruits, and bathing powders for rubbing; (5)
Fragrances—pleasant scents derived from incense, fruits, flowers, food, and drink—and the sudden sprinkling of cold water on the face immediately after eating. 6.
Ghee drunk with rock salt, especially when slightly warm, cures vomiting caused by Vāta, as well as cough and a sense of fluidity in the heart. (7)
Or milk prepared with vyoṣa and the three salts; or milk boiled with pomegranate juice; or milk boiled with ginger, curd, and coriander, mixed with an equal amount of water.

Milk boiled with an equal amount of water, or milk drunk with an equal amount of water; or clarified butter with evident rock salt; or the meat broth of wild fowl prepared with sour fruits; or unctuous food prepared with ginger, curd, and pomegranate. (6.8–9)
In this condition, lukewarm unctuous purgatives with salt are beneficial;
for the purpose of purging in cases born of Pitta, *trivṛt* should be administered with the expressed juices of grapes and sugarcane. (10)
Ghee or tilvaka oil should be administered when the pitta is aggravated and has reached the seat of kapha;
one who has undergone purification should eliminate that pitta upwards using sweet and bitter substances.

One should drink a stirred potion (mantha) or gruel (yavāgū) with parched grain, honey, and sugar; or one should eat śāli and ṣaṣṭika rice with side dishes made from mung beans and the meat of wild animals.
One should drink very cold water produced from a clod of earth that has been heated in fire, mixed with parched grain (lāja), honey, and sugar; or alternatively,
water that has been infused overnight with mung beans, uśīra, long pepper (kaṇā), and coriander (dhānya).
One may take grape juice, sugarcane juice, guḍūcī decoction, or even milk;
or [water] produced from the tender leaves of the jambu and mango, uśīra, and the shoots and sprouts of the vaṭa tree. (14)
The juice of grapes and the juice of sugarcane, or a decoction made from the tips and shoots of the *vaṭa* tree mixed with honey, when drunk while cold, cures vomiting,
fever, diarrhea, fainting, and even difficult-to-conquer thirst. (6.14–15)
Or one should drink it cold with the juice of *dhātrī*, or with water decocted from *mudga* leaves;
or [one may take] the marrow of *kola*, sugar, parched grain, honey, cow dung, and *kaṇāñjana*. (16)
One should lick a paste of *kola* pulp, sugar, lac, bee excrement, and *rasāñjana* with honey;
or else, one should consume *pathyā*, *drākṣā*, or *badara* fruits with honey.
In cases arising from *kapha*, one should induce vomiting with *nimba*, *kṛṣṇā*, *piṇḍītaka*, and mustard seeds.
One should fasten a weak patient with lukewarm water mixed with medicinal paste;
he should drink a cooled decoction of the āragvadhādi group combined with honey. (18)
