One should conquer vomiting by licking a paste of realgar, long pepper, and black pepper with the juice of bījapūraka or of kapittha, mixed with honey. (20)
One should eat wood-apple with the three pungents (vyoṣa) along with honey, or lick durālabhā with black pepper,
coca, cardamom, cow-dung juice, and honey.
That which arises from an aversion to objects is pacified by agreeable treatment;
that which arises from worms is cured by the remedies prescribed by physicians for heart-disease caused by worms. (22)
Likewise, their respective remaining [defilements] and those produced by them are likewise [to be abandoned]. (22cd)
For due to excessive vomiting, the vital wind (mātariśvā) inevitably becomes provoked by the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu);
therefore, in this condition, one should employ the procedures prescribed for excessive emesis, as well as those that are astringent and nourishing. (23)
Therefore, in this case of excessive emesis, one should employ the stabilizing and nourishing procedures prescribed [in the treatise],
such as honey-molasses confections, meat broths, medicated ghees, Kalyāṇaka, Tryūṣaṇa, and Jīvana [ghṛtas].
Milk prepared with pathya and electuaries bring about the pacification of persistent vomiting. // 24 //
6.24ab Clarified butter, jaggery, meat broths, and ghees—this concludes the treatment for vomiting; now follows the treatment for heart disease. // 24+1 //
In heart disease born of Vata, oil [should be used] along with whey, Sauvira, and buttermilk. // 25 //
Oil prepared with salts, along with urine and sour liquids, possesses the same therapeutic qualities. // 26 //
One should drink that [decoction] lukewarm with viḍa salt; it conquers abdominal tumors (gulma), flatulence, and pain.
Likewise, oil prepared with salts, along with urine and sour liquids, possesses similar qualities. // 26 //
Having boiled bilva, rāsnā, barley, kola, devadāru, punarnavā, kulattha, and the five roots (pañcamūla) in water, one should cook [the medicinal paste] in that [decoction]. // 27 //
One should employ that oil for nasal drops, internal drinking, and enemas, along with ginger, *vayaḥsthā*, salt, *kāyasthā*, asafoetida, and lotus seeds. (28)
Ghee boiled with *śuṇṭhī*, *kayasthā*, salt, *vayaḥsthā*, *hiṅgu*, *pauṣkara*, and *pathyā* overcomes pain in the flanks and heart, as well as abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
[This preparation is made] with two *palas* of *sauvarcala* salt and fifty *pathyās*. (6.28–29)
One *prastha* of ghee prepared with these [ingredients] conquers heart disease, dyspnea, and abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
[The ingredients are: pomegranate, black salt, ginger, asafoetida, and *amlavetasa*. (30)
6.30b–d: This powder—consisting of ginger, asafoetida, and sour vetasa—is excellent for destroying apatantraka, heart disease, and dyspnea. 6.31:
[The powder] made from puṣkaramūla, śaṭī, ginger, bījapūra, jaṭāmāṃsī, and abhayā [is also effective].
Yellow substances made into a paste, combined with alkali, ghee, sour liquids, and salt, remove cutting pain and colic; a lukewarm decoction of these has the same properties. (32)
It is prepared with yavānī, salt, kṣāra, vacā, jājī, and medicinal herbs,
along with pūtidāru, bījāhva, palāśa, śaṭhī, and pauṣkara.
6.33cd–6.33dv: He should drink alkaline water from barley (yavakṣāra), along with *pūtidāru*, *bījāhva*, *vijayā*, *śaṭhī*, and *pauṣkara*, as well as *yavānī*, with warm water.
By this, he shall overcome colic born of Vāta and even long-standing gulma. 33+(1)
It is split in seven nights, just as a cloud is dispersed by the wind. // 33+(1ū̆)ab //
Pañcakola, śaṭī, pathyā, jaggery, bījāhva, and pauṣkara, made into a paste with vāruṇī wine, fried in a mixture of ghee and oil, and combined with salt. (34)
In cases of pain in the heart, the flanks, or the genitals, as well as in abdominal tumors and disorders of the abdomen, one should eat [these remedies];
moreover, unctuous sudations and medicated clarified butters are beneficial here. (35)

6.35cd–36ab: For thirst, one should drink clarified butter that has been processed with the light *pañcamūla* or with ginger, or water boiled with them; or else, one may drink the supernatant liquid of *vāruṇī* wine, curd-whey, or fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*).
6.36c–v When the heart is afflicted by wind (māruta), characterized by stiffness, aching, and pain in the evening, one should administer *vāruṇī* liquor or the scum of curd (*dadhi-maṇḍa*).
This treatment is beneficial; however, when there is exhaustion from exertion and fainting, meat broths (*rasa*) are appropriate.
One suffering from heart disease should drink oil rich in fats derived from partridge, crane, peacock, quail, and cock, or "Sukumāraka" oil prepared with *balā*. (38)
6.38–39ab: Or one should administer unctuous preparations (sneha) beginning with partridge and crane meat, or the "great unctuous preparation" (mahāsneha) processed a hundred times with liquorice;
likewise, [a decoction] with rāsnā, jīvaka, jīvantī, balā, vyāghrī, and punarnavā.

One should cook a great unctuous substance (mahāsneha) with bhārgī, sthirā, vacā, and vyoṣa, along with a quarter-part of curd and whatever sour substances are available; when this is consumed, it [provides the desired result]. (40)
It is nourishing, bulk-promoting, strengthening, and a destroyer of wind (vāta) and heart disease;
it is beneficial for heart disease caused by vāta when the digestive fire is kindled and the condition involves fluid. 41.
Milk, curd, molasses, ghee, the meat of aquatic and marshy animals—these indeed should be avoided in all four types of heart disease. (42)
In the remaining cases, as well as in that vātika type associated with stiffness, dullness,
and swelling, one should employ dry and hot treatment when there is an association with kapha.

In cases of Pitta disorders, a purgative combined with grape juice, sugarcane juice, sugar, honey, and parūṣaka fruits is pleasing to the heart; once purified, the subsequent regimen should likewise alleviate Pitta.
6.44c–d A purgative that is wholesome for the heart should be administered, as well as the external and internal cleansing treatments prescribed for chest wounds, pitta disorders, and fever.
6.45 One should drink a paste of *kaṭukā* and *madhuka* with sugar and water.
[This oil] is prepared with śreyasī, sugar, grapes, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, utpala, balā, dates, kākolī, and the two types of medā.
Buffalo ghee mixed with milk cures diseases of the bile and heart. Prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, lotus-root joints, and kaserukā [are also beneficial]. (47)

One should cook ghee with those [drugs], along with ginger and *śaivala*, together with milk; when cooled, it should be taken with honey, as should that which is prepared from the group of sweet (sweetening) substances.
One should administer an enema (vasti) consisting of oil prepared with madhuka and honey;
in the case of a disorder arising from phlegm (kapha), one should induce vomiting after fomentation with a decoction of picumanda and vacā.
One should administer an enema prepared with licorice (*madhuka*), honey, and oil; [the patient] should consume *picumanda*, *vacā*, water,
the broth of *kulattha* and desert animals, pungent substances, wine, and barley.
One should drink a powder made from vacā, hiṅgu, the two types of salt, and nāgara. // 50 //

[One should take it] with warm water containing śailaja, yavānaka, kaṇā, and yavakṣāra, or likewise with fermented fruit juices, grain-sour gruel, kaulattha soup, urine, or fermented liquors. // 51 //
6.51ab A decoction of śailaja, yavānikā, kaṇā, puṣkaramūla, abhayā, śuṇṭhī, śaṭhī, rāsnā, vacā,
and kaṇā; likewise, [a decoction] of abhayā, śuṇṭhī, mādrī, pītadru, and kaṭphala.
6.52bc–cc: Likewise, a decoction of *śaṭhī*, *rāsnā*, *vacā*, and *kaṇā*; and a decoction of *abhayā* and *śuṇṭhī*.
[A medicated ghee] is prepared from a decoction of *rohītaka*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, *udumbara*, *arjuna*, *palāśa*, and *vaṭa*, combined with the powder of *vyoṣa* and *trivṛt*.
A linctus with pleasant water as a vehicle destroys disorders of *kapha*.
One should drink various alkalis along with clarified butter (*ājya*) for the treatment of *śleṣma*-derived abdominal tumors (*gulma*). (54)
6.54 For one who drinks warm water after a meal, one should employ the *rasāyana* known as Śilāhvaya or Brāhma;
likewise, one may use the electuary of Āmalaka or the *prāśa* composed by Agastya.
6.55b–d: And here, the *brāhma* elixir (*rasāyana*) should be consumed, as was prepared by Agastya;
it should be consumed by one who suffers from colic when food has been eaten excessively, when it is being digested, or when digestion is nearly complete.
That [disease] would be pacified by kuṣṭha, kṛmijit, the two types of salt, and tilvaka. // 56 //
6.56ab He who experiences colic after eating food should drink a powder of devadāru and ativiṣā with warm water;
he for whom it is more severe when the food is digested should be purged with fats and then again with fruits.

When food is being digested, or when there is a constant increase in piercing pain due to sharp-acting roots, the vāyu, its movement obstructed and having entered the stomach (āmāśaya), generally becomes aggravated. (58)
6.58dv Because it becomes aggravated in the stomach (āmāśaya), therefore its downward movement must be induced through purification, fasting, and digestive treatments;
and all anthelmintic medicine [should be used] for heart disease caused by worms. 59.
6.59d–60. In heart disease caused by worms and in thirsts, a regimen that subdues vāta and pitta is generally recommended.
In all cases, external and internal measures that are cooling, as well as palliative and purificatory, are advised.
6.60b–d. Generally, this procedure is employed; likewise, both pacifying (śamana) and purifying (śodhana) [measures] are used.

Celestial water that is cold and mixed with honey, as well as terrestrial water possessing those same qualities, [is beneficial], as is water cooled by heated clods of earth, potsherds, sand, and the like. 61.
Water boiled with sugar or with the five roots (pañcamūla), or a stirred drink (mantha) prepared with parched grain flour (lāja-saktu) and preceded by darbha grass, is recommended. 62.
Cold gruel made from raw barley, mixed with sugar and honey, as well as gruel made from *śāli* rice or from aged *kodrava*, should be used as a poultice. (63)
Food prepared with cold substances that possess a cooling potency,
along with milk mixed with sugar and honey, should be given to one who has been sprinkled with cold water.
With non-sour and non-salty juices of wild animals fried in ghee, as well as with soups of mung beans and other pulses combined with life-promoting (jīvanīya) broths. // 65 //
Nasal therapy (nasya) with juices that are not deficient in salt,
as well as milk and ghee prepared with cooling [drugs], and likewise the juice of sugarcane, are beneficial;
furthermore, gargles (gaṇḍūṣa) for pacification mentioned in the Sūtrasthāna are also recommended.

6.66b–c With cold juices of sugarcane as well; 6.66d–67a Ointments and other treatments prescribed for burning sensations and fever; remaining still; delight of the mind; and the sight and recollection of great rivers, lakes, and the like.

6.67d–68. Furthermore, when thirst arises from wind (vāta), the sight or remembrance [of water] is beneficial; curd with jaggery is recommended, as are nourishing, cooling juices and the water decocted from the vidārī-gaṇa and other such groups.
In cases arising from pitta, one may take water decocted with the *vidārī* group of drugs mixed with sugar; or the juice of ripe *udumbara* fruit;
or its decoction; or its cold infusion (*himas*); or likewise water decocted with the *śārivā* group of drugs.
And with such groups [of drugs], one should prepare cold infusions containing sugar and honey,
as well as those prepared with sweet medicinal herbs and milky trees in a similar manner.
The sprouts of the citron, the grape, the banyan, and the cane;
the roots of *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses; and *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice) boiled together in water. (71)

In fever arising from phlegm (kapha), one should drink either grapes and other such fruits, or the water decocted from the five essences (pañcasāra); or, for vomiting, one should administer emesis with water infused with nimba blossoms.
One should drink water prepared with bilva, āḍhakī, pañcakola, and the five types of darbha grass, or water processed with turmeric, mixed with honey and sugar. (73)
One should drink water prepared with *darbha* and *kacchaka*, or at night, drink green gram soup (*mudga-yūṣa*) with *vyoṣa*, *paṭolī*, and the sprouts of *nimba*.
One should also habitually consume barley-based food and apply sharp gargles, nasal drops, and linctuses.
When all [the doshas] are present, that [purgative] is desired as the destroyer; likewise, emesis is desired with trikaṭu, āruṣkara, vacā, and phalāmla, along with warm water and whey. (75)
One who knows the proper time should drink warm gruel-scum when suffering from indigestion, and cold *mantha* when thirsty;
or, when exhausted by fatigue, one should drink meat broth or *mantha* mixed with sugar. (76)
Or one should drink wine with sugar, or a churned drink (mantha) made from barley, jujube fruits, and roasted grain flour, mixed with sugar, after exposure to the sun;
and one should smear all the limbs with sesame oil-cake and sour gruel (kāñjika).
After a cold bath, one should drink wine diluted with water, or water mixed with treacle, or half-watered wine combined with sour and salty substances. (78)

6.78ab After a cold bath, one who is thirsty should drink wine diluted with water or molasses-water. 6.78cd However, one whose digestive fire has been intensified by unctuous or sharp substances should drink water that is naturally cool, combined with sour and salty flavors.
One who is thirsty after undigested food should drink warm water due to the presence of oiliness; however, once the food is digested, one should drink scum (maṇḍa).

6.79 But one whose digestive fire has become excessively sharp from the intake of unctuous substances (sneha) should drink molasses-water as cold as ice when thirsty after eating unctuous food; however, if one is thirsty after eating heavy food and drinks hot water, one should induce emesis with that [hot water].
For all wasting diseases, every nourishing medicine that is beneficial for wasting is indicated;
likewise, milk or goat's meat broth is recommended for those who are emaciated, weak, or dry. (81)
In cases of upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), milk boiled with drugs that cure wasting and cough should be administered;
if the condition arises from complications of disease, rice-water mixed with sugar and honey should be given.
6.82 When thirst arises due to disease or contagion, drinking is recommended, as is every therapeutic action considered in relation to the disease and other factors.
If one who is suffering from thirst and emaciated by a prior illness should not obtain water... 83.
6.83cd–84ab: One who is emaciated by a previous illness and suffering from thirst will, consequently, quickly meet with death or a chronic disease;
therefore, one should first conquer that thirst with wholesome food, drink, and medicines.
6.84dv One should first conquer craving; once that is conquered, any other disease can also be treated. 84ab //
In the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna):

In cases of alcoholism (madātyaya) where the humors (doṣas) are of equal strength, one should first treat whichever humor is perceived to be predominant, following the sequence of the locations of kapha (kapha-sthānānupūrvyā). // 1 //

7.1cv Generally, alcoholism (madātyaya) follows the sequence of the locations of *kapha*, ending with *pitta* and *vāta*. It is the disease that arises from drinking [alcohol] in deficient, improper, or excessive amounts. // 2 //
He is pacified by that very same liquor when drunk in equal measure;
for while liquor is similar to poison, poison acts with increasing intensity.
Due to its association with qualities such as sharpness and so forth, it requires another poison [to neutralize it];
for when it is drunk in excessive measure, being sharp, hot, sour, and burning, [it acts as an antidote].
When the moisture of food-essence is corrupted by alcohol and reaches a state of alkalinity, it produces intoxication, thirst, delusion, fever, internal burning, and confusion. (5)
When the vital air (māruta) is obstructed in the channels by a disorder aggravated by alcohol,
there arise extremely intense pains in the head, the bones, and the joints.

When the disorders of digested food and wine have subsided and there is a desire for food and lightness of body, wine itself— administered appropriately according to the prescribed method— is what cures those very disorders.
For alkaline matter quickly attains sweetness when combined with sour substances;
and among sour things, wine is the best, as it is fully capable of liquefying the humors.
7.8dv Sufficient is the drainage of the humors (doṣa-visrāvaṇa) by means of sharp and hot substances and other qualities previously mentioned for stimulating digestion;
moreover, because it is wholesome (sātmya), that very [regimen] is the supreme means for restoring the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātu).
One should administer the medicine for intoxication for seven or eight nights;
by this much time, the drink that has taken an improper course is digested. (10)
Thereafter, one should administer the appropriate remedy for whatever disease subsequently arises, having already completed the treatment for the alcoholism. (11)
7.11dv For one who has consumed an excessive amount of medicine, if vāta is predominant, one should administer wine prepared from flour and combined with bījapūraka,
vṛkṣāmla, kola, dāḍima, and dīpyaka. // 12 //
With yavānī, hapuṣā, jīraka, vyoṣa, the three salts, and fresh ginger;
with roasted meats on a spit, and with harītakī and unctuous parched grain flour (saktu); 13.

7.13b–c: [These are prepared] with the three pungents (vyoṣa), the three salts, and arjaka; roasted on a spit (śūlya) meats, and green ginger (haritaka). Hot, unctuous, sour, and salty fatty meats and broths are beneficial, as are rāgas and ṣāḍavas prepared with slices of mango and hog-plum (āmrātaka). 7.14d: [These are beneficial]. 7.15a: [These are 7.54d: [These are beneficial]. 7.55a: [These are beneficial]. 7.
Warm, unctuous, sour, and salty wines, meats, and broths are beneficial; likewise, well-prepared *rāga* and *khāṇḍava* condiments,
as well as preparations of wheat and black gram that are soft, varied, and pleasant to the palate.
Containing moist ginger, fermented grain-porridge, sour gruel, meat, and so forth. (15)
The juice of the pomegranate, the decoction of the minor five roots (kanīya-pañcamūla), and the juice of the vātsaka-vāruṇī—fragrant, salty, cold, and free from impurities—are [recommended]. (16)
7.16b–d. Or, one should take *nigada*, *vāccha*, *vāruṇī*, ginger, coriander, and likewise whey, fermented rice-gruel (*śukta*), clear sour water, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
There should also be warm oil massage, dry rubbing, bathing, and thick clothing.
There was thick incense made of agallochum, and a paste of agallochum and saffron;
there were women endowed with beautiful breasts, thighs, and hips, their slender bodies heated by youth. (18)
Beloved women are appropriate for embracing with joy and for massaging; in cases of a predominance of pitta, honey mixed with sugar or plenty of water [is beneficial]. (19)
One should prepare a very cold drink made from the juices of pomegranate, dates, bhavya, grapes, and parūṣaka, combined with sugar and parched grain flour; such a *pānaka* should be used.
Wine mixed with honey, combined with decoctions of the sweet group such as *bhavya*, grapes, and *parūṣaka*, or even with *paṭolī* and pomegranate, should be consumed;
one should eat *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice along with the meat of rabbit, deer, or grey partridge. (7.20–21)
One suffering from thirst and burning sensations should vomit up the aggravated phlegm and bile using the juices of *satīna*, mung beans, *āmalaka*, *paṭolī*, and pomegranate. (22)

Having drunk cold water, or wine mixed with abundant sugarcane juice, or grape juice, one who has undergone purgation finds the administration of refreshing drinks and the like to be supremely beneficial. (23)
Likewise, the digestive fire blazes up for him, digesting the remnants of the morbid humors and food, in cases of cough with blood-stained expectoration and pain in the sides and breasts. (24)
When there is burning thirst and agitation in the heart and chest, one should take the juice of *guḍūcī*, *bhadramustā*, or *paṭola*. (25)
One should administer [this] along with ginger as a follow-up meal consisting of partridge meat, in cases of excessive thirst or when vāta and pitta are intensely aggravated. (26)
One should administer this with dry ginger (nāgara); one should give grape juice as a cold drink to facilitate the downward movement of the humors (doṣa).
Once it is digested, one should eat with sweet and sour goat meat broth.
Thirsty, one should drink wine sparingly while protecting against intoxication, mixed with plenty of water;
or one may drink water infused with musta, pomegranate, and parched grain, or water boiled with the parṇinī group of herbs. (28)
Or [fever arises] from the roots of the *pāṭalī* or the blue lotus, or from its very nature;
or when the water element has been depleted by excessive drinking of alcohol and the fire element has become excited. (29)

Or, for one whose throat, palate, and lips are parched and who moves about after pulling out the tongue, one should, according to one's desire, have him drink water that has been struck by the midnight breeze, using the tubers of *paṭola* and blue lotus.
The juice of *kola*, pomegranate, *vṛkṣāmla*, *cukrīkā*, and *cukrikā*—this "five-sour" (*pañcāmlaka*) application to the mouth immediately subdues thirst. (31)
When the heat of the wind (pānoṣmā), intensified by bile and blood, reaches the skin, it produces a terrible burning sensation; in that case, extremely cooling treatment is prescribed.
But when that heat of the wind has reached the skin, it does not subside even when the tissues are satisfied by juices; in such a case, one should pierce the *rohiṇī* vein.
One should conquer an excess of phlegm through scraping and fasting, or one should drink [medicinal decoctions]. (7.32–33)

When the patient is free from undigested matter (āmadoṣa) and hungry, one should at the proper time have them drink a large quantity of cold water mixed with honey, along with any one of the following: ginger (śuṇṭhī), sthirā, uśīra, or duḥsparśā. // 34 //
One should take aged sugar-cane wine, honey-wine, ariṣṭa, or even sidhu, combined with parching and nourishing agents, and mixed with yavānī and ginger. (35)

One should feed [the patient] barley and wheat with a thin, small amount of broth, along with *kaulāttha* pulse, slightly mixed with ghee and characterized by warm, sour, pungent, and bitter flavors. (36)
7.36c–d With warm water, pungent and bitter substances, or with the juices of dried radish or of animals that roam arid lands; or with sour vetasa, vṛkṣāmla, paṭolī, vyoṣa, and pomegranate.
7.37a–b [One should eat] with these, along with sour fruits, vṛkṣāmla, paṭolī, the three acrids (vyoṣa), and pomegranate.

7.37–38. [A dish] prepared with pāṭalī, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and pomegranate; containing abundant pieces of ginger, black pepper, and fresh green ginger; seasoned with the acidic juices of citron and other fruits; fried in meat broth and served with rice.
It was filled with many *karīra* and *karamarda* trees, very beautiful, clearly possessing the eight types of salt, and provided with various kinds of grinding-stones. // 39 //

7.39dv–40. The *vikalpita-vimardaka* preparation is as follows: one should eat meat with fire [as a digestive stimulant] and drink Mādhava liquor along with sugar, *sauvarcala* salt, cumin, tamarind, and sour cane-juice.
One should drink Madhava wine, free from impurities, with one-eighth part each of cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper, along with the beneficial eight-fold salt (aṣṭāṅga-lavaṇa).
This is helpful in cases of alcoholism (madātyaya) where kapha predominates, as it cleanses the channels and stimulates the digestive fire.
By means of dry and hot unguents, rubbing the body, bathing, eating, fasting, engaging with women who desire him through skillful means, and by staying awake, [the fever is pacified]. // 42 //
Alcoholism characterized by a predominance of phlegm (kapha) subsides quickly; this is the treatment prescribed for each according to the strength of the respective dosha. (43)

In the case of the ten types of combined disorders (*saṃnipāta*), one should likewise apply this formulation to the remaining types as well, using *tvak*, *nāgapuṣpa*, *magadhā*, *marica*, *ajāji*, and *dhānyaka*. (44)
A refreshing drink made from *parūṣaka*, *madhūka*, *elā*, and *surāhvā* combined with sugar, along with the juice of *kapittha*, is heart-pleasing when stirred with moonlight. (45)
In all cases of alcoholism, wine that stimulates the appetite and kindles the digestive fire should be drunk;
yet one should not drink it without first agitating the mind or without impairing the body. 46.

For intoxication does not cause the disorder of alcoholism (*madātyaya*) unless it agitates the mind or impairs the body; therefore, exhilarating treatment is prescribed even when purification and pacification therapies have been performed, provided the fault of intoxication persists. (7.46–47)

If it does not subside when the phlegm has been depleted and weakness and lightness have arisen, then for that patient whose [stomach] is impaired by liquor and in whom vāta and pitta predominate, [the following should be done]. 48.
Just as rain is for a tree scorched by the summer heat, so milk quickly nourishes one who has been weakened by liquor; indeed, the depleted milk causes him to flourish.

For one emaciated by alcohol, milk when drunk nourishes [the body] very quickly; it is equal to *ojas* in all its qualities and is the opposite of alcohol. When the disease has been overcome by the milk and strength has arisen, one should discontinue it. (7.49–50)
7.50 Once the disease has been conquered by the use of milk,
one should gradually practice the administration of milk and wine in very small quantities, so that one is not touched by complications arising from the destruction of the wasting (vikṣaya). 7.51.
One should not be afflicted by complications arising from the destruction of the *viṭ* (fecal matter) or the depletion of *dhātus*, as these two conditions may occur;
however, for them, ghee, milk, nourishing enemas (*vasti*), massage, dry powdering (*udvartana*), bathing, and food and drink that conquer *vāta* are auspicious remedies. (7.51–52)
For one who drinks wine in a balanced manner, no disease arising from wine occurs;
therefore, his regimen will be described here, which leads exclusively to well-being. (53)
She who possesses the great splendor of Āśvina and the strength of Sārasvata;
she who possesses the heroic power of Indra and the majesty of Vaiṣṇava.
She who is the weapon of the god whose banner is the sea-monster (Kāma), she who is the human goal of Balarāma,
and she who is invoked in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, in the mouth of the twice-born, and in the sacrificial fire.

7.55b-v And that which is the purpose of man for strength, [the goddess] who arose from the great ocean as it was being churned by the gods and demons along with all medicinal herbs, together with Śrī, the moon, and nectar; 56.
She who persists in many forms, never relinquishing her power of intoxication through honey-wine, spring-wine, maireya, sidhu, molasses-distillate, and the like.
7.57 Drinking which, without relinquishing its power of intoxication, wanton women truly bear their name;
even a woman of good family, having drunk it, leads her mind to arrogance. 58.
Having encountered her, the limbs of even a sage’s heart are embraced by the bodiless god [of love] somewhere;
and by the threats of her arched brows, which break like waves, the mind of a proud woman is subdued.
By pleasing one [deity], she brings about the fulfillment of both, just as a woman who has obtained a troop of Apsarases delights in acquiring warriors according to her desire. (60)

Just as men, having obtained soldiers at their will, cast away their lives in battle like blades of grass— even after practicing that [meditation] for a long time in many ways and with great effort— yet it remains full of conflict. (7.60–61)
7.61 Having reached which they constantly abandon their lives through the excessive force of joy, he now serves that very same [state] as if it were before;
seeing which, he is no longer overcome by grief, agitation, discontent, or fear. 62.
Without her, neither the social gathering nor the great festival nor the garden shines for him;
and remembering her again and again many times, he grieves when separated from her. (63)

But having remembered her many times, she who was once displeasing now brings joy; she who, when pleased, is heaven itself; and by whom, abiding in the heart, one considers even Indra to be in a wretched state. (7.63–64)
Inexpressible and tasting of bliss, which is supremely to be known only by oneself—thus, in various states, she imitates her beloved. (65)
That which becomes especially dear to one who is already dear attains the state of being most beloved;
it is praised as love, as delight, as speech, and as nourishment.
When the occasion for drinking arises, gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans may drink that liquor according to the prescribed rule. 67.

Those diseases arising from fat, wind, and phlegm do not occur [among those protected] by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and mānavas; nor do those terrible diseases which do not succumb to wine when used according to the prescribed rules.
And those diseases that arise from liquor when it is not prepared according to the prescribed method— those severe ailments do not succeed [in being cured].
There is a certain state of the body in which drinking is forbidden.
Except for liquor and for meat prepared with various medicinal herbs. // 69 //
7.69 Even meat from marshy or arid regions, prepared according to the prescribed method and provided with various medicinal herbs,
how could it be properly digested without the accompaniment of wine?
And what merit would there be in the use of garlic—which destroys even the most violent diseases caused by wind—if it were devoid of liquor and meat? (71)
7.71 How much benefit might there be from such an application? How much benefit might arise from this practice?
In the extraction of deeply embedded foreign bodies, and in the application of surgical instruments, caustics, and fire, one who has drunk wine endures the physician’s boastings with ease. 7.72
7.72b–c: In procedures involving surgery, caustics, and thermal cautery, it stimulates the digestive fire, is appetizing, and dispels grief and fatigue;
there is nothing else superior to this for promoting health, strength, and nourishment.
Therefore, one who cherishes life should always drink this, which dispels grief and fatigue;
it is beneficial for those who depend on him and those who depend on them, and it is the supreme means for accomplishing the Dharma.
Having bathed and prostrated before the gods, brahmins, and teachers, and having assigned to each of his dependents their respective livelihoods,
he should then proceed to the drinking ground— which has been sprinkled with fragrant water— located near the pavilion for food.
Then, upon a lovely, well-spread bed, surrounded by friends, servants, and beloved women,
he listened to his own world-transcending fame being extolled by throngs of bards and minstrels.
And the song of the playful women, beautiful with its grace and accompanied by dance, resounded along with the sounds of soft musical instruments,
the tinkling of waist-bands with moving bells, and the warbling of pet birds.
7.77b–78a: There was singing accompanied by dance to the sounds of melodious musical instruments, with sets of waist-bands featuring clearly tinkling bells,
made of various gems, gold, and earthy materials.
With various drinking vessels made of gems and gold, originating from the *aupageya* mines, their bodies were draped in watered silk garments (*kṣauma*) adorned with diverse painted designs.
7.78b–c Even with their limbs covered in wet, variously patterned silk garments, they were capable of agitating the minds of the sages.
with beloved women whose glances are as restless as those of startled deer. // 78d //

With their beloveds, whose glances were as restless as startled deer, moving slowly and unsteadily due to the excessive weight of their breasts and hips, yet hurried by the agitation caused by the Lord;
thus they bore a gait that was unsettled and possessed the magical power to entice the hearts of the young.
It was being moved here and there simultaneously by slender-limbed women who were intoxicated by the wine of youth and whose minds were possessed by amorous playfulness.
Made exceedingly cool by the breezes from palm-leaf fans and lotus petals, it brings even its mere sight under one's control; how much more so when tasted, O Mind-born One? (81)

7.81d–82. How much more so when it is frequented by the moon-beams of mango nectar, made fragrant by the residence of jasmine, and graced by the brilliance of white flowers; bearing limbs as lovely as the body of the bodiless God of Love, shimmering like the waves reflected within a crystal shell.

Then, having first consumed jasmine (*mallikā*) with its radiant [fragrance], or a heart-pleasing powder of *tālīśa* and other ingredients, or that which establishes youthfulness (*vayaḥsthāpana*), along with crystal, pearl-oyster shell, and fine waves [of water]; and having caused those who desire it to drink that mixture with water upon a well-swept patch of ground, thereafter— (7.82–83)
7.83–84. A person who possesses fortitude and mindfulness, always practicing what is beneficial for the heart and promotes longevity without excess or deficiency,
and providing everything with appropriate treatment, [attains success].
Practicing neither less nor more, and maintaining every prescribed conduct with the proper ritual observance,
he increased his splendor through the reflection of the blossoming blue lotuses in the eyes [of the goddesses] he had conquered.
One should drink wine like the face of a beloved woman, from which the swarms of bees have been drawn away by its fragrance. // 85 //

Having thus drunk from the two cups— [the first] whose beauty was increased by the reflection of her lotus-born eyes, and [the second] which possessed a splendor enhanced by her own loveliness— he then honored all his attendants.
Having thus drunk three cups and honored all his attendants, he should then go to the dining hall and eat again in the presence of his physicians.
(7.86) Alternatively: Having thus drunk two cups and honored all his attendants, he should then go to the dining hall and eat again in the presence of his physicians. (7.86)
Combined with meat-cakes, ghee, fresh ginger, and other greens, along with sauvarcala salt. // 86c //
At night, one should drink only a small amount two or three times for the sake of embracing a woman. // 86d //
Having taken his beloved onto his lap in secret, by the pressure of his embrace between his arms... // 87a //
Her body was bristling with horripilation, perspiration had arisen upon it, and her breasts were trembling. // 87b //
If that skillful man does not hastily cause him to drink a draught of wine. // 87c //
7.87cd If that wise man does not, with impetuosity, cause her to drink the vomit of *sīdhu* wine, what then does he experience?
Thereafter, he undergoes the state of domestic life, which consists mostly of suffering. 87d.
Why should he experience in vain that household life which consists mostly of suffering? At that time,
he would rather enjoy the wine, which is more fragrant from contact with the faces of beautiful-bodied women.
Like a ruby gem that has quickly assumed the form of a liquid. // 88b //
And from the fatigue of sexual pleasure, intoxication arises even for one who drinks only a little. (88c)
Avoiding the depletion of his vital energy (ojas), he should sleep at most [the prescribed amount]. 88d.
Thus, drinking liquor according to this method, one is not deprived of the three aims of life (trivarga) and attains the supreme happiness found within this essence-less saṃsāra. (89)
This enjoyment of sovereignty is desirable even to the gods;
otherwise, in times of misfortune, wealth would become fuel for one's subsequent remorse.
Otherwise, when calamities befall him,
he would be censured as "one who possesses wealth yet is deprived of its enjoyment";
[the Creator] would have fashioned this miserly guardian of the treasure by destiny as one utterly devoid of it.
Therefore, by means of disciplined regulation, the consumption of drink is always beneficial, once one has conquered the independence of the sense organs that are greedy for their objects. (92)
Therefore,

this rule regarding drinking applies to those who possess wealth according to their circumstances; however, those who are like the Vasus in the future should drink wine in a beneficial measure, as it arises, according to their means.
As long as there is no confusion of vision, and as long as the mind does not waver, so long should a self-possessed person always abstain from intoxicants. 94.

One whose wind (vāta) is predominant should drink [medicinal oil], having been treated with massages, dry rubs, baths, garments, incense, and ointments, and having been conditioned by unctuous and warm foods and drinks. (95)
One who has been treated for a pitta disorder with various cooling measures— sweet, unctuous, and cold—
and who consumes food and drinks wine, does not suffer.
One of phlegmatic constitution who eats barley and wheat should drink wine along with the meat of animals from arid regions and with black pepper, using non-cooling adjuncts.
7.97c-d: In a kapha-type [fever], [one should use] the meat of wild animals; 7.97d: wine with black pepper.
In that case, for vāta, wine made from flour or molasses is generally beneficial;
in pitta, honey with water; in kapha, mārdvīka, ariṣṭa, and mādhava wines. 98.

7.98d–99. A person with a predominance of phlegm (ślaiṣmika) should drink *mādhvīka*, *ariṣṭa*, or *mādhava* liquor before the meal; one with a predominance of bile (paittika) should drink it after the meal; one with a predominance of wind (vātika) should drink it during the meal; but one whose humors are in equilibrium may drink according to his desire.

7.99 When the humors (doṣas) are equally aggravated, one may act according to one's preference; however, in cases of intoxication (mada), a treatment that generally subdues vāta and pitta is desired, and in cases of fainting (mūrchā) as well. In all instances, one should specifically observe the state of the pitta humor above all else. 7.100 When the humors are equally aggravated, one may act according to one's preference; however, in cases of intoxication (mada), a treatment that generally subdues vāta and pitta is desired, and in cases of fainting (mūrchā) as well.
