In all instances, one should
Cool poultices, cooling gems, sprinklings, and the breeze from fans; the juices of white sugar, grapes, sugarcane, dates, and *kāśmarya*, as well as milk. (101)
The juices prepared with the group of sweet substances, soups with pomegranate, sixty-day rice, red śāli rice, barley, and ghee constitute life-sustaining nourishment. (102)
One should take Kalyāṇaka, Mahātiktaka, or Ṣaṭpala with milk, or Agnika, or Pippalī, or Śilājatu, according to the procedure for Rasāyana. (103)
Alternatively, Triphalā should be administered with ghee, honey, and sugar;
in cases of persistent discharges, closing the mouth and nostrils is beneficial. (104)
Or one should drink human milk, and with that, administer nasal drops (nāvana). Alternatively, one should lick lotus stalks, lotus fibers, and Pippalī, along with Abhayā and honey. 105.
Or one should drink human milk,
or *durālabhā*, or *musta* with cold water;
or one should drink black pepper, the marrow of the stone of the *kola* fruit, *uśīra*, and the filaments of the lotus.

One should prepare ghee processed with the juice of *dhātrī* fruit or with a decoction of *pathyā*, and perform the prescribed treatment according to the specific dosha and the manifestation of its strength. (107)
Five activities are recommended: the sprinkling of blood, reliance upon a sentient being, knowledge, and lack of greed for sense objects. (108)

When swellings have become excessively enlarged and when fainting occurs, one should administer the sharp treatment prescribed for syncope; and in cases arising from poison, one should employ anti-poisonous measures. (109)

7.109c–d: The application of prescribed ritual renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is ordained; however, among those afflicted by poisons, that which destroys poison should be applied quickly. In the case of renunciation, very sharp nasal drops (*nasya*), collyrium (*añjana*), smoke (*dhūma*), blowing [medicines] into the nose (*pradhamana*), pricking with needles (*toda*), and [rubbing] between the nails should be employed. 7.110.

7.110c–d Inhalation of smoke, blowing [into the eyes], pricking with needles, and scratching between the nails; 7.111 tearing out the hair, burning, being bitten by dogs or scorpions, pouring bitter and sour liquids into the mouth, and rubbing with *kapikacchu* [seeds].
7.111d–112ab: One who has been bitten by a *kapikacchu* and has regained consciousness should drink the fresh juice of garlic;
he should also eat the filaments of the *bījapūraka* fruit together with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) and salt.
One should eat light food that is sharp and hot for the purification of the channels;
[one should also be treated] by means of startling experiences, recollections, and the hearing or seeing of beloved things. (113)

Light food that is pungent, sharp, and hot; exposure to the sounds of clear singing and musical instruments; the practice of physical exercise; emetics, purgatives, and medicinal smokes; and bloodletting—[these are the remedies]. // 114 //
One should attend to him constantly out of fear of a relapse;
furthermore, his mind must be protected from that which causes dissolution.
At the time of treatment, when the weather is temperate and free from clouds, one should administer [the therapy] to a patient with hemorrhoids who is not excessively weak,
whose bowels have been purified, and who has eaten a light, small amount of food that promotes the downward movement of the *vāyu*. (1)

8.1cv [The physician should treat] one whose bowels are purified, who has eaten light food, who is clean, for whom auspicious rites have been performed, who has voided excrement and urine, and who is free from distress;
[the patient] resting upon a bed, a plank, or on the lap of another person. // 2 //
With the upper body facing east, the anus directed upward toward the sun, the hips level and the waist region slightly elevated, one should then secure [the patient] with a binding cloth. (3)
It is wrapped around the thighs and the neck, held straight, supported by attendants, while the patient's anus has been anointed with ghee. (4)
Then, one should insert for him a straight enema nozzle lubricated with ghee, slowly and comfortably into the anus; then, having observed [the result] from the urging to defecate— // 5 //
Once the *durnāman* (fistula-in-ano) has entered the instrument, the physician should press it with a probe covered by a cloth and cauterize it according to the prescribed method.
8.6 When the instrument has been inserted, the *durnāman* (fistula) should be moistened with alkali; the other [type] with alkali or fire.
Or, having incised the large [fistula] of a strong patient while the instrument is withdrawn, one should then treat the patient.
One should have him, with his anus and buttocks well-anointed, enter the bath;
thereafter, for one staying in a windless chamber, one should prescribe his regimen.
8.8c–d For one staying in a windless room, one should apply [the treatment] once every seven days;
first the right [hemorrhoid], then the left, and after that the one located at the posterior end of the anus. 9.

For one who has many hemorrhoids and has been well-cauterized, there shall be the downward movement of wind, a relish for food, keenness of the digestive fire, health, and the emergence of complexion and strength. (10)
In the case of pain in the bladder, however, one should apply a smooth paste made from *varṣābhū*, *kuṣṭha*, *surabhi*, *miśī*, and the substances called *loha* and *amarā* below the navel.
In cases of obstruction of feces and urine, one should employ affusion and immersion with *varaṇa*,
*alambuṣā*, *aṇḍa*, *gokaṇṭaka*, and *punarnavā*.
8.12ab In cases of obstruction of feces and urine,
one should administer a warm decoction of *suṣavī* and *surabhī*,
or else milk or oil that destroys *vāta* along with unctuous substances.

One should administer foods that cause loose stools, as well as unctuous substances that alleviate Vata and stimulate digestion, for those whose burning sensation has subsided after being caused by Kapha and Vata. 14.
Having anointed piles characterized by stiffness, itching, pain, and swelling, one should sprinkle them with oil prepared from the roots of *bilva*, *agnika*, alkali (*kṣāra*), and *kuṣṭha*. (15)

8.15ab For swelling accompanied by irritation, itching, pain, and stiffness, one should apply a poultice of oil mixed with the fat of a snake, a cat, a camel, or a boar; thereafter, one should apply fomentation using either a solid bolus or a liquid application. 8.15cd–16ab.
Green vitriol, rock salt, rāsnā, ginger, kuṣṭha, lāṅgalī, mica, abhraka, aśvamāra, jantuhṛt, danti, and citraka. (16.1+1)
Likewise, one should cook oil with equal parts of yellow orpiment and *svarṇakṣīrī*,
along with the milky sap of the *sudhā* and *arka* plants, and four times as much cow’s urine.
Through this massage, hemorrhoids are quickly made to fall away like [the effect of] caustic alkali;
for this acts as a caustic procedure yet does not damage the anal folds. (16.1+(3))
Or with balls of unctuous roasted grain flour mixed with oil and ghee;
or with boluses of *rāsnā*, *hapuṣā*, or *kārṣṇyagandhika*.
8.17dv Or with boluses containing *kārṣaka* [seeds], the root of *arka*, *śamī* leaves, human hair, snake slough, cat skin,
and clarified butter constitute a beneficial fumigation for hemorrhoids. 18.
Likewise, with a paste made of ashvagandha, surasa, brihati, pippali, ghee, and the seeds and sprouts of jimuta ground in fermented grain-water (dhanyamla), that [wound] becomes soft. 19.
A wick (varti) that has been coated with this and dried in the shade cures hemorrhoids;
or one may use a linctus made from the roots of *sajāla* and *mūlajīmūta* combined with alkali (kṣāra). || 20 ||
A wick made from the seeds of *guñjā*, *sūraṇa*, and *kūṣmāṇḍa* possesses the same qualities;
likewise, an ointment consisting of *niśā* moistened with the milky sap of *snuk* and ground with cow’s urine [has the same effect]. // 21 //
Likewise, with the dung of a cock, black night (turmeric), and the fruits of guñjā, ground with the milk of snuhī, along with ṣaḍgranthā, halinī, and the bones of an elephant; // 22 //
With *kulīraśṛṅgī*, *vijayā*, *kuṣṭha*, *aruṣkara*, and *tutthaka*;
with the seeds and leaves produced from *śigru* and *mūlaka*; and with those produced from *aśvaghna* and *nimba*. (23)
Or [one may use] *śigru* roots and *mūlaka* seeds,
combined with *pīlu* root, *bilva*, and asafoetida; or *kuṣṭha*, *śirīṣa* seeds, long pepper, rock salt, and jaggery.
The milk of *arka*, the milk of *sudhā*, and *triphalā* constitute a plaster;
likewise, the milk of *arka*, the stem of *sudhā*, and the tender leaves of bitter *alābu*. (25)
8.25–26. Milk from the *arka* plant, the stem of *snuhī*, *karañja*, and goat’s urine constitute an excellent external application for hemorrhoids (*arśas*).
An ointment made with the *pippaly-ādi* group of drugs, combined with substances used for oil enemas (*ānuvāsana*), is also highly recommended.
With these very same medicinal herbs, one should prepare oils for massage;
through fumigation, ointments, and massages, the anal growths will discharge [their secretions]. // 27 //
8.27 One should prepare medicinal ointments and oils from these [substances]. Then, the accumulated vitiated blood is eliminated, and the patient becomes comfortable.
One should extract the blood that is not flowing from swellings that are hard and elevated.

In the case of hemorrhoids, the disease is not pacified by repeated applications of water-born [lotus] stalks, surgical instruments, needles, or tufts of grass, nor by cold, hot, unctuous, or dry treatments. (29)
8.29 When the blood is vitiated by cold, heat, unctuousness, dryness, and so forth, the physician should therefore bleed that very blood.
[One should prepare] goat's milk from which the fire-powder has been sprinkled.
By drinking that very [powder] from *bahumūla* after it has been finely ground and eating with that same [milk], one conquers hemorrhoids;
likewise, by drinking the powder of *kovidāra* roots with churning milk (*mathita*). 8.31ab.

One suffering from anal swelling and pain, with weak digestion, should drink the churned [milk] while eating; once it is digested, one should consume wholesome foods. Those afflicted by gulma should drink [the preparation] known as *hata*. (8.31–32)
One should eat asafoetida and other such ingredients with buttermilk, or consume *guḍa-harītakī*;
or one should drink *pathyā*, *vellā*, *agni*, and the bark of *kuṭaja* with buttermilk. (33)
One should drink either the *hiṅgu* group of drugs with buttermilk,
or *pathyā* with buttermilk, or *vellā*, *agni*, the bark of *kuṭaja*, *kaliṅga*, *magadhā*, *jyotis*, and *sūraṇa*, or *vaṃśa* and *vardhitā*.
Or [one may take] tripaṭu, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, and amlavetasa with lukewarm water. (34)
One should administer a satiation of buttermilk (takratarpaṇa) combined with bilva and kapittha, or with mahauṣadha and viḍalavaṇa, or with aruṣkara and yavānī.
8.35c–d Or one should give [the patient] *āruṣkara* or *yavānī*, or *hapuṣā*, *hiṅgu*, and *citraka* combined with buttermilk;
or for a month, he should eat *pīlu* fruits with buttermilk as a post-drink (anupāna). 8.36.
One should drink buttermilk every day, or even abstain from food and drink it to one's heart's content;
for one whose digestive fire is excessively weak, one should administer buttermilk alone.

For one whose digestive fire (kāyāgni) is extremely weak, the physician— who understands strength, the season, and the nature of the disorder— should administer buttermilk for seven days, ten days, half a month, or even a full month. (8.37–38)
In the evening, one should give parched grain flour with buttermilk to be licked,
or once the buttermilk has been digested, one should administer buttermilk gruel mixed with rock salt.
Thereafter, one should eat boiled *śāli* rice with clarified butter followed by buttermilk as a drink, or else with buttermilk-rice;
or one may eat *śāli* rice in appropriate measure with soups or meat broths enriched with buttermilk. (40)

One should employ three types of buttermilk—determined by the state of the humors, digestive fire, and strength—namely: that which is dry (rūkṣa), that from which half the fat has been removed, and that from which no fat has been removed at all. || 41 ||
Hemorrhoids do not grow again when struck with buttermilk;
for that [buttermilk], when poured even upon the ground, burns up grass and weeds.
8.42cd–43ab That nutrient juice which, once poured into the channels purified by buttermilk, reaches the bodily tissues (dhātus),
produces nourishment, strength, complexion, and supreme satisfaction.
A hundred disorders of wind and phlegm are also eliminated when [the milk] is churned in a vessel smeared with the fruits of the small and large *bṛhatī*. (44)
For those desiring to drink a decoction that has stood overnight to alleviate hemorrhoids and wasting,
[it should be prepared] with coriander, cumin, caraway, asafoetida, and the two types of long pepper.
Take *kāravī*, *granthika*, *śaṭhī*, *yavānī*, *agni*, and *yavānaka*;
having powdered these, let buttermilk that is not too sour be infused in a vessel of ghee. (46)
One should drink *takrāriṣṭa* (fermented buttermilk) prepared with *yavānī*, *agni*, and *yavānikā*, once it has developed a distinct sour and pungent taste according to one's preference;
it stimulates digestion, improves appetite, enhances the complexion, and facilitates the downward movement of *kapha* and *vāta*.
Having ground the bark of the root of *citraka*, one should smear it upon a jar; this destroys swelling, itching, and pain of the anus, and increases strength. (48)
One should drink buttermilk or curd produced therein to remove hemorrhoids; this same procedure applies to *bhārgī*, *āsphota*, *amṛtā*, and the five spices (*pañcakola*). (49)
One should prepare [a medicinal paste] with the powders of gaja, kaṇā, pāṭhā, kāravī, pañcakola, tumburu, ajājī, dhanikā, and the pulp of bilva.
Sour fruits, double-fried fats, gruels, soups, meat broths, and the like should be prepared;
likewise, water and ghee processed with these very same medicinal herbs act as digestive stimulants.
This sequence will be described for those with loose stools;
for those with hard stools, one should drink Vāruṇī wine mixed with salt and barley meal (saktu) enriched with fats.
Or indeed, salted preparations of buttermilk, sidhu, dhanyāmla, and vāruṇī liquor—fried in *yamaka* oil and butter before the meal and sprinkled with roasted grain flour (*saktu*). (53)

8.53–54ab: One should eat the sprouts of *karañja* fried in *yamaka* oil before a meal to facilitate the downward movement of wind and stool; or one may take ginger (*nāgara*) with jaggery, or *pāṭhā*, or jaggery, alkali, and ghee.
One should eat ginger with jaggery and *pāṭhā*, or [the same] with jaggery, alkali, and ghee;
or one should consume *harītakī* with jaggery that has been soaked in cow’s urine;
or, from two hundred *pathyā* fruits, one should take [the decoction] with a *droṇa* of urine until the urine is exhausted.

One should eat two hundred *pathyā* fruits cooked in urine with honey, two at a time; this destroys diseases arising from *kapha*, such as hemorrhoids, skin diseases, swelling, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, abdominal enlargements, and worms. (8.55–56)

One who eats the boiled paste of *ajaśṛṅgī* roots with honey will overcome glandular swellings (*granthi*), tumors (*arbuda*), scrofula (*apacī*), obesity, anemia (*pāṇḍu-roga*), and severe disorders of wind (*māruta*).
He who drinks the paste of *ajaśṛṅgī* roots with goat’s urine [attains the same]. (8.56–57)
For one who eats jaggery and eggplant, the growths in the rectum perish quickly;
likewise, by taking trivṛt with the juice of śreṣṭhā, or pathyā with buttermilk. (58)
One should eat Pathyā combined with Pippalī, fried in ghee and mixed with jaggery;
or else, one should consume Trivṛt and Dantī, which promotes the downward movement of the bowels. (59)
When the morbid humors (doṣas) residing in the rectum are destroyed, the diseases arising in the rectum go to their destruction by means of pomegranate juice, cumin, yavānī, jaggery, and ginger. (60)
8.60 When the morbid humors (doṣas) residing in the rectum have been removed, buttermilk mixed with *pāṭhā* promotes the downward movement of flatus and feces;
or else, *sīdhu* liquor made from molasses (*gauḍa*) combined with *citraka* and *mahauṣadha*.
Or one should drink wine combined with hapuṣā, pāṭhā, and sauvarcala salt;
or one should take pippalī fruits increased by groups of ten starting from ten, along with two picus of sesame seeds.
Having drunk two picus of long pepper with milk, one gains strength for both the body and the digestive fire; likewise by using *duḥsparśaka*, *bilva*, *yavānī*, or *nāgara*. (8.62–63)
Pāṭhā combined with either yavānī or nāgara, even by itself, destroys the pain of hemorrhoids; likewise,
half a *prastha* of the bark of *abhayā* boiled in flowing water [is effective].

8.64d–65ab: Half a *prastha* of *abhayā* bark, one *prastha* of *dhātrī*, ten *palas* of *kapittha*, half that amount [of *kapittha*] of *viśālā*, *lodhra*, black pepper, long pepper, *vella*, and *elavāluka*.

When each [of the previous ingredients] has been separately reduced to one-fourth and strained, one should add two palas [each] from a tula of jaggery (guḍa) and one prastha of dhātakī, and place it in a vessel of ghee.
Having given one *prastha* of *dhātakī*, this *ariṣṭa*, when consumed for a fortnight, kindles the digestive fire and destroys hemorrhoids,
malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), abdominal enlargements (*udara*), artificial poisons (*gara*), and fevers.
One should boil dantī, daśamūla, varā, and agnikā in one droṇa of water to treat swelling, splenic disorders, heart disease, abdominal tumors, consumption, vomiting, and worms. (68)
One should add a *tulā* of jaggery to the remaining liquid in the vessel;
everything else for this [preparation] shall be as before, but this one is superior due to its capacity for inducing downward movement (*ānulomī*). (69)
One should cook one *prastha* of *durālabhā* with four *āḍhaka* (droṇa) of water,
together with one *prasṛta* each of *dantī*, *pāṭhā*, *agni*, *vijayā*, *vāsā*, *āmalaka*, and *nāgara*.
In that droṇa of water, together with two palas [of the aforementioned substances], one should add a hundred palas of sugar; when it has reached the quarter-stage, the rest is as before.
One should then smear the jar with the fruit of the phalinī, black pepper, cavya, ghee, and honey.
Before a meal, one should drink ghee prepared with sour fruits for the sake of restoring natural downward movement (ānulomya),
or ghee processed with cavya and citraka, combined with barley-alkali and jaggery.
Or ghee prepared with the root of long pepper (pippalī-mūla), along with jaggery, alkali, and dry ginger;
or ghee prepared with long pepper, the root of long pepper, coriander seeds, and pomegranate.
Ghee prepared with *dhānyaka*, pomegranate,
and curd cures the obstruction of flatus, feces, and urine.
One should cook ghee with three times as much water containing the alkali of *palāśa*.

This [decoction], with an addition (pratīvāpa) of the vatsakādi group, removes obstruction of feces and urine, destroys hemorrhoids, and is an excellent digestive stimulant. [It is prepared] with the five spices (pañcakola), abhayā, alkali, yavānī, viḍa salt, and saindhava salt. (8.74b–75)
One should prepare clarified butter with pāṭhā, coriander, black pepper, and bilva, along with curd;
this quickly overcomes pain in the anus and the groin. (76)
For dysentery, prolapse of the rectum, difficulty in urination, and excessive discharge, [one should use] pāṭhā, ajamodā, dhanikā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and the five spices (pañcakola). // 77 //
Ghee prepared with bilva, curd, and four times the quantity of the fresh juice of aṅgerī destroys abdominal distension, dysuria, and dysentery. (78)

For those suffering from prolapse of the rectum, anal diseases, disorders of the grahaṇī, and wind-related ailments, one should administer well-prepared sour meat broths made from peacock, partridge, and common quail. (79)
In cases of the retention of feces and flatus, one should administer the excrement of mongooses or quails;
or the sprouts of vāstuka, agni, trivṛt, dantī, pāṭhā, amlīkā, and other such plants. (80)

Furthermore, this vegetable preparation destroys phlegm and wind; it is light and promotes digestion when fried in a mixture of two fats with asafoetida and prepared together with the liquid from curdled milk. 81.
It is prepared with the serum of curd,
along with *dhanikā* and the five spices (*pañcakola*) ground together with pomegranate juice, as well as the tender shoots of *ārdrikā* and slices of fresh ginger.
It is proper that it be made fragrant with pleasant-smelling charcoal incense, along with cumin and black pepper, and enriched with a profusion of *viḍa* and *sauvarcala* salts. (83)

For one who has an excess of wind, whose body is dry, whose digestive fire is weak, and whose stool is constipated, it is appropriate to prepare red *śāli* rice with side dishes and meat broths seasoned like vegetables, using charcoal smoke as a flavoring.
One should prepare red *śāli* rice, along with side dishes, vegetables, and meat broths;
specifically, the meat of cows, monitor lizards, goats, and camels, as well as that of carnivorous animals.
Wine made from honey, wine made from molasses, wine made from grain, rum, buttermilk, and water from fermented rice husks; // 85 //
One should drink buttermilk, water, or a small amount of boiled water,
along with coriander, coriander and ginger, or with kaṇṭakārī.
Before or during the meal, it facilitates the downward movement of flatus and feces;
for when the feces, flatus, kapha, and pitta move properly, the channels become clear. (87)

Those ailments arising in the rectum are pacified in the rectum, and the digestive fire increases, as do those conditions characterized by upward movement of wind (udāvarta) and those who have become excessively dry. (88)
In cases of upward-moving winds (viloma-vāta) accompanied by pain, an oil enema (anuvāsana) is desired;
[it should contain] long pepper (pippalī), madana, bilva, dill (śatāhvā), licorice (madhuka), and sweet flag (vacā).
Having ground kuṣṭha, śaṭhī, puṣkaramūla, citraka, and devadāru, one should cook oil combined with twice the amount of milk. // 90 //
Kuṣṭha, śaṭhī, and pauṣkara—
this is the best unctuous enema (anuvāsana) for hemorrhoids caused by obstructed wind (mūḍhavāta).
Painful discharge from the anus, colic, difficulty in urination, and dysentery. // 91 //
Weakness of the hips, thighs, and back; distension of the abdomen localized in the groins; slimy discharge from the anus; swelling of the rectum; and suppression of flatus and feces. (92)

If there is frequent straining during defecation, one should overcome it by means of an oil enema (anuvāsana), or one should administer a decoction enema (nirūha) containing milk and the five roots (pañcamūla). // 93 //
Combined with urine, oil, salt, and pastes of the *phala* group and others, this [enema] should be administered after examining whether the blood-piles are caused by Vāta or Kapha. (94)
8.94d–95ab: Then, having determined the association with either vāta or kapha, one should apply a cold treatment that is either unctuous or dry.
When the feces are dark, rough, and dry, and the flatus does not pass downward, [this indicates the need for such treatment].
If there is pain in the hips, thighs, and anus, and the cause is dryness, then vāta is the secondary factor; if the stool is loose, then kapha is the secondary factor. (96)
The anus is white, yellow, heavy, unctuous, covered with slimy mucus, and flaccid;
one should recognize the cause as being unctuous and heavy, according to the specific characteristics of the blood [in each case]. (97)

If the blood is vitiated, purification and fasting should be administered according to the patient's strength; however, one should wait until the turbidity caused by the humors has been cleared through the discharge of the blood. (98)
For the purpose of maturing the humors, for stimulating the digestive fire, and for the collection of blood, one should treat the patient primarily with bitter substances. (99)

However, if the blood of one whose humors are diminished or who has a predominance of Vāta is vitiated, one should treat it with appropriate unctuous substances administered through drinking, massage, and enemas. (100)
However, blood that is dominated by pitta and flows during the hot season should invariably be checked with astringent measures, unless it is accompanied by vāta and kapha. (101)
If blood is accompanied by phlegm, one should drink a decoction of ginger and the bark of *kuṭaja*;
or [a decoction] of *kirātatiktaka*, ginger, *dhanvayāsa*, and red sandalwood. (102)
The bark of *dārvī*, *nimba*, and *sevyā*, or the bark derived from the pomegranate;
the bark and fruit of *kuṭaja*, *tārkṣya*, honey, and *ghuṇavallabhā*. (103)
Or one should drink mayūraka made into a paste with rice-water;
or one should boil a tulā of fresh kuṭaja bark in divine water.
When the bark has lost its juice, one should add equal portions of a handful each of the finely powdered fruits of samaṅgā, phalinī, and moca into the decoction. (105)

Having purified those with Śakrayava, one should then cook it until it can be smeared with a ladle; having prepared this electuary (avaleha), one should lick it and drink [the decoction] according to the strength of one's digestive fire. // 106 //

8.106–107. Purified with *śakrayava* by those [grains], one should drink gruel (*peyā*), scum (*maṇḍa*), or goat’s or cow’s milk; or, consuming goat’s milk, one may take this linctus (*leha*). It quickly pacifies dysentery with blood (*raktātīsāra*) and disorders arising from the rectum (*pāyu*).
In cases of severe bleeding from *rakta-pitta*, whether flowing upwards or downwards, one should boil one *tulā* of *kuṭaja* bark in one *droṇa* of water until it is reduced to one-eighth. (108)
When eight parts remain, one should cook it;

having made [the following] into a paste, one should add to it: *tārkṣyaśaila* (rasāñjana), the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), the two types of *lodhra*, *mocarasa*, *balā*, and the rind of pomegranate.
One pala each of bilva, karkaṭikā, musta, samaṅgā, and dhātakī fruit, and ten palas of the bark of kuṭaja. // 110 //

Thirty palas of jaggery and twenty palas of clarified butter, purified and cooked until it reaches the consistency of a linctus, should be kept for a fortnight in grain; one who licks this [attains the desired result]. (111)
It cures all types of hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, asthma, and cough;
[namely] *lodhra*, sesame seeds, the juice of the *moca* fruit, *samaṅgā*, sandalwood, and blue lotus. (112)

Having administered [this] with goat's milk, it eradicates dyspnea and cough; one should then feed [the patient] śāli rice with that same milk. [The decoction consists of] yaṣṭyāhva, padmaka, anantā, payasyā, kṣīra, and moraṭa. (8.112b–113)
It should be drunk with sugar and honey, or with cold water;
[one should also take] the bark of *lodhra*, *kaṭvaṅga*, *kuṭaja*, *samaṅgā*, and *śālmalī*. (114)
8.114d–115. Or, one may take the barks of *samaṅgā* and *śālmalī*, or *himakusuma*, *kesara*, and *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice), with rice-water;
or *yavānī*, *indrayava*, *pāṭhā*, *bilva*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *rasāñjana*.
A powder is beneficial for the condition when there is pain and excessive bleeding;
ghee prepared with *dugdhikā* and *kaṇṭakārī* is recommended. (116)
Alternatively, [one may prepare it] with the bark and fruit of dhātakī, lodhra, and kuṭaja, along with utpala and kesara,
together with barley-alkali and the juice of pomegranate.
Fresh butter, when practiced regularly with sugar, lotus filaments, or sesame seeds, cures hemorrhoids characterized by bleeding. (118)
Goat meat, fresh butter, ghee, milk, and the flesh of wild animals; or a broth that is not sour, or slightly sour, together with the juice of vāstūka—these are the [suitable] liquids. (119)
Red rice, lake-curds, sixty-day rice, young wine, and fresh wine-scum are the supreme remedies for blood. (120)
Onions, whether used alone or combined with gruels, soups, meat broths, and the like, when administered, conquer even excessive hemorrhaging and wind disorders. (121)
When blood has been excessively discharged, hemorrhoids generally become dominated by wind; therefore, one should exert special effort to conquer that [wind]. (122)
Having observed that blood and bile are predominant while phlegm and wind are weak, one should by all means apply cooling treatments for their pacification. (123)
If there is no such relief, one should then satisfy him with unctuous and warm substances,
with lukewarm meat broths, and with medicated ghees prepared as *avapīḍakas*.
And when there is no such subsiding [of the pain], one should sprinkle it at will with lukewarm oil, milk, and ghee,
as well as the roots and flowers of *yavāsa*, *kuśa*, and *kāśa*, and of the *śālmali* tree.
Two palas each of the tender shoots of nyagrodha, udumbara, and aśvattha should be boiled with three prasthas of water and one prastha of milk. 126.
When that decoction has been reduced to milk-residue and strained, one should mix into it the paste of moca-rasa, samaṅgā, candana, and utpala. (127)
Priyaṅgu, the seeds of Kauṭaja, and the filaments of the lotus—this is the proven slimy enema (picchā-vasti), prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar. (128)
It cures dysentery, prolapse of the rectum, hemorrhage, and fever, [prepared] with liquorice, white lotus, and the like, as well as the sap of the *moca* tree and other ingredients. (129)
An oil cooked with twice the amount of milk should be administered as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
[The decoction for this consists of] madhuka, utpala, lodhra, ambu, samaṅgā, bilva, and candana. (130)
Cavikā, ativiṣā, musta, pāṭhā, alkali from barley sprouts, dārvī bark, nāgara, māṃsī, citraka, and devadāru. (131)

Ghee prepared with the fresh juice of cāṅgerī, along with those [other ingredients], conquers the three doṣas and is used for hemorrhoids, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia, fever, and loss of appetite. (132)
In cases of dysuria, prolapse of the rectum, distension of the bladder, tenesmus, slimy discharges, and pain from hemorrhoids, this supreme medicine should be administered. (133)

One should regularly employ sweet and sour, cold and hot substances in alternation, while constantly considering the strength of the digestive fire; thus one conquers the diseases caused by hemorrhoids.

8.134d–135ab. It overcomes the pain caused by hemorrhoids; having anointed one afflicted with upward-moving wind (udāvarta) with oils that alleviate cold-fever, one should apply fomentation with well-oleated boluses, and then insert an enema-salve (varti) into his anus.

One should apply [the enema] after it has been smeared with oil, made smooth by rubbing with the thumb of that same hand, and prepared with *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *pippalī*, and the fruit of *nīlinī*. (136)
With the two salts ground together and combined with jaggery and cow urine, and likewise with long pepper, rāṭha, house-soot, and mustard seeds; 137.
8.137b Or one should blow the powder of these very same [substances] into the anus through a tube, cooked with jaggery and cow’s urine.
If that fails, one should administer a very sharp, unctuous enema (vasti). 138.
This [treatment] straightens his rectal vessels, feces, urine, and flatus;
however, if there is further persistence [of the disorder], he should be purged with unctuous purgatives that subdue Vata. (139)
One should straighten the head of the rectum, for due to dryness (raukṣya), there may be an obstruction of flatus and feces in one who has received an oil enema (anuvāsya).
[The following paste is used: the three salts (tripaṭu), the three pungents (trikaṭu), śreṣṭhā, dantī, aruṣkara, and citraka.
One should cook the charred residue, soaked in oil and urine, with internal smoke, inside a clay-coated joint of two earthen bowls; this is the alkali known as Kalyāṇaka. (141)

When drunk with clarified butter, or taken with food by one who eats unctuous meals, it cures upward movement of wind (udāvarta), constipation, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors (gulma), anemia, abdominal enlargement, and worms. (142)
It destroys urinary obstruction, gravel, swelling, heart disease, disorders of the digestive tract, urinary disorders, splenic ailments, colic, dyspnea, and cough. (143)
And one should perform everything that has been prescribed for those with hemorrhoids and severe constipation. (144ab)
Then one should boil two *tulās* of putrid bark of the *droṇa* tree in water until it is reduced to one-fourth. In that [decoction], // 144c //

8.144cd–144d: One should boil two *tulās* of putrid bark (*pūti-valka*) in one *droṇa* of water until it is reduced to one-fourth; then, to that decoction, one should add eighty *palas* of jaggery (*guḍa*) and eight *palas* of the fine powder of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
This, having been produced over the course of a month, generates the supreme power of digestion from heat.

When prepared as a fermented sour gruel (*śukta*), it cures hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, and abdominal enlargements when used in accordance with the natural direction of the bowels. // 144f //

One should boil one *tulā* each of the bark of *pūtikarañja*, and two [parts] each of the roots of *citraka* and *kaṇṭakārī* in three *droṇas* of water until one-fourth remains; when strained, one should add one hundred *palas* of jaggery (*guḍa*) to it. // 145 //
One pala each of well-ground trijāta, trikaṭu, granthika, dāḍima, and aśmabheda;
pūra, puṣkaramūla, dhānya, cavya, hapuṣā, ārdraka, and sour vetasa. (146)
Having become cooled, it is combined with twenty parts of honey, along with fresh grapes, citron, and ginger;
likewise, it may be mixed at will with pieces of sugarcane, having been kept for exactly one month in a vessel of clarified butter. (147)

Cukra is like a saw for those with difficult names (diseases); it is a supreme stimulant for the digestive fire and a destroyer of anemia, chronic poisoning, abdominal enlargements, gulma, splenic disorders, flatulence, urinary stones, and strangury. 148.
A droṇa of pīlu juice, strained through cloth, was placed in the sacrificial vessel.
One should prepare it with two palas each of liquorice, madhuphala, dates, and dhātrī fruits. // 149b //
With pāṭhā, mādri, durālabhā, amla, vidula, vyoṣa, tvak, elā, and ullaka; // 149c //

8.149c–d: One *pala* each of *pāṭhā*, *mādrī*, *durālabhā*, sour *vidula*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), cinnamon bark (*tvak*), cardamom (*ellā*), *allaka*, *spṛkkā*, *kola*, cloves (*lavaṅga*), *vella*, *capalā*, *mūla*, and *agnika*.

Having prepared this with one hundred palas of jaggery and stored it in a windless place, one who drinks it for just a fortnight suppresses hemorrhoids along with abdominal tumors and quickly increases the strength of the digestive fire. (150)

8.150–151. This [preparation] pacifies hemorrhoids along with abdominal tumors (gulma), whether taken individually or in combination. Ten palas each of the ten roots (daśamūla), kumbha, the two types of pāṭhā, arka, ghuṇavallabha, and kaṭphala are burnt and then strained; subsequently, it is cooked with one droṇa of water until reduced to one-quarter. Then, one tulā of jaggery and five palas [of the aforementioned drugs] are added.
One should take one *muṣṭi* each of pāṭhā, abhayā, arka, ghuṇavallabha, and kaṭphala;
two *muṣṭis* each of the triad of pungents (vyoṣa), cavya, and abhayā; and two *muṣṭis* of yava-kṣāra.
This molasses (*guḍa*), when licked while coating the ladle, destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*), splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, urinary disorders, and loss of digestive fire.
Half a *tula* of *citraka* root should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water until it is reduced to one-fourth;
then, having added eight *pala*s of aged treacle, this should be boiled again until it reaches a consistent consistency. (153)

8.153b–154. This electuary, prepared with the powders of the three pungents (tri-kaṭuka), miśī, pathyā, kuṣṭha, mustā, varāṅga, kṛmiripu, dahana, and elā, and mixed with water in which the patient’s feet have been washed, conquers hemorrhoids, skin diseases, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, and enlargements of the abdomen when consumed regularly. It also constantly strengthens the digestive fire.

8.154c–d. This pill, consisting of jaggery, the three pungents (vyoṣa), chebulic myrobalan (varā), vella, sesame, aruṣkara, and citraka, conquers hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen;
when habitually used, it destroys piles and skin diseases.
Having cooked a *sauraṇa* tuber coated with clay in a fire using the *puṭapāka* method, one should eat it with oil and salt for the cessation of hemorrhoids (*durnāma*). (156)

Prepare boluses of jaggery from long pepper, black pepper, ginger, and leadwort, with their parts increased in sequence by one, combined with four times as much turmeric and sweet flag; these destroy hemorrhoids. (157)
Sixteen parts of *sūraṇa* powder, half as much of *citraka*, two parts of *mahauṣadha*, and one part of black pepper—this bolus, taken with jaggery, conquers chronic dysentery. (158)
This powder—composed of *pathyā*, *nāgara*, *kṛṣṇā*, *karañja*, *vellā*, and *agni*, each equal in measure to sugar—digests even a large and heavy meal like the mouth of a mare. (159)
Even a large quantity of heavy food, when combined with a powder of *kaliṅga*, *lāṅgalī*, *kṛṣṇā*, *vahni*, *apāmārga*, and rice, along with *bhūnimba*,
rock salt (*saindhava*), and jaggery (*guḍa*), forms a sweetmeat (*guḍā*) that destroys hemorrhoids.

If you wish to destroy the growths in your anus, drink for seven days *lavaṇottama*, *vahni*, *kaliṅga*, and *yava*, combined with *ciribilva* and *mahāpicumanda*, churned and stirred in buttermilk. 161.

Drink [the decoction] stirred with churned butter for seven days, if you wish to rub away the hemorrhoids; bhallātaka is said to be the foremost medicine for dry [hemorrhoids], but the bark of vatsaka is for the moist ones.
In all seasons, kālaśeya is beneficial for hemorrhoids, strengthening, and it removes impurities.

The patient suffering from hemorrhoids should consume food, drink, and medicine that break up obstructions, facilitate the downward movement of wind, and strengthen the digestive fire; anything contrary to this should be avoided. (163)

Hemorrhoids, diarrhea, and disorders of the *grahaṇī* are generally causes for one another; they exist when the digestive fire (*agni*) is suppressed and do not exist when it is kindled. Therefore, one should especially protect the digestive fire in these conditions. (164)
Therefore, one should especially protect the digestive fire among those [factors];
for diarrhea in the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna) most frequently originates from the stomach (āmāśaya).
Therefore, even in the case of fever born from wind (vāta-ja), fasting is beneficial prior to administering fire (purgation). // 1 //

9.1dv Prior to this, fasting is beneficial; one suffering from colic, abdominal distension, or excessive salivation should be made to vomit, as well as a patient with diarrhea whose accumulated doshas have been provoked by undigested food (vidagdha-āhāra). // 2 //
They lead to diarrhea; in such cases, where there is intense agitation and the humors are naturally mobile, non-intervention alone is the remedy.

However, the application of a *saṃgrahaṇa* (astringent) therapy should not be employed first in one suffering from *āmātisāra* (diarrhea caused by undigested matter), nor in cases that produce flatulence, heaviness, colic, and numbness. // 4 //

9.4a However, it should not be administered when constipating; 9.4b nor [should it be given] first when the *āmadoṣa* is predominant. When the *doṣa* is obstructed, one should drink [the medicine] boiled in water, which promotes the downward movement of life-sustaining breath (*prāṇadā*). One with moderate *doṣa* should drink it while drying up the humors.
Bhūtīka, pippalī, śuṇṭhī, vacā, dhānyaka, and harītakī;
or else, bilva, dhanikā, musta, nāgara, and vālaka. (6)
Either viḍa, pāṭhā, vacā, pathyā, kṛmijit, and nāgara;
or śuṇṭhī, ghana, vacā, mādrī, bilva, vatsaka, and hiṅgu. // 7 //
However, fasting is recommended for those with mild symptoms who suffer from diarrhea;
alternatively, [it may be treated] with *vacā* and *prativiṣā*, or with *mustā* and *parpaṭaka*.
Or one should have him drink water boiled with *hrīvera* and *nāgara*;
when the time for food has arrived, one should feed him light food as he is emaciated by hunger. (9)
9.9dv One should feed light food; thus he quickly regains his appetite, digestive fire, and strength—either with buttermilk, āvantisoma, gruel (yavāgū), or a nourishing drink (tarpaṇa). // 10 //
One should treat the patient with wine or honey according to what is suitable for them;
thereafter, one should prepare foods that are constipating, digestive stimulants, and carminatives.
9.11ab Then, with wine and honey, along with young bilva, śaṭhī, coriander, asafoetida, vṛkṣāmla, and pomegranate;
with palāśa, hapuṣā, cumin, yavānī, viḍa salt, and rock salt.
It should be prepared with the five roots (pañcamūla), the five spices (pañcakola), pāṭhā, śāliparṇī, balā, bilva, and pṛśniparṇī. // 13 //
A sour gruel made with pomegranate is beneficial when kapha and pitta are excessively aggravated;
it promotes the downward movement of vāta when combined with abhayā, pippalī root, and bilva. (14)
One who suffers from diarrhea with obstructed doshas, excessive humors, and a stimulated digestive fire should be purged with decoctions of black pepper, viḍaṅga, and triphalā. (15)

One should administer thin gruel made with wind-alleviating and digestive-stimulating drugs to one who has been purged; however, he whose undigested matter (āma) has been fully processed and whose digestive fire is kindled may pass stool even without it. (16)
It is passed repeatedly with foam and mucus, accompanied by pain and constipation;
it is scanty, slightly purged of impurities, or passed with straining (pravāhikā). (17)
9.17c–d He should drink it in very small quantities, mixed with curd, oil, ghee, and milk, along with ginger and jaggery;
or he should eat steamed jujube fruits (*badara*) with jaggery and oil.
One should feed this hungry patient with vegetables prepared with thick pulses, along with broths containing abundant fats, seasoned with curd and pomegranate. (19)
9.19d–20. One should eat śāli rice well-prepared with sesame, black gram, or green gram, seasoned with curd and pomegranate;
or [rice prepared] with śaṭī, young radish, pāṭhā, or svastika.
9.20c–21: [One may prepare a preparation] with ginger, young radish, *sūṣā*, *yavānī*, *karkāru*, *kṣīriṇī*, *cirbhaṭa*, or with *upodakā*, *jīvantī*, *vākucī*, or *vāstuka*.
Or with the juices of *suvarcalā*, *cuñcu*, or *loṇikā*; and with the meat of tortoise, partridge, jackal, peacock, *tittiri* quail, and cock. (22)

9.22dv–23ab. A gruel prepared with buttermilk (takrā yavāgū) made from the bile of a peacock, partridge, and cock, along with *bilva*, *mustā*, *akṣi-bhaiṣajya* (indrayava), *dhātakī* flowers, and *nāgara*, overcomes chronic diarrhea (*pakvātīsāra*).
Likewise, a gruel prepared with curd (*dādhikī*) [is effective].
With the sprouts of *kapittha*, *kacchurā*, *phañjī*, *yūthikā*, *vaṭa*, and *śelu*, as well as those of *dāḍimī*, *śaṇa*, *kārpāsī*, and *śālmalī*. (24)
A paste made from the tender leaves of *śālmalī* and *moca*, along with an equal amount of the paste of unripe *bilva* fruits and sesame seeds,
mixed with the sour liquid from curd, oil, and salt, cures dysentery (*pravāhikā*).
Black pepper, cumin, hog plum, *śaṭhī*, *viḍa* salt,
pomegranate, *dhātakī*, *pāṭhā*, the three myrobalans (*tri-phalā*), and the five *kola* fruits (26).
Take the pulp of wood-apple, mango, and rose-apple, along with *dīpyaka*, together with the seeds up to the awn;
grind these with six times their quantity of *bilva* fruits, and [prepare the preparation] in curd, mung-bean broth, and jaggery. // 27 //
This unvanquished powder, prepared with oil and *yamaka* (the two myrobalans), is digestive, carminative, astringent, appetizing, and a destroyer of *bimbiśī*. (28)
One should prepare a grain-soup using the pastes of kola, young bilva, śāli rice, barley, mung beans, māṣa beans, and sesame seeds. // 29 //
When there is a loss of feces and dryness of the mouth, one should feed the patient śāli rice along with curd, pomegranate, and sugar, which has been fried together in equal parts.
One should use either the cream of curd fried in *yamaka* oil with jaggery and ginger, or wine fried in *yamaka* oil, for the purpose of seasoning. (31)
One should eat sour fruit fried in *yamaka* (a mixture of equal parts ghee and oil), or a soup of *gṛñjanaka*,
or roasted barley meal (*saktu*) fried in *yamaka* and sprinkled with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
Or likewise, well-cooked mung beans served with the scum of clarified butter;
or well-prepared and strained broth derived from the meat of goats, sheep, or antelopes.
Or one may cook well-prepared, strained juice,
acidified with pomegranate essence, along with coriander, oil, and ginger;
eating red śāli rice with this and drinking it as well.
One is quickly freed from disorders caused by the depletion of *varcas* (fecal matter) by consuming young *bilva* fruit, jaggery, oil, *pippalī*, and ginger. (35)
9.35 When wind is obstructed, one who suffers from pain and dysentery should lick a compound of long pepper (*pippalī*) and ginger (*viśva-bheṣaja*).
[One should also take] the bark of *śābara*, its flower, *dhātakī*, and the leaf of *badarī*. 9.36

9.36b–d. One should lick *pathyā* (chebulic myrobalan) prepared with *dhātakī*, jujube fruit (*badarī-phala*), castor oil plant (*eraṇḍa*), wood-apple (*bilva*), barley, and *gokṣuraka*, along with sour substances, combined with honey; or alternatively, with jaggery.
This will certainly destroy diarrhea of intense onset, accompanied by excessive pain, straining (*pravāhikā*), and mixed with blood, even when its force has become aggravated. 36.1+1.
One whose flatus and feces are obstructed, and who suffers from excessive colic and dysentery, should drink [this] saturated with the cream of curd, honey, and the fresh juice of *kapittha*. (37)
One who is afflicted by thirst and has blood-stained phlegm deserves the satisfaction of milk;
one should administer milk that is warm as it flows over the twin [palate]. (38)
Alternatively, having boiled twenty mustā fruits in three times as much water with milk, one should cook it with the root of eraṇḍa or with young bilva fruits. (39)
9.39 One part of milk boiled with twenty parts of water until only the milk remains should be drunk; it destroys undigested matter (āma) accompanied by pain.
Likewise, one who drinks the fine powder of long pepper (pippalī) or that produced from black pepper [achieves the same].

Even diarrhea that has persisted for a long time is quickly destroyed in one who is free from undigested matter (āmadoṣa), afflicted by colic, and emaciated by fasting and other such depletive therapies. (41)
For one with a dry bowel, considering the digestive fire, one should administer ghee prepared with alkali,
along with curd-whey, the scum of wine, and the water of the ten roots.
Alternatively, oil prepared in the decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) along with rock salt (*sindhūttha*) and the five spices (*pañcakola*) immediately destroys pain.
[Oil may also be prepared] with six *palas* of ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), two *palas* each of *granthi*, *agni* (citraka), and rock salt (*saindhava*).
One should cook one prastha of oil with curd; this cures the pain of intestinal obstruction.
Similarly, meat, milk, and ghee combined together conquer constipation and colic.
Oil employed for drinking, enemas, and massage stands on one side;
for it is the foremost among those that conquer Vāta, as well as the pain caused by disordered wind. (45)

Like the pressure of another element, it is mobile, pervasive, and abides in its own domain; even for one with a weak digestive fire, oil, when applied by the proper method, brings about supreme well-being. (46)
Indeed, due to the crushing of another element, or by the crushing of another element, Bimbiśī does not remain in the seat of the wind when it is filled with oil. // 46 //

When the impurity has been exhausted and the other humors have fallen from their own seats, O sole hero who sets them in motion—what one afflicted with internal colic can live on by groaning, unless he is devoted to oil both internally and externally? (47)
In cases of anal pain and prolapse, one should administer clarified butter prepared with milk. (48ab)
In a decoction of *kola* (jujube), *amlā* (tamarind), and *cāṅgerī*, along with curd and ground ginger,
it is prepared by combining these very sour ingredients with a finely ground paste.

One should administer an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) combined with those same sour substances, along with coriander, black pepper, viḍalavana, cumin, the five spices (pañcakola), and pomegranate; or one prepared with daśamūla.
Or with *śaṭhī*, *śatāhvā*, and *kuṣṭha*; or with *vacā* or *citraka*—[these are used] in cases of dysentery, prolapse of the rectum, urinary obstruction, and stiffness of the waist. (51)

Oil or clarified butter boiled with sweet and sour substances should be used as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana); once the prolapsed rectum has been lubricated and gently fomented, it should be reintroduced.
One should fashion a cow-horn-shaped ligature with leather having a hole in the middle;
one should then boil a decoction of the five great roots in milk.
One should boil a decoction with milk,

or cook a rat devoid of its entrails with that [milk] like a paste of wind-alleviating drugs; one should cook oil with this, and by drinking it or applying it as an ointment, one shall conquer prolapse of the rectum.
In the case of *pitta* with *āma*, one should first undergo fasting (*laṅghana*) as previously described, avoiding sharp and hot substances;
if there is thirst, one should drink water prepared with the six parts [of the *pañcamūla*] along with *bhūnimba* and *sārivā*. 55.

For one who is hungry, gruel and similar foods are beneficial as they kindle the digestive fire; these are prepared with the Bṛhatyādi group of herbs, Abhīru, the two types of Balā, and Śūrpaparṇī. (56)
If there is a persistent complication, however, one should have [the patient] drink the ground fruit of *kuṭaja*, along with its bark and *ghuṇapriya*, mixed with honey and rice-water. (57)
The fruit of *vatsaka* ground with honey and rice-water;
or *pāṭhā*, *vatsaka* seeds, bark, *dārvī*, *granthika*, and *śuṇṭhī*;
or a decoction produced from *ativiṣā*, *bilva*, *vatsaka*, *udīcya*, and *musta*. (9.57–58)
Alternatively, [one may take] ativiṣā, mūrvā, niśā, indrayava, and tārkṣya;
or with honey, ativiṣā, śuṇṭhī, musta, indrayava, and kaṭphala. (59)
One should boil one pala of vatsaka seeds and drink the decoction;
he who subsists on this broth will quickly conquer bile-born abdominal disease. (60)
Or one should drink a decoction of mustā mixed with honey;
or a decoction of śālmalī stalks mixed with honey; or a decoction of himāhvaya. (61)
Kirātatiktaka, musta, vatsaka, rasāñjana, kaṭaṅkaṭerī, hrīvera, the pulp of bilva, and durālabhā. // 62 //
Sesame seeds, the juice of the moca fruit, lodhra, samaṅgā, lotus, blue water-lily, ginger, dhātakī flowers, pomegranate bark, and utpala. (63)
The yogas mentioned in half-verses [59–63] are to be taken with honey and rice-water.
A decoction of niśā, indrayava, lodhra, and elā conquers chronic diarrhea (pakvātisāra). 64.
A decoction made from ginger, ativiṣā, mustā, bhūnimba, amṛtā, and vatsaka cures chronic diarrhea (pakvātisāra).
This decoction removes all fevers and destroys all types of diarrhea.
With *guḍūcī*, *ativiṣā*, *dhānyaka*, *śuṇṭhī*, *bilva*, *musta*, and *vālaka*; with *pāṭhā*, *bhūnimba*, *kuṭaja*, *candana*, *uśīra*, and *padmaka*. (64–65)
This decoction should be drunk cold for the pacification of fever and diarrhea;
it destroys nausea, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, and burning sensations. (64+3)
Likewise, one should drink separately the groups of drugs beginning with *lodhra*, *ambaṣṭhā*, and *priyaṅgu*;
or [one may drink] with the bark of *kaṭvaṅga*, *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice), *phalinī*, and the sprouts of *dāḍima*.
One should prepare thin gruel, thick gruel, and dough-balls together with curd and pomegranate;
likewise, one should prepare them with the pulp of wood-apple, bilva, mango, and jambu. (66)
If there is no relief through that [milk], goat's milk should be administered during the non-fecal (nirāma) stage;
however, if due to an excess of the doshas it does not subside, one should administer a purgative to that strong patient.
Or one who passes stool mixed with blood in reverse order should drink a decoction of the fruit of *palāśa* combined with milk. (68)
Thereafter, lukewarm milk should be drunk according to one's strength;
when the morbid matter has been expelled by that means, the abdominal disease is pacified. (69)
Alternatively, *trāyamāṇā*, which is purifying, may be administered like *palāśa*; if pain persists while the *saṃsargī* enema is being prepared, [this should be used]. (70)

Trāyamāṇā is used for purification; once the morbid humors have been expelled, one should quickly administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) to that patient with śatapuṣpā, varī, bilva, and madhuka, according to the strength of the digestive fire.
Clarified butter cooked with one-fourth part oil and combined with milk is used as an *anvāsana* enema;
if diarrhea is not relieved by this, a *picchā-vasti* is most beneficial.
Having wrapped [the root] with moist *kuśa* grass and moist stalks of the *śālmali* tree,
and having smeared it with black earth, one should heat it over a fire of cow-dung.
When the clay has dried, one should crush those [ingredients] and form them into a ball the size of a fist;
one should then macerate it in a prastha of strained milk and subsequently administer it as an enema (āsthāpana).
After administering an enema containing the paste of nata, yaṣṭyāhva, ghee, honey,
and oil, the patient should bathe and eat with milk or the broth of wild game.

This enema quickly conquers diarrhea caused by pitta, fever, swelling, abdominal tumors, disorders of wind and blood, and diseases of the grahaṇī, as well as excessive discharge resulting from purgation and non-unctuous enemas. // 76 //
The bone from the *kaṭvaṅga* and *bilva*, *kapittha*, *surasā*, *añjana*, lac, the two types of *haridrā*, *hrīvera*, *kaṭphala*, and *śukanāsikā*. // 76+1 //
Having ground lodhra, moca-rasa, musta, dhātakī, and the sprouts of the vaṭa tree with rice-water, one should prepare pills (vaṭakas) the size of an akṣa.
One should drink it with that very water; it destroys fever and diarrhea.
Indeed, this is a purifier of the blood and a destroyer of swelling and diarrhea. // 76+3 //
Treacle derived from *kuṭaja*, combined with the *vatsakādi* group, the *sāmbaṣṭhādi* group, and honey, destroys all types of diarrhea. (77)

One should treat diarrhea that is free from mucus and undigested matter, yet accompanied by blood, long-standing, occurring even in one with a strong digestive fire, and characterized by various colors, using *puṭapāka* preparations. (78)
From the bark-mass of the *dīrghavṛnta* tree, which is covered with the leaves of the *śrīparṇī*,
smeared with clay, and steamed over a fire, the juice is squeezed out and cooled.
One suffering from diarrhea should drink [this] mixed with honey or sugar;
likewise, one should prepare it with the bark and the sprouts of milk-exuding trees.
9.80 Similarly, the bark of milk-exuding trees (kṣīradruma) combined with the bark of *kaṭvaṅga* and mixed with ghee, when steamed with the heat of water and taken with honey,
quickly destroys even severe diarrhea.
Furthermore, if one suffering from bile-induced diarrhea (pittātīsāra) consumes substances that increase bile,
his bile produces blood-diarrhea (raktātīsāra) accompanied by thirst and fever.
In cases of severe inflammation of the anus (gudapāka), goat's milk is beneficial, as is milk boiled with lotus, water-lily, samaṅgā, and the juice of the moca fruit. (83)
Alternatively, one should use śārivā, yaṣṭi, and lodhra, or the flowers of the vaṭa and other such trees, mixed with honey and sugar for drinking, eating, and for sprinkling upon the anus. (84)
Similarly, non-sour tastes such as sweet and others, along with clarified butter, are beneficial for drinks and food;
so too is a soup made from *kāśmarya* fruit, slightly sour and mixed with sugar. (85)
A gruel prepared with half water and half curd from a goat, combined with *hrīvera*, blue lotus, ginger, and the juice of *pṛśniparṇī*, destroys bloody diarrhea. (86)
Before a meal, one should lick fresh butter mixed with honey and sugar;
or, if the blood disorder is severe, one should eat goat or deer meat fried in ghee.

Drinking milk as an after-drink while subsisting on milk for three days, or consuming ghee produced from milk while eating the meat broth of the grey partridge, one attains health by licking [the medicine]. (88)
Having drunk the paste of śatāvarī with milk while maintaining a diet of milk, one quickly overcomes bloody diarrhea; or likewise, ghee prepared with that same [paste] accomplishes the same. (89)
Ghee prepared with lac, ginger, long pepper, katuka, and the bark of deodar, along with indrayava, should be consumed after drinking thin gruel and scum.
One shall quickly conquer even severe diarrhea caused by the three doṣas by using black earth, conch shell, licorice, honey, blood, and rice-water. (91)
Jayantyāsaṇa, priyaṅgu, and rice-water saturated with honey, along with a paste of black sesame seeds mixed with sugar constituting one-fifth part, [are effective]. (92)
9.92d–93. When drunk with goat’s milk combined with a portion of sugar, it immediately stops the flow of blood.
Having drunk sandalwood mixed with sugar and honey along with rice-water, [the same result follows].
One is freed from burning, thirst, delusion, and hemorrhage;
when there is burning or suppuration of the anus, cold affusions and ointments are beneficial. (94)
For burning sensations, thirst, and urinary disorders (prameha), cold sprinklings and ointments are beneficial.
When blood is passed in very small quantities many times, accompanied by pain,
and when the wind (vāyu) is obstructed and passes with difficulty or not at all— 95.
Then, one should prepare for him the previously mentioned feather enema (picchā-vasti),
having crushed the young shoots of the *śiṃśipā* and *kovidāra* trees.
And he should administer barley grains boiled in a decoction combined with ghee and milk in cases of slimy discharge, prolapse of the rectum, or pain during straining. (97)
A feather enema (picchā-vasti) should be administered to bring strength to those who are wounded or emaciated;
furthermore, an oil enema (anuvāsana) with ghee prepared with Prapauṇḍarīka should be given. 98.
For one who suffers from diarrhea preceded by or followed by blood mixed with feces, one should prepare Śatāvarī-ghṛta for the purpose of being taken as a linctus. (99)
Freshly extracted butter, licked with half its weight of sugar and a quarter part of honey, quickly overcomes that disorder for one who eats wholesome food. (100)
Having crushed the shoots of the nyagrodha, udumbara, and aśvattha trees, one should let them soak for a day and night in heated water; with that water, one should cook clarified butter. 101.
One should have this linctus, mixed with half as much sugar and one-quarter part honey, licked by anyone from whom blood flows either downwards or upwards. (102)

9.102–103. Whether the diarrhea is downward or upward, in cases of *śleṣmātīsāra* (kapha-type diarrhea), the measures prescribed for vata should be applied specifically to digest the undigested matter (*āmapācana*). If there is a persistent secondary complication (*anubandha*), one should drink a decoction that kindles the digestive fire (*agnidīpana*).
Bilva, karkaṭikā, musta, prāṇadā, viśvabheṣaja, vacā, viḍaṅga, bhūtīka, dhānaka, and amaradāru; or [these]. 104.
9.104d–105: Or else, *dhānyaka*, *devadāru*;
or alternatively, *pippalīmūla*, the two types of *pippalī*, *citraka*, *pāṭhā*, *agni*, *vatsaka*, *granthi*, *tiktā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *vacā*, and *abhayā*.
Alternatively, pippalī, the two types of pippalī, and citraka,
when boiled or ground into a paste, are a remedy for kaphaja diarrhea; likewise are sauvarcala salt, vacā, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, prativiṣā, and abhayā.
One suffering from diarrhea caused by phlegm (kapha) should drink [the powder] with lukewarm water;
or, having licked the pulp of a wood-apple (kapittha) mixed with the three pungents (vyoṣa), honey, and sugar. 107.
One is freed from abdominal disease by consuming *vyoṣa* with sugar and honey, or *kaṭphala* combined with honey;
likewise, by licking *kaṇā* (long pepper) mixed with honey and drinking buttermilk with *citraka*.
Or, by eating young bilva fruits, one dispels abdominal disease;
likewise, pāṭhā, moca, rasāmbhoda, dhātakī, bilva, and nāgara [are effective]. (109)
One may destroy even severe diarrhea with buttermilk mixed with jaggery, along with yavānī, pippalī-mūla, cāturjātaka, and nāgara. (110)
With equal parts of long pepper, agni, water, cumin, coriander, and sauvarcala salt;
and with vṛṣa, sour [substance], dhātakī, black pepper, bilva, pomegranate, and dīpyaka. (111)

A powder prepared from three parts each of vṛkṣāmla, dhātakī, kṛṣṇā, bilva, dāḍima, and tinduka; six parts of sugar; and eight parts of kapittha, cures diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), wasting, abdominal tumors, and diseases of the throat. (9.111–112)
Prepared with three parts of *guḍūcī*, six parts of sugar, and eight parts of *kapittha*,
it overcomes wasting diseases, abdominal tumors, and disorders of the abdomen, as well as cough, dyspnea, loss of digestive fire, hemorrhoids, catarrh, and anorexia.
One karṣa of tāvakṣīrī and two karṣas of the four spices (cāturjāta). // 113 //

Take one *karṣa* each of *tvaṅkṣīrī* and *cāturjātaka*, two *karṣas* each of *yavānī*, *dhānyaka*, *ajājī*, *granthika*, and *vyoṣa*, one *pala* each of *dāḍima* and eight *palas* of sugar; these, when combined together— 9.113cd–114ab: [The resulting preparation is known as *madhuśigru*. It cures hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargement, consumption, cough, and fever. It is beneficial for the voice and is a promoter of strength and complexion. It is especially effective against wind-disorders (*vāta*) and is a digestive stimulant. It is also a cure for dysuria and edema.
