9.114–115. One pala each of *yavānī*, *dhānyaka*, *ajāji*, *granthi*, and *vyoṣa* constitutes this powder called Dāḍimāṣṭaka, which possesses qualities similar to the Kapitthāṣṭaka. It should be administered with *khala* and other vehicles as prescribed for *vātātisāra*, according to the specific condition.
A *khala* preparation consisting of *viḍaṅga*, black pepper, *kapittha*, and dry ginger, combined with *cāṅgerī*, buttermilk, and sour *kola* fruit, overcomes diarrhea caused by *śleṣman*. (116)
When the phlegm has been diminished, one should administer the previously mentioned sour *lākṣā* compound weighing six palas, or aged ghee mixed with gruel and scum. (117)
One should drink kaṭphala, madhuka, lodhra, and the bark of the pomegranate fruit with rice-water; this destroys diarrhea caused by vāta and pitta. (117+1)
Musta, ativiṣā, dārvī, vacā, and śuṇṭhī, each taken in equal parts—this decoction, combined with honey, is for one suffering from diarrhea caused by kapha and vāta. (117+2)
One should administer yellow sandalwood, *vacā*, *lodhra*, *kaliṅga* fruit, and ginger, combined with pomegranate juice, to one suffering from diarrhea caused by *pitta* and *kapha*. (117+3)
A slimy enema (picchā-vasti) is recommended for obstruction of wind and phlegm, or when there is excessive discharge of phlegm, as well as for colic or dysentery (pravāhikā). // 118 //
In cases of obstruction caused by Vāta and Śleṣman,
[an enema] combined with Vacā, Bilva, Kaṇā, Kuṣṭha, Śatāhvā, and salts should be used;
or alternatively, one prepared with Bilva oil or with oil cooked with the drugs beginning with Vacā.
For one frequently afflicted by phlegm and wind, a lukewarm non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) is beneficial;
likewise for those with diminished phlegm, anal inflammation, long-standing diarrhea, or debility. (120)
The powerful wind humor, when situated in its own location, inevitably arises; being strong, it may suddenly destroy [the patient], therefore one should conquer it with haste. (121)
One should first conquer wind, then bile, and then phlegm; or else, one should first conquer whichever among the three is most powerful. (122)

One who is agitated by fear and grief becomes angry quickly; therefore, for those two conditions, one should perform treatments that remove wind (vāta), as well as acts of cheering and consolation. 123.
For one whose urine or flatus passes even without the expulsion [of feces], and who possesses a stimulated digestive fire and a light digestive tract, that abdominal disease is pacified. (124)

In the section on therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna), one should treat the morbid humors (doṣas) localized in the duodenum (grahaṇī) as in the case of indigestion (ajīrṇa); furthermore, one should digest the undigested matter (āma) therein according to the procedure prescribed for diarrhea (atīsāra). // 1 //
At the time of eating, one should provide thin gruel and other foods combined with the five spices (pañcakola) and so forth—
food that is pungent and light— and furthermore, administer digestive stimulants (dīpana).
In cases of undigested matter (āma), one should administer a gruel made with ativiṣā, sour ingredients, and ginger;
for drinking, one should provide water prescribed for diarrhea, as well as buttermilk, wine, and so forth. // 3 //

For those suffering from disorders of the *grahaṇī*, buttermilk is wholesome because it stimulates digestion, is constipating, and is light; furthermore, due to its sweet post-digestive transformation (*pāki*), it does not aggravate *pitta*. (4)
Because it is astringent, hot, and expanding in its action, and because it is dry, it is beneficial for phlegm (kapha).
Because it is sweet, sour, and thick, it is fresh and does not cause a burning sensation when consumed; thus, it is beneficial for wind (vāta). // 5 //
10.5ab Because of their astringent, hot, and drying qualities, one should take one *prastha* each of the four sour substances, three *palas* of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*),
four *palas* of salts, and eight *palas* of sugar.
One should add this powder to vegetables, soups, cooked rice, meat gravies, and so forth;
it cures cough, indigestion, loss of appetite, dyspnea, heart disease, anemia, splenic disorders, and abdominal tumors.

One should drink a decoction of ginger (*nāgara*), ativiṣā, and musta to alleviate heart disease, pain in the flanks, and colic; or one may drink the paste of those same drugs with warm water, or simply ginger, or even *abhayā*. (10.7d–8)
In cases of diarrhea with undigested stool (āmātisāra) accompanied by mucus (pravāha), one should drink either the *vacā* group of drugs with rock salt (*saindhava*), or likewise with wine,
or else with pomegranate juice.

Vid salt, along with bilva, citraka, and ginger, ground together and taken with lukewarm water, [is effective] against undigested matter (āmadoṣa), kapha, and vāta, as well as for pain in the abdominal cavity. (10)
Kaliṅga, hiṅgu, ativiṣā, vacā, sauvarcala, and abhayā should be drunk with warm water for vomiting, heart disease, and colic. (11)
The powder of pathyā, sauvarcala salt, and ajājī, combined with marica;
along with pippalī, nāgara, pāṭhā, śārivā, and the two types of bṛhatī. (12)
Citraka, the alkali of Kuṭaja, and likewise the five salts, reduced to powder, [should be taken] with curd, wine, its scum (maṇḍa), warm water, and sour gruel (kāñjika). // 13 //
One should drink this for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire (agni) and as a supreme remedy for wind (vāta) in the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha):
the five salts, the two alkalis, black pepper, and the five-kola group. (14)
A pill made of *dīpyaka* and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) prepared in the juice of *bījapūra*, or in the water of *kola* and pomegranate, is a supreme digestive and stimulant of the digestive fire. (15)
One pala each of tālīśapatra, cavikā, and marica;
two palas each of kṛṣṇā and its root; and three palas of śuṇṭhī. (16)
One should always consume pills made from four types of *uśīra*, each weighing one *karṣa* and finely powdered, mixed with three times as much jaggery (*guḍa*). // 17 //

Wine, broth, meat-soup, fermented liquor (ariṣṭa), whey, thin gruel, and milk, taken as after-drinks, [are beneficial] for those whose vomiting, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and pains in the flanks and heart are caused by vāta and kapha. (18)
For the cessation of fever, swelling, anemia, abdominal tumors, alcoholism, hemorrhoids, excessive salivation, chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and cough. // 19 //

One should administer Abhayā at the site of a tumor (nāgara-sthāna), and likewise in cases of intestinal obstruction; in cases of vomiting and other Pitta-related disorders, it should be combined with four times its weight of sugar.
In this very case of constipation (viḍ-graha), one should administer [the powder];
alternatively, boluses (vaṭaka) should be prepared with jaggery or sugar. For indeed, through contact with fire, they attain lightness.
Then, for one whose wind and grahaṇī disease have reached maturity,
the physician should administer ghee processed with digestive stimulants in small quantities.
Then, for one whose wind-disorder of the *grahaṇī* is fully matured, once the digestive fire has been slightly kindled, and who has had their feces, urine, and flatus suppressed,
one should administer a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*) after two or three days of oleation and sudation, following anointing with oil.
Then, once the Vata has been pacified by castor oil, ghee, or Tilvaka oil mixed with alkali, one should administer a purgative to eliminate the displaced Doshas. (24)

Then, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) to that patient whose internal channels are purified and dry, and who has bound feces, using oil processed with digestive stimulants, sour substances, and vata-alleviating drugs. (25)

Once the enema has been established, the patient has undergone purgation, and has been properly administered an oil enema, one should again practice the habitual use of ghee while consuming light food.

Or, having been properly administered an oil enema (anuvāsana), one should take ghee prepared with the five roots (pañcamūla), abhayā, vyoṣa, pippalīmūla, saindhava, rāsnā, the two types of kṣāra, ajājī, viḍaṅga, and śaṭī. (10.26)
With sour gruel (*śukta*), the juice of *mātuluṅga*, fresh ginger, dried radish, sour jujube (*kola*), *cukrikā*, and pomegranate; (28)
Cooked with buttermilk, whey, the scum of wine, fermented gruel, water from boiled husks, and sour rice-gruel, this preparation is supreme for kindling the digestive fire. (29)

Or one should administer clarified butter prepared with the juice of bījapūraka, which removes colic, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, dyspnea, cough, and disorders of wind and phlegm. (30)
Oil prepared with these [herbs] for the purpose of anointing overcomes tremors;
or one may drink the powder of these medicinal herbs with lukewarm water.
When vāta is enveloped by kapha, or when kapha is accompanied by āma and provoked by vāyu,
the pitta that extinguishes the digestive fire should be eliminated by means of purgation or emesis.

Having [administered emetics], one should kindle the digestive fire with foods that are bitter, light, constipating, appetizing, and non-burning, as well as with bitter powders and unctuous substances.
Paṭola, nimba, trāyantī, tiktā, tiktaka, parpaṭa, the bark and fruit of kuṭaja, mūrvā, the fruit of madhuśigru, and vacā. (34)
Dārvī-tvak, padmaka, uśīra, yavānī, musta, candana, saurāṣṭrī, ativiṣā, vyoṣa, tvak, elā, pattra, and dāru. (35)
This powder, to be licked with honey or drunk with wine or water, cures heart disease, anemia, disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors, colic, loss of appetite, and fever. (36)
It destroys jaundice, disorders of the combined humors (saṃnipāta), and diseases of the mouth.
Take equal parts of bhūnimba, kaṭukā, mustā, the three pungents (try-ūṣaṇa), and indrayava. (37)
One should powder sixteen parts of the bark of *vatsaka* from the *citraka* plant;
when drunk with jaggery and cold water, it cures disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī-doṣa*) and abdominal tumors (*gulma*). (38)
Long pepper, ativiṣā, mustā, pāṭhā, bilva, and rasāñjana conquer jaundice, fever, anemia, urinary disorders, loss of appetite, and diarrhea. (39)

The powder made from the bark and fruit of *kuṭaja*, along with *tiktā* and *dhātakī*, which cures urinary disorders, loss of appetite, and diarrhea, should be taken with honey and rice-water in cases of *paittika* (bile-related) *grahaṇī* disease. (10.39)
Chandana, padmaka, uśīra, pāṭhā, mūrvā, and kuṭannaṭa are desired for the treatment of dysentery, hemorrhoids, pain in the rectum, and the onset of bleeding. (41)
Ṣaḍgrantha, śārivā, āsphotā, saptaparṇa, and āṭarūṣaka; paṭola, udumbara, aśvattha, vaṭa, plakṣa, and kapītana. (42)
One should boil two-pala portions each of vaṭa, plakṣa, kapītana, kaṭukā, rohiṇī, mustā,
and nimba in one droṇa of water; with that decoction, one should cook ghee using [the paste] measured at one picu each.

In cases of pitta-type grahaṇī, one should drink [the decoction] of kirātatikta, indrayava, vīrā, māgadhikā, and utpala; as well as the "bitter" (tiktaka) formulation mentioned in the treatment of kuṣṭha.

When the *grahaṇī* is afflicted by *śleṣman*, after emesis has been induced with sharp [emetics], one should gradually increase the digestive fire (*agni*) using pungent, sour, salty, and alkaline substances. (45)
One should prepare gruel and other drinks with the five pungent fruits (pañcakola), chebulic myrobalan (āmalaka), coriander (dhānya), patha, fragrant palāśa, and plenty of citron (bījapūra). // 46 //
One droṇa of madhūka flowers, half that amount of viḍaṅga, half of that again of citraka, and one āḍhaka of bhallātaka. (47)
One should boil eight palas of this mañjiṣṭhā in three droṇas of water;
when reduced to one droṇa, it should be cooled and mixed with half an āḍhaka of honey. (48)
One should employ that fermented liquor (*āsava*) which has been stored for a month in a jar scented with cardamom, lotus stalks, agallochum, and sandalwood. (49)
10.49c–d This [preparation], having been kept for a month in a jar, when consumed, kindles the digestive fire (grahaṇī), is nourishing, and subdues pitta and blood disorders;
it is a destroyer of consumption, skin diseases, leucoderma, and urinary disorders. 50.
10.50b–d. The decoction of Madhūka flowers, boiled down to half its original quantity, is nourishing and subdues raktapitta;
it should be prepared as before, cooled, and combined with a quarter part honey.
10.51 Drinking one kuḍava of madhūka flowers while eating wholesome food, one may conquer all disorders of the grahaṇī;
likewise, one should drink the expressed juices of grapes, sugarcane, and dates that have been fermented.
One karṣa each of hiṅgu, tiktā, vacā, mādrī, pāṭhā, indrayava, gokṣura, and pañcakola, along with one pala each of the five salts (paṭupañcaka). // 53 //
Having crushed two kuḍavas each of ghee and oil, along with two prasthas of curd,
one should boil them over a mild fire until the liquid has been reduced.

Then, having incinerated it until the smoke has vanished, one should reduce it to powder, soak it in clarified butter, and drink a handful (pāṇitala) of it; once that has been digested, one should eat sweet food.
It destroys all diseases of wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman), as well as poisons and artificial toxins (viṣa-gara).
[One should take] bhūnimba, rohiṇī, tiktā, paṭola, nimba, and parpaṭa. (56)
Having burnt [these] with buffalo urine, one should drink it as an increaser of the digestive fire:
the two types of *haridrā*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *citraka*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*. (57)
Mustā processed with goat's urine is an alkali that increases digestive fire.
[Take] four palas from the stem of Sudhā and three palas each from the three salts. (58)
10.58d–59. Having burnt the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the salts, one *kuḍava* of eggplant (*vārtāka*), eight *pala* of *arka*, and two *pala* of *citraka*,
[one should form] pills with the juice of eggplant to be taken after meals.
One *kuḍava* each of eggplant and *arka* [leaves],
when eaten, quickly digest consumed food; they are beneficial for cough, dyspnea, and hemorrhoids, and they alleviate cholera, catarrh, and heart disease.
Mātuluṅga, śaṭhī, rāsnā, the three pungents (kaṭutraya), and harītakī; svarjikā, the alkali called yāvaśūka, and the five salts (pañcapaṭu). // 61 //
The powder of the three pungents (kaṭutraya) and harītakī, when drunk with lukewarm water, increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire.
In cases of kapha-type grahaṇī disorder associated with vāta, one should cook ghee with these [drugs].
The *dhānvantara* [ghee], the *ṣaṭpala*, the *bhallātaka-ghṛta*, and *abhaya*; as well as *viḍa*, *kāca*, *uṣa*, salt, *svarjikā*, and *yāvaśūka*.
One should burn saptalā, kaṇṭakārī, and citraka together;
then, one should cook half an āḍhaka of the alkali that has been strained seven times [from this mixture]. (64)
One āḍhaka of ghee should be drunk to increase the strength of the digestive fire;
during the accumulation [of fat], one should employ these five procedures according to one's strength.
In cases of excessive salivation caused by phlegm (kapha) and weak digestive fire, one should employ dry and bitter substances that stimulate digestion;
for a person who is emaciated, these should be applied alternately with unctuous and dry substances when there is an aggravation of phlegm.
For one whose body is emaciated by wasting, a digestive stimulant combined with unctuous substances is prescribed;
for one with an excess of bile, a digestive stimulant combined with bitter and sweet substances is prescribed. (67)
Oil combined with sour and salty substances is recommended for those with excessive Vāta;
one should know that oil alone is the supreme stimulant for a weak digestive fire.

Even very heavy food is not sufficient to pacify a fever kindled by [excessive] unctuousness, for one whose digestive fire is weak and whose phlegm is diminished, even when the stool is digested, it remains loose. (69)
One should release it; he should drink ghee mixed with potent medicine in small quantities.
By that means, [the vāyu] is brought back to its own path and engaged in its own function. // 70 //
Being equal [to the fire], it kindles the fire, for it is the stimulator of the fire;
and it discharges the fecal matter with difficulty because of its hardness. (71)
10.71b–72a. For this [salt] is indeed an inflamer of the fire;

a person whose digestion is sluggish due to dryness should drink ghee mixed with salts, or, when the digestive fire is weak, he should drink clarified butter or oil along with digestive stimulants (*dīpana*).

In cases of weak digestion due to excessive intake of fats, or from upward movement of gases (udāvarta), alkaline powders, fermented liquors (āsava), and medicinal decoctions (ariṣṭa) should be administered, as well as non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) and unctuous enemas (sneha-vasti). // 73 //
In cases of udāvarta caused by the excessive increase of the doṣas, one who has been properly purified when the digestive fire is weak should follow the dietary regimen.
However, for one who is free from disease but whose digestive fire remains weak, ghee alone is the digestive stimulant.
Once thoroughly purified, the patient should follow the dietary regimen.
For those who are emaciated by travel or fasting, one should have them drink ghee with gruel;
that [ghee] is strengthening, digestive, and nourishing when administered alongside food.

However, because of the danger of a long-term complication, one should feed those men who have become emaciated, wasted, and thin the meat-juices of carnivorous animals mixed with sour substances. (76)
Because they are light, hot, pungent, and purifying, they quickly kindle the digestive fire;
and because they increase the flesh with flesh, they are supreme increasers of strength. (77)

10.77 When properly administered, oleation (sneha), fermented liquors (āsava), spirits (surā), medicinal extracts (ariṣṭa), powders (cūrṇa), decoctions (kvātha), and wholesome diets— due to their qualities of being light, hot, pungent, and purifying— increase the strength of the body and the digestive fire.
Just as an external fire, such as a blazing pillar, is produced by heartwood and fuel, so too is the fire within the digestive tract generated by food. (79)
The bodily fire does not blaze through lack of food, nor does it blaze from overeating;
just as a fire without fuel, or a small fire covered by too much fuel, does not burn. (80)

When the phlegm is diminished and the wind is joined with fuel, the increased bile in its own location, following the wind, further increases the fire; then that fire, accompanied by the wind, becomes small. (10.80–81)

Having quickly digested the food and depleted all the bodily constituents (dhātus) as well as the vital essence (ojas), it causes death; such a person is not healthy, and he faints once the meal has been digested. (82)
That [fire] would kill him; otherwise, he remains healthy.
Diseases such as thirst, cough, burning sensations, and fainting arise from excessive digestive fire (*aty-agni*).
That excessive fire should be treated with substances that are heavy, unctuous, mild, thick, cold, and stable. (10.82–83)
One should bring him to peace with food and drink, just as one extinguishes a blazing fire with water;
even when his previous meal is not yet digested, one should repeatedly offer him further food.
One should provide him with foods,
ensuring that he finds no lack of fuel so that he does not perish;
[these include] *kṛsarā*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), unctuous foods, flour-based preparations, and various products of molasses.
10.85b–d Thus one should not cause him distress;
he should eat the flesh of aquatic and marshy animals that have been cooked, especially smooth fish and those that dwell in still waters. 86.
One should eat well-prepared mutton, which wards off excessive digestive fire;
or, when thirsty, one should drink milk mixed with beeswax, or ghee. 87.
One should take wheat flour thoroughly saturated with milk and abundant ghee,
or fatty substances (snehas) devoid of oil and combined with the meat-broth of animals from marshy regions.
Alternatively, one should administer milk boiled with *śyāmā* and *trivṛt* as a purgative;
this repeatedly removes the *pitta*, and the patient should be given a meal of milk-rice (*pāyasa*). (89)
Whatever food is heavy, oily, and increases phlegm—all that is beneficial for those with excessive digestive fire; and sleeping during the day after eating is likewise beneficial. (90)
Fire digests food; when devoid of food, it digests the humors (doṣas).
When the humors are exhausted, it digests the bodily constituents (dhātus); and when the constituents are depleted, it consumes life itself. 91.

"Thinking, 'This food is inherently incompatible, yet this [other food] possesses the power of combination and preparation,' and so forth—acting according to their own whims without understanding this is the strength of one who possesses the power of the sacred fire. (92)
Therefore, one should protect the fire with every effort; for when that is lost, the person goes to destruction itself.
When seized by defects, one is devoured by hosts of diseases; but when it is kept in balance, one shall be free from illness and long-lived. 93.
One should properly insert [the instrument] into the opening of the *liṅga* or into the vagina;
one should apply camphor, which is the primary remedy for removing the pain of urine. 0+1.

In the case of a wind-born disorder below the navel, one should apply vāta-alleviating oil during difficult labor; furthermore, one should foment the body thoroughly with unctuous substances using bolus-sweats, affusions, and immersions. // 1 //
With the ten roots, balā, eraṇḍa, yava, abhīru, punarnavā, kulattha, kola, pattūra, vṛścīva, and upalabhedaka; // 2 //
Oil, ghee, and the fats of boar and bear, prepared with decoctions and pastes along with the five salts, when administered internally, are excellent for removing colic. (3)
One should employ these substances— along with oils and fruits— in drinks, food, boluses, and poultices, making them slightly sour and rich in unctuousness.
One should drink wine enriched with sauvarcala salt to alleviate pain in the urine; in cases of Pitta-type disorders, one should employ cold affusions, plasters, and immersions.
One should drink water boiled with gokṣuraka, vidārī, kaseruka,
and the five roots known as tṛṇa-pañcamūla, together with honey and sugar.
By drinking vṛṣaka, the seeds of trapusa, ervāru, and laṭvā, along with saffron, with grape juice, one overcomes all urinary obstructions (mūtrāghāta).
One should drink a paste of *ervāru* seeds, *yaṣṭyāhva*, and *dārvī* with rice-water, or a paste of *drākṣā* with water that has been allowed to stand overnight. // 8 //
In cases arising from *kapha*, one should employ emesis, sudation, and food that is sharp, hot, and pungent;
one should also habitually consume preparations of barley, alkali, and whey (*kālaśeya*). (9)
One should drink *sūkṣmailā* with wine, or with the juice of *dhātrī* fruit;
or one may take *sārasāsthi*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *elā*, and *vyoṣa* with honey and urine. (10)
One should cause [the patient] to drink either the natural juice of Kaṇṭakārī mixed with honey, or the seeds of Śitivāraka ground into a fine powder with buttermilk. // 11 //
Dhava, saptāhva, kuṭaja, guḍūcī, caturaṅgula,
kembuka, elā, and karañja should be boiled together with honey until they are properly prepared.
11.12c–d Or one should drink gruel prepared with *kaṭukailā* and *karañja*, or powdered *pravāla* with rice-water; or *pāṭalā* alkali mixed with oil, having been strained seven times. // 13 //
From the sprouts of the *pāṭalī* and *yava*, from the *pāribhadra* and even from sesame, one should prepare wine combined with cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper, using alkaline water. (14)
One should drink these with molasses as a side-dish, or lick them individually; in cases of the combined derangement (saṃnipāta), all of this is beneficial according to the specific condition. (15)
Even when it has arisen recently, in cases such as vātavasti and others, urinary calculus (aśmarī) is considered a terrible disease, resembling the God of Death himself. (16)

In cases such as vātavasti and others, the condition is curable with medicines while it is still young; once it has grown severe, it requires excision. In its early stages, the sequential application of oleation and other therapies is prescribed.
Pāṣāṇabheda, vasuka, vaśira, aśmantaka, varī, kapotavaṅkā, atibalā, bhallūka, uśīra, and kacchaka. // 18 //

11.18d–19: *Bhallūka*, *uśīra*, *kaṇṭaka*, *vṛkṣādanī*, the leaf and fruit of *śāka*, the two types of *vyāghrī*, *guṇṭha*, *trikaṇṭaka*, barley, *kulattha* beans, *kola* fruits, *varuṇa*, and the fruit of *kataka*.
Ghee boiled with a decoction of these [drugs] along with an added paste (*pratīvāpa*) of *ūṣaka* and other ingredients, when drunk, quickly breaks up urinary calculi (*aśmarī*) produced by Vata. (20)
One should drink the paste of the roots of *gandharvahasta*, *bṛhatī*, *vyāghrī*, *gokṣuraka*, and *ikṣurā* with curd and honey to break up urinary calculi. (21)
Kuśa, kāśa, śara, guṇṭha, itkaṭa, moraṭa, aśmabhit, darbha, vidārī, vārāhī, śālimūla, and trikaṇṭaka. // 22 //
One should cook ghee in a decoction of bhallūka, pāṭalī, pāṭhā, pattūra, kuraṇṭaka, the two types of punarnavā, and śirīṣa. (23)
The powder of the seeds of *trapusa* and others, along with blue lotus (*indīvara*), licorice (*madhuka*), and realgar (*śilājatu*), breaks up bile-stones (*pittāśmarī*). (24)
The two groups beginning with *varuṇa* are wind-destroying; [the second group consists of] cardamom, *hareṇukā*, *guggulu*, black pepper, costus, *citraka*, and *surāhvaya*. (25)
Ghee prepared with these [drugs] ground into a paste, along with the *ūṣakādi* group of drugs and water, quickly breaks up urinary calculi born of *kapha*. (26)

One should prepare [the medicine] with substances such as alkali, milk, and barley gruel, each according to its own requirements, as well as with the fruits of *picuka*, *aṅkola*, *kataka*, *śāka*, and *indīvara*. (27)
Warm water mixed with jaggery, when drunk, is the supreme means for precipitating gravel (śarkarā). [The following are also effective:
the bones of a crane, a camel, and a donkey; śvadaṃṣṭrā; and tālapattrikā. (28)
Ajamoda, the root of the Kadamba tree, and Viśva— the medicinal herb— drunk with warm water and ghee,
or sugar drunk with wine or warm water, will break up gravel. (11.28–29)
The medicinal root of *bilva* and the powder of *nṛtyakuṇḍaka* seeds,
combined with honey and drunk for seven days with goat’s milk, causes the removal of urinary calculi.

A lukewarm decoction of the seeds of *nṛtyakuṇḍala*, the seeds of *markaṭaka*, and the root of *śigru* causes the expulsion of urinary calculi (*aśmarī*). [Likewise does a decoction] derived from sesame, *apāmārga*, plantain, *palāśa*, and barley. (11.30–31)
An alkaline preparation should be drunk with goat's urine for gravel and urinary calculi;
or one may drink the root of *kapotavaṅkā* alone with wine or other liquids. (32)
Or, afflicted by these pains, one should drink milk prepared with that [decoction],
or milk prepared with the seeds of *harītakī*, or again, milk boiled with *punarnavā*.
One who eats milk-rice should take the root of *barhiśikhā* with rice-water;
this should be administered in cases of urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*), and from here one should apply the treatment to the remaining conditions as well. (34)
Water, milk, or clarified butter prepared with the *bṛhatī* group of herbs and double the amount of *gokṣura* conquers all disorders of the urine. (35)
One should drink devadāru, ghana, mūrvā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and harītakī with wine, milk, or water in all cases of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta). // 36 //
Or one may take the juice of dhanvayāsa, or a decoction of kakubha, or triphalā ground with warm water and combined with rock salt. (37)
One should administer gruel mixed with treacle in a decoction of vyāghrī and gokṣuraka, or in a decoction of vīratarādi, or even in the broth of a cock. (38)
Or one should eat *śilājatu* consecrated with the *Vīratara* mantra and so forth;
or, having drunk wine or a decoction, one may travel by chariot or horse. (39)
Alternatively, by drinking medicinal wine free from toxins,
the stone is likewise dislodged due to the agitation caused by its rapid movement.
In every case, the group of drugs beginning with *vīratara* should be employed.

For the purpose of clearing the rectum, one should regularly employ sesame oil, *tailvaka* ghee, and enema therapy; specifically, one should administer urethral enemas (*uttara-vasti*) once the seminal calculi have been cleared. (41)

11.41d–42. And in the case of seminal calculi (*śukrāśmarī*), once the urinary tract has been purified by those [measures], a strong man, being well-satiated, should consume aphrodisiac meats, such as those of the rooster, for the purification of the seminal receptacle.
If, despite these accomplished remedies, he does not attain peace, then the physician may at will attend to the passionate man with women who bestow intoxication.
11.43dv If there is no peace [of the disease], then, having informed the king, "The physician [has failed]," one should properly apply the surgical instrument.
Without treatment, death is certain; with treatment, there is doubt [as to the outcome]. 11.44ab/11.44cd (Note: The numbering follows the source's intent to combine the two halves of verse 44).
Even for a physician who is well-established and has repeatedly achieved success in his practice, [he should treat] the patient who has been lubricated, purified, and slightly emaciated. 45.

Then, for the patient who has been lubricated, purified, and slightly emaciated— whose body has been anointed and fomented, who has not yet eaten, and for whom auspicious rites have been performed— [the procedure should be undertaken].
[She was] resting on the lap of a man whose knees were pressed against his thighs. // 46 //
Sitting on a cloth or a cushion with the body turned face upwards toward the east,
he should then firmly bind his bent knees and elbows with a cloth.
While the patient remains with him, supported and comforted,
one should apply oil all around the navel and below it on the left side.
Having crushed it with the fist, one should press down until the stone has gone downward; then, with the index and middle fingers smeared with oil and having grown long nails... 49.
Having inserted two fingers into the anus on the left side and followed along the anal canal,
one should reach the stone with strength and effort at the junction of the anus and the penis.
Having positioned the anus and drawn the rectal folds inward, one should insert the enema bag so that it is free of wrinkles and not overly extended;
then, pressing with both fingers, one should squeeze it until it bulges like a knot. 11.51.
One should extract a foreign body, avoiding the raphe, by making an incision one barley-corn in width;
one should remove it in such a way that it is not shattered by the force of the stone.

The entire [rectum] is at the snake’s mouth; however, for women, the bladder is situated on the side, resting upon the uterus; therefore, their surgical instrument is shaped like a lap (utsaṅgavat). 53.
If one performs the placement otherwise than this, there will be a wound with a discharge of urine;
furthermore, for the man, there may even be a single instance of urinary incontinence. 54.
The rupture of the bladder is the cause of urinary calculi; it does not succeed if [the calculus] is double.
Once the foreign body has been removed, one should have the patient immersed in a tub of warm water.
Likewise, the bladder is not filled by the enema fluid; however, once it is full, one should press it.
Then, for the purification of the urine, water from milk-producing trees should be injected into the end of the penis.

11.56c–d: One should apply the water of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*) to the penis; inside the penis, one should apply the same. Having saturated [the area] with jaggery (*guḍa*), and having anointed the wound with honey and ghee, one should drink two times a day lukewarm gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared with urine-purifying drugs, mixed with ghee. 11.57.
For three days or ten days, he should eat a small amount of rice with milk enriched with plenty of jaggery;
thereafter, he should consume it with sour fruits and the meat-broths of animals that roam the wilderness.
Having washed the wound with a decoction of milky trees, one should apply an ointment made of *prapauṇḍarīka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, and eye-medicines. // 59 //
One should cook oil for the anointing of the ulcer with these very same ingredients combined with niśā;
one should then foment it for ten days, and after seven nights, restore it to its own natural channel.
One should apply fomentation for ten days; likewise, if the urine does not flow, one should cauterize the urinary stone wound with fire.
However, once it has returned to its own natural passage, one should treat it with predominantly sweet substances.
Even when his wound has healed, he should not mount that [tree] by means of a bladder-bag;
nor should he swim in water using elephants, snakes, horses, trees, women, or chariots as floats.
One should avoid these eight with the surgical knife: the urinary and seminal ducts, the bladder and the testicles, the raphe (sevanī), the anus, the urethral meatus, and the vagina. (63)

In the section on therapeutics, for a strong patient suffering from urinary disorders (meha), one should first administer emesis and purgation after the patient has been oleated with a decoction made from mustard, ariṣṭa, nikumbha, akṣa, and karañja.

The oil should be prepared with *trikaṇṭaka* and other ingredients as appropriate, or with a fatty substance (*sneha*) to which *musta*, *devāhva*, and *nāgara* have been added as a medicinal paste (*prativāpa*). // 2 //
Then one should administer a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) with a decoction of the surasādi group;
however, one afflicted by pitta should be purified and then satiated with the meat juices of the nyagrodhādi group. // 3 //

12.3cv However, in one afflicted by pitta, [the use of] nyagrodha and other such drugs causes urinary retention, pain, abdominal tumors (gulma), emaciation, and so forth due to depletion; therefore, one should employ pacifying (śamana) treatments to prevent further complications. // 4 //
For one whose condition cannot be purified by those [measures], one should administer those very same remedies in all types of urinary disorders (sarva-meha),
having soaked turmeric in the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) and mixing it with honey, to be taken in the morning.
Alternatively, dārvī, surāhva, triphalā, and mustā may be boiled in water;
or else, citraka, triphalā, dārvī, and kaliṅga may be taken with honey. (6)
Or one may take the juice of *guḍūcī* or *āmalaka* mixed with honey.
Of lodhra, abhayā, toyada, and kaṭphala; of pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, arjuna, and dhanvana. // 7cd //
In cases of phlegm (kapha), three decoctions made from gāyatrī, dārvī, kṛmihṛt, and dhava, combined with honey, [are recommended]. // 7ef //

In cases of pitta, three decoctions—of uśīra, lodhra, arjuna, and candana; of paṭola, nimba, āmalaka, and amṛtā; and of lodhra-water, kālīyaka, and dhātakī—should be administered mixed with honey. (8)
According to their respective natures, these [substances] provide drinks, food, and the nourishment of barley and wheat. (9ab)

In cases of prameha where vāta is predominant, one should prescribe oleation therapies using barley and wheat; furthermore, preparations such as cakes, parched flour, and *vāṭya* made from barley are beneficial. (12.9b–10)
Then there are the excrement of elephants, horses, and goats, or that produced from bamboo;
grasses and grains such as mung beans and the like, and aged *śāli* rice along with *ṣaṣṭika* rice. (11)
The *śrī-kukkuṭa* is sour; likewise is the *khalaka* made from the husks of sesame and mustard seeds.
*Kapittha*, *tinduka*, and *jambū*—these are used to prepare *rāga-ṣāḍava* condiments. (12)
Bitter vegetables, excellent honey, dry foods with roasted grain flour (saktu), the meat of wild animals roasted on spits, dried meats, and iron preparations [are beneficial]. 13.
Madya, ariṣṭa, and āsava are fermented liquors; sīdhu is produced from boiled juice; likewise are the water from the heartwood of asana and other trees, darbha-water, and honey-water.
One should drink well-prepared barley flour mixed with honey and *sīdhu* liquor, after the barley has been soaked overnight in a decoction of the best drugs and dried during the day. (15)
One should eat the well-powdered flowers of *śāla*, *saptāhva*, *kampilla*, *vṛkṣaka*, *akṣa*, *kapittha*, and *rohītaka* with honey. (16)
In cases of urinary disorders caused by kapha and pitta, one should drink [the powder] with the juice of dhātrī, or with [a paste of] trikaṇṭaka, niśā, lodhra, somavalka, vacā, and arjuna. // 17 //
One should cook [the oil] with padmaka, kāśmantaka, ariṣṭa, candana, aguru, dīpyaka, paṭola, musta, mañjiṣṭhā, mādrī, and bhallātaka. (18)
Oil is used for disorders of vāta and kapha; ghee for pitta; and a mixture of both for combined (miśra) disorders. [The ingredients are]:
daśamūla, śaṭhī, dantī, surāhva, and two types of punarnavā. (19)
The roots of snuhī and arka, pathyā, bhūkadamba, aruṣkara, the two types of karañja, the root of varuṇa, pippalī, and that which is pauṣkara; 20.
12.20c–d One should boil ten palas each of the roots of *karañja* and *varuṇa*, along with one prastha each of *yava*, *kola*, and *kulattha*,
in eight times the amount of water, until reduced to one-fourth. 12.21a–b [This decoction should be used as follows:]...
With that [milk], one should prepare [the ghee] using two parts each of pippalī, cavya, vacā, nicula, and rohiṣa, along with trivṛt, viḍaṅga, kampilla, bhārgī, and viśva. // 22 //

One should prepare one *prastha* of ghee with *bhārgī* and *bilva*; it conquers all those types of urinary disorders (*meha*), pustules, and poisons, as well as anemia, abscesses, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, consumption, swellings, and toxic abdominal enlargements.
This Dhānvantara ghee cures dyspnea, cough, vomiting, enlargement of the spleen, gout, leprosy, insanity, and epilepsy. (24)
Lodhra, mūrvā, śaṭhī, vella, bhārgī, nata, nakha, plava, kaliṅga, kuṣṭha, kramuka, priyaṅgu, ativiṣā, and agnika; (25)
Two *viśālā*, *caturjāta*, *bhūnimba*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *yavānī*, *pauṣkara*, *pāṭhā*, *granthi*, *cavya*, and the three fruits (*phalatraya*). // 26 //
When one *karṣa* of [the powder] has been placed in a water-pitcher, and the cold infusion has been strained down to a quarter-remnant,
one should add two *prasthas* of honey and preserve it for half a month with neglectful indifference.
This Lodhra-asava cures urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, vitiligo, skin diseases, anorexia, worms, anemia, disorders of the digestive tract, and obesity. (28)
One should prepare twenty palas each of asana and the other ingredients separately;
when two parts of water have been added, one should throw two hundred palas of jaggery into that while it stands on the fire.
Half an āḍhaka of honey and one pala of the paste (kalkita) of the Vatsakādi group should be placed in a vessel of ghee that has been smeared with honey and powdered pippalī.
12.30b–c. One should place the paste of the *vatsakādi* group, having been kept in a strong lac-encrusted vessel, within a heap of barley;
one should repeatedly immerse [the vessel] therein while it is heated by charcoal from the *khadira* tree.
Thin leaves of sharp iron, processed until the iron is completely consumed, when swallowed, remain within the body and possess qualities superior to the previous [iron preparation]. (32)
Rough body rubs, vigorous exercise, staying awake at night,
and whatever else destroys phlegm and fat— both externally and internally— is beneficial.
Having drunk from a balance-scale of excellent, refined water produced from stone,
he partook of *śāli* rice with the essence-water itself, accompanied by juices derived from the meat of wild animals.

12.34d–35ab: One should overcome all types of urinary disorders (meha), even those with many complications, as well as scrofula (gaṇḍamālā), tumors (arbuda), glandular swellings (granthi), obesity (sthaulya), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara), by means of *śāli* rice taken with the juices of wild animals (*jāṅgalaja*).
It cures worms, elephantiasis, and swellings; furthermore, it is a supreme elixir.
One who possesses no wealth, who lacks an umbrella, shoes, or a staff, and who follows the conduct of a sage [should use this].
Sandalwood, blue lotus, grapes, uśīra, and punarnavā;
liquorice, śrīkhaṇḍa, the three myrobalans, blue lotus, and śārivā. (36.1+1)
Śamī, bamboo fruit, lodhra, the three aromatics (trijātaka), nāgakeśara, padmaka, and powdered long pepper—along with an equal amount of auspicious sugar. (36.1–2)
One should drink this powder in the morning with rice-water,
for urinary disorders (prameha), blood-bile (rakta-pitta), and severe painful conditions (kṛcchra).
He may travel a hundred yojanas, or he may dig out reservoirs of water;
or, subsisting on cow dung and urine, he may wander together with the cows themselves. (37)
One should nourish a person who is emaciated with medicinal foods that do not increase fat or urine;
pustules such as śarāvikā and others should be treated like swellings (śopha).
The unripe swellings are treated like ulcers, as are those that have ripened; their premonitory symptoms are the same.
For drinking, the juice of milky trees and goat's urine are recommended. (39)
Strong purification is generally required, for those suffering from urinary disorders (mehin) are difficult to purge;
one should prepare an ointment for wound healing using the *elādi* group of drugs mixed with oil.
For the medicinal powder used for rubbing (udvartana), one should use a decoction from the Aragvadhadi group;
for sprinkling (pariṣeka), the Asanadi group; and for drinks and food, the Vatsakadi group.
12.41c–d / For sprinkling, food, and other purposes, one should use pāṭhā, citraka, śārṅgeṣṭā, śārivā,
kaṇṭakārikā, saptāhva, the root of kuṭaja, somavalka, and nṛpadruma. 12.42 / [These are to be used] for sprinkling, as well as for food and other requirements.

Having powdered it, one should lick it with honey; likewise, the powder of *navāyasa* [should be used] by one who has fallen into the state of *madhumeha* (diabetes mellitus) and has been abandoned by physicians. (43)
One suffering from prameha should consume an equal measure of śilājatu and punarnavā. (43½)
In the section on therapeutics,
one should treat every abscess while it is still immature (āmam) just like a swelling;
blood should be removed continuously, but once it has suppurated, the treatment should be like that for an ulcer.
A wound caused by wind (vātaja) should be washed with water decocted with the five roots mixed with an abundance of salts;
one should then apply an ointment consisting of the Bhadradī-varga, liquorice (yaṣṭyāhva), and sesame seeds. // 2 //
Having purified [the wound] with a purgative formulation of *traivṛta*, one should heal it with *traivṛta* prepared with the *vidārī* group of drugs. // 3 //
One should wash [the area] with milk-water and then apply a paste of liquorice, immortality-root (amṛtā), and sesame seeds;
for a bile-related [inflammation], one should treat it with ghee prepared with mañjiṣṭhā, uśīra, and padmaka.
One should promote healing with milk, the two types of *niśā*, *śreṣṭhā*, and *yaṣṭī* mixed with milk;
or, in the case of a wound born of *kapha*, one should use the tender leaves, bark, and fruits of the *nyagrodha* group of trees.
Having washed [the area] with *āragvadha* and other [decoctions], one should apply a plaster made of parched grain flour (*saktu*), *kumbha*, turmeric (*niśā*),
and sesame seeds, along with *kulatthikā*, *dantī*, *trivṛt*, *chyāmā*, *agni*, and *tilvaka*.
13.6ab Washed with water from the *āragvadha* tree, one should prepare a healing oil containing rock salt and cow’s urine.
In cases arising from blood or external [factors], treatment should be performed as for a *pitta*-type abscess. // 7 //

In the case of an internal abscess (vidradhi) that has arisen and is not yet suppurated, one should drink a decoction of the *varuṇādi* group in the forenoon, with the addition of the *ūṣakādi* group as a medicinal adjunct (*pratīvāpa*).

13.8bv When the [doshas] remain unripened and situated internally, one should administer ghee processed with purgative substances, and have the patient drink both of these; one should likewise prepare a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) and an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) using those very same substances. // 9 //
Madhuśigru, when applied as a drink, food, or ointment,
and sown as a medicinal seed according to the specific dosha, destroys an unripened abscess (vidradhi).
Equal parts of trāyantī, triphalā, nimba, kaṭukā, and madhuka;
and four parts each of trivṛt and paṭola root [are taken] separately. (11)

Eight *masūra* beans, dehusked, [taken] with their decoction and ghee, conquer abscesses (*vidradhi*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), erysipelas (*vīsarpa*), burning sensations, delusion, intoxication, and fever. (12)
Fever, fainting, vomiting, heart disease, hemorrhagic disorders, skin diseases, and jaundice are cured by preparing one *kuḍava* of *trāyamāṇā* boiled in eight times its quantity of water. (13)
One *kuḍava* each of its juice, the fresh juice of *dhātrī*, milk, and ghee;
and one *karṣa* each of the pasted paste of *tiktā*, *trāyantī*, and *dhanvayāsaka*. (14)
One should cook mustā, tāmalakī, vīrā, jīvantī, candana, and utpala together in a single preparation; that ghee possesses the same qualities as the previous one. (15)
One should cook ghee in a decoction of grapes, madhūka, dates, vidārī, śatāvarī, parūṣaka fruits, and triphalā. (16)

Combined with the paste (kalka) of milk, sugarcane, āmalakī, and prāṇadā, that [mixture], when cooled and containing one-fourth part sugar and honey, possesses qualities identical to those mentioned previously. (17)
In a decoction of milk, sugarcane, and *dhātrī*, combined with the paste of *prāṇadā*,
one should drain the blood from a swelling using instruments such as the *śṛṅga* (horn) or by means of a vein, according to its proximity.
This applies to an abscess (*vidradhi*) that is ripening, whether located within the abdominal cavity (*koṣṭha*) or protruding externally.
Having diagnosed [the condition], one should apply a poultice when the swelling is localized and situated upon a pin (śūla);
likewise when there is numbness from pressure on its sides, or when burning sensations and other symptoms are slight. (19)
Once it has become suppurated, one should lance the abscess and treat it like an ulcer; this is also the sign of a suppurated internal abscess. (20)
Once matured, it fills the channels and then moves either upward or downward;
one who eats wholesome food should simply observe that naturally occurring disorder.
13.21b–22a. The physician, guarding against complications, should keep the patient either upward or downward for ten or twelve days;
if the discharge flows improperly, he should treat it with a decoction of the *varuṇādi* group mixed with lukewarm water.
The physician should protect the patient from complications;
he should administer madhuśigru or a gruel prepared with it.
Furthermore, food taken with soups made from barley, jujube, and horse gram is recommended. (13.22b–23)
After ten days have passed, one should perform purification using *trāyantī* ghee or *tailvaka* oil according to one's strength;
once purified, one should drink bitter medicine mixed with honey. (24)
One should treat this condition in every respect according to the specific doṣa, as one would a gulma;
likewise, guggulu is indicated in all stages and in all types of abscesses (vidradhi).
