Moreover, because it causes rapid suppuration, it is called *vidradhi* (abscess);
and when it occurs in association with urinary disorders (*meha*), one should apply the treatment for those *pramehas*.
A decoction of *śaubhāñjanaka* combined with *hiṅgu* and rock salt, when consumed every morning, destroys abscesses before long. (27+1)
The three pungents (kaṭutrika), tiktarohiṇī, musta, kirātatikta, and barley; along with saptaparṇa, ativiṣā, durālabhā, the root of paṭola, and trāyamāṇā. // 27+2 //
Guḍūcī, cavya, viḍaṅga, nimba, priyaṅgu, nīlotpala, lodhra, añjana, dhātakī, mocarasa, the three fruits (triphalā), nāgara, bilva, kapittha, and śārivā. // 27+3 //
These [drugs] should be in equal parts, but *citraka* should be double that amount; the bark of *kuṭaja* should be one-sixteenth part.
Well-ground into a fine powder and mixed with cold water, a person should drink half a *pala* of this combined with jaggery. (27+4)
When hungry, soft food consisting of rabbit, quail, or partridge meat is beneficial;
it destroys tumors arising from phlegm and bile, and one shines like the full autumn moon. (27.5)

The three pungent spices (kaṭu-trika) combined with jaggery, when administered, conquer cough due to indigestion, consumption, anemia, fever, diarrhea, disorders of the small intestine (grahaṇī), scrofula (apacī), urinary disorders (prameha), oliguria (mūtra-kṣaya), hernia (vardhma), and abscesses (vidradhi). // 27+6 //
Half a pala of bhūnimba, one pala of niśā, and likewise two palas of dārvī. // 27+7a //
Furthermore, make the *punarnavā* half the size of the *dārvī*; likewise, the *pragraha* is equal to the *dārvī*.
One pala of duḥsparśa should be used together with half that amount of kaṭukā. // 27+7c //
A pala should be equal to four aśvāhvas and seven niśās, plus one-quarter of an amṛta.
This, together with seven karṣas of vatsaka, should be made into a very fine powder. // 27+8a //
One should drink five, four, or three days' worth of the fresh juice of vāsā.
Furthermore, that should be drunk daily with molasses-water when the sun is positioned in front. // 27.8c //
This powder is the supreme secret for making those suffering from abscesses free from pain. // 27.8d //

This entire essence of the science of health must never, under any circumstances, be given to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a brother, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who does not wish for one's welfare. (27+9)
One should treat everything as if it were a wound on the breast, but one should not apply poultices;
rather, while protecting the milk-carrying ducts, one should incise [the abscess] at the dark areola.
In all stages, beginning with the undigested state (āmādi), one should milk that breast dry;
it should be purified with trivṛt when there is an increase of unctuousness, and with fatty substances when the condition is characterized by mobility.

Then, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) using a decoction and paste of *kauśāmbī*, *tilvaka*, *airaṇḍa*, *sukumāraka*, and *miśraka*, along with unctuous substances that subdue wind (*anila*). // 30 //
Once it has been nourished with meat broth, one should subsequently administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) using liquorice oil.
When suppuration has occurred, vata-alleviating fomentations and plasters should be applied; once it has burst open, the treatment for an ulcer (vraṇa-kriyā) should be performed.
In cases where [the disease] arises from pitta and blood, whether it is in the stage of undigested (āma) or digested (pakva) toxins,
one should apply treatments for swelling and ulcers as appropriate, and constantly extract the blood.

In cases of the phlegmatic type (ślaiṣmika), one should drink a paste made from *pītadāru* with cow’s urine; furthermore, apart from the procedure for inducing emaciation (*vimlāpana*), the regimen prescribed for phlegmatic glandular swellings (*śleṣma-granthi*) is beneficial for this condition. (33)

13.33c–d & 13.34ab: Except for cases where there is no resolution of swelling, once the abscess has ripened and been incised, an oil prepared with *sumana*, *aruṣkara*, *aṅkola*, and *saptaparṇa* is desired for the purification of the wound (*vraṇa-śodhana*).
And for a tumor born of fat (medoja), one should apply a paste made from paṭola, nimba, rajanī, viḍaṅga, and kuṭaja, ground with urine and well-steamed with the drugs of the surasādi group. // 35 //

Or, avoiding the fruit-bearing vein, one should properly incise [the tumor] with a Vṛddhipattra instrument using substances for head-purgation (śiro-vireka), once the fatty tissue has been well-removed.
13.36 When the fat has been properly extracted, one should rub the wound with honey, green vitriol (kāsīsa), and rock salt (saindhava) and then suture it;
an ointment should also be applied for the purification of the fat. 13.37 [continued]
One should apply oil prepared with realgar, cardamom, jasmine, granthiparṇa, and bhallātaka until the wound has healed, and one should habitually employ oleation and sudation therapies.

One should pierce below the suture a swelling produced by urine, which has been fomented and wrapped with an oily cloth bandage, and drain it according to the requirements of the abdominal cavity. (39)
And one should heal a wound caused by the intestines when it is bound with a dressing;
until the testicles have descended, the treatment is like that for an increase of wind (vāta).
One should cook one *tulā* of *punarnavā*, along with ten *palas* each of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *payasyā*, *aśvagandhā*, *eraṇḍa*, and *śatāvarī*. (41)
Combined with two *darbha* blades, *śara*, *kāśa*, the root of sugarcane, and *poṭagala*, when eight parts of water remain in the fire, thirty *palas* of jaggery [should be added]. (42)
One should add one *prastha* each of castor oil, ghee, and milk, along with two *pala* portions each of long pepper, its root, and rock salt. (43)
Licorice, raisins, caraway, and ginger—this [mixture] prepared with these is called Sukumāra; it is a very gentle rejuvenative elixir.
For those who are delicate, for lords, and for those whose nature is pleasure, there should be no restriction regarding things to be avoided, such as wind, heat, travel, and riding in vehicles. (45)
For men who are lords of a multitude of women, it destroys misfortune and the age of strife;
through its use at all times, it bestows luster, charm, and nourishment.

It is excellent for treating swellings, abscesses, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, disorders of the female genital tract, and pain in the penis caused by Vāta; as well as for edema, abdominal enlargement, sciatica, splenic disorders, and constipation. (47)
A decoction prepared from rāsnā, yaṣṭīmadhu, amṛtā, eraṇḍa, balā, and gokṣura, when mixed with castor oil, quickly destroys enlargement of the intestines (antravṛddhi). // 47+1 //
If the swelling does not subside through oleation, recakas, and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana),
one should first perform the procedure of enema (vasti-karma) and then cauterize the area located at the groin.
The Maruts, for the purpose of obstructing the path with fire, drank the yellow ligament upon the thumb, which was as thin as a thread and curved like a half-moon. 49.

Having lifted it with a needle, one should cauterize it transversely after cutting it, wherever the disease is located; others, however, say that one should cauterize on the other side of the [needle's] entry point, or else on the ring finger.

This procedure is prescribed for abdominal tumors (gulma) caused by vāta and kapha, as well as for splenic enlargement (plīhan); it is also applied to the little finger, the ring finger, and to the disease known as viśvācī. (51)
The roots of the bilva, the kapittha, the aralu, the agni, and the two types of bṛhatī. // 51.1a //
From the Śyāmā, Pūtikarañja, and Śigruka trees, [one obtains] Viśvauṣadha and Aruṣkara. 51+1b.
Combined with black pepper, granthika, vella, the five salts, alkali, and ajamoda. // 51+1c //
When drunk with *kāñjika* water and stirred with [the aforementioned ingredients], then ground into a powder, it overcomes abdominal enlargement (*vardhma*). // 51.1d //
A plaster consisting of cumin, kuṣṭha, gomedaka, hapuṣā, and jujube fruits, mixed with fermented rice-gruel (āranāla), is a supreme medicine for conquering swelling (vardhma). // 51+2 //
A lukewarm plaster made from wheat flour and *kanduruka* mixed with goat’s milk is a supreme remedy for conquering *vardhma*. (51+3)
Immediately upon the crow's death, the wise man should apply a paste made from its flesh; after a moment, the swelling will vanish, and he shall be free from pain instantly.
In the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna),
one should treat a Vātika Gulma characterized by obstructed feces and flatus, accompanied by intense pain,
and arising from dryness and cold, with oils used for Vāta disorders. // 1 //
One should administer sudation to a person who has been made unctuous by means of drinks, food, inunctions, and massages, especially in cases of distension, pain, stiffness, and constipation. // 2 //
Having softened the channels, conquered the violent wind, and broken up the obstructions, sudation applied to one who has been oleated dispels the gulma. // 3 //
The internal administration of fats (sneha-pāna) is beneficial for gulma, especially when it is located above the navel;
when it has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), enemas (vasti) are indicated; and when it resides in both regions, both treatments should be employed.
When the fire is kindled, in cases of Vata-type Gulma, and when there is obstruction of flatus and feces, one should administer nourishing foods and drinks that are unctuous and warm. (5)

In a gulma born of vāta, repeated administration of oil-drinks, as well as non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), should be employed while protecting against the provocation of kapha and pitta.

14.6dv One should know that the procedure of enema (vasti-karma) is supreme for protecting against phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta); for it destroys the abdominal tumor (gulma), since it first conquers the wind (māruta) in its own location and thereby immediately removes the tumor. // 7 //
Therefore, when administered repeatedly with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) along with unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), disorders consisting of vāta, pitta, and kapha are pacified. // 8 //
With asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, the three pungents (vyoṣa), viḍa salt, pomegranate, dīpyaka, puṣkaramūla, cumin, dhānyāmla, vetasa, alkali, and citraka; // 9 //
One should prepare clarified butter with śaṭhī, vacā, jagandhā, elā, and surasa, combined with curd; this removes colic and abdominal distension for those suffering from vāta-type gulma.
With hapuṣā, uṣaṇa, pṛthvīkā, pañcakolaka, and dīpyaka, along with ajājī, saindhava, curd, milk, and meat broth; 11.
One should cook ghee with pomegranate, radish, and jujube;
it destroys Vata-type Gulma, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, and pains in the flanks, heart, and viscera. (12)
Daśamūla, balā, kālā, suṣavī, and the two types of punarnavā [are used] for disorders of the female reproductive tract, hemorrhoids, grahaṇī, cough, dyspnea, anorexia, and fever. (13)
14.13cd–14ab. One should boil the ten roots (daśamūla), balā, kālī, puṣkara, eraṇḍa, rāsnā, aśvagandhā, bhārgī, amṛtā, śaṭhī,
and gandhapalāśa in one droṇa of water until two palas remain.
In this decoction made from one *prastha* each of barley, *kola*, horse gram (*kulattha*), and black gram (*māṣa*), one should cook one *prastha* of ghee along with a vessel of curd. (15)
It should be combined with the natural juices produced from pomegranate, hog-plum, and citron,
as well as with thin gruel-water, fermented rice-water, and vinegar, along with finely ground pastes.
With bhārgī, tumburu, ṣaḍgranthā, granthi, rāsnā, agni, and dhānyaka; with yavānaka, yavānī, amlavetasa, and asitajīraka. (17)
With cumin, asafoetida, hapuṣā, kāravī, vṛṣaka, uṣaka, nikumbha, kumbha, mūrvā, ibha, pippalī, vella, and pomegranate; 18.
With *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *trapusa*, *ervāru* seeds, *hiṃsrā*, *aśmabheda*, *miśi*, the two types of alkali (*kṣāra*), *surasa*, *śārivā*, and the fruits of *nīlinī* (19);

When seasoned with the three pungents (tri-kaṭu) and the two salts (tri-paṭu), that [milk] prepared with curd (dādhika) quickly dispels those aforementioned diseases, even the most difficult ones, when practiced regularly. (20)

[One should treat] epilepsy, insanity, urinary obstruction, and diseases of the wind (vāta) with [a compound of] the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three fruits (triphalā), coriander (dhānyaka), long pepper (cavikā), vella, and leadwort (citraka). // 21 //
Ghee cooked with the paste of *apasmāra*, *agara*, and *unmāda*, along with milk, cures *vāta-gulma*.
[One should take] one *tulā* of garlic bulbs and five *palas* each of the following: (14.22)
One should cook the five roots and the great [drugs] with half a bhāra of water until one-fourth remains; to that, one should add half as much pomegranate juice and fermented liquor (surā). 23.
Taking fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) and curd, one should grind half-pala portions of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa),
the three fruits (triphalā), asafoetida (hiṅgu), yavānī, cavya, and dīpyaka.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with sour *vetasa*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), and *devadāru*; this is a supreme remedy that conquers all disorders of *vāta* and *gulma*. (25)

One should boil *sāmla*, vetasa, *sindhūttha*, and *devadāru* with six *pala*s of ghee, or one should drink the ghee prescribed for *rājayakṣman*. Alternatively, milk may be used with *prasannā* wine, *surā* wine, or pomegranate juice. (14.25–26)
In cases of vāta-gulma, a medicated ghee prepared with *dadhi-sara* (the liquid part of curd) should be administered to destroy the disease;
however, if the increased kapha has suppressed the digestive fire and caused loss of appetite, [this should be avoided].

It produces nausea, heaviness, and drowsiness; one should eliminate it by recognizing that the internal receptacle (āśaya) contains oleaginous matter in cases of colic, constipation, and obstruction. (28)

Powders and boluses of *niryūha* should be administered with medicinal ghee, or with the decoctions of *kola*, pomegranate, warm water, buttermilk, wine, sour liquids, or fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*). (29)
One should drink the powders with curd at dawn, or before a meal;
or the powders of *mātuluṅga* (citron), which have been repeatedly saturated with its juice.
One should prepare vaṭakas that are more effective than even the bow [in their potency] against phlegm and wind. // 31ab //
Hiṅgu, vacā, vijayā, paśugandhā, dāḍima, dīpyaka, dhānyaka, and pāṭhā. // 31cd //
Puṣkaramūla, śaṭhī, hapuṣā, agni, the two types of kṣāra, the three salts, and the three pungents. // 31ef //
This powder, consisting of ajāji, cavya, tintiḍīka, and vetasāmla, destroys colic arising from vāyu, āma, and kapha located in the heart, flanks, bladder, sacrum, vagina, and anus. (32)

It cures severe abdominal tumors, obstruction of flatus, feces, and urine, constriction of the throat, cardiac oppression, anemia, loss of appetite, splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, hiccups, hernia, flatulence, dyspnea, cough, and loss of digestive fire. (33)
Salt, yavānī, dīpyaka, kaṇā, and nāgara, each increasing in quantity by one part respectively, with harītakī powder equal in measure to the whole—this is Vaiśvānara itself. (34)
14.34cv Equal parts of all [the ingredients] and *harītakī*—14.34cv equal parts of all [the ingredients] and *vijayā*—14.34dv this powder is indeed the "Fire" (*vaiśvānara*) itself:
the three pungents (*tri-kaṭuka*), *ajamodā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and the two types of cumin (*jīraka*). // 35a //
To eight parts of ghee mixed with equal amounts [of the other ingredients], one-eighth part of asafoetida is added. // 35b //
The first morsel of food was mixed with ghee. // 35c //
This powder, taken with clarified butter as the very first morsel of food,
generates digestive fire and destroys vāta-gulma.
It generates a great internal fire and indeed destroys vāta-gulma (wind-disorder abdominal tumors) when combined with hiṅgu, ugrā, viḍa, śuṇṭhī, ajājī, vijayā, and the one called vāṭyā.
The powder [is made] from the roots of Kumbha and Nikumbha, increased by successive parts. // 36b //
Taken with lukewarm water, this [medicine] cures abdominal diseases such as gulma and udara. (36c)
Like a tiger forcibly crushing herds of deer, it violently overcomes diseases. // 36d //
Of rock salt, yellow myrobalan, long pepper, and bishop’s weed. // 37a //
Let them drink the powders with lukewarm water. // 37b //
That which arises from phlegm and wind goes to destruction. // 37c //
Like a flood of disease pierced by an iron arrow. // 37d //
Pūtīka leaves, gaja-cirbhaṭa, cavya, and vahni— // 38a //
And [he prepared] a bed spread with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and having salt as its pillow. // 38b //
Having burned and pulverized it, one should employ it mixed with curd-whey. // 38c //
In cases of abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, edema, anemia, and diseases arising from the rectum. // 38d //

14.38–39ab: In cases arising from gulma, abdominal enlargement, edema, and anemia, one should take asafoetida (hiṅgu) with three times as much rock salt (saindhava), and from this, three times as much castor oil (airaṇḍa-taila).
That juice of garlic, prepared with three times its quantity [of other ingredients], destroys abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, hernia, and colic;
likewise, the juice of citron, asafoetida, pomegranate, viḍa salt, and rock salt [are effective]. (40)
It should be drunk with the scum of wine (*surā-maṇḍa*) to alleviate the pain of wind-type abdominal tumors (*vāta-gulma*):
one *karṣa* of ginger, two [palas] of jaggery, and one *pala* of washed black sesame seeds. (41)
By chewing these together and consuming them with warm milk as an after-drink, one may overcome vāta-gulma and fever;
it also conquers vāta-related heart disease, gulma, hemorrhoids, pain in the female reproductive tract, and constipation. (14.41–42)
One suffering from vāta-gulma should drink castor oil with clear wine when the kapha is weak and the vāyu is predominant; however, it should be taken with milk when pitta is predominant.
If the pitta is aggravated or if there is burning sensation in one suffering from vāta-gulma,
that patient should be administered a purgative along with unctuous and carminative substances.
And while the fever persists in this manner, one should bleed that person who is afflicted by it;
then, one should prepare four palas of pure, dried garlic.
One should boil [the aforementioned drugs] with eight times the amount of milk and water until only the milk remains; this cures vātagulma, udāvarta, gṛdhrasī, and irregular fever (viṣamajvara). 46.
That milk, along with oil, *prasannā*, cow urine, *āranāla*, and *yavāgraja* [sour gruel], quickly cures heart disease, abscesses, and consumption. (47)
That milk, when drunk alone, quickly destroys gulma, abdominal enlargement, and flatulence; it should be prepared in one place [with these ingredients].
A decoction of citraka, granthika, eraṇḍa, and śuṇṭhī is exceedingly beneficial.

In cases of colic, constipation, and intestinal obstruction, [one should use] roots of *puṣkara* and castor (*eraṇḍa*), along with *yava*, *dhanvayavāsaka*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *viḍa* salt, and rock salt (*saindhava*). (49)
The root of vāṭyāhva, eraṇḍa, and darbha, along with dāru and mahauṣadha, when boiled in water and drunk, removes burning and pain in the digestive tract (koṣṭha). (50)
Shilājatu, when boiled with water and drunk, conquers pain in the abdomen, back, and shoulders;
or it may be taken with milk or with water boiled with a small quantity of the five roots (pañcamūla). (51)
14.51b–v: A person suffering from vāta-gulma should drink vāṭya [preparation] which overcomes pain in the abdomen, back, and shoulders;
however, in the case of udāvarta, one should feed them unctuous food with soups made of peas (paippalika) or with the juice of radishes (mūlaka).
One whose flatus and feces are obstructed should eat barley-gruel with warm milk,
or consume boiled grains (kulmāṣa) mixed with abundant fat and a high amount of salt.
Ghee mixed with nīlinī, trivṛtā, dantī, pathyā, and kampillaka, along with feces, viḍa salt, kṣāra, and nāgara, should be administered.
One should boil one *pala* each of nīlinī, triphalā, rāsnā, balā, kaṭukarohiṇī, viḍaṅga, and vyāghrī in one *āḍhaka* of water.
When one-eighth of the liquid remains, one should cook a *prastha* of ghee, having combined it with a *prastha* of curd and two *palas* of the milky sap of *sudhā*. (56)
Then one should give a pala of ghee mixed with the scum of gruel;
once it has been properly digested and the patient has been well-purged, one should feed him a meal of meat broth.
This Nīlinī ghee cures abdominal tumors, skin diseases, ascites, facial freckles, edema, anemia, fever, leucoderma, splenic enlargement, and insanity. (58)
Fowl, peacocks, partridges, cranes, and quails;
rice, wine, and clarified butter—this is the treatment for wind-induced abdominal tumors (vātagulma). 59.
For those suffering from Vata-type Gulma, food that is measured, warm, liquid, and unctuous should be prescribed;
likewise, Varuni wine served with its scum (māṇḍa) or water boiled with coriander (dhānyaka) should be drunk.
When a Pitta-type gulma has arisen with oily and hot qualities, purgation is beneficial;
one may administer a mixture of grapes, *abhayā*, jaggery, and juice, or *kampilla* mixed with honey. (61)
Alternatively, for a gulma born of dryness and heat, one should administer Kampilla with liquid honey as prescribed in the Kalpa section, or that which was prescribed for Rakta-pitta.
Furthermore, bitter ghee (tikta-sarpis) or ghee prepared with Vāsā is the supreme pacifying treatment.
Milk boiled with a decoction of the five drugs known as *tṛṇapañcaka*, or with the *jīvanīya* group, or with the *nyagrodhādi* group, [should be used]. (63)
In that case as well, the physician should quickly administer a laxative for the emergency,
using either clarified butter prepared with purgative drugs or even milk.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the juices of *āmalaka* and sugarcane, adding a quarter-part of *pathyā*.
This prepared ghee, when drunk, cures *pitta-gulma*. (65)
Or one should drink Tailvaka ghee, or that which was prescribed for pitta-type abscess (pittavidradhi),
along with grapes, payasyā, madhuka, candana, padmaka, and honey.
One should drink two palas of trāyamāṇā, boiled in two prasthas of water, with rice-water for the pacification of pitta-gulma. (67)
One should drink it when it has been purified, reduced to one-eighth, and made lukewarm, equal in quantity to milk;
thereafter, one should drink warm milk over it according to one's strength. (68)
By this, the pitta-type gulma of one whose doshas have been eliminated is pacified;
in cases of burning sensation, there should be anointing with cold ghees and an application of cooling medicinal herbs mixed with clarified butter.

Contact with lotus leaves and vessels containing moving water [is beneficial] in cases of burning sensations (vidāha) and its premonitory symptoms, as well as in colic (śūla) and the attenuation of the digestive fire (vahni-mārdava).
In cases of pitta-type gulma especially, one should repeatedly extract blood;
for when their roots are severed, they do not undergo further inflammation and the gulmas go to destruction.

For blood turns sour when it is corrupted, yet in this case there was neither that corruption nor pain; the patient's humors had been removed, his body refreshed, and he was nourished with the juices of wild game.

Once the patient has been comforted, though some pain remains, one should again administer medicated ghee, either because the blood-bile (rakta-pitta) has increased excessively or because the proper treatment was not obtained. (73)

When a gulma is about to suppurate, all treatments should be like those for a pitta-type abscess (pitta-vidradhi): śāli rice, cow’s milk and goat’s milk, paṭolī, meat from wild animals, and ghee. (74)
Emblic myrobalan, *parūṣaka*, grapes, dates, pomegranate, sugar, food, and water boiled with *balā*, *bṛhatī*, and other such herbs [are recommended]. (75)
In the case of a disease born of phlegm (kapha), one should first induce emesis; however, if the patient is not fit for emesis, one should first administer a fast.
Thereafter, one should stimulate the digestive fire with a combination of bitter, hot, and pungent substances.

In the case of a tumor born of *kapha*, one should first induce emesis with the *hiṅgv-ādi* group of drugs, or with double the amount of alkali (*kṣāra*) combined with *hiṅgu* and *amlavetasa*. This applies if the tumor is deeply seated, constricted, numb, hard, or stable. (14.76–77)
After applying sudation, one should subsequently pacify a gulma associated with abdominal distension and other such symptoms;
those suffering from kaphaja gulma should drink ghee prepared with alkali and pungent substances. (78)

After purification, one should subsequently administer ghee boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla), along with the three pungents (vyoṣa), alkali, salt, asafoetida (hiṅgu), viḍa salt, and pomegranate; this quickly conquers kapha-type gulma. (14.78)
Two palas of bhallātaka and one pala of pañcamūla should be boiled in one āḍhaka of water; with that decoction reduced to one-fourth, [the following should be prepared]. (80)
One should cook equal quantities of ghee and milk with one *akṣa* each of viḍaṅga,
hiṅgu, sindhūttha (rock salt), yāvaśūka, śaṭhī, and viḍa salt.
This Bhallātaka ghee, prepared with dvīpī, rāsnā, yaṣṭyāhva, ṣaḍgranthā, kaṇā, and nāgara, is supreme for removing kapha-type gulma. (82)
It conquers splenic disorders, anemia, dyspnea, malabsorption syndrome, and cough; thereafter, one should apply sudation to his body and to all parts of the abdomen affected by gulma.

14.83b–d – It cures disorders of the *grahaṇī*, cough, and all types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*). Whatever treatment is administered after first applying oleation and sudation attains success; it does not succeed when applied without such preparation.

When the body has been lubricated and fomented and the abdominal tumor (gulma) has become softened, one should apply the aforementioned medicinal cupping jar; once it has adhered, one should remove it.
Then, having placed a cloth in between, the physician who knows the proper measure should break up the gulma;
he should apply pressure as available using a finger, a patha-leaf, or a mirror.
One should wipe away only the tumor itself and must not touch the intestines or the heart;
and having smeared it with sesame, castor, linseed, and mustard seeds, [one should proceed]. (87)
Alternatively, having smeared [the abdomen] with mustard seeds,
one should apply sudation using iron vessels that are comfortably warm;
thus, the phlegm-tumor (kapha-gulma) that has spread from its site should be expelled by means of purgatives.
One should cleanse him with unctuous enemas prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla).
One should cook [a decoction] using one pala each of pippalī, āmalaka, drākṣā, śyāmā, and the other [specified] ingredients.
One prastha each of castor oil and clarified butter, cooked with six times the amount of milk,
constitutes this "Mixed" unctuous preparation (miśraka-sneha), which is beneficial as a laxative for those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma).
In cases of enlargement, abscesses, and colic, as well as in disorders of Vata, one should drink the "Amrita" ghee or Nīlinī-ghee in a dose of two Palas.
Likewise, one should cook twenty-five palas of dantī with two palas of the substance called sukumāra in a droṇa of water, using either clarified butter (ghṛta) or oil (audarika). 14.91–92ab.
Likewise, one should cook that same quantity of Citraka and Pathyā in two Prasthas of their decoction; once strained, one should add jaggery equal in weight to the Dantī.
14.93b–94. When that decoction has been boiled down to one-fourth its original volume, four *pala*s of oil and a *pala* of powdered *trivṛt* should be added.
Likewise, two *karṣa*s each of *kaṇā* (long pepper) and *śuṇṭhī* (dry ginger) are added. Once the linctus is prepared and cooled, [it is ready for use].
One should administer honey and oil in equal proportions, along with a fourth part of the four spices (catur-jātaka);
then, one should eat a single *harītakī* together with a *pala* of this electuary. 95.
One who is oleated is purged easily and comfortably; being free from disease, one passes a dose of impurities equal to a prastha.
[This cures] abdominal tumors, heart disease, chronic diarrhea, edema, flatulence, and poisoning from *udara*. (96)
Dantī and Harītakī destroy skin diseases, nausea, anorexia, splenic disorders, malabsorption syndrome, and irregular fevers; they also cure anemia along with jaundice. (97)
14.97–98. Having licked one karṣa of the powder of *trivṛt*— well-impregnated with lime-water, milk, and liquid [sugar]— which causes paleness and jaundice,
mixed with honey and ghee, one is properly purged.
One should drink either kuṣṭha, śyāmā, trivṛt, dantī, vijayā, alkali, and guggulu together with cow’s urine, or guggulu alone with it. (99)
One should administer non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), prepared according to the methods described in the Kalpa-sthāna, for the destruction of gulma;
[especially when it is] firmly rooted, extensive, hard, immobile, and heavy. (100)
One should conquer gulma with concealed internal masses through the application of alkaline preparations (kṣāra), fermented liquors (ariṣṭa), and thermal cautery (agni-karma),
administering them either on alternate days, every two days, or after allowing a rest period of three days.

For one intent on increasing or diminishing the strength of the bodily humors, alkaline preparations (kṣāra) prescribed for hemorrhoids, urinary calculi, and disorders of the digestive tract should be employed when phlegm (kapha) is predominant. (102)
Devadāru, trivṛt, dantī, kaṭukā, pañcakolaka, svarjikā, yāvaśūka, śreṣṭhā, pāṭhā, and upakuñcikā. (103)

One part each of kuṣṭha and sarpasugandhā, two parts each of the five salts (paṭupañcaka), and one pala each [of the remaining ingredients], powdered and saturated with oil, muscle fat, curd, and ghee. (104)

One should cook it inside a jar until it is thoroughly cooked; then, having taken that alkali from the fire-colored jar, one should drink it with milk, clarified butter, buttermilk, wine, and so forth. (105)
It cures gulma, udāvarta, vardhma, hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargement, grahaṇī, and worms;
as well as epilepsy, poisoning, insanity, disorders of the female reproductive tract, diseases of the semen, and urinary calculi. (106)
This alkaline medicine shall pacify the poison arising from rats and snakes;
for one who consumes meat broth, milk, and ghee, it also subdues sweet and unctuous phlegm.
Having cut through and pierced [the tissues] from within due to its caustic nature, the alkali causes them to fall away downward;
this occurs in those with weak digestive fire and loss of appetite who consume fatty substances along with wines that are wholesome for them. (108)

Having repeatedly cut through and pierced the receptacle (āśaya) due to its alkaline nature, the caustic agent (kṣāra) causes it to fall downward. One should administer fermented liquors (āsava) and medicinal decoctions (ariṣṭa), as prescribed, for the purification of the channels.
Old śāli rice, sixty-day rice, horse gram, and the meat of wild animals. 109.
Circibilva, agni, tarkārī, yavānī, and sprouts of varuṇa;
young śigru, tender bilva fruits, and both fresh and dried radish. (110)
14.110c–v Young roots of śigru, bījapūraka, hiṅgu, sour vetasa, kṣāra, and pomegranate;
vyoṣa, buttermilk, ghee, oil, and boiled rice; and vāruṇī liquor for drinking.

Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), whey (mastu), or buttermilk (takra) mixed with the powder of yavānī and viḍa salt; or water boiled with the five roots (pañcamūla); or aged grape wine (mārdvīka). // 112 //
Wine mixed with long pepper, long pepper root, leadwort, cumin, and rock salt, along with *jagala*, quickly conquers abdominal tumors (*gulma*). (113)

14.113d–114. And the *jāṅgala* type [of fever] is treated with mixed therapies: emetics, fasting, sudation, the drinking of ghee, purgatives, enemas (*vasti*), alkalis (*kṣāra*), fermented liquors (*āsava*), medicinal wines (*ariṣṭa*), pills (*guṭikā*), and wholesome diets.

If a kapha-type gulma does not subside due to its deeply rooted nature, it should be treated with enemas, alkali, fermented liquors (āsava), and medicinal spirits (ariṣṭa), along with a diet suitable for those suffering from gulma.
Once the blood has been removed, one should perform cauterization on that [wound] at the end with arrows and other instruments. // 115 //
Then the physician, having covered the area around the tumor with a cloth, should avoid the umbilicus, the bladder, the intestines, the heart, and the line of hair. (116)
One should not touch [the patient] too firmly with a burning arrow, or with a piece of iron produced from a fire-drill, or with a piece of wood from the tinduka tree. (117)
Then, once the intensity of the fire has been pacified by cooling measures— just as treatment is applied to a wound—
the digestive fire should be rekindled with thin gruels and other foods after the patient has undergone fasting.

A physician who knows the proper time should apply his respective treatments, either individually or combined, in cases of mixed disorders; likewise, when a woman whose time for delivery has passed develops a gulma arising from blood.

To one whose body has been lubricated and fomented, one should administer an unctuous purgative (sneha-virecana) consisting of sesame decoction mixed with the powders of ghee, jaggery, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and bhārgī. // 120 //
For a woman suffering from a blood-born gulma (abdominal tumor) and suppressed menstruation,
a drink should be prepared from bhārgī, kṛṣṇā, the bark of karañja, granthika, and amaradāru.
Powdered sesame seeds drunk with their own decoction alleviate the pain of abdominal tumors (gulma).
Two potfuls of palāśa alkali are mixed with two potfuls each of oil and ghee. (122)
One should administer a dose of [medicinal oil] that has been cooked to produce softening of the gulma;
if it is not thus broken up, one should then give a vaginal purgative.
Then, one should give pungent fish, having soaked them in either minced meat mixed with alkali, or in lime-water, or in both of these. 124.
For the purpose of purifying the vagina, one should insert well-impregnated tampons made from the bile of a boar and a fish, or else yeast mixed with jaggery and alkali. (125)
One should have her lick an alkaline preparation that removes *rakta-pitta* with honey and ghee;
furthermore, one should administer garlic, strong liquor, and fish to her. (126)
An enema containing milk, cow urine, alkali, and the ten roots (daśamūla) is beneficial when bleeding has ceased; it is effective for breaking up abdominal tumors (gulma). // 127 //

14.127ab When [the fetus] has entered [the birth canal], one should administer an enema (vasti) containing honey and cow’s urine to the woman whose body has been anointed with the "yamaka" oil; then there should be waiting [for labor to progress]. 14.128cd Her food should consist of meat broth and rice, and her drink should be young wine (surā).
When blood flows excessively, treatments that remove blood and bile (raktapitta) should be administered;
however, for one afflicted by the pain of wind (vāta), all wind-alleviating treatments should be performed again. 129.
These [medicines] destroy abdominal distension and the like, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and phlegm (balāsa), as appropriate. // 129u //
In the Section on Therapeutics: Due to the excessive accumulation of the doshas and the consequent obstruction of the channels, abdominal enlargement (udara) arises;
therefore, one should regularly administer purgation for this condition. //1//
15.1b–d Because it obstructs the channels and the pathways,
one should have [the patient] drink castor oil along with urine or even with milk; or else,
for one or two months, cow’s urine or buffalo urine.

One should drink cow's urine for one or two months while subsisting on cow's milk, or else subsist on camel's milk; this is especially indicated for those afflicted by burning sensations, flatulence, excessive thirst, vomiting, and fainting. (15.2cd–3ab)
For those who are dry, have an excess of vāta, and desire the purification of the bodily humors (doṣas),
one should administer unctuous medicated ghees that destroy abdominal diseases.
Six palas of the ten roots (daśamūla) boiled in two āḍhakas of whey (mastu), along with three palas of ginger (nāgara), one prastha of ghee, and likewise one āḍhaka of oil; // 5 //

Having prepared three palas of ginger with one prastha of buttermilk, one should drink this; it removes all types of abdominal enlargements and is supremely beneficial for gulma arising from kapha and vāta. (15.5cd–6)
One suffering from abdominal enlargement should drink one *prastha* of ghee prepared with four parts water, two parts urine, and one *pala* each of the paste of *citraka* and alkali. (7)
Or one should administer ghee prepared with water containing barley, kola, kulattha, and the five roots (pañcamūla), along with surā and sauvīraka.
When unctuousness has been produced by these [measures], when the strength is restored and the wind (māruta) is pacified,
and when the seat of the humors (doṣāśaya) has become relaxed, one should administer a purgative as prescribed in the ritual manuals (kalpa).
One karṣa each of paṭola root, triphalā, niśā, and vella;
and two, three, and four parts respectively of kampilla, nīlinī, and kumbha. (10)
Having powdered it, one should drink it with urine; first a gruel, then with meat broths.
Once purged, one should eat the meat of wild animals, and thereafter drink milk for six days.
One should drink this boiled [mixture] combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa), and thus drink it again and again;
this powder destroys all types of abdominal enlargements (udarāṇi), even those in which fluid has accumulated. 12.
One should drink gavākṣī, śaṅkhinī, dantī, the bark of tilvaka, and vacā with the juice of karkandhu, mṛdvīkā, and kola, or with water, urine, or sīdhu. // 13 //
Yavānī, hapuṣā, dhānyaka, śatapuṣpā, upakuñcikā, kāravī, the root of pippalī, ajagandhā, śaṭhī, and vacā. (14)
Citraka, ajājīka, vyoṣa, svarṇakṣīrī, the three fruits (triphalā), the two alkalis (dvau kṣārau), pauṣkaramūla, kuṣṭha, and the five salts (lavaṇapañcaka). // 15 //
Take equal parts of viḍaṅga and three parts of dantī;
trivṛt and viśālā are each double that amount, and sātalā is four times that amount. (16)
This powder named Nārāyaṇa destroys hosts of diseases; having encountered it, diseases do not increase, just as the Asuras do not prosper upon encountering Viṣṇu. (17)

Having obtained this [medicine], those suffering from abdominal enlargement (udara) should drink it with buttermilk; those with abdominal tumors (gulma), with a decoction of jujube (badara); in cases of constipation (ānāha) and wind-disease, with wine; and in diseases of vāta, with clear wine (prasannā). (15.17c–v, 18)
In cases of constipation, it should be taken with the cream of curd; for hemorrhoids, with pomegranate juice; for cutting pain, with *vṛkṣāmla*; and for indigestion, with warm water. (19)
In cases of fistula-in-ano, anemia, cough, dyspnea, throat obstruction, heart disease, disorders of the small intestine, skin diseases, weak digestion, and fever; (20)
This purgative should be drunk as appropriate by one with a lubricated bowel in cases of fang-poison, root-poison, gara-poison, and artificial poisons. (21)
Hapuṣā, kāñcanakṣīrī, triphalā, the fruit of nīlinī, trāyantī, rohiṇī, tiktā, sātalā, trivṛtā, and vacā. (22)
One should powder rock salt, black salt, and long pepper, and [administer them] with pomegranate juice, the fruit juices of the three myrobalans, meat broth, urine, or lukewarm water. // 23 //

This [mixture] is to be drunk in all cases of gulma, in splenic disorders, in all types of abdominal enlargements, in vitiligo, in skin diseases, in chronic fever, in lassitude, and in irregular digestion. (24)
In cases of swelling, hemorrhoids, anemia, jaundice, and melanoderma, one should quickly pacify the deranged vāta, pitta, and kapha by means of purgation. (25)
One should drink the powder of nīlinī, nicula, vyoṣa, the two types of kṣāra, the five salts, and citraka with clarified butter to cure abdominal enlargement and gulma. (26)
As before, one who has been emaciated by the purgative should drink milk at intervals; however, in the case of an urgent illness, one should administer the milk of a camel, a cow, or a goat. (27)
For those who are particularly weak, one should administer fats specifically for the purpose of purgation;
an āḍhaka of ghee mixed with a prastha of finely powdered harītakī [is recommended]. (28)
15.28 Having melted the oil itself over a fire for the purpose of purgation and stirred it with a churning stick, one should place it in a vessel of barley husks;
then, after a month has passed, having removed and strained it, one should cook it again.
Combined with the decoction of *harītakī* and sour curd, it cures abdominal enlargement, artificial poison, tumors, constipation, abdominal lumps, and abscesses. (30)
This [mixture], prepared from cow’s milk mixed with the latex of *snuk*, boiled, cooled, and stirred with a whisk, cures leprosy, insanity, and epilepsy when drunk. (31)
The ghee that is produced when prepared with the milk of the *snuk* plant possesses those same qualities;
likewise, one *droṇa* of milk combined with half a *prastha* of *sudhā* milk and curd [yields similar results]. (32)
Having churned curd that has been prepared by adding half a *prastha* [of water], one should drink that clarified butter (*sarpis*) processed with *trivṛt*, which possesses those same qualities;
likewise, one should drink a *prastha* of clarified butter prepared in eight times the amount of milk.
One should cook milk with eight times its quantity of water along with a paste of one pala of snuk-milk and six palas of trivṛt;
thereafter, one should drink a gruel (peyā), meat broth, sweet juice, or milk.
Once the ghee has been digested and he has undergone purgation, he should drink lukewarm water prepared with ginger;
thereafter, he should take liquid gruel (peyā), and then soup made from horse gram (kulattha).
One who has undergone drying therapy (rūkṣa) should drink ghee for three days in this manner, or even longer if he is given supplementary food;
he should drink the ghee again and again according to this very same sequence.

A skilled physician should administer these prepared ghees for the pacification of abdominal tumors (gulma), poisons (gara), disorders of the humors (doṣa), and abdominal enlargements (udara). // 37 //
Or one should drink ghee prepared with a paste of *pīlu*, which breaks up abdominal distension (*ānāha*);
or one may drink *tailvaka-ghṛta*, *nīlinī-ghṛta*, or *miśraka-sneha*. (38)

Having had the humors removed, the patient with abdominal enlargement should gradually eat light rice prepared from *śāli* paddy; he should consume it for the purpose of alleviating the drying of the humors. (39)
Or one may take a thousand myrobalans with cow's urine, followed by milk;
or a thousand long peppers that have been well-impregnated with the milky sap of the *snuk* plant. (40)
Or one may follow the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen while subsisting on milk, or consume *śilājatu*;
likewise, one may take *guggulu* with milk, or similarly with an equal amount of fresh ginger juice. // 41 //
Or one should drink a paste of *pippalī* in increasing doses, or a paste of *citraka* and *amaradāru* with milk;
likewise, for a month, one may take *hastipippalī* and *viśvabheṣaja* combined.

Having drunk milk with a paste made of equal parts of *viḍaṅga*, *citraka*, *dantī*, *cavya*, and the three acrids (*vyoṣa*), each the size of a *kola* fruit, one shall conquer even advanced abdominal enlargement.
Or one should eat food mixed with the milk and ghee of *snuhī* for a month;
or one may consume a bolus (*utkārikā*) made from *pathyā* and *kaṇā* that has been soaked in *snuhī* milk.
If the wind (vāyu) should cause pain in the sides, stiffness, or a gripping sensation in the heart, one should then drink oil mixed with the alkali of *bilva*. 45.
Or it may be cooked with the separately prepared alkalis derived from *tuṇṭuka*, *balā*, *palāśa*, and the stalks of sesame, or from *kadalī*, *apāmārga*, and *tarkārī*. (46)

When kapha is occluded by vāta, or pitta by those two (kapha and vāta), or when vāta itself is occluded, castor oil combined with its own appropriate medicinal drugs is beneficial for a strong patient. 47.
One should apply an external plaster to the abdomen using devadāru, palāśa, arka, hastipippalī, śigru, and aśvakarṇa, along with cow's urine. (48)
One should sprinkle [the area] with decoctions and urines prepared from vṛścikālī, vacā, śuṇṭhī, pañcamūla, punarnavā, varṣābhū, dhānyaka, and kuṣṭha. (49)
Once the abdomen has been purged and its flaccidity removed, it should be fomented with *śālvaṇa* and other poultices;
one should then wrap it with a cloth, so that the wind does not cause it to distend again.

15.50b–c. If a person who has been well-purged with emetics such as *śālvaṇa* and others should again experience flatulence (*ādhmāna*), one should treat him with non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*) that are well-oleated and contain sour and salty substances.
15.51d. [One should treat him] with non-unctuous enemas that are well-oleated, sour, and salty.
Or, when the wind, even if supported by other factors, causes a person to become distended, sharp enemas containing alkali and cow's urine are recommended for him. (52)

Thus have the general procedures for those with abdominal enlargement (jaṭharin) been declared. Now, for a strong patient with vātodara, ghee boiled with the vidārigandhādi group [of herbs] should be administered. (53)
15.53 Thus has the general treatment for those suffering from abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara) been declared as effective.
Thereafter, one should administer a purgative to the patient whose body has been lubricated and fomented,
using either Tailvaka oil or Miśraka ghee many times.
Once the preparation is complete, one should administer the milk for the sake of strength;
however, it must be discontinued before the onset of nausea, and once strength has been regained, the milk may be resumed gradually.
15.55cv Prior to the onset of nausea, one should turn back [the patient] by means of broths or meat juices that are mildly sour and salty, once the digestive fire has been stimulated;
then, for one suffering from udāvarta, one should again administer an unctuous enema after performing oleation and sudation.
With an enema (vasti) prepared with the ten roots (daśamūlī) combined with sharp purgatives, and with sesame oil and castor oil boiled with Vāta-subduing and sour substances. // 57 //

15.57b–v. In cases of throbbing, convulsions, pain in the joints, bones, flanks, back, and the sacrum (trika), as well as dryness, constipation, flatulence, and a stimulated digestive fire, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla).
For one who has not undergone purgation, pacifying treatments such as enemas, milk, and ghee should be administered;
in the case of Pitta-type fever, the patient should be strengthened with sweet-prepared ghee after first applying oleation.
One should administer a purgative prepared from śyāmā, tribhaṇḍī, and triphalā;
thereafter, a nirūha enema enriched with sugar, honey, and ghee is beneficial for him.
An oil enema (sneha-vasti) prepared with a decoction of *nyagrodha* and other such drugs should be administered;
however, for one who is weak, one should first cleanse the patient with milk enemas (*kṣīra-vasti*) before performing an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*).
Once the strength of the digestive fire has been restored, one should repeatedly administer unctuous purgation with milk mixed with the paste of trivṛt, or with urubūka oil boiled with it.

15.62 When the digestive fire has been restored, one should administer an unctuous enema to that patient with a decoction of *mūrvā* and *urubūka*, or with a decoction of *sātalā* and *trāyamāṇā*, or with *āragvadha*.
In cases involving phlegm (*kapha*), it should be given with urine; in cases involving wind (*vāta*), with bitter ghee.

15.63–64ab. He should eat with *saptalā* and *trāyamāṇā*, or with milk boiled with one of these [drugs], or with milk boiled with the *vidāryādi* group. Furthermore, he should apply a poultice (*upanāha*) of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to his abdomen.
Furthermore, by steadily following the sequence of milk, enemas,
and purgatives, one who is diligent shall surely conquer pitta-type abdominal enlargement.

15.65–66ab: Since one should conquer pitta-type abdominal enlargement with a decoction prepared from the *vatsakādi* group, and having lubricated a patient with kapha-type enlargement using clarified butter, one should first apply sudation and then administer a strong purgative prepared with the milk of *snuk*.
One should administer foods that are pungent, alkaline, and dispel kapha;
thereafter, a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) rich in urine, the three pungents (trikaṭu), and oil is beneficial for him. (67)

An oil enema (sneha-vasti) prepared with a decoction of muṣkaka and other such herbs, as well as food taken with the milk boiled with that same decoction, or with the soup of kulattha beans, [are recommended]. 68.

One should administer fermented liquors (ariṣṭas) and alkalis in cases of sluggish digestion, loss of appetite, nausea, alcoholism, and abdominal enlargement caused by the thickening and hardening of kapha.

15.69 When kapha is stagnant in a fixed abdomen (sthirodara), accompanied by numbness, loss of appetite, and nausea, one should administer asafoetida, upakulyā, the three fruits (triphalā), devadāru, the two types of niśā,
bhallātaka, the fruit of śigru, kaṭukā, tiktaka, and vacā.
One should burn śuṇṭhī, mādrī, ghana, kuṣṭha, sarala, and the five salts (paṭu-pañcaka) after having crushed them into small pieces, using curd and the four types of fats (sneha). // 71 //
Then, one should drink "cat-foot" (biḍāla-padaka) salt from alkaline earth, with the smoke [of the preparation] held within the mouth,
along with wine, the whey of curd, warm water, ariṣṭa, and surā-āsava.
15.72–73. With the decoctions of *jalāriṣṭa* and *sudhāsava*,

one may destroy abdominal enlargement, tumors, *aṣṭhīlā*, scrotal swellings (*tūṇyau*), edema, choleraic dysentery (*viṣūcikā*), diseases of the spleen and heart, hemorrhoids, and upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*).
One may conquer kaphaja udara in a weak patient by drinking a preparation of powdered iron mixed with *ariṣṭa* and cow's urine, as well as by drinking alkaline oils. (74)

One should apply a poultice (upanāhya) to the abdomen made of white mustard seeds, fermenting agents (kiṇva), and the seeds of radish, ground into a paste; and in this condition, one should repeatedly employ fomentation (sveda). // 75 //

15.75–76. For one whose strength and digestive fire are not excessively diminished, one should perform fomentation on the abdomen with the pastes of [the aforementioned drugs] in cases of abdominal enlargement caused by *saṃnipāta*.
However, this procedure should be rejected if it is performed in accordance with a predominance of the *doṣas* [that would otherwise be aggravated].

Oil produced from the fruits of *dantī* and *dravantī* is recommended for drinking, especially in cases of abdominal enlargement (*jaṭhara*) involving all three *doṣas* when other treatments have failed. (77)
Having consulted with her kinsmen, one should give her the root of *kākādanī*, *guñjā*, and *karavīraka* mixed with wine for her to drink. (78)
Or one may give food and drink mixed with poison, or a stationary poison, or a fruit upon which an enraged serpent has released its venom. (79)
Therefore, his mass of defects—firm, latent, and following wrong paths—is quickly shattered by the swiftly destructive poison and flows outward. (80)
In that manner, it attains freedom from disease, or else [the patient] enters another body;
however, once the humors have been removed, one should have him drink milk after he has bathed in cold water.
Or one should eat the greens of trivṛt with gruel, or those of māṇḍūka or vāstuka, or kāla-śāka, or that known as yava, prepared with their own expressed juices. // 82 //

For one month, the patient should abstain from food, consuming neither sour nor salty substances and avoiding fats; then, whether the body has been previously fomented or not, when thirsty, he should drink the expressed juice [of meat]. 83.

15.83–84. After one month has passed in this manner, once the humors have been thus removed by means of potherbs, thereafter, for the sake of the patient who is now weakened, one should administer the milk of a young camel to sustain his life.

In cases of splenic enlargement (plīhodara), after the patient has been oleated and fomented according to the specific dosha and has eaten a meal with curd, one should perform venesection on the left arm. (85)
Once strength has been regained, one should again administer sea-shell-derived alkali that has been purified by being soaked in oil and then processed with milk. (86)

One should take the juice of *amlavetasa* enriched with the powder of *viḍa* salt and *kaṇā*, or a decoction of *naktamāla* or *śaubhāñjana* mixed with *saindhava* salt, *agni* (citraka), and *kaṇā*. (87)
One should administer the powder of hiṅgu and other ingredients, along with alkali and ghee, according to one's strength;
likewise, one may take long pepper, ginger, and dantī in equal parts, with double the amount of chebulic myrobalan. (88)
One should drink this powder— consisting of equal parts of *viḍaṅga* and *citraka*, twice as much *abhayā*, and a half-part of *saktu*—
with warm water; or else, one may take *viḍaṅga*, *citraka*, roasted grain flour (*saktu*), ghee, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *vacā*.
Having burnt [the plant] in a skull, one should drink it with milk to cure abdominal tumors (gulma) and splenic disorders (plīhā).
When bound with leaves of the *badaraka* tree crushed together with oil, it likewise cures these conditions.
Furthermore, spleen disease caused by a pestle is destroyed in one who subsists on milk;
likewise, Rohītaka creepers cut into pieces along with Abhayā [are effective] when placed in water.

One should distill that [juice] in urine and drink it after it has stood for seven nights; it removes jaundice, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, worms, urinary disorders, and abdominal enlargements. (92)
One should macerate twenty-five palas of the bark of *rohītaka* in urine; having prepared this,
one should formulate a decoction combined with two prasthas of *kola*.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with five-pala portions of each of those [five spices] and an equal amount of powdered *rohītaka* bark.
When applied quickly, this [mixture] of the alkali of plantain, sesame stalks, and *kṣuraka* pacifies the enlargement of the spleen. (95)

It pacifies the enlargement of the spleen; indeed, it pacifies the excessive enlargement of the spleen. Furthermore, oil cooked with the alkali of *ikṣuraka* overcomes splenic disorders born of *kapha* and *vāta* when consumed.
If there is no pacification, one should apply cauterization according to the procedure for abdominal tumors (gulma).

In cases where the bile has not reached the gallbladder or the fluids, in splenic disorders, and when wind and phlegm are predominant, as well as in Pitta-type conditions, life-prolonging medicated ghees and milk enemas should be administered. (97)
Bloodletting, purification, and the drinking of milk are recommended;
for the liver, the treatment is as for the spleen, but the vein is on the right arm. 98.

To one who has undergone sudation and suffers from abdominal distension, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) containing urine and sharp medicinal herbs, along with oil and salt, followed by an unctuous enema (anuvāsana). // 99 //
Foods that cause downward discharge, a sharp purgative for him, and such treatments as remove udāvarta and pacify vāta should be administered. (100)
Except for chidrodara, one should treat it like śleṣmodara;
as soon as fluid has accumulated, it should be drained, and thus the physician should manage the condition. (101)
In cases of abdominal dropsy (udakodara), one should first employ strong (tīkṣṇa) drugs that remove the defects of the water, combined with urine and various alkaline substances (kṣāra). 102.
One should treat him with foods that are digestive stimulants and phlegm-subduing;
one should cook goat dung-ash, strained in urine, over a fire. (103)
When it has become solidified, one should add one karṣa of powdered pippalī, pippalīmūla, śuṇṭhī, and the five salts. (104)
Nikumbha, kumbha, triphalā, svarṇakṣīrī, viṣāṇikā, svarjikākṣāra, ṣaḍgranthā, sātalā, and that which is produced from yavaśūka. (105)
Having made pills from *kola* fruits and soaked them in fermented gruel (*sauvīraka*), one should drink them in cases of non-bilious edema (*ajāraka*), swelling, and ascites (*udakodara*). 106.

15.106 When dropsy has become advanced and is not relieved by medicines, the physician— when requested by the patient’s kinsmen and the king— should employ surgery for the three types of abdominal enlargements beginning with *baddhodara*.
For one whose body has been lubricated and fomented, and for whom the intestines have been secured below the navel,
one should incise the abdomen, leaving a space of four finger-breadths on the left side.
Having extracted the intestines to a length of four finger-breadths,
one should examine them and remove any hair, impurities, mucus, stones, or other such debris.
In the case of a perforation, however, having extracted the foreign body and cleansed the intestinal leakage, one should cause centipedes to bite the perforation;
once they have attached themselves, one should then extract [the perforation].
Having cleansed the intestine of the oozing discharge,
one should reposition the body parts and the intestines according to their proper places; then, having lubricated them with honey and ghee, one should suture the external wound.
15.111b–112a. One should insert [the instrument] into its proper place, then coat it with black earth mixed with a stick, and bind it.
Remaining in a windless place and subsisting on milk, the patient should then stay in a vat of oil.

When the abdomen, which has been smeared with oil that subdues wind, is fomented with hot water while still containing water, and is wrapped with a cloth band around the waist, [the procedure should be performed]. 113.
When the abdomen is encircled and the location of the bound opening has been identified, one should pierce it to the depth of one finger-breadth;
having inserted a tube into that [opening], one should drain half of the fluid.
Then, having drawn out its tube and having anointed the wound with oil and salt, one should bind it and wrap the abdomen with a cloth.
On the third or fourth day, and so on up to the sixteenth day,
one should drain the water from it little by little, allowing it to rest at intervals.

15.116b–117. Or, for up to sixteen days, one should wrap the abdomen very tightly with a cloth, or loosely. Once the [fluid] has flowed out, the patient, having undergone fasting, should drink a thin gruel (peyā) prepared without fat or salt.
15.117b–c. And the abdomen may become either flaccid or firm;
one should subsist on milk for six months. For three months, one should drink gruel with milk;
for another three months, one should eat [solid food] with milk alone, or with the juice of sour fruits, or with meat broth. 118.
By consuming small quantities of aged śyāmāka and kodrava grains with little oil and salt, one who is self-restrained shall conquer ascites within a year. (119)
Restrained regarding things to be avoided, and having conquered his senses, he should eat what is prescribed and not what is not prescribed;
for almost everything that enters the stomach arises from a combination of the humors (doṣas). 120.
Therefore, treatment that pacifies wind and the other humors is recommended in all cases;
for when the abdomen is filled with the humors, the digestive fire becomes weak. (121)
Therefore, all therapeutic actions are highly commended; likewise, foods that are appetizing, digestive stimulants, light,
and containing the five roots (pañcamūla), with slight acidity, pungency, oiliness, and bitterness, are recommended.
One should feed the man as much as he desires a gruel prepared with milk, using sixty-day rice grains and the urine of cows that have been previously treated.
One should drink sugarcane juice afterwards for the cessation of abdominal enlargements;
in this way, the wind, bile, and phlegm of these patients return to their respective locations. (124)
Excessively hot, sour, salty, dry, constipating, cold, and heavy; jaggery, vegetables prepared with oil, and water for drinking and immersion baths—[these should be avoided]. 125.
One should avoid water that is excessively hot, salty, physical exertion, travel, sleeping during the day, and riding in vehicles.
Buttermilk that is neither too clear, too thick, nor too sweet is recommended for drinking.
In cases of Vāta, it should be taken with Kaṇā and salt; in Pitta, with Soṣaṇa and sugar; and in Kaphaja Udara, with Yavānī, Saindhava, Ajājī, honey, and Vyōṣa. (127)

In the abdomen of a patient with *nicaya*, one should apply a paste combined with the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), alkali (*kṣāra*), and salts, along with honey, oil, *vacā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *śatāhvā*, *kuṣṭha*, and rock salt (*saindhava*). (128)
15.128c–d In the case of an enlarged spleen (plīha), [one should administer] honey, oil, varā, and ginger; however, if it is obstructed (baddha), [one should use] hapuṣā, yavānī, paṭu, and ajāji.
For an internal cavity (chidra), [use] honey with kṛṣṇā; for abdominal dropsy (salilodara), [use] the three pungents (vyoṣa).
For those suffering from loss of appetite, nausea, abdominal distension, weak digestion, and diarrhea, as well as for those afflicted by wind and phlegm disorders, buttermilk acts like nectar. (130)
After all the medicinal applications, one should subsequently administer milk;
it stabilizes all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), provides strength, and removes the persistence of the humors (*doṣas*). (131)
For those whose limbs are nourished by medicinal herbs, even milk acts as nectar. 131½.
In the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna),
a patient suffering from anemia (pāṇḍv-āmaya) should first drink the ghee known as Kalyāṇaka,
or the Mahātikta ghee prepared with the Aragvadhādi group of drugs. (1)
A patient suffering from jaundice should drink ghee prepared with one *kuḍava* of pomegranate, half a *kuḍava* of coriander,
one *pala* each of *citraka* and ginger, and half a *pala* of long pepper. (16.1ab)

Twenty palas of ghee, cooked with one āḍhaka of water and the [powdered] paste of these [drugs], cures heart disease, anemia, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, and afflictions caused by vāta and kapha. (3)
It is an illuminator, a destroyer of dyspnea and cough, and it facilitates the downward movement of obstructed wind;
it is highly recommended for women who have difficult labors and for those who are barren. (4)
One should induce emesis with sharp [emetics] for a person who has been oleated, and then purify one who has been re-oleated, using milk mixed with urine or even milk alone, many times over. // 5 //
One should drink the juice of *dantī* fruit, slightly warmed, in which one *añjali* of *kāśmarya* or one *añjali* of *drākṣā* has been soaked and crushed; this conquers the disease of *pāṇḍu*.
16.6a–c: One should take *pathyā* (harītakī) ground with warm urine in the juice of one *pala* of *dantī*, or the three fruits (*phalatrika*) processed with that same [juice];
or [one may take] *svarṇakṣīrī*, *trivṛt*, *śyāmā*, *bhadradāru*, and *mahauṣadha*.
One should drink [the medicine] ground with a handful of cow’s urine, or boiled with that same urine;
or one should drink milk prepared with these [drugs] to facilitate the downward movement of the humors.
Or, one may drink iron dust that has been kept in urine for seven days with milk;
once the milk is digested, one should eat with milk or with a sweet meat broth. // 9 //
Once purified, one should lick a paste of *pathyā* (chebulic myrobalan) melted with honey and ghee from both sides [of the mouth].
[The following are also used: *viśālā*, *kaṭukā*, *mustā*, *kuṣṭha*, *dāru*, and *kaliṅgaka*. (10)
Pathyā, softened with honey and ghee, along with viśālā, kaṭukā, mustā, kuṣṭha, dāru, and kaliṅgaka—one karṣa each; two picus of mūrvā; and half a karṣa of ghuṇapriyā.
Having drunk that powder with pleasant waters, one should then lick honey.
It conquers anemia, fever, burning sensations, cough, dyspnea, anorexia, abdominal tumors, flatulence, colic, and hemorrhagic disorders (rakta-pitta). // 12 //
A decoction made from vāsā, guḍūcī, triphalā, kaṭvī, bhūnimba, and nimba, when combined with honey, destroys anemia (pāṇḍu), bilious hemorrhage (pittāsra), and jaundice (kāmalā). (13)
Equal parts of the powder of vyoṣa, agni, vella, triphalā, and musta, along with iron filings, should be administered with buttermilk, honey, ghee, and warm water. (14)
This destroys jaundice, anemia, heart disease, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and urinary disorders;
it consists of equal measures of jaggery, ginger, iron rust (maṇḍūra), and sesame seeds. 15.
One should give pills made with double the amount of long pepper (pippalī) to a patient suffering from anemia (pāṇḍu-roga);
[the other ingredients are] mākṣika-taṅkaṇa, the bark of dārvī, cavya, granthika, and devadāru. (16)
Then, one should powder this group of nine beginning with vyoṣa in double quantity,
and thereafter add maṇḍūra that resembles collyrium in eightfold quantity compared to all of the former.

16.17 Having separately decocted the nine ingredients beginning with *vyoṣa* in cow's urine until they are fit for making pills (*vaṭaka*), one should add them [to the base] and form the pills; these one should eat while subsisting on buttermilk (*takra*).
These iron-powder pills (maṇḍūra-vaṭaka) bestow life upon those suffering from jaundice; they also cure skin diseases, chronic anemia, edema, stiffness of the thighs, and loss of appetite. (19)
They pacify hemorrhoids, jaundice, urinary disorders, and splenic enlargement;
[these are] five palas each of mica, bitumen, silver, and iron dross. (20)
One pala each of citraka, triphalā, vyoṣa, and viḍaṅga, mixed with eight palas of sugar, should be powdered and quickly consumed with honey. (21)
16.21–22. These [medicines], powdered and combined with honey, or powdered and mixed with honey while still warm, cure anemia, poisoning, cough, consumption, irregular fever,
skin diseases, chronic indigestion, urinary disorders, edema, dyspnea, and loss of appetite.

This [mixture] specifically cures epilepsy, jaundice, and diseases of the rectum, when prepared with *kauṭaja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *nimba*, *paṭola*, *ghana* (musta), and *nāgara*. (23)
The ten-day-prepared juices, increased two or three times over, [are mixed with] eight palas of *śilājatu* and an equal amount of white sugar. (24)
One pala each of tvakkṣīrī, pippalī, dhātrī, and karkaṭākhyā; one pala each of the fruit and root of nidigdhikā; and trijātaka in appropriate measure. (25)
16.25cv One should prepare boluses (*guḍa*) equal in size to an *akṣa* fruit from the fruits and roots of *nidigdhā*, combined with three *pala* of honey;
these should be taken with pomegranate juice, milk, bird broth, water, wine, or fermented liquors (*āsava*). 16.26.

Having consumed those [powders] combined with three palas of honey, one should drink [the decoction], either while fasting or after having eaten; it cures anemia, skin diseases, fever, splenic disorders, Tamaka-shwasa, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano. (16.26–27)

It cures diseases of the heart, urinary disorders, putrefaction, seminal defects, digestive fire disorders, consumption, poisoning, abdominal enlargements, cough, hemorrhaging, dysentery, internal hemorrhage, swellings, abdominal tumors, and throat ailments. (28)
These auspicious formulations, which remove all the *doṣas*, destroy urinary disorders (*meha*), abdominal enlargements (*vardhma*), and delusions (*bhrama*).
One *prastha* of grapes (*drākṣā*), one *prastha* of long pepper (*kaṇā*), and likewise half a *tulā* of sugar (*śarkarā*) [should be taken]. (29)
Having powdered two palas each of madhuka, śuṇṭhī, and tvakkṣīrī, one should throw them into a droṇa of dhātrī fruit juice and cook it like a linctus (leha). // 30 //
One should lick one *pāṇitala* measure of this [mixture], cooled and combined with a *prastha* of honey;
it cures *halīmaka*, anemia (*pāṇḍu-roga*), and jaundice (*kāmalā*). // 31 //

Water boiled with the minor five roots (kanīya-pañcamūla) is recommended for drinking and food; likewise, the juice of grapes and emblic myrobalan is beneficial for those suffering from anemia (pāṇḍu) and jaundice (kāmalā).

Thus has the medical treatment for anemia (pāṇḍu-roga) been described in general; it should be applied by the wise after making distinctions according to the specific strength of each individual humor (doṣa). // 33 //
16.33b–d. Pandu-roga is conquered by the physician through treatments primarily consisting of oleation when caused by Vāta; bitter and cold remedies when caused by Pitta;
pungent, dry, and hot remedies when caused by Kapha; and a combination of these when caused by all three Doshas (Sāṃnipātika).

In the case of a kapha-type [fever], one should administer pungent, sharp, and hot [medicines]; in that arising from the combination of all three doshas (saṃnipāta), one should first expel the mild [dosha] from the body using sharp purificatory therapies. Once the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha) has been purified, however, one should employ strengthening medicated ghees (sarpis).
One should extinguish the [burning] from the body with clay; once the internal cavity is purified, one should administer the following:

the three pungents (vyoṣa), bilva, the two types of turmeric (rajanī), the three myrobalans (triphalā), the two types of punarnavā, mustā, iron powder (ayo-rajas), pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, and devadāru. (16.35–36)
Ghee boiled with vṛścikālī, bhārgī, and milk quickly pacifies all disorders caused by [the consumption of] clay. (37)

Similarly, if there is a craving for that [earth], one should provide earth treated with saffron, yaṣṭimadhu, long pepper, milk, and young grass for the purpose of breaking the aversion to earth. (38)

Furthermore, medicinal remedies should be administered according to the specific derangement of the humors (doṣas), using the flowers of Vellāgni and Nimba, or Pāṭhā and Mūrvā, as appropriate for the particular type of morbid matter displaced from its site. (39)

In cases of jaundice (kāmalā), however, one should administer that which pacifies pitta and is not antagonistic to anemia (pāṇḍu-roga): a hundred fruits of *pathyā* boiled in their own juice, with the paste of fifty of their stalks added. (40)
One *prastha* of this prepared ghee cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), and anemia (*pāṇḍu-roga*).
[This is prepared] with the juice of *āragvadha*, sugarcane, or *vidārī* and *āmalaka*. (41)
One should administer a dose the size of a bilva fruit containing the three pungents (try-ūṣaṇa) to cure jaundice;
or one may drink the paste of nikumbha with double the amount of jaggery and cold water. (42)

or the juice of *triphalā*, *guḍūcī*, *dārvī*, or *nimba*.
One should administer honey-mixed [preparations] every morning to one afflicted by jaundice;
a collyrium made from niśā, gairika, and dhātrī removes jaundice. (44)
