When the wind (vāyu), aggravated by dry, cold, heavy, sweet [substances], physical exertion, and suppression of natural urges, displaces the bile (pitta) to the exterior while being itself overwhelmed by phlegm (kapha); // 46 //
At that time, the man’s eyes, urine, and skin become yellow, his feces white, and he suffers from flatulence, constipation, and a heavy heart. (47)

When pitta has taken refuge in the peripheral tissues (śākhā), it should be understood that weakness, low digestive fire, pain in the flanks, hiccups, dyspnea, anorexia, and fever will gradually become slight. (48)
One should feed him with juices that are dry, pungent, and sour, produced from peacock, partridge, and cock,
as well as with soups made from dried radish and from horse gram (kulattha).
That which is very sour, pungent, sharp, salty, and hot is recommended;
likewise, one should lick the three acrid drugs (vyoṣa) with the juice of bījapūraka according to the state of the internal organs.
One's own bile returns to it, whereby even one's feces become colored;
and the wind subsides along with complications such as flatulence. (51)
For this patient whose complications have subsided, the treatment for jaundice should be administered;
in the case of Kumbhakāmalā, one should drink realgar and lac with cow's urine.
A woman suffering from halīmaka should take for a month either honey-ore, or dross produced from gold,
prepared with the fresh juice of guḍūcī and milk.
One who has been lubricated with buffalo ghee should drink the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) mixed with *trivṛt*; once purged by that, he should eat sweet food that alleviates pitta and vāta. (54)
One should habitually employ the previously mentioned grape electuary, sweet medicated ghees, non-unctuous enemas (yāpana), milk enemas, and unctuous enemas (sānuvāsana).

One should drink preparations of *mārdvīkāriṣṭa* according to the proper method for the increase of the digestive fire, as well as the *kāsika* electuary of *abhayā*, *pippalī*, *madhuka*, and *balā*. (56)

16.56c–v Or, one skilled in the treatment of jaundice (pāṇḍu-roga) should administer a linctus of kāsīsa and abhayā with milk, according to the specific humor involved and the patient's strength; as well as the therapeutic regimen prescribed for swelling (śopha).

Equal parts of iron filings, sesame, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and jujube (kola), along with an amount of honey-ore powder (mākṣika-dhātu-cūrṇa) equal to all of these combined—these, made into a bolus (modaka) and taken with honey followed by buttermilk, are recommended even for long-standing cases of jaundice (pāṇḍvāmaya). // 57+1 //

In the section on therapeutics (*cikitsāsthāna*), throughout the *Sarvāṅgasāra*, regarding swelling (*śvayathu*) born of the humors (*doṣa*) when it is still in the stage of undigested toxins (*sāma*):
after first drying it up [with astringents] and eating light food, one should drink [the medicine] with warm water. (1)
Nāgara, ativiṣā, dāru, viḍaṅga, indrayava, and uṣaṇa;
or else, vijayā, śuṇṭhī, devadāru, and punarnavā. (2)
One with an abundance of *doṣas* should take new iron for purification, along with *mūtra-harītakī*, or *kaṭukā*, *kumbhāyasa*, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) with a decoction of *varā*. (3)

For purification, one with weak digestion who suffers from undigested matter (āma), heaviness, and obstructed stools should regularly consume *mūtra-harītakī*, or likewise *guggulu*, or *jatū* derived from stone (*śailasaṃbhava*). 17.3b–d.

Buttermilk mixed with sauvarcala salt, the three pungents (vyoṣa), honey, jaggery, and chebulic myrobalan; or else, buttermilk followed by an after-drink of jaggery and dry ginger—these are likewise [recommended].

Or one may take ginger with an equal amount of jaggery, increasing the dose by half a *prakuñca* every day until it reaches a maximum of five *palas*, consuming a diet of broth, milk, or meat soup for one month. (6)

This application overcomes gulma, abdominal enlargement, hemorrhoids, edema, urinary disorders, dyspnea, catarrh, intestinal torpor, indigestion, jaundice, consumption, mental disorders, cough, and phlegm. (7)

Having prepared ghee with the paste and the expressed juice of fresh ginger (ārdraka-nāgara) along with milk, even one overcome by swelling, sneezing, abdominal enlargement, and loss of digestive fire becomes free from disease upon drinking it. // 8 //
Likewise, the juice of fresh ginger (nāgara) should be drunk; thereafter, when it has been digested, one should eat food with milk.
Alternatively, one should forcibly overcome swelling caused by the three doṣas by consuming realgar (śilāhvaya) with the juice of triphalā. // 8+1 //
A decoction of punarnavā, nimba, paṭola, śuṇṭhī, tiktā, amṛtā, dārvī, and abhayā destroys edema of the entire body, abdominal enlargement, cough, colic, dyspnea, and the disease of jaundice. (8+2)
One who is afflicted by edema, suffering from constipation and bound-up impurities, should drink milk prepared with the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), trivṛtā, dantī, and citraka. (9)
One who subsists on milk should consume the urine of a cow or a buffalo along with milk for seven days or a month; alternatively, one may subsist on camel's milk.
17.10d–11: It may be prepared with camel’s milk,
along with *yavānaka*, barley-alkali (*yava-kṣāra*), *yavānī*, the five-spice group (*pañca-kolaka*),
black pepper, pomegranate, *pāṭhā*, *dhānakā*, and sour *vetasa*.
One should prepare one karṣa of young bilva in one āḍhaka of water;
a prastha of ghee cooked with that [decoction] cures swelling, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and urinary disorders.

Alternatively, one who knows the proper time should employ ghee cooked with *citraka* from curd that contains *citraka*, combined with that same buttermilk; or likewise, [ghee] cooked with *citraka* [from plain curd], which possesses those same qualities.
One should cook one hundred *pathyā* fruits in a *kaṃsa* measure of the decoction of *daśamūla*, together with *dhānvantara*, *mahātiktaka*, *kalyāṇaka*, and *abhayā-ghṛta*. (14)
Having added a *tulā* of jaggery to that linctus, one should add the powdered *trijātaka*, *trikaṭuka*, and a small amount of *yavaśūka*. (15)
And half a *prastha* of that [milk] mixed with honey and applied during the cold season destroys it when used. (16ab)
It cures increased swelling, fever, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, emaciation, flatulence, acid eructation, and blood-bile (rakta-pitta). // 16cd //
Discoloration, defects of urine, flatus, and semen, dyspnea, anorexia, splenic enlargement, and poisoning from *udara*—[these are the symptoms]. // 16ef //
Old barley and śāli rice, boiled with water decocted from the ten roots (daśamūla). // 17ab //
A diet consisting of small quantities of food with mild fats is beneficial for swelling (śvayathu),
along with soups made from mung beans, horse gram, and broken rice, seasoned with alkali and the three pungents (vyoṣa).
17.18b–c. In cases of swelling (śvayathu), food consisting of meat from wild animals, as well as that from tortoises, monitor lizards, and porcupines, is beneficial;
likewise, unsour curd (mathita) for drinking, along with medicinal wines (madya). 19.
With cumin, *śaṭhī*, *jivantī*, *kāravī*, lotus seeds, and *agnika*;
with the pulp of *bilva*, barley-alkali, and *vṛkṣāmla*, each measured in the quantity of a jujube fruit; // 20 //

Prepared with milk, clarified butter, and oil, and properly fried, it is highly beneficial for those suffering from swelling, diarrhea, heart disease, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, weak digestion, and urinary disorders. (21)
And likewise, for the purpose of recitation, it is prepared with the five spices (pañcakola) along with the virtues [of those ingredients],
together with śaileya, kuṣṭha, sthauṇeya, reṇukā, aguru, and padmaka.
With śrīveṣṭaka, nakha, spṛkkā, devadāru, and priyaṅgu; with māṃsī, māgadhikā, vanyā, dhānyā, dhyāmaka, and vālaka. (23)

One should prepare an unguent oil from *caturjātaka*, *tālīśa*, *mustā*, and *gandhapalāśaka*; [this oil may be used as] an ointment, while water [prepared with these same ingredients] is for bathing. (24)
Or one may bathe with water from the *nimba*, *varṣābhū*, *naktamāla*, and *arka* plants for swelling in a single limb; or with *varṣābhū*, *karavīraka*, and *kiṃśuka* for similar conditions.
With viśālā, triphalā, lodhra, nalikā, and devadāru; with hiṃsrā, kośātakī, mādrī, tālaparṇī, and jayantī. (26)
An application of a lukewarm paste made from *sthūlākākādanī*, *śāla*, *nākulī*, *vṛṣaparṇī*, *vṛddhi*, *ṛddhi*, and *hastikarṇa* is beneficial. (27)
Now, in a swelling caused by Vata, one should drink Trivṛt for half a month;
however, in the case of obstruction of flatus and feces, one should take that very same [Trivṛt] with castor oil.
One should likewise administer [medicines] mixed with milk or meat broths before the meal;
furthermore, one should apply sudation, oil massages that subdue Vāta, and ointments for cases localized in a single limb.
In cases of Pitta-type fever, one should drink bitter ghee prepared with mātuluṅga, agnimantha, śuṇṭhī, hiṃsrā, and amarāhvaya, or else ghee boiled with the drugs of the nyagrodhādi group.
Milk is used for thirst, burning sensations, and delusion; cooling ointments and massages are also beneficial.
Patola root, trāyantī, yaṣṭyāhva (liquorice), kaṭukā, and abhayā [are likewise employed]. (31)

The decoction of those [drugs] drunk with ghee cures saṃnipāta, erysipelas (visarpa), swelling, burning sensations, and fever caused by poison.
One should drink oil prepared with the āragvadhādi group for conditions arising from kapha.

17.33b–34. When there is obstruction of the channels, diminished digestive fire, and loss of appetite, one whose internal organs are congested should habitually employ alkaline powders, fermented liquors (āsava), medicated spirits (ariṣṭa), urine, and buttermilk to alleviate swelling, burning sensations, intoxication, and fever.
One should employ black sesamum, old oil-cake, drumstick bark, sand, and linseed—ground into a paste with urine and made pleasantly warm—for application and massage. (35)
When the urine-water has been prepared with kuṣṭha, tarkārī, and citraka, or with kulattha and nāgara, one should bathe; or one should apply a plaster of caṇḍā and aguru.
A paste consisting of kālājaśṛṅgī, saralā, bastagandhā, hayāhvayā, and ekaiṣīkā should be applied for swelling that is localized to a single limb. (37)
An ointment consisting of liquorice, milk, and sesame seeds combined with fresh butter, or else with the stalks of the *śāla* leaf, destroys swelling caused by *āruṣkara*. (37+1)

One should perform purification by bloodletting according to the specific humor involved and its proximity; however, when the humors are mixed, one should perform the treatment according to the strength of the predominant humor.

Ajāji, pāṭhā, ghanapippalī, pañcakola, vyāghrī, rajanī, bhūnimba, and mahauṣadhi, when drunk with lukewarm water, destroy swelling caused by the three doṣas that is long-standing and fully developed. (39)

The two types of Amṛtā, Śivātikā, Surakāṣṭha, along with Pura and cow's urine, cure swelling, abdominal enlargement, skin diseases, anemia, worms, urinary disorders, and the upward movement of kapha and vāta. (40)

Thus, regarding one's own [condition], wholesome treatment has been stated: for swelling born of a wound, bloodletting is required; for that born of poison, the use of purgatives, cold applications, ghee-pastes, affusions, and venesection—along with anti-poisonous remedies—is desired. (41)
Village-grown meat, marshy meat, weak meat, dried vegetables, and sesame-based food; 42a.
Gauḍa liquor, flour-based food, curd with salt, slimy substances, and sour wine. // 42b //
Gauḍa liquor, flour-based foods, curd with salt, waterless sour wine,
parched grain, dried meat, eating in equal quantities [of incompatible foods], as well as heavy, unwholesome, and burning food.
One suffering from the disease of swelling should avoid sexual intercourse during the day and at night, as well as dreaming [of such acts]. // 42d //
In the section on therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna),
at the very outset regarding erysipelas (visarpa), fasting and drying therapies are beneficial;
bloodletting, emesis, and purgation are also advised, but oleation is not.
Emetic therapy (pracchardana) that destroys visarpa consists of madanaphala combined with yaṣṭīmadhu and indrayava, or else combined with the leaves of paṭola, pippalī, and nimba. // 2 //
Trivṛt powder, combined with the juice of trāyantī or grapes,
or with the three myrobalans (triphalā), acts as a purgative when taken with milk or clarified butter.
When the *doṣa* has entered the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), purification (*viśodhana*) should be applied, especially so;
however, for one whose *doṣa* is not to be purified or when it is slight, pacification (*śamana*) with sandalwood and blue lotus should be used. (4)
Either musta, nimba, and paṭola, or the paṭolādi group itself, or śārivā, āmalaka, uśīra, and musta, boiled in water; // 5 //
One suffering from thirst and erysipelas (visarpa) should drink either a decoction or a cold infusion of durālabhā, parpaṭaka, guḍūcī, and viśvabheṣaja. // 6 //
Dārvī, paṭola, kaṭukā, masūra, and triphalā, likewise along with nimba, yaṣṭī, and trāyantī, should be boiled and then mixed with ghee.
Amṛtā, vṛṣa, paṭola, mustaka, and saptaparṇa. // 7+1a //
Khadira, black cane, nimba leaf, and the two types of turmeric. // 7+1b //
Various spreading poisons, leprosy, eruptive boils, and itching.
It removes measles, cold-pitta, and fever. // 7+1d //
When the blood is vitiated in the vessels (śākhā), one should first remove the blood itself;
for the putrefaction of skin, flesh, and sinews arises from the putrefaction of the blood. // 8 //
When phlegm is devoid of its oily essence and diminished, and wind and bile are predominant, bitter ghee or ghee boiled with *mahātiktā* or *trāyamāṇā* is beneficial. (9)

Once the blood has been removed and the internal morbidity located within the skin, flesh, and joints has been purified, external treatments such as medicinal plasters (pradeha) and the like should be applied for the immediate pacification of visarpa. 10.
Śatāhvā, musta, vārāhī, vaṃśa, ārtagala, dhānyaka, surāhvā, kṛṣṇagandhā, and kuṣṭha constitute a paste for use in cases of instability [of the fetus]. (11)
18.11 For a mobile [type of hemorrhage], *kuṣṭha* is the external application;
for [mobile] *pitta*, the *nyagrodhādi* group as well as the *padmotpalādi* group [is used].
And for a *bisa-granthi*, there should be an application (*lepa*) soaked in clarified butter washed a hundred times;
or cold lotus-mud, or pearl ground into powder. (13)
Conch shell, coral, oyster shell, or red ochre mixed with clarified butter;
along with triphalā, padmaka, uśīra, samaṅgā, and karavīraka—(14).
An ointment made from *samaṅgā*, *karavīra*, the roots of *nalada*, and *anantā* destroys *śleṣmavisarpa*.
[Likewise, an ointment of] *dhava*, *saptāhva*, *khadira*, *devadāru*, and *kuraṇṭaka* [is effective].
An ointment consisting of Musta and Āragvadha, or the group of drugs beginning with Varuṇa, or the leaves of Āragvadha and the bark derived from Śleṣmātaka [should be used]. (16)
Indrāṇī-śāka, kākāhvā, and śirīṣa flowers should be used respectively for irrigation, wound massage, oblation, ointment, and powder. (17)
With these very medicinal herbs— indrāṇī, śāka, kākāhvā, and śirīṣa flowers— one should prepare ointments enriched with ghee for application when [the disease] is located in the seat of vāyu,
whether accompanied by āma and situated in the seat of kapha, or situated in the seat of pitta. (18)
Neither cold nor hot, wholesome, and dry, they should be mixed with ghee in cases of raktapitta;
they should be extremely cold, thin, and placed between layers of thin cloth. (19)
18.19d Those [remedies] situated within thin clothing should be applied anew at every moment; those same [remedies] are of mild potency.
When the humors (doṣas) are combined, this combined treatment is recommended. // 20 //
One should smear the fire with ghee that has been washed a hundred times, or with pure [ghee] alone;
one should sprinkle it with cold ghee-scum or with water decocted from Madhuka. // 21 //
Mahātiktaka is supremely beneficial when used for drinking, as an external application, or for irrigation with cold water, rainwater, milk, or sugarcane juice. (22)
18.22–23. Having properly performed the treatment for the condition known as *granthi* (as previously described) with white water and lotus-water to destroy blood and bile (*raktapitta*),
one should apply poultice fomentation (*piṇḍasveda*) and compresses (*upanāhana*) as desired to alleviate phlegm and wind (*kaphānila*).

In cases of pain from glandular swellings (granthi) or erysipelas (visarpa), one should sprinkle [the area] with warm oil prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla), or likewise with urine or water boiled with them. // 24 //
Or one should apply a warm paste made from ground black hellebore (*kṛṣṇagandhā*), or from the bark of *naktamāla*, or from dried radishes, or from *kaliṅga*. (25)
A plaster composed of dantī, the root-bark of citraka, the milky sap of sudhā and arka,
jaggery, the kernel of bhallātaka, and kāsīsa would split even a stone.
The latex of *snuhī* and *arka*, along with jaggery, [cures] a glandular swelling located in the external channels; how much more so one arising from *kapha*?
One should break up even a long-standing glandular swelling with these medicinal remedies. (18.26)
With soups of radishes and horse gram, seasoned with alkali and pomegranate;
or with meals of wheat or barley, accompanied by sidhu wine, honey, and sugar.
18.28c–d With meals of wheat and barley, accompanied by sidhu wine, honey, and sugar, or with the scum of vāruṇī liquor mixed with honey and the juice of mātuluṅga;
18.29 with the administration of triphalā, and with pippalī combined with honey.
18.29dv By means of applications of *devadāru* and *guḍūcī* combined with long pepper (*pippalī*) and honey, as well as of *girija*,
and by means of applications of *musta*, *bhallātaka*, parched grain flour (*saktu*), and honey; 18.30.

By means of fumigations, head-purgatives, and the previously mentioned methods for breaking up abdominal tumors (gulma), as well as by the application of pressure from heated iron, gold, salt, stones, and other such objects. // 31 //
If, despite being established in strength through these various perfected practices, the knot—which is as hard as stone—does not subside at all, [then one must apply further effort]. (32)

Then, cauterization with alkali, or even with arrows of gold, is beneficial for it; or, having caused it to suppurate with drugs that induce suppuration, one should incise it and extract [the foreign body].
Having caused it to ripen with digestive agents, one should repeatedly let out the blood that has become provoked;
and once the blood has been removed, one should administer medicine that conquers wind and phlegm.
When the area is excessively moistened by burning and suppuration, treatment should be like that for external and internal ulcers;
oil prepared with dārvī, viḍaṅga, and kampilla is beneficial for the ulcer. (35)

Ghee prepared with the fresh juice of *dūrvā* grass is indicated when *kapha* and *pitta* predominate; on one side stand all other therapeutic measures, and on the other side stands bloodletting. (36)
For erysipelas (visarpa) does not arise unless it is associated with blood and bile;
since blood itself is its substrate, one should therefore repeatedly deplete the blood.
Clarified butter should not be given to one with excessive morbid humors (doṣas) unless it acts as a purgative; for by that [butter], the obstructed humor may cook the skin, blood, and flesh. (38)
In the section on therapeutics, one should first treat all types of leprosy (kuṣṭha) with the internal administration of fats (sneha).
In that regard, oil or ghee prepared [with appropriate herbs] is beneficial when vāta is predominant. (1)
The ten roots, amṛtā, eraṇḍa, śārṅga, aṣṭā, meṣaśṛṅgī, paṭola, nimba, kaṭukā, dārvī, pāṭhā, and durālabhā. // 2 //

One should boil one pala each of parpaṭa and trāyamāṇā in two āḍhakas of water; when reduced to one-eighth, [one should add] with that decoction [an amount] measured by one karṣa each of the following: // 3 //
One should cook twelve palas of ghee with trāyantī, musta, bhūnimba, kaliṅga, kaṇa, and candana; that "bitter" (tiktaka) preparation overcomes [the diseases].
[It cures] bile-born skin diseases, erysipelas, pustules, burning sensations, thirst, vertigo, itching, anemia, swellings, malignant sinus tracts, ulcers, and scrofula. (5)
It also cures boils, abscesses, abdominal tumors, swellings, insanity, intoxication,
heart disease, blindness, facial disfigurement, chronic diarrhea, vitiligo, and jaundice.
It cures fistula-in-ano, epilepsy, abdominal enlargement, menorrhagia, artificial poison, hemorrhoids, blood-bile, and other extremely difficult diseases born of bile (pitta). // 7 //
Parpaṭaka with its covering, śamyāka, kaṭukā, vacā, triphalā, padmaka, pāṭhā, the two types of rajanī, the two types of śāriva, and kaṇa; // 8 //
Nimba, candana, yaṣṭyāhva, viśālā, indrayava, amṛtā, kirātatiktaka, sevya, vṛṣa, mūrvā, and śatāvarī [are to be used]. // 9 //
One should prepare ghee with eight parts of water and twice as much juice of *āmalakī*, using *paṭola*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *trāyantī*, and *dhanvayāsaka*.
The *tikta* (bitter) and *mahā-tikta* (great bitter) [decoctions] are considered superior in their qualities;
for cases where *kapha* is predominant, ghee should be prepared with *nimba*, *saptāhva*, and *citraka*.
In all cases, one should drink a decoction of kuṣṭha, uṣaṇa, vacā, śāla, priyāla, and caturaṅgula, along with aruṣkaraja, taubara, and sārṣapa.
One should take oil or ghee boiled with *kṛmijit*, *pathyā*, and *bhallātaka*;
or ghee boiled a hundred times with the root of *āragvadha*. (13)

19.13b–d: Drinking ghee boiled seven times with *pathyā*, *bhallātaka*, and water decocted with *khadira*, one quickly conquers skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). Anointing with these very same unctuous substances (*sneha*) as appropriate is also beneficial. 19.14.
One should drink Kuṣṭha; it quickly conquers [the disease].
Purification should be applied to one who has been lubricated, as that which was described for Visarpa.
Furthermore, one should venesect the veins in the forehead, hands, and feet.
In cases of minor kuṣṭha, one should apply scarification and the [medicines] beginning with horn as appropriate;
furthermore, one should nourish the patient from time to time with unctuous substances that destroy kuṣṭha.
For a leper who has been freed from blood and purged, whose internal organs are emptied, the wind will not be able to shatter his body. (17)
Ghee cooked with the paste of vāsā, amṛtā, nimba, varā, paṭola, vyāghrī, karañja, and udaka is known as Vajraka; it destroys erysipelas, fever, jaundice, blood disorders, and skin diseases. (18)
With one *picu* each of triphalā, trikaṭu, the two types of kaṇṭakārī, kaṭukā, kumbha, nikumbha, rājavṛkṣa, vacā, ativiṣā, agnika, and pāṭhā, along with a handful of fresh vajra-milk; 19.

One *prastha* of ghee prepared with these ground ingredients acts as an unctuous purgative for those with a hard bowel; it destroys difficult cases of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), vitiligo (*śvitra*), splenic enlargement, hernia, urinary calculi, and abdominal tumors. This is known as Mahāvajraka. (20)

Having boiled one āḍhaka of dantī in a droṇa of water, one should cook ghee with that decoction; when one pala of dhāmārgava is added and drunk, it effects purification from both the upper and lower tracts. (21)
One should boil one *droṇa* of *āvartakī* until it is reduced to one-eighth;
then, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee in that decoction along with its roots. (22)

Having drunk that [mixture], one should eat unrefined *kodrava* grain with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) once it has been well digested after an interval of one day—one who desires to conquer leprosy, vitiligo, and scrofulous swellings, and who desires abundant progeny, a retentive memory, and mindfulness. (23)
19.23b–c. An ascetic should eat *lelītaka* fat prepared with *kodrava* grain and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), combined with honey and the juice of *jātī*.
Or, it may be taken with equal parts of ghee, along with *asanā* water and the *gāyatrī* mantra, as a cure for leprosy. 19.24.
Rice, barley, wheat, koradūṣa, and priyaṅgu;
mung beans, lentils, tubarī, bitter vegetables, and meat from wild animals. (25)
Wine blended with varā, paṭola, khadira, nimba, and aruṣkara, containing medicinal ingredients within, as well as buttermilk mixed with indurājī, [should be administered]. (26)
Food and drink that are beneficial for leprosy (kuṣṭha) should be consumed, but one must strictly avoid sour, salty, and pungent items;
furthermore, one should especially renounce curd, milk, molasses, products from marshy regions, sesame, and black gram.
Patola root, triphalā, and viśālā—each in three parts reduced by one-third; trāyamāṇā and kaṭurohiṇī in half-parts, combined with a quarter-part of nāgara. (28)
This powder, one pala in weight, should be soaked until it becomes soft and then boiled in water; one should drink it for the purification of the bodily humors (*doṣas*).
Once it has been digested, one should eat old *śāli* rice with the meat broths of wild animals and birds. (29)

This formulation destroys leprosy, vitiligo, disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, difficult urination, and jaundice within six nights; it also cures pain in the heart and bladder, as well as irregular fevers. (30)

19.30c–31. By means of this six-night regimen, one who has conquered his self, using three *pala* each of the essence of *viḍaṅga*, *āmalaka*, and *abhayā*, along with twelve *māṣa* of jaggery from a jar, destroys [diseases] within a month.

It is said that the Yakṣa Māṇibhadra taught this proven formula to the mendicant Mumukṣu for [the cure of] leprosy, vitiligo, asthma, cough, abdominal disease, hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, splenic enlargement, tumors, pain, parasites, and abdominal masses—[thereby] saving the life of the monk. (32)
Bhūnimba, nimba, triphalā, padmaka, ativiṣā, kaṇā, mūrvā, paṭolī, the two types of niśā (haridrā and dāruharidrā), pāṭhā, tiktā, and indravāruṇī. // 33 //
Equal parts of kaliṅga and vacā, with each subsequent ingredient doubled in quantity, one should lick as a powder—consisting of dantī, trivṛt, and brāhmī—with honey and ghee. (34)

This is the supreme medicine for skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (meha), and numbness (prasupti); alternatively, one should lick a paste of triphalā, viḍaṅga, and pippalī with oil, clarified butter, and honey. (35)

The decoction of *vṛkṣaka*, taken with a paste of *kākodumbarikā*, *vella*, *nimba*, *abda*, and *vyoṣa*, destroys all skin diseases when drunk by those afflicted with leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and urinary disorders (*meha*). (19.35–36)
After drinking a decoction of *kuṭaja*,
*agni*, *nimba*, *nṛpataru*, *khadira*, *āsana*, and *saptaparṇa*,
one should consume *abhayā* (chebulic myrobalan) prepared with honey and ghee to destroy all skin diseases and leprosy.
A decoction of the bark of *dārvī*, *khadira*, and *nimba* is a destroyer of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). // 37½ //

A decoction prepared from niśottamā, nimba, paṭola root, tiktā, vacā, and red yaṣṭikā, when well-administered, eradicates kapha, pitta, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha), just as the heat of summer destroys [the cold]. // 38 //
Ghee boiled with these very medicinal herbs as an internal tonic overcomes Māruta-kuṣṭha;
one should likewise prepare [medicines] from khadira, nimba, guḍūcī, devadāru, and rajanī separately.
With pāṭhā, dārvī, vahni, ghuṇeṣṭā, and kaṭukā. // 40a //
Or urine mixed with Śakrayavas, or warm water. // 40b //
A leper who drinks [this] for a month shall be free from disease, as shall one suffering from hemorrhoids. 40c.
One who has urinary disorders, swelling, jaundice, consumption, and worms. // 40d //
Lac, danti, sweet juice, vara, dvipi, patha, and vidanga— // 41a //
Lākṣā, dantī, madhurasa, varā, dvīpī,
pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, pratyakpuṣpī, the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), rajanī, saptaparṇa, and āṭarūṣa.
19.41b–c A powder made from *pratyakpuṣpī*, the three pungents (*tri-kaṭu*), turmeric (*rajanī*), *saptaparṇa*, *āṭarūṣa*, *raktā*, *nimba*, *surataru*, and the two types of *pañcamūla*.
Having drunk it for a month while consuming wholesome food, one conquers leprosy with cow's urine.

Nigella sativa, Pippali, ginger, Vella, and Saurashtra salt, heated with fire and increased in quantity in successive order, when made into pills and drunk with cow’s urine, likewise destroy even the most dreadful forms of leprosy. 42.

This pill, prepared from the three pungents, *uttamā*, sesame, *aruṣkara*, clarified butter, honey, and white sugar, is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*) that conquers skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), acts as an aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*), and consists of seven ingredients. (43)

This pill is a rejuvenative (rasāyana); it is cooling for the mind and heart, aphrodisiac, and effective against skin diseases (kuṣṭha) when taken for seven days. [It is prepared] with candraśakala, agni, rajanī, viḍaṅga, tubarāsthī, aruṣkara, and triphalā.
These pills, prepared with one part jaggery, destroy all types of skin diseases when used habitually.
A bolus made from viḍaṅga, bhallātaka, vākucī, dvīpī, vārāhī, harītakī, lāṅgalī, black sesame, and upakulyā, combined with jaggery, destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha). // 45 //

Śaśāṅkalekhā, taken as a linctus with the pith of viḍaṅga, long pepper, the root of agni (hutāśa), black salt (sāyomala), āmalaka, and oil, destroys even the most difficult skin diseases (kuṣṭha). (46)
A bolus made of *śaśāṅkalekhā* with the roots of *viḍaṅga*, along with *pathyā*, sesame, jaggery, and *aruṣkara*, overcomes *kuṣṭha*; or alternatively,
one prepared with jaggery, *aruṣkara*, *jantughna*, and *somarājī*.

One who eats sparingly and wholesome food should consume the powder of *khadira* wood mixed with *viḍaṅga*, mountain-resin (*adrijatu*), honey, and clarified butter; this destroys *kiṭibha*, vitiligo, and ringworm. (48)
One who licks a mixture of sugar, oil, kṛmighna, dhātrī, iron rust, and pippalī overcomes all types of skin diseases, even those that are extremely severe. (49)
Musta, vyoṣa, triphalā, mañjiṣṭhā, dāru, the two pañcamūlas, the bark of saptacchada and nimba, viśālā, citraka, and mūrvā. (50)
This powder, combined with nine parts of *tarpaṇa* and a portion of honey, should be consumed daily as a habitual regimen; it destroys *kuṣṭha*. (51)
It destroys swelling, anemia, leucoderma, disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, scrotal enlargement, fistula-in-ano, pustules, itching, urticaria, and apacī. (52)

Through the application of elixirs (rasāyana), one should practice with the tubers and bones [of the aforementioned plants], as well as *bhallātaka*, *vākucikā*, the root of *vahni*, and the substance called *śilā*. (53)
Thus, when the internal doshas have been conquered and reside in the skin, pacifying treatments such as external pastes are beneficial;
for leprosy (kuṣṭha) that has been provoked by a strong paste increases further in a body that remains impure.
For chronic and hard ringworm lesions, fomentation with poultices is beneficial;
once the raised patches have been sweated and softened, they should be scraped with instruments and then treated with medicinal plasters.

In those cases of leprosy (kuṣṭha) which resist surgical instruments and destroy the sense of touch, an alkaline solution (kṣāra) should be applied after first draining the blood and the morbid humors (doṣa). 56.

In cases of thick, rough, dormant, stable, or chronic leprosy (kuṣṭha), as well as for one whose disease has been suppressed by other remedies, an ointment should be prepared with poisons accompanied by mantras, followed by anti-poisonous (agada) treatments. 57.
19.57–58. Kuṣṭhas that are numbed by poisons, or rendered numb by mantras and medicinal decoctions, and which lack perspiration and itching,
should be rubbed with dried cow dung, foam, or instruments, and then an ointment should be applied.
Mustā, triphalā, madana, karañja, āragvadha, kaliṅgayava, saptāhvā, kuṣṭha, phalinī, dārvī, and siddhārthaka constitute the bath [mixture]. (59)
This decoction acts as an emetic, a purgative, a cosmetic, and likewise a rub;
it overcomes skin disorders, leprosy, and swelling, and destroys jaundice. // 60 //
A decoction of the roots of karavīra, nimba, kuṭaja, śamyāka, and citraka, prepared until it coats the ladle, destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) when applied as an ointment with urine. (61)
A proven ointment consisting of the root of white karavīra, the fruit of kuṭaja and karañja, the bark of dārvī, and the young shoots of sumana, removes skin diseases (kuṣṭha). // 62 //
The bark of śirīṣa, the flower of kārpāsī, the leaves of rājavṛkṣa, and ground kākamācī—this fourfold ointment destroys kuṣṭha. // 63 //

A superior ointment for removing vitiligo and skin diseases consists of vyoṣa, mustard, niśā, soot, barley awn, salt, citraka, and kuṣṭha; these are made into pills the size of a jujube fruit, with one part of poison added. (64)

One should prepare equal quantities of the powders of nimba, the two types of haridrā, surasa, paṭola, kuṣṭha, aśvagandhā, suradāru, śigru, along with sarṣapa, tumburu, dhānyaka, vanya, and caṇḍā. // 65 //
One should first endeavor to rub the body, which has been anointed with oil, with these [herbs] ground with buttermilk;
thus his itching, pustules, urticaria, skin diseases, and swellings will be pacified. (66)
By this [application], his itching, pustules, and urticarial patches [are cured].
Mustā, amṛtā, saṅga, kaṭaṅkaṭerī, kāsīsa, kampillaka, kuṣṭha, lodhra, gandhopala, sarjarasa, viḍaṅga, manaḥśilā, āla, and the bark of karavīraka [are used].
One should apply these powders for the purpose of dusting over a body smeared with oil;
thus, ringworm accompanied by itching, kiṭibha, scabies, and eczema do not exist.
A paste made from mustard seeds cooked over a fire of chaff, when applied to the cheeks, destroys scabies just as a surge of passion overcomes shame. (69)
Realgar, orpiment, black pepper, oil, and the milk of the *arka* plant constitute an ointment that removes leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
Likewise, the seeds of *karañja* and *prapunāṭa*, ground together with cow’s urine, cure leprosy when applied as a paste. (70)
With guggulu, marica, viḍaṅga, sarṣapa, kāsīsa, sarjarasa, musta, śrīveṣṭa, kālagandha, manaḥśilā, kuṣṭha, and kampilla; (71)
With these, combined with both types of *haridrā* and mixed with oil from a wheelwright’s shop, and heated by the rays of the sun, leprosy—whether rubbed or internal—is destroyed. (72)
Black pepper, *tamāla* leaf, costus, realgar, and *kāsīsa*, mixed with oil and kept in a copper vessel for seven days; 73.
For one who resorts to heat, even a white leprosy (sidhma) that is not smeared with [medicines] departs within seven days;
for one who is pure and abstains from bathing, fresh vitiligo (kilāsa) disappears after nine months.
Jyotiṣmatī oil prepared in alkaline water from peacock feathers, strained seven times, destroys sidhma when used for massage. (75)
A paste made from the root of *vāyasajaṅghā*, the leaves of *vamani*, and the seed of radish, applied with buttermilk on a Saturday, is a proven remedy for removing *sidhma* (vitiligo). // 76 //
Jīvantī, mañjiṣṭhā, dārvī, kampillaka, milk, and tuttha—this is the preparation for cooking ghee and oil; once it is perfected, resin (sarjarasa) is added to the finished product.
It should be applied together with beeswax; by this, cracked feet (vipādikā) are indeed destroyed when anointed.
Leucoderma, ringworm, kiṭibha, leprosy, and alasaka are all pacified.
The root of *saptāhva*, the bark of *śirīṣa*, *aśvamāra*, *arka*, *mālatī*, *citraka*, *āsphota*, and *nimba*;
the seeds of *kārañja*, mustard, *prāpuṇāṭa*, *śreṣṭhā*, *jantughna*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and the two types of *haridrā*. (79)

Oil prepared with these [drugs] along with urine is called Vajraka; when used as an ointment, it is equal to a thunderbolt (vajra) in its power to destroy skin diseases, malignant sinus ulcers, and disorders arising from phlegm and wind. (80)
Eraṇḍa, tārkṣya, ghana, nīpa, kadamba, and bhārgī. // 81a //
—along with kampilla, vella, phalinī, and suravāruṇī. // 81b //
Nirguṇḍī, aruṣkara, surāhva, and suvarṇadugdhā. // 81c //
—With śrīveṣṭa, guggulu, śilā, paṭu, tāla, and viśva. // 81d //
Oil prepared with equal parts of snuhī and arka milks is known as Mahāvajra;
it possesses qualities exceeding those of Vajraka and destroys vitiligo, hemorrhoids, tumors, and cervical warts. (82)
Oil prepared with kuṣṭha, aśvamāra, bhṛṅga, arka, urine, snuhī milk, and rock salt, when administered as an ointment, destroys poison and is supreme for conquering skin diseases (kuṣṭha). 83.
A bitter oil prepared with beeswax, vermilion, borax, blue vitriol, and the product of *tārkṣya* quickly eradicates scabies and eczema. (84)

19.84b–d: Kaṭutaila (pungent oil), along with haritāla, tutthaka, and tārkṣyaka, quickly subdues pāmā and vicarcikā. Lākṣā, vyoṣa, prāpuṇāṭa, its seeds, śrīveṣṭa, kuṣṭha, and siddhārthaka [are used for this purpose].
A plaster of turmeric mixed with *takra* (buttermilk) is prescribed for ringworm, as is the seed derived from radish.
Citraka, śobhāñjanaka, guḍūcī, apāmārga, devadāru, khadira, dhava, śyāmā, dantī, and dravantī constitute a medicinal paste. 86.

Lac, rasāñjana, cardamom, and punarnavā—these six, applied as ointments with curd-whey in one-quarter parts each, are said to destroy wind and phlegm in those afflicted by skin diseases (kuṣṭha). // 87 //

Water-lily, blue lotus, iron-filamented lotus, leaf-lotus, floating lotus, sandalwood, and lotus-stalks—these, taken in successively increasing proportions, form a prepared ointment for skin diseases caused by Pitta and Kapha. (88)
For burning kuṣṭha lesions, anointment should be performed with bitter ghee or washed ghee, as well as with oils combined with sandalwood, madhuka, prapauṇḍarīka, and utpala. (89)
When the limbs fall off, or when there is burning, eruptive boils, or sloughing of the skin, cold plasters and affusions, bloodletting, purgation, and bitter ghee [are indicated]. (90)
Khadira, vṛṣa, nimba, kuṭaja, śreṣṭhā, kṛmijit, paṭola, and madhuparṇī—when used both internally and externally with cow's urine, they destroy worms and skin diseases. (91)
Water boiled with Khadira wood, when habitually used for the acts of anointing, massaging, bathing, drinking, and eating, destroys all skin diseases. (91+1)
In cases of kuṣṭha where vāta is predominant, ghee should be administered; where kapha is predominant, emesis;
and where pitta is predominant, bloodletting and purgation should be performed first.
Purgation is the foremost treatment for blood disorders;
those medicinal pastes which are prescribed for skin diseases (kuṣṭha) become immediately effective when the blood and morbid humors have been removed and the internal cavities have been purified.

When the humors have been removed, when the blood has been extracted, when both external and internal pacification has been performed, and when oleation is applied at the proper time, curable leprosy does not persist. (94)

A leper with many morbid humors (doṣas) should be purified repeatedly while carefully protecting his life; for if the humors are removed in excessive measure, the wind (vāyu), finding the patient weak, may quickly destroy him. (95)

One should undergo emetics every fortnight, and purgatives below [the navel] every month; purification occurs at the crown of the head every three nights, and bloodletting should be performed every sixth month. (96)
Every sixth month, bloodletting should be performed for one who has vomited poorly or whose purgation was inadequate.
This leper is pervaded by the provoked humors. // 97b //
Thus, without doubt, it reaches a state of being truly incurable. 97c
Therefore, one should eliminate all of his faults. // 97d //
Diligence in vows, self-restraint, discipline, service, renunciation, and virtuous conduct. // 98a //
Worship of the twice-born, the gods, and the preceptors; loving-kindness toward all sentient beings. // 98b //
The propitiations of Śiva, the Son of Śiva (Śaṅkara), Tārā, and the Sun. // 98c //
The propitiation of the Jinas, the sons of the Jinas, Tārā, and the Sun removes leprosy by manifesting and uprooting impure sins.
The treatment for vitiligo (śvitra) is even more loathsome than that for leprosy (kuṣṭha), and it proceeds much more rapidly toward incurability;
therefore, one should strive to pacify it as if a house were on fire. //1//
One should specifically employ purification therapies for the body even before [the application of other treatments];
for vitiligo, the juice of *malayū* mixed with jaggery is considered the foremost emetic.

Having drunk that and having anointed one's body, one should, according to one's strength, expose oneself to the heat of the sun's rays; once the body has been purged, one should drink *peyā* (gruel) for three days whenever thirst arises. // 3 //
One should prick with a thorn those pustules that arise on a limb afflicted with vitiligo;
once the pus has flowed out from the pustules, one should drink [the medicine] every morning for three days. // 4 //
Every morning for a fortnight, one should drink a decoction of *malayū*, *asanā*, *priyaṅgu*, and *śatapuṣpā* boiled with water;
or, according to one's strength, the alkali of the *palāśa* tree mixed with treacle.

Having drunk a paste of *indurājikā* with a decoction of the bark of the *phalgv-akṣa* tree, when eruptions have appeared while remaining in a warm place, one's meal should consist of buttermilk (*takra*) without salt. // 6 //

Cow’s urine combined with *citraka* and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), placed in a jar of clarified butter and mixed with honey, should be drunk by one afflicted with vitiligo after a fortnight; furthermore, the regimen prescribed for skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) should be followed for him. (7)
After a fortnight, those afflicted with vitiligo should drink this *mārkaṇḍa* [juice]; or else, one should taste it roasted in oil and kept in an iron vessel.
Thereafter, for the destruction of vitiligo, one should drink milk boiled with *bījaka*. (8)
The tender leaves of *pūtīkārkī*, *vyādhighāta*, and *snuhī*, ground with urine, when applied as a plaster, destroy vitiligo, scabies, ringworm, itch, boils, and malignant sinus ulcers. (9)
An ointment made from burnt leather of an island-dwelling animal or of an elephant, combined with oil, is excellent for leucoderma;
even a single stinking insect, when smeared with the alkali produced from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, destroys leucoderma.
20.10d–11. One [ingredient], when smeared with alkali, destroys white leprosy (*śvitra*) alone.
At night, one should soak crushed parts [of plants] in cow urine; during the day, one should dry them in the shade until they form blisters.
Having done this for three days, one should then grind them finely and apply a paste with the milk of *snuhī* to destroy white leprosy.
An ointment consisting of the soot produced from a black cobra, melted with oil of *akṣa*, or likewise *hrīvera* burnt together and soaked in peacock bile [is used]. 12.

20.12 A plaster made with *akṣa* oil, melted with a *kuḍava* of *avalguja* seeds mixed with a fourth part of yellow orpiment and ground with cow urine, is the best for restoring the natural color to vitiligo.

When the alkali produced from well-burnt elephant dung has been strained with elephant urine, one should add the seeds of *avalguja* in a proportion of one-tenth to a measure of one *droṇa*, and cook them together. (14)

When alkali or elephant dung-ash has been well-burnt and filtered in elephant urine, one should repeatedly apply it after rubbing the area until it reaches a smooth consistency; by this means, one may conquer vitiligo (*śvitra*), or *kuṣṭha*, *maṣa*, or *tilakālaka*, or whatever excess flesh (*adhimāṃsa*) may have grown upon a wound. (20.14–15)

Having cooked together bhallātaka, the roots of dvīpī, sudhārka, and guñjā fruit, the powder of the three pungents (try-ūṣaṇa) and conch shell, tuttha along with kuṣṭha, the five salts, the two alkalis (kṣāra), and lāṅgalikā; // 16 //

The powder of *bhallātaka*, the root of *dvīpisudhārka*, *guñjā* fruit, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and conch shell, made thick with the milks of *snuh* and *arka* and placed in an iron vessel— this one should apply as an ointment using a probe.
In cases of leprosy, vitiligo, black moles, freckles, hemorrhoids, and warts; 17.
For some whose sins have been exhausted, vitiligo is pacified through purification, bloodletting, drying treatments, and the consumption of parched grain flour. (18)

When the abdomen containing worms has been lubricated and fomented with jaggery, milk, fish, and other such substances, and the worms and phlegm have been provoked, the patient should be made to rest comfortably for that night. (19)
Having boiled the *surasādi* group of drugs in urine until it is reduced to half its volume,
one should add a paste of *kaṇā*, *gāla*, and *kṛmijit* to that decoction.
On that same day, one should administer an oil enema containing *svarjikā* alkali; once he has been cleared by that [non-unctuous enema], one should have him drink a purgative.
Then, one should administer a paste of trivṛt stirred with a decoction of madanaphala and pippalī,
combined with pañcakola, once the body has been purified through both upward and downward channels.
One should perform affusions with decoctions of pungent, bitter, and astringent substances;
then, at the appropriate time, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) using Viḍaṅga oil.

One should sprinkle [the head] with decoctions (kaṣāya) and follow the procedures prescribed for the treatment of diseases of the head. For disorders located in the head, one should consume food that is excessively bitter and pungent, and contains little oil. // 24 //
One should feed [the patient] food with little fat,
prepared with viḍaṅga, kṛṣṇā, marica, pippalīmūla, and śigru;
he should drink gruel boiled with buttermilk and mixed with svarjikākṣāra.
One should drink the juice of śirīṣa, kiṇihī, pāribhadraka, and kembuka together with viḍaṅga, kṛṣṇā, madhuka, and svarjikā-kṣāra;
or one may drink the juice of palāśa seeds, pattūra, and pūtika separately.
Or one should lick the drugs beginning with *surasā* (Surasādi group) mixed with honey, each separately combined with honey;
or horse dung powder, processed a hundred times with a decoction of *viḍaṅga*. (27)

One suffering from worms should lick [the powder] with honey, or it may be processed with the juices of *varā*; when worms have migrated to the head, that same powder should be used as a nasal insufflation (*pradhamana*). (28)
One should eat a cake made from well-ground sprouts of *ākhukarṇī* mixed with flour, having cooked it, and afterwards drink sour gruel (*dhānyāmla*). // 29 //
20.29 Or one may take the tender shoots of *ākhuparṇī* with the five spices (*pañcakola*) and salt, along with thin buttermilk;
this same procedure applies to the sprouts of *nīpa*, *mārkava*, and *nirguṇḍī*.
20.30 Or one should prepare foodstuffs mixed with the ground powders of nimba, apāmārga, nirguṇḍī, and viḍaṅga;
or [food] combined with half-parts of viḍaṅga seeds, kept in the sun. // 31 //
One should administer Āruṣkara oil— prepared with one part [of the drug] for every half-part [of the base oil] and heated in the sun— for drinking and for enema (vasti).
One should likewise prepare the oils of Devadāru and Sarala in the same manner, separately.
In cases arising from feces, one should especially administer enemas and purgatives;
in those born of phlegm, one should employ head-purgation, emesis, and palliative treatments. (33)

One should apply the remedies for blood-born diseases according to the treatment for skin disorders (kuṣṭha), and the procedure for Indra-lupta should also be employed here for those cases where the hair is being consumed.
One who desires to be free from worms should, in brief, avoid milks, meats, ghee, molasses, curds, and leafy vegetables, as well as sour and sweet flavors. (35)
In the section on therapeutics, one should first treat a person with unobstructed [vāta] using oleation therapies;
subsequently, one should treat that person by administering internal potions of ghee, muscle fat, marrow, and oil. (1)
Having comforted the patient exhausted by the oleation therapy with milk, one should oleate them again with soups or with the meat-broths of domestic, aquatic, or marshy animals, combined with fats.
Then, one should apply sudation with milk-porridges, rice-and-pulse mixtures seasoned with sour and salty substances, along with enemas, nasal drops, nourishing foods, and well-oleated meals.
The limb, repeatedly anointed with substances such as *śaṅkara* mixed with fats, and having been massaged with oil and fomented, is then bent, stiffened, and accompanied by pain. (4)
21.4cv Once a limb has been lubricated with oil and fomented, it can indeed be easily bent according to one's will;
for even dry pieces of wood [can be bent] by the application of oil and fomentation. // 5 //
21.5dv By means of oleation, sudation, and poultices, it is possible to bring even the limbs of the living to a state of functional flexibility; how much more so [the body as a whole]?
[For these treatments counteract] exhilaration, piercing pain, distressing pain, stretching, swelling, stiffness, and rigidity.
When applied quickly, it pacifies the heat of one who has undergone sudation, induces softness, and nourishes the dried-up tissues with its oiliness. (7)
When administered promptly, it quickly nourishes his strength,
digestive fire, physical vigor, and vital breaths; furthermore, one should repeatedly treat him with oleation and sudation therapies.

21.8b–v And one should further increase his vital energy (prāṇa); thus, in a digestive tract softened by oleation, wind-related diseases do not persist. If, however, due to the presence of morbid humors (doṣas), he is not relieved by this procedure, [then other measures should be taken]. // 9 //
One should purify that [patient] with mild medicines combined with unctuous substances, or with ghee prepared with *tilvaka*, or indeed with ghee prepared with *sātalā*. (10)
One should drink either milk or castor oil, which are auspicious and remove the humors;
for the impurities have accumulated through foods that are unctuous, sour, salty, and hot. (11)
By obstructing the channels, one should block the wind; therefore, one should cause it to move in its natural direction.
One who is weak and unfit for purgation should be treated with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha). 12.
By obstructing the channels, one should arrest the wind (vāyu) in a person through digestive stimulants (dīpana), carminatives (pācanīya), or foods combined with those;
once the person has been thoroughly purified and the digestive fire (agni) has been rekindled, oleation (sneha) and sudation (sveda) are again beneficial. // 13 //
When the wind has reached the stomach, one who has vomited and been readmitted to food should administer the *vacā* group of drugs weighing six *dharaṇas* with lukewarm water. (14)

Enema therapy (vasti-karma) below the navel and the pressed-in enema (avapīḍaka) are recommended; furthermore, alkalis, powders, and similar substances that are digestive and appetizing are beneficial when located in the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha). // 16 //

When [the disease] is located in the heart, milk boiled with *sthirā* should be used as a head-enema (*śirovasti*); when it has reached the head, unctuous nasal drops (*nāvana*), medicinal smoke (*dhūma*), and the satiation of the ears and other sense organs should be employed. (17)
For [fever] localized in the skin, one should employ sudation, oil massage, avoidance of wind, and pleasant food;
for that located in the blood, cold poultices, purgation, and bloodletting are indicated. (18)

Sudation and oil massages are recommended when the disease resides in the muscle and fat; purgation, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), and palliative measures are indicated when it resides in the bone; one should conquer the disease located in the marrow by means of unctuous therapies both externally and internally. (21.18–19)
When semen is located there, exhilaration and food that increase strength and semen are beneficial;
however, seeing that the path is obstructed, one should administer a purgative. (20)

21.20b–d. It is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and beneficial when consumed after a purgation; one should perform the previously mentioned treatment for those whose fetus has been dried up by Vāta, as well as for children who are becoming emaciated.
For one who has vomited and then eaten, milk prepared with sugar, *kāśmarya*, and *madhuka* is used for restoration;
if [the poison] has reached the ligaments, joints, or vessels, oleation, fomentation, and poultices should be applied.
In the case of contraction, an oil massage with oil prepared from māṣa and rock salt is indicated;
when blood has flowed out, an ointment consisting of soot, salt, and oil should be applied.
When a limb is numb and constricted, a poultice (upanāhana) should be applied;
likewise for one afflicted by apatānaka who does not have drooping eyes or trembling. (24)
One should treat that patient with haste whose penis is not stiff, who does not perspire, who is free from external extension, and who has not struck his buttocks against the bed. (25)
In that case, once the limbs have first been well-anointed and fomented,
one should administer a sharp nasal medication (nasya) for the purification of the channels, followed by the drinking of clear ghee.
If it is boiled with the decoction, curd, milk, and meat-broth of the Vidāryādi group, the Vāyu will not pervade excessively, nor will it suddenly spread. (27)

Having boiled a decoction of kulattha, barley, and kola, along with the group of drugs beginning with bhadradāru, as well as the meat of marshy animals, one should [prepare it] with sour liquids and even with milk. (28)
One should cook a great quantity of oil with a sweet infusion as an additive;
it may be used for sprinkling, massage, immersion baths, food, drinks, nasal medication, and oil enemas. (29)
It destroys the wind, as do those various applications of oleation and sudation when properly administered; furthermore, between the intervals of the urges, one should repeatedly purge his head.
When the breaths have been released through compressions, sharp blowpipes, and phlegm-destroying treatments, he likewise regains consciousness. (31)
Ghee prepared with sauvarcala salt, abhayā, and vyoṣa is indicated when vāta is predominant.
Having boiled eight *palas* of *tilvaka*, one *prastha* of *varā* (one *pala* each), and the five roots of *guru* along with *eraṇḍa*,
*siṃhī*, and *trivṛt* in a jar of water, one should cook [the medicine] with that decoction reduced to one-quarter.

A prastha of ghee prepared with curd, barley-alkali, and three bilva fruits, when consumed, destroys corrupted vātas located in a single part or throughout the entire body, as well as disorders of the female reproductive tract, gulma, enlargement of the spleen, and abdominal dropsy. (33)

The procedure for *dadhnas* (sour milk) in a vessel containing barley-gruel and three *bilva* fruits should be understood to be like that for *tilvaka*; it is also [applicable] for *ramyaka* and *aśoka*.

21.34b–c This same treatment should also be applied for Śamyāka and Ākāśoka, as well as in pure Vāta-apatānaka. In cases of combined doṣas, one should administer a combined powder; in those associated with Kapha, a powder [of the respective drugs]. 21.35d–36a [The physician] should give it mixed with honey, ghee, or meat broth, according to the patient's strength. It cures apatānaka, ardita, and all diseases arising from Vāta. 21.36b–c This powder, known as *Vātaśūla-nibarhaṇa*, destroys the pain of Vāta and is beneficial for all types of Vāta disorders. 21.36d–37a One should prepare a powder from these very same drugs, excluding the *Śamyāka* and *Ākāśoka*. 21.37b–c This is called *Sarvavātaghna-cūrṇa*; it is the best among powders for destroying Vāta. 21.37d–38a One should take one part each of *śuṇṭhī*, *pippalī*, *yavakṣāra*, and *sauvarcala-lavaṇa*. 21.38b–c Two parts of *hiṅgu*, three parts of *viḍa-lavaṇa*, and four parts of *rāmaṭha*. 21.38d–39a Five parts of *citraka*, six parts of *ajamodā*, and seven parts of *bhārgī*. 21.39b–c Eight parts of *gaurasarṣapa*, nine parts of *śatapuṣpā*, and ten parts of *śatāhvā*. 21.39d–40a Eleven parts of *pippalīmūla*, twelve parts of *yavānī*, and thirteen parts of *ajagandhā*. 21.40b–c Fourteen parts of *hapuṣā*, fifteen parts of *balā*, and sixteen parts of *vacā*. 21.40d–41a Seventeen parts of *elā*, eighteen parts of *kuṣṭha*, and nineteen parts of *vyoṣa*. 21.41b–c Twenty parts of *musta*, twenty-one parts of *tālīśapatra*, and twenty-two parts of *tvac*. 21.41d–42a Twenty-three parts of *pāṭhā*, twenty-four parts of *abhayā*, and twenty-five parts of *cavya*. 21.42b–c Twenty-six parts of *jīraka*, twenty-seven parts of *māgadhyāḥ*, and twenty-eight parts of *dhānyaka*. 21.42d–43a Twenty-nine parts of *marica*, thirty parts of *śarkarā*, and thirty-one parts of *guggulu*. 21.43b–c This powder, known as *Triṃśacchata*, is the best among powders for Tumburu, abhayā, hiṅgu, pauṣkara, and the three salts should be drunk with water decocted from barley in cases of pain in the heart and flanks, and in apatantraka.
One should drink asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, dry ginger, pomegranate, and sour vetasa;
or that which is prescribed for kapha, vāta, and heart disease is also recommended. (37)
The treatment for the two types of facial paralysis, external and internal, is like that for Ardita;
there is also lying in a vat of oil. Among these, the internal type is very difficult to cure. (38)
One whose teeth and face have changed color, whose limbs are limp, whose consciousness is lost, who perspires, and who is paralyzed by the bow, does not live for ten nights. (39)
One who perspires and suffers from rigidity of the bow (dhanuḥ-stambha) during the [acute] stages will live;
otherwise, if the stages are mild, he will survive but be hunched, dull-witted, lame, withered,
paralyzed on one side, crippled, or deformed.

21.40d–41. Even if a person is lame or maimed, in the case of a dislocation of the jaw (hanu-sraṃsa), the skilled physician should apply oil and fomentation to the jaws and restore them to their natural position; he should also elevate the chin by opening the mouth wide.
One should bend [the body] while remaining in a secluded place; the rest should be performed as in the case of *ekāyāma*.
In the case of tongue-stiffness (*jihvā-stambha*), treatment for wind disorders (*vāta-cikitsita*) should be applied according to the specific condition. (42)
In the case of speech-seizure (vāg-graha), a person should drink warm water with *vetasāmla*, or likewise the juice of *mātuluṅga* combined with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and *sauvarcala* salt. 42+1.
In Ardita (facial paralysis), nasal drops, head oil, and the filling of the ears and eyes with oil are indicated;
if swelling is present, emesis is prescribed, and if accompanied by burning and redness, venesection should be performed. (43)
A man should eat a bean-cake combined with fresh butter;
it destroys even an irresistible facial paralysis within seven days—of this there is no doubt. (43+1)
In hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta), oleation therapy combined with unctuous substances is beneficial, as is purgation;
for the paralyzed arm, nasal medication (nasya) and unctuous substances taken after meals are recommended.
A lukewarm decoction of māṣa, balā, śuka-śimbī, kaṭtṛṇa, rāsnā, aśvagandhā, and urubūka, mixed with asafoetida and salt, should be administered as a nasal drop or drunk. (44.1+1)
It removes the wind-disorder of the flanks, stiffness of the neck, and pain with ringing in the ears;
it certainly conquers even the most difficult-to-overcome facial paralysis within seven days. (44.1+2)
Gudamañjarī, khapura, and the root of vṛṣabhī, ground with cold water and employed in the procedure of nasal administration (nāvana), removes the pain of avabāhuka and throat ailments. 44+1.

Having eaten in the evening, one should drink a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), balā, and māṣa, mixed with oil and ghee; this should also be used as a nasal drop (nasya) in cases of viśvācī and avabāhuka.
In the case of thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha), neither oleation nor purification is beneficial;
because of the abundance of phlegm, undigested matter, and fat, one should therefore employ methods to diminish them through skillful means.

21.45ab In cases of thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha), one should not apply oleation; rather, dry treatment is indicated, such as barley, *śyāmāka* millet, and *kodrava* grain. These are recommended with salt-free vegetables, along with small amounts of oil and boiled water.

For those who drink honey, water, and *ariṣṭa*, one should administer the *vatsakādi*, *haridrādi*, or *vacādi* groups of drugs along with rock salt (*saindhava*), using the meat of wild animals (*jāṅgala*) prepared without ghee.
In cases of *āḍhya-vāta*, one should drink six *dharaṇas* with pleasant water; or alternatively, one should lick a paste made of *śreṣṭhā*, *cavya*, *tiktā*, *kaṇā*, and *ghana* with honey.
In cases of *āmavāta*, one should drink either the "six-footed" (*ṣaṭcaraṇa*) decoction with warm water, or else [the following]:
chavya, tikta, kaṇā, ghana, citraka, indrayava, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, ativiṣā, and niśā.
This practice called the Six Supports is a means for pacifying diseases of wind.
One should habitually consume a paste made from *cavya*, *pathyā*, *agni*, and *suradāru* with honey,
or one should regularly take *pathyā* and mountain-born *guggulu* with urines.
By consuming an equal amount of guggulu along with vyoṣa, agni, musta, triphalā, and viḍaṅga, one conquers all diseases arising from fat, phlegm, undigested matter, and wind. (50)
In this way, the wind (vāyu) that is overcome by phlegm (kapha) and accompanied by fat (medas) is indeed pacified;
[one should apply] sudations, affusions, and massages combined with alkali and urine. 51.
One should apply an ointment and perform a plastering with *karañja* fruits, mustard seeds, and cow’s urine; or likewise with the roots of *arka*, *tarkārī*, *nimba*, and *surāhva*.

For the purpose of reducing phlegm, one should employ this [diet] consisting of honey, mustard seeds, baked clods of earth, and anthill soil; and once physical exercise has become tolerable, one should engage in it.
One should cross over dry land, approach women according to one's ability,
and ford a river against the current only after ensuring the lake has still water and the crossing is safe.
In this condition, when phlegm and fat have diminished, one should administer oleation and other therapies;
furthermore, the remaining treatments should be applied after considering the location, the affected tissues (dūṣyas), and other factors. // 55 //
Having considered the location and the affected tissues (*dūṣya*),
the root of a large *nimba* tree ground with water, when drunk,
will quickly destroy even an incurable *gṛdhrasī*.
In the case of *vātakaṇṭaka*, one should perform bloodletting from the *tūṇī* and *pratūṇī* vessels; or one may apply a poultice of *lavana* with ghee, or *kṣāra* and *hiṅgu*, repeatedly. (55.1–2)
Or one should drink castor oil, or else cauterize [the area] with needles;
[the eyes] should be anointed with groats mixed with ghee, but not combined with milk.
Or, having smeared their feet with the bark of the śālmalī tree, intense heat arises.

One whose body and gait are afflicted by wind, drinking a decoction of *sahacara*, *suradāru*, and *nāgara* boiled in water and mixed with oil, attains a gait that is both swift and slow according to his desire. (56)
Having ground together rāsnā, mahauṣadha, dvīpī, pippalī, śaṭhī, and pauṣkara, one should cook ghee; this is a supreme remedy for diseases caused by vāta. (57)
One should boil ten palas each of nimba, amṛtā, vṛṣa, paṭola, and nidigdhikā separately in a jar of water until the liquid is reduced to one-eighth;
then, with that decoction, one should cook one prastha of ghee along with a paste consisting of one picu each of the [same] ingredients.
21.58 With nimba, amṛtā, vṛṣa, paṭola, karañjaka, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, suradāru, gajapippalī, upakulyā, the two types of kṣāra, nāgara, niśā, miśi,
cavya, kuṣṭha, tejovatī, marica, vatsaka, dīpyaka, agni, rohiṇī, aruṣkara, vacā, kaṇamūla, and yavānī; [these should be used].

Mañjiṣṭhā, ativiṣā, viṣā, and yavānī, along with five palas of purified guggulu—when this is consumed, it dispels even powerful vāta located in the joints, bones, and marrow, as well as such diseases as kuṣṭha. (60)
When consumed, it forcefully expels powerful wind (vāta) and cures diseases of the channels,
ulcers, tumors, fistula-in-ano, cervical lymphadenitis, all ailments above the clavicle, abdominal tumors,
urinary disorders arising from the rectum, consumption, loss of appetite, dyspnea, catarrh, cough, edema, heart disease, anemia, intoxication, abscesses, and gout (vātarakta).

Rāsnā, āṭarūṣa, suradāru, amṛtā, śatāvarī, eraṇḍa, puṣkaramūla, dhānyaka, śuṇṭhī, pathyā, along with gokṣura, śaileya, śaṭī, and ativiṣā—these, when boiled and administered, truly destroy heart disease, diseases of the flanks, intoxication, abscesses, and vātarakta, as well as all ailments born of vāta. One should cook the scum of ghee in milk boiled with *balā* and *bilva*;
one *śukti* or one *prakuñca* of this should be used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) when wind has reached the head. (62)
In the same way, fat derived from crocodiles, fish, tortoises, and *culūka* frogs is proven effective;
it should be applied especially when the wind alone is the predominant humor. (63)

One should boil old oil-cake and the five roots separately; then, with these two decoctions combined, one should cook oil along with eight parts of milk. By drinking this, wind disorders are destroyed, especially those associated with phlegm. (64)

One *prastha* of oil, equal in quantity to milk, should be cooked with a decoction of *prasāriṇī* weighing one *tulā*, along with two parts each of *medā*, *miśī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *kuṣṭha*, *rāsnā*, and *kucandana*. (65)
One should cook [this] with the pastes (kalka) of jīvaka, ṛṣabha, the pair of kākolī, and amaradāru; it destroys all diseases caused by vāta.
One should boil fifty palas of the combined *sahācarā* with its roots and branches, along with the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and *abhīru*, in water until one-quarter remains. (67)

In that [oil], one should use *sevya*, *nakha*, *kuṣṭha*, *hima*, *elā*, *spṛk*, *priyaṅgu*, *nalikā*, *ambu*, *śilājatu*, *lohitā*, *analada*, *loha*, *surāhva*, *kopanā*, *miśī*, *turuṣka*, and *nata*. (68)

An oil preparation of one *pātra* cooked with an equal amount of milk, when consumed regularly, overcomes difficult cases of Vāta disorders—including tremors, convulsions, stiffness, and wasting—as well as abdominal tumors (*gulma*), insanity (*unmāda*), chronic catarrh (*pīnasa*), and diseases of the female reproductive tract. (69)
One should cook one *āḍhaka* of oil with an equal amount of milk in the decoction of one *tulā* of *sahacara*, adding ten *palas* of the paste of its roots and four times as much milk. (21.69–70)
Alternatively, [one may prepare it] from nata, ṣaḍgranthā, sthirā, kuṣṭha, and surāhvaya, along with elā, nalada, śaileya, śatāhvā, and raktacandana. (71)

When this [oil] is prepared, one should add eighteen palas of sugar powder; this oil, esteemed by Bheda, cures difficult urinary disorders and diseases of Vāta. (21.71) [The ingredients are: sthirā, kuṣṭha, surāhvaya, śatāhvā, and raktacandana. (21.71bd) [The verse continues: ...śatāhvā-rakta-candanān. When this is cooked, one should add eighteen palas of powdered sugar.
That oil, approved by Bheda, [remedies] painful conditions and ailments of the wind. (72)

One should conquer disorders such as vātakuṇḍalikā, insanity, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids by using one hundred parts of balā and a quarter part of chinnaruhā, with rāsnā constituting one-eighth part. (73)

Having boiled [the ingredients] in one hundred āḍhakas of water until the liquid remains at one-hundredth part, one should add one āḍhaka of oil along with equal quantities of curd-whey, sugarcane juice, and fermented gruel. (74)
One should cook [the oil] with half a part of goat's milk and these paste-ingredients (kalkas) measured by one pala each: śaṭhī, sarala, dāru, elā, mañjiṣṭhā, aguru, and candana. (75)
With padmaka, atibalā, mustā, śūrpaparṇī, hareṇu, yaṣṭyāhvā, surasa, vyāghranakha, ṛṣabhaka, and jīvaka; // 76 //
With the juice of *palāśa*, musk, *nalikā*, and the heartwood of *jātī*;
with *spṛkkā*, saffron, *śaileya*, *jātī*, *kaṭuphala*, and water. // 77 //
With water from *jātī* and *kaṭphala*,
and with *tvak*, *kunduruka*, camphor, *turuṣka*, *śrīnivāsaka*,
*lavaṅga*, *nakha*, *kaṅkola*, *kuṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, and *priyaṅgu*.
When the decoction has been prepared with sthauṇeya, tagara, dhyāma, vacā, madanaka, plava,
and nāgakeśara, one should add [the powder] once it has been removed from the heat.
Then, that filtered leaf-paste, prepared according to the prescribed method with vacā, madana, and sprouts, when administered,
cures cough, dyspnea, fever, vomiting, fainting, abdominal tumors, chest wounds, and consumption. (21.79b–80)
This excellent Bala-oil destroys enlargement of the spleen, consumption, epilepsy, and misfortune; it is the foremost destroyer of diseases caused by Vata. (81)

When these unctuous substances are properly administered at the right time through drinking, nasal drops, enemas, and massage, they quickly pacify the vitiated *vātās* and cause barren women to bear sons. (82)
Barren women may be made to bear sons when the phlegm (śleṣman), having been liquefied by oleation and sudation, is situated in the colon (pakvāśaya);
or when the bile (pitta) manifests its symptoms, one should conquer that [condition] with enemas (vasti).

When [the blood] is located in the colon (pakvāśaya), one should repeatedly extract the blood from a patient suffering from vāta-śoṇita after they have been treated with oleation (snigdha). (Cikitsāsthāna 21.83b-v)
One should restrain the breath in very small measures, according to the specific disorder and one's own strength. // 1 //
One should extract [the blood] with leeches in cases of redness, swelling, piercing pain, and burning;
and with horns or gourds in cases accompanied by a tingling sensation, itching, pain, and aching. (2)
Or [blood] may be removed by means of hidden vessels as it moves from one part of the body to another;
however, blood should not be drawn when there is exhaustion of the limbs, nor when the condition is dry or dominated by Vāta. // 3 //
However, one should not perform bloodletting when there is witheredness of the limbs (22.3c), nor when the swelling is dry or dominated by Vāta (22.3d).
Due to the depletion of blood, the Vāyu would cause deep-seated swelling, stiffness, tremors, diseases of the tendons and vessels, exhaustion, and other disorders arising from Vāta. //4//
In vātarakta where vāta is predominant, one should first administer oleation and then purge with purgatives combined with fats; thereafter, one should cause the patient to drink aged ghee.
Ghee prepared with equal parts of śrāvaṇī, kṣīrakākolī, kṣīriṇī, jīvaka,
and ṛṣabhaka, along with milk, cures vātarakta.
Or one should drink ghee prepared with grape and madhūka decoctions along with sugar candy;
likewise, one may drink milk boiled in the fresh juice of guḍūcī.
Or one should cause [the patient] to drink oil, milk,
and sugar well-blended together with balā, śatāvarī, rāsnā, daśamūla, and pīlu.
Milk boiled with black castor (*śyāmairaṇḍa*) and *sthirā* destroys the affliction of Vāta;
milk that is warm from the udder, or mixed with urine, facilitates the downward movement of the bodily humors (*doṣa*). (9)
In the case of Pitta-type fever, one should boil śatāvarī, tikta, paṭola, triphalā, and amṛtā, and then drink either ghee or milk prepared with these sweet and bitter herbs. (10)
A person with an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas) should drink castor oil with milk for the purpose of purgation; once it has been digested, he should eat rice with milk. 11.
Or one should administer a decoction of *abhayā* fried in ghee;
or a powder of *trivṛt* with milk as an after-drink, or with grape juice. (12)
Or one should eliminate his impurity with enemas of milk mixed with ghee;
for indeed, there is no treatment for vātarakta equal to the enema. (13)
Specifically, in cases of pain in the anus, flanks, thighs, joints, bones, and the abdomen, one should drink a decoction of Musta, Dhātrī, and Haridrā when Kapha is predominant. (14)

One should cause the patient, who has been vomited after drinking an appropriate quantity of unctuous substance, to undergo mild drying therapy using musta, drākṣā, and haridrā with honey, or triphalā, or likewise guḍūcī. (22.14cd–15ab)
Or, according to one's strength, one may take *guḍūcī*.
[One may also take] *triphalā*, *vyoṣa*, *pattra*, *elā*, *tvakṣīrī*, *citraka*, *vacā*, *viḍaṅga*, *pippalīmūla*, *romaśā*, *vṛṣaka*, and *tvac*. (22.15b–16)
One should grind together equal parts of romasha, vrshaka, tvak, riddhi, langaliki, and chavya.
Having smeared an iron vessel with this in the early morning, one should consume it at midday.
In cases of vātāsra (hemorrhagic disorders), even when all the doṣas are involved and accompanied by severe pain,
a decoction of kokilākṣaka is highly beneficial when drunk while consuming its leaves as a vegetable.
When drunk by one who subsists on vegetables,
it subdues vāta-rakta just as the practice of compassion subdues anger;
[likewise,] *lelītakī* and fat [are taken] with the juices of the five roots (*pañcamūla*) or of *dhātrī*.
"Even if there is a small wound on the body, the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) shall conquer [the pain] by drinking [the juice];
thus the internal rite has been indicated, and after this follows the external one. (20)
Having boiled eight *pala*s of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) in one *āḍhaka* of water until one-fourth remains,
one should add sixteen *pala*s of purified *guggulu* to it.
Then, once that has solidified, one should add two karṣas each of harītakī and viḍaṅga, and one pala each of kaṭukā and guḍūcī, after making them into a paste.
One should consume Trivṛt and Dantī in the measure of one Karṣa, along with a desired after-drink;
this destroys even the various forms of Vātarakta, whether it is flowing, dried up, or cracked open. (20.1+3)
Having overcome wounds, cough, leprosy, abdominal tumors, swelling, dropsy, anemia, urinary disorders, and hemorrhoids, as well as the defects of old age, it makes the body youthful. (20.1+4)

One *āḍhaka* of fermented rice gruel (*āranāla*) cooked with a quarter-part of *sarjarasa* resin and a large quantity of water, when churned, is a supreme remedy for the pain of fever and burning sensations. (21)
That *piṇḍataila*, containing beeswax, madder, resin of the *sarja* tree, and *śārivā*,
removes the pain of *vātarakta* when used as an ointment.
Milk boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla) immediately relieves colic;
likewise, a lukewarm affusion with ghee is effective when the condition is dominated by vāyu.

Or one should sprinkle the patient—who suffers from stiffness, convulsions, and pain—with the four unctuous substances prepared with sweet drugs; they should be lukewarm, but cold if there is a burning sensation. (24)
In the same manner, [one should apply] decoctions of cow’s milk, sheep’s milk, or goat’s milk mixed with oil, or of the *jīvanīya* group, or of the minor *pañcamūla*. (25)

Wine made from grapes, sugarcane juice, and fermented liquor; curd-whey, sour gruel, and sour rice-water; as well as rice-water, honey, and sugar-water—these are recommended for the purpose of sprinkling. (26)

Beloved women, speaking sweet words, with hands and breasts moistened with sandalwood paste—cool to the touch and pleasant to the skin—they destroy the burning heat, the pain, and the exhaustion. (27)
If there is redness, pain, and burning sensation, one should remove the blood and apply a plaster made of *prapauṇḍarīka*,
*mañjiṣṭhā*, *dārvī*, *madhuka*, and *candana*.
An ointment made from sugar, elakā, parched grain flour, lentils, uśīra, and padmaka destroys pain, burning sensations, erysipelas, redness, and swelling. (29)

22.29–30. A *kṛśara* dish prepared with sugar-candy (*sitopala*), sugar-cane juice (*kāsa*), sugarcane (*ikṣu*), lentils (*masūra*), *airaka*, and parched grain flour (*saktu*), enriched with Vata-alleviating substances, is unctuous and cures colic.
Likewise, a poultice (*upanāhana*) made from balls of sesame and mustard seeds is a destroyer of pain.

22.31c–d Those [fatty substances] prepared with life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, along with milk or muscle fat (vasā),
destroy stiffness, piercing pain, aching, stretching, swelling, and rigidity of the limbs.
22.32a–b [They are] also effective when prepared with life-promoting drugs and milk, or even with muscle fat alone.
Clarified butter, the root of sahacara, and jīvantī, with goat’s milk, form a paste;
likewise, sesame seeds ground and then fried, quenched in milk, [form another].
For the cessation of pain when Vata is predominant, one should apply a plaster of linseed ground with milk, or the fruits of castor oil plant, or dill.
22.34 An ointment of *umā* ground with milk,
or ghee cooked with urine, alkali, and wine, is beneficial for massage;
or fermented vinegar (*śukta*) prepared with honey is likewise used for sprinkling and massage when *kapha* predominates.
22.35ab A decoction of *mustā*, alkali, and sugar, when prepared, used for sprinkling and massage, is indicated when *kapha* is predominant.
22.35cd–36ab House-soot (*gṛhadhūma*), *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *śatāhvā*,
and the two types of *rajanī* (turmeric and *daruharidrā*) constitute a paste that relieves pain in *vātarakta* where *vāta* and *kapha* are predominant.
Likewise, the seed of Madhuśigru is beneficial when combined with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla);
having been smeared for a short while, one should sprinkle it with acidic liquids in cases where Vāta and Kapha predominate.
One should treat the superficial type with ointments, massages, affusions, and immersions;
the deep type with purgatives, non-unctuous enemas, and the drinking of unctuous substances. (38)

In cases where wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman) predominate, applications such as plasters should be lukewarm; for if cold substances are used, there will be an increase in burning sensation, swelling, pain, and itching due to the obstructive nature of the treatment. // 39 //
In cases where pitta and blood predominate in vātarakta, cooling applications such as plasters are indicated;
for through hot treatments, burning, heat, pain, redness, sweating, and cracking arise. (40)
One hundred palas of licorice (madhuyaṣṭī) should be boiled down to one-fourth in water;
then, one āḍhaka of oil with an equal amount of milk should be cooked with pastes (kalka) weighing one pala each.
With *sthirā*, *tāmalakī*, *dūrvā*, *payasyā*, *abhīru*, and *candana*;
