with *loha*, *haṃsapadī*, *māṃsī*, the two types of *medā*, and *madhuparṇī*—(42)
With kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, śatapuṣpā, ṛddhi, and padmaka;
with jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, jīvantī, tvak, pattra, nakha, and vālaka. (43)
Prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, śārivā, aindrī, and vitunnaka, when employed in four ways, alleviate vāta-rakta, pitta disorders, burning sensations, and the pain of fever. (44)

Through fourfold application, this oil destroys wind-blood disorders (vātāsṛj) accompanied by complications and pain in the limbs, as well as those that have spread throughout all the body parts; it likewise cures the affliction of burning heat from wind, blood, and bile, as well as fever, and it promotes strength and complexion.
One should cook oil with equal parts of milk and the decoction and paste of *balā*;
having processed it a hundred or a thousand times, it cures gout (*vātāsṛg*) and diseases caused by *vāta*.
This is the foremost elixir (rasāyana), which clarifies the sense organs, promotes longevity, provides nourishment, improves the voice, and destroys defects of the semen and blood. (46)
When the wind (vāyu) is provoked by the obstruction of the channels due to an excessive increase of either fat (medas) or phlegm (kapha),
oleation and nourishing therapies are not recommended at the outset.
Having administered there the treatment for vātarakta as prescribed for āḍhyavāta, one should then apply unctuous medicine (snehana) and that which purifies the blood. 48.

When there is a simultaneous disturbance of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the other elements, one should prescribe the medicine according to what has been specified, according to the disease, according to proximity, and according to the patient's strength. (49)

When the *āmadoṣa* has been eliminated from the *sāma* (undigested) state by means of sudation, fasting, digestive treatments, and dry applications such as ointments and affusions, one should administer therapies that alleviate *vāta* alone. (50)
Emaciation, convulsions, contraction, stiffness, sleepiness, trembling, drooping of the jaw, facial paralysis, lameness, club-foot, and the condition of khuda-vāta; 51.
Fractures at the joints, paralysis of the limbs, and diseases affecting the fat, marrow, and bones—these may be cured with effort if they are recent, owing to the depth of their location. (52)
Therefore, one should conquer these nine strong and harmless [conditions] by means of cold and hot treatments applied repeatedly when vāyu is occluded by pitta. (53)
One should administer ghee in an alternating manner and cause the patient to drink *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) decoctions;
[the diet should consist of] the meat of animals from arid lands, barley, and *śāli* rice, along with mild purgation using milk. (54)

Enemas containing milk, milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūla) and balā, and oil-anointing enemas (anuvāsana) prepared with oils processed with sweet medicinal herbs should be administered at the appropriate time. (55)
At the appropriate time, an oil enema (anuvāsana) prepared with sweet medicinal herbs should be administered;
furthermore, there should be affusion (secanam) with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhu), balā-oil, ghee, and milk,
or with water cooled by a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla), or simply with cold water.

22.56 When [the heart] is obstructed by *kapha*, [one should treat it] with cold water; likewise, barley-based foods, meat of wild animals and birds, sharp sudations, non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*), emesis, and purgation [are indicated].
Old ghee and oil produced from sesame or mustard seeds are beneficial.
When [the disease] is associated with both kapha and pitta, one should first conquer the pitta. // 58 //
In the case of blood associated with vāta, one should perform the treatment for vātarakta;
fomentation, massage, meat soups, milk, and unctuous substances are beneficial when [vāta] is covered by muscle tissue (māṃsa). // 59 //

22.59 When [the vāta] is covered by muscle tissue (māṃsa), oleation therapy is beneficial; it is the physician’s proven remedy for urinary disorders (prameha), obesity (medas), and vāta. For vāta located in the rich [tissues], the "Great Oleation" (mahāsneha) is prescribed; when located in the bones and marrow, the previously mentioned [oleation] is used; and when covered by semen, the same applies.
When [the digestive fire] is obstructed by food, one should administer digestive (pācanīya) treatments, emetics, digestive stimulants (dīpana), and light [dietary measures].
When it is obstructed by urine, one should use diuretics (mūtralāni), sudations (sveda), and urethral enemas (uttara-vasti). // 61 //
22.61–62. Fomentations, urethral enemas (uttara-vasti), castor oil, and unctuous enemas that promote evacuation are indicated when [the doshas] are located in the feces.
Whatever is not antagonistic to kapha and pitta, and whatever promotes the downward movement of vāta, should be employed.
Even when obstructed in all its locations, it quickly performs its function within the vital air (mātariśvan);
it is non-mucilaginous, unctuous, and the cause of purification for the channels.

When all sites are obstructed, however, *yāpana* enemas—mostly sweet and accompanied by oil enemas (*anuvāsana*)—should be administered quickly. Having carefully considered the excess of strength, a mild purgative (*virecana*) should be employed. (22.63–64)
A mild purgation of the body is recommended, as is the use of all types of rejuvenative elixirs (rasāyana),
especially those of śilājatu and purified guggulu taken with milk.
Likewise, the leha of Bhārgava consists of eleven white and non-white [substances];
when the apāna is obstructed, every kind of digestive stimulant (dīpana) and absorbent (grāhin) medicine [is indicated]. 66.
22.66b–c: Eleven [medicines] are white and black;
one should perform the downward movement of vāta and the purification of the urinary bladder.
Thus, the treatment for those [doshas] that are obstructed has been stated in brief. 67.
The physician, having reflected upon this himself, should perform [the treatment] for the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth;
he should direct the udāna upward and cause the apāna to flow in its natural downward direction. 68.
The wise one should pacify the *samāna* breath; he should employ the *vyāna* in three ways.
The *prāṇa* must be protected even from the four [other winds], for upon its stability depends the stability of the body. (69)

One should likewise apply the Vyāna in three ways and lead it to its own respective locations; thus, one should treat the Vātas that have entered wrong paths and all obstructions, provided they are free from the association of Pitta and blood. (22.69–70)
Garlic, when consumed according to the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana), destroys [diseases];
it removes pitta when [the channels] are obstructed by pitta and promotes the downward movement of vāta. (71)

Likewise, when [the channels] are obstructed by blood, one should employ that same treatment as well as the medicine taught by Khuḍa, various remedies for blood, bile, and wind, and diverse rejuvenative elixirs (rasāyana). // 72 //
This section, which teaches the correct medical treatment according to its specific causes, is the fruit of Ayurveda, for it brings about the immediate destruction of suffering. (73)

22.73 This is known by its synonyms as *auṣadha* (medicine): it is the immediate destroyer of pain, the beneficial treatment, the wholesome regimen, the expiation, the physician’s victory, the remedy, the pacifier, and the praised cure. 74.
In the Section on Therapeutics, Madana is the best for emesis, and the root of Trivṛt is the best for purgation;
however, in other cases, the specific [drug] varies according to the particular disease. (1)
Having taken fruits that are neither too pale nor too green,
during the day under an auspicious constellation, in the middle of the summer and spring seasons.

Those fruits should be pale yellow and not too green; having wiped them clean with a bundle of *kuśa* grass, one should place them inside, tie it up, and smear it [with clay]. After applying cow dung over the bundle, one should deposit it in the midst of grain. (3)
Having wiped [the seeds] with a bundle of *kuśa* grass, and having subsequently smeared the bundle with cow dung, one should remove those seeds—
which have become soft and possess a pleasant fragrance from the *kuśa* wrapping— after eight days have passed, and then dry them in the sun. (4)
1.4av When they have become mild and are desired for intoxication; 1.4cv Extracted when eight days have passed; 1.4cv Having extracted [them] once eight days have elapsed;
1.4cv Having extracted [them] once eight days have gone by.
Then, having extracted the seeds from those [pippalīs] once they are thoroughly dried,
one should crush them with curd, honey, clarified butter, and sesame paste, and dry them again.
Having first mixed it with one and a half *cuvits* of curd, honey, water, and meat-paste, one should store it well protected and employ it at the time of action;
then, taking a dose from that, one should crush it and let it soak.
Or one may [bathe] at night in water infused with licorice (madhuyaṣṭī), or with kovidāra,
karbudāra, bimba, nīpa, or vidula.
1.7 Or else, one should drink that decoction of *jīmūtaka*, or *bimbī*, or *śaṇapuṣpī*, or *sadāpuṣpī*, or *pratyakpuṣpī* in water;
having crushed and strained it, one should drink it in the morning.

Alternatively, with water containing *pratyakpuṣpā* flowers, one should properly induce emesis according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtra; this is likewise indicated in cases of phlegm disorders, fever, coryza, abdominal tumors, and internal abscesses. // 9 //
It is good that one should vomit by means of that; therefore, one should cause vomiting, specifically inducing emesis until the appearance of bile.
Alternatively, one may use the powder of *phala* and *pippalī*, impregnated with its own decoction. (1.9b–10)

One suffering from fever, loss of appetite, dyspepsia, glandular swellings, scrofula, tumors, or abdominal enlargement should drink a powder of *triphalā* mixed with one-third its weight of *kovidāra* and other [herbs], using water boiled with *kovidāra* and the rest.

One should drink [it] in cases of fever, poisoning, and spitting; one should drink [it] in cases of fever, poisoning, and sweating; one should drink [it] in cases of fever, anorexia, and spitting; one should drink [it] likewise in cases of fever and anorexia. 1.11dv.
In cases of glandular swellings, scrofula, tumors, and abdominal enlargements when pitta has reached the seat of kapha, one should use water from clouds and the like;
in cases of burning in the heart and downward hemorrhaging of pitta, milk boiled with that [water] and long pepper should be used. (12)

In cases of phlegm-induced vomiting, excessive salivation, and tamaka-shvāsa, however, one should administer kṣaireyī (rice-pudding), or the whey of curd, or curd itself produced from boiled milk. 13.

1.13bv–14. In cases of excessive salivation (praseka) and tamaka-shwasa, ghee prepared from milk that has been processed with the decoction and paste of madanaphala and other fruits should be administered for emesis, when the digestive fire is overcome by kapha and the body is becoming emaciated.

1.14 In cases of emaciation or a drying body, one should administer emesis using the expressed juice of *bhallātaka* seeds or their pulp, boiled according to the procedure for *bhallātaka*. Having licked this preparation until it reaches the consistency of a paste that adheres to a ladle, one will easily vomit.
One should incorporate that electuary into various foods and drinks, as well as their decoctions;
there is also a decoction produced from the fruit pulp with vatsakādi added as a counter-injection. (16)
Combined with a decoction of either nimba or arka, it subdues all diseases arising from over-nutrition, even those that have taken deep root. (17)
1.17dv For those conditions arising from the excessive nourishment of *śleṣman*,

one who is satisfied by eating the scum of gruel, meat broth, and so forth, should comfortably vomit while smelling a garland that has been well-dried with the fine powders of *rāṣṭra*, flowers, and fruits. 18.
1.18bv – with powders, the garland is dried; 1.18bv – with powders, the garland is well-smeared;
1.18bv – with powders, the wreath is well-smeared;
1.18cv – a man should vomit [substances such as] juices and the like.
In this very way, when the fruit is absent, one may imagine it as a flower or an unripe bud;
and among clouds and the like, which are like fruits, the cloud (*jīmūta*) is especially so. (19)
In the same way, when the fruit has not yet been obtained,
it should be administered to those suffering from fever, dyspnea, cough, hiccups, and other such ailments.
When the flower has matured into fruit, milk prepared with this [plant] should be drunk as gruel.
If the milk is hairy, it is a continuous flow of milk; if hairless, it is superior curd (dadhyuttara).
When the milk has been boiled and turned sour, and the resulting curd is greenish-yellow, it is called *jāta*. (21)
When it has turned greenish-yellow,
one should drink the scum of *vāruṇī* liquor after squeezing and filtering it.
In cases of loss of appetite due to phlegm, cough, anemia, and pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), [this should be used]. // 22 //
And this same reasoning should also be applied to the gourds, the kośātakī fruits, and to those born from creepers whose fruits have fully ripened and dried. (23)
One afflicted by vāta and pitta should drink one *śukti* (two karṣas) of the powder of bamboo-born fruits (*veṇu-janman*) or those born from the *ūni* plant, mixed with milk;
or alternatively, having crushed two or even three [fruits], one should drink them with a decoction of the best bitter herbs (*tiktottama*). (1.23–24)

1.24–25. Having crushed two or three [drugs] from the group of nine beginning with *āragvadha*, or having prepared a decoction of any one of them, one suffering from fever caused by *pitta* and *kapha* should drink that strained decoction after it has been cooled.
Having strained that decoction through a cloth and purified it,
one should drink it with cold water along with the paste (kalka) or powder (cūrṇa) of jīmūta;
in cases of pitta-type fever, it should be taken lukewarm, and in cases of fever arising from kapha and vāta, or from kapha alone, it should be taken warm.
The powder or paste of *jīmūta* is recommended for those afflicted by cough, dyspnea, poisoning, vomiting, and fever who are emaciated by *kapha*; likewise,
*ikṣvāku* is praised for inducing emesis in a person who is fainting.

1.27bv – For one afflicted by fever and depleted of kapha; 1.27cv – Ikṣvāku is best for inducing emesis. Milk boiled with its sprouts, from which the fruits and flowers have been removed, should be administered in cases of fever caused by pitta and śleṣman when pitta is predominant. // 28 //
Prepared with that [juice] and with coral sprouts (pravāla), one should administer it in cases of a predominance of pitta.
When the milk has remained for a day after the fruit has been digested in the middle of the stomach, it turns into curd;
at that time, in cases of cough born of kapha, dyspnea, and vomiting, one should cause it to be drunk. (1.28–29)

When the fruit is ripe and its pulp has been extracted, one should have the patient drink the pulp with whey (mastu) in cases of dyspnea and vomiting; or those afflicted by anemia (pāṇḍu), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), or poison should drink it.
Alternatively, they may drink buttermilk (takra) cooked with that [pulp], along with honey and rock salt (saindhava).

One suffering from anemia, skin diseases, or affliction by poison should soak the seeds in goat’s milk and drink them with that same milk; this is for cases of poisoning, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, glandular swellings, goiters, and elephantiasis. (1.30bv–31)
Or one may drink a churned beverage (mantha) made with roasted grain flour (saktu) saturated with the fresh juice of the bottle gourd (tumbī),
in cases of fever arising from phlegm (kapha), cough, diseases of the throat, and loss of appetite.
In cases of abdominal tumors (gulma) and persistent fever, a person should drink a medicinal paste with meat broth;
in this way, he vomits effectively and does not suffer from weakness.
In cases of abdominal tumors (gulma), fever,

and excessive salivation, one accustomed to the pleasure of excellent fragrances should induce vomiting by smelling a garland that has been sprinkled with the dried juices of the bottle-gourd (tumbī) flowers along with the flowers themselves.
1.34ab Dried with the juices of the fruit of the *tumbī* vine, 1.34d the fragrance is perfectly suited for comfort;
1.34d the fragrance is perfectly suited for the comfort of the excellence of scent; 1.34d the fragrance is perfectly suited for comfort.

In cases of cough, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and goiter; when vāta is located in the seat of phlegm (kapha-āśaya); when kapha is situated in the throat and mouth; and in disorders arising from the accumulation of kapha. // 35 //
1.35d–36ab: However, for diseases born from the accumulation of *kapha* that are chronic and extensive, *dhāmārgava* is recommended;
likewise are *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *vīrā*, *kapikacchū*, and *śatāvarī*.
Linctuses made from the powders of Kākoli, Śrāvaṇī, Medā, Mahāmedā, and Madhūlikā, each combined separately with the powder of Dhāmārgava, [are used]. (37)
In cases of cough and burning of the heart, these [medicines] mixed with honey and sugar and taken as a liquid are recommended;
they should be followed by a drink of warm water when kapha is associated with pitta and heat. (38)

1.38b–c: These [drugs] are recommended when combined with honey and sugar; a paste of them, taken with a broth of coriander and *tumburu*, destroys poison. Alternatively, [the paste may be taken] with the juice of *bimbī*, *punarnavā*, or *kāsamarda*. (39)
1.39–40. One should drink either one or two *dhāmārgava* seeds crushed in the juice of *bimbi* or *punarnavā*.
Alternatively, one may consume ghee prepared from milk boiled with that [decoction], or ghee processed with the *phala* group of drugs and others.

Kṣveḍa, which is extremely pungent, sharp, and hot, is recommended for severe cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya), splenic disorders (plīha), edema (śopha), abdominal tumors (gulma), and poisoning (gara), among others. (41)
And in cases of severe [dysuria], meat from marshy animals is recommended when boiled in a decoction of the six drugs beginning with *pṛthakphala*;
one should drink that broth, prepared together with *kośātakī*, along with salt. (1.42)
1.42–43. One may take a decoction of *kośātakī* prepared with an equal amount of the "fruit-group" (*phalādi*) and *pippalī*; or one prepared in the juice of *kṣveḍa*;
or one should drink a decoction of *kṣveḍa* boiled with sugarcane juice.

Or it may be prepared with the juice of *kṣveḍa*. One should drink [this] *kauṭaja* [preparation] boiled in a decoction of *kṣveḍa* for those who are delicate, when there is an aggravation of *pitta*, blood, and *kapha*.
It is highly esteemed in cases of fever, erysipelas (*visarpa*), heart disease, *khuḍa*, and skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
For children who are very delicate, one should administer *kuṭaja* with water of mustard, *madhūka*, or salt;
or else, one should give *kuṭaja* seeds combined with *kṛsarā*.
For seven days, one should administer that powder separately, moistened with goat’s milk, along with the decoctions of *phala*, *jīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *jīvantī*, and *jīvaka*. (46)

1.46ab–47. "For seven days, it should be treated with *arka*-milk; this is declared as the general direction for the procedure (*kalpa*) regarding the foremost emetic medicines. By means of this seed-method, the wise person may devise other [preparations] as well."
By this method, the wise man should devise other [preparations] as well and apply others as well. (Kalpasthāna 1.47cd–1.47dv)
Trivṛt is astringent-sweet and dry; it is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), pacifies phlegm and bile, and aggravates wind due to its dryness. (1)
Astringent, sweet, and dry; due to its dryness, it aggravates Vāta. Now, when combined with medicinal substances that remove Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha, [it becomes beneficial].
Having attained a specific ritual procedure (kalpa), one becomes a conqueror of all diseases. // 2 //
That root is said to be of two kinds: dark (śyāma) and darkish-red (śyāmāruṇa), known as trivṛt.
Of these two, the one called trivṛt is superior, being free from harmful side effects and easy to administer.
That [emetic] is beneficial for those who are delicate, infants, the elderly, and those with soft bowels;
it brings about fainting, delusion, and causes irritation and abrasion of the heart and throat. (4)
2.4dv–Because it performs sharp and rapid action, that [emetic] which bestows both drawing out and tearing is also praised for a harsh bowel,
for a great accumulation of humors (doṣa), and for a patient capable of enduring hardship. // 5 //
In a person with a cruel constitution, excessive *doṣas*, or a great accumulation of *doṣas*, one should take a piece of wood that is deep-reaching, smooth, and not spread out sideways;
having extracted it, one should discard it and allow the bark to dry. (6)
2.6bv And that which is not spread obliquely;

then, at the proper time, one should drink a small amount of powder of ginger and rock salt with sour liquids in a wind-disease (vātāmaya), but with ghee, sugar, and honey in a bile-disease (paitta). 7.
2.7av Then, at the proper time, that powder; 2.7av then, at the proper time, that powder; 2.7av then, at the proper time, the powder of *trivṛt*;
2.7av then, by the lapse of time, that powder; 2.7cv one suffering from wind-disorders (*vātāmayin*) should drink it with sour substances; 2.7dv [if] in bile (*pitta*).

In cases of diseases caused by phlegm (kapha), [the enema should be prepared] with ghee, sugar, honey, milk, grapes, sugarcane, kāśmarya, the sweet cluster [of fruits], and the juice of varā; or with the juice of pīlu, urine, wine, sour liquids, and fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika). // 8 //

Combined with powders of the five types of *kola* and other phlegm-subduing substances according to the proper method, and prepared with the paste and decoction of *trivṛt*, this [mixture] is a cooling drink served with sugar. (9)
2.9c–d One should administer [this] combined with the paste and decoction of *trivṛt*, along with substances that alleviate *kapha*.
A linctus (leha) joined with honey and the three aromatics (*tri-jāta*) is a heart-pleasing purgative.
*Ajagandhā*, *tavakṣīrī*, *vidārī*, sugar, and *trivṛt* [are used for this]. 10.
2.10cv Having licked a powder of *ajagandhā* and *tukākṣīrī* with honey and ghee, one who is afflicted by *saṃnipāta* fever, stiffness, thirst, and burning sensations is effectively purged. // 11 //

One should apply that powder internally with honey and ghee; having cut a piece of sugarcane into two parts and combined them, one should cook it by the *puṭapāka* method and eat it once it has been steamed.
2.12b Having cut the pieces of sugarcane into two; 2.12c And having combined that, it should be well-steamed.

Having combined those steamed ingredients with equal parts of *bhṛṅga*, *elā*, and *nīlī*, along with *trivṛt* and sugar, one should drink this powder as a nourishing draught (*tarpaṇa*) mixed with fruit juice, honey, and roasted grain flour (*saktu*). // 13 //

2.13ab Nīlī, equal in quantity to both bark and cardamom, is a harmless purgative for diseases arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha, as well as for those with weak digestive fire and for very delicate persons.
Viḍaṅga seeds, varā, yava-śūka, kaṇā, and trivṛt—each of these taken in half the quantity [of the preceding]; that [mixture] should be licked with honey, ghee, or jaggery. // 15 //
It eliminates abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, cough, chlorosis, anorexia, and many other diseases caused by kapha and vāta. (16)
Viḍaṅga, pippalī root, triphalā, dhānyaka, citraka, marīca, indrayava, ajājī, pippalī, and hastipippalī; (17)
2.17b–d: One karṣa each of the powders of triphalā, dhānyaka, citraka, pippalī, hastipippalī, dīpyaka, and the five salts;
along with eight palas each of sesame oil and the powder of trivṛt.

Having cooked two parts— each measuring eight palas— of the juice of *dhātrī* fruits along with three *prasthas* of the juice of *dhātrī* fruits and half a *tulā* of jaggery over a mild fire, one should then consume the appropriate dose without dietary restrictions. (2.18d–19)
Then, one who is not restricted by a fixed dose should take three *tulās* of half-jaggery (*guḍa*).
This cures weak digestion, fever, fainting, dysuria, and anorexia. (19+1ab)

It destroys leprosy, hemorrhoids, jaundice, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, enlargement of the abdomen, fistula-in-ano, malabsorption syndrome, and anemia; furthermore, it is a promoter of virility. (20)
The electuary named Kalyāṇaka is suitable for all seasons;
it consists of trikaṭu, the three aromatics (trijātaka), ambhoda, kṛmighna, āmalaka, and trivṛt.
All these ingredients, equal in quantity and combined with honey, are made into pills;
they are used for dysuria, fever, vomiting, cough, emaciation, vertigo, and wasting.
Equal parts of all [the ingredients] together with sugar, made into pills with honey,
one should eat upon rising in the morning and drink cold water afterwards.
These are recommended for fever, anemia, weak digestion, and all types of poisoning;
this formulation is praised as being free from complications and beneficial for those suffering from bile disorders. (23)
Trivṛt, kuṭaja seeds, pippalī, and viśvabheṣaja, combined with honey and grape juice, constitute a purgative for the rainy season. (24)
At the end of the rainy season, one should take trivṛt, durālabhā, musta, sugar, udīcya, candana, drākṣā, yaṣṭimadhu, and sātala with water. (25)

2.25c–d: [One should take] *trivṛt*, *citraka*, *pāṭhā*, cumin (*ajājī*), *sarala*, and *vacā* with grape-water and *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice) during the summer season when the clouds have ceased. 2.25d: [Or one may take it] with cool water during the summer season when the clouds have ceased.
And during the winter, one should drink the powder of *svarṇakṣīrī* with warm water. // 26 //
Trivṛt mixed with an equal amount of sugar is a purgative for the summer season; likewise, trivṛt, trāyantī, hapuṣā, sātalā, and kaṭurohiṇī [are used]. (27)

Having powdered svarṇakṣīrī and steeped it in cow’s urine for three days, this formulation is suitable for all seasons; it removes impurities and defects from those who have been treated with unctuous therapies. (28)
Śyāmā, trivṛt, durālabhā, hastipippalī, vatsaka, nīlinī, kaṭukā, mustā, and śreṣṭhā—these, when well-powdered and combined, [form a remedy]. (29)
It is recommended for those who are dry at all times, taken with meat broth, ghee, or warm water;
it is also beneficial for those suffering from fever, heart disease, gout, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and similar ailments. (30)

Saindhava salt, pippalī root, and abhayā, each succeeding one being double the amount of the preceding, should be drunk as a powder with warm water; this is a pleasant purgative for those in good health. (30.1+1)

The powder of *rājavṛkṣa* drunk with warm water is especially wholesome; it is mild, sweet, and cooling, suitable for children, the elderly, those with chest wounds, the emaciated, and delicate persons. (2.30.1+1)
The *caturaṅgula* should be employed because it is soft and does not decay; furthermore, at the time of fruition, one should gather its matured fruit. (32)
One should place the load of those virtuous substances upon sands;
after seven nights, one should lift them up and dry them in the sun.
Then one should dry it in the sun;
thereafter, having extracted the marrow, one should place it in a clean vessel.
One should administer that with grape juice to a patient suffering from burning sensations and upward-moving wind (udāvarta).

A child should be made to drink the medicinal decoction until he is four years old, or until he is twelve; or else, one should have him drink it until his knees are submerged up to four finger-breadths.
It should be prepared separately with whey, the scum of wine, or the juice of *dhātrī* fruits, or combined with *sauvīraka* vinegar, or with the paste of the three sweets (*traivṛta*). // 36 //
One should add jaggery and its marrow to a decoction of *dantī*;
this *ariṣṭa* should be kept for a month or even for a fortnight before being administered.
Having removed the inner bark from the skin of the *tilvaka* root, one should dry it, powder it, and then filter two parts of that [powder]. (38)
One should saturate it a third time with a decoction of *lodhra* itself;
then, one should again saturate that portion with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*). (39)
2.39 Having dried the powder and then processed it again with a decoction of *lodhra*, one should drink it from the palm of the hand with whey,
urine, the scum of wine (*surā-maṇḍa*), and the juices of *kola* and *dhātrī* fruits.
Then one should make it into a dry powder;
having again made it into a dry powder, it should be taken with the decoction and paste of *tilvaka*, along with sugar.
This electuary, prepared with ghee, is an excellent purgative. // 41 //
And that [ghee] is the best purgative;

it breaks up even a massive accumulation of the humors (doṣas) as effectively as sudhā. Because it causes distressing displacement [of the humors] very quickly, one should not administer it for that purpose. 2.42cd–42ef.
One should not administer it immediately thereafter to those with severe displacement of the humors or displacement of the digestive tract;
nor to one with a soft bowel, one who is weak, a child, an elderly person, or one suffering from a chronic disease.
It should be prescribed for those suffering from abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, poisoning, skin diseases, and diabetes mellitus. // 43 //
In cases of jaundice, latent poison, swelling, and mental confusion caused by the derangement of the humors, that [ghee] is best when it is thickened with many sharp thorns. (44)
When she is two or three years old, especially at the end of the winter season,
one should cut her with a blade and extract the milk from there.

Having mixed the milk of *sudhā* either individually with an equal amount of the decoction of *bilva* and so forth, or with that of the two *bṛhatī*s, one should then dry it over charcoal embers. (46)
One should drink [the medicine] after making it into pills with whey, urine, wine, and so forth; [using] the nine excellent drugs beginning with trivṛt, along with svarṇakṣīrī and sātala. (47)
For seven days, one should drink [the juice] having drunk the milk of *snuk*, or one should drink it with its juice or with clarified butter;
likewise, one may take *vyoṣa*, *uttamā*, *kumbha*, *nikumbha*, and *agni* with jaggery-water.
2.48dv–49. One should take *nikumbha* and the others with molasses-water;
the fruit of *śaṅkhinī* should be taken after being dried and dehusked, as should the root of *saptalā*. These two are sharp and purgative.
In cases of abdominal diseases caused by phlegm (śleṣmāmayodara), poisoning (gara), edema (śvayathu), and the like,
one should prepare a bolus of the size of an akṣa fruit from those two [drugs], combined with wine and salt.
In heart disease caused by vāta and kapha, one should apply this same treatment as well as for abdominal tumors (gulma).
[One should use] the root of dantī that is firm and thick like a tooth, produced from the juice of dantī and dravantī. (51)
In the same way, one should employ [this treatment] in cases of gulma that is copper-colored, dark-brown, sharp, hot, quick-acting,
and expansive; it is heavy, provokes vāta, and dissolves pitta and śleṣman.
2.52b–c That [ointment], smeared with honey and long pepper (pippalī) and wrapped in clay and darbha grass, should be heated;
it should then be dried in mild sunlight, for fire and the sun destroy its tendency to cause spreading (vikāśitvam). 53.
That [milk], mixed with honey and long pepper (pippalī), or combined with honey and long pepper,
one should drink when its [digestive] power has been diminished, along with whey, wine, buttermilk, the juice of *pīlu*, or fermented liquors (*āsava*).

One with a body afflicted by excessive secretions, one suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma), one with urinary disorders (prameha), one with abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara), or one with edema (śopha). 54.

One suffering from *abhiṣyanda*, one with a slender body, one with abdominal tumors (*gulma*), one who is pale, one with worms in the intestines, or one with fistula-in-ano— [these should take] that [medicine] prepared with the decoction and paste [of the aforementioned drugs] along with the juice of *daśamūla*. (2.54–55)
Ghee overcomes erysipelas, abscesses, alajī, and burning sensations in the armpits;
oil, however, conquers abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, constipation, and disorders of kapha and vāta. (56)
Excessive unctuousness, retention of feces, semen, and flatus, and pain from wind—these nine conditions are most effectively treated by purgation with the drugs beginning with *trivṛt*. (57)
One should also prepare a "great unctuous" (mahā-sneha) formulation containing feces, semen, and *harītakī* according to the procedure for *trivṛt*.
In eight *pala* of jaggery, there should be twenty *pathyā* fruits and one *pala* each of [the other ingredients]. (2.58)
Having prepared one *karṣa* each of *dantī* and *citraka*, and ten each of *pippalī* and *trivṛt*, one should administer one bolus (*modaka*) on every tenth day. (59)
One should drink warm water and eat all of these according to this procedure; these require no dietary restrictions and are destroyers of all diseases. (60)
2.60 Drinking warm water after eating is especially beneficial for those suffering from *grahaṇī*, anemia, itching, urticaria, and hemorrhoids.
[It ensures that] even a small amount [of food] yields great benefit, while a large amount results in little effect. 61.
[These] are beneficial for itching, skin diseases, and hemorrhoids. One should [prepare them] by means of the methods of combination, separation, time, and processing. (2.61)

2.61–62. Purgatives should be administered according to the season, the patient's constitution, and the appropriate method, combined with cinnamon, saffron, *āmrātaka*, pomegranate, cardamom, white sugar, honey, and citron; or with various wines that are agreeable to the mind.

2.62cv And with various kinds of wines that are agreeable to the mind, emesis [should be induced] by one whose digestive tract is soft, or who has hunger and little phlegm, according to the Kalpasthāna.
Or if one who is weak consumes an excessive amount of very sharp or cold food while it has not yet been digested; // 1 //
If the oil goes downward, there is loss of the desired effect and the arising of impurities;
one should then cause it to move upward again by administering unctuous matter while recollecting the previous transgression. (2)
3.2dv Recalling the previous sequence, purgation administered to one who has not digested [the previous meal] or who has an excess of phlegm moves upward;
likewise, if it is excessively sharp, hot, salty, unpalatable, or given in too great a quantity. // 3 //
In that case, if the previously mentioned failure or success does not occur even so,
yet the intention remains firm, then one should not administer the third [dose].

Except for a medicine that is habituated, or one that is heart-pleasing and free from harmful side effects, administering an old, dry medicine to a person whose body has not been oleated or fomented [is harmful]. (5)
3.5ab–cd: Except for what is wholesome (sātmya) and what is beneficial to the heart, [emesis] cannot expel the humors (doṣas) if administered to one whose body has not been oleated and fomented;
it may produce diseases, including displacement [of the humors], swelling, hiccups, darkness of vision, and thirst. 6.

3.6cv For one who has been treated with oleation and sudation, whose digestive fire is kindled, and for whom the medicine has been digested, [the following signs indicate success]: loss of consciousness, swelling, hiccups, cramps in the calves, itching, weakness in the thighs, discoloration, and very little flatus. // 7 //

3.7cv If one administers [purgatives] in insufficient quantity to a person who has been properly oleated and sudated, or if they are suppressed by cold substances, or if they are administered while the *āma* (undigested morbid matter) is still present, causing it to become agitated;
all such improper administration (*ayoga*) will produce those very same diseases.
If the bowels are obstructed by cold or undigested (āma) matter, one should eliminate the morbid humors (malas) after inducing nausea. Having induced nausea, one should remove the impurities.
That patient, having been anointed with oil and salt and fomented with prastara and saṃkara methods, [should be treated].
Once the oil has taken effect, one should feed the patient with the meat-juices of wild animals and then administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
Once the patient has been fomented with bedding and straw,
they should be treated with an appropriate dose of oil prepared with *phala*, *māgadhikā*, and *dāru*.
Having been lubricated with unctuous substances that alleviate *vāta*, one should then purify [the channels] again with a sharp [purgative].
For one who has many defects, is dry, and has weak digestion, a small dose of medicine causes the humors to become agitated;
together with upward-moving wind (udāvarta), it obstructs the pathways by means of those very humors.
3.11cd–12ab: By obstructing the channels, the humors (doṣas) cause intense distension of the umbilical region, as well as pain in the back, sides, and head;
they also produce severe dyspnea and the retention of feces, urine, and flatus.
3.12ab One should cause intense distension [of the abdomen] which causes pain in the navel, back, flanks, and head.

All therapeutic measures that alleviate *udāvarta*—such as massage, sudation, suppositories (*varti*), and so forth, along with non-unctuous and unctuous enemas (*nirūha-anuvāsana*)—are recommended for one suffering from abdominal distension (*ādhmāta*). 3.13ab/13.0001–02 //
A well-prepared gruel made with the five roots, barley-alkali, vacā, bhūtīka, and rock salt destroys colic, constipation, and flatulence. (14)

3.14 One should drink the five spices (pañcakola), alkali of barley (yavakṣāra), long pepper (pippalī), pomegranate alkali (dāḍimakṣāra), asafoetida (hiṅgu), dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and sour vetasa (amlavetasa), together with rock salt (saindhava), along with fermented liquors (madya), clarified butter (sarpiḥ), or warm water.

In cases of dysentery, discharge, piercing pain, or cutting pain, the vital winds (māruta) and other humors become aggravated due to the suppression of natural urges following the ingestion of medicinal drugs. // 16 //

In cases of dysentery (pravāhikā) and excessive discharge (parisrāva), when the aggravated [doshas] reach the heart and cause excruciating cutting pain, they produce a terrible cardiac seizure (hṛd-graha),
accompanied by hiccups, pain in the flanks, cough, debility, salivation, and rolling of the eyes.
Devoid of consciousness, he gnaws his tongue and grinds his teeth;
the physician should not fall into confusion regarding this state, but should quickly cause him to vomit. 18.
One whose consciousness is clouded by pitta grinds his teeth when given sweet [drugs], while one whose consciousness is clouded by kapha does so when given pungent ones;
thereafter, one should digest the remaining morbid humors with digestive (pācanīya) agents.
Then, by means of digestive (pācanīya) [drugs], one should quickly digest the remainder of the doshas and gradually increase his bodily fire (kāyāgni) and strength.
For one who vomits excessively due to vāyu and whose heart is afflicted: // 20 //
3.20b–c. One should administer [the purgative] in gradual stages; to that patient, one should give unctuous, sour, and salty substances, or otherwise if pitta and kapha are predominant.
[The following complications arise] from the suppression of the urges after the medicine has been drunk, or by the action of kapha: 3.21.
3.21ab For one who has been excessively obstructed or excessively purified, the wind (māruta) seizes the limbs with unctuous, sour, and salty [food], causing stiffness,
trembling, pricking pain, exhaustion, twisting, distress, and splitting sensations.
In one whose [channels] are purified, the obstructed wind moves upward, causing exhaustion, aversion, and piercing pains.
In that condition, all wind-alleviating measures such as oleation and sudation are recommended;
likewise, potent medicine is advised for one who is hungry and has a soft bowel. (3.22–23)
Having quickly removed the feces, bile, and phlegm, it causes the liquid tissues to flow out;
if there is excessive application of this, one should scrape away the remaining medicinal substance with sweet [substances]. (24)
3.24b–c. One should cause the liquid elements of the tissues (dhātus) to flow out;
in the case of excessive emesis, purgation (reka) should be employed, and in the case of excessive purgation, mild emesis.
Furthermore, one should arrest that [excessive discharge] with very cold affusions (pariṣeka), immersions (avagāha), and so forth. 3.25.
After emesis, excessive purgation should be applied; collyrium, sandalwood, and uśīra [should be used], or goat's blood with sugar-water.
One should drink a *mantha* (gruel) made with parched grain flour (*lāja-cūrṇa*), which is the supreme remedy for excessive administration.
3.26 When there is excessive force in emesis, one should be sprinkled with cold water and drink a churned potion (mantha) made from collyrium, sandalwood, uśīra, marrow, blood, sugar, and water,
In cases of excessive belching and vomiting, one should have the patient lick a powder made of *mūrvā*, *dhānyaka*, and *mustā*, along with *madhūka* and *añjana*, mixed with honey. (28)
3.28b–c. In cases of fainting (mūrchā), [one should administer] emetics made from *dhānya* and *mustā*.
When the tongue has entered the mouth, gargles (*kavaḍagraha*) that are unctuous, sour, and salty are beneficial; likewise, soups and meat broths that are pleasing to the heart are wholesome. 3.29.
3.29c–d: Unctuous, sour, and salty foods that are pleasing to the heart are beneficial; goat meat broth is also wholesome. 3.29e–f: Other men should eat sour fruits before him;
once [the stone] has emerged, one should reinsert it coated with a paste of sesame and grapes.
And other people stand before him;
one should apply [this] paste smeared over [the body],
prepared with ghee and meat, for diseases of speech, seizure, and wind.
One who knows the proper time should administer thin gruel, as well as oleation and sudation.
And through excessive application, medicine takes away the life-blood;
that is called "taking life" because it seizes one's vitality. (32)
3.32–33. It bestows life upon men;
one should give food along with that blood to a dog or a crow.
Whether [the patient] has eaten or not, one should declare "life" or "bile" as proclaimed by the physicians.

3.33cv One should declare the *jīva* [digit] when it has been eaten; 3.33cv one should declare the *jīva* when that has been eaten; 3.33cv one should declare the *jīva* when it has been eaten and then not eaten;
3.33dv one should indicate *pitta* when it has not been eaten.
A white cloth that has been dyed, when washed with lukewarm water, becomes discolored; this indicates the presence of pitta, whereas if it remains pure, it indicates blood.
3.34d–35ab: However, when the bile is purified, it may cause thirst, fainting, and intoxication for one afflicted by them until death;
therefore, one should quickly perform treatment that cures blood-bile diarrhea and protects his life.
One should perform the life-prolonging rites for him until death. He should drink the fresh blood of deer, cows, buffaloes, or goats while they are still living;
for that blood quickly enters his own life-force, thereby restoring his vitality.
For that [blood] quickly sustains life;
therefore, one should sprinkle that very blood, squeezed with *darbha* grass, into the bladder.
Milk boiled with *śyāmā*, *kāśmarya*, *madhuka*, *dūrvā*, and *uśīra* [should also be used].
Or one should administer an enema (vasti) combined with ghee-scum and collyrium for the alleviation of fever;
or a very cold piccha-vasti, or an oil enema (anuvāsana) with ghee-scum. // 38 //
Having extracted the prolapsed rectum and stabilized it with astringent decoctions, one should reinsert it;
and for one who has lost consciousness, one should cause the sounds of Sāman chants, flutes, songs, and the like to be heard.
3.39bv Having caused [the decoction] to solidify, one should employ it.
In the Section on Pharmaceutics (Kalpasthāna), one should take one pala each of balā, guḍūcī, triphalā, rāsnā, and the two groups of five roots (dvi-pañcamūla).
One should boil eight fruits and half a *tulā* of goat meat in water until one-fourth remains. (1)

Purified with the pastes of *yavānī*, *phala*, *bilva*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *śatāhvā*, *ghana*, and *pippalī*, combined with jaggery, honey, ghee, and oil, it should be applied lukewarm and mixed with salt. (2)

This enema, purified with *yavānī*, *phala*, *bilva*, and *kuṣṭha*, is supreme for crushing all diseases; it is beneficial for those in good health, providing life-sustenance and nourishment. Furthermore, in whichever enema a medicinal paste (*kalka*) is not specifically mentioned, one should always add this very same paste therein. (3)
4.3cv Furthermore, in that case where no paste has been prescribed,
a decoction of the two groups of five roots (dvi-pañcamūla) combined with sour liquids, along with goat meat and the previously mentioned pastes,
mixed with the three unctuous substances (tri-sneha), is declared to be the most excellent non-unctuous enema (nirūha), which cures all diseases caused by Vāta. // 4 //

4.4b-v From the well-cooked meat broth of goat, together with the previous paste, along with *balā*, *paṭolī*, the minor *pañcamūla*, *trāyantikā*, castor root, and barley, one *prastha* of juice should be prepared; this should be cooked again until it reaches the quantity of one *prastha* combined with half a *prastha* of goat's milk. // 5 //

Combined with a paste of priyaṅgu, kṛṣṇā, and ghanā, along with oil, clarified butter, honey, and rock salt, this [preparation] is digestive, bestows flesh and strength, and immediately imparts strength to the eyes. (6)

Three palas of castor root, one pala of *palāśa*, and one pala each of the minor pentad roots (*laghu-pañcamūla*), along with *rāsnā*, *balā*, *chinnaruhā*, *aśvagandhā*, *punarnavā*, *āragvadha*, and *devadāru*. (7)
4.7bv Likewise, one should boil one pala each of *palāśa* and the light *pañcamūla*, along with eight fruits, in two *āḍhaka* measures of water until one-eighth remains;
then add *vacā*, *śatāhvā*, *hapuṣā*, *priyaṅgu*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *kaṇā*, seeds of *vatsaka*, and *musta*.

One should administer well-ground *sahatārkṣyaśaila* (gandhaka) in the measure of an *akṣa*, combined with a portion of salt, along with honey, oil, and urine; this enema (*vasti*) is purgative and digestive-stimulant. (9)
4.9 This enema (vasti) is digestive and carminative; it conquers pain in the calves, thighs, feet, sacrum, abdomen, heart, and genitals, as well as heaviness and constipation.
It also cures abdominal tumors (gulma), urinary stones, hernias, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), and various diseases arising from kapha and vāta located in the rectum.

4.10cd–dv: Milk boiled with liquorice (yaṣṭyāhva), lodhra, chebulic myrobalan (abhaya), sandalwood (candana), and lotuses (kamala) and water lilies (utpala) is the foremost remedy for abdominal tumors (gulma), urinary stones (aśman), scrotal enlargement (vardhma), disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-vikāra), and various diseases born of phlegm (kapha) and wind (vāta).
This [milk], well-cooled and combined with sugar, honey, ghee, and the *jīvanīya* [drugs], destroys diseases caused by *pitta*. // 11 //
4.11cd–dv: This [milk], well-cooled, mixed with sugar and honey, along with the *jīvanīya* [herbs], destroys diseases of *pitta*.
[One should also use] *rāsnā*, *vṛṣa*, *lohitikā*, *anantā*, *balā*, and the two smaller *tṛṇapañcamūla*s.
Half a pala each of gopāṅganā, candana, padmaka, yaṣṭyāhva, and lodhra. // 12 //

4.12cv Milk half-an-āḍhaka in measure, boiled with water-free decoction and juice of *gopāṅganā*, *candana*, and *padmakāhvaya*, [along with] *jīvanti*, marrow of *medā*, *ṛddhi*, *varī*, *vidārī*, *vīrā*, two kinds of *kākoli*, and *kaseruka*— [this should be used]. // 13 //
With sugar, *jīvaka*, lotus pollen, *prapauṇḍarīka*, blue lotus, white lotus, *lodhra*, *ātmaguptā*, liquorice, *nāgāhvaya*, *muñjātaka*, and sandalwood; (14)
4.14c–v: One should administer a cold Nirūha enema prepared with iron filings, Atmaguptā, and Madhuyaṣṭikā, ground together and mixed with ghee, honey, and rock salt (saindhava).
Once the enema has returned, the patient, having had his body sprinkled with water, should eat Śāli rice with the meat-broth of desert animals or with milk.

It destroys burning sensations, diarrhea, menorrhagia, hemorrhagic disorders, bile diseases, heart disease, anemia, and irregular fevers; it also cures abdominal tumors, urinary retention, jaundice, and all other diseases caused by pitta. // 16 //
It cures burning sensations, diarrhea, menorrhagia, acid dyspepsia (amlapitta),
heart disease, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and irregular fevers.
[The decoction is made from] kośātakī, āragvadha, devadāru, mūrvā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, kuṭaja, arka, and pāṭhā.
Having boiled kulattha and bṛhatī in water, there should be ten handfuls (prasṛta) of that decoction. // 17 //

These, combined with mustard seeds, *elā*, *madana*, and *kuṣṭha* in the measure of an *akṣa*, along with one *prasṛta* each of honey, oil, *phalāhvaya* (castor) oil, alkali, and mustard oil; // 18 //

4.18 One should administer an oil enema (nirūha) consisting of alkali, oil, and mustard seeds for one suffering from diseases of phlegm (kapha), for those with weak digestion, and for those who have an aversion to food.
I shall now describe mild, unctuous enemas (sneha-nirūha) made with one *prasṛta* each of these [substances], intended for those accustomed to comfort. 4.19

Now, I shall describe separately, in terms of *prasṛta* measures, these mild non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*) for children, as well as unctuous enemas (*snehana*) for those whose bodily functions have been deranged. (20)
4.20c–d For those whose [bodily constituents] have been impaired by [excessive] action (karma), two *prasṛta* measures of milk should be used, along with three measures each of honey, oil, and ghee.
An enema churned with a churning stick (*khaja*) destroys Vāta and produces strength and complexion. 4.21.
One part each of oil, clear wine (prasannā), honey, and ghee,
along with two parts of the decoction of the roots of the bilvādi group and two parts of horse-gram (kaulattha)— this [mixture] conquers vāta.
4.22 A single *prasṛta* each of the decoctions of *tailapaṭola*, *nimba*, *bhūtīka*, *rāsnā*, and *saptacchada*,
along with one *prasṛta* of clarified butter (*ājya*) and a paste (*kalka*) of mustard seeds, constitutes an enema (*vasti*).
4.23ab Of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *pūtīka*, *rāsnā*, and *saptacchada* water, [one] handful each, and from clarified butter;
this "Five Bitter" (*pañcatikta*) [decoction] destroys excessive secretions (*abhiṣyanda*), worms, skin diseases, and urinary disorders.
Four [substances] are derived from oil, cow urine, curd-whey, and sour gruel. // 24 //

It destroys worms, skin diseases, and delusion; it conquers worms, skin diseases, and urinary disorders. A handful [of this powder], ground with mustard seeds, breaks up constipation and abdominal distension.
[This formulation consists of] milk, sugarcane juice, śrīparṇī, rāsnā, vidārī, honey, and ghee.
4.25bv Breaking up the obstruction of stool and distension; 4.25bv Breaking up the obstruction of stool and distension;
4.25dv A single *prasṛta* enema each of vidārī, honey, and ghee, with the paste of kṛṣṇā, produces virility.
Therefore, I shall now describe the proven enemas (siddha-vasti) that should be employed at all times. // 26 //

Free from affliction, yielding great fruit, providing strength and nourishment, and bringing happiness—[these are the qualities of] honey and oil [taken] in equal parts, with one *karṣa* of rock salt (*saindhava*) and two *picu* of *miśī*. (27)

A Nirūha enema prepared with the decoction of castor root and Madhu-taila is a rejuvenative (rasāyana) that cures urinary disorders (prameha), hemorrhoids (arśas), worms, abdominal tumors (gulma), and hernia (antra-vṛddhi). // 28 //
This Nirūha enema, containing honey and oil along with Yaṣṭīmadhuka, removes worms, abdominal tumors (gulma), and hernia; it is beneficial for the eyes and conquers raktapitta.
This Yāpana enema contains a thick paste and consists of honey, oil, meat-broth, and ghee.
It conquers pain in the anus, knees, thighs, scrotum, bladder, and penis;
one should prepare it with parts measured in handfuls (prasṛta) along with ghee, honey, muscle fat, and oil. (30)

A decoction of castor root, combined with half an akṣa of rock salt (saindhava) and half a pala of hapuṣā, along with honey, oil, and rock salt, provides relief for the anus, calves, thighs, and scrotum. (4.30–31)
Honey, oil, rock salt, vacā, pillalī, and madanaphala— this is the "well-yoked chariot" (yuktaratha) enema;
or that decoction [of madanaphala] with honey, ṣaḍgranthā, śatāhvā, hiṅgu, and rock salt.
The decoction of those [drugs], along with honey, *ṣaḍgranthā*, *śatāhvā*, asafoetida,
rock salt, *suradāru*, and *rāsnā*, constitutes an auspicious enema (*vasti*) that removes the [bodily] humors.
Likewise, a decoction of the five roots (*pañcamūla*), oil, *māgadhikā* (long pepper), and honey [form another such preparation].

4.33a Suradāru, vacā, and rāsnā; 4.33b that enema (vasti) removes the doshas. 4.33b That enema, combined with saindhava salt and madhuka, is known as the Siddhavasti, the supreme remover of the doshas.
One should boil two roots of *pañcamūla*, the three fruits (*triphalā*), *phala* (myrobalan), and *bilva*. // 34 //
And with cow’s urine, one should grind pāṭhā, vatsaka, and toyada (musta) along with their fruits, together with honey, oil, alkali, and salt. (35)

An enema combined with alkali or salt is highly recommended for diseases of phlegm (kapha), anemia (pāṇḍu-roga), cholera-like dysentery (viṣūcī), obstructions of semen and flatus, and abdominal rumbling (vasti-āṭopa). 4.36cd–37ab.
4.36dv In cases of abdominal distension (vastyāṭopa), the following [decoction] is highly esteemed:
mustā, pāṭhā, amṛtā, eraṇḍa, balā, rāsnā, punarnavā, mañjiṣṭhā, āragvadha, uśīra, trāyamāṇā, akṣa, and rohiṇī.
One pala each of balā, rāsnā, punarnavā, trāyamāṇā, akṣa, rohiṇī,
and the minor five roots (kanīya-pañcamūla), along with eight madana fruits, should be boiled in one āḍhaka of water until reduced to one-fourth; this decoction should then be strained.

Combined with two prasthas of milk, one should cook it again until only the milk remains; this should then be mixed with a quarter-part of wild animal broth, along with ghee, honey, and rock salt. (39)
An enema prepared with the powders of yaṣṭī, miśī, śyāmā, kaliṅgaka, and rasāñjana, when applied lukewarm, increases muscle mass, digestive fire, strength, and semen. (40)
It cures disorders of wind and blood, fainting, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, retention of feces and urine, irregular fevers, erysipelas, hernia, flatulence, and dysentery. (41)
It cures vātarakta, prameha, hemorrhoids, gulma, retention of feces and urine,
and pains in the groin, thighs, waist, abdomen, neck, ears, and head.
It destroys hemorrhage, fainting, insanity, swelling, cough, urinary calculi, and earwax obstructions. // 42 //

A decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) with water is beneficial for the eyes, bestows sons, and serves as a restorative tonic for kings; it is also light and effective for deer and those who have been wounded. 43.
4.43bv Among the sustaining [meats], the *rasāyana* [is the best]. 4.43cv Of deer that are light-brown (*laghu-babhrūṇām*), 4.43cv Of deer with light plumage (*laghu-barhāṇām*),
4.43cv Of deer that are light-grey (*laghu-vaḍrāṇām*), 4.43cv Of deer that are light-brown (*laghu-vabhrāṇām*).
For small herds of deer,
an ointment made from the pastes of hapuṣā, miśi, and gāṅgeyī is the best for removing wind disorders.
This non-unctuous enema (nirūha), combined with a large quantity of unctuous substance (sneha), is an excellent aphrodisiac.

Or, it is excellent as a paste made from Vata-alleviating [substances]. A peacock, devoid of its feathers, bile, intestines, feet, excrement, and beak, should be combined with the light *pañcamūla* and *pālika*. (4.45)
Having boiled milk and water until only the milk remains, one should add ghee and honey, along with a paste of vidārī, kaṇā, yaṣṭī, śatāhvā, and phala. (46)
An enema containing a paste of *śatāhvā* fruit combined with a small amount of salt is supremely effective for increasing strength and semen.
This same preparation may also be applied separately using the meat of the common quail (*tittiri*) and other such birds.

Among all the birds that scratch the ground (viṣkira), those that peck (pratuda), and those that are powerful (prasaha), as well as among the aquatic birds and fish, this [diet]— excluding milk— is the supreme producer of strength and complexion.
One should prepare ten palas each of the flesh of the monitor lizard, mongoose, cat, porcupine, and rat, along with the five roots, in milk. (49)
That milk, combined with the paste of *phala* and *vaidehī*, the two salts, sugar, oil, honey, and clarified butter, should be employed as an enema (*vasti*) as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). (50)
Sugar, oil, honey,

and ghee [should be used] for those whose chest is exhausted by physical exertion, whose sensory faculties, strength, and vital essence (*ojas*) are depleted, and for those suffering from disorders of obstructed semen, feces, urine, or *khuḍa*-type wind (*vāta*). (4.50–51)

This supreme aphrodisiac restores youthfulness to those whose bodies are broken, shattered, or afflicted by constipation, seminal disorders, or the exhaustion caused by elephants, horses, and chariots. 4.51–52.
4.52d–53ab: This is the most excellent aphrodisiac (vājīkaraṇa);
it should be eaten with prepared milk along with *ātmaguptā*, *uccaṭā*, and sugar.
One should also prepare unrestrictive fats (snehas) using these proven ingredients.

4.53–54. Now, the unctuous enemas (sneha-vasti) that are enriched with excellent qualities, which cure the humors (doṣa), and for which specific post-procedural restrictions (parihāra) are prescribed, will be described.
[The decoction should be prepared from] daśamūla, balā, rāsnā, aśvagandhā, and punarnavā.
4.54ab Guḍūcī, eraṇḍa, bhūtīka, bhārgī, vṛṣaka, rohiṣa, śatāvarī, sahacara, and kākanāsā— one pala each of these— destroy the doṣas and require no restrictive regimen (niṣparihāra). // 55 //
Take one *pala* each of *guḍūcī*, *airaṇḍa*, *pūtīka*, and *kākanāsā*; and one *prasṛta* each of barley, black gram, linseed, jujube, and horse gram.
Having boiled it until one *droṇa* of water remains, [one should use] that decoction. // 56 //
One should cook one āḍhaka of oil with one pala each of the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs as a paste;
this is an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) that cures all disorders of vāta.
One should cook one *āḍhaka* of oil with these pastes; it conquers all disorders of vāta.
Similarly, the fat (*vasā*) of marshy animals, prepared with the *jīvanīya* drugs, [is effective].
Oil prepared with *śatāhvā*, *ciribilva*, and acidic substances [is likewise] for vāta.

4.58c–d: Similarly, oil prepared with *śatāhvā*, barley, *bilva*, and sour liquids [is used] for Vāta; likewise, ghee heated to the color of fire with *saindhava* salt conquers Vāta. [One should also use] *jīvantī*, *madana*, *medā*, *śrāvaṇī*, *madhuka*, and *balā*.
4.59: [These, along with] *jīvantī*, *madana*, *medā*, *śrāvaṇī*, *madhuka*, and *balā*...
Śatāvarī, ṛṣabhaka, kālā, kākanāsā, śatāvarī, svaguptā, kṣīrakākolī, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, śaṭhī, and vacā. (60)
Having ground [the herbs], one should cook oil and ghee in four times as much milk;
this is nourishing, destroys Vāta and Pitta, and increases strength, semen, and digestive fire. // 61 //

Having ground [these], one should prepare oil and ghee in four times the amount of milk; this enema (anuvāsana) removes disorders of the female reproductive tract and semen, promotes the birth of a son,
and consists of rock salt, madana, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, nicula, and vacā.
4.62ab An oil enema (anuvāsana) that removes the menstrual blood, semen, and wind, and which leads to the birth of a son, consists of:
4.62cd hrīvera, madhuka, bhārgī, devadāru, and kaṭphala; nāgara, puṣkara, medā, cavikā, citraka, and śaṭhī.

4.63–64ab. *Hrīvera*, *padmaka*, *bhārgī*, *viḍaṅga*, *ativiṣā*, *śyāmā*, *hareṇu*, *nīlinī*, *sthirā*, *bilva*, *ajamodā*, *capalā*, *dantī*, and *rāsnā*—with these taken in equal parts: 4.64cd. [One should prepare a decoction with] these [drugs].
Viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, and śyāmā; bilva, ajamodā,
and capalā—
castor oil or other oils processed with these should be administered to destroy diseases caused by phlegm (kapha).
It cures enlargement of the spleen, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, urinary disorders, and excessive vāta. (65)

Castor oil (eraṇḍa-taila) should be prepared [as an enema]; it removes diseases born of kapha and vāta, and when used as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana), it quickly destroys abdominal distension (ānāha) and urinary calculi (aśmarī).
Alternatively, oil may be prepared with the five roots (pañcamūla) or with the bilva group of herbs.

One should prepare an oil that subdues *kapha*, or one cooked with *kapha*-destroying substances; an unctuous enema (*anvāsana*) prepared with eight times the amount of sour fruits is indicated for *kapha*.
4.67c–d When [the bladder] has become softened and numbed by eightfold sour fruits, another sharp enema is desired;
when it has been drawn out by sharp [drugs], a smooth, sweet, cold, and mild [enema] is required. 4.68cd–69ab.

4.68 When the soft tissue has become numb, sharpness [of the instrument] should be applied at the appropriate time using urine, pilu, fire (ash), salt, alkali, and mustard seeds; however, softness should be restored with milk, clarified butter, and similar substances.
4.69a Sharpness [of the digestive fire] is produced by urine, bilva, and agni; 4.69d Mildness is produced by milk, clarified butter (ājya), and so forth;
4.69d Mildness is indeed produced by milk and other such substances;
4.69d Mildness is produced by ghee and milk.
An enema administered after having analyzed the strength, age, disease, humors, and constitution, using the respective groups of medicinal substances, cures each of its corresponding diseases. (70)
Having carefully examined the constitutional types (*prakṛti*), the enema (*vasti*) thus administered removes each respective disorder (*doṣa*).

One should administer enemas composed of drugs appropriate for that purpose—cold ones for those afflicted by heat, warm ones for those afflicted by cold, and comfortably lukewarm ones for others—after due deliberation. (4.71)

One should not administer nourishing enemas (br̥ṃhaṇīya-vasti) in diseases that require purification; likewise, those who are obese, those requiring purification, and men afflicted by skin diseases (kuṣṭha) or urinary disorders (meha) [should not receive them]. // 72 //
One should administer purificatory therapies for diseases that require cleansing,
except in the case of those who are emaciated, wounded, weak, fainting, thin, dehydrated, or whose bodies have been recently purified.
One should also administer purificatory therapies to those whose life-force is bound up within the morbid humors (doṣas).
If administered to one whose body has not been lubricated or fomented, whose digestive tract is heavy,
or who is given a dose that is cold, deficient in oiliness and salt, or even if it is thick— (these factors cause complications). // 1 //

5.1dv Whether the enema (vasti) consists merely of liquids or is even thick, if it agitates that dosha but fails to expel it due to weakness, it causes inadequate administration (ayoga); by this, there occurs retention of flatus, urine, and feces. // 2 //
5.2ab That enema, having caused the morbid humor (doṣa) to become stagnant, results in pain at the navel and bladder, a burning sensation, a coating on the heart,
swelling in the anus, itching, eruptions, discoloration, restlessness, and weakness of the digestive fire. // 3 //
Pain in the navel and bladder, constipation, itching, swelling, and discoloration of the skin; [or] itching, swelling, and discoloration of the eyes—
these occur in a patient with diarrhea and moderate doshas for whom the two previously prescribed decoctions have been administered.
Therefore, among those, the drinking of that single warm [substance] is recommended. // 4 //
5.4dv In that condition, drinks, fruit-purgatives, as well as sudations, and purgation at the appropriate time are prescribed;
[the decoction] containing bilva root, trivṛt, devadāru, barley, kola, and kulattha [is used]. 5.5ab.
One should administer an enema containing wine and other liquids along with urine and the aforementioned paste;
this is appropriate when the patient has diminished vitality, is dominated by the humors (doṣas), is dry, or has a hard bowel.
5.6ab There, an enema containing wine and meat may have its path obstructed by doshas; thus blocked, it would obstruct the wind (vāyu).
That wind, having gone astray, would cause flatulence and pain in the vital organs (marman). // 7 //
It causes a burning sensation in the anus and abdomen, pain in the scrotum and groin, and constricts the heart; with piercing pains, the patient runs hither and thither. (8)
For one whose limbs have been well-anointed and fomented, one should apply an enema (varti) there;
the Nirūha enema should consist of the Bilva group of drugs along with Pīlu, mustard seeds, and urine.
For one whose limbs have been anointed and fomented— whose body has been well-anointed and fomented— an oil enema (anuvāsana) prepared with *saralā* and *devadāru* should be administered.
For one who suppresses the natural urges while suffering from an excessive degree of wind, [this occurs]. // 10 //

5.10b Or an oil enema (anuvāsana) that has been prepared [improperly]; 5.10d or an enema that is squeezed with excessive force, or one that is unsmeared with oil, lacking salt, or lacking heat; or one that is too small in quantity or contains too few medicinal ingredients; or one that is too mild—[all these] may be driven upward by the wind (māruta) through the mouth and nostrils.
It emerges, bringing about fainting, nausea, thirst, burning sensations, and so forth; seeing these symptoms of the disorder of fainting, one should sprinkle his face with cold water. (12)
One should induce thirst, burning sensations, and other such symptoms; one should perform fanning until exhaustion is relieved and practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
With the face turned downward, one should massage the back, sides, and abdomen with warm hands. (5.13)

5.13 One should exercise until exhaustion is dispelled; one should exercise until exhaustion is no longer present; one should exercise until exhaustion is destroyed. One should massage the back, the sides, and the abdomen.

One should pull [the enema bag] by the hair and shake it, or frighten it with beasts of prey and fanged animals; likewise, one should use weapons, firebrands, or royal officers, for in this way the enema (vasti) moves downward. 14.

5.14b–c One should frighten [the victim] with beasts of prey and fanged animals; one should apply pressure to the throat with the hands or a cloth so that he does not die, for by the obstruction of the *prāṇa* and *udāna* breaths, the path [of consciousness] becomes even more clearly established. 15.
The downward-moving wind (apāna) quickly draws that [semen] back into the bladder;
one should then cause the patient to drink a paste of kuṣṭha and kramuka mixed with sour substances. // 16 //
5.16b–d: Likewise, he should immediately extract [the fetus]; or, one should have her drink a paste of *kuṣṭha* and *kramuka* combined with sour substances.
Because of its heat, sharpness, and fluidity, it will cause his bladder to move downward.
Or, a paste of trivṛt and pathyā with cow's urine acts as a downward purgative. // 17 //

And when [the poison] is located in the colon (pakvāśaya), once it has been induced to move downward with a paste (kalka) and the patient has undergone sudation, a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) prepared with the ten roots (daśamūlī) and cooked with barley,
jujube (kola), and horse gram (kulattha), along with urine, should be administered. (5.18)
5.18–19. An enema prepared with cow’s urine, or cooked with cow’s urine together with *amṛtā*, bamboo shoots,
the bark and leaves of *pūtikarañja*, *śaṭhī*, *devāhva*, and *rohiṣa*, should be administered as prescribed.
An enema prepared with oil, jaggery, and rock salt, containing a paste of purgative drugs and the five roots beginning with *bilva*, is indicated for [diseases] located in the chest. (20)
If the head is afflicted, one should administer nasal drops (nāvana), medicated smoke (dhūma), or cover the head with mustard seeds;
or, in the case of one who has been excessively fomented, an enema (vasti) that is too hot, sharp, sour, or thick [should be used]. 21.
If administered repeatedly for a minor ailment or in a person with a mild digestive tract, it may reach a state of excessive action (atiyoga) and cause pain in the abdomen. // 22 //

By means of excessive purgation, that [condition] is treated with an enema (vasti) having similar properties—containing alkali, acid, sharp, hot, and salty substances—for one suffering from pitta. (23)
5.23dv–5.24ab. Furthermore, the salty [enema] burns, scrapes, and lacerates the rectum of one with a pitta disorder, causing it to discharge [mucus].
It causes the rectum to discharge vitiated blood and bile in many colors.

5.24b-v It causes profuse discharge of blood with great force, and the patient repeatedly falls into a state of fainting; in that case, treatment that cures hemorrhagic diarrhea caused by *rakta-pitta* is recommended. (25)
5.25ab Through excessive use, one frequently falls into a state of delusion; 5.25cd or one repeatedly falls into a state of delusion.
In cases of burning sensations and other such symptoms, one should drink a paste of trivṛt with grape juice.
For that [cold water], having removed bile, feces, and wind, overcomes burning sensations and other such ailments. // 26 //
5.26 Having suppressed burning sensations and other such symptoms, and once purified, one should drink cold gruel mixed with sugar.
For one who has been excessively purged or whose feces are diminished, one should administer food.

5.27b–c One should administer gruel mixed with sugar, or boiled rice with black gram soup, or curd, or wine, as a drink. Thus is the successful management of complications arising from enemas; now the procedure for unctuous enemas will be described. // 28 //
5.28dv The [details regarding] unctuous enemas (sneha-vasti) will be explained [later]. 5.28dv Now, the preparation of the unctuous substance (sneha-kalpa) will be described:

it should be cold and small in dose when vāta is predominant; very hot when pitta is predominant; and mild when kapha is predominant. It should be heavy after excessive eating, and likewise weak in potency when there is an accumulation of feces.
The affection bestowed by them, being overwhelmed even by these symptoms— stiffness, trembling of the thighs, lassitude, flatulence, fever, colic, and aching of the limbs— does not return.
5.30b–c: One should recognize that when oil is obstructed by vāyu, it does not descend due to oppression, but rather causes pain in the flanks and a twisting sensation;
this should be treated with unctuous, sour, salty, and hot substances, along with rāsnā, pītadru, and oils. 5.31a–b: [One should treat it] with rāsnā, pītadru, and oils.
One should properly eliminate [the doshas] with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) prepared with sauvīraka, surā, kola, kulattha, and yava, along with cow's urine and the five roots (pāñcamūla). // 32 //

One should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) in the evening after a meal, using sauvīraka, surā, aṅkolla, and the five roots (pañcamūla) along with urine, or with those same two oils, for those suffering from thirst,
burning sensations, redness, delusion, discoloration, and tamaka fever.
One should recognize that [the fever] covered by pitta is caused by those same two oils; one should eliminate it with enemas (vasti) containing sweet and bitter substances.
[It is characterized] by drowsiness, cold fever, lassitude, excessive salivation, loss of appetite, and heaviness. // 34 //
5.34b–35. One should expel that [unabsorbed oil] with bitter substances; one should recognize that the oil is occluded by kapha through fainting and malaise.
It should be removed with decoctions that are bitter, pungent, and astringent, prepared with wine and urine.
One should recognize [the condition] by its fainting and exhaustion;
one should eliminate it with enemas prepared with wine and cow's urine, combined with fruit-oils and sour liquids.
[It is characterized] by vomiting, fainting, loss of appetite, malaise, colic, drowsiness, and aching of the limbs. // 36 //

5.36–37ab. One should recognize that [fever] as being obstructed by overeating when it is accompanied by colic, drowsiness, body-aches, and the symptoms of undigested matter (āma), along with a burning sensation. Its digestion is brought about by decoctions and powders of pungent and salty substances.
5.37b–v One should recognize that [fever] as being obstructed by *āma*; in that case, a mild purgative is beneficial, and everything prescribed for *āma* is wholesome.
[It is further characterized] by the retention of feces, urine, and flatus, pain, heaviness, flatulence, and cardiac oppression.

Having recognized that the oleaginous substance (sneha) is obstructed by feces, one should treat it with oleation and sudation using suppositories (varti), as well as with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) prepared with Śyāmā, Bilva, and other such drugs. // 39 //
One should properly expel [the doshas] by means of the procedure that removes udāvarta;
this should be done when the patient has not eaten, or when the anus is swollen, or when he has consumed only a small measure of liquid gruel (peyā). // 40 //

Or, by means of a preparation that removes *udāvarta*, [the oil] may be administered; however, for one who has eaten only the quantity of gruel prescribed for the enema, the unobstructed oil, having been introduced into the rectum, rushes upward with force and reaches the upper body, even passing through the channels above the throat. (5.40–41)

5.41cv Then, for the upper body from the throat upwards, a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) prepared with *mūtrāśyāmā* and *trivṛt*, containing barley, *kola*, and *kulattha*, along with oil processed with those same ingredients, should be administered, as well as an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*). 42.
One should effect its eradication by means of emesis, throat-stirring, gripping the throat, purgation, and treatments that suppress vomiting as it rises from the throat. (43)
One should not administer unrefined oil, for it will smear the rectum; this may then cause pain, delusion, itching, and swelling. The treatment for this is as follows: 44.

One should not administer an unripened oil enema; for if one does so, it may cause vomiting, delusion, pain in the thighs, and fainting. Likewise, a sharp oil enema prepared with the juice of *arka* leaves [should be used].
But if [the food] is bound without being allowed to breathe, or if it is given entirely without remainder, // 45 //

5.45cv If [the enema] is administered without being held back or while it is still attached, or 5.45dv if it is administered without being fully expelled or while it remains entirely inside, the agitated *vāyu* enters and causes piercing pain and colic.
In that case, there should be oil massage, fomentation of the rectum, and foods that subdue Vāta.
5.46dv Furthermore, if wind-alleviating foods are served too quickly, or if [the enema] is withdrawn, or suddenly pulled out,
there may occur stiffness and pain in the waist, anus, calves, thighs, and bladder, as well as piercing sensations.
In that case, food that subdues Vāta, as well as sudation, oil massages, and enemas [are indicated].
When the rectum is pressed and then released during the procedure, the Vāyu becomes obstructed within. (48)
A strong enema may cause pain in the chest and head, as well as a sinking sensation in the thighs;
in that case, an enema containing the fruits of the *bilvādi* group, the roots of the *śyāmādi* group, and urine should be administered. (49)

5.49 In that case, an enema (vasti) consisting of the bilvādi group, along with the fruits of śyāmādi and urine, should be administered. If [the medicine] is excessively pressed, it may remain in the abdomen or rise to the throat; in such cases, an enema, purgation (vireka), and treatments for throat irritation and similar conditions should be employed. 50.
5.50b–c. Or, while standing, he may vomit it up;
once purified by emetics and other therapies, his body, strength, and digestive fire become diminished, like a fresh egg or a vessel filled with oil. 5.51.
Once the patient has been purified by therapeutic procedures such as emesis and the like, the physician should diligently protect him from all improper conduct. Thereafter,
he should administer sweet and palatable foods, followed by those of sour and salty tastes.
5.52b–c: Compared to everything else, the sweet and bitter tastes are more [palatable] than the astringent and pungent;
among tastes that are mutual opposites, as are the unctuous and the dry.
By using [the regimen] in reverse order, one should gradually restore it to its natural state.
When it can endure everything and possesses stable strength, it should be known as having returned to its natural state. // 54 //
In the section on the site (Kalpasthāna):
In a desert region that is common [to many], level, with good soil, and pure;
and free from cemeteries, sacred shrines, pits, and anthills. // 1 //
6.1 In a region that is arid yet temperate, on ground free from cremation grounds, shrines, and the like, where the water flows clockwise, strewn with *kuśa* and *rohiṣa* grass,
unploughed by the furrow, and untrampled by more powerful trees; // 2 //

6.2bv Medicinal plants grown on ground prepared with *kuśa* and *rohiṣa* grasses are recommended, provided they are endowed with excellent color, taste, and other qualities; that they have not been eaten by insects, nor scorched by fire, nor damaged by any deformities. // 3 //
