6.3c–d That which is not inhabited by living creatures, nor burnt by fire, nor devoured by abnormal beings; 6.3d–4 That which has been utilized at the proper time for shade, sunlight, water, and so forth;
that which has deeply penetrated the earth with great roots and is situated toward the northern direction.
6.4dv To those situated in the northern direction—
whether they be the Brahmins Mahendra, Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa, or even the cattle— be appeased through austerity or through splendor for the sake of auspiciousness! 4+(1)

6.4+(1) Whether by means of austerities or by means of fiery powers, O twice-born ones, you must indeed become tranquil for the sake of peace; with this mantra, a wise man should bring even every remedy under control. 4+(2)ab //
Then, one of virtuous conduct, faithful, pure, and having fasted, should take the medicine while it is fresh and administer it at the proper time. (5)
If that [gift] is not obtained with milk, it remains valid for no more than one year,
except in the case of molasses, ghee, honey, grain, black pepper, and viḍaṅga.
6.6cv Except for ghee, jaggery, honey, milk, and the excrement and urine of a *bāṣkayaṇa* (a calf one year old), which may be accepted even from those free of disease;
likewise, the feathers, horns, hooves, and so forth of animals endowed with youth and strength [may be taken]. // 7 //
6.7bv And that feces and urine are free from pain; 6.7dv [The animal's] tail,
horns, hooves, and so forth [are affected by] bile.
The five tastes, excluding salt, are the sources of decoctions (kaṣāya).
Their preparations consist of: juice (rasa), paste (kalka), boiled decoction (śṛta), cold infusion (śīta), and hot infusion (phāṇṭa). // 8 //
6.8dv And *phāṇṭa*—these are the five types of decoctions (*kaṣāya*); each preceding one is more potent than the next.
That which flows from [the plant] immediately after being uprooted and crushed, when pressed through a cloth, is the *phāṇṭa*. // 9 //

6.9ab Furthermore, among the five decoctions, each preceding one possesses greater strength. 6.9cd [That which flows from] freshly uprooted and crushed [medicinal plants], when pressed through a cloth, 6.9d [is the most potent].
That which is [administered] as it is is designated as its own juice (svarasa); a paste (kalka) is ground and saturated with liquid;
a powder (cūrṇa) is unsaturated; a decoction (kvātha) is boiled; and a cold infusion (śīta) is that which has stood in liquid overnight. // 10 //

6.10dv Cold [water], used at night, in a liquid state, and immediately strained after being freshly pressed, is a *phāṇṭa* decoction; in determining its dosage, one should employ it according to the strength of the disease and other factors, as per the statement of the Sage. 11.

6.11ab However, for that which is freshly crushed and purified, there is no fixed dosage; rather, having considered the disease, the constitution of the patient, strength, age, as well as place and time, the pharmaceutical preparation should be administered accordingly.
There is no fixed rule for the dosage; it depends on the humors, the digestive fire, strength, and age.
However, the standard measure for a decoction (svarasa) is specified as four palas.
One karṣa of a powder (peṣya) should be stirred into three palas of liquid.

6.13ab The method for measuring [liquids] is specified: one should prepare a decoction from one *pala* of substance, reduced to half a *prastha*, with one-fourth remaining; when cooled, it is mixed with six *palas* [of sugar], and after that, another four *palas*.

And after that, another [measure] with four [parts]; but after that, when the quantity of oil is not specified in the cooking process, Śaunaka further teaches that the paste, the oil, and the liquid should be combined in an increasing ratio of four times each.
When the unctuous substance has been prepared, one should gradually add a fourth, sixth, or eighth part of the paste to pure water, decoctions, or expressed juices respectively. 16.

One should add the solid ingredients separately in equal measure to the liquid, starting from five parts of liquid; however, the paste should not cling to the fingers, nor should the oil make a crackling sound when heated over the fire.
6.17ab However, one should add five or more liquids separately, equal in measure to the oily substance (sneha).
When there is no dry substance [to weigh], then that which has been freshly extracted should be used; double that amount should be employed for liquids such as a *kuḍava* and so forth. 17.1+1.
And when there is excellence of color and so forth, one should extract it quickly;
for the subsiding of the froth of ghee occurs [when it is fresh], whereas its emergence occurs with oil. (18)
6.18d–19. From that [oil] is produced the medicinal extract (*leha*);
its characteristics are the presence of threads, sinking in water, and lack of flow.
Its cooking (*pāka*) is of three kinds: mild (*manda*), sticky (*cikkaṇa*), and rough-sticky (*khara-cikkaṇa*).

6.19b–c: Immersion is not a refuge for the dull-witted; when the dregs are like paste, it is sticky like *madana*; and when it is somewhat black, the latter [type] sinks while being rolled into a wick. 6.19d: And the last [type] sinks slightly while being made into a wick.

And while it is still functioning, the last [dosha] is the one present; once it has been burnt, it should be expelled thereafter. However, if it remains undigested (āma), it causes the subsidence of the digestive fire (agni-sāda).
It should be soft for nasal administration, rough for massage, and unctuous for drinking and enema.
One should know that the śāṇa, pāṇitala, muṣṭi, kuḍava, prastha, āḍhaka, droṇa, and vaha increase fourfold in succession.
One should employ double the quantity for moist substances such as *kuḍava* and the like, as well as for liquids;
water is used for grinding and mixing, while in the cooking of fats, no liquid is used.
One should divide into equal portions where no specific measure has been mentioned;
and one should reduce to a paste (kalka) that medicine for which no specific method of preparation has been specified.
When the constituent parts have been mentioned, that itself shall be the basis even if they are not well-known.
Two *śāṇas* make a *vaṭaka*, a *kola*, a *badara*, and a *draṅkṣaṇa*. (25)
6.25 In cases where [weights] are not specifically mentioned and are not well-known, the root [measure] should be understood for things such as bark and the like:
two *śāṇas* make one *vaṭaka*; a *kola* is six *vaṃśyas*; a *marīci* consists of six *vaṃśyas*; and six *marīcis* make one *sarṣapa*.
Eight *taṇḍula*s are a *sarṣapa*; two of those are a *dhānyamāṣa*, and [eight] of those are a *yava*.
Two *dhānyamāṣas* make one *yava*; two of those make one *aṇḍikā*; four of those make one *māṣaka*, as do four *śāṇakas*.
6.25.1+(2)a So many [four] are said to be a *māṣa*; 6.25.1+(2)b with four of those *guñjās* a *māṣa* is formed; 6.25.1+(2)c this is remembered by the sages as a *śāṇa*.

Four *turyās* are traditionally said to be a *śāṇaka*; likewise, an *akṣa*, a *picu*, a *pāṇitala*, a *suvarṇa*, a *kavaḍagraha*, a *karṣa*, a *biḍālapadaka*, a *tinduka*, and a *pāṇimānikā* [are each equal]. (26)
6.26b–d. A *kavaḍagraha* is equal to one *suvarṇa*; a *tinduka* is a *pāṇimānikā*.
When the meaning is not distinct, the terms *śukti*, *aṣṭamikā*, and *picu* are synonymous;
likewise are *pala*, *prakuñca*, *bilva*, *muṣṭi*, *āmra*, and *caturthikā*. 6.27. [The same applies to these measures.]

6.27 Thus, these words refer to the same meaning: "two *pala*s are a *prasṛta*; those two [*prasṛta*s] are an *añjali*; two [*añjali*s] are a *mānikā*; an *āḍhaka* is a vessel; a *kaṃsa*, a *droṇa*, a *kumbha*, a *ghaṭa*, and an *armaṇa* [are synonyms for a measure]. 6.28 [Continued: "Two *āḍhaka*s are a *droṇa*; two *droṇa*s are a *khārī*; twenty *khārī*s are a *vāha*; four *vāha*s are a *kuvya*. 6.29 "A *kuvya* is also called a *bhāra*; a *kuvya* of sesame seeds is known as a *kharva*; a *kharva* of gold is a *niṣka*; a *niṣka* of silver is a *dharaṇa*. 6.30 "A *dharaṇa* of copper is a *paṇa*; a *paṇa* of iron is a *śatamāna*; a *śatamāna* of lead is a *dharaṇa*; a *dharaṇa* of tin is a *karṣa*. 6.31 "A *karṣa* of silver is a *māṣa*; a *māṣa* of gold is a *māṣaka*; a *māṣaka* of copper is a *kākiṇī*; a *kākiṇī* of lead is a *kākini*. 6.32 "A *kākini* of tin is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of iron is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of wood is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of stone is a *kākini*. 6.33 "A *kākini* of glass is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of clay is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of cotton is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of wool is a *kākini*. 6.34 "A *kākini* of silk is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of linen is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of hemp is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of jute is a *kākini*. 6.35 "A *kākini* of flax is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of bark-cloth is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of leather is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of hide is a *kākini*. 6.36 "A *kākini* of bone is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of horn is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of ivory is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of tusk is a *kākini*. 6.37 "A *kākini* of shell is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of pearl is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of coral is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of ruby is a *kākini*. 6.38 "A *kākini* of sapphire is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of emerald is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of diamond is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of lapis lazuli is a *kākini*. 6.39 "A *kākini* of crystal is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of quartz is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of amber is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of agate is a *kākini*. 6.40 "A *kākini* of onyx is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of carnelian is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of topaz is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of cat's-eye is a *kākini*. 6.41 "A *kākini* of moonstone is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of sunstone is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of fire-crystal is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of water-crystal is a *kākini*. 6.42 "A *kākini* of gold is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of silver is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of copper is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of bronze is a *kākini*. 6.43 "A *kākini* of bell-metal is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of brass is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of steel is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of iron is a *kākini*. 6.44 "A *kākini* of lead is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of tin is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of mercury is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of quicksilver is a *kākini*. 6.45 "A *kākini* of poison is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of salt is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of sugar is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of honey is a *kākini*. 6.46 "A *kākini* of ghee is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of oil is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of milk is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of curd is a *kākini*. 6.47 "A *kākini* of buttermilk is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of whey is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of molasses is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of jaggery is a *kākini*. 6.48 "A *kākini* of rice is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of barley is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of wheat is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of millet is a *kākini*. 6.49 "A *kākini* of beans is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of lentils is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of chickpeas is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of peas is a *kākini*. 6.50 "A *kākini* of sesame is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of mustard is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of linseed is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of hemp-seed is a *kākini*. 6.51 "A *kākini* of jute-seed is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of cotton-seed is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of flax-seed is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of bark-seed is a *kākini*. 6.52 "A *kākini* of fruit is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of flower is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of leaf is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of root is a *kākini*. 6.53 "A *kākini* of bulb is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of tuber is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of spice is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of condiment is a *kākini*. 6.54 "A *kākini* of medicine is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of incense is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of perfume is a *kākini*; a *kākini* of unguent is a *kākini*. 6.55 "A *kākini* of cloth
Two *pala*s make one *prasṛti*; two of those make one *tulā*, which is one hundred *pala*s; twenty of those are called a *bhāra*.
The earth is for the most part covered by the Himavat and Vindhya mountains.
6.29 One hundred palas of those [herbs] constitute one tulā; among them, the first group is mild and wholesome, while the latter consists of fiery and mountainous medicinal plants.

6.29 Therein, the first [medicine] is said to be cooling (saumya), the second fiery (āgneya), and the third is the Vindhyan herb (vaidhya). Immediately after birth, the infant should be cleansed of the placenta (ulba) with rock salt (saindhava) and ghee.
And one should sprinkle the woman, distressed by the pains of childbirth, with oil prepared from *balā*. // 1 //
One should also strike two stones at his ear-root;
then, one should recite this mantra into his right ear: // 2 //
From limb after limb you are produced; from the heart you are born.
You are indeed the self (ātman) named "son"; live for a hundred autumns! // 3 //
O Saṃjīva, may you live for a hundred autumns;
you are one whose life-span is a hundred years, so may you attain long life.
1.4dv For four days, one should protect the navel of the person who has recovered from the thread at a distance of four finger-breadths;
having tied it above and extended it, one should fasten it around the neck. // 5 //
Having tied [the cord] with 1.5 *cuvits* and extended it upwards, one should fasten it around the neck with 1.5 *dvats*.
One should then sprinkle the navel with *kuṣṭha*-oil and subsequently bathe it with a decoction of milk-tree bark or with water scented with all fragrant substances. // 6 //
One should sprinkle and bathe the navel with Kuṣṭha-oil,
using lukewarm water, and immerse it in heated silver and gold.
Then, with the right index finger, one should press down on the palate and cover it.
One should apply an oil-soaked cotton pad to the head and administer a dose the size of a hareṇu seed for the sake of intelligence, longevity, and strength, having consecrated it with mantras.
1.8bv One should administer a medicinal gruel (*prāśa*) for him, consisting of a paste of *aindrī*, *brāhmī*, *vacā*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, along with ghee and honey.
[Alternatively,] gold, *vacā*, *brāhmī*, *tāpya*, and *pathyā* should be reduced to a fine powder. // 9 //
One should lick a powder of *kuṣṭha* and *pathyā* processed with *rajī*, combined with honey and ghee; or else, a powder of *hema* and *dhātrī*.
Thereafter, one should induce emesis with the water of a pregnant woman (*garbhāmbhas*) mixed with *saindhava* salt and clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). // 10 //
Then, one should cause [the child] to vomit using womb-water (*garbhāmbhas*), rock salt (*saindhava*), and *vacā* mixed with ghee (*sarpiṣ*).
Thereafter, one should perform the birth-rites (*jātakarman*) according to the Prajāpati procedure.
This is because, at the time of delivery, the vessels situated in the heart become dilated.
The breast milk of women flows forth on the third or fourth day;
therefore, on the first day, one should [administer] honey and ghee three times. (12)
One should have the child consume [the medicine] mixed with *anantā* and purified by mantras;
then, on the second day, that which is prepared with *lakṣmaṇā*, and on the third day, ghee. (13)
For this child whose breast-feeding has been previously prohibited,
one should administer fresh butter at two times of the day, measured by the palm of his hand, as a drink to follow the breast milk.

The child should drink only his mother’s milk, for that is sufficient for the growth of the body; however, if she is unable to provide it, two wet-nurses who are affectionate toward him should be appointed.
1.15b–d. That [is] for the growth of the body;
[the couple should be] free from physical defects, celibate, equal in terms of caste and constitution, free from disease, middle-aged, having living offspring, and not greedy.
One should also carefully attend to her with wholesome food and conduct;
for sexual intercourse, anger, fasting, and over-exertion are the causes of the loss of breast milk. (17)
For breast milk, one should avoid wines other than *sīdhu*, the meat juices of marshy animals, milky plants, and the opposites of grief and so forth. (18)

The milk of milky plants, when consumed by a pregnant woman who has eaten incompatible food, is hungry, lacks self-control, and whose bodily constituents (dhātus) are vitiated, causes disease in the infant. 1.18c–d, 1.19.
1.19 In the absence of breast milk due to incompatible food and activity, one should drink goat's or cow's milk that possesses similar qualities;
or [one may take] the five roots (pañcamūla) of the *hrasva* group, or those of the *sthira* group, combined with sugar.
Having performed special rites of protection and offerings on the sixth night with roots such as those of the *bṛhatī* group,
his kinsmen, maintaining supreme joy, should remain awake throughout that night.
When the tenth day is complete, one should perform the rising from confinement according to the rites appropriate to one's own family,
and perform the honored naming ceremony for the child.
1.22bv Bearing, according to the prescribed rite,
on their limbs realgar, gorocana, agallochum, and sandalwood—
beings appropriate to their own lineage, or [names] associated with a lunar mansion deity and consisting of an equal number of syllables.

Then, the wise physician should perform an examination of the lifespan of the child—who is lying with the head toward the east or north—using the forms described according to the various constitutions (prakṛti). 24.
The bedding, coverlets, and garments were clean, washed, free of wrinkles, soft, and perfumed with incense that wards off demons.
A crow, dissected and prepared as a medicinal paste combined with *trivṛt*, is used for fumigation;
likewise, a child should always wear auspicious gems originating from the horns of living rhinoceroses and other such animals.

The heron (kaṅka) is both dissected and praised. One should wear the most excellent medicinal herbs—such as brāhmī, aindrī, and the group beginning with jīvaka—found on living lions and other such creatures.
One should especially and constantly hold vācā with both hands, the neck, and the head.
One should cause him to wear excellent medicinal herbs—

those that promote longevity, intelligence, memory, and health, and provide protection against demons— on the sixth, seventh, or eighth month, on an auspicious day, provided he is free from illness. (1.27–28)
1.28c–29. In the sixth, seventh, or eighth month, at the onset of winter, the physician should pierce the ears of the child while he is held by his nurse and being consoled;
first the right ear of a male child, but the left of a female.
Holding a needle with his right hand and a probe with the other hand,
he applies it slightly toward the cheek, at the center of the ear-base.
[The fetus] is properly covered only by the placenta, illuminated by the rays of the sun,
motionless like clarified butter, and marked with the essence of lac-dye.
One should pierce once, straight and with lightness, at the opening created by fate;
not upwards, nor to the side, nor downwards, for the vessels are situated there.

From that piercing [of the channels], there arise blackish, parched, and red discolorations, as well as passion, disease, and fever, accompanied by swelling, burning sensations, agitation, stiffness of the neck (manyā-stambha), and facial paralysis (apatānaka). // 33 //
1.33bv Due to the obstruction of those [channels], there arise passion, disease, and fever; one should quickly administer their treatment after differentiating it according to the specific ailment.
1.34c–d. To prevent bleeding from the site of the puncture, one should apply a thread pierced by a needle and soaked in oil;
likewise, one should sprinkle it with raw oil using an awl. 1.35.
One should pierce the earlobe with a needle, and then insert a thicker wick;
after three days, once it has healed, one should gradually increase its size.
After three days, one should replace that thick wick with another. Once it has healed, one should gradually withdraw the child from the breast;
then, one should provide the milk mentioned previously along with light, nourishing solid food.
When a child has teethed, one should gradually wean him from the breast during the cold season. For a child who has ceased nursing,
a nourishing sweetmeat (*modaka*) should be prepared using the marrow of *priyāla* fruit, *madhuka*, honey, parched rice (*lāja*), and sugar, and administered to satisfy the infant.
The digestive stimulant [is prepared] with long pepper, bilva, cardamom, sugar, parched rice, and barley flour;
the astringent [is prepared] with dhātakī flowers, sugar, parched rice, and refreshing drinks. (39)
One should treat his diseases with mild, non-depressing medicines;
except in cases of life-threatening illness, one should strictly avoid administering purgatives.
One should not frighten an uncooperative patient with medicines that are non-poisonous yet cause trembling; for when he is terrified, the seizing spirits (grahas) take hold of him.
One should protect him from wind, from the touch of others, and from fasting. // 41 //
1.41ab And one should frighten the disobedient [disciple] by the dropping of a garment or by a harsh touch.
1.41cd By the dropping of a garment or by a touch from another; 1.41d one should protect him from transgression.
Ghee prepared with *brāhmī*, *siddhārthaka*, *vacā*, *śārivā*, *kuṣṭha*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and long pepper (*kaṇa*), when drunk, produces eloquence, intelligence, and memory. (42)
Vacā, indulekhā, maṇḍūkī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and śatāvarī increase longevity, destroy evil spirits and demons, and eliminate possession and insanity. (43)
Having made into a paste one pala each of vacā, indulekhā, maṇḍūkī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, śatāvarī, brahmasomā, amṛtā, and brāhmī,
one should cook one prastha of ghee with eight parts of milk. (1.43–44)
Having made a paste of one pala each of Brahmasomā, Amṛtā, and Brāhmī,
with four times as much milk, that [mixture] when drunk for a prastha [measure] is auspicious, life-prolonging, and a producer of eloquence, intellect, memory, and wisdom.
With goat's milk, abhayā, vyoṣa, pāṭhā, ugrā, śigru, and saindhava; // 45 //
Sārasvata ghee, prepared with pāṭhā, ugrā, śakra, and saindhava, is supreme for producing speech, intelligence, memory,
and digestive fire.
With vacā, amṛtā, śaṭhī, pathyā, śaṅkhinī, vella, and nāgara. // 46 //
1.46bv It produces eloquence, intelligence, memory, and wisdom. 1.46cv Ghee prepared with *vacā*, *amṛtā*, *varī*, *pathyā*, and *apāmārga* possesses the same qualities as the previous [preparation].
Gold, white *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *arkapuṣpī*, and *kāñcanā* [are used for this purpose].
1.47c–d: Gold, white *vacā*, and *kuṣṭha*; 1.47d: *śaṅkhapuṣpī* with *kāñcanā*;
*śaṅkhapuṣpī* with *rocanā*.
Gold, *matsyākṣaka*, conch-shell, *kaiḍarya*, gold, and *vacā*.
These four portions, declared as such, should be soaked in honey and ghee. // 48 //
Hemā, matsyākṣaka, phaṇijī, kaiḍarya, kanaka, and vacā—
these auspicious substances, when consumed mixed with honey and ghee or licked for a year, bestow physical vigor, intelligence, strength, and a healthy complexion.
With vacā, yaṣṭyāhva, sindhūttha, pathyā, nāgara, and dīpyaka. // 49 //
Speech is purified by licking clarified butter mixed with kuṣṭha, kaṇa, and jīraka. // 49 //
Speech is purified by licking clarified butter.
In the Uttarasthāna, the child is said to be of three types: the breast-fed, the solid-food-eater, and one who subsists on both.
From those two, when they are undisturbed, comes health; from them, when they are disturbed, arises disease. // 1 //
That water which attains oneness with the [other] waters and is not affected by defects is pure; however, water corrupted by wind floats upon the surface of the water. // 2 //
2.2dv When vitiated by wind (vāta), the stool floats on water, is discolored, frothy, and dry, causing obstruction of feces and urine.
From bile (pitta), it is hot, sour, and pungent, marked by yellow streaks, and causes a burning sensation in the water. // 3 //
From *kapha*, it is salty, thick, slimy, and sinks in water;
from their combination (*saṃsarga*), it possesses mixed symptoms; and from the combination of all three (*sāṃnipātika*), it possesses the symptoms of all three.
When administered, it produces those diseases according to its own specific properties;
one should recognize the pain of an infant by their frequent crying. (5)

2.5. One should know that a child’s fever is either sharp or not sharp depending on which part of the body it touches intensely, or where it is unable to bear being touched; likewise, one should know there is pain in the head from the closing of the eyes.
2.6ab One should touch intensely oneself that place which is incapable of being touched [by another].
7. By means of pressing the heart, tongue, lips, teeth, and breath with the fist;
and by means of obstruction in the abdomen, vomiting, biting the breasts, and gurgling in the intestines.
2.7bv – by gasping and being squeezed by the fists; 2.7dv – by loathing breast milk, intestinal rumbling, distension, bending of the back, and upward swelling of the abdomen;
also by retention of feces and urine in the bladder and groin, by terror, and by gazing in all directions. // 8 //
Then one should perform the treatment for the wet-nurse according to the specific humor and the specific disease;
in that case, if the breast milk is characterized by Vāta, she should drink Daśamūla for three days. (9)
Alternatively, [one may take] agni, vacā, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, kuṣṭha, dīpyaka, along with bhārgī, devadāru, sarala, vṛścikālī, kaṇā, and uṣaṇa. (10)
Then one should drink any one of the ghees that alleviate diseases of Vata; subsequently, having consumed clear Surā liquor, one should thus undergo mild purgation with unctuous substances.

Clarified butter (ghṛta) beneficial for diseases of Vāta should be administered; thereafter, one should perform enema therapy (vasti-karma) and other Vāta-alleviating measures such as sudation (sveda).
[The enema should be] mixed with the powders of Rāsnā, Ajamodā, Sarala, and Devadāru. (2.11b–12)
The child should lick ghee prepared with those [drugs], or ghee cooked with them along with sugar;
when the bile is deranged, [one should use] amṛtā, abhīru, paṭolī, nimba, and candana.
The nurse and the prince should drink [this] after boiling it with *śārivā*; or else, they should boil *triphalā*, *musta*, *bhūnimba*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*. (14)
The groups of drugs beginning with Śārivādi, Paṭolādi, and Padmakādi—clarified butters prepared with these are curative of pitta and act as purgatives. (15)
Furthermore, in the case of the phlegmatic type (śleṣmātmake), one should employ cooling treatments such as massages and ointments;
one should also have the child drink ghee mixed with liquorice (yaṣṭyāhva) and rock salt (saindhava). // 16 //
Alternatively, one should smear the breasts and the lips of the infant with Sindhu-stone, long pepper, and honey, ground together with honey and Rāṭha flowers.
2.17ab With rock salt, long pepper, liquor, 2.17ab with rock salt, long pepper, and nut grass,
2.17ab with rock salt, long pepper, and mūrvā, 2.17b ground together and mixed with honey.
In this way, the fool may vomit easily, but one should cause the nurse to vomit with pungent substances;
thereafter, she who has come into contact with the food should drink a decoction of mustā and other such drugs.
In the same manner, [one may use] tagara, pṛthvīkā, suradāru, and kaliṅgaka;
or alternatively, ativiṣā, musta, ṣaḍgranthā, and the five types of kolaka. (19)
2.19bv–2.19dv: *suradāru*, *kaliṅgaka*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, and the five types of *kolaka* [are used].
When the breast milk is vitiated by the three *doṣas*, it becomes foul-smelling, undigested (*āma*), resembling water, obstructed, clear, intermittent, and frothy when discharged. 20.
The feces are of various colors and painful, while the urine is yellow, white, or thick;
there is fever, anorexia, thirst, vomiting, dry eructations, and yawning. (21)
Breaking of the limbs, tossing of the limbs, moaning, trembling, dizziness, inflammation of the nose, eyes, and mouth, and other such symptoms arise from that disease. (22)
2.22b–c. Ringing in the ears, trembling, vertigo, and milk-indigestion—these they call the most dreadful complication known as *kṣīrālasaka*.
In that case, one should quickly treat both the wet-nurse and the infant with emetics.
When the purgative enema (saṃsargī) has been prepared, one should add the group of drugs beginning with vacā,
or the group beginning with niśā, or else mādrī, pāṭhā, tiktā, ghanā, and amayā.
Pāṭhā, śuṇṭhī, amṛtā, tikta, tiktā, devāhva, śārivā, along with musta, mūrvā, and indrayava, are excellent for removing defects of breast milk. (25)
Regarding the consequence: "One who knows the proper time should treat a disease according to its nature;
for the eruption of teeth is the cause of all diseases. (26)
Specifically, it gives rise to fever, diarrhea, dysentery, cough, vomiting, headache, ophthalmia, pustules, and erysipelas. (27)
When the backs of cats are broken, when the crests of peacocks sprout, and when the teeth of children erupt, there is indeed nothing that does not cause distress. (28)

2.28cv Regarding the eruption of teeth in children, the physician’s treatment should be applied after analyzing the specific humor (doṣa), the specific disease, the specific aggravation, and the specific fear, as well as the place, time, and other relevant factors. // 29 //

2.29bv According to the predominance, according to the strength; 2.29bv according to the predominance, according to the age; 2.29bv according to the predominance, according to the constitution—those very same doshas and dhatus, as well as diseases such as fever and others, [arise].
Therefore, that very same thing is the medicine, though its dosage is smaller.
2.30b–c And diseases such as fever arise for them because of their delicacy, their small physical stature, and their failure to consume all types of food.
Children must always be treated with unctuous substances, due to their habitual consumption of ghee and milk. 31.
2.31b–c Due to the consumption of all kinds of food, those [symptoms] arise immediately; therefore, a wise physician should administer a mild emetic to them.
One who is satiated with breast milk should be made to vomit, as should one who consumes milk and milk-based foods. 32.
For one who has drunk a thin gruel mixed with ghee and is eating solid food, an enema should be administered;
when purgation is required, it should be treated with an asthapana enema, and with a marsha enema for after-treatment.
One should administer purgatives and other such treatments using *dhātrī* (myrobalan) alone, as previously described;
[alternatively, one may use] *mūrvā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *varā* (chebulic myrobalan), *kola* (jujube), the bark of *jambū*, *dāru* (deodar), and mustard seeds.
One should also administer purgatives and other such treatments. Mūrvā, vyoṣa, vacā, kola, pāṭhā,
and varāṅga,
when licked with honey, are excellent for removing defects of the breast milk.
One should rub the edges of the teeth with a powder mixed with honey. // 35 //
2.35b–v: Or, those [medicines] which eliminate defects of breast milk [should be used], or [milk processed] with long pepper (pippalī), dhātakī flowers, and emblic myrobalan (dhātrī) fruit;
or [the milk may be taken] mixed with the powder of dried meat of common quail (lāva) or partridge (tittiri), and honey.
Or, the powder saturated with the juice of *dhātrī* fruit or the juice of flowers quickly makes the mouths of children like a forest of teeth and filaments.
With vacā, the two types of bṛhatī, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, ativiṣā, and ghanā; // 37 //
Ghee prepared with sweet [herbs] is effective for the eruption of teeth; likewise is ghee prepared with turmeric, devadāru, sarala, śreyasī, and the two types of bṛhatī. (38)
2.38c–d Rajani, dāru, and saralā; 2.38d śreyasī and the two types of bṛhatī,
along with pṛśniparṇī and śatāhvā— when licked with honey and ghee,
this is excellent for stimulating the grahaṇī and for promoting the downward movement of vāta.
It cures diarrhea, fever, dyspnea, jaundice, anemia, and cough;
it is honored for all diseases of children and bestows strength and complexion. (40)
2.40bv–41. It cures jaundice and anemia with samaṅgā, dhātakī, lodhra, kuṭannaṭa, the two types of balā,
mahāsahā, kṣudrasahā, mudga, and the tender fruits of bilva.
Ghee prepared with water boiled with *kuṭannaṭa*, *balā* (or *vaṭā*), and the fruit of *kārpāsī*, combined with milk and whey, quickly destroys diseases arising from the eruption of teeth. (2.42)
This [treatment] devised by the Elder Kāśyapa for various ailments should not be applied with excessive restraint to children during the eruption of teeth. (43)
2.43cd–44ab: Diseases arising from the eruption of teeth subside spontaneously once the teeth have emerged;
however, they persist in a child who consumes excessive daytime sleep, cold water, phlegm-producing substances, or breast milk.
2.44dv–45. In an infant who drinks phlegmatic breast milk, when the channels carrying the nutrient fluid (rasa) are obstructed by phlegm,
loss of appetite, catarrh, fever, and cough arise.
Then the boy withers; thereafter, his face and eyes become glossy and white.
[One should administer] rock salt, trikaṭu, śārṅgeṣṭā, pāṭhā, and giri-kadambaka. (46)

2.46d–47. For one who is wasting away, one should administer pāṭhā and girikadambaka with honey and ghee in cases of loss of appetite and similar conditions; likewise, the powder of aśoka, rohiṇī, and pañcakola should be administered.
Or, a powder of badarī, dhātakī, and dhātrī, quickly stirred with ghee;
or [a preparation] with sthirā, vacā, the two types of bṛhatī, kākolī, pippalī, and nata. (48)

Or, half a *prastha* of clarified butter prepared with one *karṣa* each of *nicula*, *utpala*, *varṣābhū*, *bhārgī*, and *musta*, along with a powder soaked in clarified butter, is the supreme cleanser of the channels. (2.48b–49)
That [milk] which contains *siṃhī*, *aśvagandhā*, *surasā*, and *kaṇā* possesses those same qualities;
likewise [the milk] with *yaṣṭyāhva*, *pippalī*, *lodhra*, *padmaka*, *utpala*, and *candana*. (50)
Ghee prepared with tālīśa and śārivā conquers wasting diseases (śoṣa), as does that prepared with śṛṅgī, madhūlikā, bhārgī, pippalī, and devadāru. (51)
Ghee prepared with a paste of aśvagandhā, the two types of kākolī, rāsnā, ṛṣabhaka, jīvaka, śūrpaparṇī, and viḍaṅga [is beneficial]. (52)

For one who is wasting away, a decoction prepared with *vaca*, *vayaḥsthā*, *tagara*, *kāyasthā*, and *coraka* is supremely nourishing when placed upon a head-ornament fashioned from the skull of a rabbit. (53)
Oil prepared with bastamūtra and surā is beneficial for massage.
One prastha of oil, an equal amount of lac juice, and four times as much whey [should be cooked together]. (54)
2.54b–d: Four times as much whey (mastu) as oil; oil equal in measure to lac-juice;
one prastha of oil with four times as much whey [is prepared] with aśvagandhā, niśā, dāru, kauntī, kuṣṭha, abda, and candana.
With equal parts of mūrvā, rohiṇī, rāsnā, śatāhvā, and madhuka. // 55 //
This oil known as Siddhalākṣādika, when used for massage, is strengthening and cures fever, consumption, insanity, dyspnea, epilepsy, and disorders of Vāta. (56)
This destroys yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūtas, and is recommended for pregnant women;
one should have the infant lick a linctus of ativiṣā, śṛṅgī, and pippalī mixed with honey. (57)
Or, for one afflicted by cough, fever, and vomiting who drinks and yet vomits even a single dose of ativiṣā, [one should administer] breast milk mixed with honey and ghee. (58)
One who is afflicted by fever and vomiting, and who vomits whatever breast milk he drinks,
should be made to lick two *vārtākī* fruits mixed with honey and ghee, as well as *pañcakola*.
Long pepper, the five salts, Vidanga, and Paribhadra; // 59 //

One should lick a paste of long pepper (pippalī), the five salts, kṛmijit, and pāribhadraka; likewise, one should lick viḍaṅga and pāribhadraka, or similarly, the three pungents (vyoṣa), or the soot of hair and skin.
By way of gain, there is birth as a porcupine, a hedgehog, a monitor lizard, a bear, or a peacock. // 60 //
Ghee prepared with the juice of khadira, arjuna, tālīśa, kuṣṭha, and candana, along with milk, cures vomiting. (61)
When the wind located at the base of the jaw, which has the teeth and the bone of the jaw-region as its range, becomes aggravated in a child, then the teeth do not erupt. (61+1)
The wind residing at the root of the jaw dries up the regions of the teeth,
or purifies the regions of the teeth.
In one who eats dry food and has a predominance of wind (vāta), the wind agitates the vessels located in the jaw;
thus, while the person is asleep, it produces a sound with the teeth.
If one is born with teeth already present, or for whom the upper teeth erupt first,
one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) during that portent and give [a gift] to a twice-born man.
2.62cd–63ab: One should perform a propitiatory rite (*śāntika*) for the twice-born and give them a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); one should also worship the deity Bāla Naigameṣa.
When phlegm (*kapha*) becomes aggravated in the palate-flesh, it produces *tālukaṇṭaka*.
2.63b–64. One should also worship Sainikeśa; by that [rite], a depression in the palate region arises at the top of the head.
[The symptoms include] falling of the palate, aversion to the breasts, drinking with difficulty, and liquid excrement.
Thirst, pain in the mouth, itching, eye-pain, stiffness of the neck, and vomiting [occur];
in that case, one should lift the patient up and rub [the area] with barley-alkali and honey. (65)
Likewise, the palate [is treated] with a paste of long pepper, dry ginger, cow dung juice, rock salt,
ginger, turmeric, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and banyan sprouts.
Having bound it and smeared it with cow dung, one should then sweat it in a kiln;
thereafter, one should smear the palate and mouth with the juice and sprinkle the eyes with it. // 67 //
Having drunk a paste of harītakī, vacā, and kuṣṭha mixed with honey along with breast milk, the child is freed from tālukaṇṭaka. (68)
Due to the accumulation of impurities or from sweating, a copper-colored ulcer arises within the rectum, produced by blood and phlegm, accompanied by itching and many complications. (69)
Some call that disorder *mātṛkā-doṣa*, others *ahi-pūtana*; some call it *pṛṣṭhāru*, *guda-kuṭṭa*, and others *anāmika*. (70)
2.70 Some call it *anāmaka*, others call it *pūtana*,
and still others indeed call it *pūtana*; it causes itching on the back and itching of the anus.
Pṛṣṭhāru and gudakiṭṭa (2.70c–v); pṛṣṭhāru and gudakuṣṭha:
in these cases, the mother’s milk should be purified with drugs that remove pitta and kapha.
And boiled water that has cooled, mixed with cold water, as an intermediate drink. // 71 //
One should apply a cold,
cooling plaster of sugar, honey, *tārkṣya* (rasāñjana), and *śaila* (śilājatu) to the ulcer, and sprinkle it with a decoction of the barks of *triphalā*, *badarī*, and *plakṣa*.
One should smear [the area] with green vitriol, gorocanā, blue vitriol, realgar, and rasāñjana, ground with an acidic liquid, or one should dust it with their powders. // 73 //
Alternatively, [the eye] may be treated with very fine *yaṣṭī*, conch-shell, *sauvīraka* collyrium, and *añjana*;
or with *śārivā* and the navel of a conch; or else with the bark of the *asana* tree. (74)

In a case where the itching caused by passion is intense, one should effect the extraction of blood using leeches; furthermore, all treatments that cure bile-related ulcers are recommended for anal fissures. 75.
Clarified butter cooked with pāṭhā, vella, the two types of rajanī, musta, bhārgī, punarnavā, bilva, the three pungents (try-ūṣaṇa), and vṛścikālī is recommended for anal discharge.
By consuming [clay] in the proper measure, one is liberated from diseases arising from the earth. // 77ab //
If there is a medicine for this disease, that breast has been smeared with it. (77cd)
Having remained for a moment, it should then be washed and subsequently drunk; thus one shall conquer each respective disease. (77ef)
2.77fv That yellow [medicine] shall conquer that disease.
In ancient times, they were created by the wielder of the trident (Śiva) for the protection of Guha.
The five male-bodied and seven female-bodied grahas. // 1 //
Skanda, Viśākha, the one called Meṣa, Śvagraha, the one designated as Pitṛ, Śakuni, Pūtanā, Śītapūtanā, and Dṛṣṭipūtanā. // 2 //
3.2 Skanda, Viśākha, Meṣāsya,
Mukhamaṇḍitikā, and likewise Revatī and Śuṣkarevatī—
the symptoms of those who are seized by these [spirits] are constant weeping and fever.

3.3ab Like that, there is the ornamenting of the face; likewise, the general form [of the symptoms] consists of terror, yawning, twitching of the eyebrows, dejection, salivation of foam, upward gazing, biting of the lips and teeth, and wakefulness. (4)
3.4bv – yawning, knitting of the eyebrows, dejection, weeping, moaning, aversion to breast milk, and abnormality of voice;
[the child] suddenly scratches all over the limbs of its own nurse with its nails. // 5 //
In that condition, with discharge from one eye, he repeatedly tosses his head;
one side of his body is paralyzed, his limbs are stiff, he perspires, and his neck is bent. (6)
The head is repeatedly tossed about;
he gnashes his teeth, loathes the breast, and weeps discordantly while trembling.
With a distorted face, vomiting saliva profusely, he stares intensely upward. (7)

3.7bv Trembling, he cries out with a discordant voice; 3.7cv With a distorted face, he spits saliva, smelling of fat and blood, agitated, with clenched fists and bound feces; the infant has one eye and cheek twitching along with the eyebrow, and both eyes are bloodshot. // 8 //
Afflicted by the aggregates, he will certainly suffer either mutilation or death; there will be frequent loss of consciousness, the plucking out of hair, and the bending of the neck. (9)

Or death may occur swiftly; there is loss of consciousness, and as the patient yawns with his hair disheveled, there is the discharge of feces and urine, vomiting of froth, upward gazing, and the twitching of the hands, eyebrows, and feet. (3.9b–3.10)
The pressing of the breasts with one's own tongue, fever, wakefulness due to agitation, and the smell of pus and blood are the characteristics of Skandāpasmāra. 11.
Swelling of the hands and feet, twitching, vomiting of froth, clenching of the fists, diarrhea, weakness of voice, and discoloration of the skin. // 12 //
3.12ab Distension of the abdomen, twitching of the hands, feet, and face, 3.12b foaming at the mouth,
3.12b twitching, the expulsion of froth, 3.12b twitching, convulsions, and vertigo.
Moaning, groaning, vomiting, coughing, hiccups, sleeplessness, biting of the lips, contraction and stiffness of the limbs, and an odor resembling that of a goat [occur]. (13)
3.13a–c: Moaning, labored breathing, vomiting; moaning, stiffness, vomiting;
moaning, noisy sounds, vomiting;
looking upward, laughing, and bending at the waist—these are symptoms of fever.
Fainting and swelling of one eye are the symptoms of the Naigameṣa graha.
Trembling, horripilation, perspiration, closing of the eyes, outward extension [of the limbs], biting the tongue, and gurgling within the throat; // 15 //
Trembling, horripilation, running, having the odor of feces, and barking like a dog;
horripilation, repeated terror, sudden weeping, and fever. (3.15–16)

3.16b–c: Barking like a dog at a female dog; 3.17: horripilation, frequent labored breathing, coughing, diarrhea, vomiting, yawning, thirst, a cadaverous odor, and convulsions, tossing about, emaciation, stiffness, and discoloration of the limbs.
In the case of a child seized by Pitṛgraha, there may be clenching of the fists, discharge from the eyes, drooping of the limbs, diarrhea, and ulcers on the tongue, palate, and throat. (18)
Blisters accompanied by burning, pain, and suppuration may repeatedly appear in the joints;
they dissolve at night and during the day, and suppuration may also occur in the mouth or the anus. (19)
In the Śakunī seizure, there is fear, a foul odor, and fever;
in the Pūtanā seizure, there is vomiting, trembling, drowsiness, and wakefulness at night. (20)
Hiccup, flatulence, diarrhea, thirst, suppression of urine, drooping of the limbs, horripilation, and a foul odor like that of a crow [are present]. (21)
In Śītapūtanā, there is shivering, crying, a sidelong gaze, thirst,
rumbling in the intestines, diarrhea, and a body odor like that of fat.
One side of the body is cold while the other is hot;
there is vomiting by Andhapūtanā, as well as fever, cough, and sleeplessness. (23)

3.23d–24: Fever, cough, weak digestive fire, breaking up of the stool, discoloration, foul odor, emaciation of the limbs, impairment of vision, excessive pain, itching, the appearance of *pothakī* eruptions, and swelling.
3.24cv impairment of vision, pain, and itching; 3.24cv impairment of vision, pain in the eye, and itching;
3.24cv impairment of vision, excessive pain, and itching;
3.24cv impairment of vision, excessive pain, and itching; 3.24cv impairment of vision, pain in the eye, and itching; 3.24dv [same as above].

The appearance of *pothakī* pustules, swelling, a sense of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), agitation of the heart, aversion to the breasts, discoloration, and harshness of voice; 3.24dv—[these are the symptoms]. 3.24dv—The appearance of *pothakī* pustules, swelling, a sense of emptiness, agitation of the heart, aversion to the breasts, discoloration, and harshness of voice.
Trembling, a fishy odor, or else a sour odor [arise]. (25)

3.25bv – discoloration and harshness of voice; 3.25cv – vomiting and a fishy odor from the mouth; with a beautiful face, hands, feet, and mouth; an abdomen covered with dark-colored veins; and fever. 3.26.
Through *mukhamaṇḍikā*, there is loveliness of the hands and feet; through *arocaka*, there is a lack of relish, exhaustion of the limbs, and an odor like cow's urine;
in *revatī*, there is a dark-blue discoloration and rubbing of the ears, nose, and eyes. (3.27)
3.27–28. In the Revatī [fever], there is a dark-blue discoloration, cough, hiccups, tossing of the eyes, distortion of the face, redness,
a smell like that of a goat, fever, emaciation, and green, liquid stools.
In Śuṣkarevatī, there arises in due course the wasting away of all limbs, loss of hair, aversion to food, weakness of voice, and discoloration of the complexion. (29)
In Śuṣkarevatī,
there arises the condition of having multi-colored feces, as well as knots and veins in the abdomen.
Lamentation, a vulture-like odor, persistence for a long duration, knotty swellings on the abdomen, and various kinds of feces—[these are the signs]. // 30 //
One should abandon that child whose tongue is depressed in the center, whose palate is dark-brown, and who, though eating various kinds of food, suffers emaciation. (31)
3.31 A depression in the center of the tongue indicates one seized by thirst; with sunken eyes, he is killed by Śuṣkarevatī.
A desire for violence, pleasure, and worship is the cause of being seized by a Graha.
In that case, whether he be a child or an adult, one whose nature is violent will have a runny nose, a wounded tongue, and will cry out loudly in great distress with tearful eyes. (33)
3.33cv With his tongue wounded, he moans intensely; 3.33cv with his tongue wounded, he groans deeply;
3.33cv with his tongue wounded, he vomits profusely; 3.33dv being miserable, his eyes are filled with tears.
He is born with an ugly complexion, base speech, and a foul odor; emaciated, he soils himself with urine and excrement and feels no disgust. (34)

But a foul odor arises; he does not feel disgust when he seizes [the corpse], and being frantic, he strikes himself as well as others with his hands, or likewise kills them with weapons, wood, and so forth, or enters a blazing fire. (3.34b–35)
3.35–36. Raising his hands in a state of rage, he may plunge into water, fall into a well, or perform other such acts;
he may also bring on thirst, burning sensations, delusions, and vomiting of pus.
One who suffers from thirst, burning sensations, and delusion; whose pus and blood issue from all the orifices; in whom fatal signs (ariṣṭa) have arisen—such a person one should abandon.
One who is fond of solitude, women, sexual pleasure, conversation, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments [is also to be avoided].
And if signs of impending death (riṣṭa) arise, one should abandon him;
he is difficult to cure if he is cheerful yet despondent, afflicted by a desire for sexual pleasure,
dejected, touching his face, and having dry lips, throat, and palate.
3.38c–d. Dejected, he touches his mouth; looking about apprehensively, he cries out, broods, and falls into a state of dejection.
Even when food is offered despite his desire for it, he does not wish to eat.
One should know that [a mantra] grasped by one desiring an offering (bali) is a means for attaining happiness;
however, one who desires to kill [an enemy] should conquer it through fire-oblations (homa) performed with perfected mantras. // 40 //
3.40ab One who possesses great desire seizes [the victim], while the other two do so according to their desire by means of offering the "pleasure-oblation" (ratibali) and so forth.
Then, one should place the child—the victim to be seized—in a secluded shelter. 41.
In a place sprinkled and swept three times a day, where fire is always maintained, and where ashes, flowers, leaves, seeds, food, and mustard are scattered about; 42.
3.42ab Sprinkled and swept three times a day; 3.42ab Sprinkled and cleansed three times a day; 3.42ab Sprinkled and swept three times during the day;
3.42ab Sprinkled and cleansed three times during the day; 3.42cd With many scattered flowers.
In that place where evil is destroyed by lamps ignited with demon-slaying oil, and where attendants abstain from sexual intercourse, intoxicants, and meat; (43)
In a lamp that has destroyed all evil,
[the patient] should be anointed with aged ghee and sprinkled with lukewarm water prepared with *balā*, *nimba*, *vaijayantī*, and *nṛpadruma*.
With *pāribhadraka*, *kaṭvaṅga*, *jambū*, *varuṇa*, and *kaṭtṛṇa*; with *kapotavaṅkā*, *apāmārga*, *pāṭalā*, *madhu*, and *śigru*. (45)

One should perform an incense offering for one who has bathed using *pāṭalī* and *madhuśigru*, or *mālatī* and *madhuśigru*, as well as *kākajaṅghā*, *mahāśvetā*, *kapittha*, milky trees (*kṣīri-pādapa*), along with *kadamba* and *karañja*. (3.45–46)
With *kapittha* trees, milk-trees (*kṣīrapādapa*),

and the skins of leopards, tigers, snakes, lions, and bears mixed with ghee; and with putrid [substances], the ten-ingredient [formula] (*daśāṅga*), white mustard, *vacā*, *bhallātaka*, and *dīpyaka*.
3.47c–d A fumigation prepared with *pūtī*, *daśāṅgī*, white mustard, and *kuṣṭha*, along with clarified butter, liberates one from all seizing spirits (*graha*).
3.48 White mustard seeds, neem leaves, the root of *aśvakhura*, and *vacā* [are used for fumigation].
Incense prepared with these along with *kuṣṭha* [is effective]. Horse’s urine, *aśvakhura*, and *vacā*;
horse’s hoof, *vacā*, birch bark (*bhūrjapattra*), and ghee—this incense wards off all seizing spirits (*graha*).
Anantā, āmrāsthi, tagara, marica, and the sweet group [of drugs]. // 49 //

3.49bv It destroys all seizing spirits (grahas). 3.49cv–dv With ananta, copper-colored bone (āmra-sthi), tagara, marica, madhura-gaṇa, śṛgālavinnā, and mustā— having made these into a paste, one should cook ghee with them.
Combined with the juice of the ten roots and milk, that [preparation] is supreme for overcoming the influence of the planets.
One should cook ghee in a decoction of rāsnā, the two types of aṃśumatī, vṛddha-pañcamūla, balā, and musta, with the paste of śārivā, vyoṣa, and citraka. (51)
From rāsnā, the two types of aṃśumatī, pattra, lodhra, pañcamūla, vacā, ghanā,
pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, madhuka, payasyā, hiṅgu, and dāru;
This, along with knots (granthika) and indrayava, is always beneficial for the child. 52.

3.52d–53. However, [a preparation] made with śārivā, surabhi, brāhmī, śaṅkhinī, kuṣṭha, and mustard seeds is always beneficial for an infant; it removes all diseases and malevolent spirits (grahas), stimulates the digestive fire, and bestows strength and a healthy complexion.
3.53bv It stimulates digestion and increases strength. 3.53dv One should cook ghee with śaṅkhinī, black mustard, vacā, aśvagandhā, and surasa;
that [ghee], by means of drinking and anointing, shall destroy all planetary afflictions (grahas). 54.
Vacā, aśvagandhā, surasā, cow horn, hide, hair, snake slough, the dung of a bull and a dog,
nimba leaves, ghee, kaṭukā, madana, and the two types of bṛhatī. // 55 //
Cow-horn, hide,
tail-hair, bone, cotton-seed, bone, barley, goat-hair, devāhva, mustard, peacock-feather, śrīvāsa, chaff, hair, and asafoetida.
3.56av Cottonseed, barley, and vacā; 3.56av Cottonseed, vacā, and bilva; 3.56av Cottonseed, vacā, and lodhra;
3.56av Peacock feather and śrīvāsa; 3.56av Peacock feather and śrīvāsa; 3.56bv [Peacock feather and śrīvāsa].
Lodhra, devāhva, and mustard (3.56b); devāhva, barley, and mustard (3.56c); peacock feather, śrīvāsa, (3.56d); human hair, and asafoetida.
An earthen vessel, treated with goat's urine and ground into a fine powder, as well as its incense, is beneficial for all living beings suffering from irregular fever. (57)
3.57c–d: All ghees that are beneficial for fumigation, as well as those which will be described in the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā), should be employed;
likewise, one who knows the mantras and tantras should perform offerings, oblations, and ritual ablutions.

[One should avoid] the bark and leaves of the *pūtikarañja*, as well as those from the milk-exuding trees (*kṣīrin*), the *barbara*, the *tumbī*, the *viśālā*, the *āragvadha*, the *śamī*, the *bilva*, and the *kapittha*. (59)
3.59av From the bark and leaves of the *pūtikarañja*,
3.59bv from the milky trees (*kṣīrin*), and also from the *vedara* [tree], 3.59bv from the roots of the *barbara*, and also from the *vardhara*.

Having boiled water with *śamī*, *bilva*, and *kapittha*, bathing children with it at night is auspicious; it removes complications according to their severity and even the afflictions caused by the seizing spirits (*graha*). (60)
3.60dv: One should treat the afflictions caused by planetary influences and other calamities with the same medicines prescribed for the prevention of childhood diseases. 3.60u: Thus it is said.
3.60 One should treat [the patient] with medicines appropriate for the [specific] condition.
In the Uttarasthāna, one should examine knowledge, discernment, speech, activity, strength, and virility.
Where there is no human agency in a person, one should say that it is possession by a spirit. // 1 //
One should declare that a person is possessed by whichever being they imitate through their physical form, natural disposition, speech, gait, and other such behaviors. // 2 //
That [restraint] is of eighteen kinds, distinguished by the various classes such as gods and dānavas;
its cause, however, is either immediate attachment to those [objects] or what was previously performed. (3)
4.3dv Or rather, the transgression of wisdom previously committed is greatly intensified by that which gives rise to desire and the like;
with his religious vows and conduct destroyed, he even oversteps those worthy of honor. // 4 //
4.4dv By transgressing against those worthy of worship, that sinful man who has thus broken the bounds of propriety and brings destruction upon himself—
even the gods and other beings slay him, for the planetary spirits strike at his vulnerabilities. // 5 //
A vulnerability consists of the undertaking of sinful actions, the ripening of undesirable karma, remaining alone in a deserted place, or staying at night in places such as cremation grounds. (6)
Nakedness, reviling one's guru, engaging in sexual pleasure through improper means, worshipping deities while impure, and being defiled by the birth-impurity of others; // 7 //

4.7cd–dv: Through impurity, there is no propitiation of the deities; through contamination by the birth-impurity of others, the performance of fire-offerings (*homa*), mantras, and oblations (*bali*) becomes defective.
Furthermore, there is a transgression of the conduct prescribed for the daily routine and so forth when it is undertaken in a summary manner. 8.
4.8dv–And the reverse of those [times] has been declared:
on the first and thirteenth days of the bright fortnight, the gods seize men;
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight and the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, the Dānava spirits seize them.
On the twelfth day, the Dānava grahas;
on the fourteenth, the Gandharvas; and again on the twelfth, the Uragas;
on the fifth, the seventh, and the eleventh of the bright fortnight, however, are the Dhaneśvaras.
On the fifth and the seventh day of the bright fortnight, [the Grahas are active]; on the eleventh day, the Lords of Wealth (Dhaneśvaras);

on the eighth, the fifth, and the full moon days of the bright fortnight, the Brahma-Rākṣasas; and during the ninth, twelfth, and other festival days of the dark fortnight, the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and others [are active]. (4.10cd–11)
On the eighth and fifth days of the bright fortnight, on the full moon, and on the two new moons, the Brahma-rākṣasas [are active]; on the tenth and ninth days, others, namely the Pitṛs;
and teachers, elders, and so forth generally manifest at the twilights. One should observe the time accordingly.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, [the patient] has a face like a blooming lotus, a gentle gaze, and is free from anger;
he speaks little, has minimal perspiration, feces, and urine, and has no desire for food. (13)
4.13cd–14ab One who speaks little, whose sweat, feces, and urine are minimal, who is supremely devoted to the gods and the twice-born, pure, and refined in speech;
who closes his eyes for a long time, is fragrant, and is a granter of boons.
One should know that he who delights in white garlands, garments, rivers, mountains, and lofty mansions, and who is sleepless and invincible, has been brought under the power of the gods. 15.
Wearing white garlands and garments, fond of high mountain dwellings,
with a squinting gaze, evil-minded, a hater of gurus, gods, and brahmins, fearless, proud, brave, wrathful, and industrious.
4.16 One should know that a person who is fearless, proud, and cruel,
who says "I am Rudra," "I am Skanda," or "I am Viśākha," and who has a taste for liquor and meat, is possessed by a Daitya-graha.

One should recognize that a person who has been brought under the influence of the Daitya Graha has a taste for liquor and meat; he follows his own whims, is fragrant, cheerful, and engages in singing and dancing. Rudra, Skanda, and Piśāca—I am [the one who possesses him].
Delighting in bathing and garden excursions, and fond of red garments, garlands, and ointments. // 18 //
4.18a–b: One who is refined by his own virtuous conduct, fragrant, joyful, and engaged in singing and dancing; 4.18c–d: one who delights in bathing and gardens, and is full of passion.
One should describe him as being devoted to amorous play, inhabited by Gandharvas, red-eyed, wrathful, with a fixed gaze, moving with a crooked gait, and fickle. (19)

4.19 One who delights in love and garlands, who is described by amorous gestures, who pants incessantly, whose tongue is restless, who licks the corners of his mouth, who bathes in beloved milk and molasses, and who lies with his face turned downward; 20.

One should know that [the horse] is presided over by a serpent if it trembles at the sight of a sunshade, has disordered, terrified, and blood-red eyes, possesses a pleasant fragrance, and is endowed with great luster. // 21 //
One who delights in dancing, storytelling, singing, bathing, garlands, and ointments; who has a taste for fish and meat; and who is joyful, contented, strong, and free from distress. (22)
Delighting in dancing, storytelling, and song; having a taste for fish and meat;
joyful, contented, strong, and free from distress—or rather, contented, strong, and imperishable.
Moving his hand forward, asking "What shall I give to whom?", speaking in secret, and showing contempt for physicians and the twice-born; (23)
One should recognize as being possessed by a yakṣa a person who slanders the twice-born, has little anger, moves quickly,
is fond of laughter and dancing, acts with ferocity, and strikes at vulnerable points.
One who has little anger, whose gait is stolen away, who is fond of laughter and dance,
who performs fierce laughter and dancing,
who is abusive, swift in movement, and a hater of gods, brahmins, and physicians;
One who strikes oneself with wood, weapons, and so forth, while uttering the word "Bhoh. // 25 //
4.25 One should recognize that a person who utters the word "cow" while striking [others],
who recites the scriptures and the Vedas, who has a wrathful gaze, who raises his eyebrows in a frown, and who is full of agitation, is possessed by Brahma-rākṣasas.
4.26b–c. Seized by a Brahma-rākṣasa, he ran about striking out, shrieking with a terrifying face;
though without food, the night-walker became powerful and lost all sleep.
4.27b–c He is weeping, with a terrifying face, shameless, impure, brave, cruel, and harsh-spoken;
he is irascible and fond of red garlands, women, wine, and meat.
4.28dv–29ab. One should declare that a dog which is fond of clouds, wine, and meat; which licks blood or flesh; which licks its own lips; and which laughs at mealtime, is possessed by a *rākṣasa*.
And seeing him licking blood and flesh from his lips,
with an uneasy mind, not staying in one place but running about,
fond of dancing to remnants of food, of gandharvas, laughter, wine, and meat; (4.29–30)
With a dejected face due to being rebuked, weeping without apparent cause,
scratching himself with his nails, his body and voice were coarse and wasted.
One who reports his own suffering and so forth, who speaks both coherently and incoherently, whose memory is lost, whose delight is gone, who is restless, naked, and filthy.
4.32 Seeing one who announced his sorrows, wearing rags from the street as a garment and adorned with a garland of grass; and likewise seeing one mounting a wooden horse or a heap of refuse.

One should recognize a person who climbs a heap of wood, stone, or refuse-piles as being possessed by a *piśāca*; likewise, one should know that a person who eats excessively is possessed by a *piśāca*.
Having the appearance, actions, and odor of a hungry ghost, he is terrified and loathes food. // 34 //
4.34 One should declare a man who is timid, averse to food, and cuts grass to be seized by a *preta*;
likewise one who talks excessively, has a black face, and walks with a swaying gait.
One should say that he has swollen, pendulous testicles and is possessed by a *kūṣmāṇḍa* demon;
he wanders about, clad in rags, carrying pieces of wood, clods of earth, and the like. (36)
Having seized wood, iron, and so forth,
he runs naked with a terrified gaze, adorned with grass; he frequents cremation grounds, deserted temples, streets, and solitary trees.
One should recognize as being presided over by Niṣāda that person whose eyes are constantly fixed upon sesame, rice, liquor, and meat, and who utters harsh words. (38)
4.38bv One with stuck eyes and red eyes; 4.38bv one with constantly red eyes;
4.38bv one with blood [in the mouth] and red eyes—one should know him as possessed by Karkoṭaka.
One should recognize a man afflicted by the Aukiraṇa [demon] as one who begs for water and food, whose eyes are bloodshot with terror, and who speaks harsh words. (39)
A man running while seeking water and food, his eyes terrified by blood, afflicted by the *autkiraṇa* [demon]. A man.
A man afflicted by the autumnal heat,
tormented by the cold of winter,
fond of perfumes, garlands, and pleasures, truthful in speech, and trembling.
And one should know that excessive sleepiness is caused by being brought under the influence of a vetāla. // 40 //
One who delights in perfumes and garlands, who speaks the truth, who is prone to lamentation, and who has been brought under control by a *vaitāla* spirit.
With a lackluster gaze, a dejected face, and a parched palate;
with trembling eyelashes, drowsy, and with a sluggish digestive fire. (41)
One should recognize that a person who wears their garment over the right shoulder, who is fond of sesame, meat, and molasses,
and whose speech is faltering, has been brought under the influence of a paternal spirit (pitṛ-graha).
4.42 One should recognize faltering speech as resulting from the curses of gurus, elders, ṛṣis, or siddhas, or from anxiety;
one should declare the specific possession according to its own corresponding speech, diet, and behavior. 4.3 //
4.43ab According to the nature of the curses and thoughts of the gurus, elders, sages, and perfected ones, 4.43cd Through their dwellings, food, and activities, each according to its own [kind].
One should describe that seizure as being followed by a troop of youths, with the patient naked and hair standing on end;
with an unsettled mind, it is long-lasting— one should abandon such a case as possessed by a graha.
In the Uttarasthāna:
One should conquer the elemental spirits through non-violence, the desire for peace, recitation, fire-offerings, oblations, and vows;
and through austerity, virtuous conduct, meditative concentration, generosity, wisdom, compassion, and so forth. // 1 //

One should conquer the affliction arising from *bhūtas* through non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). [The following are the remedies: austerity (*tapas*), moral conduct (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), meditation (*dhyāna*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *alana*, *nepālī*, garlic (*laśuna*), the root of the sun-plant (*arkajaṭā*), *jaṭā*, *ajalomī*, *golomī*, *bhūtakeśī*, *vacā*, and *latā*. (2)
5.2bv – garlic, arka, jaṭāmāṃsī; 5.2dv – bhūtakeśī, vacā, and latā. Bhūtakeśī, vacā, balā, kukkuṭī, and that called sarpagandhā; tilā, kāṇā, and vikāṇikā;
vajraproktā, vayaḥsthā, śṛṅgī, and mohanavallī as well. (3)
5.3bv *tilāḥ kālavikaṇike* / 5.3bv *tilāḥ kāṇaviṣāṇike* / 5.3bv *tathā kāṇavikaṇike* / 5.3cv *vajraproktā vayaḥsthā vā*

Sroto-jañjana destroys demons; there is another medicinal herb that likewise destroys demons, [prepared] from the bile of a donkey, horse, porcupine, camel, bear, monitor lizard, mongoose, and hedgehog.

5.4dv–From the lizard, the mongoose, and the fish; from the panther, the cat, the cow, the lion, the tiger, and marine creatures—one should prepare ghee with their skin, bile, teeth, and nails in this group. //5//
Either old or fresh oil should be used for drinking, nasal administration, and massage;
and their powder should be employed as an inhalation.
One should employ these [substances] as pills, in collyrium, or as an avapīḍana;
likewise, one should use their paste as a pralepa, and their decoction for sprinkling (pariṣecana).
5.7bv This application as an eye-salve (añjana) with a pressing-stick (sāvapīḍaka) shall bring to pacification seizures, insanity, and epilepsy;
[using] gajāhvā, pippalī root, the three pungents (vyoṣa), āmalaka, and mustard seeds (sarṣapa). // 8 //

One should administer the bile of the monitor lizard, mongoose, cat, and crocodile, ground with water, for nasal drops, massage, and affusion to ward off the influence of the seizing spirits (grahas).
5.9bv – ground with the bile of a rabbit; 5.9bv – ground with the bile of a bear:
white mustard, *vacā*, asafoetida, *priyaṅgu*, the two types of *rajanī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, white *kaṭabhī*, *varā*, and white *adrikarṇikā*. (10)

5.10c–d Mañjiṣṭhā, śvetakaṭabhī, varā, and śvetādrikarṇikā; 5.11 the leaf of nimba, the seeds of naktamāla and śirīṣa, surāhva, and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa)— with these, one should prepare ghee in four times the quantity of cow’s urine.
5.11cd–12ab. White mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*) prepared with four times as much cow urine, when administered internally or used as nasal drops (*nasya*),
quickly destroys all planetary afflictions (*graha*), especially those of demonic origin.
An elixir prepared with these very same medicinal herbs and goat's urine cures sorcery, misfortune, poison, insanity, fever, epilepsy, and sin. (13)
5.13bv – When employed for drinking, nasal administration, collyrium, ointment, bathing, or rubbing, it removes fever, epilepsy, and evil influences;
it is described as possessing the same qualities as previously mentioned, and it brings success at the royal court.
5.14c–d This [formula] is prescribed with its constituent qualities as before:
siddhārthaka, vyoṣa, vacā, aśvagandhā, the two types of niśā, hiṅgu, palāṇḍu-kanda, the seed of karañja, the flower of śirīṣa, and the fruit, bark, and wood of the kapittha tree. 5.15.
For two nights, [one should take] asafoetida and the bulb of the onion; likewise, the pulp and the fruit of the *kapittha* tree,
or the fruit and the flower of the *kapittha* tree, or the fruit and the bark.

One should prepare boluses from the roots of *śyoṇāka*, *kiṇihī*, sugar, *māṇimantha*, *nata*, and *kuṣṭha* taken from the *kapittha* tree, well-soaked in the urine of a goat and clarified with cow’s bile. (16)

They restore to life those blinded by the darkness of madness from malignant sores, those who have hanged themselves, those whose bodies are submerged in water, those struck by poisoned weapons, and those bitten by venomous serpents, by means of ointments, nasal drops, and medicinal plasters. (17)

5.17 They cure those suffering from malignant ulcers, insanity, darkness, and blindness at night; they cure those who hang themselves or whose bodies are submerged in water by means of collyrium, nasal drops, and ointments. They cure them.
By means of collyrium, potions,
and ointments made from cotton seeds, peacock feathers, *bṛhatī*, discarded flower offerings, and *piṇḍītaka* [18a].
5.18 With cotton seeds, peacock feathers, *bṛhatī*, discarded flower-offerings, *piṇḍītaka* bark, *māṃsī*, *vṛṣadaṃśa* excrement, husks, *vacā*, hair, and snake sloughs; 5.18b.
5.18b—with cinnamon-bark, bamboo, vṛṣadaṃśa, excrement, husks, vacā, hair, and snake-skin; 5.18b—with cinnamon-bark, bamboo, vṛṣadaṃśa, feces, nails, vacā, hair, and snake-skin;
5.18b—with cinnamon-bark, māṃsī, vṛṣadaṃśa, excrement, husks, vacā, hair, and snake-skin.
Incense prepared from equal parts of nāgakesara, the horn of a goat, asafoetida, and black pepper [is used]. // 18c //
It is the supreme destroyer of Skanda, insanity, piśācas, rākṣasas, possession by spirits, and fever. 18d.
5.18 This supreme remedy destroys possession by Skanda, insanity, piśācas, rākṣasas, and surās, as well as the influence of grahas;
it is prepared with the three pungents (trikaṭuka), leaves, saffron (kuṅkuma), granthika, alkali (kṣāra), siṃhī, niśā, dāru, siddhārtha, the two [types of] ambu, and śakrāhvaya.
With white garlic, the three fruits, uśīra, tiktā, vacā, tuttha, yaṣṭī, balā, red cardamom, realgar, and padmaka. // 19b //
With curd, tagara, the essence of madhūka, priyāhvā, viṣākhyā, viṣā, tārkṣya, śaila, along with cavya and āmaya, [these should be] made into a paste. // 19c //
Ghee prepared with an equal portion of fresh urine is known as Bhūtarāva; when drunk, it is considered a supreme destroyer of the grahas. (19d)
Nata, madhuka, karañja, lākṣā, paṭolī, samaṅgā, vacā, pāṭalī, hiṅgu, siddhārtha, siṃhī, the two niśās, latā, and rohiṇī. // 20a //

Nata, madhuka, karañja, lākṣā, paṭolī, samaṅgā, vacā, pāṭalā, hiṅgu, siddhārtha, siṃhī, the two types of niśā, latā, rohiṇī, badara, the three pungent fruits (kaṭu-phala-trika), kāṇḍa, dāru, kṛmighna, ajagandhā, amarā, aṅkolla, kośātakī, śigru, and nimba.
with mango trees called *dendrā*.
[The compound consists of: badara, kaṭuphalatrikā, kāṇḍa, dāru, kṛmighna, ajagandhā, surāṅkolla, kośātakī, śigru, nimba, ambuda, and indrāhvaya;
[and] madana, kaṭuphalatrikā, kāṇḍa, dāru, kṛmighna, ajagandhā, amarāṅkolla, kośātakī, śigru, nimba.
With *ambudendra* (musta),
*madana*, *kaṭuphala*, *trikaṭu*, *kāṇḍa*, *dāru*, *kṛmighna*, *ajagandhā*, *surāṅkolla*, *kośātakī*, *śigru*, and *nimba*.

With equal parts of the paste made from madana, kaṭuphala, trikaṭu, kāṇḍa, dāru, kṛmighna, ajagandhā, amṛtā, kola, kośātakī, śigru, nimba, ambuda, indrāhvaya, gada, śukataru, puṣpa, bīja, ugrā, yaṣṭī, adrikarṇī, nikumbha, agni, and bilva;
Ghee prepared with a group of urines. // 20c //

When administered according to the prescribed rules and applied through all the proper procedures, it quickly destroys all planetary afflictions, insanity, leprosy, and fevers; that is known as Mahābhūtarāva. (20d)

When administered according to the prescribed rules and applied with all the sequential procedures, it quickly destroys all types of planetary seizures (graha), insanity (unmāda), leprosy (kuṣṭha), and fevers; that [preparation] is known as Mahābhūtarāva.
When administered for a long time and applied with all the sequential procedures, it quickly destroys [these ailments].
One should remember that those [afflictions] such as all types of planetary seizures (*graha*), insanity, leprosy, and fever are known as the "Roar of the Great Elements" (*mahābhūtarāva*).

The planets seize those individuals specifically on their respective days; therefore, the physician should administer offerings (*bali*), oblations (*homa*), and other treatments on those specific days. (21)
Bathing garments, fat, meat, liquor, milk, molasses, and so forth—whatever is pleasing to whom at whatever time, that one should bring for them at that time. (22)
Bathing, clothing, fat, meat, liquor, milk,
molasses, gems, perfumes, garlands, seeds, honey, clarified butter,
and all kinds of edible foods— this is the general rule that applies to all of them. (5.22–23)
Red perfumes and garlands, and all kinds of food,
should be offered by everyone to the gods, sages, teachers, elders, and the perfected ones (siddhas) in the abode of the gods.
There, in the northern direction, one should also present an offering (bali) to the deity.
In the west, at the proper time, one should offer a bali with garments and ornaments to the Daityas at the crossroads, and to the Gandharvas on the path of cattle.
In the case of possession by a *pitṛ* or a *nāga*, [one should perform the rite] at a river; for a *nāga*, in the southeast;
for a *yakṣa*, in a *yakṣa* sanctuary or at the confluence of two rivers. // 26 //
5.26 When uttering the name of a deceased ancestor, [one should avoid] a river, a crossroads, a terrifying place belonging to a *rākṣasa*, and dense thickets;
for the *rākṣasas* are in the south, while the *brahmarākṣasas* are in the east.
5.27b–28. In terrifying or dense forests, or in an empty dwelling where a Piśāca resides in the western direction,
[the offerings are] pure white garlands, perfumes, milk-rice, and boiled rice.
When [the moon] has taken recourse to the western direction, or is situated in the western quarter,
an offering to the gods is desired consisting of curd and a white umbrella,
along with asafoetida, mustard seeds, vacha, and the three pungents (vyoṣa), each measured at half a pala. (5.28–29)
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee in cow’s urine possessing four times its quantity;
by drinking it, using it as nasal drops (*nāvana*), or applying it as an ointment (*abhyaṅga*), there is liberation from the influence of the Deva-grahas. (30)
For a Daitya, snuffing and collyrium made of *vacā*, *hiṅgu*, and garlic with goat's urine yield great results; likewise do *uśīra*, *kamala*, and *utpala*. (31)

5.31–32. For nasal drops (nasya) and collyrium (añjana), one should use *vacā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and *nāgā* (Nardostachys jatamansi); for [the elephant’s] food, with *sumana* flowers, parched grain (*lāja*), molasses, cakes (*apūpa*), molasses-rice (*guḍaudana*), fine rice-pudding (*paramānna*), honey, milk, black clay, and *nāgakeśara*.
An offering is made with vacā, padma, uśīra, and petals of the red lotus;
likewise, white pattra, lodhra, tagara, and nāga-sarṣapa.
5.33ab Ground vacā, pāṭhā, and uśīra with cold water is beneficial for nasal drops (nāvana) and collyrium (añjana).
For yakṣas, [offer] rice mixed with milk, curd, and ghee, along with guggulu.
Devadāru, utpala, padma, uśīra, cloth, gold, and silver—these should be prepared as an offering; urine, clarified butter, and milk should be placed together in one [vessel]. 35.
5.35b–d: Uśīra, cloth, and sandalwood; 5.35b–d: Uśīra, cloth, and woolen blanket—these, prepared in equal proportions, are beneficial for drinking, nasal drops, and massage.
Harītakī, the two types of haridrā, garlic, marica, and vacā [are also used]. 36.
5.36–37. One pala each of *nimba* leaves and *pānīya* (liquorice) should be prepared as a paste with goat urine for use as nasal drops (*nāvana*) and collyrium (*añjana*).
An offering (*bali*) should be made to Brahmā and the *Rakṣasas*. Furthermore, one full *āḍhaka* measure of barley should be prepared.
5.37cd–38ab: One *āḍhaka* of barley flour, one jar (*kumbha*) of water, minced meat, an umbrella, a garment, and ointment—
one should cook these with twenty *pala* of *gāyatrī* boiled in water, using half-*palika* portions [of the other ingredients].

5.38–39. A water-pitcher [should be prepared] with minced meat mixed with the three pungents (try-ūṣaṇa), the three fruits (tri-phalā), asafoetida (hiṅgu), six-partite root (ṣaḍgranthā), miśī, and mustard seeds;
along with nimba leaves and garlic, seven kuḍavas of clarified butter [are added].
That [cow's urine] is beneficial when used in drinks, nasal drops, and massages, provided it is three times the amount of cow's urine;
likewise, the flesh of a Rakshasa, white flowers, and mixed rice are beneficial.
5.40ab Prepared with three parts cow’s urine, it is beneficial for drinking and for massage. 5.40cd The offering consists of flowers, mixed rice,
raw and cooked meat, and *niṣpāva* beans sprinkled with blood.
And the bark, root, flowers, and fruits of the naktamāla and śirīṣa. // 41 //
The root, flowers, and fruits [of the *pāṭalā*]; likewise, the root of the black *pāṭalā*, the root of the *bilva*, the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*),
asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *indrayava*, white mustard (*siddhārtha*), garlic (*laśuna*), and the fruit of *āmalakī*.
This medicine, combined with goat's urine, should be applied as a nasal drop (nasya) or as a collyrium (añjana).
Ghee prepared with these same [drugs] and four times the amount of cow's urine is likewise effective. (43)
The medicine processed with goat’s urine,
when administered as a drink, anointment, or nasal drop, wards off *rakṣas* and *graha* spirits.
For *piśācas*, the offering consists of rum, oil-cake, minced meat, and curd.
Radish, salt, ghee, cooked rice with curd, barley gruel, the two types of turmeric, mañjiṣṭhā, miśī, rock salt, and ginger. (45)
5.45bv With abundant boiled rice and barley gruel (yāvaka), 5.45bv preceded by boiled rice and barley gruel;
5.45dv [mixed] with miśī, rock salt (saindhava), and ginger (nāgara); with asafoetida (hiṅgu), priyaṅgu, the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), garlic (laśuna), the three fruits (tri-phalā), and vacā.
Ghee [is prepared] with the flowers of pāṭalī, śvetakaṭabhī, and śirīṣa. // 46 //
Garlic, the three myrobalans, and vacā; paṭolī and white kaṭabhī;
or pāṭalā and white kaṭabhī—prepared with one-fourth part cow’s urine, this [oil] is beneficial for drinking and for massage.
One should employ collyrium and nasal drops made from those very same ingredients ground with goat's urine. // 47 //
