For those who are like celestial sages, ancestors, or gandharvas, one should avoid harsh treatments such as nasal medication;
instead, one should administer mild medicine, such as the drinking of clarified butter.
Except for a *piśāca*, one should not act in opposition toward anyone;
for when provoked to anger, those beings of great power destroy even a patient along with his physician.
By reciting the mantra of Īśvara, the twelve-armed Lord Āryāvalokita, and the remedy for all diseases, one shall conquer all seizing spirits (grahas). 50.
5.50cv He who treats all diseases, 5.50cv and the treatment for all diseases,
5.50cv as well as the treatment for all diseases, likewise [treats] madnesses, epilepsies, or other disturbances of the mind.
And one should always cause him to hear the pure Mahāmāyūrī vidyā. 51 //
Or other delusions of the mind; one who is pure should always cause him to hear [the scriptures].
He should worship Sthāṇu, the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa), and his hosts known as the Pramathas.
By reciting their perfected mantras, he drives away all planetary influences.
Whatever beneficial [teachings] will be stated in the two subsequent chapters, and whatever has been stated here, one should apply all of that to one another. (53)

5.53cv As it has been stated here, all of that is found in the Uttarasthāna: there are six types of insanity (unmāda), arising respectively from each of the doṣas, their combination, mental affliction, and poison.
Unmāda (insanity) is defined as an intoxication of the mind caused by its own defects that have led it onto a wrong path.
[It arises] from bodily and mental afflictions, from unwholesome food and drink, and from the improper consumption of corrupted, unsuitable, or impure substances. // 2 //
6.2 Due to physical and mental defects, from the consumption of unwholesome, impure, and irregular substances,
and from the onset of the force of disease in one who is despondent and of little fortitude;
And for one who is diminished, [this occurs] due to irregularity in activity and the transgression of honoring those worthy of honor. // 3 //

6.3bv Due to the onset of the force of disease, or due to the confusion caused by the force of disease; through mental disturbances, or by poison and secondary poisons—by these means, the humors (doṣas) become corrupted in the heart of one who lacks fortitude. // 4 //

6.4b–c By means of poison or artificial poisons (upaviṣa), they produce turbidity in the intellect of one whose vital essence (sattva) has been depleted; having obstructed the mind-carrying channels, they induce insanity through the resulting confusion of intellect, discernment, and memory. //5//
The body, deprived of both suffering and happiness, wanders like a chariot with a fallen driver; its undertakings are unreflective, and therein lies the emaciation of its limbs caused by the wind.
6.6ab Devoid of both suffering and happiness, the embodied being engages in weeping, crying out, laughing, smiling, and dancing in inappropriate places;
as well as singing, playing musical instruments, speaking, tossing the limbs about, and slapping [the body]. // 7 //
Constantly imitating the sounds of flutes, lutes, and other instruments without using words; the continuous emergence of froth from the mouth; wandering about; and excessive talkativeness. (8)
6.8ab Repeatedly producing sounds from flutes, lutes, and the like; 6.8cd Constant wandering and excessive talkativeness.
Adorning oneself with what are not ornaments, the effort to travel by means that are no vehicles, greed for foods and drinks, and the humiliation felt upon obtaining them. (9)

6.9dv Upon obtaining those [objects], there is a sense of contempt; 6.9dv upon obtaining those [objects], there is contempt, reddened eyes with bulging pupils, and when food is digested, the arising of disease;
from bile (pitta) comes threatening, anger, and the attacking with fists, clods of earth, and so forth. // 10 //
6.10 Having eyes that are reddened and swollen, a desire for cool shade and water, nakedness, a yellowish complexion,
and seeing false flames of fire, stars, and lamps. // 11 //
6.11b Yellowish discoloration of the eyes and skin; 6.11c A flame appearing even when no fire is present; 6.11c A lack of appetite, vomiting, and diminished desire for food and speech due to *kapha*.
Desire for women, delighting in seclusion, and the flowing of saliva and nasal mucus. // 12 //
A sense of disgust, aversion to cleanliness, sleepiness, swelling of the face, and powerful insanity that arises at night and immediately after eating [are the symptoms]. (13)
One should recognize as a terrible insanity that which arises from the convergence of all the sense bases and their configurations; the physician should avoid treating such a case. (14)

6.14bv – From that same combination [of humors], one who is afflicted by the unbearable loss of wealth, beloved ones, and so forth, becomes pale, dejected, and repeatedly fainting, lamenting "Alas! Alas! (15).
He weeps for no apparent reason, dies, and holds those qualities in high esteem; with a mind afflicted by grief, brooding and sleepless, he acts restlessly. (16)
One who weeps for no apparent reason,
laughs with a darkened face, whose complexion, strength, and sensory faculties have perished,
and who is agitated even during intervals between paroxysms with bloodshot eyes— one should avoid such a person.

6.17b–d. One whose complexion has faded and whose strength and senses are impaired should be treated for insanity caused by Vāta. First, one should administer the drinking of unctuous substances; however, if the channels are obstructed, a mild purification with unctuous agents should be employed.
Even when Kapha and Pitta are predominant, one should first administer emesis along with purgation;
for one who has been oleated and sweated, enemas and head-purgation (errhines) should also be given. // 19 //
Even when [the disease] arises from kapha and pitta, first [administer] unctuous and sudorific treatments,
as well as enemas and head-purgatives; thus, for one whose body has been purified, the mind attains clarity.
If there is still persistence even in this manner, however, strong nasal drops and collyrium [should be administered].

6.20 Just so, for one whose body is purified, [the physician may employ] exhilaration, encouragement, intimidation, fear, beating, and threats; as well as massage, rubbing with powders, ointments, fumigation, and the drinking of clarified butter.
6.21–22. One should employ the inhalation of smoke and the drinking of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*); for these lead the mind of one who has been purified back to its natural state (*prakṛti*).
[One should prepare] an *āḍhaka* of clarified butter with two *pala* portions each of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), and the three acrid drugs (*vyoṣa*).
This proven formulation, prepared with cow’s urine, is supreme for curing insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy.
Two *prasthas* of the fresh juice of *brāhmī* and one *prastha* of ghee are cooked together [with the aforementioned ingredients]. (23)
With one akṣa measure each of the pastes (kalka) of vyoṣa, śyāmā, trivṛt, dantī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, nṛpadruma, saptalā, and kṛmihara; // 24 //
6.24 With the pastes of vyoṣa, śyāmā, trivṛt, bimbī, sātalā, and kṛmijit— each of these taken in the measure of one akṣa— one should administer them,
increasing by one pala at a time, up to a maximum dose of four palas.
It removes insanity, leprosy, and epilepsy, and grants sons to the barren woman. // 25 //

The *brāhmī* ghee, prepared with *varā*, *viśālā*, *bhadrā*, *elā*, *devadāru*, and *elavāluka*, is known to bestow eloquence, clarity of voice, memory, and intelligence, and is considered auspicious. (26)

6.26 With *varā*, *viśālā*, *utpala*, *pattra*, *elā*, the two types of *śārivā*, the two types of *rajanī*, the two types of *sthirā*, *phalinī*, and *nata*; with *bṛhatī*, *kuṣṭha*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *nāgakeśara*, and *dāḍima*— 6.27 [These constitute the formulation.]
One should cook ghee with one karṣa each of vella, tālīśapatra, elā, mālatī buds, utpala, dantī, padmaka, and hima.
6.28bv With *mālatī*, *kumuda*, and *utpala*; 6.28cv with *rudantī*, *padmaka*, and *himā*:
[this] paste [is used] in cases of possession by spirits, seizures, insanity, cough, epilepsy, and sins;
[it is also used] for anemia, itching, poison, wasting, delusion, urinary disorders, artificial poison, and fever.
It conquers cough, epilepsy, and evil influences (6.29b). It is used in cases of jaundice, itching, poisoning, swelling, lack of semen, or sterility;
when the mind is afflicted by fate, when one lacks intelligence, when speech falters, when there is a desire for memory, or when the digestive fire is weak (6.29c–6.30b).

6.30–31 This auspicious ghee, which bestows strength, blessings, longevity, beauty, good fortune, and nourishment, is excellent for women who have not yet conceived or whose menstrual flow is scant, and it is also preeminent for the *puṃsavana* rite.
Having boiled twenty-one drugs, beginning with the two types of śārivā, in water,
one should cook ghee in that decoction with four times as much milk from a cow that has recently calved.

6.32dv In four times the amount of milk from a cow that has calved once (gṛṣṭi-kṣīra), [one should prepare] this supreme Mahākalyāṇaka [ghṛta] with vīrā, the two types of medā, kākolī, kapikacchū, viṣāṇī, and śūrpaparṇī. 6.33ab In four times the amount of milk from a cow that has calved once, [one should prepare] this supreme Mahākalyāṇaka [ghṛta] with vīrā, the two types of medā, kākolī, 6.33 Vīrarddhi, medā, and kākolī are known as Mahākalyāṇaka;
it is nourishing, destroys the disorder of the three humors (saṃnipāta), and is superior to the former in its qualities.
Jaṭilā, pūtanā, keśī, cāraṭī, markaṭī, and vacā [are also included]. 34.
Trāyamāṇā, jayā, vīrā, coraka, kaṭurohiṇī, vayaḥsthā, śūkarī, chattrā, sāticchattrā, and palaṅkaṣā. // 35 //
6.35–36: With *aticchattrā*, *palankaṣā*,
*mahāpuruṣadantā*, *kāyasthā*, the two kinds of *nākulī*, *kaṭaṃbharā*, *vṛścikālī*, and *śāliparṇī*, [one should prepare] ghee.

Having taken kaṭambharā, vṛścikālī, and sthirā, ghee prepared with these destroys quartan fever, insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy; this is the ghee named Mahāpaiśācaka, which is like nectar. (6.36–37)
This proven remedy for quartan fever and insanity (unmāda) bestows intelligence, wisdom, and memory, and promotes the growth of the limbs in children.
[It consists of] brāhmī, aindrī, viḍaṅga, the three pungents (vyoṣa), asafoetida (hiṅgu), jaṭā, and murā. (6.37–38)
It promotes memory and intelligence, and increases the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) of children.
[One should take] *rāsnā*, garlic which destroys poison, *viśalyā*, *surasā*, *vacā*, *jyotiṣmatī*, *nāgavinna*, *anantā* together with *harītakī*.
6.39 Having ground rāsnā, viṣaghnī, garlic, and kāṅkṣī with elephant urine and dried them in the shade, one should prepare a wick (varti).
This [wick], used as nasal drops, collyrium, ointment, or smoke, is a destroyer of insanity (unmāda).
Kācchī with elephant urine, and saurāṣṭrī with goat urine; fumigations destroy insanity,
as do various types of pressed-out juices (avapīḍās) and mustard seeds combined with fats.
One should perform an oil massage with pungent oil and cause that dust to be blown away from him.
This sharp-smoking fumigation, containing asafoetida and prepared from the fat of jackals, porcupines, owls, leeches, bulls, and goats, as described in the Sūtrasthāna, is beneficial.

6.42a–d: One should perform [the treatment] with asafoetida and pungent smoke, and with the urine, bile, feces, hair, nails, and skin derived from leeches, bulls, and goats— or from leeches, wolves, and goats.
Incense, fumigation, collyrium, anointing, medicinal plasters, and affusion. // 43 //
One should constantly fumigate this [area] with the highly putrid flesh of dogs, cows, and fish;
this is generally recommended for disorders of wind and phlegm, whereas it is praised for those of the bile type.
Bitter and life-sustaining ghee, mixed unctuous substances, and food and drink that are cold, sweet, and light [are recommended]. (45)
Or one should venesect at the site prescribed for the condition, or [venesect] one who is satiated with fatty meat;
having thus laid the patient to rest in a windless place, he is freed from the confusion of the mind. (46)
One should have him venesectioned at the prescribed site,
or, having thrown him into a waterless well, one should let him wither from hunger;
or a friend should console him with words consistent with dharma and artha.
6.47c–d He should console him with friends, or he should show him the destruction of something dear, or display wonders;
or he should place him bound, smeared with mustard oil, face up in the sun. 6.48.
6.48ab Or he should announce the destruction of what was desired. 6.48cd Or he should place it face-up in the sun, or touch it with *kapikacchū* plants, or with heated iron, oil, or water;
or, having beaten it with whips, he should bind it and cast it into a pit. 49.
6.49d–50b. Or else, having bound him, one should cast him into a pit, or into a house that is pitch-black and devoid of weapons, stones, or people;
or [one should deliver] him to a snake whose fangs have been extracted, or to tamed lions and elephants.
Or he should terrify them with Kirātas, enemies, and thieves brandishing weapons in their hands. // 50+(1)ab //
6.50+(1) Or else, by thieves or enemies, or again by the king's men who have led him outside and bound him securely,
they shall terrify him with threats of execution by the king's command.
For the fear for one's life is considered greater than the fear of bodily suffering;
by that [fear], his mind, which is agitated in every way, attains tranquility.
6.52d–53ab: When the mind has withdrawn from all sides, this successful action should be employed with due regard for place, time, and other factors.
However, if one's mind is afflicted by the loss of a beloved object— 53ab: [then it is not so].

6.53ab Once the [therapeutic] procedures have been established, they should be applied; one should bring that [patient] to tranquility through consolations and reassurances regarding the attainment of something similar to that [cause].
[One should treat] those arising from desire, grief, fear, anger, joy, envy, and greed. 54.

6.54a His attainment of something similar to that; 6.54b one should appease him with consolations and reassurances; 6.54b one should demonstrate [this] with dear reassurances; 6.54b one should lead him to tranquility with consolations and reassurances.
One should bring these very [humors] to a state of equilibrium through their mutual opposites;
one should observe the persistence of the elements, which manifests as a form exceeding the stated symptoms.
6.55c–d If one observes that the insanity is possessed by a spirit (bhūta), then one should administer the medicine prescribed for spirits;
and one should offer a bali-oblation consisting of minced meat, barley gruel, and balls of parched grain flour. 56.
6.56 If that [insanity] occurs in one suffering from *unmāda*,
one should provide unctuous and sweet food, rice drenched in blood,
both cooked and raw meats, *surā* wine, *maireya*, and *āsava*.
6.57c–d: Meats that have been cooked and raw; 6.57d: *surā*, *maireya*, and *āsava* liquors.
[One should avoid] the flowers of the *atimukta*, the *jāti*, and the *sahacara*;
and [places such as] crossroads, the watering places for cattle, and the confluences of rivers. 58.
One who has desisted from meat and intoxicants, who eats wholesome food, is self-restrained and pure—
that being endowed with sattva is not afflicted by innate or adventitious forms of madness.
6.59 Even for one who has abstained from meat and wine, clarity regarding the objects of the senses, as well as the intellect, self, and mind,
and the state of the bodily elements being established in their natural condition, are the characteristics of freedom from insanity.

6.60ab Clarity of the sense faculties is the characteristic of one who has recovered from insanity. Uttarasthāna: Epilepsy (apasmāra) is indeed the loss of memory resulting from the overwhelming of the intellect and the vital essence (sattva).
It arises when the mind is struck by anxiety, grief, fear, and the like. // 1 //

7.1b Due to the agitation of the humors (mala) located in the mind and body— arising from the confusion of intellect, vital essence (sattva), and other factors— just as in insanity, when the vital essence (sattva) is struck, the heart is pervaded, and the channels (kha) that carry consciousness are obstructed; // 2 //
Entering darkness with a deluded mind, he performs loathsome actions,
gnashing his teeth, vomiting foam, and tossing about his hands and feet.
Trembling with his hands and feet, seeing forms that are not there, he stumbles and falls to the ground; when the force of the affliction has passed, he awakens with his eyes and brows distorted. (4)
After some time, he again behaves in this very same way;
epilepsy is of four types, caused by wind (vāta) and the others, as well as by their combination (nicaya).

When this form is about to arise, there occurs a trembling of the heart, a sense of emptiness, vertigo, the appearance of darkness, meditation, the raising of the eyebrows, and a distortion of the eyes. (6)

7.6 When this [state] arises, there is loss of form, inability to hear sounds, perspiration, the flowing of saliva and nasal mucus, lack of digestion, aversion to food, fainting, abdominal distension, and loss of strength. // 7 //
Loss of sleep, aching of the limbs, thirst, singing and dancing in dreams, and the drinking and urinating of oil and wine [are its signs]. (8)
Therein, due to wind (vāta), his thighs throb, he falls down again and again, suffers from epilepsy,
and regains consciousness while crying out discordantly.
7.9b And he breathes continuously and repeatedly with his eyes bulging; he vomits foam, trembles, tosses his head, gnashes his teeth, and has his neck distended. // 10 //
He tosses his limbs about on all sides, with uneven and bent fingers;
his eyes, skin, nails, and face become rough, dark-brown, and reddish, and he gazes upon blackness. (11)
One whose form is restless, harsh, deformed, and with a distorted face, loses consciousness repeatedly due to pitta, yet regains it again. // 12 //

The supreme form is extremely fickle; it is harsh, coarse, with yellow foam, eyes, mouth, and skin. It strikes the earth, appearing with a terrifying, blazing, and wrathful form, and is possessed by thirst. // 13 //
From kapha, there is slow grasping and slow awakening;
movement is minimal, saliva is abundant, and the eyes, nails, and mouth are white. (14)
One should see forms that appear white and avoid all [other] signs.
Then follows the preliminary awakening of the intellect, mind, heart, and space, which were previously unawakened. 15.
In cases of epilepsy, one should treat the vātika type primarily with strong emetics and other procedures,
while the paitta type should generally be treated with purgatives, accompanied by a predominance of enemas.
One should treat epilepsy caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika) primarily with emetic therapies, once the patient has been thoroughly purified from all [humors] and properly reassured. // 17 //
Listen now to the pacifying yogas for the purpose of liberation from epilepsy:
clarified butter boiled with cow dung, its own juice, milk, curd, and urine. (18)

One should drink [the decoction of] the two groups of five roots (dvi-pañcamūla), triphalā, the two types of niśā, and the bark of kuṭaja, which brings an end to epilepsy, fever, insanity, and jaundice. (19)
7.19cd–20ab: The two groups of five roots (dvi-pañca-mūlī), triphalā, saptaparṇa, apāmārga, nīlinī, kaṭurohiṇī, śamyāka, the root-tuft of puṣkara, phalgu-root, and durālabhā.

7.20c–d. Having boiled two palas each of śyoṇāka, puṣkaramūla (jaṭā), and dvi-palā in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth, [one should add] bhārgī, pāṭhā, āḍhakī, kumbha, nikumbha, vyoṣa, and rohiṣa.
7.21. [With these: bhārgī, pāṭhā, āḍhakī, kumbha, nikumbha, vyoṣa, and rohiṣa.

7.21ab One should cook two palas each of mūrvā, bhūtika, bhūnimba, śreyasī, the two types of śārivā, madayantī, agni, and nicula in one droṇa of water, along with one akṣa each of these, to prepare ghee.
7.22 Similarly, one *prastha* each of *mūrvā*, *pūtika*, and *bhūnimba* [is boiled] with the aforementioned liquids; this is the great *pañcagavya*.
It is the supreme remedy for fever, epilepsy, abdominal diseases, and fistula-in-ano.
Ghee boiled with the juice of Brāhmī, Vacā, Kuṣṭha, and Śaṅkhapuṣpī removes swelling, hemorrhoids, jaundice, anemia, abdominal tumors, cough, and demonic possession. (24)

7.24b–c — One *prastha* of oil and one *prastha* of clarified butter, [cooked] with one *pala* each of the *jīvanīya* drugs, removes abdominal tumors (*gulma*), cough, and vertigo; it is intellect-promoting (*medhya*) and conquers insanity, misfortune, epilepsy, and sin. (25)
One should cook [the paste] in one droṇa of milk until it is prepared; this is a liberation from epilepsy.
[It may also be cooked] in a bronze vessel with milk and sugarcane juice, or in eight times the amount of the decoction of kāśmarya. (26)
One should cook one prastha of ghee with one karṣa each of the life-sustaining (jīvanīya) drugs;
that quickly destroys epilepsy arising from vāta and pitta. // 27 //
In the same manner, milk boiled with a decoction of kāśa, vidārī, ikṣu, and kuśa, or ghee cooked with the juice of kūṣmāṇḍa in eighteen times its quantity, [is beneficial]. (28)

Milk boiled with a decoction of *kuśa* grass, mixed with a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhu*, removes epilepsy and bestows intelligence, speech, and a clear voice. The bile of tawny cows is supremely beneficial when used as an errhine (*nāvana*). (7.28–29)
A paste of yaṣṭīmadhu used as a nasal drop (nāvana) is supremely beneficial for epilepsy; it removes [the disorder], bestows intellect, speech, and voice,
and is highly esteemed for use with the [flesh] of dogs, jackals, cats, lions, and other such animals.
Of the iguana, the mongoose, and the elephant, as well as of the spotted deer, the bear, and the cow. // 30 //

Oil prepared with the bile of bulls, bears, cows, wolves, and hyenas is recommended for use as a nasal drop (nasya) and for massage (abhyaṅga). [It may also be prepared] with triphalā, vyōṣa, pītadru, barley-alkali, and phaṇijjaka. (7.30–31)
One should prepare oil from *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *apāmārga*, and *kārañja* seeds; this oil, cooked with goat’s urine, is recommended for use as nasal drops (*nasya*) or for massage (*abhyaṅga*).
Alternatively, the physician may administer it as a beneficial nasal powder (*cūrṇa*) or blow it into the nose. (7.31–32)
Oil should be prepared by cooking it with the seeds of *śyāmā*, *apāmārga*, and *kārañja*,
along with [the fat] derived from a mongoose, an owl, a cat, a vulture, insects, a snake, and a crow.
One should employ its beak, wings, and excrement as incense for this [rite]. // 33 //
One should administer smoke therapy to him, or one should apply incense to him.
He should practice the habit of consuming garlic with oil or with milk, or he should take the juice of śatāvarī, the juice of kuṣṭha, or vacā combined with honey. (34)

Apasmāra arises from the simultaneous provocation of the bodily and mental humors (doṣas) when they are enraged; it originates from this [cause] and takes its seat in the great vital organs (mahā-marma). (35)
Therefore, one should treat this [disease], which is difficult to cure, with rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana);
and one should always protect the patient afflicted by it from the dangers of fire, water, and other such hazards.

"Therefore, one should always protect him with elixirs (rasāyana), and that afflicted person from fire, water, poison, and the like; for you have acted in this manner toward one who was liberated from mental affliction."
One should not speak of desired objects, for that would cause his afflicted mind to swell.
In the Uttarasthāna:
The *malas*, provoked by unwholesome factors described in the etiology of all diseases—especially those detrimental to the eyes—mostly follow the course of *pitta*. (1)
The vessels, having spread upward, take refuge in the various parts of the eye—the eyelids, the junctions, the white portion, the black portion, the pupil, or the entire eye. (2)
Having reached the vessels located in the eyelid, they become unstable and produce diseases;
in one who has just risen from sleep, it causes a painful stiffness of the eyelid.
The eyes appear as if filled with dust, there is difficulty in opening them, and tears flow;
because it subsides upon rubbing, they call that *kṛcchronmīla*. // 4 //
The wind, shaking the eyelids, repeatedly causes their opening and closing;
that which is the closing of the eyelid when they are shut is known as *animeṣa*, provided it is free from disease.
With its joints loosened and devoid of movement, it is indeed inferior and struck by wind (vāta).
Due to bile (pitta), many black specks appear within the eyelid like the seeds of the kumbhīka plant.

8.6c–d: Due to pitta, numerous pustules arise within the eyelids like the seeds of a *kumbhīka* fruit; they swell up and then burst, being known as *kumbhī*. They are accompanied by burning, discharge, and pricking pain, appear reddish, and are intolerant to touch. (7)

8.7bv Pustules known as *kumbhī* arise from *pitta*; they call that condition *pittotkliṣṭa-vartman*. *Pitta*, having taken its seat at the edge of the eyelid, causes itching and a burning sensation. // 8 //

8.8dv When *pitta* is localized at the edge of the eyelid, it causes the falling out of the eyelashes; this they call *pakṣma-śāta*. White pustules, resembling mustard seeds and dense, arise from *kapha*; these are called *pothakī*. // 9 //

Furthermore, there is the falling out or the loosening of the eyelashes; the eyelid (vartman) becomes afflicted with swelling, coating, pain, itching, and slimy tears due to the provocation of phlegm (kapha), characterized by stiffness, moisture, and coating. // 10 //
A hard, whitish swelling that suppurates, accompanied by itching, arises from Kapha;
it is the size of a jujube fruit, or slightly smaller than that, and is called Lagana. (11)
8.11dv A small red pustule, or even one slightly smaller than that, which is surrounded by similar pustules,
is called *utsaṅga*. Likewise, *utkliṣṭa* is characterized by streaks and is intolerant to touch.

8.12a Pustules red with red [blood], 8.12b covered with pustules similar to those, 8.12c are called *utsaṅga*; likewise, *utkliṣṭa* is a fleshy growth (*adhimāṃsa*) at the edge of the eyelid that is stiff, oily, and accompanied by burning and pain.
It is red, it flows with blood, and whenever it is cut, it grows back again. // 13 //
Located either in the middle or at the edge of the eyelid, a firm, copper-colored pustule the size of a mung bean, accompanied by itching and pain, is called añjananāmikā. (14)
When the eyelid is swollen on the outside due to the humors (doṣas), while its interior is covered with fine openings,
accompanied by discharge and filled with internal fluid like a lotus stalk, that is called Bisavartma.
When the eyelid, though irritated,
suddenly becomes swollen and then turns pale due to the provocation of the three [doshas] along with blood, that is known as *utkliṣṭa-vartma*.

8.16d They call that *utkliṣṭa-vartman* (elevated eyelid) [when it is] dark-brown due to impurities mixed with blood, accompanied by darkness, pain, discharge, and swelling; *śliṣṭa* is so named when the two eyelids are stuck together, characterized by itching, edema, and redness. // 17 //
In the *vartman* (eyelid), there are hard, rough pustules resembling sand; this is *sikatāvartman*. The black [pustules] are *kardama*, resembling mud. (18)
Kukūṇaka is a thick accumulation of flesh, uniform and of the same color as the skin, occurring only in an infant and caused by the eruption of teeth. (19)
By that [disease], the child may have swollen, copper-colored eyes, be unable to look, experience pain and sliminess in the eyelids, and rub the ears, nose, and eyes. (20)

8.20b–21. His eyes become copper-colored and he is unable to look; there is a contraction of the eyelids due to the obstruction of the lashes, as well as roughness and inward-turning of the hairs within the eyelids, or other such symptoms.

Likewise, [this disease] arises from the eyelids; as if rubbed by sharp-pointed thorns, the eye swells and burns due to the wind and other humors. When these [thorns] are extracted, relief occurs within a few days. (8.21)
When rubbed by those [factors], the eye weeps or is inflamed;
it is afflicted by wind and the other [humors], and even when extracted, there is only slight relief for a short time.
Alaji is a hard, elevated, copper-colored glandular swelling at the outer corner of the eye (kanīnaka) on the eyelid;
when it is ripe, it exudes blood and pus and repeatedly becomes distended. (23)
An Arbuda is a painless, knotted swelling resembling a lump of flesh at the edge of the eyelid;
it is caused by the humors (doṣas) along with blood, being irregular in shape and mobile on its outer surface. (24)
These twenty-four diseases are located in the eyelids;
among them, the first is curable by medicines, while the next two and the hemorrhoids (arśas) should be avoided.
Obstruction of the eyelashes (pakṣmoparodha) should be palliated; the remaining [conditions] one should treat with the scalpel.
One should crush the falling out of the eyelashes (pakṣmasadana) and excise any tumor (arbuda) among them as well. // 26 //
One should crush [the drug] for the treatment of pakṣma-śadana;
it destroys lagaṇa, kumbhīkā, bisotsaṅga, añjanālajī, pothakī, śyāva, sikatā, and the four types of śliṣṭa and utkliṣṭa.
One should scratch [the skin] where there is mud, where it is thick, and where there are *kukūṇaka* eruptions. // 27 // u // ab //
In the Uttarasthāna, for chronic blepharospasm (kṛcchronmīla), one should administer old ghee processed with the paste of grapes and water, mixed with sugar;
furthermore, unctuous treatments such as nasal drops, medicated smoke, and collyrium should be employed. // 1 //

The eyelid of a patient with Kumbhīkā-vartman, after being scraped and rubbed with rock salt (saindhava), should be sprinkled with a decoction of liquorice (yaṣṭī), emblic myrobalan (dhātrī), and patola (paṭolī). // 2 //
For one who has been established in a windless place by trusted attendants, who is pure and lying supine, the eyelid should be fomented with a cloth warmed by lukewarm water from the outside. (3)
Having rolled it up and secured it between the left thumb and fingers with a cloth interposed, the eyelid will neither slip nor move; thus, in every respect, the procedure is performed.
9.4cv It does not slip nor does it waver;
having made that [line] oblique with the edge of the mandala, one should mark it with the footprints of the weapon.
One should draw [the design] with that very [line], or else with leaves produced from vegetables such as *śephālikā* and the like. // 5 //
Wiping away the blood with a pad made of *śāka*, *śephālikā*, and other such plants, or with the foam of the ocean,
once the bleeding has ceased, one should rub the well-incised wound with honey and [astringent] powders. // 6 //
Having washed it with warm water after applying the respective [medicines] as prescribed,
one should sprinkle it with ghee, anoint it, and bind it with honey and clarified butter.
9.7cv Having sprinkled [the ear] with ghee and anointed it, and having placed a bolus of barley-flour into both the upper and lower parts of the ear,
one should perform an appropriate irrigation on the second day once the patient has been released [from the bandage]. // 8 //
On the fourth day, one should administer nasal therapy (nasya) and other treatments; on the fifth day, one should release [the bandage].
[The wound] becomes even, resembling the color of a fingernail, and is no longer afflicted by swelling, itching, rubbing, or similar discomforts.
One should know that the eyelid has been well-scrubbed; one should scrub again in case of the opposite.
From excessive scrubbing arise pain, irritation of the lashes, sinking of the lid, and drooping. (10)
In that condition, the therapeutic sequence beginning with oleation and sudation, which pacifies Vata, is desired;
after massaging with fresh butter, one should apply a plaster of white Lodhra. // 11 //
Then one should cook it by the *puṭapāka* method using a paste of castor root;
once steamed, it should be washed, dried, powdered, and made into a sachet.
The milk of a woman or a goat, rubbed [with these substances], serves as an eye-drop;
likewise, it is prepared when smeared with a paste of *śāli* rice grains. (13)
9.13ab If the eyes have been excessively scraped, one should apply a paste of curd-whey (dadhi-mastu) made from the milk of a woman or a goat;
or, for one who eats the meat of wild animals, an irrigation with whey alone may be used.
Having pierced the hard, elevated pustules with the opening of a rice grain, one should squeeze them out; the remaining procedure is as before. 15.
Having incised a hard, elevated pustule with a *vrīhivaktra* instrument,
this same procedure for scraping and excising applies to every part of the passage.
For those [conditions] afflicted by pitta and āsrava, [the treatment] is with ghee prepared with the sweet group of drugs.
For one who has been treated with oleation, venesection is indicated; Trivṛt is the best purgative.
Once the eyelid has been scarified and blood has been let, irrigation is beneficial for the ulcerated eye. (17)

Trivṛt is the best for purgation. When the blood has been scraped away and drained, a wash with liquorice decoction should be applied; however, if the eyelashes have fallen out, one should prick the hair follicles with a needle, and milk boiled with sandalwood should be used as a wash. (9.17–18)

An irrigation with a decoction of yaṣṭīmadhu, or bloodletting by leeches, or an irrigation with milk or sugarcane juice [is indicated]; likewise, emesis, nasal drops, and ghee boiled with sweet and cooling substances [should be employed]. 9.18–19ab.
Having powdered flower-sulfate (puṣpakāsīsa), one should saturate it with the juices of *surasā* for ten days; when applied as a collyrium, this is excellent for the falling out of eyelashes.
The pustules, having been written upon with a stylus and rubbed with ginger and rock salt,
should be washed with warm water and sprinkled with a decoction of khadira, āḍhakī, and śigru.
One should sprinkle a *pothakī* ulcer that has been written upon with a stylus, rubbed with ginger and rock salt,
and washed with warm water, with a decoction of the two best types of *niśā*, *madhuka*, and honey; or [with a decoction] prepared with water.
When [the eye] is afflicted by kapha and has been scarified, it should be rubbed with honey. // 22 //

With fine powders of rock salt (*saindhava*), green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), red chalk (*manohvā*), *kaṇa*, and *tārkṣya-ja*, all emetics, collyria, nasal drops, and other remedies that conquer *kapha* are beneficial. (23)
This same treatment should be performed for *lagaṇa* as well; if it is not pacified, one should cauterize it with fire.
For *kukūṇaka*, ghee boiled with the best *khadira* and nimba leaves should be used. (24)
The physician, having fomentated and incised the swelling called *añjananāmikā*, should squeeze out its contents and apply a plaster of *nimba* leaves boiled with ghee,
combined with realgar (*śilā*), cardamom (*elā*), rock salt (*saindhava*), and *nata*, along with honey.
Having fomented her, one should break open the *añjananāmikā* vein located at the junction of the shoulders and squeeze out the blood;
then, after drinking [the milk], the wet nurse should vomit it up using black liquorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*), mustard seeds, and rock salt.
One should cause her to purge with a decoction of abhayā, pippalī, and drākṣā. // 25 //
One should apply an ointment of mustā, the two types of rajanī, and kṛṣṇā to the breasts;
fumigate them with mustard seeds mixed with ghee, and once they are purified, one should have the woman drink a decoction.
The eyelid of an infant, having been scarified, should be washed with water produced from *paṭola*, *musta*, *mṛdvīkā*, *guḍūcī*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
or with lotus-flowers after blood has been let.
One should sprinkle [the child] with a decoction of the leaves of dhātrī, aśmantaka, and jambū;
for since children generally consume milk and ghee, their diseases are mostly born of phlegm (śleṣman). // 28 //
Therefore, emesis alone is honored as the foremost treatment for all diseases at the outset;
[the remedy consists of] rock salt, long pepper, seeds of Apāmārga, clarified butter, breast milk, and honey. (29)
For an infant who consumes milk, milk-rice, and solid food in gradual succession, one should administer a powder of *vacā* with honey, along with *madana* and *madhuka*. (30)
For a child who gradually develops [the disease],
emesis is indicated in all diseases, especially in *kukūṇaka*;
moreover, clarified butter prepared with the juice of *saptalā* should be administered for the purification of both [the upper and lower tracts].
In cases of *kukūṇaka*, a medicinal wick (*varti*) made from lodhra, liquorice, *rohiṇī*, nimba leaves, and copper dust—all ground together—is beneficial. (32)
Or, iron dust burnt with milk, honey, and ghee, together with cardamom, garlic, kataka, conch-shell, long pepper, and phanijjaka; (33)
Alternatively, a wick made from the burnt powder of *lodhra* or from *kaṭphala* ground with wine should be applied for *kukūṇaka* and *pothakī*.
When the eyelashes have grown excessively thick and are obstructing vision, the body of the patient should first be purified, and then [the treatment] should be applied to the lashes.
Having cast aside two parts below the eyebrows and one part from the eyelashes,
he should cut [the hair] crosswise to the measure of a barleycorn, in the shape of a barleycorn, using a moist cloth.
When the blood in that [wound] has become scanty, it should be removed;
one should then suture it with a curved needle at intervals of the size of a mung bean.
Having tied a cloth band upon the forehead, one should insert the sewing thread there—neither too tight nor too loose—and then join it with a needle. (37)
One should not apply a honey-and-ghee poultice nor perform bandaging on this [wound];
rather, in the case of pain, one should irrigate it with decoctions of the *nyagrodha* group mixed with milk.
On the fifth day, having removed the thread, one should dust the wound with powder; one should apply red ochre to the wound and administer strong nasal drops, collyrium, and so forth. (39)
And sharp nasal drops, collyriums, and so forth; if there is no relief, one should cauterize the fold of skin that serves as the seat of the eyelid disorder by turning it outward.
Having removed the excessive eyelash with forceps, one should cauterize its base.
Furthermore, cauterization with a needle-pointed instrument glowing like fire is for an external *alajī* ulcer;
whereas for a ruptured *arbuda* tumor that has been well-incised, cauterization with alkali or fire is prescribed.
In the Uttarasthāna:
When the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated, it reaches the channels that carry water;
it causes tears to flow from the junction of the eyelid and the white of the eye, and from the corner of the eye (kanīnaka). // 1 //
10.1dv–Due to a white film over the junction [of the eyelids] and the pupil, the eye becomes painful, discolored, and swollen; that is *jalāsrava*.
From *kapha*, in *kaphāsrava*, a white, slimy, and thick discharge flows. // 2 //

From *kapha*, there is a white discharge of *kapha*; due to *kapha*, a swelling arises that has sharp points, resembling alkaline bubbles, with a broad base and strength, glossy, the same color as the skin, soft, and slimy. (3)
10.3dv An *upanāha* (conjunctive swelling) is of the same color as the skin, soft, slimy, large, non-suppurating, itchy, and painless.
From the vitiated blood (*rakta*), there is a discharge of blood, and the eye sheds copious, hot, copper-colored tears. // 4 //

From blood, there is a flow of blood that is copper-colored; or hot tears may flow profusely. A pustule, accompanied by burning and pain, arises on the white of the eye (śukla) at the junction of the eyelid (vartma).
The *parvaṇī* is copper-colored, resembles a mung bean when split open, and exudes blood. // 5 //
In Pūyāsrava, the impurities flow as pus and tears from the eyelid junctions and the inner corner of the eye;
due to the suppuration of the skin and flesh, they repeatedly discharge pus along with tears.

10.6b–d: From the eyelid margin, the junction, and the kanīnaka (the inner corner of the eye), there arises a minute ulcer characterized by suppuration of the skin and flesh, accompanied by lacrimation and preceded by swelling and inflammation. This is known as pūyālasa.
In the joint of the little finger, it becomes distended, discharging pus, and accompanied by pain. // 7 //
The *alajī* is a swelling within the corner of the eye (*kanīna*), accompanied by pain, pricking, and a burning sensation;
or it occurs at the outer corner (*apāṅga*) or the corner (*kanīna*), characterized by itching and the falling out of eyelashes. (8)
Pūyāsrāvin, Kṛmigranthi, Granthi accompanied by worms and painful, Upanāha, Kṛmigranthi, Pūyālasaka, and Parvaṇī; // 9 //
One should treat the five types of *sālajī* with surgical instruments and eliminate the secretions (*āsrava*).
One should apply cauterization (*pitta*) to white spots that have become black, dark-brown, or yellow. (10)
Or, when all white [parts] are like a mirror smeared with filth, accompanied by burning and pain—this disease is known as Śuktikā, characterized by the breaking of stool, thirst, and fever. (11)
10.11b–d All white [lesions] are without burning or pain due to Kapha; Śuklārma is a white, uniform, and whitish growth of flesh that increases slowly.
Śopha, however, is painless, the same color as the surrounding tissue, thick, and not soft. 12.
A guru that is glossy and resembles a drop of water is known as *balāsagrathita*;
one should call it *piṣṭaka* when it is covered with white, flour-like, and raised dots. // 13 //
10.13d–14. That which is known as *balāsa-granthi* is characterized by a white, painful swelling covered with red streaks;
whereas that which arises from blood (*śoṇita*) is called *sirotpāta*, being without swelling, tearing, or discharge.

If neglected, sirōtpāta causes swelling, lacrimation, and exudation; it increases those very streaks (rājīs) and produces sirāharṣa with blood, whereby the eye becomes incapable of looking upward. 10.14c–d, 15.

10.15c–d: One should treat sirā-harṣa (vein-trembling) with tears; by that, the eye becomes incapable of vision. 10.16: Sirājāla (vein-network) is a large, red, thick, and elevated network of vessels.
Śoṇitārma (blood-tumor) is similar, while adhimāṃsaka (flesh-growth) is smooth and lotus-colored.

The *nīruja* (non-painful) type is smooth, white, and marked with spots; the *bindu* (spot-type) is red like the blood of a hare; the *mṛdu* (soft), *āśu* (rapid), and *vṛddhi* (increasing) types are flesh-colored and painless; and the *prastārin* (spreading) type is dark red.

A *prastāry-arman* is characterized by tears mixed with mucus; a *snāva-arman* resembles a ligament; and that which is thick and broad, dark-brown like a mass of dried blood, is [an *adhimāṃsaka*]. (18)

Adhimāṃsārma consists of eruptions resembling mustard seeds that are covered by veins, located near the black part of the eye, and characterized by burning and itching; they are known as "vein-born" (sirā-saṃjñā). // 19 //
One should treat with medicines the six types— adhimāṃsa, arma, rugdāha, śukti, harṣa, and sirotpāta— and piṣṭaka, grathita, and arjuna with surgical instruments. (10.19–20)

10.20–21. Armas characterized by scales, itching, and protruding vessels, those with a crust like flour-paste, knotted growths, or the *arjuna* type— whether newly arisen or of the five types previously mentioned— are to be excised, provided they have turned black and are covered with flesh, sinews, and veins.
10.21b–c That which has been described as fivefold, like a flayed skin, elevated, and reaching the pupil (dṛṣṭiprāpta), one should avoid;
as well as [the condition where] bile (pitta) is in the black part (kṛṣṇa) or in the pupil (dṛṣṭi), accompanied by whiteness (śukra), pricking pain (todo), lacrimation (aśru), and redness (rāga).

10.22b–d One should avoid [treating] the *dṛṣṭiprāpta* [type]; however, when the *śukra* (cornea) is incised like [a vessel with] piercing pain, bleeding, and redness, it produces a scar that forms the black circle (*kṛṣṇamaṇḍala*).
This lesion of the *śukra* is somewhat sunken and resembles a ripe *jambu* fruit.

That [disease] is difficult to cure, but it is palliable when there is a perforation of the second layer (paṭala). In that case, there is an abundance of pricking pain and other symptoms, and the blackness resembles that produced by being pierced with a needle. (24)

That which has reached the third layer (paṭala), is incurable, and is covered with ulcers, is incurable; that which is as white as a conch shell due to phlegm (kapha) and has very little pain, being pure and white, is curable. (25)
Flowing with copper-colored, slimy blood, accompanied by excessive pain and copper-colored pustules, and characterized by a swelling as black as goat dung—this *asṛjājaka* should be rejected. (26)
10.26a–d: It may have copper-colored, slimy tears; it may have copper-colored, slimy blood; its elevation may resemble goat dung; and it is black. These types of *asṛjājaka* should be rejected.

The vitreous humor (sirā-śukra), when affected by the humors along with blood, causes the black portion (kṛṣṇa-maṇḍala) to be covered with vessels that are copper-colored and accompanied by pricking pain and burning. (27)

One should discard that [blood] which is signless, warm, cold, clear, thick, or frothy; when mixed with the humors (doṣas) and blood, it is drawn out black at once, yet assumes a white appearance. (28)
10.28b–c: And that which has thick tears should be abandoned; that which flows with thick tears should be abandoned; and that which sheds thick tears should be abandoned. 10.28c–d:
When the humors, along with blood, affect the eye, it becomes black.
It has the appearance of being smeared with white clouds, is shaped like the half-moon of a flat bean, and is afflicted by extremely intense pain, redness, burning, and swelling. // 29 //
One should avoid that semen which, due to overcooking, causes intense pain, or for which there is destruction of the penis, or which is dark-brown or reddish inside. (30)
A *śūkaka* that is excessively elevated or deeply sunken, accompanied by tears, covered with sinus tracts or ulcers, chronic, irregular, or severed in its center, [should be rejected]. (31)

10.31b–d: Covered by blood, channels, and ulcers—these five diseases have been described in the *Kṛṣṇa* [chapter], according to the distinction between those that are curable and those that are incurable.
In the Uttarasthāna:
The physician should foment the *upanāha* (abscess), incise it with a *vrīhimukha* instrument, scarify it with a *maṇḍalāgra*, and then apply medicinal paste (*pratisāraṇa*). // 1 //
An incision made with a *vrīhimukha* instrument should then be bound as before with long pepper, honey, and rock salt;
one should then irrigate it with a decoction of *paṭola* leaves and *āmalaka*.
The *parvanī* [root] is grasped with a hook from three parts of the external joint;
it should be increased by half using the growth-leaf, otherwise there would be the movement of tears.
11.3ab At the joints, [the incision] should be made with a hook from the internal and external junctions at one-third [of the distance]. 11.3cd Otherwise, there would be a course for the arrow;
otherwise, there would be a flow of blood.
The treatment for pūyālasa is like that for carma-kustha, involving rubbing with honey and rock salt;
one should then venesect the patient and apply a poultice.
11.4dv Thereafter, one should apply a poultice and perform all the procedures prescribed for *akṣipāka* according to the rules,
using finely powdered rock salt (*saindhava*), fresh ginger (*ārdraka*), ferrous sulfate (*kāsīsa*), iron, and copper. // 5 //
One should apply either a powdered collyrium with honey or a medicinal extract (rasakriyā).
Having fomented the worm-nodule (krimigranthi) with dried cow dung, one should then incise and scrape it.
One should rub [the affected area] with triphalā, honey, kāsīsa, and saindhava salt;
the treatment for śukti and the piṣṭaka known as balāsa is the same as that for pitta-abhiṣyanda.
11.7dv For those [eye diseases] called *balāsa* and *piṣṭaka*, one should treat them like *kaphābhiṣyanda*, avoiding venesection;
[one may apply] as an ointment *vyoṣa* and *kaṭphala* moistened with the juice of *bījapūra*. 8.

A wick (varti) made from jasmine buds, rock salt, deodar, and great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadha), ground together with clear wine (prasannā), is an eye-salve (añjana) that destroys swelling and itching. (9)
The medicinal treatment for erythema ab igne (utpāta) and horripilation (harṣa) is the same as that for ocular hemorrhage (rakta-syanda), including the application of *arjuna* bark.
For *sirotpāta* specifically, an ointment (*añjana*) made of ghee and honey is especially recommended. 11.9d–10.
In the case of sirā-harṣa (vein irritation), finely ground rasāñjana with honey is beneficial; for arjuna (corneal opacity), eye-drops consisting of sugar, whey, and honey are recommended. (11)
Rock crystal, saffron, conch shell, and madhuka mixed with honey;
or collyrium with honey, conch shell, and sea-foam together with sugar.

Sphaṭika, kuṅkuma, śaṅkha, kāsīsa, and añjana with honey—these five are said to be the remedies for arma; likewise, that which is thin, smoky-grey, red, resembling curd, or like semen, for these too this is the medicine. (11.12–13)
While lying on one's back, the other [eye], which has been sweated and anointed with rock salt, should be closed and rubbed with the juice of a citron. 14.
Thus, when his eyes are inflamed and the eyelids and their flesh are throbbing, he should apply clarified butter to the head, and especially to the eyelids. (15)

11.15b–16. When the *arman* (pterygium) or *adhimāṃsaka* (caruncle) is powerful, one should look toward the outer corner (*apāṅga*); when the *arman* has grown large from the pupil (*kanīnaka*), a fold (*valī*) will form there. Having suspended the *arman* with a hook (*baḍiśa*) at that spot, [one should proceed].
One should release [the thread] from there, neither too long, using a small needle, a larger needle, or a string;
then, one should release it all around with the tip of the mandala once it has been set free. 17.
11.17 Having pulled it out so as not too far, and having brought the canthus near until one-fourth remains, one should cut the canthus while protecting the tear-carrying channels. 18.

One should excise the *kanīnaka* while protecting it; by piercing the *kanīnaka*, tears flow through the canal into the eye. Likewise, when the *arman* has grown large, one should pierce the *kanīnaka* from the outer corner (*apāṅga*) for the sake of the patient's vision. (11.18–19)
From the injury of the pupil, tears flow quickly;
from the piercing of the pupil, a tear-duct is formed in the eye.
Properly excised, rubbed with honey, trikaṭu, and rock salt, sprinkled with warm ghee, and then anointed with honey and ghee. (20)
One should bind it and then release it, sprinkling [the patient] on the third and subsequent days with milk processed with *karañja* seeds, as well as with decoctions. (21)
With honey, the two types of niśā, lodhra, paṭolī, yaṣṭi,
kiṃśuka, and kuraṇṭa buds, one should certainly release [the patient] on the seventh day.

11.22c–d When [the eyelid] is properly incised with [incisions] resembling *koraṇṭa* buds, health is restored; however, from insufficient or excessive incision, diseases arise. One should overcome these through irrigation, collyrium, and so forth, as well as by scraping and nourishing treatments.
White sugar, realgar, elecampane, the best salt (rock salt), and dry ginger—each measured at half a karṣa—and half a pala of *tārkṣya* (rasāñjana), all well-mixed with honey. 24.
Half a pala of collyrium saturated with honey conquers phlegm-induced blindness, pilla, cataracts, pterygium, and dryness.
One should take the bark of any one of the three fruits (triphalā) and grind it into a paste with water. 11.25cd–25.
11.25b–26. Having burnt it covered with a shallow dish (*śarāva*) on a potsherd (*kapāla*), one should then reduce it to powder.
It should then be processed (*bhāvita*) separately with the juices of each of the remaining medicinal herbs.
That soot, once dried, should be ground again and combined with two salts;
Nimi has declared these three to be the most excellent collyriums for scraping.

Regarding the network of vessels (sirājāla), those vessels which are hardened and do not respond to scraping medicines—just as in the case of *arma*—the treatment for those [conditions] and for pustules (*piṭikā*) is as follows: 28.
In cases of semen disorders, unctuous and dry treatments are best according to the specific doshas; bitter substances, upward bloodletting, purgation, affusion, and so forth are recommended. (29)

11.29ab Regarding seminal disorders, due to the persistence of the *doṣas*, unctuous or dry treatments are recommended; ghee is the best for both unctuous and dry conditions. 11.29cd Bitter [medicines] are desired for upward bleeding, as are purgation, bloodletting, affusion, and so forth.
In cases of *kṣata-śukra*, one should drink ghee that has been cooked three times with *trivṛt* water; subsequently, one should remove blood from the eye using venesection or leeches. (30)
Sprinkling with milk from a goat mixed with sugar, along with *utpala*, *kākolī*, *drākṣā*, *yaṣṭī*, and *vidārī*—or else with water—is [prescribed] by the perfected ones. (31)
For the pacification of the tears of passion and suffering, the supreme collyrium is an ointment-stick made from jasmine buds, lac, red ochre, and sandalwood. (32)
[Tooth-powders] made from the teeth of elephants, boars, camels, cows, horses, goats, and donkeys clarify the bile and blood, and destroy wounds and seminal disorders. (33)

11.33a–d. A tooth-stick (dantavarti) made from the products of a cow, a donkey, or the sea— mixed with conch-shell, pearl-oyster, and sea-foam, and containing one-quarter part black pepper— pacifies pitta and blood, and may also eliminate pervasive seminal injury (kṣataśukra).
A wick made of *tāmalapatra*, cow-tusk, conch-shell, sea-foam, donkey-bone, and copper, [applied] with urine, destroys all types of seminal disorders (*śukraka*). (35)
Copper with goat’s urine;
gems, teeth, horns, and metals; the three pungents (try-ūṣaṇa), cardamom (truṭī), karañja seeds, garlic, and medicines for treating wounds. // 36 //
Collyrium destroys the vitiated *śukra* located in the skin, whether it is ulcerated, non-ulcerated, or deep-seated;
it raises the sunken [eye] through the intake of fats, nasal medication (*nasya*), and liquid collyrium (*rasāñjana*). (37)

One should treat seminal impurity (śukraka) that is either painful or painless with a poultice cooked in milk; when the semen is purified, one should use a decoction of turmeric (niśā), licorice (yaṣṭī), śārivā, and śābarā.

11.38–39. Sprinkling with water prepared from śārivā, or with a lukewarm water-soaked pouch of *lodhra*, or [a poultice] made of *bṛhatī* root, *yaṣṭimadhu*, copper filings, rock salt (*saindhava*), and ginger (*nāgara*).
A copper vessel smeared with substances ground with the juice of *dhātrī* fruits should then be fumigated many times with barley, clarified butter, and *āmalakī* leaves.
One should prepare pills from those [substances], ground with water and honey;
known as "Mahānīla," they are supreme for removing pure semen.
When the semen is stable and thick, one should repeatedly extract the blood,
and frequently administer head-purgatives, body-purgatives, and fomentations in a closed vessel (puṭapāka).
One should perform aphrodisiac stimulation with black pepper, long pepper, śirīṣa fruit, and rock salt, or with salt dissolved in a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā). // 43 //

One should perform rubbing with a decoction of the three fruits (triphalā), or a decoction of mustard seeds and the three fruits; or one may apply these two collyrium formulations mentioned in the half-verse:
[one] with conch shell, kola seeds, kataka, grapes, madhuka, and honey. (11.43–44)

An alkaline solution derived from *lāṅgalikā*, combined with the impurities of fermented liquor, ivory, and the ocean, along with *śirīṣa* flowers, the juice of *dhātrī* and *phaṇijjaka*, [is used]. (45)
An ointment made from the ashes of *khara-dantī* and the salt from the ocean,
combined with an alkaline solution derived from *lāṅgalikā* (or *lāṅgalikī*),
which has been soaked, dried, and powdered, is an aphrodisiac collyrium that arouses virility.
Alternatively, dehusked mung beans, ground into a paste and combined with conch-shell powder and honey, [should be used]. // 46 //
11.46b–47. Semen, *añjana* ointment, the pith of *madhūka*, honey, the marrow of *vākṣa*, along with honey;
the teeth of a cow, donkey, horse, and camel; conch shell; and sea foam.
The pith of the *madhūka* tree, sweetened with honey, forms a medicinal wick (*varti*) which,
when applied with the juice of the *arjuna* tree, destroys prominent seminal discharge (*śukra*).
One should scrape away the discharge— whether it is protruding, accompanied by a foreign body, or merely excessive— using instruments such as a lancet.
Pounded [together], it destroys *śukraka*. It also destroys vitiated *śukraka*.
However, for *sirā-śukra* which does not cause loss of vision, the treatment is like that for *vraṇa-śukra*.
[The remedy consists of] *puṇḍra*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *kākolī*, *siṃhī*, iron, *niśā*, and collyrium. (11.49)
A medicinal wick (varti) made from [the drug] ground with goat’s milk, fumigated with ghee and barley,
and [mixed with] emblic myrobalan leaves, applied in rotation, is the supreme collyrium (añjana) for this condition.

In this case, medicinal wicks and collyriums are beneficial. If there is no subsiding, one should employ surgical instruments as prescribed for *arman* (pterygium) and for the condition called *ajakā*.
In the case of incurable *ajakā*, as well as in *śukra* and other similar conditions, the same [surgical] measures should be applied.

One should effect the subsiding of the sensation [of desire] through the drinking of unctuous substances, bloodletting, and so forth, in order to overcome the loathsomeness [of the body] and to achieve the reduction of the accumulation of semen. (52)
11.52d–53. Ashes produced from coconut husks, marking-nut seeds (*bhallātaka*), palmyra palm, bamboo, and bamboo shoots serve as a means for achieving whiteness and elevation.
One should cause these to be washed with water and then saturate ash produced from camel bones with that same liquid.

This powder is an eye-salve that removes discoloration in cases of semen-disorders (śukra) that are otherwise incurable; and when practiced regularly, it is also sufficient for the cure of those cases that are curable.
Having pierced the goat's [wound] from the side with a needle and drained the fluid, one should press it evenly with the thumb and fill it with fat moistened with water. // 55 //

Having bound the wound with powdered beef and releasing it once it has been bound, when the wound has healed after seven nights—becoming level and stable in its dark portion—[the procedure is complete]. (56)
An unguent of oil should be applied, as well as nasal drops (nasya) with milk and ghee;
nevertheless, if there is renewed distension, one should perform procedures such as incision and excision.
11.57cv Nevertheless, when it has swollen again, one should proceed by means of skillful technique so that there is no excessive cutting during immersion. 11.57d //ab //

One should apply [the collyrium] with skill so that it is neither too frequent nor too constant; likewise, one should administer ghee boiled with *śukra* internally, both as a drink and as an unguent.
For the vision, having once attained its strength, does not diminish even when sharp collyriums are applied constantly.
11.58dv When the impurity follows the vessels and has first reached the first layer (paṭala), the vision is restored by the continuous application of sharp collyriums.
One perceives the unmanifest form, and the manifest as well, through the absence of causal signs.
12.1b When [the visual consciousness] has reached the first layer (*paṭala*), form is perceived indistinctly;
when it has reached the second layer, one sees even what is non-existent.
However, even if it is existent, one does not see what is nearby with effort, nor what is distant or subtle. // 2 //

One does not see what is distant or subtle, nor does one perceive forms situated at a distance or nearby correctly; when there is a circular defect in the eye, one sees things as if they were circles. (12.2cd–3ab)

When [the object] is situated in the middle of the vision, it appears as one thing in two ways; when situated in many places, it appears in many ways. When it has entered within the range of vision, there is a reversal of shortness and length. // 4 //

12.4dv: A reversal of short and long [distances]; a near object appears far away, and what is situated below appears high; one does not see what is far off when it is situated above, nor does one see what is at the side when it is situated at the side. This is the disease known as *timira*. // 5 //
When a defect resides in the third layer [of the eye], it acquires the nature of glass;
therefore, one sees what is above but not below, as if covered by a thin cloth.

12.6cv Looking upwards with that [wind], one does not see below; the vision becomes colored according to the specific humor and gradually deteriorates. Even so, for one who neglects it, the disease reaches the fourth layer (paṭala). // 7 //
12.7 According to the specific dosha involved,

the impurity (mala), causing the destruction of the [visual] signs, may cover the circle of vision (dṛṣṭi-maṇḍala). In that regard, when there is timira caused by vāta, one sees as if [the objects] were distorted.
He repeatedly sees a clear appearance with a flickering, reddish luster; and when he disregards it, he sees lattices, hair, gnats, and rays of light. (9)
12.9a–d: One whose vision has become like glass (kācī-bhūta) sees objects repeatedly as hazy with smoke, reddish in luster, or clear;
yet when this condition is neglected, the eye becomes bloodshot and one sees a face without a nose.
One perceives the moon, lamps, and so forth as being manifold, and considers what is crooked to be straight. // 10 //
Advanced cataract (vṛddha-kāca) makes the vision as if veiled by dust or smoke;
it may appear clear, reddish, extensive, or minute, and it destroys one's sight.

12.11c–d When the eye-vessels are contracted by Vāta, that condition is known as *liṅganāśa*; it appears bright red and extensive, the pupil enters deep within, and the vision becomes profoundly dimmed. // 12 //

In the case of *timira* born from bile (*pitta*), one generally sees [objects] illuminated by lightning, fireflies, or lamps, resembling the color of a peacock's or partridge's feather, and mostly blue. (13)

12.13–14. The eye, appearing like the glow of a firefly or illuminated by its light, resembles the feathers of a peacock or a partridge; it perceives glass as having the blue luster of glass, and likewise sees halos around the sun and moon, flames, rays of light, and rainbows.

In *kāca* (cataract), the vision appears like the color of bell-metal or blue, or as dark as a bumblebee; in *liṅganāśa*, the vision is glossy yet devoid of light. Due to *pitta*, the condition called *hrasvā* occurs, which is short and characterized by short-sightedness.
When [the eye] is afflicted by bile, it is called Pitta-vidagdha; it is yellow, and one perceives objects as having a yellowish appearance.
In the case of Kapha-timira, one generally sees things as glossy and white. // 16 //
12.16b–c. When yellow, it appears yellowish, as if strewn with conch shells, the moon, jasmine flowers, and white water-lilies;
but when glassy, it is like being strewn with lusterless moons, suns, lamps, and the like. 12.17.

12.17b–d. And that vision would appear as if covered by white water-lilies; however, in the case of *liṅganāśa*, it is observed that phlegm (*kapha*) becomes solidified, localized in the eye, glossy, and destroys sight. 18.
Like a drop of water resting upon a lotus leaf, it is flickering;
in the heat it contracts, and in the shade it spreads.

12.19b–c Residing within the folds of a lotus leaf, possessing a whiteness like that of a conch shell, jasmine, the moon, the white water-lily, or crystal; in the case of *rakta-timira*, one sees redness and perceives things as if enveloped in darkness.
12.20d–a [The patient] sees everything as having become dark.
A vision reddened or blackened by glass sees things accordingly;
likewise, even when the visual faculty is destroyed, the vision is similarly devoid of luster and its sight is impaired.

In cases of combined or simultaneous involvement [of the humors], one should recognize the mixed symptoms; moreover, conditions such as *timira* (blindness/darkness) may arise suddenly, and through these, the eyes become clearly disordered.

By these [three causes], one's vision becomes distorted and clouded; by the remaining two, the vision in *timira* becomes clearly clouded. A variegated discoloration arises in the sight of one whose vision is thick with impurities, appearing like that of a mongoose.
Blind from birth, he saw nothing there by day, yet at night he beheld a marvel: when the sun’s rays had settled upon its setting peak, they reached the pillar.
Defects obscure the vision; that other disease is blindness caused by defects.
When touched by the rays of the sun, the impurities fall away from the path of sight. (25)
Those who have dissolved and become latent manifest their presence clearly here during the day, like one who has been heated by the heat and suddenly immerses himself in cold water. (26)
When the three doṣas are combined with blood, the heat ascends and reaches the eyes; there is burning pain, the pupil becomes turbid white, and during the day there is blurred vision. (27)
Blindness occurs at night; that is known as *vidagdhoṣṇā*.
When the vision is covered by the humors along with blood due to excessive consumption of sour food, [it is called *raktābhiṣyanda*]. // 28 //
That [condition] is known as being afflicted by moisture, itching, and turbidity due to burning acidity;
for one tormented by grief, fever, and diseases of the head, the [disturbances of] wind and the other [humors] arise. (29)
12.29b–d. That [condition] is considered to be caused by burning with sour substances; it makes the eyes turbid with smoke and causes the vision to become smoky (*dhūmara*).
For one of little fortitude who suddenly beholds a wondrous form, that [condition] arises.

12.30ab They make the vision of those with smoky vision turbid with smoke; that is *dhūsara*. 12.30b That which makes the vision [turbid] is *dhūmaka*. 12.30cd Vāta and the other [humors], when localized in the eye, [cause it to see] a brilliant light such as that of the sun.
They cause the vital energy to dry up and the vision to become robbed of its sight. // 31 //
12.31 Whether it be radiant, like the sun and so forth,
or the color of lapis lazuli, steady, naturally stable, and as if free from distress—
this destruction of the signs (liṅga-nāśa) is called "adventitious" (aupasargika); one should avoid it here.

Except for those caused by phlegm (kapha), those involving loss of vision, those that are deep-seated, and even those of short duration—these six types of cataracts (kāca) and nocturnal blindness (nakulāndhya) are palliable; the remaining types one should treat with curative intent. (33)
12.33cv Six types of cataracts (kāca) and nakulāndhya—thus twelve diseases of the vision have been specified; [with the others,] there are twenty-seven in total. 12.33ū̆ab //
In the Uttarasthāna:
Timira turns into Kāca through neglect, and Kāca likewise leads to blindness.
Therefore, among eye diseases, one should treat the terrible Timira immediately. (1)
One should boil one *tulā* of *jīvantī* in a *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-quarter;
into that decoction, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with double the amount of milk.

To that decoction, twice as much milk should be added along with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *kākolī*, long pepper (*pippalī*), *lodhra*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *śatāhvā*, licorice (*madhuka*), grapes (*drākṣā*), sugar, *dāru*, and the three myrobalans (*phala-traya*). (13.2cd–3ab)
When drunk at night by farmers, it is the supreme remover of darkness (cataract), [prepared] with grapes, sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of kākolī, and jīvaka. (4)
13.4b This is the supreme remedy for all forms of *timira*.
One should cook one *prastha* of aged ghee with equal parts of milk and one *picu* each of sugar, *śatāvarī*, *medā*, *puṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, and blue lotus.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the following until it is fully digested:
*paṭola*, *nimba*, *kaṭukā*, *dārvī*, *sevya*, *varā*, and *vṛṣa*. This destroys *kāca*, *timira*, blood-shot vessels, and headaches. (13.5cd–6ab)
One pala each of dhanvayāsa, trāyantī, and parpaṭaka,
along with one prastha of āmalaka fruits, should be boiled separately in abundant water.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with half-pala weights of the ground paste of those [drugs] in an āḍhaka of water,
along with musta, bhūnimba, yaṣṭyāhva, kuṭaja, udīcya, and candana.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with half a pala each of pippalī in an āḍhaka of that [decoction]; this medicated ghee conquers diseases of the nose, ears, and mouth,
and it destroys abscesses, fever, malignant ulcers, erysipelas, scrofula, and skin diseases.
That ghee, prepared with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and cavya, conquers diseases of the nose, ears, and eyes; it specifically removes abscesses,
fever, and vitiated blood, as well as seminal disorders, cataracts, night-blindness, and the burning sensation caused by heat and sourness.
Eight palas of the three myrobalans (triphalā) should be boiled in one āḍhaka of water until one-fourth remains.

It cures night-blindness and relieves burning sensations caused by heat and sourness. When one-quarter part of this [decoction] is combined with one *āḍhaka* of water and an equal amount of milk, along with a paste of one *pala* of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), half a *prastha* of ghee is cooked; it may then be taken with sugar or honey. (13.10–11)
One suffering from *timira* (blindness) should drink that [milk] mixed with it, or the juice of *varā* (triphala) combined with *yaṣṭīmadhu*,
the two *kākolīs*, *vyāghrī*, *kṛṣṇā*, *amṛtā*, and *utpala*.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with equal parts of pālikas (one pala each) of sugar and grapes,
along with goat’s milk, the fat of the varā plant, and the fresh juices of mārkava, each separately.
This is known as the Great Traiphala, which conquers the distortions of vision;
then, licking the Traiphala at night with an oblation of Traiphala [ghee], he should consume the three fruits.
13.14b–d. Furthermore, one who consumes *āmalaka* water mixed with *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and saturated with honey for one month, while eating wholesome food, will remove disorders of vision. 15.
"One obtains the vision of Suparṇa," so said the venerable Nimi.
[This is achieved] by means of *tāpya*, iron, gold, *yaṣṭyāhva*, white sugar, old ghee, and honey. (16)
This excellent, darkness-dispelling Varā should be combined as desired;
or one suffering from the disease of timira should habitually consume a decoction of Varā with ghee. 17.
Or cakes, soups, or parched grain flour mixed with the powder of the three myrobalans;
or milk-rice combined with *varā*, served cold with honey and sugar. (18)

A patient suffering from *timira* should constantly eat *pathyā* (harītakī) either with cakes, buttermilk, or roasted barley flour, or before a meal, each separately combined with raisins, sugar, and honey. (13.18–19)
13.19–20ab. Or, before breakfast,
one should place sixty-four parts of *srotoñjana*— each combined with a single part of copper, iron, silver, and gold— inside the interior of a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*).
Having blown [the crucible] until it has cooled, one should then pour that [substance] into the decoctions of the mercury-group (rasaskandha) seven times, separately for each.
Then, one should employ a powdered collyrium consisting of three parts each of beryl, pearl, and conch shell; it removes all types of cataracts.

All of that [removes] darkness (timira) when prepared with spikenard, the three aromatics, costus, saffron, blue lotus, chebulic myrobalan, blue vitriol, white glass, conch shell, cuttlefish bone, black pepper, collyrium, and licorice. (13.22–23)

When the Moon is with its lord Aśvinī, one desiring the pacification of cataracts, film, blood-vessels, itching, ophthalmia, and other such ailments, should apply well-ground [medicines] as collyrium to both eyes. (24)
Two parts each of black pepper, excellent salt, long pepper, and sea-foam, along with nine parts of *sauvīra* salt, ground together under the asterism Citrā, conquers diseases caused by phlegm. (25)
13.25dv When finely ground with *citrā*, it overcomes diseases caused by *kapha*.

Realgar (*manohvā*), blue vitriol (*tuttha*), musk (*kastūrī*), spikenard (*māṃsī*), sandalwood (*malaya*), and yellow pigment (*rocanā*), combined with ten parts of camphor (*karpūra*), constitute an eye-salve (*añjana*) of eighty-fold potency. 25+(1)

13.25+(1) Ground together with *dara* and camphor, this [ointment] is beneficial for the six types of cataracts when prepared under the asterisms of Citrā, Aśvinī, or Puṣya; it clarifies the vision, as declared by Cakṣuṣeṇa. 25+(2)
One should sprinkle conch-shell [powder] seven times separately with the natural juices of grapes and lotus stalks, as well as with milk, wine, fat, and celestial water. (26)
That powder, ground and placed in a conch shell, is a collyrium that clarifies the vision; it is recommended for all eye diseases and was formulated by the Lord of Videha. (27)

That [mercury] is powdered and mixed with ghee, burnt in a conch shell using *bādara* charcoal, and then successively sprinkled with *tuttha*, goat’s milk, clarified butter, and honey; from this, two *pala*s [are taken]. (13.27–28)
And likewise, Tuttha (copper sulfate) should be infused and heated in succession with one karṣa each of tāpya (borax),

marica (black pepper), srotoñjana (antimony), kaṭukā (Picrorhiza), nata (Cinnamomum tamala), paṭu (salt), lodhra, śilājatu, pathyā (Terminalia chebula), kaṇā (Piper longum), elā (cardamom), añjana (collyrium), and phenaka (sea foam).
Equal parts of *yaṣṭī* (liquorice) and *pala* (Cassia fistula), powdered and blown into a crucible,
when well-practiced [as a collyrium], destroys cataracts, night-blindness, and blood-red streaks.
This powder, like the sun, especially dispels cataracts (timira) just as the sun [dispels darkness];
it consists of thirty parts of snake [ash] and five parts of sulphur (gandhapāṣāṇa).
Two parts each of śulba and tālaka, one part of vaṅga, and three parts of añjana,
placed in an andhamūṣā crucible and heated until melted, yield pure añjana.
Two parts each of copper and silver, when blown [into a crucible] placed within a blind-muṣā,
become a destroyer of darkness in the world, like a second sun.
13.33 In this world, [this remedy] removes cataracts when applied to cow urine, the liquid of dried cow dung, sour *kāñjika*, and breast milk.
In cow urine, goat's milk, sour *kāñjika* gruel, clarified butter,
poison, and honey.
The tuttha which has been heated many times and poured [into acid]... // 33e //
That would make a man's vision equal to that of Garuḍa. // 33f //
Gold purified by fire, along with conch-shells, stone, red ochre, and collyrium;
and a human skull, a Sahi, and a hen’s egg—a man who has gone through these for seven, two, seven, and three times respectively [attains success]. (33+1)

This collyrium made from *sauvīra* salt, having been purified by being successively saturated with the fresh juice of *bhṛṅga*, goat’s milk, cow’s urine, cow’s milk, a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and grape juice, destroys cataracts (*timira*). // 33+2 //
Take the best water, the juice of *bhṛṅga*, ghee with poison, goat’s milk, and the juice of *yaṣṭī*; these, along with lead, should each be processed separately seven times. (34)
The juice of *śreṣṭhā* and the juice of *bhṛṅga*,
heated repeatedly and administered as a probe (*śalākā*) to the eye— whether combined with collyrium (*añjana*) or used alone—
destroys blurred vision (*taimira*), cataracts (*arman*), discharge (*srāva*), thickening (*paicchilya*), *pailla*, itching (*kaṇḍū*), numbness (*jāḍya*), and blood-streaks (*rakta-rājī*). // 35 //
Mercury and the serpent [mineral] are equal in measure;
then, an ointment equal to those two, combined with a small amount of camphor, is an ointment that removes darkness (cataracts).

Collyrium combined with a small amount of camphor is the best remedy for cataracts; it is the nectar for the eyes. The face of that vulture, which once had cheeks radiant as the rising sun, now belongs to one who has died in due time; [it is covered] with cow dung.
Equal parts of burnt ghee and collyrium (añjana) should be ground together; this formulation bestows the strength of vision of a vulture. (37)
Collyrium that has been burnt with an oblation in the mouth of a black cobra,
mixed with powdered *nalada* leaves, protects the eyes even when they are pierced by a star-like speck.

13.38b–c. This *bhāskara-añjana* for the eyes is prepared by taking two parts of *nāgāñjana*, five of *aśmāla*, one of *śilā*, twelve of *arka*, and two of *vaṅga*; these are burnt until the smoke has ceased, mixed with *nalada* leaves, placed in an *andhamūṣā* crucible, and sprinkled with goat’s milk. (38+1)

One should wrap the "hero-stone" from a stream with ajamoda and banyan leaves; this sixfold preparation conquers cataracts when it has been soiled and smeared with clay, then heated by a fire of cow-dung. (38+2)
The fine powder of copper, iron, magnetite, sulphur, and malachite, along with *bhṛṅgaraja* fried in iron, when used for seven days, conquers diseases of the eye. (38+3)
13.38–39. Having placed the well-disguised dust of *tārkṣya*, a dead black snake, and four scorpions into a jar of milk,
one should let them soak for three weeks and then churn it.

Having moistened [the eyes], one should then churn them; whatever fresh butter (*navanīta*) may be produced therefrom, one should nourish a cock with it. By means of its excrement as an ointment (*añjana*), a blind person certainly regains his sight.
The fat of a black cobra, conch shell, the fruit of the *kataka* tree, and collyrium—this medicinal preparation (rasakriyā) quickly bestows sight upon the blind. (41)
