Five picus of long pepper, one pala and one picu of purified copper sulfate (tuttha), and one picu of liquorice—this collyrium, burnt while moist with milk, is called Apratisāra; it is excellent for cataracts (timira). 42.

Ten *marica* (black pepper) seeds, two *pala* of *akṣa*-seed, black pepper, *āmalaka*, bark, *tuttha*, and *yaṣṭimadhu*, ground with water and formed into pills, dried in the shade, destroy cataracts (*timira*) before long. (13.42cd–43ab)

The formulation known as "sixfold honey" (*ṣaṇ-mākṣika*), consisting of long pepper (*marica*), emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), mineral pitch (*jalodbhava-tuttha*), antimony collyrium (*añjana*), and gold ore (*tāpya-dhātu*) in increasing proportions, destroys cataracts, opacities, inflammation, pterygium, and itching. (44)
It destroys darkness, cataracts, moisture, film, itching, and [other ailments];
it is a destroyer of *timira*, *arman*, *kleda*, *kāca*, and *kaṇḍū*.
[The ingredients are] gems, silver, crystal, gold, *srotoñjana*, copper, iron, along with conch shell.
Bad sandalwood and red ochre, as well as powdered collyrium, destroy all eye diseases. (45)
Sesame oil, vibhītaka oil, the natural juice of bhṛṅgarāja, and a decoction of aśana, when cooked in an iron vessel and administered as a nasal drop (nasya), bestows strength upon the vision. (46)
One should restore the strength of vision through nasal therapy according to the specific doshas, and treat the patient repeatedly with oleation, bloodletting, purgation, and errhines; furthermore,
one should employ collyrium, head-enema, enema therapy, saturation, ointments, and affusions.
This proof is common [to all]; therefore, hear the refutation for each [of these] faults. (48ab)
In that case, for cataract (timira) born of wind (vāta), one should then drink ghee cooked with the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla),
four times the amount of milk, and a paste (kalka) of śreṣṭhā.
One should administer a purgative consisting of a decoction of triphalā and pañcamūla, combined with milk and castor oil. (50)
One should employ a purgative mixed with castor oil.
One should boil one *tulā* of *jīvantī*, including its root system, in a *droṇa* of water.
When that decoction has been reduced to one-eighth, one should add one *prastha* of oil along with an equal amount of milk.
One *prastha* of oil, equal in quantity to milk,
should be cooked in an iron vessel with one *pala* each of the three types of *balā*, *jīvantī*, and the roots of *varī*, and four *palas* of *yaṣṭī*. (13.51–52)

Iron kept for a month in a decoction of *balā*, *trijātaka*, and *jīvantī* destroys diseases of the upper body caused by wind and bile (*vātapitta*) when used as an errhine (*nāvana*); it is especially effective for those localized in the eyes.
If kept for a month in an iron vessel, it especially cures eye diseases and bestows nourishment upon the hair, face, neck, and shoulders, as well as beauty and luster.
[This is prepared] with white castor root, *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *siṃhī* fruit, *dāruharidrā*, *vacā*, and *tagara*.

Oil cooked with *ghoṣā*, the roots of *bilva*, and milk, which promotes nourishment, beauty, and luster, used as nasal drops (*nasya*), overcomes the pain of all diseases arising from wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*) above the clavicle. 13.54b–55a.

13.55–56ab. A collyrium made from the fat of a tiger or a boar, combined with *śatāhvā* and the roots of *bilva*, is highly recommended; likewise, fat derived from a vulture, a snake, or a cock, each mixed separately with *madhuka*, is also praised.

And for the application of collyrium, rock salt (sroto-ja) should be successively infused into juice, milk, and ghee; when used as before, this is the unsurpassed destroyer of cataracts (timira). (57)

If [the disease] does not subside by means of meat broth, milk, and ghee in succession, then one should perform a satiation therapy (tarpaṇa) with *śatāhvā*, *kuṣṭha*, *nalada*, the two types of *kākolī*, and *yaṣṭi*. 13.58ab–58cd.
Ghee cooked with prapauṇḍarīka, sarala, pippalī, and devadāru, along with eight times its quantity of milk, is an excellent nourishing tonic. (59)
In the same manner, fat from the meat of a black antelope, prepared with milk and stirred with a churning stick,
should have its essence extracted and processed with madhuka, uśīra, and sandalwood.
One should separately prepare the fat of the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the partridge, the francolin, and the peacock by this very same procedure.

One should employ *puṭapāka* (sealed cooking) of porcupine, hedgehog, and monitor lizard; of partridge, gallinaceous birds, and monitor lizard; and of bear, partridge, and peacock, for the purposes of clarification (*prasādana*) and oleation (*snehana*).
And in this case, as in the treatment for vāta-type chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) along with an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).

In cases of *timira* born of *pitta*, after administering a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*) or an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*), one should have the patient drink ghee prepared with the *jīvanīya* drugs and the three myrobalans (*phala-traya*).
Once the patient has been lubricated, one should perform venesection.
One should administer purgation with powders of sugar, cardamom, and trivṛt mixed with honey;
one should also apply very cold sprinklings, ointments, and other treatments to the eyes, mouth, and head. (64)
A medicinal wick (varti) made from śārivā, padmaka, uśīra, pearls, and śābara sandalwood is recommended for collyrium; likewise, a powder made from pattra, utpala, and añjana is prescribed.
13.65c–d: An ointment stick (varti), a collyrium powder (añjana-cūrṇa), and likewise [ointments] made from lotus, blue water-lily, and añjana;
with nāgapuṣpa, camphor, yaṣṭimadhu, and golden ochre;
with sauvīrāñjana, tutthaka, śṛṅgī, dhātrī fruit, crystal, and camphor.

One part each of the five [ingredients], three parts of *añjana*, and one part of *añjana* destroy cataracts (*timira*); likewise, clarified butter boiled with milk, the *jīvanīya* group of herbs, and white lotus, used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), [achieves the same]. (67)
In cases arising from phlegm (kapha), one should administer ghee prepared with a decoction of amṛtā, varā, and kaṇā;
after the patient has drunk it, one should perform venesection and subsequently give a purgative.

One should prepare a decoction from betel nut (*pūga*), *abhayā*, ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), *kumbha*, and *nikumbha*, combined with a paste (*kalka*) of *hrīvera*, *dāru*, the two types of turmeric (*niśā*), and long pepper, along with milk. (69)

Oil cooked with a decoction of the two [types of] *pañcamūla* is used for nasal administration (*nāvana*), along with conch shell, *priyaṅgu*, *nepālī*, the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), and the three fruits (*phalatrika*). (70)

For the purification of vision, there should be a stainless wick; furthermore, the *kokilā* [preparation] is made from black iron filings, *vyoṣa*, rock salt, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and collyrium.
Furthermore, the *kaulikā* suppository should consist of the bones from the forehead of a rabbit, cow, donkey, lion, camel, and bird;
white cow-hair, black pepper, conch-shell, sandalwood, and cuttlefish bone.
A wick made from this powder ground with breast milk, ghee, and cow’s milk conquers *timira* and *śukra*.
In cases arising from blood (*rakta-ja*), the treatment is successful as in *pitta*; one should clarify the blood with cooling remedies. (73)
The pith of Madhūka, Añjana, copper, the three pungents (Trikaṭuka), Viḍaṅga, Pauṇḍarīka, along with salt, Tuttha, Triphalā, and Lodhra, ground with rainwater; 73+1.
This fourteen-ingredient medicinal wick, which destroys eye diseases, was inscribed upon a stone pillar for the benefit of the world; it specifically removes darkness. (73+2)
One part of Māgadhikā and two parts of Harītakī, ground with water, form this medicinal wick (varti) which removes cataracts, films, opacities, itching, and tearing. 73+3.

By means of grapes, *nalada*, *lodhra*, and *yaṣṭi*, along with conch, copper, white lotus, *padmaka*, and blue water-lily, prepared with goat's milk, blood-born cataracts (timira) are quickly destroyed. (74)
With grapes, *nalada*, *lodhra*, *yaṣṭikā*,
conch-shell, copper, *himapadma*,
and *padmaka* (or *padmapattraka*).
In cases arising from the combination of two or three doṣas, treatment should be administered according to the predominance of the specific doṣa.
A proven formulation consists of madhūka, kṛmijit, marica, and amaradāru. (75)
Oil for nasal drops (nāvana) mixed with milk, and an ointment for the face made from a paste of nata, nīlotpala, anantā, yaṣṭyāhva, and suniṣaṇṇaka; // 76 //
The oil prepared for nasal irrigation (nāvana) is recommended for use in the head-bleeding procedure (śiro-vasti);
one should add powdered black pepper and rock salt to a decoction of uśīra.
That prepared oil for nasal drops (nāvana), having been strained, should be cooked again with ghee; when it has become thick, one should add honey.
Once this has cooled, it is beneficial as a collyrium (añjana) for all types of cataracts (timira).
13.78 Having boiled that again with ghee, one should let it soak in water containing the bones of nocturnal beings filled with marrow, combined with *srotoñjana* collyrium. 79.

13.79c–d. These [powders] should be combined with *srotoñjana* for one month or twenty nights; then, having removed them, one should dry them, followed by *meṣaśṛṅgī*, its flowers, and *yaṣṭyāhvā*. 13.80.
These [drugs], along with yaṣṭi, when ground into a powder, constitute the best collyrium for *sāṃnipātika* timira;
this same procedure applies to *kāca* as well, provided one avoids venesection and instead uses pressure applied by a mechanical instrument.

13.81cd–82ab: The vessels (sirā), when compressed by the instrument, may cause blindness due to the pressure on the vessels; therefore, one should apply leeches to drain the blood. [The ingredients for the collyrium are: jaggery, foam, antimony, long pepper, black pepper, and the powder of saffron.
Therefore, for the sake of curing blindness, one should administer this medicinal preparation of mercury with honey as a collyrium to remove *kāca*.
In cases of *nakulāndhya* arising from the three *doṣas*, the procedure prescribed for *timira* should be followed.
13.83–84. Just as in the treatment for *timira*, therapeutic actions are performed with juices, medicinal preparations, ghee, honey, cow-dung, and fresh extracts.
For night-blindness (*niśāndha*), collyrium made from *tārkṣya* (mercury), *gairika* (red ochre), *tālīśa*, and *niśā* (turmeric) is beneficial.
13.84cd–85ab: For night-blindness, collyrium ground with curd is beneficial; black pepper rubbed with curd is the best collyrium for night-blindness.
[One may also use] *karañjika*, blue lotus, golden ochre, and the filaments of the lotus.

13.85b–c. This collyrium is the best for night-blindness (rātry-andha). A wick made from powdered kārañjika, utpala, and gold, ground with cow-dung water, destroys blindness caused by the [three] humors (doṣāndha).
Or, it may be prepared with goat’s urine and kauntī, kṛṣṇā, sroto-ja, and saindhava.

13.86b–v. A wick (varti) composed of kālānusāri, the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), the three fruits (tri-phalā), alum, realgar, and phenā, mixed with goat’s milk, destroys blindness caused by the humors (doṣa); such wicks are beneficial for night-blindness (rātry-andha).
13.87d–88. For night-blindness, medicinal wicks (varti) are beneficial.
One should cook long peppers (pippalī) by placing them inside the center of a liver without burning them.
Once dried, these should be rubbed with honey; this is the best collyrium (añjana) for night-blindness.
Collyrium is the best remedy for night-blindness (*niśāndhya*), and collyrium is the best remedy for nocturnal blindness (*naktāndhya*).
One should eat the spleen and liver of a buffalo with oil and ghee,
and one should also consume the sprouts of *jīvantī* prepared in clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Likewise, ghee fried with the leaves of *atimuktaka*, *eraṇḍa*, *śephālī*, and *abhīru* is honored when drunk by one born from a jar (Agastya). 90.
Ghee prepared with the leaves of the *kumbhayoni* (Arka) plant is highly esteemed for internal consumption.
In cases of *dhūmaka*, acid dyspepsia (*amlapitta*), heat, and burning sensations, one should administer a purgative using aged ghee after first applying oleation,
and one should apply cold poultices all over the body with cooling substances.
An ointment cooked with cow dung, juice, milk, and clarified butter is recommended;
a medicinal extract (rasakriyā) prepared by adding powders of gold, red ochre, and tālīśa is also advised. (92)
Ghee cooked with eight parts of milk and combined with medā, śābaraka, ānantā, mañjiṣṭhā, dāruharidrā, and yaṣṭimadhu, along with oil, is beneficial as a nasal drop (nāvana). // 93 //

Satiating therapy with milk and ghee should be employed; if [the condition] does not subside, venesection is indicated. [This disease arises] from anxiety, injury, fear, grief, dryness, and sitting in a squatting posture (utkaṭaka). // 94 //

From the consumption of dry, sour, and pungent foods; from the improper administration of purgatives, nasal therapy, emetics, and medicinal soot-pastes (puṭapāka); from vomiting undigested food; and from the suppression of hunger, thirst, and other natural urges. // 95 //
And until the end of the eye disease, one should see like a person suffering from *timira*;
in that state, one should apply medicine according to the specific [condition], having observed the humors (*doṣa*) and other factors. // 96 //

For one whose vision is impaired by gazing at a solar eclipse, fire, lightning, and the like, nourishing treatment with unctuous and cooling substances such as clarified butter should be administered; likewise, an ointment made of gold rubbed with clarified butter should be applied. (97)
As long as one desires to live, men should at all times exert effort in guarding their eyesight;
for this world is useless for blind men, whose days and nights are equal, even though wealth exists. 98.

The three myrobalans, the flowing of blood, purification, mental tranquility, collyrium, nasal medication, subsisting on bird-flesh, worship of the feet, and the drinking of ghee—these always constitute the protection of the eyes. 99.

13.99b–d The pacification of the mind, collyrium, nasal drops, and the offering of a seat and feet; 13.99e–f constant abstention from unwholesome food and from gazing intensely at bright lights, moving objects, or minute things.
This supreme protection for the eyes of men was taught by the sage Nimi. 100.
In the Uttarasthāna,
one should examine a well-formed penis that is free from the loss of the glans caused by phlegm (kaphodbhava-liṅganāśa) and devoid of the six complications beginning with āvartakī. // 1 //
For that which has not yet formed is unstable, thin like curd-whey;
even when drawn out with a probe, it rises back up again. // 2 //

Furthermore, it moves upward again and produces intense pain, while repeatedly obstructing the vision; it is quickly filled with other phlegmatic humors, and thus, accompanied by complications, it persists for a long time. (14.2dv)
14.3dv That loss of vision caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika), accompanied by other complications, occurs after a long time; indeed, because of the whiteness of phlegm, it is white.
Due to its being overcome by other doshas, that disease becomes bluish-black.
In that disease, there occurs a bluish discoloration (ānīlatā), and a state of near-blackness (ānīlikā) arises in the ailment. In this condition, the vision is unsteady with whirling circles;
it is reddish-black and becomes extremely dense, as if covered by a layer of sugar, sunlight, and water droplets.
14.5bv The *āvartakī* eye is reddish-white with streaks; it is covered with lines resembling the awns of rice.
It has an uneven, cut, or burnt appearance and is painful; it is known as *chinnāṃśukā*.
The *dṛṣṭi* is a dark-brown color like bell-metal; the *candrakī* has the appearance of the moon;
the *chattrābhā* is multicolored; and the *chattrakī* is a type of *nīlikā*. // 7 //
One should not perform venesection on those unfit for it, nor on those suffering from thirst, nasal catarrh, or cough;
nor on those with indigestion, the timid, those who have vomited, or those afflicted by pain in the head, ears, or eyes. (8)
14.8bv Not for those suffering from eye disease, nasal catarrh, or cough; rather,
during the intermediate season, after the patient has been purified and well-nourished, in a well-lit place during the forenoon, the physician, seated on a stool whose height reaches his knees— 9.

When the eyes of one who is restrained and seated have been fanned with breath from the mouth until they are perspiring, and when the thumbs have massaged the eyes so that impurities are seen to leap forth from the vision; 10.
While gazing at one's own nose with the head held motionless,
[the gaze] should be directed half a finger-breadth below the black part of the eye, and likewise half of that half from the outer corner of the eye.

While looking at one's own nose, [the practitioner] should hold the probe steadily with the index finger, middle finger, and thumb at a distance of half a half-measure from the outer corner of the eye;
One should pierce the left eye with the right hand and the other with the left;
when well-pierced, there will be a sound, no pain, and a flow of drops of water.
While consoling the patient, one should sprinkle the eye with breast milk;
then, with the tip of the probe, one should scrape the circumference of the eye.
14.14cd–15ab Without causing pain, one should slowly withdraw the circle of vision toward the nose; then,
by means of hiccups, one should expel the phlegm located within the circle of vision.
14.15c–d: One should remove [the probe] by suction when the morbid humor (doṣa) is stable; when it is mobile, one should foment the eye from the outside.
Then, once the forms are seen, one should slowly withdraw the probe. 16.
Whether the *doṣa* is stable or mobile,

one should then have the patient lie down with their eyes bound after inserting a cotton swab soaked in ghee; for a single puncture, the patient should be positioned on their side opposite the site to be pierced, and for a double puncture, they should be placed supine.
14.17c–d Having treated him with another side [of the body],

while he lies on a bed in a windless place with his head and feet anointed and intent on what is beneficial, one should encourage sneezing, coughing, belching, spitting, and the drinking of water. 14.18ab [The physician should do this] until the patient, having been cleared of the morbid humors, breathes freely and feels lightness in the chest.

14.18b–d: One should avoid lying on the head or body, engaging in [other] wholesome activities, remaining with the face downward, bathing, brushing the teeth, and eating for seven days; furthermore, the same restrictions as those prescribed after drinking oleaginous substances (sneha) apply here.
One should apply a lukewarm pouring of ghee as much as possible for pain;
or one should eat a liquid preparation made from the three pungents (vyoṣa) and āmalaka with ghee. (20)
Or, after three days, one should sprinkle his eyes with decoctions of wind-alleviating herbs while avoiding [solid] gruel;
however, on the seventh day, one should by all means remove the bandage from the eye.
One should conform to restraint until stability of vision is attained;
one should not suddenly look at subtle or brilliant forms. // 22 //

Swelling, redness, pain, and other symptoms, as well as the onset of *adhimantha*, arise from unwholesome practices and defects in bloodletting; one should treat these according to their respective natures. (23)
14.23cd–14.24ab Due to improper treatment and the defects of the piercing, one should treat those [conditions] according to their respective [remedies].
Dūrvā, barley, gairika, and śārivā, made into a paste with ghee, should be applied as a facial plaster for the subsiding of pain and redness. 14.24ab [End of verse 14.24a]
Likewise, sesame seeds mixed with mustard and soaked in the juice of *mātuluṅga*, along with *payasyā*, *śārivā*, *pattra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *madhuyaṣṭī* [should be applied]. // 25 //
An application of goat's milk combined with these [drugs], lukewarm, provides supreme relief.
Goat's milk [mixed] with *lodhra*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *mṛdvīkā*, and *madhuka* [is likewise beneficial]. (26)
14.26 An ointment combined with goat’s milk should be applied,
or a decoction used as an eye-drop (āścyotana) should be employed to destroy pain and redness;
alternatively, [a preparation] with madhuka, utpala, and kuṣṭha, or with drākṣā, lākṣā, and sugar may be used.
14.27c–d: With *madhuka*, *utpala*, *kuṣṭha*, and *elā*, combined with grape juice and lac;
or with grapes, lac, and sugar;
or with grapes, lac, and juice.
Ghee boiled in four times its quantity of milk processed with Vātaghna drugs, with the addition of the Padmakādi group as a medicinal paste, is recommended for all therapeutic procedures.

If there is no subsiding [of the symptoms], one should perform venesection on the patient after he has been lubricated and fomented; one should also carry out the procedure described for *mantha*, and once the wound has healed from the incision, apply mild collyrium.

14.29 When a wound has healed, a mild collyrium should be applied, made from the root of *āḍhakī*, black pepper, yellow orpiment, and *rasāñjana*. For a pierced eye, a medicinal wick (*varti*) made from these along with jaggery, ground with celestial water (*divyāmbu*), should be employed.
Jātī, śirīṣa, dhava, meṣaviṣāṇī, and puṣpavaiḍūrya—these, along with pearls, should be well-ground with milk.
A thin copper plate should be smeared with this [mixture] and, after seven days, it should again be ground with milk alone. 31.

14.31 A compound of *jātī*, *śirīṣa*, *dhava*, *meṣaviṣāṇa*, *puṣpa*, and *piṇḍāñjana*, dried in the shade, is beneficial for an eye that has been pierced; it restores clarity and strengthens the vision.
It is said to possess qualities and applications equal to those of *srotoñjana*, coral, *śilājatu*, sea-foam, and *tīkṣṇāñjana*.
14.32cv When the eyes are congested by Vāta due to substances such as conch-shell, coral, stone, sea-foam, and pungent [substances], there is constriction of the nose and slight swelling.
Pain, throbbing, and piercing sensations in the temples, eyes, eyebrows, and forehead. // 1 //

In the case of *abhiṣyanda* (ocular congestion) caused by Vāta, there is pricking, throbbing, and splitting pain in the temples, eyes, eyebrows, forehead, and face; the eye-secretion (*dūṣikā*) is scanty and dry, the tears are cold and clear, and the pains are shifting.
The opening and closing of his eyes was as difficult as the crawling of living beings.
15.2bv Clear tears, shifting pains, and the eye appearing as if swollen or covered with fine splinters;
its subsidence occurs through unctuous and warm treatments—that is *abhiṣyanda* when neglected. // 3 //

15.3cv When there is a desire for unctuous and hot things and [the condition] is pacified, it becomes *adhimantha*; in that case, there is ringing in the ears, dizziness, and the forehead, eyes, eyebrows, and so forth feel as if they are being churned like a fire-drill. // 4 //
Even he whose mental agitation has been destroyed may, through negligence, experience various kinds of sensations and incur an ulcer in his vision as well as the loss of sight. (5)
The wind, moving from the eyes, the temples, or from other locations, causes intense pain, a lack of lubrication, redness, and swelling in the eye. (6)
15.6b–d. Or, it may turn toward another side; with tears flowing all around, it contracts—that is designated as *anyatovāta*.
Similarly, in the course of a vāta disorder, the eye becomes squinted (*jihma*) or sunken (*ūna*).
15.7c–d Just like that, the eye becomes squinted; 15.7d–e or, in the course of a Vāta disorder,
it becomes swollen, with burning, a sensation of fuming, swelling, and a dark-brown discoloration of the outer eyelids.
Internal moisture, yellowish-warm tears, passion, and a vision of yellowish light. // 8 //
The condition of having eyes wounded and smeared with alkaline matter is a symptom of *pittābhiṣyanda* (vitiated bile in the eyes);
it has the appearance of being strewn with glowing embers and a luster similar to a mass of liver. // 9 //
In Adhimantha, the eye becomes affected; in Syanda caused by Kapha, there is stiffness, great swelling, itching, drowsiness, and a lack of desire for food. (10)
In Adhimantha, the eyes have a discharge and tears like thick, oily, and abundant white mucus;
the black portion (kṛṣṇa-maṇḍala) is sunken, while the white portion (śukla-maṇḍala) is elevated.
15.11b–d— Like slimy mucus, there is discharge of blood and tears, salivation, inflation of the nostrils, and the eyes feel as if filled with dust;
there is red streaks in the tears, discharge of mucus, and the appearance of red circles.
15.12c–d: There is the appearance of red streaks, dūṣīkā, and white circles. In raktasyanda, the eye exhibits the symptoms of pittasyanda;
in mantha, the eye has copper-colored margins and a pain like that of being plucked out. 15.13 //
Due to passion, it withers like a bandhūka flower and becomes incapable of touch;
it appears black like a corpse submerged in blood, yet its appearance is like fire.
All types of *adhimantha* [eye diseases] cause excessive pain according to their respective natures; those located in the temples, teeth, cheeks, and skull produce extreme agony. (15)

In one afflicted by vāta and pitta, the eyes experience friction, pricking, tearing, and a sense of being smeared; the eyelids become dry and rough, and the opening and closing of the eyes is difficult. (16)

15.16ab That which is characterized by an excess of vāta and pitta, accompanied by friction, contraction, dryness, a desire for cold things, pain, and suppuration, is called *śuṣkādi-pāka*; it occurs with swelling when all three doṣas are involved. // 17 //
15.17a–b: There is contraction and dryness; through contraction, there is a state of parchedness. 15.17b–d:
Accompanied by a desire for cold, colic, and suppuration, there is swelling with blood, along with excessive pain, burning, spitting, and so forth.
A white circle arises, resembling a ripe udumbara fruit. // 18 //

In the case of slight swelling, the suppuration (pāka) is characterized by tears that are repeatedly warm, cold, clear, slimy, transparent, and thick; it is likewise recognized by other such symptoms. 19.

15.19c–d In Akṣipākātyaya, there is slight swelling, slight inflammation, redness, and turbid lacrimation; the black and white parts of the eye are smeared with phlegm and characterized by moisture and redness. 15.20.
15.20c–v When smeared with *kapha*, it becomes black; there is a burning sensation, obstruction of vision, and unstable pains.
The essence of food is turned sour by the humors (*mala*) in which *pitta* and blood predominate.
Having ascended to the eye via the vessels, it makes the eye dusky-red, accompanied by swelling, burning, suppuration, and tearing, and causes very blurred vision. (22)

Having stated that these sixteen diseases, which affect the entire eye, are caused by *amloṣita*, one should avoid treating those cases where *adhimantha* has been destroyed, as well as those with *sākṣipāka* and *atyaya*. (23)

Among these, the *adhimantha* arising from Vāta destroys vision in five nights; that born of Kapha (*śleṣma*) in seven days; and that produced by blood (*rakta*) likewise destroys it in three nights. Furthermore, the Pitta-type (*paittika*) caused by improper conduct destroys vision instantly. (15.23–24)
15.24b-v: Adhimantha caused by kapha [is cured] in seven days. In the case of the prodromal symptoms of the discharge (syanda), strong gargling and nasal drops [should be administered].
One should observe the fast, except when it arises from anger or from wind-related disorders.
To pacify burning, inflammation, redness, tearing, and swelling, one should prepare *biḍālaka* everywhere with leaf, cardamom, black pepper, gold, and red ochre. //2//
[One should use] rasāñjana, yaṣṭīmadhu, nata, candana, and saindhava;
or saindhava, nāgara, and tārkṣya fried in ghee with rice-scum (maṇḍa). // 3 //
16.3dv Rubbed with a paste of ghee, *badarī* leaves, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *pathyā*, *āmalaka*,
and *tutthaka* should be burnt by the internal-smoke method; or that powder [should be applied] immediately in cases of swelling caused by *vāta*.
In cases born of vāta, meat from the Śabara region fried in ghee should be employed;
in cases of pitta and rakta, it should be used with māṃsī, padmaka, kālīya, and yaṣṭyāhva.

That which grows in the Śabara country should be employed; [it is used] with māṃsī, padmaka, kākolī, manohvā, phalinī, and honey in cases of kapha, but in all cases when it arises from all three doṣas.
One part of white pepper, four parts of realgar, and eight parts of red arsenic. // 5cd //
Having ground it and bound it in a cloth, one should apply it as a covering over the eyes immediately upon becoming enraged. 5ef.
When [the eye] is thus excessively constricted, this bandage should be applied as soon as the [doshas] have become aggravated.
An external paste made of *dhātūka*, ginger, *abhayā*, and *tārkṣya* destroys diseases of the eye. 5.1(1)+1ab.
An external application of mineral pitch (*dhātu*), dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), chebulic myrobalan (*abhayā*), and *tārkṣya* cures eye diseases.

One should apply an external ointment to the eye using *harītakī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *tārkṣyaśīla*, and red ochre (*gairika*), each rubbed with its own hand; this is for the purpose of pacifying all eye diseases. (5.1[2]+1)

Wild *kulattha* beans, well-steamed, stripped of their husks with the fingernails, and bound within a cloth soaked in the juice of dried cow-dung cakes—when their powder is applied as a single dusting at midnight, it instantly dispels the inflammation of the eyes. (6)
16.6ab Forest-born [plants] soaked in the juice of dried cow dung,
their forms wrapped in cloth and bound with very fine, loose cloth, along with *ghoṣā*, *abhayā*, *tutthaka*, *yaṣṭi*, and *lodhra*,
when their forms are submerged in fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*) placed in a copper vessel, conquer various kinds of afflictions in the eye. // 7 //
16.7 With *ghoṣā*, *abhayā*, *tutthaka*, *yaṣṭi*, and *lodhra*—
with *vyoṣa*, *abhayā*, *tutthaka*, *yaṣṭi*, and *lodhra*—
well-ground into an extremely fine powder and bound together in a loose cloth.
With sixteen *pala* of water, one *pala* of *kaṭaṅkaṭerī* is prepared, its form submerged in clear copper-colored fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*) bound within loose cloth.
When all the humors (doṣas) are provoked in the eyes, an irrigation (seka) consisting of one-eighth part [of the decoction] mixed with honey should be used. // 8 //

16.8 When applied with honey, the juice of *śigru* sprouts quickly overcomes all types of eye affliction arising from the provocation of all the *doṣas*, as well as the various pains of the eyes born from the combination of *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*. (9)

The young leaves and root of the *urubūka* plant, prepared by boiling them in goat's milk, or a warm bolus of parched grain flour (*saktu-piṇḍikā*), immediately destroys the pain of vāta-type ophthalmia (*vātābhiṣyanda*). (10)

Having powdered the root, it is prepared in goat’s milk as an eye-drop for disorders born of Vāta; a lukewarm decoction of the Bilvādi group with Eranda, Jaṭā, Bṛhatī, and Madhuśigru is also beneficial. (16.10–11)
An excellent collyrium for eye pain is prepared from *hrīvera*, *vakra*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, and the bark of *udumbara*, boiled with water and goat’s milk. (12)
16.12b Prepared with *udumbara* bark, or prepared with *udumbara* and *plakṣa*.
This eye-drop, consisting of *lodhra*, *āmalaka*, *rasāñjana*, *bimbitikā* leaves, *tubarikā*, and *tuttha*, forcibly and immediately removes the provocation [of the humors] of the eyes. 12+1.
A decoction made of mañjiṣṭhā, turmeric, lac, grapes, ṛddhi, madhuka, and blue lotus, cooled and mixed with sugar, is a sprinkling that conquers raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders). 13.

Powdered *kaseru* and *yaṣṭyāhva*, together with grapes, the two types of *madhuka*, and blue lotus, placed loosely in a cloth strainer and immersed in celestial water, is beneficial for ophthalmia born of blood and bile. (16.13b–14)
16.14b–c. A plaster consisting of *puṇḍrāyaṣṭī*, *niśā*, and *mūrvā*, soaked in goat’s milk mixed with sugar, applied to a loose bandage, removes burning, pain, redness, and tearing. 15.
White lodhra and madhuka, finely powdered and fried in ghee, placed within a cloth and softened with breast milk, conquer disorders of pitta, rakta, and injury. (16)

In cases of kapha-type disorders, a warm eye-drop (āścyotana) prepared from the juices of nāgara, triphalā, nimba, vāsā, and lodhra should be used; in cases involving all three doṣas (sāṃnipātika), it should be prepared with these drugs combined.
In cases of kapha, one should drink old ghee processed with the juices of vāsā and lodhra; in cases of vāta, [old ghee] combined with sugar;
and in cases of pitta, [ghee] prepared with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and sprinkled with yava-kṣāra. // 18 //
In the case of pitta, one should repeatedly cause the blood to flow out mixed with sugar; thereafter, having administered unctuous therapy, one should purge the patient.
An application of vesavāra made from marshy animals should be used as a plaster for the head and face.
In cases of piercing pain (śūla) or burning sensation (dāha), one should apply cold treatments combined with milk and ghee;
furthermore, having observed the specific condition, one should employ the treatments for the suppression of timira as appropriate.
This entire procedure is also recommended for the *mantha* and other [remedies]. If there is no pacification by any means, one should apply cauterization above the eyebrows during the *mantha*.
One should smear silver with rough cow's curd until it turns blue;
once dry, a wick made with whey destroys the disease of wind-afflicted eyes. (22)

When [the eye] has been smeared and has turned blue, [apply the following]: jasmine buds, conch shell, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), licorice (*madhuka*), and *balā*—ground with divine water (cow’s urine)—form a wick that removes bile and blood. (16.22–23)
16.23 Sumana, kṣāraka, conch shell, rock salt, triphalā, vyoṣa, the navel of a conch shell, sea foam, aileyaka, and sarja resin—
these form a wick that cures diseases of the eyes caused by phlegm (śleṣman).

One should boil eight palas each of prapauṇḍarīka, yaṣṭyāhva, and dārvī in one droṇa of water; once the liquid is strained and boiled again until it becomes thick, one should add [the following]: // 25 //
Ten palas of *puṣpāñjana* and one *karṣa* of black pepper, made into a powder or a wick (*varti*), [cures] all types of *abhiṣyanda*. (26)
It destroys the afflictions of passion and friction and immediately clarifies the vision;
this Pāśupata yoga is the supreme secret of physicians. (27)
In the case of dry inflammation of the eyes (śuṣkākṣi-pāka), one should drink clarified butter and perform eye-satiation with it;
furthermore, nasal drops (nasya) should be administered using either life-prolonging (jīvanīya) ghee or the subtle oil (aṇu-taila).
In this condition, nasal medication with *cāṇu* oil is beneficial, as is a lukewarm sprinkling with milk mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*).
An ointment (*añjana*) made from *mahauṣadha* ground with breast milk and combined with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) is also recommended.
16.29c–d. Hair mixed with ghee and rubbed on breast-milk, or fat derived from marshy animals, along with a little rock salt and ginger;
these hairs, smeared with ghee and rubbed on a mirror, [should be placed] within a hollowed-out cup. 16.30. [One should place them] inside a pair of hollowed-out cups.
16.30ab. Fat derived from marshy animals, burnt and ground with clarified butter, forms an excellent collyrium when placed in a metal vessel.
For one who has undergone oleation therapy, one should perform venesection in cases of swelling, whether extensive or slight. 16.31.
16.31c–d In cases of both significant swelling and slight swelling,

once the patient has been oleated, purgation should be administered with a decoction of *drākṣā* and *pathyā*, along with *trivṛt* and ghee. 16.32 White *lodhra*, fried in ghee and reduced to powder, should be placed inside a piece of cloth.

White *lodhra* fried in ghee and crushed with warm water, when used as an irrigation, is an excellent reliever of pain; alternatively, a decoction of *dārvī* and *prapauṇḍarīka* is beneficial for eye-drops (*āścyotana*). 16.32–33.
One should apply a plaster to the head made of dārvī, prapauṇḍarīka, yaṣṭīmadhu, hima, utpala, and milk.
And one should employ emollients that alleviate itching, redness, lacrimation, and pain. (33½)
Copper rubbed with urine and applied to the eye, or fumigated with clarified butter, relieves pain;
likewise, copper rubbed with the liquid of cow's curd, combined with long pepper and rock salt, is most excellent. (34)

A conch shell rubbed with breast milk and smeared with ghee, fumigated with the leaves of the *śamī* tree and with barley, when applied to the eyes, quickly destroys the condition known as *saṃdhāva*, as well as friction and extremely intense pain. (35)
The fruit of the Udumbara tree, rubbed on iron and fumigated with breast milk. // 36ab //
The resin of the *śigru* leaf, well-ground in a copper vessel with clarified butter and *śamī* leaves, overcomes burning pain, redness, and tearing of the eyes. (37)
The resin of *śigru* sprouts, rubbed in a copper vessel with two types of *niśā*, *triphalā*, and *mustā*, ground together with the milk of a woman,
and applied as a wash with sugar and honey, removes the pain of injury.
Tutthaka (blue vitriol) that has been sprinkled twenty-five times with cow’s urine, or with breast milk or goat’s milk, when ground into a paste with the milk of a young woman,
serves as an ointment for sudden inflammation of the eyes.
Incensed with ghee, it destroys swelling, friction, lacrimation, and pain;
likewise, a fragment of a clay pot rubbed on bell-metal and well-incensed with sesame-water [achieves the same]. (38)

When the eyes are anointed with a paste made from nimba leaves smeared with clarified butter, it overcomes grinding pain, tearing, and redness; once the medicinal application has worn off, the eyes are free from pain. (39)
An eye-drop should be prepared with breast milk; one should not apply more than three drops of these, consisting of *tālīśapattra*, *capalā*, *nata*, iron filings, and collyrium.

Having smeared copper with bentonite, iron, and *rasāñjana*, along with jasmine buds, *kāsīsa*, and rock salt, ground together with urine, one should keep it for seven days and then grind it again. (16.40dv–41)
Pills should be prepared with urine alone and dried in the shade;
when rubbed with breast milk, they destroy itching, tearing, swelling, and itching of the eyes. (42)
One should prepare pills with urine and dry them in the shade.
A paste made from the bark of *vyāghrī*, *madhuka*, copper dust, and goat’s milk, fumigated with the smoke of *śamī*, *āmalaka* leaves, and clarified butter, removes swelling and pain. (16.42–43)

One should apply *raja* ground with goat’s milk for the treatment of *pittābhiṣyanda* when it is acid-irritated; likewise for *kukūṇaka*, which arises from the provocation of *kapha*, *pitta*, and blood, and from their accumulation. (16.43bv–44)
Pakṣmoparodha, śuṣkākṣipāka, pūyālasa, bisa, pothakī, amlapita, alpākhya, syanda, and mantha—these [occur] without the involvement of vāta. (45)
These eighteen, known as pillās, persist for a long duration;
their respective treatments have been stated separately, and shall now be further explained. (46)

16.46dv–47ab. Having thus described each [of the aforementioned conditions], the treatment for those suffering from the disease called *pillā* is now stated generally for cases where the condition has become chronic (*pillī-bhūta*).
For one who has been treated with oleation, whose wind has been expelled by emesis, and whose blood has been removed by venesection:
16.47b–48. Then, for one suffering from eye diseases of the eyelids who has undergone purgation, one should scrape along the eyelid margins until they are purified.
[The recipe consists of] one *pala* of *tutthaka* (copper sulfate) and twenty white peppers (*marica*).
16.48 After the patient has been purged, one should scrape along the eyelid until it is thoroughly cleansed.

Having ground [the ingredients] with thirty palas of sour gruel (kāñjika), one should place them in a copper vessel; this makes even cataracts (pillā) that have persisted for many years disappear. 16.49
Sprinkling that [wash] destroys ointment-residues, tears, itching, and swelling;
as do the seeds of *karañja*, *surasā*, and the buds of *sumana*. (50)
Having crushed *sumanaḥ* and *kṣāraka*, one should prepare a decoction; when it has been strained, a medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) should be made from it.
This collyrium is a remedy for *pilla* and promotes the growth of eyelashes. (16.50–51)
Rasāñjana, sarjarasa, rītipuṣpa, manaḥśilā, samudraphena, salt, gairika, and black pepper. // 52 //
16.52b–c: *Jātī* flower, realgar, sea-foam, salt, and collyrium ground with honey are an excellent remedy for destroying moisture and itching.
Alternatively, *tagara* ground with the juice of *abhayā* destroys *pilla*. 53.
Devadāru treated with goat's urine along with oil, as well as rock salt, the three myrobalans, Pippalī, Kaṭukā, and Śaṅkhanābhi; (54)
A wick made of *devadāru* mixed with fat, or with copper powder, destroys *pilla* and *śukraka*;
or else, a powder of *puṣpa-kāsīsa* saturated with the juice of *surasā*.
This collyrium, applied for ten days to copper, overcomes the falling out of eyelashes and cataracts. (55½)
Take sour gruel (sauvīraka) and collyrium in equal parts, along with very fine copper powder;
when this powder is applied to the eyelids using even a single probe, it causes new hair to grow upon the lashes. (56)

16.56b–c: Together with those two, one should add fine copper powder; this [mixture] used for eye-salves (pilla) promotes the growth of hair. Cotton that has been processed seven times with the juice of lac, nirguṇḍī, bhṛṅga, and dārvī is excellent [for this purpose].
A lamp should be lit with clarified butter; the soot produced from that is the best for the purpose of healing eye ointments.
That ink is the best for the purpose of healing ulcers; likewise, frequent scraping of the eyelid and bloodletting [are recommended].
One afflicted by the disease pilla should repeatedly undergo purgation and constantly employ eye-drops, collyrium, nasal medication, and the inhalation of medicinal smoke. (59)
If the suppuration and swelling have not subsided at the end, one should apply cauterization with a fine probe.
Thus, there are ninety-four [types of eye diseases] categorized by their causes, symptoms, and treatments. (60)

When a pūyālasa (suppurating ulcer) has not been pacified, [the total number of diseases] is ninety-four; thus, the diseases of the eyes have been described in their entirety as distinct from one another.
Furthermore, one who desires the well-being of his eyes should always employ these remedies, even when he is in good health.
Old barley, wheat, śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, and kodrava,
as well as mung beans and other such grains that destroy kapha and pitta, should be thoroughly saturated with abundant ghee.
Likewise, one should consume vegetables, meat from wild animals, pomegranate, white sugar, rock salt, the three myrobalans, grapes, and celestial water for drinking. (63)

One should use a sunshade and footwear, purify the humors according to the prescribed rules, avoid the suppression of natural urges, and abstain from eating before the previous meal is digested or overeating. (64)
16.64d–65ab: Indigestion, overeating, and the like; anger, grief, sleeping by day, staying awake at night, and exposure to the sun;
foods and medicines that cause a burning sensation or constipation—[these are the causes of the aggravation of wind].
16.65b–d: And staying awake at night; whatever food or medicine causes burning or constipation; [and] whatever conduct, food, or medicine [is harmful].
Two vessels, situated broadly between the feet, extend in many branches to the eyes;
they carry to the eyes the applications of ointments, powders, and unguents applied to the feet. (66)

16.66ab–dv: Two [types of worms] are situated widely in the middle of the foot; 16.66cd: those joined to the foot lead to the eyes through contact with heat, friction, pressure, and so forth; being corrupted, they vitiate the eyes.
Therefore, one should always employ shoes, ointments, and washing, which are beneficial for the eyes. 67.
By means of striking,
pressing, and so forth with the palms, or with clods of earth and the like— Uttarasthāna 16.67av.
The wind (marut) becomes aggravated by chronic catarrh, playing in water, scratching the ears, improper application of sound, and other provocative factors. // 1 //
Having reached the channels of the ears, it causes pain within the passage like a rushing torrent, as well as hemicrania, stiffness, and a distaste for cold things. (2)
After a long time, once it has reached maturity, it may discharge a small amount of lymph; the ear suddenly feels empty, as if experiencing shifting and throbbing sensations. (3)
From pitta, there is piercing pain accompanied by burning, a desire for cold things, swelling, and fever;
it suppurates quickly, and when fully suppurated, it discharges yellow lymph.
17.4b–d—There is a desire for cold, swelling, fever, and serous discharge (lasīkā); whatever [part of the body] it touches, that undergoes suppuration.
Due to kapha, there is heaviness of the head, jaws, and neck, as well as dullness and pain. // 5 //

Itching, swelling, a desire for heat, and a thick white discharge resulting from suppuration occur when the ear is afflicted by injury and other such factors, causing pain within the auditory passage. (6)
From suppuration, there is a thick white discharge;
blood flows with pain similar to that of Pitta, or with some additional symptoms.
When all the Doshas are combined, there is colic, swelling, fever, and intense pain. //7//
Through a change of state, a desire for heat or cold arises, like the dullness of hearing;
it becomes ripened and flows with white, black, red, thick, and pus-like discharges. (8)
When the wind (pavana) is situated within the sound-carrying channels (sirā), one repeatedly hears various sounds without any apparent cause; this they call Karṇanāda (tinnitus). // 9 //
When the wind (vāyu) is accompanied by phlegm (śleṣman), or when the sound [of breath] is neglected,
it may cause hearing with great difficulty at first, and eventually lead to deafness.
17.10d–11: Or, when the phlegm (śleṣman) has been dried up by vāta, it gradually coats the auditory canal, causing deafness;
then there occurs pain, heaviness, and obstruction, which is designated as *pratīnāha*.
Itching and swelling in the ear caused by kapha are known by that same name [kaṇḍū-śopha];
when kapha is vitiated by pitta, it becomes either painful or even painless. (12)

17.12b–d: These two [types] are known as stable and are so named. Furthermore, when the ear—vitiated by Vāta and the other [doshas]—produces pain, or even painlessness, along with thick, putrid, and profuse discharge, it causes *pūtikarṇaka* (putrid ear disease), a painful condition arising from the moisture of flesh and blood.
17.13–14. When creatures, feeding on the pain born of the moisture of flesh and blood, cause intense agony, that is *krimikarṇaka* (ear-worm).
It arises from scratching the ear when an ulcer has formed, and it possesses the aforementioned symptoms.
17.14c–d Due to scratching the auditory canal, an abscess (vidradhi) arises, as well as other swellings described previously, such as hemorrhoids (arśas) and tumors (arbuda).
In these conditions, pain, putridity of the ear, and deafness cause affliction.
17.15b–d: A tumor arising from the six types of hemorrhoids is described; deafness also arises from wind (vāta) in the womb. A constricted auditory canal is called *kucikarṇaka*.
A single or multiple firm fleshy sprout within the womb that is free from pain [is also a type of tumor]. 16.

17.16b–d: *Śaṣkulī* and *kuñcikarṇaka*; when a sprout of flesh remains within the ear-cavity, it is *pippalī*, the size of a long pepper (*pippalī-māna*); from the derangement of all three humors (*saṃnipāta*), *vidārikā* arises.
That swelling which is of the same color as the skin, painful, and stiff—if it is neglected, [it becomes a fistula]. // 17 //
When matured, it exudes a secretion resembling pungent oil; it heals with difficulty, and once healed, it invariably causes the earlobe to contract. (18)
When the Vāyu located in the vessels causes the earlobe to grow back with difficulty after being cut, it produces the condition known as Pālī-śoṣa (wasting of the lobe).
When the lobe becomes thin yet firm like a string due to Vāta, it is called Tantrikā.
In a delicate person, due to long-term neglect, if [the ear] is suddenly made to grow, there arises a painful swelling at the ear-lobe that is reddish and characterized by cracking. (20)

That condition is called *paripoṭa*; it arises from wind (*vāta*) and bile-blood (*pitta-śoṇita*), and is caused by the weight of heavy ornaments and the like; it is dark-brown in color and characterized by pain, burning, and suppuration. (21)
Swelling accompanied by eruptions, pustules, redness, heat, and moisture occurs at the earlobe;
swelling of the entire lobe due to Vāta and Kapha is painless and firm. (22)
It is stiff, the same color as the skin, itchy, and characterized by unmantha and gallira;
when the ear is pierced improperly and the swelling increases, there is itching, burning, suppuration, and pain. (23)
17.23b–d. That swelling arising from the combination of all three humors (saṃnipāta) is called Unmantha or Gallika; it increases suffering.
Those caused by phlegm, blood, and worms are minute, accompanied by itching, discharge, and pain. 17.24ab. [They are] minute, with itching, discharge, and pain.
Neglected, these pustules known as *lehyā* lick the rim [of the anus]; for they are characterized by *pippalī*, *sarvaja* pain, *vidārī*, and *kucikarṇaka*. (25)
17.25ab Those eruptions (piṭikās) are called lihyākhya; 17.25cd vidārī and kūcikarṇaka—among these, one (vidārī) is incurable, one (kūcikarṇaka) is palliable, and the others should be treated.
Thus, twenty-five diseases of the ear have been described according to their classification. 17.26ab/17.25cd–26ab.

In the case of earache caused by Vāta, one who has eaten meat broth should drink clarified butter prepared with Vāta-subduing drugs at night; furthermore, the ear should be fomented and filled [with that ghee]. // 1 //

From the leaves produced by the *aśvattha*, *bilva*, *arka*, and *eraṇḍa* trees, which have been separately smeared with oil and rock salt and then subjected to *puṭapāka* (sealed cooking), [the juice is extracted]. // 2 //
Likewise, it may be cooked with slightly warm juices of radish or aralu, or boiled in sour substances that remove wind (vāta) or in animal urines. (3)
Great unguent quickly destroys even most intense pain [when applied] from a large piece of the five roots (pañcamūla) wood wrapped in linen. // 4 //
Oil poured onto the blazing tip [of a wick] provides immediate relief from pain;
likewise, oil from *bhadrakāṣṭha*, *kuṣṭha*, and *sārala* wood should be employed in the same manner. (5)
18.5bv Oil provides immediate relief from pain;
here, that which is prescribed for wind-diseases (*vātavyādhi*) and coryza (*pratiśyāya*) is beneficial.
One should avoid bathing the head and drinking cold water even during the day. (6)
18.6cv One should avoid bathing the head in cases of pitta-type headache. For such pain, one should administer a purgative with ghee mixed with sugar.
Breast milk boiled with grapes and liquorice is recommended for filling the ears. // 7 //
One should prepare [a decoction] with yaṣṭī, anantā, hima, uśīra, kākolī, lodhra, jīvaka, mṛṇāla, bisa, mañjiṣṭhā, and śārivā. // 8 //
One *kuḍava* of oil combined with one *prastha* of liquorice juice and two *prasthas* of milk—this [mixture] is used for nasal drops, ear-filling, and massage. (9)

The burning pain and distress of the piercing (śūla) are destroyed by honey alone, or by [medicinal pastes] such as those beginning with yaṣṭīmadhu mixed with ghee; one should apply these all around the ears. 10.
In cases arising from kapha, one should administer emesis using ghee processed with long pepper (pippalī) to provide oleation;
furthermore, one should employ medicinal smoking (dhūma), nasal drops (nāvana), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), and sudation (sveda) that alleviate kapha.
The fresh juice of garlic, ginger, drumstick, *muraṅgī*, radish, and plantain is excellent when used lukewarm as an ear-drop. (12)
18.12b–c: [One may use] the juice of *surangi*, *mūlaka*, and *bhṛṅga*.
Having placed sprouts of *arka* ground with sour liquids, smeared with oil, and mixed with salt, inside a hollowed-out stem of *snuhī* covered by its own leaves; 18.13: [one should apply it].
When that [vessel] has been made and covered with a lid, one should heat it by means of *puṭapāka* (herbivore-style cooking); this juice is supreme for conquering colic (*śūla*).
One should fill [the vessel] with the juice of *bījapūra* and *kapittha*. 18.13–14.
Or, having filled [the ear] with sour gruel (śukta), one should sprinkle it with froth; and oil prepared with goat’s urine, sheep’s urine, and bamboo bark is also used for filling. // 15 //
One should fill [the cavity] with prepared oil,
or indeed with prepared mustard oil processed with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *tumburu*, and ginger (*nāgara*).
In cases arising from blood, treatment should be performed as for pitta, and one should quickly release the vein (*sirā*).

When the ear is suppurated and discharging pus, one should employ fumigation, mouthfuls of medicated smoke, nasal drops, the application of tubes (nāḍī), and whatever treatments remove malignant ulcers. // 17 //
Having cleansed the wound and smeared it twice daily with cotton-wool swabs,
one should fumigate it with guggulu resin and then fill it with honey.
One should apply a cotton wick soaked in a decoction and treacle of the Sura-sādi group, and dust it with very fine powders of those same ingredients. (19)
One should habitually consume or employ [the food] smeared with treacle;
this regimen is the remedy that eliminates colic, moistening, and heaviness.
With priyaṅgu, madhuka, ambaṣṭhā, dhātakī, utpala, and parṇī. // 20 //
One should cook oil with mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, lākṣā, and the juice of kapittha; when used as a filling, it quickly arrests the discharge. (21)
In cases of deafness and tinnitus, one should administer the medicine prescribed for vāta-type earache;
if there is an association with phlegm (śleṣman), one should first conquer the phlegm through emesis and other such means. // 22 //
One should cook oil with four times as much juice extracted from the leaves of eraṇḍa, śigru, varuṇa, and mūlaka, and eight times as much milk.
That [oil], combined with the paste of castor, drumstick, young *yaṣṭyāhvā*, milk, and *kākoli*,
destroys tinnitus, deafness, and pain through nasal drops, massage, and ear-filling. (18.23–24)

That oil, when cooked with a paste (kalka) of prativiṣā, hiṅgu, miśī, tvak, svarjikā, and uṣaṇa, along with fermented gruel (śukta), destroys pain, discharge, deafness, and tinnitus upon filling [the ear] with it. (18.24b–25)
18.25d–26. Oil derived from mustard seeds is beneficial for filling the ears to alleviate pain, discharge, ringing, and tinnitus.
Likewise, the alkali of dried radish pieces, asafoetida, and ginger are also useful.
Śatapuṣpā, vacā, kuṣṭha, dāru, śigru, rasāñjana, sauvarcala, yavakṣāra, svarjika, audbhida, and saindhava. (27)

Bhūrja-granthi, viḍa salt, and mustā, along with four times as much honey and fermented gruel (śukta), and likewise the juice of mātuluṅga and the fresh juice of kadalī—[these are combined] with those [other ingredients]. // 28 //
Heated oil, when used as an ear-filling treatment, quickly overcomes even the most difficult cases of itching, discharge, deafness, putridity of the ear, pain, and worms. (29)
This excellent alkaline oil (kṣāra-taila) is best for itching, piercing pain, deafness, burning sensations, and diseases of the mouth and teeth; furthermore,
if the ears feel as if they were numb, one should then let out blood from them.
18.30dv One should remove blood from the ears when they are swollen and moistened, and one should administer emetics for impaired hearing.
One should avoid treating deafness in children and the elderly, as well as that which has been long-standing.
In the case of *pratīnāha*, after moistening [the ear] with oleation and sudation, one should cleanse it;
subsequently, using an ear-cleansing instrument, one should fill the ear with oil. // 32 //
18.32d–33. One should fill the ear with oil mixed with sour gruel (śukta), rock salt (saindhava), honey, or the juice of citron (mātuluṅga).
If dryness arises due to excessive purification, filling with the scum of clarified butter (ghṛtamaṇḍa) is indicated.

18.33ab Filling [the ear] quickly with sour gruel (śukta) and rock salt, or with the juice of mātuluṅga, or with the scum of ghee (ghṛtamaṇḍa)— this procedure [is used] even when the ear is full of impurities. 18.33d It removes itching and phlegm from the ear.

In such cases, nasal medication (nasya) and other treatments should be applied as previously described; furthermore, an ointment made of pungent and hot substances should be used here for external application. // 34 //

18.34d–35ab: For both *pūtikarṇa* (foul-smelling ear) and *kṛmikarṇaka* (ear with worms), one should apply an after-paste (*anulepana*) consisting of pungent and hot substances as prescribed for ear-discharge (*karṇasrāva*).
In the case of *kṛmikarṇaka*, filling the ear specifically with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) is especially recommended.

In cases of putrid ear (pūtikarṇa) and ear infested with worms (kṛmikarṇa), emesis preceded by [appropriate] measures is beneficial; for an abscess of the ear (karṇavidradhi), the treatment for abscesses should be applied.
For an abscess resulting from injury (kṣatavidradhi), the measures prescribed for earache arising from pitta should be performed.

18.36 Emesis is first beneficial in cases of ear polyps and tumors, as it is in nasal diseases; ear-vidārikā should be treated like ear-abscess, according to the manifestation of the respective doṣas. 18.37 [The treatment] should be carried out according to the predominance of the specific doṣa.

In the case of drying of the earlobe (pālī-śoṣa), one should apply nasal drops (nasya) and ointments (lepana) as in the treatment for pain in the ear due to Vāta, and administer fomentation (sveda); once the lobe has been fomented, one should rub it with sesame seeds.
Then, one should daily perform an oil massage with nourishing oils prepared from priyāla seeds, yaṣṭyāhva, hayagandhā, and barley. (39)
Oil cooked with śatāvarī, vājigandhā, payasyā, eraṇḍa, and jīvaka, along with milk, is the supreme means for nourishing the lips. (40)
Oil cooked with the paste of the *jīvanīya* [herbs], milk, and the decoction of the meat of marshy animals nourishes and increases the growth of the earlobes. (41)
18.41c–d Having cut away the excessively wasted earlobe with a decoction of the meat of marshy animals, one should join the remaining portion and nourish it.
This same procedure applies to the condition called *tantrikā* as well as to *paripoṭa*. 18.42.

In the case of a swelling (utpāta), after blood has been removed by leeches, an application of cooling substances should be made with the tender leaves of *jambu* and *āmra*, *balā*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *lodhra*, sesame, and blue lotus.
Oil prepared with fermented grain-liquor (dhānyāmla), mañjiṣṭhā, kadamba, and śārivā should be used for massage, as should the medicated ghees mentioned in the treatment of visarpa.
This accomplished oil for massage is used as an ointment in the Unmantha procedure; it is prepared with the fat of a monitor lizard and a porcupine,
along with *tālapattrī*, *aśvagandhā*, *arka*, *vākucī* fruit, and rock salt.

18.45b–d: A sharp nasal medication (nāvana) prepared with the fat of a monitor lizard (*godhā*) and a crab (*karka*), along with *vākucī*, sesame, rock salt (*saindhava*), *surasā*, and *lāṅgalī*, [is used].
For a poorly punctured [nostril], one should sprinkle it with a decoction of *aśmantaka*, *jambu*, and mango leaves.
This sharp nasal drop (nāvana), having been prepared with oil, should be used after anointing the earlobe;
one should then dust it with very fine powders derived from madhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, prapuṇḍarīka, and niśā.
Oil prepared with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *niśā* (turmeric), *pauṇḍarīka*, and *niśā* is beneficial for massage; likewise, oil processed with lac (*lākṣā*) and *viḍaṅga* is beneficial for anointing.
For a *parilehikā* ulcer, one should repeatedly apply fomentations using boluses made of cow dung.
One should smear [the wound] with the essence of *viḍaṅga* mixed with the urine of a she-goat and a paste of the seeds of *kauṭaja*, *iṅguda*, and *kārañja*, along with the bark of *śamyāka*. (49)
Alternatively, one should cook pungent oil with those [same ingredients] for anointing;
or, with nimba leaves, black pepper, and madana, one should prepare it for an ointment in the case of a leech-wound.

Having examined the appropriate method for binding a severed ear of one who is pure, one should apply a pure medicinal paste at the time of healing; for that which was recently severed, purification is required.
18.51 When [the bone] has been properly severed, it should then be cleansed; having knotted the hairline and performed the incision and scraping,
one should set the joint so that it is perfectly even, neither depressed nor protruding.

Having anointed it with honey and ghee, covered it with a cotton plug (*picu*) or a linen pad (*plota*), and bound it with a thread that is neither too tight nor too loose, one should sprinkle it with powders.
Then, one should prescribe wound-healing treatments and proper conduct;
after seven days, once the wound has been treated with unrefined oil, one should gradually remove the bandage.
18.54 When the wound has been treated with blood-stabilizing measures, is well-healed, covered with hair, with its joints closed,
even, firm, well-proportioned, and free from disease, one should gradually enlarge the ear.
18.55c–56. Suvarṣmāṇa, suroma, jalaśūka, svayaṃguptā, the two types of rajanī, the fruit of bṛhatī, aśvagandhā, balā, hastipippalī, and gaurasarṣapa.
The root of *kośātaka*, *aśvaghna*, *rūpikā*, and *saptaparṇa*; *chucchundarī* that has died a natural death; and a house inhabited by honey-bees—[these are the ingredients]. (57)
With these pastes— jatūkā, jala-janmā, and likewise śabarakandaka— one should cook buffalo ghee with oil until it becomes thick.
Likewise, *śabarakandaka* with the urine of an elephant or a horse is an excellent application for increasing the size of the ears; furthermore,
it may be used to restore a severed nose to its natural state in one who is healthy and has been purified.
One should cut the skin and flesh level with the nose from the cheek; protecting the area adjacent to the nose, one should bring it to thinness.
Then one should suture the swelling with a needle provided with lint;
furthermore, in the case of a nose that has been cut or incised, one should turn the skin back over it.
18.61c–d When the nose has been cleanly excised, one should apply a cheek-flap and carefully suture the nose;
one should elevate it from within by means of two tubes for the sake of easy respiration.

One should apply a cheek-binding (kapola-bandha) or a cheek-splint (kapola-vadhrī). Having sprinkled it with raw oil, one should then dust it with a very fine powder of pattraṅga, madhuka, añjana, and other blood-stilling agents. (18.62–63)
With *pataṅga*, *madhuka*, and *añjana*, along with other blood-stabilizing [substances],
one should then apply honey and ghee, bandage it, and prescribe the regimen.
Having recognized any change in the stage [of healing], one should thereafter perform the procedure for fresh wounds (*sadyovraṇavidhi*).
18.64b–65. Having secured the procedure, he should then give instructions; once the wound has healed, he should excise any excess flesh and the skin from the edge of the nose.
Then, he should suture it very smoothly and further increase any deficient portion.
18.65b–v: And when [the skin] has been drawn down from the side of the nose like a flap and fixed in its proper place, this same procedure applies even if it was recently severed.
For one whose lip is missing, the procedure is like that for the reconstruction of the nose, provided a connection for a tube is made.
18.66bv Even in the case of an immediate incision, this procedure [is prescribed]. (Uttarasthāna) [The wound is aggravated] by dew, wind, dust, talking, excessive sleep, and staying awake.
With a pillow that is too low or too high, or with yellow water, or otherwise. // 1 //

Due to excessive drinking of water, sexual intercourse, vomiting, weeping, suppression [of natural urges], and so forth, the humors (doṣas), with vāta being predominant, become aggravated and reach a state of thickening within the nose. // 2 //

19.2cv The aggravated *doṣas*, with *vāta* predominant, when increased, produce coryza that grows progressively and causes wasting. Among those, in coryza caused by *vāta*, there is extreme dryness of the mouth and frequent sneezing. (3)
There is obstruction of the nose, piercing pain, and distress in the teeth, temples, and head;
one feels as if ants are crawling all around the eyebrows. (4)
19.4cv Like insects, they crawl;
there is loss of voice, delayed suppuration, and the discharge of cold, clear phlegm.
From pitta, there arise thirst, fever, pustules in the nose, and vertigo. // 5 //

From pitta arise thirst, fever, and pustules in the nose; from kapha, suppuration at the tip of the nose, dryness, heat, and the discharge of copper-colored or yellow phlegm. From kapha also arise cough, loss of appetite, dyspnea, vomiting, and heaviness of the limbs. (19.5cd–6)
Sweetness in the mouth, itching, and the discharge of oily, white phlegm characterize the type caused by all three doshas;
it possesses all the symptoms of the individual types and is subject to sudden aggravation and subsidence. (7)
When vitiated blood reaches the nasal vessels, it causes *pratiśyāya* (nasal catarrh) characterized by a discharge that is unctuous, white, and thick.
There is numbness of the chest, copper-colored eyes, labored breathing, and a foul odor [from the breath]. (8)
There is itching in the ears, eyes, and nose, and the symptoms mentioned for pitta-type [fever] are also present here. All types of coryza (pratiśyāya) become malignant if neglected. // 9 //

19.9b And here, the symptoms arising from pitta are present due to an excess of the aforementioned complications; it afflicts all the sense organs and is accompanied by loss of digestive fire, fever, dyspnea, cough, and pain in the chest and flanks. // 10 //
It frequently becomes irritated without cause, causing foul breath and swelling;
it repeatedly produces nasal discharge, dryness, purification, and obstruction. (11)
It causes foul odor and dryness of the mouth, and there is an oozing of blackish-red, knotted phlegm resembling pus;
furthermore, long, glossy, white, minute worms multiply therein. // 12 //
Resembling pus, blackish, or red, knotted, and discharging phlegm—
these are the signs of suppuration. Among them, lightness of the limbs and the cessation of sneezing [indicate recovery].
Phlegm is viscous, yellowish, and causes a lack of discernment regarding taste and smell. (13)
19.13d–14. Furthermore, there is loss of the perception of taste and smell due to pungent inhalations, the application of sunlight, threads, grass, and the like;
or by other things that aggravate the wind (*vāta*), [which affect] the cartilage of the nostrils.
When the wind (vāyu), provoked by the use of pungent snuffs or by exposure to the sun, becomes enraged and is obstructed, it moves toward the *śṛṅgāṭaka* (the junction of the nasal passages).
When it returns, it produces excessive sneezing; that is known as *bhṛśakṣava*.

Obstructed while moving toward the *śṛṅgāṭaka*, that wind, causing excessive sneezing (*kṣavathu*), dries up the nasal passages and produces phlegm; thereafter, it causes the sensation of the nostrils being filled with awns and difficult breathing. (19.15–16)

One should dry out the nasal passages; when the throat appears as if filled with awns (*śūka*) and the nose likewise appears as if filled with awns, this is known as *nāsikā-śoṣa* (nasal wasting), which arises from *nāsānāha* (nasal constriction).
It is like the nose being bound by wind obstructed by phlegm. // 17 //
Due to the suppression of exhalation and inhalation, as if the two channels were obstructed, the bile in the nostrils cooks the skin and flesh, causing burning and pain. (18)
That inflammation of the nose is characterized by a discharge arising from phlegm; it is clear, resembling water, and occurs incessantly, especially at night. (19)
When *kapha* is excessively increased in the nose, it obstructs the channels and produces *apīnasa*,
characterized by wheezing breath and pain exceeding that of ordinary *pīnasa*.
19.20b–c. When obstructed in the channels, it flows out like the discharge from an ulcer; by this, his nose becomes excessively moist.
21. He constantly discharges thick, slimy, yellow, and mature nasal mucus (siṅghāṇaka).
When the nose is as if scorched by blood, unable to endure touch either externally or internally, the breath becomes like smoke, and that radiance burns as it were. (22)
When the wind and foul phlegm, corrupted by impurities at the root of the palate,
exit through the mouth and nose with a putrid odor, they call that condition *pūtināsa*.
Due to accumulation or injury, pus and blood may flow from the nose;
that is called *pūyarakta* (pus-blood), which causes burning and pain in the head. (24)
When the wind (vāyu), obstructed within the nose by bile (pitta) and phlegm (śleṣman), dries up the phlegm, that dried phlegm attains the state of a pouch; this is indeed called *puṭaka*. // 25 //
19.25c–v: That [kapha] produces dryness of the orifices, hemorrhoids, and tumors; one should distinguish them according to their respective symptoms of the doshas.
In all [types], there is difficult breathing, chronic rhinitis, and constant sneezing.
19.26dv Chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), constant sneezing, nasal catarrh, nasal speech, fetid breath, and headache—
among these eighteen [symptoms], one should treat malignant rhinitis (duṣṭa-pīnasa). 19.27ab [The physician] should manage [the condition] by means of palliative measures.
19.27b–d: Putrid nose and headache; one should treat these eighteen types of malignant chronic rhinitis (duṣṭa-pīnasa), but one should avoid [treating] incurable malignant chronic rhinitis.
In the Uttarasthāna:

In all cases of chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), one should first resort to a windless chamber, cow's urine, oleation, sudation, emesis, medicated smoking, gargling, and the holding of liquids in the mouth. // 1 //
20.1b One should dwell in a windless chamber; clothing should be heavy and warm, and the head should be well-wrapped with a thick covering.
Food should be light, sour, salty, unctuous, hot, and not liquid. (2)
Light, sour, salty, and unctuous;
consisting primarily of the meat of dryland animals, jaggery, milk, chickpeas, and an abundance of the three pungents (tri-kaṭu);
rich in barley and wheat, and accompanied by curd and pomegranate—this is the diet for the Sārika bird. (3)

Soup prepared with curd and pomegranate, or soup made from young radish or from horse gram (kulattha), is highly recommended; one should drink lukewarm water decocted with the ten roots (daśamūla) or aged vāruṇī wine. // 4 //
One should smell coraka, tarkārī, vacā, jājī,
upakuñcikā, vyoṣa, tālīśa, cavikā, tintiḍīka, and amlavetasa.
Having powdered realgar, viḍaṅga, asafoetida, vacā, the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), and asafoetida, when inhaled as a snuff, chronic catarrh is destroyed. (5.1+1)
In the same way, [it is prepared] with *doraka*, *vallī*, *elā*, *lava*, *tārkṣya*, *dvijīraka*... // 5.1+2ab //
Two palas each of cumin seeds and black salt, one-fourth pala each of cinnamon, cardamom, and cinnamon leaves,
and half a tula of aged jaggery— these, when cooked together, are formed into boluses (vaṭakī).
The bark of *śatāhvā*, *balā*, the roots of *śyoṇāka*, *airaṇḍa*, and *bilva* destroy chronic catarrh, dyspnea, and cough; it is supreme for promoting appetite and improving the voice. (7)

One should inhale the smoke of *sāragvadha* mixed with fat, ghee, and *madana*; or else, having placed roasted barley flour (*saktu*) with ghee inside a hollowed-out earthen vessel (*mallaka*), one should inhale its smoke.
One should avoid bathing, grief, anger, excessive sleeping, and cold water;
in cases of vāta-type coryza, one should drink ghee prepared with vāta-alleviating drugs.
One should administer the treatments prescribed for facial paralysis (ardita), such as sudation and nasal therapy, using either the *paṭupañcaka* group of drugs or the *vidāryādi* group.
In cases arising from pitta and blood, one should drink ghee boiled with the drugs of the sweet group;
furthermore, one should apply cooling affusions and cooling medicinal plasters.

One should cook oil with the barks of *dhava*, *triphalā*, *śyāmā*, *śrīparṇī*, *yaṣṭimadhu*, and *tilvaka*, along with *niśā*, in ten times the amount of milk; this is used for nasal administration (*nāvana*).

20.12b–c. In cases arising from *kapha*, fasting, an application (*lepa*) on the head with white mustard seeds, or drinking clarified butter mixed with alkali and then inducing emesis, as well as nasal drops (*nāvana*) made from the ground [seeds], [should be employed]. 13.

Having drunk ghee mixed with alkali, one should conquer the disease arising from all three doshas by using ghees that are pungent and sharp, along with enemas of goat's urine, and by means of nasal drops (nasya) and gargles (kavala) containing salt, the three acrid spices (vyoṣa), vella, vatsaka, and cumin. // 14 //
One should treat malignant chronic rhinitis (duṣṭa-pīnasa) by administering a sequence of treatments for consumption (yakṣma) and worms (kṛmi),
using a compound of the three pungents (vyoṣa), śukanāsā (urubūka), kṛmighna, devadāru, mādrī, gada, and iṅguda.

One should prepare a sequence for treating consumption (yakṣma) and worms (kṛmi): dāru, mādrī, ambuda, iṅguda, the seed of vārtāka, trivṛt, siddhārtha, pūtimatsyaka, the flowers of agnimantha, and the fruits of pīlu and śigru. (20.15–16)
One should prepare a wick with linen as its core using horse dung juice, urine, and elephant urine combined together, and inhale the resulting smoke through both the nose and the mouth. (17)

In cases of sneezing and the condition known as *puṭaka*, the administration of sharp medicinal powders by blowing (*pradhamana*) is beneficial, using a paste or decoction of ginger, costus, long pepper, *vella*, and grapes. (18)
Oil or clarified butter prepared [with the aforementioned drugs] serves as a nasal drop (nasya) that dispels the discharge from the nose;
in cases of dryness of the nose (nāsā-śoṣa), one should administer Bala-oil through drinking and other means, along with meals consisting of meat broths.

In cases of nasal obstruction (nāsānāha), this procedure involves the application of unctuous smoke and sudation; furthermore, during suppuration and for the purpose of stimulating digestion, sharp pitta-alleviating treatments such as errhines (nasya) and the like should be administered in a flowing manner.
Strong nasal therapy (nasya) and other measures are recommended for putrid nose (pūtināsā) as they are for phlegmatic coryza (kaphapīnasa).
The treatment for pūtināsā and pīnasa consists of lac (lākṣā), karañja, black pepper (marica), vella, asafoetida (hiṅgu), long pepper (kaṇā), and jaggery (guḍa). // 21 //

After emesis has been performed, one should administer a nasal medication (nasya) consisting of sheep’s urine mixed with the juices of *śigru*, *siṃhī*, and *nikumbha*, along with *vyoṣa* and rock salt.
Oil prepared with *vella* and *surasā* is highly beneficial for nasal medication (*nāvana*).
In cases of fresh *pūyarakta*, one should follow the same procedure as for *raktapīnasa*. // 23 //
20.23–24. When hemorrhoids have become excessively enlarged, one should perform the same treatment as for blood-nasal catarrh (raktapīnasa).

Once the polypoid growths of the hemorrhoids have been cauterized like a sinus tract (nāḍī), apply a paste composed of nikumbha, kumbha, rock salt (sindhūttha), realgar (manohvā), long pepper (kaṇā), and saltpeter (agnika).
When the piles and polyps have been cauterized, one should insert into the nostril a wick smeared with honey and mixed with a paste [of the aforementioned drugs].
In this case, one should also employ nasal drops (nāvana) from the *śigru* group, as prescribed for putrid nose (pūtināsā). // 25 //
20.25ab [One should prepare] fish, buffalo, and boar meat, along with garlic and radish, mixed with medicinal pastes (kalka), smeared with ghee and honey, according to the *Uttarasthāna*.
Black gram soup, curd, milk, sour gruel, sugarcane juice, and molasses. // 1 //
21.1ab For one who consumes fish, buffalo, and pork, sleeps on the ground, and hates the cleaning of the teeth, as well as for one accustomed to smoking, emetics, gargles, and bloodletting— // 2 //
When the aggravated humors, with phlegm predominant, become enraged, they produce diseases within the mouth.
Among these, the condition called *khaṇḍauṣṭha* occurs when the lip is split in two by the wind (*vāta*).
21.3bv They produce diseases within the mouth; in the case of *oṣṭhakopa* (lip disease) caused by Vāta, the lips become stiff and intensely painful.
They crack, slough off, and become rough, black, and coarse. // 4 //
From pitta, they are yellowish, bear with sharp pain, and are covered with eruptions shaped like mustard seeds;
from kapha, however, they have much discharge and undergo rapid suppuration.

21.5c–d: Due to *saṃnipāta*, [the swelling] is characterized by large pustules, excessive moisture, intolerance to cold, heaviness, swelling, and being covered with pustules of the same color as the skin; it has various appearances, a foul odor, and slimy discharge.
Foul-smelling, discharging, and slimy; excessively malodorous and very sticky;
suddenly withered or swollen and painful; undergoing irregular suppuration; afflicted by blood and discharging blood; and having the luster of blood—[these are the signs]. //7//
In this case, when the blood is depleted, a tumor (arbuda) resembling a date fruit may arise;
from the flesh, two masses like lumps of meat appear, which gradually become infested with worms. (8)
Swelling and moisture resembling oil, accompanied by itching, are soft due to fat;
