those caused by injury burst open and are repeatedly torn asunder. (9)
The lips become itchy and soft due to an excess of fat (medas), or they may repeatedly burst and then knit back together; they also become itchy.
From wind and phlegm (vāta-kapha), a water-tumor (jalārbuda) arises on the lip, resembling a bubble on the surface of water.
Gaṇḍālajī is a stable swelling on the cheek accompanied by burning sensations and fever;
due to Vāta, the teeth cannot tolerate heat and experience increased pain upon contact with cold. (11)
It feels as if the teeth are being pierced by a spear; that condition is called *śīta* (cold) and *dālana* (tearing).
In *danta-harṣa* (trembling of the teeth), the teeth cannot endure exposure to wind, sour foods, or cold. (12)
When there is a disorder of the teeth, the twice-born [teeth] become unable to tolerate cold foods; they become painful as if from eating sour things, and as if they were loose.
In the case of *dantabheda*, the twice-born [teeth] are accompanied by pricking pain, splitting pain, and cracking.

21.13b–d: They were painful as if they had been shaken, accompanied by the sensation of splitting pain; Cāla was more agonized by the gnawing with his moving teeth, while Karāla’s was the protrusion of his formidable fangs.
21.14d–e The emergence of the teeth: when there is an excess of teeth, it is called *adhidanta* (supernumerary tooth), and it is indeed said to be *vardhana*.
When such a tooth is forming, there is extreme pain; once it has emerged, the pain subsides. 15.

21.15c–d: As it arises while [the tooth] is growing, pain subsides once it has been born. Due to lack of cleaning, the impurity on the tooth—either phlegm dried by wind or [other matter]—becomes foul-smelling and hardened; that, when neglected, becomes *śarkarā* (tartar).

21.16c–d The foul odor becomes fixed; 21.16d that sugar-like deposit, if neglected, causes the fragments of the jawbone to crumble from the tooth into tiny pieces. 17. The *śyāva* [type of caries], having turned black due to blood, bile, and wind, is a disease of the teeth.
The *kapālikā* [disease] shatters the tooth sockets into minute fragments; the *śyāva* [disease], caused by blood, bile, and wind, brings the teeth to a state of dark-brown discoloration.

Relying upon the root of the tooth, when the marrow within the hollow of the tooth has been dried up by the humors with aggravated wind and filled with the impurities of food, [the disease arises]. (18)
Due to its putrefaction, subtle worms are born; from that, there arises a violent pain without apparent cause, accompanied by agitation, dark in color, and shifting. (19)
When it is destroyed and discharges pus and blood, it is called *kṛmidantaka* (worm-infested tooth).
When the teeth discharge foul-smelling blood without any apparent cause due to phlegm and blood, [it is *pūtivaktra*]. // 20 //
21.20 When copious pus and blood flow out, and the gums become soft, moist, and blackened,
this is *śītāda*, also known as *upakuśa*; it is an inflammation (*pāka*) arising from *pitta* and blood.
The gums are burned, becoming red, swollen, itchy, and bleeding; they become distended as long as the blood remains there. (22)
The teeth become loose and painful, and the mouth becomes foul-smelling.
A swelling, firm and resembling the stone of a jujube fruit, appears on two or three teeth. (23)
From kapha and blood, danta-puppuṭa arises with intense pain and ripens quickly;
it is a heavy swelling, both internal and external, in the gums caused by the humors along with blood. (24)
When it bursts open, the dental abscess (danta-vidradhi) discharges pus and blood accompanied by pain and burning;
it is a swelling at the roots of the teeth, characterized by pain and arising from pitta and blood. (25)

21.25b–d. In the case of *pūyāsra* (pus-blood), there is a dental abscess (*danta-vidradhi*) characterized by salivary discharge; it is called *suṣira* because it erodes the gums and destroys the teeth.
Arising from the combination of all three humors (*saṃnipāta*), it is accompanied by fever and the discharge of pus and blood.

21.26c–d That which arises from the combination of all three doshas (saṃnipāta) is called mahāsuṣira; its ligaments and teeth become shattered, and there is a swelling at the edge of the gums resembling a wooden peg, causing pain in the jaw and ears. 27.

21.27b–v When the supports of the teeth are shattered, that condition caused by phlegm (śleṣman) is called adhimāṃsaka; it obstructs the ingestion of food. When the gums are rubbed, a great swelling arises.
That in which the teeth waver is called Vidarbha, born from injury;
it is that which neglects diseases affecting the gums, even those that are curable. (29)

21.29b–c. That Vaidarbha [type of ulcer], born from trauma, has its morbid humor (doṣa) flowing internally; it produces a minute channel that repeatedly discharges pus, penetrating the skin, flesh, and bone.
21.30. It flows repeatedly with pus, tearing through the skin, flesh, and bone.
Furthermore, those five types are to be recognized by their own respective characteristics as previously described:
that which is rough like a leaf of the *śāka* plant, that which is numb, and that which is cracked when vitiated by *vāta*. (31)

Due to pitta, the tongue is characterized by burning and pain; due to blood, it is covered with fleshy sprouts resembling the thorns of the śālmali tree; and due to kapha, it becomes thick and heavy. (32)
21.32–33ab. When dominated by kapha, it is heavy;
from kapha and pitta, there arises a raised swelling below [the tongue] that causes stiffness of the tongue.
When ripened, it has the smell of fish; this is alasaka, which destroys the flesh.

In the condition known as Prabandhana, there is a swelling beneath the tongue resembling the tip of the tongue itself; it is accompanied by sprout-like growths, caused by phlegm, bile, and blood, and is characterized by excessive salivation, loss of taste, stiffness, and roughness. (34)
21.34 A *pralambana* (pendulous tongue) is a condition where the tongue hangs down; it is accompanied by pain and itching and causes an obstruction to speech and eating.
An *upajihvā* (frenulum linguae) is exactly like that, but it is situated on the upper surface of the tongue.
When the flesh of the palate is vitiated by Vāta, numerous hard, painful, and dense pustules accompanied by discharge arise; these are known as tālupiṭikā. (36)
21.36b–c: Numerous, dense, painful, and rough pustules accompanied by discharge arise from kapha at the base of the palate.
21.37: A soft, hanging swelling resembling a fish-bladder, slimy and exuding secretions, appears at the root of the palate, causing the obstruction of food through the nose.
Galaśuṇḍikā causes obstruction of the throat, thirst, cough, and vomiting. Tālusamhati is a mass of flesh, free from disease, located in the middle of the palate. // 38 //
An arbuda is a red swelling in the middle of the palate shaped like a lotus;
a kacchapa is a tortoise-shaped growth arising from phlegm that increases slowly and is painless. (39)
A *kolābha* (gourd-like) swelling caused by phlegm and fat is painless and firm;
one caused by bile is called *pāka*, characterized by suppuration, discharge of pus and blood, and great pain. // 40 //
From wind, bile, fever, and exhaustion, there arises dryness of the palate known by that name;
originating from the constriction of the tongue, these are severe obstructions in the throat that block the passage. (41)
The Rohiṇī swelling arises from Vāta; it causes rapid accumulation of flesh-sprouts, acts swiftly, produces dryness of the throat and mouth, and causes pain in the jaw and ears. (42)
21.42b–c Rohiṇī is quick-acting;

arising from pitta, it is accompanied by fever, burning heat, thirst, delusion, and a sensation of smoke rising in the throat; it appears rapidly, suppurates quickly, is intensely red, and cannot bear being touched.

Due to phlegm (kapha), it is slimy and pale; due to blood, it is covered with pustules; resembling a heated coal, it causes pain in the ear and has the appearance of that which arises from bile (pitta). // 44 //

Due to the accumulation of the humors, primarily with an excess of phlegm (kapha), a swelling arises that is deep-seated in its maturation, possesses all the characteristic signs, and is firm and elevated like a jujube fruit (kola). // 45 //
Like a grain of millet, a *śālūka* is located in the throat and obstructs the passage;
a *vṛnda*, being round and elevated, causes burning fever and is situated on the side of the throat. (46)
Located at the joint of the jaw in the throat, resembling the fruit of the *kārpāsī* plant, slimy, with mild pain, and swelling, yet hard, it is called *tuṇḍikerikā*. (47)
21.47b–d. A terrible swelling, resembling the fruit of the karpāsī plant, occurring both externally and internally, acts like a bolt barring the passage of the throat;
it is known as galauha, and it causes heaviness of the head, drowsiness, salivation, and fever.
Valaya is a swelling that is not very painful; likewise, a māṃsakīla is a fleshy protuberance in the throat, caused by the doṣas, which may be single or multiple and is slightly painful. (49)
Accompanied by labored breathing and difficulty in swallowing, it has a broad base and is covered with fleshy growths; it is characterized by intense thirst, fever, and pain in the head. (50)

The *galāyuka* has a broad base; it is a massed coil (*varti*) like a *śataghnī* weapon that causes intense pain. Pervading the entire throat, it arises and ripens quickly, causing great agony. (21.50b–51)
21.51ab An internal swelling resembling a cluster of *śataghnī* weapons, which causes extreme pain and discharges pus-like matter, is *galavidradhi* (throat abscess).
21.52cd When the humors produce a non-suppurating swelling at the tip of the tongue or in the region of the throat, it is [known as] *jihvāgra-śopha*.
It produces a firm, painless growth of blood; that is a tumor (arbuda) of the throat. // 53ab //
That painless tumor of the throat is called *galārbuda*;
when it occurs externally due to wind, phlegm, and fat, it becomes a *galagaṇḍa*.
Increasing over time, it hangs down like a scrotum and causes extreme pain. 53ef.

Hanging down like a testicle, painless, and black or reddish, it is characterized by intense pricking due to Vāta; when enlarged, it causes dryness of the palate and throat as well as a bad taste in the mouth, and it is marked by black streaks.

Due to Kapha, [the swelling] is stable, of the same color as the skin, itchy, cold to the touch, and heavy; when increased, it causes a coating in the palate and throat, as well as a sweet taste in the mouth. (55)
When increased, fat produces a swelling in the palate and throat; it follows the decrease or increase of phlegm.
When increased in the throat, it causes a sound in the body and results in diminished voice.

When the movement of the wind (vāyu) is obstructed by phlegm (śleṣman), the throat becomes dry, the voice is impaired, and one breathes with persistent distress; by this condition, the voice is lost due to the affliction of the wind. (57)
The wind, having entered all the channels, produces ulcers within the mouth;
it makes the lips reddish-brown, rough, and with flickering skin.
When the tongue is cold-tolerant, heavy, cracked, and covered with papillae,
and it opens the mouth only with great difficulty, that is the ripening (pāka) of the mouth.
21.59 When the wind, obstructed below the mouth by hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, phlegm, and the like, moves upward toward the face,
it causes foul breath; this condition is known as *ūrdhvaguda*.
21.60d–61. However, when it arises from pitta, that upward-moving disease causes a burning sensation and heat in the mouth, and a bitter taste in the mouth.
The ulcers are like those caused by an alkaline solution applied to a wound; and the same is true when it arises from blood.
In the type born of kapha, there is sweetness in the mouth, and the ulcers are itchy and slimy;
the kapha forms a tumor (arbuda) that takes refuge within the cheeks, appearing dusky-white.
Kapha produces a tumor that is dark-brown or pale;
it increases when it is rubbed, cut, or pressed.
Mouth-sores (mukhapāka) may occur with all the humors accompanied by blood, exhibiting the characteristics of all [the doshas].
One should consider that [use] as causing laceration or cutting;
it causes piercing or cutting, as well as foul-smelling breath, for those who are averse to using tooth-sticks and the like.
[The same applies to brushing] the lips, cheeks, teeth, their roots, the tongue, the palate, and the throat. (21.63–64)
In the mouth and everywhere else, seventy-five diseases have been described:
eleven, one, ten, thirteen, and six respectively. (65)
Among them, eight, eighteen, and eight [types] respectively are incurable;
[these include] Karāla, those with fleshy lips and blood-red lips, and the Arbudas, excluding the one caused by water.
21.66b–c Among these, in due order, those that are incurable are:
kacchapa, tālupiṭikā, galaugha, suṣira, mahān,
svaraghna, ūrdhvaguda, śyāva, śataghnī, valaya, and alasā.
21.67c–v: From the combination of all [doshas] arise svaraghna, ūrdhvagada, śyāvanāḍī, oṣṭhakopa, and from blood, rohiṇī;
when the teeth crack, it is dantabheda; and when the uvula is inflamed, it is upajihvikā.
Goiter, loss of voice, and labored breathing occurring after many years are palliative; however, one should conquer hoarseness and chest pain with surgery and medicines. 69.
21.69a–b: Diseases of the throat, goiter, loss of voice, and [diseases of] the lips: having incised the edges of the lip and sutured them, one should treat it like a wound.
With yaṣṭī, jyotiṣmatī, lodhra, śrāvaṇī, śāriva, and utpala. // 1 //
One should prepare oil for anointment from *paṭolī* and *kākamācī*, and an oil for nasal administration prepared with the wind-alleviating and sweet groups of drugs. (2)
A cotton pad soaked in a proven great unctuous preparation (mahāsneha) is beneficial when applied to the lips;
likewise, incense made from deodar, beeswax, guggulu, and amaradāru is beneficial. // 3 //
One should apply a rubbing with that same [mixture] combined with the powder of yaṣṭyāhva;
one should foment the lip of the sinus with castor leaves prepared with milk.
One should apply a rubbing (pratisāraṇa) with those very same substances mixed with a powder of yaṣṭyāhva;
for a cracked lip, one should administer nasal drops (nasya) and perform head-satiation (tarpaṇa) on the head.
For lips arising from pitta or injury (abhighāta), one should treat them with leeches.
A rubbing ointment should be prepared with lodhra, sarjarasa, honey, and madhuka;
for anointing, ghee processed with guḍūcī, yaṣṭimadhu, and pattaṅga is recommended.
In this case, as well as in a blood-born abscess, the treatment is the same as for a pitta-born abscess;
this very same procedure should be applied when it is acute, but in the case of an abscess on the lip caused by phlegm, [the following applies].

This very same treatment should be applied. However, when *kapha* predominates in the lips, once the blood has been removed, one should perform rubbing with *pāṭhā*, alkali, honey, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, therapies that eliminate *kapha*—such as medicated smoke, nasal drops, and gargles—should be employed. (8)

When the swelling is softened, opened, and its fatty tissue has been removed, one should cauterize a fat-born tumor with fire and rub it with *priyaṅgu*, *lodhra*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and honey. // 9 //
For a *jalārbuda* that has been opened and purified, a sharp rubbing with honey is the treatment;
however, for one that is deeply embedded or excessively enlarged, caustic alkali (*kṣāra*) or fire (*agni*) are the remedies. (10)

Rubbing with honey and strong [medicines], alkali, and fire are the remedies. One should treat *alajī* on the cheek according to the swelling protocol during its various stages, such as the undigested (*āma*) stage.
Once the patient has been fomented and the tooth has become cold, one should scarify and cauterize the gum margin.
And it should be rubbed with oil [mixed] with honey, sugar, rock salt, pomegranate bark, *varā*, *tārkṣya*, *kāntā*, jambu stone, and ginger. (12)

In cases of hypersensitivity of the teeth (danta-harṣa) and their loosening (bheda), one should administer a gargle with the decoctions of milky trees, as well as nasal drops (nāvana) of aṇu-taila; furthermore, all treatments that alleviate vāta should be employed.
In cases of toothache as well as hypersensitivity (harṣa), all treatments that alleviate vāta should be employed. Milk boiled with sesame and liquorice should be held as a mouth gargle;
likewise, water from the ten roots (daśamūla) mixed with unctuous substances should be used as a gargle for loose teeth.
22.14c–d: When the *dvija* (teeth) are loose, gargles with water decocted with the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and fats should be used;
for rubbing, *tuttha*, *lodhra*, *kaṇā*, *śreṣṭhā*, *pattaṅga*, and *paṭu* are best. 22.15:
Unctuous, cooling, and habitual treatments such as nasal drops (*nasya*), food boluses (*kavaḍa*), and so forth, should be administered according to the specific condition.
When the gums, the cheeks, and so forth, as well as the tooth itself, are coated with a caustic and become decayed,
one should treat them at that time just like a carious tooth that has been extracted.
When the redness is unstable and the area is inflamed, treatment should be like that for a wound;
without injuring the roots of the teeth, one should remove the tartar from the teeth. (17)
Then one should rub [the area] with alkaline powders mixed with honey;
in the case of Kapālikā as well, one should act in this same manner and perform the treatment prescribed by Harṣa.

One should conquer caries with stable roots by means of sudation followed by bloodletting, and for unstable caries, by means of unctuous applications, gargles, nasal drops, and diets that remove the instability. (19)
22.19b–c. One should cauterize a tooth that is weak, decayed by worms, or hollow with jaggery or beeswax.
Filling [the cavity] with the milky sap of *saptacchada* and *arka* overcomes worm-infestation and toothache. 20.
The powder derived from asafoetida, katphala, kāsīsa, svarjikā, kuṣṭha, and vella,
when applied to the teeth while held in a cloth or smeared with ghee, quickly conquers dental pain.

22.21dv Ghee placed on a cloth, or lac-dye, or rock salt, or asafoetida with the smoke of *vella*, or moss prepared in fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), or lukewarm [substances] held in the mouth; or [these may be] held in the teeth. // 21+1 //
22.21+1b Or [one may apply] house-smoke mixed with asafoetida;
or the root of *varāhakarṇī*; or the root-fiber (*jaṭā*) of *śarapuṅkhā*;
or a wick made from the fruits of *avalguja* combined with the root-fiber of *bījapūra*.
One should cause him to take a gargle of oil prepared with these very same decoctions,
or combined with those derived from castor, the two types of vyāghrī, and bhūkadamba.

One should hold oil as a mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa) prepared with vyāghrī, bhūrja, and kadambaka. When the pain remains severe and unrelieved despite these various therapeutic applications, one should extract even a firmly rooted tooth that has already been loosened from its base. // 23 //
Then, using a small forceps or a tooth-extractor, [extract the tooth];
thereafter, a gargle of oil mixed with the powder of yaṣṭyāhva (liquorice) or honey [should be used].
Then, a gargle with honey should be used;
thereafter, one should employ as nasal drops oil prepared with vidārī, yaṣṭyāhva, śṛṅgāṭaka, and kaseru, along with ten times the amount of milk.
One should not extract a tooth from those who are emaciated, weak, or elderly, nor from those afflicted by wind (vāta); nor should one extract an upper tooth, for it causes many complications.
For these as well, during extraction, a sequence of unctuous, sweet, and cold applications is beneficial;
once the blood has been drained, if there is coldness and so forth, one should apply a rubbing with honey.

22.27 When these [drugs] have been extracted along with unctuous *mustā*, *arjunatvak*, the three fruits (*triphalā*), *phalinī*, *tārkṣya*, and *nāgara*, their decoction may be used as a gargle or as nasal drops; likewise, oil prepared with sweet [substances] [is beneficial].
The gums of the teeth, having been fomented with warm water applications, should be scraped repeatedly with a circular blade or with leaves of śāka and other plants. (29)
Then, they should be treated with the scum of clarified butter, honey, and melted [substances],
along with lac, priyaṅgu, pattaṅga, the best salt (saindhava), and red ochre.

22.30b–c: A lukewarm gargle consisting of the scum of ghee (ghṛtamaṇḍa) mixed with honey, along with kuṣṭha, śuṇṭhī, marica, yaṣṭīmadhu, and rasāñjana; or alternatively, oil [mixed with these] may be used as a gargle. 22.31a: [This should be done] after [the previous treatment].
22.31 Oil, or ghee prepared with drugs of the sweet group, is beneficial when used as a bolus or as nasal drops.
In the case of *danta-puppuṭaka*, after it has been fomented, incised, split, or scraped, [the aforementioned treatments are applied].
Alternatively, ghee prepared with the "sweet" (madhura) drugs,
along with liquorice (yaṣṭyāhva), sarjikā, dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and rock salt (saindhava), should be used as a rubbing agent (pratisāraṇa).
For an abscess (vidradhi), gargles and plasters consisting of pungent, sharp, hot, and dry substances should be applied.
One should apply friction with *kaṭukā*, *kuṣṭha*, *vṛścikālī*, and *yava*.
One should protect against suppuration with cooling applications; once suppurated, it should be incised, and if deep-seated, it should be cauterized. (34)
In cases of perforation, incision, or laceration, a medicinal paste (pratisāraṇa) mixed with honey should be applied using lodhra,
musta, miśī, śreṣṭhā, tārkṣyaja, pattaṅga, and kiṃśuka.
In cases of hollowing, incision, or scraping, gargling with decoctions of those [same] drugs along with *kaṭphala* is prescribed;
likewise, with *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *lodhra*, *utpala*, *anantā*, *śārivā*, *aguru*, and *candana*.
A decoction prepared with *kaṭphala*,
red ochre (*gairika*), sugar, and *puṇḍra*, as well as oil processed with these, should be used for nasal administration (*nāvana*).
After excising the excess flesh (*adhimāṃsaka*), one should rub the area with powders mixed with honey.
A gargle consisting of a decoction of vacā, tejovatī, pāṭhā, svarjikā, yavaśūka, paṭola, nimba, and triphalā is beneficial. (38)
In the case of Vidarbha, one should cleanse the roots of the teeth with a round-headed instrument (maṇḍalāgra) using svarjikā, yavaśūka, and jatu.
Thereafter, one should apply alkaline medicine (kṣāra), as well as nasal drops (nasya) and cool gargles (gaṇḍūṣa).
Having purified both parts of the body, one should then treat the head;
having extracted a tooth whose root extends into the sinus, one should cauterize it with fire.

A hunchbacked woman who has many suitors, when filled with jaggery or *madana* fruit, [is effective]; likewise, running [with a mixture] of *jāti*, *madana*, *khadira*, and *svādukaṇṭaka* [is used for the same purpose]. 41.
One should apply a full dose of *guḍa* (molasses) or honey to the face while it is turned downward,
or administer mouthfuls of water from milky trees (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*), as well as nasal drops (*nasya*) prepared from that same [water].
For thorns caused by Vāta, one should also perform the treatments prescribed for the provocation of Vāta in the lips.

When the tongue is afflicted by pitta-born disorders, when it is abraded and bleeding, the application of sweet substances as a powder for rubbing (pratisāraṇa), as a mouthwash (gaṇḍūṣa), and as nasal drops (nāvana) is beneficial. (43)
In cases arising from phlegm, one should likewise use sharp [medicines] such as mustard seeds, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and so forth;
the same applies to acute tongue-palsy (jihvālāsa), yet one should not touch it with a surgical instrument.

In cases arising from *kapha*, one should likewise employ sharp measures. Having raised the tongue and drawn out the *adhi-jihvikā* (ranula) with a hook, one should excise it with a scalpel (*maṇḍalāgra*), followed by rubbing with sharp and hot substances and other treatments. (22.44–45)
Having cauterized the uvula, one should rub it with barley-alkali;
a swelling of the palate (śuṇḍikā) caused by phlegm should be treated with nasal drops, gargles, and rubbing, using drugs that destroy phlegm.
Resembling the seed of an ervāru gourd, it is situated at the tip of the tongue in the uvula, spread out without visible veins, and suspended by means of a hook or similar instrument. // 47 //
When the tip [of the growth] is situated on the tongue, one should excise it with a scalpel at the front of the tongue, neither too far forward nor from the root.
If excised too much, death may occur due to loss of blood; if excised insufficiently, the disease increases.
22.48b–d. It should not be placed too far forward nor too far back [in the mouth].

For a cracked lip, one should apply a rubbing powder of black pepper (*marica*), ativiṣā, pāṭhā, vacā, kuṣṭha, and kuṭannaṭa, along with salt and honey; furthermore, a gargle (*kavaḍa*) should be used.

In cases of *saṃghāta*, *puppuṭa*, and *kūrma* [types of nasal polyps], one should first perform scarification and then proceed with treatment using water decoctions of *kaṭukā*, *ativiṣā*, *pāṭhā*, *nimba*, *rāsnā*, and *vacā*.

In the case of inflammation of the palate that is not yet suppurated, one should apply rubbing with *kāsīsa*, honey, and *tārkṣya* (rasāñjana), and administer gargles consisting of cooling, astringent, and sweet medicinal herbs. (51)

In the case of dryness of the palate in one who does not suffer from thirst, ghee taken after meals, a drink of water boiled with long pepper (kaṇā) and ginger (śuṇṭhī), and holding mouthfuls of acidic liquids are recommended. (53)

22.53–54ab. For one suffering from thirst with dryness of the palate, unctuous juices of desert meat, milk, and ghee [are indicated], as well as nasal drops (nāvana). In diseases of the throat, bloodletting and procedures such as sharp nasal therapy (tīkṣṇa-nasya) should be performed.
A decoction made from the bark of *dārvī*, *nimba*, *tārkṣya*, and *kaliṅga* should be drunk;
or alternatively, a decoction of *harītakī* mixed with honey should be consumed. // 55 //
With the best [qualities], trikaṭu, yavakṣāra, dārvī, dvīpī, rasāñjana, pāṭhā, tejinī, and nimba, prepared with fermented gruel (śukta) and cow’s urine. // 56 //
In this case, a bolus or a pill is prepared as a local application (pratisāraṇa),
consisting of nicula, kaṭabhī, musta, devadāru, and mahauṣadha.
In this case, a bolus or pill [should be used]. A lukewarm paste of *nicula*, *kaṭabhī*, *mustā*, *vacā*, *dantī*, and *mūrvā* removes pain and swelling.
Furthermore, once the internal and external [parts] of *vāta-rohiṇikā* have been fomented, one should scarify it.
Quickly [extract it] with a fingernail-sword, or with a sharp, well-prepared nail;
[administer] the five roots decoction as a mouthful, oil as a gargle and nasal drop. 59.
Having drained a swelling born of pitta, one should rub it with sugar, honey, priyaṅgu, lodhra, and pattaṅga; and a gargle should be prepared from these same ingredients boiled together.
A decoction of grapes and *parūṣaka* is beneficial for gargling;
one should treat [the patient] in this very manner after rejecting the possibility of blood production. (61)
One should counteract phlegm-born [diseases] with pungent substances containing salt and smoke;
furthermore, oil prepared for use as nasal drops (nasya) or mouth-rinse (gaṇḍūṣa) is highly recommended. 62.
With apāmārga fruit, śvetā, dantī, jantughna, and saindhava; and likewise for vṛnda, śālūka, tuṇḍikerī, and gilāyu. (63)
In cases of *tuṇḍikerī*, goiter, and abscesses,
once the pus has been drained, a gargle and rubbing with *śreṣṭhā*, *rocanā*, *tārkṣya*, *gairika*, *lodhra*, *paṭu*, *pattaṅga*, and *kaṇā* are recommended.
22.64dv—Holding a mouthful [of water] with droplets; rubbing with droplets.
A goiter of the throat born of wind (pavana) should be treated by fomentation and the draining of blood, using sesame seeds, *laṭvā* seeds, flax (*umā*), *priyāla*, and *śaṇa*. 65.
Once the wound has been fomented and the blood has flowed out, it should be treated with poultices once the ulceration has healed, and then repeatedly smeared with a paste made of *śigru*,
*tilvaka*, *tarkārī*, *gajakṛṣṇā*, and *punarnavā*.

And with the roots of *kālāmṛta* and *arka*, and flowers produced from *karahāṭa*, ground together with a single reed-shaft (*ekaiṣīkā*) and mixed with wine or sour gruel (*kāñjika*), [one should perform the rite]. 67.

One should cause [the patient] to drink oil prepared with the roots of *tāla* and *arka*, flowers of *karaghāṭa*, *guḍūcī*, *nimba*, *kuṭaja*, *haṃsapadī*, the two types of *balā*, along with *kṛṣṇā* and *devadāru*.

This same treatment should also be performed for [fevers] born of phlegm (kapha), though excessive sudation and depleting measures are required; furthermore, an external paste of ajagandhā, ativiṣā, viśalyā, and viṣāṇikā should be applied.
Having boiled *guñjā*, *lābu*, and *śukāhvā* with the alkaline paste of *palāśa* and the alkali of *haṭha* strained through urine, one who eats *kodrava* grain should drink it. (70)
Barley alkali boiled with urine, or barley alkali strained through urine, or oil prepared with the *vatsakādi* group of drugs along with the five salts and rock salt.
One should habitually employ phlegm-subduing treatments such as medicated smoking, emesis, and nasal drops.
22.71c–d: One should practice the use of phlegm-subduing medicated smokes (dhūma) and gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), as well as emetics and other such therapies.

In cases arising from fat (medas), one should perform venesection (sirā-vidhya) and follow a regimen that subdues phlegm (kapha). Furthermore, one should have the patient drink the powder of the *asanādi* group with urine every morning. 72.
When there is no subsiding, one should treat all [the conditions] like a wound after purifying them;
for mouth ulcers, mouth-washes mixed with honey should be employed. (73)
If there is no subsiding, after performing surgical incision, mouth-cleansing decoctions should be employed,
such as those boiled from *triphalā*, *pāṭhā*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *jātī* sprouts; or else, one should either gargle with or consume the *kuṭhera* group of herbs.

22.74c–d. In cases of mouth ulcers caused by Vāta, after rubbing [the affected area] and consuming [the medicine], one should apply a powder of *kṛṣṇā*, *paṭu*, and *elā* as a local rub (*pratisāraṇa*).
Oil prepared with Vāta-alleviating drugs is beneficial for use as a gargle (*kavaḍa*) and as nasal drops (*nasya*).

In cases of *pittāsra* (blood-bile), the procedure consists of treatments that subdue blood and bile, as well as those that subdue *kapha*. For *kapha*, one should scarify hard and firm pustules using the leaves of vegetables and similar plants. (76)

In cases of *pittāsṛj* (hemorrhagic disorders), one should administer treatments that subdue *raktapitta*; in cases of *saṃnipāta* (combined humors), one should perform treatment according to the manifestation of the specific *doṣas*. However, when a tumor (*arbuda*) is newly formed and has not yet grown large, once it has been excised, a rubbing ointment (*pratisāraṇa*) should be applied.
A gargle is recommended consisting of a decoction of svarjikā, nāgara, and honey;
alternatively, one made from the paste of guḍūcī and nimba, combined with honey and oil. (78)

One who eats barley-based food should likewise perform nasal drops and massages with pungent oil; when vomiting has occurred and the mouth is foul-smelling, a sharp medicinal smoke along with nasal drops should be administered. (79)
Water containing *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī*, *lodhra*, *phalinī*, and *padmaka*, with these powdered substances sprinkled inside the mouth, serves as a gargle. (80)
One should apply the powdering [of the affected area] with these powders, and one should also practice the nasal drops (nāvana) and other treatments prescribed for śītāda and kuṣṭha.
The three fruits, dvīpi, kirātatikta, yaṣṭyāhva, siddhārtha, and the three pungents (kaṭutrika). // 81cd //
Mustā, the two types of haridrā, yavaśūka, vṛkṣāmlaka, āmla, agnimantha, and vetasa; // 81ef //

The bark of the aśvattha, jambu, āmra, dhanañjaya, and ahimāra, as well as the heartwood of khadira—these should be boiled until they reach a thick consistency, and pills should be prepared by mixing them with the powder of those same ingredients. (82)

When held in the mouth, these [medicines] constantly destroy even the most difficult diseases of the throat, lips, palate, and so forth—specifically *rohiṇikā*, dryness of the mouth, and halitosis—as prescribed by the Lord of Videha. (83)
Having boiled a decoction of *khadira* wood in a water-pot, one should grind with that water *candana*, *joṅgaka*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), *paripelava*, *vālaka*, and *uśīra*. // 84 //
With *surataru*, *lodhra*, *drākṣā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *coca*, *padmaka*, and *viḍaṅga*; with *spṛkkā*, *nata*, *nakha*, *kaṭphala*, *sūkṣmailā*, *dhyāmaka*, and *pattaṅga*. // 85 //

One should cook one prastha of oil with [the aforementioned] ingredients in portions of one karṣa each; when used as a drink, nasal drop, or mouth gargle, it destroys all diseases of the mouth and produces the vision of a vulture and the hearing of a boar. (86)
22.86b–c: Used as a drink, nasal drop, or gargle in doses of one karṣa each, it destroys all diseases of the mouth.

When used as an external rub (udvartana), and when the face is anointed with this [mixture] of *prapuṇāṭa*, *lodhra*, and *dārvī*, the face becomes free from freckles, dark spots, and impurities, and acquires a luster equal to the moon. 87.

Having boiled one hundred palas of *bāṇa*— free from dark spots, with its mouth and impurities removed— in a jar of water, one should add half a pala each of *khadira*, *jambū*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *anantā*, copper, *ahimāra*, and blue lotus to this decoction.

One should cook one *prastha* of oil with *khadira*, *jambū*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *anantā*, and *lodhra*, using these substances ground into a fine paste. When this oil is held in the mouth, it destroys all diseases of the oral cavity; specifically, it provides stability to a loose set of teeth.
One should cook one *prastha* of oil with these substances finely ground; when that [oil] is applied, it provides comfort.
One should boil two *tulas* of the heartwood of *khadira* and one *tulā* of the bark of *arimeda*.
When this four-pitcher remnant of the feet has been purified again by boiling until it becomes thick, [one should proceed]. (90)
One should boil two *tula*s of the heartwood of *khadira* and one *tula* of the bark of *arimeda*. When this has been strained, one should boil it again until it becomes thick from the decoction.

One should add very fine powder of copper sulfate, realgar, blue vitriol, water, cinnabar, red ochre, the two types of sandalwood, lodhra, punnāga, yaṣṭimadhu, lac, and the two types of collyrium. (91)
One should add one akṣa of very fine powder;
one should add one karṣa of very fine powder.

The two types of sandalwood, śyāmā, puṇḍrāhvā, dhātakī, kaṭphala, the two types of niśā, triphalā, the four spices (caturjāta), joṅgaka, musta, mañjiṣṭhā, the sprouts of nyagrodha, māṃsī, and yavāsaka. // 92 //
When that [decoction] has cooled, one should add one *pālikā* each of *dhānyaka*, *praroha*, *vacā*, *māṃsī*, *yavāsaka*, *padmaka*, *elā*, and *samaṅgā*; likewise,
one *pālikā* each of *jātīpattra*, *jātīphala*, *lavaṅga*, and *kaṅkollaka*.
One should add *padmaka*, *kailaya*, and *samaṅgā* separately to each cold infusion (*pālikā*), along with *nakhī*, *lavaṅga*, and *kaṅkolla*; then,
one should add a *kuḍava* measure of crystal-white, fragrant camphor (*karpūra*) into it.
One should always have these pills prepared; when held in the mouth, they remove those diseases.

One should prepare these pills; by substituting the decoction drugs [with oil], one should cook the oil using this very same method of preparation. They say that this [oil] is for the eradication of all diseases, but for the stabilization of the teeth, this [pill] alone is primary. // 95 //
22.95 By applying a reversal of the decoction and medicinal ingredients, this has been stated for the purpose of pacifying all diseases of the mouth;
they call that [method] "reversal" (vyayana) in the case of every oral disease.
These pills made from *khadira* wood and this oil prepared from *arimeda* are renowned;
by practicing them daily, even one who is already healthy becomes possessed of firm teeth. 96.
22.96 Even an old man becomes firm in his teeth by means of a decoction of *kṣudrā*, *guḍūcī*, *sumanaḥpravāla*, *dārvī*, *yavāsa*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
This gargle, when combined with honey, destroys all diseases located in the mouth. 97.
22.97–98. A powder made from *drākṣā*, *guḍūcī*, *sumana* sprouts, *pāṭhā*, *dārvī* bark, *kuṣṭha*, *mustā*, *samaṅgā*, *tiktā*, *pītāṅgī*, *lodhra*, and *tejovatī*,
mixed with honey, destroys pain, itching, suppuration, and discharge of the gums when used as a rubbing powder.

In disorders of the mouth, teeth, and throat, a black powder (kālaka) composed of house-soot, *tārkṣya*, *pāṭhā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), alkali, *agni* (citraka), iron, *varā* (triphalā), and *tejahva* (musta), mixed with honey, should be held in the mouth. (99)

22.99–100. A powder made from the bark of *dārvī*, rock salt (*sindhūdbhava*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *yāvaśūka*, and yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), should be held in the mouth with honey and kept for a period of time; this yellow powder, taken with honey and clarified butter, cures diseases of the teeth, mouth, and throat.

This medicinal preparation (rasakriyā), cooked with cow’s urine and consisting of the two alkalis, dhūmaka, varā, the five salts (pañcapaṭu), vyoṣa, vella, girija, and tārkṣya, destroys diseases of the throat. 101.
22.101–102 Drinking a decoction of the two alkalis, house-soot, and *varā* with cow’s urine,
and consuming *pathyā* fruits whose bodies have been dissolved in a decoction of cow’s urine and infused with water, *miśi*, and *kuṣṭha*—
even minute oral diseases do not touch such a man who eats this, just as misfortunes do not touch a king who listens [to wise counsel].
One should drink a decoction of saptacchada, uśīra, paṭola, musta, harītakī, tiktaka, rohiṇī, yaṣṭyāhvā, rājadruma, and candana to alleviate inflammation of the mouth. (103)

The decoction of paṭola, śuṇṭhī, triphalā, viśālā, trāyantī, tiktā, the two types of niśā, and amṛtā, when drunk with honey or held in the mouth, destroys all diseases of the mouth without exception. (104)

The juice of *dārvī* boiled down until it becomes a solid extract, mixed with red ochre (*gairika*) and honey, when kept in the mouth, quickly removes all diseases arising from the mouth, including stomatitis, sinus-like ulcers, and oral wounds. (22.104–105)
In this same manner, preparations should be made separately from paṭola, nimba, yaṣṭyāhva, vāsā, jāti, arimeda, khadira, and varā. (106)
A mouthful of water boiled with *khadira*, *āragvadha*, *pārtha*, *madayantī*, and *ahimāraka* should be held in the mouth for the pacification of weak teeth. 107.
Diseases arising in the mouth, the roots of the teeth, and the throat are generally characterized by a predominance of phlegm and blood;
therefore, one should repeatedly drain the vitiated blood from them. (108)
Purgation of the body and head, emesis, and pungent or bitter foods and drinks are generally recommended for them, as well as any treatment that removes phlegm and blood. (109)

Barley, grass, and grains; foods prepared with split pulses soaked in alkaline water and devoid of fat; soups and solid foods that are beneficial, as well as anything else that destroys phlegm—these are wholesome. (110)

Barley, grass, and grain that have been eaten and processed with alkaline substances and deprived of their oiliness cause those situated in the path of the vital breath (prāṇa) to obstruct even the respiration of one who is negligent.
Therefore, one should quickly apply medical treatment for diseases of the throat.
Uttarasthāna:
By means of smoke, heat, frost, water, excessive play, sleep, and wakefulness;
by excessive sweating, mental anguish, east wind, suppression of tears, and weeping. (1)

23.1c–d: [Insanity arises] from the onset of wind (vāta), excessive drinking of water and wine, worms, the suppression of natural urges, aversion to pillows, cleansing, and massage, and from looking downward for long periods. // 2 //

Furthermore, the humors located in the head produce diseases through unwholesome odors, putrid food, harsh speech, and so forth; therein, due to the provocation of the wind (vāta), [the following occurs]: //3//

23.3ab Due to unwholesome odors or contaminated water, the temples are intensely pricked and the frontal bone likewise feels as if it is splitting; the space between the eyebrows and the forehead suffer extreme pain, as if they were falling apart. // 4 //
23.4cv The space between the eyebrows and the forehead are oppressed; the ears seem to ring and the eyes feel as if they are being pulled out.
The entire head seems to spin, as if it were being released from its joints. // 5 //
The network of veins throbs excessively; there is constriction of the neck and jaw; intolerance to light; nasal discharge; and sudden onset and subsiding of pain. (6)
Softness [of the head] arises from massage, oiling, sweating, and bandaging;
this pain in one half of the head is known as *ardhāvabhedaka*.
It becomes aggravated after a fortnight or a month and subsides by itself;
however, when excessively increased, it may destroy the eye or the ear.
In head-fever arising from pitta, there is a sensation of fumes in the head, fever, perspiration, burning in the eyes, fainting, and relief at night from cold applications. (9)

In the case of [diseases] born from phlegm (kapha), there is a lack of relish, heaviness, numbness, and coldness of the head; sluggishness of the vessels, lassitude, and dull pain that increases during the day and at night. 10.

Drowsiness, swelling of the eyes and temples, itching of the ears, and vomiting [occur]; from blood there is pain exceeding that of bile; by the combination of all [three humors], it possesses all the symptoms. (11)
When the blood and flesh at the head are moistened by mixed foods,
and when the *sannipāta* (the combination of the humors) is provoked, living organisms are born in the head.
Drinking the blood from your head, those terrible beings cause agonizing pains that produce mental derangement, fever, cough, and loss of strength. (13)
Roughness, swelling, piercing pain, cutting, burning, throbbing, and putridity [occur];
in the *kapāla* [vessel], there is itching, dryness, and drowsiness in the palate and the head. (14)
In [the case of] roughness and swelling caused by insects, there is piercing, cutting, burning, cracking, and putrefaction; there is itching,
swelling, and drowsiness— or rather, itching, swelling, and lack of drowsiness—
and copper-colored clear nasal discharge and ringing in the ears.
When the humors (malas) are dominated by wind (vāta), they cause a shaking of the head known as that [condition]. // 15 //

When vāta and the other [doshas], dominated by pitta and accompanied by blood, affect the temple region (śaṅkha), there occurs swelling along with intense burning, pain, redness, delirium, fever, thirst, and vertigo. (16)
With a bitter mouth and a yellow face, that Śaṅkhaka acts swiftly;
it destroys life within three nights, yet if properly treated, it may also be quickly cured.
23.17 When properly treated, it is quickly cured; however,
when wind (vāta) is associated with bile (pitta) in the temples, eyes, eyebrows, and forehead,
it causes a throbbing pain that arises following the rising of the sun.

Thus, the ten diseases located in the head, including sūryāvarta, have been described;
now, nine diseases of the skull (kapāla) will be explained in the head itself. 20.
When the wind (vāyu) is vitiated in the skull (kapāla), a swelling of the same color as the skin and free from pain arises even in one still in the womb; one should know that condition as upaśīrṣaka.
One should describe the pustules, tumors, and abscesses according to the arising of their respective humors;
on the skull, they are characterized by excessive moisture due to bile, blood, phlegm, and parasites.
Arūṃṣikā consists of pustules resembling millet or white mustard seeds;
it causes itching, hair loss, numbness, dryness, and the cracking of the skin. (23)
One should know that *dāruṇaka* is a very fine cracking of the skin caused by *kapha* and *vāta*, which produces dryness;
it occurs when *pitta*, following the hair follicles, is congealed together with *vāta*. (23.23dv–24)
One should know that this is *dāruṇaka*;
it causes the hair to fall out, and then the phlegm, along with blood, obstructs the hair follicles of this person, whereby the growth of other hairs becomes impossible. (23.24b–25)
They call this *indralupta*, and others say it is *rujyā*; some also call it *āceti*.
The birth of *khalati* (baldness) is likewise [due to] the gradual wearing away (*śātana*) of hair there.
23.26ab That is Indra-lupta, and [the defects] born from it; 23.26ab that is Indra-lupta, and [the defects] beginning with jha; 23.26ab that is Indra-lupta, and [the defects] beginning with tha;
23.26ab that is Indra-lupta, and [the defects] beginning with ru. 23.26cd But in that regard, there is a hundredfold [classification] according to the sequence.
In that case, however, the ulceration occurs gradually: from Vāta it has the appearance of being burnt by fire; from Pitta it is covered with perspiring vessels.
From phlegm (kapha), one should diagnose thick skin and colors on the skin according to their respective [characteristics]. // 27 //

From pitta, it is glossy and covered with vessels; from pitta, it is yellow and covered with vessels. When caused by all the doshas, it takes on every form; that [disease], which has the luster of a fingernail, is incurable.
Like one burnt by fire, she becomes hairless and suffers from a burning sensation. // 28 //

23.28d–29. Furthermore, the bodily heat produced by grief, exhaustion, and anger arises accompanied by the humors (doṣas). When that heat, along with the humors, reaches the head, it cooks the hair; from this, graying occurs.
That which is cracked by wind (vāta) is dark-brown, rough, dry, and resembles water;
from bile (pitta) it is accompanied by burning and has a yellowish luster; from phlegm (kapha) it is unctuous and subject to increase.
One should know that [the swelling] which is large and very white has all mixed characteristics;
another, arising from headache, is discolored and cannot bear being touched. (31)

When the condition is thick and accompanied by white hair, it is incurable; indeed, baldness (khalati) and premature graying (palita) caused by the derangement of all three humors (saṃnipāta), as well as those arising from the natural transformation of the body, require rejuvenative therapy (rasāyana).

In the Uttarasthāna, for headache caused by Vāta, one should employ the procedures prescribed for Vāta diseases. Having anointed the head with ghee, one should drink it at night, followed by warm milk. (1)
Having anointed one's head with ghee at night,
one should drink clarified butter followed by milk;
likewise, one should eat mung beans, horse gram, or green gram mixed with ghee.
One should cause [the patient] to drink either the oil of sesame seeds or their paste together with milk. // 2 //
Poultices, fomentation, and sudation prepared with meat and grains are beneficial;
as is sprinkling with milk processed with Vātaghna, Daśamūla, and other such drugs. (3)
An unctuous nasal drop (nasya), as well as medicated smoke (dhūma) and the saturation of the head and ears, [should be employed].
One should cook milk mixed with half its amount of water over the group of drugs beginning with *varuṇa* that has been ground into a paste.
When the group beginning with *varuṇa* has been crushed and the milk remains as the residue, one should churn that cooled liquid and extract the essence (*sāra*).
Then, clarified butter prepared with the "sweet" (*madhuraka*) drugs is highly recommended as a nasal medication (*nasya*). //5//
In this group, ghee cooked with milk should be drunk along with sugar;
likewise, cotton seeds, bark, musta, and jasmine buds [are used]. 6.
In that [mixture], cotton-seed pulp, bark, musta, and *sumanas*-alkalis, cooked in milk,
ground with warm water, form an errhine (*nasya*) that removes all pain of the head.
Ghee boiled with sugar and saffron is for cases arising from the combination of pitta and blood.
One should apply plasters containing ghee made from kuṣṭha, kuṭila, utpala, and candana;
however, out of fear of aggravating the vāta, one should not perform bloodletting in this condition.

Thus, when there is no pacification and the condition is unstable, the application of cauterization (dāha) is desired in cases of kapha, as previously described; this same treatment is also applied in hemiplegia (ardhāvabhedaka), following the same sequence of the doshas.
24.9b In cases of kapha, [the treatment] is warm as previously described; 24.9d the procedure follows the specific involvement of the doṣas.
24.9d The procedure according to the involvement of the doṣas is as follows: the seeds of *śirīṣa* and the root of *apāmārga*, combined with *viḍa* salt, used as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
Alternatively, for an ointment, one may use *sthirā* juice or *prapunnāṭa* ground with sour substances.
In this case of Sūryāvarta, a plaster of *sthirā* juice may also be applied; however, one should extract the blood by means of venesection.
In the event of a headache arising from pitta, one should perform venesection on the patient after he has been treated with oleation.
In the case of Sūryāvarta, however,
cold applications as ointments for the head and face, affusions, purificatory measures, and enemas should be employed;
furthermore, milk and ghee boiled with the drugs of the Jīvanīya group should be used for drinking and as nasal drops.
This same procedure should be performed for blood-born fever as well, after first rejecting the use of conch-shell;
however, in cases of burning pain caused by phlegm, one should induce vomiting with pungent substances mixed with aged ghee.

Sudation, medicinal pastes, nasal drops, and other treatments using dry, sharp, and hot medicines are recommended here; furthermore, fasting is advised, and one should employ a mixed regimen when the humors are combined.
24.14c–d In this case, fasting is recommended; blood should be administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*), by which the parasites become unconscious.
Intoxicated by the smell of blood, they emerge through the nostrils and the mouth. 24.15 //
If [the parasites] emerge from the nose or the mouth,
one should then perform their expulsion by means of very sharp nasal medication (nasya) and medicated smoke (dhūma).
[The preparation for this consists of] viḍaṅga, svarjikā, dantī, and hiṅgu, boiled with cow's urine.
The oils of *kaṭuka*, *nimba*, *iṅgudī*, and *pīlu* used individually as nasal drops, or [the oil] processed with goat’s urine as a nasal drop, conquers worms; it is the supreme worm-conqueror. (17)
24.17c–d One should administer a nasal drop (nasya) of goat’s urine processed with [the aforementioned drugs] and smoke therapy using medicinal substances combined with putrid fish.
Because the blood has been consumed by parasites, one should not extract the blood in this case. 24.18ab/18//
A rotten fish, having killed worms due to its foul odor, [is used] for diseases born of wind (vāta).
In cases of tremors caused by wind (vāta) accompanied by heat, one should apply the procedure for burning [the head] except when there is no burning sensation;
this should be employed in the case of *upaśīrṣaka* occurring after a new birth.
One should apply the treatment for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) once suppuration has occurred; for an abscess (vidradhi), the procedures prescribed therein are indicated.
For inflammatory swellings (piṭikā) and tumors (arbuda), whether immature or suppurated, one should act according to what is appropriate for each.
In the case of *arūṃṣikā*, after blood has been extracted by leeches, the area should be sprinkled with neem water,
smeared with abundant salt, and then plastered with the juice of horse dung.
Or with well-ground pastes of *paṭola* and *nimba* leaves together with *haridrā*, or even with the dregs of cow's urine that have been fermented, along with the feathers of a cock.
Or Kuṣṭha roasted in a skull and powdered, combined with oil, as an ointment for the head destroys itching, discharge, burning, and pain. (23)
An oil prepared with *mālatī*, *citraka*, *aśvaghna*, and *naktamāla* is for anointing the head when it is afflicted by *cācā*, *arūṃṣika*, or when it has been scraped with a razor. (24)
24.24ab: In cases of oil massage (abhyaṅga) or shaving with a razor, if there is no relief, one should strive for the purification of the head through emesis and other such means. 24.24cd:
In the case of Daruṇaka, one should venesect the vessel at the forehead and practice cleansing massages.
One should administer nasal drops, a head enema, and an external ointment made with honey along with priyāla seeds, madhuka, kuṣṭha, māṣa, and mustard.
Nasal drops (nāvana), head-enema (mūrdha-vasti), and likewise enemas (vasti) prepared with lac, śamyāka leaves, iḍagaja, and emblic myrobalan fruits;
as well as washing with water containing the alkali of koradūṣa and grass, are beneficial. // 27 //

Washing with water is beneficial in Indra-lupta; having pierced a vein near the affected area, one should apply a thick plaster of kasīsa, manohvā, tutthaka, and koṣaṇa after dusting it [with powder]. 24.27–28.

24.28bv After venesection, one should apply a plaster made from the *vanya* and *amaratara* trees, or likewise with the roots and fruits of *guñjā*, or with the roots of *lāṅgalikā*, or with the juice of *karavīra*. // 29 //

Or with *kuṭannaṭa* and *maru*, or with *dhānyāka* and *amarataru*, along with honey; or with the juice of small eggplants (*kṣudravārtāka*), or with the juice of *dhattūra* leaves, or with the juice of *bhallātaka*. // 30 //
24.30 With honey and *kṣudra-bṛhatī*, or with the fruit of *bhallātaka*;
or else with honey, clarified butter, sesame flowers, and *trikaṇṭaka*—ink made from elephant tusk smeared with oil is the supreme medicine for *ācāma*. 31.

Or else, ink is the supreme medicine for the emergence of white hair; likewise, ink produced from the horn of a ram [is used]. One should avoid sprinkling with water until the hair has fully grown out.
As long as the hair has not yet grown back, and while the regrowth of hair persists— even in cases of baldness,
graying, wrinkles, or yellowish hair— one should treat the condition with nasal medication, facial and head massage, and medicinal ointments. (24.32–33)
The ascetic should administer as nasal drops oil prepared with the *bṛhaty-ādi* group and the *jīvanīya* drugs;
or, while subsisting on milk, he should administer for a month oil extracted from *nimba*.
The seeds of śelū, akṣa, tila, and rāmā, processed with the fresh juices of nīlī, śirīṣa, koraṇṭa, and bhṛṅga, [should be used] in an amount equal to kākāṇḍakī. // 35 //
Having ground iron with goat’s milk and smeared it [with the paste], when heated by the rays of the sun,
the oil that drips from it, when consumed with milk and used as an errhine (nasya), brings an end to graying hair.
Having ground iron [powder] with goat’s milk, one should heat it with the rays of the sun; then, from that milk, along with *sahacara*, *bhṛṅgaraja*, and the juice of *saurasa*,
one *kuḍava* of oil should be prepared by boiling with four *prasthas* of these ingredients, supplemented by one *pala* of *yaṣṭī*.
From milk, from *sahacara*, from *bhṛṅga*,
from silver,
and from the juice of *saurasa*.

Or, while seated on a stone seat, with [the medicine] placed in a vessel or in the horn of a ram, one should administer a nasal drop consisting of *dugdhikā* and *karavīraka*, finely ground together with milk. (38)

24.38ab Nasal medication (nasya) should be administered using a vessel made of stone or produced from rock; having extracted the hair-whitening agent (palita), it should be applied to the site that removes gray hair.
[The ingredients are: milk, *priyāla*, *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice), the group of vitalizing drugs (*jīvanīya-gaṇa*), and sesame seeds.
A black paste is beneficial for the face, as are turmeric, hair, and folds of skin; likewise, sesame seeds, āmalaka, lotus filaments, madhuka, and honey [are beneficial]. 40.
24.40b–41 This mixture, beneficial for removing tawny hair and wrinkles, nourishes and dyes the hair when applied as a paste to the head:
spikenard (māṃsī), costus (kuṣṭha), black sesame seeds, śārivā, and blue water-lily (utpala).
One should nourish and dye the hair on the head by applying this as an ointment;
honey and [substances] ground with milk are supreme for the growth of hair.
Iron filings, *bhṛṅgaraja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and black earth [are also used]. (24.41–42)
One month’s standing of *palita* with its roots in sugarcane juice will turn it white;
likewise, gruels left for three days in *māṣa*, *kodrava*, or fermented grain-water [will have the same effect]. (43)
24.43c–d A paste made from *yava*, *kodrava*, and fermented grain (*dhānyāmla*),
combined with iron filings and a large amount of white [pigment], will dye even a crane white.
24.44 With *prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, *pippalī*, *candana*, and *utpala*...
24.44a Crushed iron and abundant kuṣṭha; 24.44a crushed iron and abundant fermented vinegar (śuktā); 24.44a crushed iron with abundant fermented vinegar;
24.44a crushed iron with abundant white [substance] and fermented vinegar.

Cook this oil, which contains *bhṛṅgaraja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), blue lotus (*utpala*), *sārī*, iron filings, and cow dung; it removes terrible ailments and makes the hair, even when shaved, thick and firm. (44.1+1)

Oil prepared with the juice of *dhātrī* and combined with copper filings and cow dung, when used as nasal drops (*nasya*) and for massage (*abhyañjana*), destroys all diseases of the head and grey hair when practiced regularly. (24.44.1+1bv–45)
Clarified butter boiled with madhūka, yaṣṭī, kṛmijit, viśva, and bhṛṅga, when administered as nasal drops (nasya) by pouring six drops into each nostril, removes all diseases of the head. 45+1.

That nasal medication (nasya) known as *ṣaḍbindu* should be prepared by cooking a combination (*yamaka*) of the exudates of *varī* and *jīvanti* with milk, along with the *jīvanīya* drugs. This nasal medication conquers all diseases of the upper body and the regions above the clavicles.
One should cook ghee with the milky exudations of *varī* and *jīvanti*, along with milk;
or one should cook ghee with milk and the feathers, bile, intestines, feet, feces, and beak of a peacock, excluding these parts.
Combined with three palas each of the ten roots, balā, rāsnā, and madhuka. // 47 //

Having boiled three *pala* of *madhuka* together with water until it is free from scum and has reached the consistency of *tuṇḍa*, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with an equal amount of milk in that [decoction], using the sweet medicinal substances as a paste; this conquers all diseases of the upper body and the head. (24.47b–d)
That [decoction] should be administered through drinking, enemas, massages, and nasal drops;
with this very decoction, one should cook one prastha of ghee.
With milk four times the quantity [of the paste], and with one-karṣa portions of these pastes—
jīvantī, triphalā, medā, mṛdvīkā, ṛddhi, and parūṣaka— [one should prepare the medicine].
With samaṅgā, cavikā, bhārgī, kāśmarī, and karkaṭāhvaya;
with ātmaguptā, mahāmedā, the tops of tāla and kharjūra fruits; (51)
With tāla, kharjūra, and mustaka;
with mṛṇāla, bisa, kharjūra, yaṣṭīmadhuka, and jīvaka;
and with śatāvarī, vidārī, ikṣu, the two types of bṛhatī, and the two types of śārivā.
With pairs of bṛhatī and śrāvaṇī;
with mūrvā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, ṛṣabhaka, śṛṅgāṭaka, and kaseruka;
and with rāsnā, sthirā, tāmalakī, sūkṣmailā, śaṭhī, and pauṣkara.

This formulation known as Madhukākṣoṭa-vātāma-mahāmāyūra is superior to the Māyūra in its qualities;
it cures the loss of bodily tissues, sensory faculties, and voice, as well as dyspnea, cough, and facial paralysis.
In cases of defects in the female reproductive tract, blood, or semen, this is recommended as it bestows sons upon barren women;
one should prepare it with rats, cocks, swans, and rabbits. (56)
24.56c–57. By means of rats, crabs, and swans, two hundred and thirty-one diseases located above the clavicle have been explained in detail, each distinct from the others.
The seers know the Puruṣa as having two hundred and thirty-one roots above and branches below;
therefore, one should very swiftly conquer diseases by striking at their root.
One should be diligent in protecting that head by which all the sense-faculties and by which the vital breaths are supported in this body. (59)
A paste of blue lotus, along with utpala, kuṣṭha, pippalī, madhuka, śatāhvā, and ginger, applied as an ointment to the head, brings about the immediate destruction of head diseases. (59+1)
In the Uttarasthāna:

A wound is of two kinds, distinguished as endogenous (nija) and exogenous (āgantuka), further divided into those that are vitiated (duṣṭa) and those that are pure (śuddha). The endogenous arises from the bodily humors (doṣas), while the exogenous is born from external causes. (1)
25.1d An "adventitious" [element] is one governed by external causes, while a "pure" [element] is one not so governed;
it may be characterized by being covered or uncovered, or by hardness or softness. // 2 //
Hardness or softness as well, excessive protrusion or subsidence, excessive heat or excessive cold,
redness, paleness, blackness, and the discharge of putrid pus; (3)
Covered with putrid flesh, veins, and sinews, it has a wide opening and intense pain;
it is afflicted by complications such as inflammation, burning, swelling, and itching. (4)
One should recognize the appearance of a malignant ulcer by its long duration;
it is of fifteen types according to the humors, including blood, among which that caused by wind (māruta) is as follows: // 5 //
25.5c–d. When [the ulcer] is afflicted by the five types of *doṣas* separately, it becomes respectively dark-brown, black, reddish, or resembling ashes, pigeon-colored, or bone;
its thin and scanty discharge is like whey, meat-juice, dregs of boiled rice, or water.
Or else, it resembles the bone of a pigeon;
it is fleshless, characterized by pricking and splitting pains, dry, and crackles with a *caṭacaṭā* sound.
Arising quickly due to bile (*pitta*), it becomes yellow, blue, tawny, or reddish-brown. // 7 //
25.7cv Due to Pitta, [the ulcer] has the luster of fire, is yellow, and resembles urine, the ash-water of the *kiṃśuka* flower, or oil; it exudes heat and flows profusely.
It possesses a pain like that of a wound sprinkled with alkali, and is characterized by redness, heat, and suppuration. // 8 //
Due to *kapha*, it is pale, itchy, characterized by a profuse discharge of thick white matter, has thick lips, is hard, covered with a network of ligaments and veins, and is slightly painful. (9)
Red as a coral, it should discharge blood-stained pus; its odor is like that of a horse's stall, and it is accompanied by the symptoms of the Pitta humor. (10)
25.10b It may discharge pus mixed with blood; 25.10c its odor is like that of a stallion’s stall.
One should recognize [the condition] through the combination of two, three, or all [of these signs], due to the mixture of symptoms.
The tongue is lustrous, soft, and smooth; the lips have darkish eruptions and are even. // 11 //
25.11 A wound that has dark lips, is free of pustules, even or slightly elevated in the center, and is clean and without complications [is healing].
Skin, muscle, vessels, ligaments, joints, and bones are the locations where wounds reside. 12.
The visceral cavity (koṣṭha) and the vital points (marman)—these eight [locations] are increasingly difficult to treat.
A wound is easily curable when the patient possesses integrity of mind, flesh, digestive fire, youth, and strength. (13)
25.13–14: A wound occurring in those endowed with youth and strength that is circular, elongated, triangular, or quadrangular;
likewise one located in the buttocks, anus, penis, lips, the region between the shoulders, the mouth, or the cheeks [is difficult to heal].

25.14dv–25.15ab: A [fistula] arising on the back, the chest, the face, or the cheeks is curable with difficulty; likewise those occurring in the eyes, teeth, nose, outer corners of the eyes, the navel, the raphe (sevanī), the abdomen, the ears, the sides, the armpits, or the breasts.

Bhagaṇḍara is characterized by the discharge of foam, pus, and wind; it is accompanied by piercing pain, emits an upward odor, has an internal opening, and is likewise situated in the pelvic bone. // 16 //

The ulcers of those suffering from skin diseases, those afflicted by poisons, those with consumption, and those with honey-like diabetes are cured only with great difficulty; as are those who have ulcer upon ulcer. (17)
25.17 Furthermore, those whose ulcers do not heal while they suffer from erysipelas, fever, diarrhea, or cough;
those who are thirsty, sleepless, dyspneic, or have undigested food (avipāka)— [their ulcers likewise do not heal].
25.18c–d For those who are thirsty or drowsy, or when the cranial bone is split open and the brain matter is visible;
due to the moistening of the sinews, the cutting of the vessels, the depth [of the wound], or being devoured by worms. 25.19.

Due to the breaking of bone, due to the presence of a foreign body, due to the presence of poison, due to unexpected trauma, due to improper bandaging, due to excessive lubrication, due to dryness, and due to the rubbing of hair and so forth. // 20 //
Due to agitation, impurity of the digestive tract, over-satiety, excessive emaciation, drinking liquor, sleeping during the day, sexual intercourse, and staying awake at night; // 21 //
25.21c–d A wound does not heal—even if it is curable—due to the drinking of intoxicants, sleeping during the day, or improper treatment.

[It is incurable] when its interior resembles the color of a pigeon and is devoid of moisture. 25.22ab [A wound is incurable] when its interior is devoid of moisture and resembles the color of a pigeon.
Even if it is curable, it does not heal;

however, when it becomes firm and covered with pustules, one should declare that it is healing. Now, during this stage of swelling, purification should be applied according to the proximity [of the affected part]. (25.22–23)
For those who have been purified, swellings accompanied by firm, pustular eruptions will quickly subside, as will the ulcer; therefore,
one should constantly apply cooling treatments during the stage of swelling.
25.24cv One should, however, apply cooling treatments; for by that, the aggravated dosas and the digestive fire (agnidoṣa) are suddenly pacified like a fire [extinguished by water].
This applies in cases of swelling, ulcers, or when the area is hard, discolored, and accompanied by pain. // 25 //
In cases of poisoning specifically involving water-born substances, one should extract the blood;
once the vitiated blood has been removed, there is an immediate subsiding of swelling, redness, and pain. (26)
One should extract the blood with leeches and other means;

and after the blood has been repeatedly removed, one should apply very cold applications—both in touch and potency—that are extremely smooth and ground on that same day, using milk, sugarcane juice, or liquid extracts. // 27 //

25.27dv A poultice made from milk, sugarcane juice, and their own expressed juices, combined with ghee washed a hundred times and other non-drying substances, applied repeatedly in the reverse direction (pratiloma) is beneficial; as are affusions and massages prepared with those same ingredients.
An external application made from the bark of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *vetasa*, and copious quantities of ghee is the supreme means for cooling and subduing swelling. (29)
25.29c–d A poultice and abundant ghee [are indicated] for swellings and even such ulcers that are dominated by Vāta, are stiff, hard, extremely painful, and have had their blood drained. 30.

Fomentation with soups of marshy animals, vesavāra, and similar preparations is beneficial; furthermore, sesame seeds that have been fried and then quenched in milk, ground into a paste, remove burning sensations and pain. (31)
Having anointed stable swellings with mild pain with unctuous substances that alleviate vāta and kapha,
and having fomented them, one should apply [pressure] very gradually using a bamboo tube.
One should massage [the area] with the palm or the thumb for the purpose of softening it;
then one should apply an ointment made of barley, wheat, and mung beans that have been cooked and ground into a paste.
One should apply a paste made from proven, ground ingredients; or one should apply a proven, ground paste; or one should apply a paste ground with milk.
If it does not dissolve in this way, then one should apply a poultice (upanāhana).
Likewise, one who is unskilled attains peace, while one who is skilled attains maturation.
A bolus made of kola, sesame, and wool, mixed with curd, sour gruel, parched grain flour (saktu),
fermenting agent (kiṇva), kuṣṭha, and salt, and applied while lukewarm, is recommended for poulticing (upanāhana).

When a well-cooked, consolidated swelling has been sufficiently compressed with pressure, a bolus made of jujube fruits (*kola*), sesame, dried meat (*vallūra*), sour curd, and parched grain flour (*saktu*) is desired for the purpose of incision in a case where incision is required, even in one who is very delicate. (25.35–36)
Guggulu, linseed, go-danta, svarṇakṣīrī, pigeon dung, alkalis, medicinal herbs, and various salts effect the bursting open of a suppurated swelling. (37)

25.37c–d For abscesses containing pus, having narrow openings, elevated margins, or located even in vital spots (marmans), one should apply alkaline medicines and alkali itself, pressing them from all sides with non-unctuous squeezing agents. 25.38 //

One should observe with equanimity if the medicinal paste dries while under pressure; furthermore, one should not apply it to the opening of the vessel, for in that way the morbid humor (doṣa) would overflow.
Kalāya, barley, wheat, māṣa, mudga, and hareṇu beans; and for substances that are slimy, the application of barks and roots as a press-juice [is recommended]. 40.

25.40cv For substances that are slimy, or for the seven [procedures] beginning with washing, the two groups starting with *surasā* and *āragvadha* should be employed in cases of severely corrupted ulcers, as well as in urinary disorders (*meha*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and wounds. 41.

Alternatively, the decoction used for washing is derived from the leaves of *paṭolī* and *nimba*; however, if [the area] is not yet purified, it should be derived from the bark of the *nyagrodha* group of trees once it has been purified. 42.
Alternatively, for washing,
a decoction of *paṭolī*, sesame, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, the two types of *niśā*,
and *nimba* leaves is used; and an ointment consisting of these along with *paṭu* (rock salt) purifies the ulcer.

25.43–44. A sharp physician should cleanse wounds by means of a suppository (varti) made from *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *lāṅgalī*, honey, and rock salt (*saindhava*); this should be used for cleansing narrow-mouthed wounds located in joints or vital spots (*marma*).
One should fumigate those afflicted by wind (vāta), who are subject to outflows (sāsrava) and suffer from intense pain,
with barley, clarified butter, birch bark, madana, śrīveṣṭaka, and surāhvaya.
One should thoroughly pacify deep ulcers aggravated by pitta, rakta, and poison with very cold treatments; however, in an ulcer that is dry or has little flesh, elevation (utsādana) is beneficial.
One should eat the flesh of carnivorous animals, prepared according to the prescribed ritual, along with nyagrodha, padmaka, and the others, as well as aśvagandhā, balā, and sesame seeds. 47.
25.47dv Prepared and applied; 25.47dv prepared and administered. For one of pure mind, meat increases by means of the meat-eater’s meat.
It is a desiccant for wounds with protruding, soft flesh. // 48 //

25.48b–d. For those [ulcers] that have increased, possess pure luster, are elevated with flesh, hard, itchy, and long-standing, [one should treat them] with nutmeg buds, ferrous sulfate (kāsīsa), realgar (manohvā), orpiment (haritāla), and sal-ammoniac (purāgnika).
One should cleanse with alkaline therapy those wounds that are very difficult to purify, as well as those discharging urine caused by urinary stones and others that discharge blood. (50)
One should treat with alkaline therapy (kṣāra-karman) ulcers that are extremely difficult to cure,
as well as other types of wounds, severed joints, and those for which the prescribed purifying treatments have been applied.
Those who are being purified but do not become pure should be purified by means of the fire-rite.
25.51b Those which do not succeed when treated with the aforementioned therapeutic measures, 25.51c those conditions that remain incurable [by other means],
25.51d should be treated with the application of fire (cauterization).
25.51d Those [conditions] are curable by means of fire-treatment.
The planting of pure [tissues] should be applied for the purpose of healing that which has been described as causing excision;
[the drugs used are] aśvagandhā, ruhā, lodhra, kaṭphala, and madhuyaṣṭikā.
25.52ab For the healing of clean wounds, *samaṅgā* and *dhātakī* flowers are to be employed; they are the supreme healers of ulcers.
[They are indicated] for those from which putrid flesh has been removed, for those where flesh remains, and for those that do not heal. 53ab.
A paste of sesame seeds combined with madhuka should effect wound healing;
being unctuous, hot, bitter, sweet, and astringent, it conquers all [types of wounds]. (54)
One should apply a paste for the purpose of healing;
this paste, consisting of sesame seeds combined with *madhuka*, along with astringent decoctions, is a conqueror of all [wounds].
Combined with honey and nimba leaves, it is a supreme purifier;
combined with the two previously mentioned substances and ghee, it acts as a rapid healer.
When properly applied, it is an excellent purifier; when properly applied, it may also be a healer.
Experts in this field recommend a paste of barley as being like sesame for wounds that are accompanied by blood, pitta, poison, or exogenous trauma, and which are deep-seated and inflamed.
One should heal [wounds] with clarified butter (ājya) boiled with milk, healing herbs, and astringents;
for those born of phlegm (kapha) and wind (vāta), one should use oil prepared with healing herbs.
Powdered *kācchī*, *lodhra*, *abhayā*, *sarja*, *sindūra*, *añjana*, and *tutthaka*, combined with oil and *madana* seeds, is an excellent healing agent for wound closure. (58)
A powder of equal parts of kākṣī, lodhra, abhayā, and sarjarasa—[the bark] of trees with firm flesh and thick bark—is recommended;
[likewise, a powder] derived from kakubha, udumbara, aśvattha, jambu, kaṭphala, and lodhra. (59)
For wounds located in the skin, a powder is prescribed; wounds dusted with these skin-powders [heal].
[The powder is made] from lac, realgar, mañjiṣṭhā, yellow orpiment, and the two types of turmeric.
When dusted with the powder of *tvak*, the wound quickly contracts its skin.
An ointment consisting of that same powder mixed with clarified butter and honey is supreme for purifying the skin.
[This is prepared] with *kālīyaka*, *latāmrā*, bone, gold, *kālā*, and the best of juices (*rasottama*). (25.60–61)
An application of elephant tusk burnt without smoke, along with ghee, honey, cow dung juice, and *rasāñjana*, is an excellent application for restoring the natural skin color. (25.61–62)

It becomes a hair-restorer of the same color as the skin. A plaster consisting of oil, *rasāñjana*, and soot produced from the four [types of animals], nails, hair, bones, skin, horns, and hooves, when saturated with oil, likewise produces hair. (25.62–63)
For one suffering from a wound, one should prescribe the wholesome and unwholesome foods as stated in the section on surgical procedures (*śastra-karma*).
The two groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*) and the wind-subduing (*vātaghna*) group are beneficial for those with a predominance of *vāta*. (64)

25.64ab Regarding those with wounds, one should prescribe what has been stated concerning the surgical procedure (śastra-karma) and what is wholesome or unwholesome; 25.64cd likewise, [the formulations] beginning with Nyagrodha and Padmaka are for when Pitta is vitiated. 65ab The Āragvadha group destroys Kapha and is used in cases of Kapha; however, in cases arising from a combination of humors, mixed [formulations] should be used. 65cd–66ab [The physician] should apply these according to the specific condition, whether it be a single humor, a combination, or a complication. 66cd–67ab One should administer them by means of enemas, nasal drops, or as a paste, or even as food and drink, according to the requirements. 67cd–68ab By this method, the physician should treat all types of wounds, whether caused by trauma, disease, or poison, until they are healed. 68cd–69ab One should avoid excessive heat, cold, and wind, as well as heavy foods, physical exertion, and sexual intercourse. 69cd–70ab By following this regimen, the patient shall quickly attain freedom from disease and regain his former strength and complexion. 70cd–71ab Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wounds," in the Section on Therapeutics of the *Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā*, composed by Vāgbhaṭa. 71cd–72ab Now, we shall explain the chapter on the treatment of hemorrhoids, which is the twenty-sixth in the Section on Therapeutics. 72cd–73ab Hemorrhoids are said to be of five types: three arising from the humors, one from blood, and one exogenous. They are located in the rectum, which consists of three folds. 73cd–74ab The first fold is for the passage of feces, the second for urine and semen, and the third is the opening of the anus. 74cd–75ab When the channels of the rectum are obstructed by the vitiated humors, they become thickened and protrude like the ears of a boar; these are known as hemorrhoids. 75cd–76ab They are called arśas because they do not leave their place, nor do they move elsewhere, nor do they perish. 76cd–77ab They are named after the boar because they resemble its ears, and they are called hemorrhoids because they cause bleeding. 77cd–78ab They are classified as external, internal, or both, and are further divided into two groups: those that are curable and those that are incurable. 78cd–79ab Those located
