in the first fold are curable, while those in the second and third folds are difficult to cure and incurable respectively. 79cd–80ab When they are small, soft, and not causing much pain, they are curable; otherwise, they are considered incurable. 80cd–81ab When they are accompanied by complications such as fistula-in-ano, prolapse, or obstruction, they are incurable. 81cd–82ab When they are located in the rectum, they are called internal, and when they protrude outside, they are called external. 82cd–83ab When both types are present, they are called mixed; these are the classifications of hemorrhoids. 83cd–84ab Now, listen to the symptoms of each type according to the specific humor involved. 84cd–85ab When Vāta is predominant, the hemorrhoids are blackish-brown, rough, and painful, and they protrude and retract frequently. 85cd–86ab When Pitta is predominant, they are red or yellowish-red, hot, and cause burning and bleeding. 86cd–87ab When Kapha is predominant, they are white or pale, heavy, itchy, and grow slowly. 87cd–88ab When blood is predominant, they are red and bleed profusely, resembling the color of a fresh lotus. 88cd–89ab When all three humors are combined, the symptoms are mixed, and the disease is very severe and difficult to treat. 89cd–90ab One should recognize the exogenous type as being caused by trauma or parasites, appearing as a fleshy growth. 90cd–91ab Now, listen to the general premonitory symptoms of hemorrhoids. 91cd–92ab A sense of fullness in the abdomen, heaviness in the thighs, and weakness in the waist and back are the early signs. 92cd–93ab Flatulence, constipation, and a feeling of incomplete evacuation are also present. 93cd–94ab When the hemorrhoids are provoked, there is pain in the rectum, anus, and bladder, and a discharge of mucus and blood. 94cd–95ab One should avoid heavy, oily, and cold foods, as well as physical strain and suppression of natural urges. 95cd–96ab For the treatment of hemorrhoids, one should employ mild purgatives, enemas, and bloodletting as required. 96cd–97ab The use of medicinal pastes, fumigations, and ointments is also recommended. 97cd–98ab One should encourage the patient to eat light, dry, and warm foods, and to practice gentle exercise. 98cd–99ab By following this regimen, the hemorrhoids will gradually subside, and the patient will regain his health. 99cd–100ab Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Hemorrhoids," in the Section on Therapeutics of the *Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā*, composed by Vāgbhaṭa. 100cd–101ab Now, we shall explain the chapter on the treatment of abdominal enlargements, which is the twenty-seventh in the Section on Therapeutics. 101cd–102ab Abdominal enlargement is of seven types: six arising from the humors and one exogenous. It is caused by the accumulation of wind, bile, phlegm, or their combinations. 102cd–103ab When the digestive fire is weak and the channels are obstructed, the humors accumulate in the abdomen and cause swelling. 103cd–104ab The patient suffers from pain, distension, and a lack of appetite, and the abdomen becomes hard and enlarged. 104cd–105ab One should avoid fatty foods, heavy meals, and physical exertion. 105cd–106ab For the treatment of abdominal enlargement, one should employ fasting, purgation, and the administration of medicinal oils. 106cd–107ab Fomentation, massage, and the use of medicinal pastes are also beneficial. 107cd–108ab One should encourage the patient to eat light, easily digestible foods, and to practice gentle walking. 108cd–109ab By following this regimen, the abdominal enlargement will gradually diminish, and the patient will regain his strength. 109cd–110ab Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Abdominal Enlargement," in the Section on Therapeutics of the *Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā*, composed by Vāgbhaṭa. 110cd–111ab Now, we shall explain the chapter on the treatment of urinary disorders, which is the twenty-eighth in the Section on Therapeutics. 111cd–112ab Urinary disorders are of eight types: six arising from the humors, one from blood, and one exogenous. They are caused by the vitiation of the urine. 112cd–113ab When the urine is vitiated by Vāta, the patient passes it with difficulty, and it is frothy and scanty. 113cd–114ab When Pitta is predominant, the urine is yellow or red, hot, and causes a burning sensation. 114cd–115ab When Kapha is predominant, the urine is white or turbid, and the patient feels a sense of heaviness. 115cd–116ab When blood is predominant, the urine is red and resembles the color of blood. 116cd–117ab When all three humors are combined, the symptoms are mixed, and the disease is very severe. 117cd–118ab One should avoid salty, sour, and pungent foods, as well as alcohol and physical strain. 118cd–119ab For the treatment of urinary disorders, one should employ diuretics, purgatives, and the administration of medicinal oils. 119cd–120ab Fomentation, massage, and the use of medicinal pastes are also beneficial. 120

In cases of kapha or those arising from a combination of doshas, these [medicines] should be used mixed with kapha-subduing agents. With these, one should employ seven treatments— irrigation, ointment, medicated ghee, oil, *rasakriyā*,
powder, and suppository— applied to the ulcer as appropriate.
25.66ab By means of these, treatments consisting of washes, ointments, ghee, oils, and meat broths [are prepared].
67a Jātī, nimba, paṭola leaves, kaṭukā, dārvī, niśā, and śārivā—
—With mañjiṣṭhā, abhayā, siktha, tuttha, madhuka, and combined with the seeds of naktāhva. // 67b //

Clarified butter should be prepared with mañjiṣṭhā, abhayā, siktha, tuttha, madhuka, and the seeds of naktāhva; by this, those [diseases] that have reached the vital points (marmans), which are characterized by minute openings and excessive moisture, are cured.
Clarified butter prepared with this [decoction] heals ulcers that have small openings,
are located in vital parts (marmans), are exuding, moist, deep-seated, painful, and spreading; such wounds become purified and heal.
Deep wounds accompanied by pain and sinus tracts are purified and heal when treated with oil prepared in four times the quantity of *kākamācī* juice.
This is highly beneficial for healing even those wounds that possess sinus tracts. (67.67)
25.67+1 Even among those who follow various destinies, the Uttara-sthāna is superior;
for those wounds that suddenly arise from injury are [treated] therein.
Even though they are infinite, that limb is said to be possessed of eight aspects. // 1 //
Rubbed, excised, severed, hanging, fallen, pierced, split, and crushed; among these, "rubbed" refers to that which has been smeared with lymph. (2)
26.2bv–It may be hanging down or drooping, or it may be accompanied by a trace of blood; after being cut, it may ooze with a burning sensation.
Furthermore, it may be deeply incised, severed, or even torn apart. (3)
That which hangs down when the remaining bones have fallen away from the body is called *pātita*;
however, that which is pierced by a fine arrow-head (*sūkṣma-aśalya*) but excludes the internal cavities (*koṣṭha*) is called *viddha*. // 4 //

26.4 One [body] has long bones hanging down with some remaining; another is shattered, crushed, and drenched in marrow and blood; through the trauma of blows and crushing, it has become broadened along with its bones. // 5 //
26.5cv Due to injuries, trauma, or accidents resulting from blows and pressure, one should immediately irrigate those fresh wounds with Yaṣṭyāhva (liquorice) ghee,
or again with lukewarm Balā oil for intense pain. // 6 //

For the purpose of suppressing the heat of the injury and for that which has spread at that time, applications (lepa) and other treatments that are astringent, cold, sweet, and unctuous are beneficial. (7)
In the case of long, fresh wounds,
one should especially employ honey and ghee for the purpose of healing, as well as cooling treatments that subdue pitta.
26.8cv One should administer honey and clarified butter in cases accompanied by swelling; purification (śodhana) via the upper and lower tracts should be performed.
Fasting is beneficial, as is a light meal, and the continuous bloodletting [of blood]. 9 //
26.9cv Fasting is beneficial in that case; this regimen is especially desired when [the tooth] is bruised or fractured.
For from those two, very little blood flows, and by that means suppuration arises quickly. // 10 //
Blood flows excessively, except in cases of injury;
then, due to the loss of blood, the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated, causing extreme pain.
26.11 He vomits blood excessively, and generally elsewhere than from a wound.

One should administer the drinking of fats, affusion, sudation, ointments, and poultices prepared with Vata-alleviating drugs, as well as an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) prepared with Vata-alleviating herbs. 26.12

One should administer an unctuous enema prepared with Vata-alleviating drugs. This regimen, beneficial for fresh wounds, is prescribed for a period of seven days; once the force [of the disease] has subsided after seven days, one should follow the previously mentioned procedure. // 13 //
26.13 Thus has been described the seven-day regimen; generally, this common procedure will now be explained separately.
Having quickly suppressed the pain in a rubbed wound, one should apply medicinal powders. 26.14
In the case of a wound that has been incised, for those that are severed or hanging, one should perform suturing according to the prescribed method, followed by bandaging and compression. (15)
26.15cd–16: A ruptured eye that is not torn apart, though it has been quickly bound and compressed, and which hangs down,
the physician should replace in its proper position, ensuring the vessels are not dislocated.

26.16b–d. However, that which is protruding and hangs down, the physician, having repositioned it into its proper place, should pierce the vein with a needle and press it with the hand shielded by a lotus petal.
Then, for him, clarified butter (havis) is beneficial for sprinkling, nasal administration, and satiation.

26.17–18. The sacrificial oblation (havis) prepared with goat’s milk and boiled with liquorice (yaṣṭyāhva), jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, and blue lotus (utpala), when used as a saturating enema (tarpaṇa), is supreme;
for it indeed conquers all injuries to the eyes.
When the eyes are impaired by pressure on the throat, one should perform vomiting, coughing, or sneezing;
or else, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) or apply the same treatment as for an injured eye. (19)
If the eye is depressed, there is pain in the throat; if it is displaced from its site and sutured, there may be vomiting, nausea, and sneezing.
If the ear is displaced, one should fill the canal with oil.
If the nape of the neck (kṛkāṭikā) is severed, even if the wind (māruta) is escaping, [it should be treated].

26.20 If the ear has fallen from its place, it should be sutured; having inserted it evenly, one should fill the canal with oil, bind it after suturing it quickly and without gaps, and in this case, irrigation with goat's ghee is recommended. 26.21.

Having positioned it evenly, one should bind it; there, with goat-ghee, the patient should eat his food while lying on his back and remain well-restrained. [This applies when] a fracture in the branches is oblique, or when it is properly positioned within the trunk. (26.21–22)
Having sewn it with a vellita-bandha stitch, one should bind it with a thick cloth;
when the wound has healed, a goṣ-phaṇā-bandha should be applied using leather.
When a wound has reached the shoulder [of the scrotum],

the following should be done: having sprinkled the feet and the eyes with water for one whose testicles are hanging down, one should draw the testicles inward and suture them with a stitch known as *tunna*.
The suturing should be performed with a thread combined with cotton, and a "cow-horn" bandage (goṣphaṇā-bandha) should be applied by wrapping a cloth around the waist.
One should not apply an oil-pouring irrigation (sneha-seka) there, for the wound would otherwise become moist. // 25 //
For in that [condition], the ulcers indeed become moistened; therefore, the ulcers are dried by means of *kālānusārya*, *aguru*, *elā*, *jātī*, *candana*, and *parpaṭa*.
Oil prepared with *śilā*, *dārvī*, *amṛtā*, and *tuttha* is also a healing agent for closing the wounds.

Having completely cauterized the severed stump with oil mixed with *jātī*, sandalwood, and *padmaka* according to the proper method, one should bind it with a *kośa-bandha* (tube-like bandage) and thereafter treat it like an ordinary wound. // 27 //

26.27b–28. After cauterizing with oil according to the prescribed methods, the procedure for a pierced wound from which the foreign body has been extracted, or for one that has been crushed or split open, should be performed. Once the foreign body has been removed from the head, one should insert a wick made of hair.
If the brain matter (mastuluṅga) flows out, he becomes enraged and may kill him; otherwise, if it is unstable, he will die.
As the wound heals, one should gradually remove the hair, one strand at a time. 29.
26.29 When the brain matter has flowed out, one who is enraged should eat the brains of other living beings.
Once the foreign body has been removed from the limb, one should have a wick of unctuous substance inserted into another part of the body. 30.
Those wounds which are deeply seated, narrow-mouthed, and have bled, one should irrigate with *cakrataila* administered through a fine nozzle. 31.
When the visceral cavity is ruptured and filled with blood, there is fainting, pain in the heart and flanks, fever, burning sensation, thirst, flatulence, and a lack of desire for food. (32)
There is obstruction of feces, urine, and flatus; dyspnea, perspiration, and redness of the eyes;
a metallic taste in the mouth, and a foul odor in the body. (33)
When blood is located in the stomach, one may even vomit blood;
moreover, one is torn apart by excessive flatulence and piercing pain. (34)
And it perishes by means of colic; furthermore, it is distinguished by colic.
When blood is located in the colon (pakvāśaya), there will be pain and heaviness;
below the navel there will be coldness, and the discharge of blood from the orifices.
Even though the underlying intention is undivided, it is filled by subtle streams, just as the bladder on its side is filled by flowing blood and urine. (36)
In that regard, one should avoid a dog that has blood in its mouth, whose feet, breath, and face are cold, whose eyes are red, whose face is pale, and which is bloated.

If [the doshas] are located in the stomach (āmāśaya), emesis is beneficial; if they have reached the large intestine (pakvāśaya), purgation and non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) with non-unctuous, hot cleansing agents are indicated. (38)
26.38b–d: When [the disease] resides in the colon (pakvāśaya),
purification with ununctuous, warm decoctions of barley, jujube, and horse gram— devoid of fats— is beneficial.
One should eat food or drink gruel mixed with rock salt. // 39 //
One whose blood has flowed excessively should drink [blood] mixed with rock salt; however, one with a perforated abdomen (bhinna-koṣṭha) should drink blood.
The perforation of the abdomen is known to be of two kinds, distinguished by whether the intestines are merely distressed (kliṣṭa) or severed (chinna). // 40 //
But when blood has flowed out excessively, due to the rupture of moistened or severed intestines,
or the rupture of adherent or cut intestines,
fainting and other symptoms are slight in the first case, whereas in the second they are extremely distressing.
A person whose intestines are defiled or who is filled with doubt does not live once their intestines have been severed. // 41 //

26.41c–d: A person whose intestines are moistened, or whose intestines are afflicted, or whose intestines are adhered, is in a state of uncertainty regarding survival; one whose intestines are ruptured does not live at all.
He whose feces, urine, and flatus pass according to their respective paths will undoubtedly survive even when the abdominal cavity is ruptured, provided he is free from other complications. (42)
The intestine, when not torn, having emerged, may be reinserted; it should not be done otherwise.
However, some say that even if it has been seized by the head of a *utpaṅgila* [fish], it may be so treated. 43.
26.43cv seized by Urogala-śirograsta; 26.43cv seized by Uroṅgila-śirograsta; 26.43cv seized by Pupuṅgala-śirograsta;
26.43cv seized by Vayaṅgila-śirograsta.
Having washed the [wound] smeared with grass, blood, and dust with milk,
and having trimmed his nails, he should slowly insert it [the instrument], lubricated with ghee.
One should moisten the dried [powder] with milk, saturate it abundantly with ghee, touch the throat with a finger, and even cause a sensation of shock with water. (45)
Likewise, the intestines enter within and cause pain at that time;
however, due to the minuteness of the wound or because of their great number, the intestine may not enter the abdominal cavity.
26.46b–c. At that time, one should press [the abdomen] with a force equal to that [of the extraction]; having opened the belly, one should insert [the intestine].
Once the intestine is properly positioned in its place, one should sew up the wound. 47.

26.47cv When [the blood] has been properly positioned in its place, that provoked [wind], having departed from its site, takes away life; one should then wrap it with a bandage and sprinkle it with ghee. 48.
Having joined together the severed part and the vital tissue that has become inflamed with the aforementioned powders soaked in honey and ghee,
one should then apply a medicinal pad and bandage it in successive layers.
Then, for the sake of mild treatment and to facilitate the downward movement of feces and flatus, one should have the patient drink lukewarm milk mixed with *citrā*-oil. (49)
Then, one should have him drink lukewarm milk mixed with *citrataila*.
Furthermore, he should maintain the prescribed bandaging of the wound for one year.
A wick that has emerged from the abdomen due to fat should be removed with ash or clay.

26.50b–c. Having applied the aforementioned bandaging of the wound, or having covered it with smooth roots decocted in astringent liquids, the skillful physician should then bind it firmly with a thread and increase [the size of the plug]. 51.
Then, at the base, one should apply smooth powders evenly; thereafter, with a sharp instrument heated by fire, one should cut it in a single stroke.
Otherwise, there may be pain, flatulence, or death as the vessel is being severed.
When the wound has been bound with honey and the food is well digested, one should drink ghee, or milk boiled with sugar, citrā, lac, and gokṣuraka. (53)
When the wound has been bound with honey, one who has well digested his food should drink ghee;
this is the supreme method for conquering pain and burning, as previously described, along with liquorice (*yaṣṭyāhva*).
For a fatty tumor (*medo-granthi*), the oil prescribed therein is beneficial for massage.

26.54c–55. Furthermore, for a tumor arising from fat (*medo-granthi*), one should use *tālīśa*, *padmaka*, *māṃsī*, *hareṇu*, *aguru*, *candana*, the two types of *haridrā*, lotus seeds (*padma-bīja*), *uśīra*, and *madhuka*; with these [one should prepare the treatment].
This oil, prescribed for acute wounds when they have healed, is the best for promoting healing;
it is also used for those struck by hidden blows, those who have fallen from great heights, and those injured by uneven falls. (56)
26.56c–57. For one struck by a blow from a confused assailant, one should administer treatments that conquer Vāta and blood (Rakta), such as satiation, massage, and anointing.
This applies to those whose bodies are dislocated, who are crushed, emaciated, or struck in a vital spot (marman). One who is thus struck is considered "slain" (hatam).

26.57ab One should indeed perform the massage, oil-enema, and purification prescribed for vātarakta; 26.57cd [one should treat] one who is emaciated, struck in a vital spot (marman), or severely injured.
One should cause him to dwell in a vat filled with oil while he consumes meat broth.
In the Uttarasthāna:
Fractures of the bones are of two kinds—those involving the joints and those not involving the joints—caused by falls, blows, and the like.
When the joints are dislocated, there is an inability to extend or contract [the limb]. // 1 //
27.1b–c: Fracture of the bone may occur at a joint or away from a joint; in the other case (fracture away from a joint), there is intense swelling and excessive pain in all stages.
There is a lack of power even when performing a slight effort, and there is a sensation of pain accompanied by sound. // 2 //

27.2b–c: "In all circumstances, one who suffers excessive pain is thus characterized by defeat (*bhaṅga*); however, that defeat is divided in many ways according to its specific distinctions. The means for establishing each of these [types] is as follows. (3)
It will be taught in such a way that it may be of practical use:
namely, how a bone, though composed of many subtle particles, produces sound upon being touched. (4)
27.4cv That bone which is extensively fissured, where a fragment of bone has entered the middle of the split bone,
and that which is fractured by trauma with only a small portion remaining; // 5 //

27.5 A fracture caused by trauma, or one that rises up when pressed, or one that sinks into the marrow like a wound— these are difficult to cure, even for those who are emaciated, weak, afflicted with vāta, or eat little. (6)
One should avoid a fracture where the pelvic bone is split, dislocated from its joint, displaced, crushed toward the pubic region, or comminuted. (7)
27.7ab When the skull at the waist is fractured, when the frontal bone is disjointed, and likewise when it is crushed;
and when there is a fracture of the temples, the head, the back, or between the breasts. (8)
Even a bone that has been correctly restrained may undergo transformation due to improper placement, faulty binding, or even agitation; therefore, one should avoid such [a bone]. // 9 //
27.9dv One should avoid from the very beginning any deformity, as well as anything that is poorly formed, whether it be a bone or even a joint;
young bones are crushed, while the long tubular bones (nalaka) are broken. 10.
27.10c–d: Young bones are bent, and the long bones (nalaka) are broken;

the cranial plates (kapāla) are split, while others mostly burst open. Then, that which is depressed should be raised, and that which is elevated should be pressed down. 27.11ab: [The physician] should apply traction to what is sunken and compression to what is protruding.
The skull bones are split;
one should pull [the head] back when it is excessively thrust forward, and turn it upward when it has gone downward.
By means of pulling, pressing, lifting, contracting the skin, and binding— // 12 //

27.12 He should pull tight all the joints of the body situated below, whether they are displaced or not, and whether they are moving or stationary; having thus properly stabilized [the body] with these means of stabilization so that it is motionless— 13.
Having properly stabilized them so they are motionless,
one should then wrap them comfortably with strips of cloth soaked in abundant ghee,
using [leaves] derived from the *kadamba*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, and *palāśa* trees.
Or with bamboo tubes— whether broad or slender, well-positioned, very smooth, provided with supports, or even made of bark or wood-shavings.
27.15c–v One should apply a uniform bandage over the cloth with very smooth *kuśa*-grass splints provided with supports;
for with a loose bandage, stability of the joint does not arise.
27.16 If stability of the joint does not arise, there occurs intense pain along with the onset of burning, suppuration, and swelling.
One should release the bandage every three days during the rainy season and summer, but after seven days in winter. // 17 //

27.17ab However, in cases where there is intense pain or a burning sensation common to both, one should sprinkle [the area] with a cold decoction of the *nyagrodhādi* group after five days, or according to the requirements of the fracture. // 18 //

Or, depending on the nature of the aggravated *doṣas* in the fracture, the wise physician should apply *cakrataila*, either lukewarm or with milk boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūla*), to alleviate the pain. (27.18–19)
27.19 One should apply a lukewarm decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla), combined with wind-alleviating (vātaghna) herbs, after considering the specific location and time; furthermore,
one should continuously administer very cold affusions and plasters.

Having considered the place and time, one who has suffered a fracture should drink every morning, cooled and mixed with lac, the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time, prepared with Vata-alleviating drugs, along with clarified butter and sweet medicinal herbs. (27.20–21)

In the case of a fracture accompanied by an ulcer, the ulcer should first be treated with astringent decoctions (kaṣāya) mixed with honey and ghee; thereafter, the remaining procedure as prescribed for fractures should be followed.
27.22c–d Or, having cauterized with astringent decoctions those hanging pieces of flesh from the wound and having smeared them with honey and ghee,
the physician should join the wounds together and apply bandages. 23.
Having recognized that they have become even and well-settled, one should dust them with the powdered fruits of *phalinī*, *lodhra*, and *kaṭphala*, combined with *samaṅgā* and *dhātakī*. (24)
Or, with the powders of dhātakī and lodhra, wounds heal quickly; thus has the treatment for fractures been described for one of stable constitution during the winter season. (25)
In one who is well-nourished and has few humors (doṣas), [the disease] is easily curable; otherwise, it is difficult.
It is [increased] by one, two, or three times [the normal intensity] respectively for those in the first, middle, and final stages of life. // 26 //

27.26b–c. Otherwise, even for one who is easy to treat, the joint may become stiff within months; therefore, for those following the prescribed regimen, stability of the joint will occur. For fractures of the hips, calves, or thighs, lying on a door-slab (kaṭāha-śayana) is beneficial. // 27 //
27.27b–d. For one who observes the prescribed regimen for the purpose of restraint, five binding pegs (kīla) should be applied:
two each on the sides of the calves and thighs, and one peg on the sole. 28.
Whether in the hips, the spinal column, the chest, or likewise the collarbones, one should apply this same procedure for fractures of dislocated joints during the process of healing. (29)

One should apply this procedure to the chest, the shoulders, as well as the face and the eye-sockets; furthermore, one should treat joints that have been dislocated for a long time by first making them supple through oleation and sudation.
By means of the prescribed methods and through one's own intelligence, one should lead [the disciple] to their respective station.
When joints that have been dislocated for a long time, or those that have healed improperly due to uneven treatment, are set using the prescribed methods and with skillful technique,
they may be restored. However,
in the case of a fracture where the joint has not healed properly or has been treated with excessive force, [it remains difficult].
Having crushed it, one should restrain the fracture; thereafter, one should treat it as in the case of a fracture.

27.31 When a fracture has healed without union, or when it has been treated with harsh remedies for a displaced fracture, the physician should strive to ensure that the fracture does not undergo suppuration. A joint whose flesh, vessels, and ligaments have suppurated does not attain firm adhesion.
27.32 Just as a fracture does not reach suppuration, one should administer the oleation therapies prescribed for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) to the patient with a fracture;
one should employ the four modes of administration, strengthening tonics, and practice the procedure of enema (bastikarma).

One should treat a fracture with nourishing, non-burning substances such as rice, clarified butter, meat broth, milk, and the like, administered in the proper measure to ensure the firm union of the joints. (34)
Illness is not recommended for him, for it causes the joints to become dislocated. (35ab)
Salt, pungent, alkaline, sour, sexual intercourse, and sunlight. // 35cd //
One should avoid physical exertion, as well as broken or dry food. // 35ef //
One should soak seven nights of black sesame seeds, free from dust and bound in a firm cloth, in water;
then, spreading them out, one should dry them daily in milk and likewise in water boiled with *madhuka*. (36)
One should dry them day after day by rubbing them with these [medicines], and having clearly distinguished them again, one should thoroughly dry those who have drunk milk as before.
Having removed the husks and freed them from dust, one should grind them well and employ the fine powder [in the preparation]. // 37 //

Having crushed them, one should employ the powders along with *nalada*, *vālaka*, red *yaṣṭikā*, *nakha*, *miśī*, *plava*, *kuṣṭha*, the three types of *balā*, *aguru*, *kuṅkuma*, *candana*, *sārivā*, *sarala*, *sarjarasa*, and *amaradāru*.
Then, one should press that sesame paste together with the *padmakādi* group of substances and all fragrant medicinal herbs, using milk that has been processed with them. (39)

Then, one should cook that oil with sesame paste and [the following ingredients]: śaileya, rāsnā, aṃśumatī, kaseru, kālānusārī, nata, pattra, lodhra, along with kṣīraśukla, milk, dūrvā, and the drugs beginning with nalada.
27.40cv With bark and milk, or with *dūrvā* grass and milk; 27.40cv with milk and *dūrvā* grass;
27.40cv with milk and *dūrvā* grass.

This supreme fragrant oil, which brings stability to the bones, quickly conquers even the most potent disorders born of wind and bile, whether they are localized or systemic, through various modes of application. 41.
27.41cv Even those [diseases] born of vāta and pitta that are extremely virulent and pervasive, through various applications, [are cured]. 27.41dv —
Uttarasthāna.
By riding on the backs of elephants and horses, by sitting in hard and elevated postures, and by practicing other factors declared to be the causes of hemorrhoids (arśas). //1//

28.1bv–2ab: By sitting on hard or uneven seats, by the sight of undesirable things, by the ripening of past karma, or immediately upon being censured by the virtuous, there generally appears first a pustule, either one finger-width or two finger-widths in size. // 2 //

Due to the ripening of undesirable or even desired karma, there may arise an ulcer (vraṇa) in the anus, either internal or external, characterized by corrupted blood and flesh; because it is situated near the bladder and the receptacle of urine, it is of a discharging nature. // 3 //
An ulcer within or without the anus is *bhagaṃdara*; it tears apart everything in one who fails to take action, as the genitals, bladder, and rectum are torn by numerous [channels]. (28.3)
That is *bhagaṇḍara* (fistula-in-ano), and it is of all [types]. Through its minute openings, it gradually discharges flatus, urine, feces, and semen.
It is known to be caused by the *doṣas* individually, in combination, or by all together; the eighth is considered to be of traumatic origin (*āgantuka*). //5//
The eighth is known as the accidental (āgantuka).

They say that when it is unripe, it is called a pustule (piṭikā), but when it has reached suppuration, it is a fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara)—one with deep-seated roots, accompanied by swelling, abundant pain, and prone to recurring inflammation. // 6 //
One should recognize a carbuncle that causes fistula as such, and not otherwise;
in that case, it is dark-red and causes pricking, tearing, throbbing, and pain. (7)
The swelling arises from wind or bile, elevated like the neck of a camel;
it is reddish, thin, rich in heat, and accompanied by the smoky fumes of fever. // 8 //
28.8cv The [eruption] born of phlegm (kapha) is reddish, thin, subtle, stable, glossy, deeply rooted, pale, and itchy;
that born of wind and bile (vāta-pitta) is dusky-brown or copper-colored, accompanied by burning and heat, and characterized by severe pain. // 9 //
28.9cv A [boil] that is dark-brownish copper-colored, accompanied by burning and pain, pale with a slight dark tint, and difficult to suppurate arises from kapha and vāta;
one equal in size to the big toe, caused by all three doṣas, involves various kinds of pain. // 10 //

Afflicted by colic, loss of appetite, thirst, burning sensations, fever, and vomiting, these [diseases], when they become suppurated through negligence, turn into ulcers; among them, those born of Vata are as follows: 11.
It is gradually filled with minute-mouthed apertures like a hundred-pored sponge, constantly discharging a clear, frothy exudation. (12)

It is torn by small-mouthed openings like the mouths of a hundred *paunaka* insects; this is known as *śatapauṇaka*. However, that which resembles the neck of a camel (*uṣṭragrīva*) arises from bile (*pitta*).
That which exudes much slimy discharge (*picchā*) is a case of *parisrāvin* arising from phlegm (*kapha*).
From the combination of wind and bile, a circular path arises that encircles the anus;
it forms a perimeter all around, like a rampart with its surrounding moat. (14)
28.14d–15. Furthermore, when the rectum is straight like a rampart or a moat, it may be torn by a straight course [of the disease] due to wind and phlegm;
however, when phlegm and bile are provoked, they do so by resorting to the pre-existing hemorrhoids (dur-nāma).

28.15bv Through the passage [of the fetus], the rectum is torn; 28.15cv As for phlegm and bile, the previously mentioned symptoms occur at the base of the hemorrhoids, followed by swelling accompanied by itching, burning, and so forth.
It quickly becomes suppurated and burst open, moistening the root of his hemorrhoid.
This hemorrhoid, known as *śambūkāvarta*, arises from all three humors; it resembles a conch-shell spiral and constantly discharges [pus] through various openings. (17)
In this [state], the channels tear the anus with their terrible forceful pains when fragments of bone, swallowed out of greed for flesh, reach the rectum. (18)
As it exits obliquely from the wound, its course becomes deviant; consequently, when the flesh has burst open with pus, it moves through that putrid matter. (19)
28.19 When it exits transversely, it causes pain; then, when the anus has been torn by pus, worms are born there, which eat around the rectum.
They tear it apart before long, and that [disease] becomes a hemorrhoidal ulcer with its course diverted from the natural path.
Worms are born from them; that [type] arising from injury follows an upward path.
One should recognize pain, burning, itching, and other symptoms in these [worm-infested ulcers] according to the prohibitions regarding wounds.
Among those six types which are difficult to cure, one should abandon the two arising from the combination of humors and from injury.
28.21 One should recognize [the condition] by its differentiation from other ulcers;
it has reached the *pravāhiṇī* fold or is supported by the *sevanī*.
Then, one should treat this very pustule with great care. 22.

Just as [a wound] does not undergo suppuration through cleansing, the application of blood-letting, irrigation, and so forth, but when it has reached suppuration, it is treated with oleation, fomentation, and immersion baths. (23)
Having restrained it as if treating hemorrhoids, one should examine the fistula-in-ano correctly—whether it is directed inward or outward, or whether its opening is internal or external. (24)
Having sought it out whether it is directed downward, upward, or inward, one should properly incise it with a surgical instrument;
then, once it is turned outward, one should treat it completely with an alkaline solution.
Or, like a physician [cauterizing] the neck of a camel with fire or caustic, one should make incisions at intervals of one finger-breadth and cut open the *śatapona* [vessel]. (26)

In the case of *śataponaka*, one should make an incision by leaving a single interval between the channels; once those have healed, the remaining ones [should be treated], for otherwise death occurs when the anus is ruptured.
In the case of *parikṣepin* as well, it is the same, using alkaline threads (*kṣārasūtra*) as described for the channels. // 27 //

In cases of hemorrhoids (arśas) and fistula-in-ano (bhagandara), one should first treat the hemorrhoids; once they have been abandoned [by healing], the wound-born [fistula] should be treated. Then, for those with a foreign body (śalya), the foreign body must first be removed. (28)
28.28 One should apply medicinal pastes to the hemorrhoids, extract them, and likewise administer anti-parasitic ointments and food.
Fomentations such as *piṇḍa-sveda* and *nāḍī-sveda*, when well-oleated, are highly esteemed for pain. // 29 //
One should extract [the material] in that manner and likewise apply it; one should extract it and likewise apply it.
In all cases, where there are many perforations, one should join them after examining the cuts.
The *go-tīrtha*, the *sarvatobhadra*, the *dala*, the *lāṅgala*, and the *lāṅgala* [arrangements]. // 30 //
28.30 In all cases, when the incision is made with the instrument directed toward the side on a surface with many openings, it is considered a *gotīrthaka*.
When the incision is made on all sides, it is a *sarvatobhadra*; when the incision is on the side, it is an *ardhalāṅgala*.

With a blade applied to the sides, one should cauterize with fire both the *lāṅgalaka* [sinus] on both sides and all the channels of discharge (*āsrāvamārga*) completely; thus, it will not recur again. (28.31–32)

28.32c–d The physician should strive to clear the channels of discharge completely and to purify the internal cavity; from time to time, an ointment consisting of the paste of *triphalā* mixed with the juice of cat-bone (*biḍālāsthi*) should be applied to the ulcer. 28.33.
One should strive for the purification of the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha-śuddhi). For the thorough cleansing of the internal organs (koṣṭha-saṃśuddhi),
one should employ a preparation made from the juice and paste of triphalā,
combined with jyotiṣmatī, malaya, lāṅgalī, śelu, pāṭhā, kumbhāgni, sarja, karavīra, vacā, sudhā, and arka.
One should cook this oil for the purpose of massage; they say it is most beneficial for those suffering from fistula-in-ano. (34)
They say that oil prepared with *kumbhī*, *agni*, *sarjī*, *karavīra*, *vacā*, *sudhā*, and *arka* is supremely beneficial; likewise,
this same [oil] is excellent when combined with *madhuka*, *lodhra*, *kaṇā*, *truṭi*, *reṇukā*, the two types of *rajanī*, *phalinī*, *paṭu*, and *śārivā*.
Kamala, kesara, padmaka, dhātakī, madana, sarjarasa, āmaya, and rodikā. // 35 //
Oil cooked with these— madana, sarja, rasāñjana, and lodhra, along with the leaves of bījapūra—
cures fistula-in-ano, scrofula, skin diseases, diabetes, and ulcers.

Viḍaṅga essence, triphalā, māgadhikā, and kaṇā, when licked together with honey and oil, act as healers for worms, skin diseases, fistula-in-ano, urinary disorders, wounds, sinus tracts, and ulcers. // 37 //
Triphalā, māgadhikā, and uṣaṇā, when licked,
promote the healing of wounds, sinus tracts, and ulcers.
Amṛtā, truṭi, vella, vatsaka, kali, pathyā, āmalaka, and guggulu [likewise act as healers].
This honey, gradually increased in dose and melted [with other ingredients], conquers boils, enlargement of the scrotum, and fistula-in-ano. // 38 //
This [mixture], increased in stages, saturated with honey, combined with *māgadhikā*, *agni*, *kaliṅga*, and *viḍaṅga*, along with *bilva* and *ghṛta*, six *pala*s each of *varā*,
and an equal amount of *guggulu*, when taken with honey, destroys all diseases. (28.38–39)
With *māgadhikā*, *agni*, *kaliṅga*, and *viḍaṅga* each equal in measure to the ghee,
along with six *pala* of *varā*;
there should be five *pala* of *guggulu*, and one *pala* each of *māgadhikā* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) separately.
Taken with a karṣa of powdered cinnamon bark and licked with honey, it destroys skin diseases, fistula-in-ano, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids. (40)
That same [medicinal substance], well-impregnated with the powder of ginger and with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), especially overcomes diseases of wind (vāta). 41.

One who habitually consumes the dust produced from the heartwood of the finest khadira tree, processed with the juice of aśana, along with equal parts of mahiṣākṣa and honey, destroys skin diseases, urinary disorders, pustules, and fistulas. (42)
One should practice [the regimen] with honey processed with fire and water, or processed with *āsana* and water.
This honey, equal in measure to the substance known as *mahiṣa*, destroys fistulas (*bhagaṇdara*).
This specific [remedy] has been stated; however, the remaining [remedies] are for the preparation of side dishes (*vyañjana*).
Having correctly understood [the treatment] through the section on wounds and by means of repeated study, one should apply the appropriate remedy. // 43 //
Having correctly understood the medicinal treatment, one should administer it. Once the wound has healed,
one should avoid riding on horseback, suppressing natural urges, alcohol, sexual intercourse, indigestion, unwholesome food,
and various forms of rash behavior for a year or even longer.
One should avoid [these] for a year and more.
In the Uttarasthāna, it is stated:
"The humors (malāḥ), when dominated by phlegm (kapha), affect the fat, flesh, and blood."
That swelling which is round and elevated is known as a *granthi* (node), so called because of its knotted nature. // 1 //
29.1d That [swelling] is called a *granthi* (knot) because of its knotted nature.
There are nine types arising from the humors (*doṣa*), blood, muscle, fat, bone, vessels, and wounds.
Among them, the one caused by Vāta is accompanied by stretching, pricking, and splitting sensations, and is blackish in color. // 2 //
Moving from one place to another without cause, characterized by sudden loss and increase, it is like an unbound bladder that, when burst, flows with clear blood. (3)
From pitta, it is accompanied by burning, appears yellow or red, and suppurates quickly; when burst, it exudes warm blood. From kapha, it is painless and thick. (4)
When the blood is vitiated by the humors (doṣas) while living beings are fainting, there arises a cold, flesh-colored, itchy swelling; when suppurated, it discharges thick pus. // 5 //
Relying upon the vessels and the flesh, accompanied by numbness and characterized by pitta, it brings about a tumor (granthi) when the flesh is corrupted by fleshy foods. (6)
It is glossy, large, hard, bound with veins, and has the appearance of phlegm;
when increased by fatty tissues, it is carried into the fat, the flesh, or the skin. (7)
The Vāyu produces a knot that is very unctuous, soft, and mobile;
it has a shape similar to phlegm (śleṣman) and its appearance waxes and wanes according to the body's depletion and nourishment. (8)
When it is fractured, it exudes a thick fat that is coppery, black, or white;
however, that which has become elevated or depressed due to a fracture of the bone or a traumatic blow [is treated differently]. // 9 //
29.9 When that [abscess] is ruptured, it discharges thick fat, pus, and copper-colored or black fluid.
Due to a fracture of the bone or a traumatic injury,
or from a pedestrian suddenly plunging into water, there occurs a bony swelling (asthi-granthi).
Or, from one who is exhausted by physical exertion, the network of vessels along with the blood [is affected]. // 10 //
The Vayu, by compressing, contracting, bending, and drying [the tissues], produces a painless, motionless knot; that is called Siraja-granthi. // 11 //

When the wound has not yet healed or has only just begun to heal, if the patient consumes all kinds of [heavy] foods, or if the body is still moist or lacks a bandage, or if it has been struck by a stone, the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated and causes contraction. // 29.11ab–12a //
When Vata dries up blood that is unflowing, corrupted, and clotted within a wound, it produces a painful, itching swelling; this is known as *vraṇagranthi*. (13)

29.13 When the aggravated *vāyu*, having quickly reached a wound located at a vital point (*marman*), [causes it to become incurable]; those [tumors] born of the *doṣas*, blood, or fat are curable, but not those that are thick, rough, mobile, located in vital points, the throat, or the abdomen; furthermore, a large tumor arising from a glandular swelling is called an *arbuda*.

29.14b–d: But those that are thick, rough, and mobile are not [granthi]; rather, a large, knotted growth is an *arbuda*. It has the same characteristics as that [granthi], but it is of six types according to the humors (*doṣa*) and other factors; because it is generally abundant in fat and phlegm (*kapha*), and because of its firmness, it does not suppurate. 15.
The morbid humor (doṣa), having contracted and compressed the blood located within the vessels, causes it to suppurate; that mass of flesh becomes swollen and discharging. (16)
Having contracted [the wound] and pressed it from behind,
or having contracted it and pressed it within,
it becomes a mass of flesh accompanied by discharge.
Covered with sprouts of flesh, it grows rapidly and then exudes a great quantity of foul blood constantly; that is a *śoṇitār-buda* (blood-tumor). // 17 //
29.17b–d. Once increased, it then flows out quickly; among those [types], the two born of blood and flesh should be rejected, while the other four should be treated.
Those [fistulas] dominated by phlegm (kapha) extend downward into the groin, thighs, and other parts of the lower body.
The humors (doṣas), having reached the flesh and blood, gradually take hold of the feet over time and produce a dense swelling; that is designated as ślīpada.
29.19 That is called *ślīpada* (elephantiasis); it is characterized by cracking, is black, painful without apparent cause, and rough due to *vāta*.
From *pitta*, however, it is yellow, accompanied by burning sensations and fever.
Elephantiasis (ślīpada) caused by vāta is dry;
that caused by pitta is accompanied by burning and fever;
and that caused by kapha is heavy, unctuous, painless, and large, covered with sprouts of flesh.
One should discard that which has passed a year, even if it is very large and well-permeated by moisture. // 21 //
29.21b–d. Some, however, say that when it is greatly covered with sprouts of flesh on the hands, nose, lips, and ears, it is called *ślīpada*, just as it occurs on the feet;
and this disease arises most intensely in marshy regions (*anūpa*).
29.22b–c. Others, however, say that the impurities located in the fat, situated in the feet, throat, neck, eyes, armpits, and groins,
form growths similar in color to the fat, which are hard, glossy, and shaped like eggplants or myrobalans.
29.23–24. Those located in the fat tissue produce many deep-seated swellings in the throat, neck, and eyes that take a long time to suppurate.
Some of these suppurate with little pain, others discharge [pus], and still others are excessively itchy.
Some suppurate with little pain, others discharge pus and are extremely itchy; some disappear, while others persist for a long time.
This condition, known as Gaṇḍamālā or Apacī, fluctuates in its decline and growth like the dūrvā grass.

One should abandon that [treatment] in cases accompanied by fever, vomiting, pain in the flanks, cough, and rhinitis; likewise when there is no suppuration of the swelling, or when the ulcer is subject to unwholesome practices. (26)

29.26–27. In a wound, pus belonging to one who consumes unwholesome food enters deep into the muscle and other tissues and spreads far away. Because it travels a great distance, that condition is called *nāḍī* (a sinus); it is so named because it flows like a channel (*nāḍī*). It is characterized by pain in the flanks, dyspnea, and catarrh.
The channel of others is not straight; that very same [channel] is the path that has many courses.
It is [disturbed] by humors (doṣas) located separately or together, and the fifth cause is a foreign body (śalya). 28.
29.28c–d Due to the doshas individually or combined, [the fistula] caused by vata is painful, has a narrow opening, is discolored, and ejects frothy matter;
it flows excessively at night. That caused by pitta produces thirst, fever, and burning sensations. // 29 //
Flowing with yellow, warm, putrid, and pus-like secretions, it exudes excessively during the day;
due to phlegm (kapha), it is thick, slimy, oozing, itchy, and hard. (30)

If the discharge is yellow, hot, putrid, and pus-like, or if there is yellow, hot, putrid, and pus-like tearing, and if there is excessive moisture at night, one should abandon the patient when all these signs appear together in every form. (29.30)
One should extract a foreign body located within by all these means, for if it remains unextracted, it produces a sinus and causes its discharge.
It forms a sinus and discharges from it pus that is mixed with foam, thin, scanty, warm, bloody, and constantly painful.

29.31. In cases of undigested (āmaja) swellings at the joints, one should apply a thin, clear, warm decoction mixed with foam; the treatment should be carried out according to the specific requirements, as in the case of general swelling.
With ghee prepared from *bṛhatī*, *citraka*, *vyāghrī*, and *kaṇā*. // 1 //
One who desires purification should apply oleation; for one who has been purified, an ointment with sharp [medicines] should be applied.
Having repeatedly fomented the glandular swelling, one should massage it again and again. // 2 //

This is specifically the procedure for [hemorrhoids] born of wind; however, in those born of pitta and blood, leeches and all cooling measures are used, while in those born of phlegm, the regimen for wind is applied. // 3 //
Nevertheless, having excised this while it is still unripe, one should cauterize it with fire once the bleeding has ceased;
for it is better to remove it entirely, as that which remains will certainly grow back again.
Furthermore, it swells up quickly; one should treat the two nodules arising from a flesh-wound in this very same manner.
This same procedure should also be performed for a tumor born of fat, using heated fruits and other such items.
In this very manner, one should incise [the swelling] and likewise rub it with oil smeared over a double layer of cloth;
or, having incised it with a surgical instrument once the fat has been thoroughly extracted, one should cauterize it.

One should cleanse [the area] with oil smeared with sesame seeds; once the fat has been removed, one should cauterize a newly formed vascular knot (sirā-granthi). Furthermore, *sāhacara* oil should be drunk, as well as poultices made with drugs that subdue Vāta, enema therapy (vasti-karma), and venesection (sirā-vyadha). //7//

In the case of arbuda, one should treat it like a granthi, which is highly beneficial according to its specific nature; in the case of ślīpada born of vāta, one should perform venesection after the area has been lubricated, fomented, and treated with poultices.
With goat dung, the root of *śigru*, lac, *surasa*, and sour gruel. // 8.1+(1)ab //
Covered with a thick mass of leaves from the *upodakā* plant, mixed with lac-juice and fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*), or with salt, alkali, and *kāñjika*.
Having applied [the paste], one should bind it with a cloth; thus, the *navārbuda* ulcer is indeed pacified.

30.8.1+(2) av [It is] covered with *upodaka*, *arka*, oil-cakes (*piṇyāka*), and *arka*-leaves (*arka-cchada*); thickly coated when old with *arka*-leaves, lime (*sudhā*), sea salt (*sāmudra*), molasses (*guḍa*), and sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
A small ball bound within the secret place dissolves knots and tumors.
Having bound a basket [filled] with equal parts of aged and fresh *arka* leaves, lime, and sea salt, and having covered it with water, one should place it inside.
Having bound the *piṇḍikā* with secret applications,
[there is] the dissolution of knots and tumors.
And one should have him drink castor oil produced from *eraṇḍa*, combined with cow's urine, for one month, after having opened a vein two finger-breadths above the ankle. (9)
When the [previous] food has been digested, one should eat old food accompanied by milk boiled with dry ginger;
or one should drink the *traivṛta* [ghee]; if there is still no relief, one should cauterize with fire.
In the case of Pitta-type [fever], venesection should be performed below the ankle, and all Pitta-alleviating measures should be employed.
In the case of Kapha-type [fever], one should pierce the vein at the big toe and habitually consume barley.
One should apply astringent decoctions mixed with honey, as well as *vardhamāna* and *abhayā*,
or else smear the area with the roots of mustard and eggplant, or with *dhanvayāsa*.

For the purification of the upper and lower tracts, one should drink a decoction prepared from the roots of *dhānyaka* or *yavānī*; likewise, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) processed with *dantī*, *dravantī*, *trivṛtā*, *jālinī*, and *devadālī* is effective for *apacī*. (30.12–13)
One should employ smoking, gargling, and nasal drops that destroy phlegm and fat;
one should let blood through venesection and drink the urine of a peacock.
By drinking one pala, half a pala, or even one karṣa of the bark of *kāñcanāra* with warm water, one eliminates *gaṇḍamālā*. (14+(1))
One should apply a *karṣa* of unripe tumors with warm water using *nākulī*, *paṭu*, and *nāgara*.
Once they have been fomented, one should massage hard tumors with a pouch of salt.
A paste made by grinding the seeds of śamī, mūlaka, and śigru, along with barley and mustard, with sour gruel and buttermilk, dissolves glandular swellings and goiters. (16)
With seeds from the roots of *śamī*,
radish, and *śigru*,
together with barley and mustard seeds.
Having crushed neem leaves together with prepared marking-nut fruits,
one should burn them in a pair of shallow earthen bowls along with an equal amount of white mustard seeds.
30.16+(1)a With aged neem leaves; 30.16+(1)b together with moist bhallātaka fruits; 30.16+(1)b together with fresh bhallātaka fruits.
This, ground with goat’s urine, is an ointment for *gaṇḍamālā*. // 16+(2)ab //
30.16+(2) One should conquer *gaṇḍamālā* that is oozing blood and about to suppurate by applying medicinal pastes that remove *pitta* and *kapha*.
Those that are not yet suppurated should be extracted and treated with alkali or fire.
With the fruits of *kākādanī*, *lāṅgalikā*, and *nahikottuṇḍikī*;
and with *jīmūtaka* seeds, *karkoṭī*, *viśālā*, and *kṛtavedhana*. (18)
One should cook [the medicine] with half-pala portions of nalikā, uttuṇḍikī, and their fruits, combined with pāṭhā, along with one karṣa of poison.
One prastha of karañja oil [should be cooked] with one āḍhaka of the fresh juice of nirguṇḍī. // 19 //
30.19 When combined with *pathyā* (harītakī) in half-pala portions,
this [mixture] forms a paste that cures long-standing, pus-discharging *gaṇḍa* swellings— even those nearly incurable— through internal consumption, external anointing, and nasal administration.
Oil cooked with a one-fourth part paste of *lāṅgalikī* tubers and four times as much of the juice of *nirguṇḍī* destroys *apacī* when used as nasal drops and other such applications. (21)
When one-fourth part of the paste and four times the amount of water have been added,
[one should cook it] with bhadraśrī, dāru, marica, the two types of haridrā, trivṛt, ghanasāra, manaḥśilā, alaktaka, nalada, viśālā, and karavīraka.
30.22–23. With one *pala* each of *bhadra*, *śrīdāru*, black pepper (*marica*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), alum (*ala*), and *madana*, together with half a *pala* of poison,
ground with cow’s urine and combined with the juice of *brāhmī*, the milk of *arka*, and the liquid from cow dung.

One *prastha* of prepared mustard oil, when consumed through drinking and other means, quickly cures skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), malignant sinus tracts (*duṣṭa-nāḍī*), ulcers, and scrofulous swellings (*apacī*). (24)
30.24c–d: Kuṣṭha, when practiced through drinking and other means, [overcomes] corrupted channels, ulcers, and scrofula (apacī).
30.25: Oil prepared with vacā, harītakī, lākṣā, kaṭurohiṇī, and candana, when drunk, conquers scrofula along with its very root.
The root produced from the *śarapuṅkha* plant, ground with rice-water, conquers malignant skin diseases, scrofula, poisons, and vermin when used as a nasal drop or an ointment. (26)
With the roots of uttamakāraṇī, pīluparṇī, and sahācara; together with lodhra, abhayā, yaṣṭyāhva, śatāhvā, dvīpi, and dāru. // 27 //
Oil prepared with the roots of *uttamavāruṇī* (or *uttaravāruṇī*, or *uttaravāriṇī*) and an equal amount of milk, when used as nasal drops (*nasya*) or for massage (*abhyaṅga*), is highly esteemed.
The hooves of cows, goats, sheep, and horses are burned and applied as an ointment with pungent oil. // 28 //

30.28cv The hooves of a cow, an elephant, or a horse, when burnt with *aiṅguda* resin, or a black snake, or a crow that has died of its own accord— these, when applied to the side or the calf of the other [limb] during a lack of pacification of the disease, [bring relief]. 29.
30.29c–d. If the disease is not pacified, one should remove the fat from the other side—whether situated in the calf or above or below the bladder—and cauterize it with fire.
Having measured the distance from the heel upwards while the patient is standing, one should measure that same distance from the heel [to determine the site]. // 30 //
"Thereafter, one should remove the knots," so said the blessed Nimi. (31ab)
Leaving twelve finger-breadths toward the heel and the indravasti on the other side of the gadā, [one should perform the procedure]. 31cd.
"Having split [the tumor] open like fish-eggs, one should extract the masses from the middle," so says Suśruta (31ef).
Having divided the well-measured body of the being from the ankle to the ear into eight parts, one should divide the smallest part;
others say that one should pierce at the level of the nose, straight down below the "king of gods" (the navel), at a distance of one eye-span.

30.32c–d: Others say that for those with wind disorders (vāta) suitable for poultices, one should incise the nasal septum at its straightness, below the "king of gods" vessel (surarājavasti), to the depth of an eye; once the sinus tract has been properly opened, one should apply an ointment.
With oils prepared from *pratyakpuṣpī* fruits, ground together with rock salt.
For the Pitta-type [toothache], one should use sesame, mañjiṣṭhā, nāgadantī, and the two types of niśā;
for the Kapha-type, sesame, saurāṣṭrī, nikumbha, ariṣṭa, and saindhava.

One should apply a plaster of sesame, honey, and clarified butter to a wound caused by a splinter that has been excised and cleansed; for a wound not caused by a weapon, one should pierce it at the edge with a probe and direct it properly.
One should repeatedly incise the track with a thread soaked in an alkaline solution; this is the treatment for ulcers that are malignant, narrow-mouthed, deep-seated, and so forth. (36)
One should repeatedly fill the passage with wicks or oils; these are also recommended for use in sinus tracts (nāḍī).
Furthermore, the paste of cañcu fruit applied as an ointment is supreme for curing sinus ulcers.

The paste consisting of the bark of the *ghoṇṭā* fruit, salt, lac, the leaf of the *būka* tree, and the milk of a woman, combined with the milks of *snuh* and *arka*, when made into a wick, destroys the sinus in a short time. (38)
The leaf of *cukra* and the milk of a woman; the leaf of *vṛṣa* and the milk of a woman.
Sea salt, *sauvarcala* salt, rock salt, well-ripened *ghoṇṭā* fruit, house-soot, the sprouts of *āmrāta* and *gāyatri*, as well as *kaṭaṅkaṭerī* and *cetakī*. (30.38–39)
When kaṭaṅkaṭerī, ketakī,
and dīnikā are applied as a paste, an ointment, a powder, or a suppository,
fleeting fortune perishes like a lack of progress among the fickle, just as instability vanishes when one is steady.
30.40b–d. While these [medicinal substances] are being used as a suppository (varti),
there arises in the upper part [of the rectum] a swelling that is unctuous, the same color as the skin, knotted, painless, and resembling a mung bean.
A pustule caused by phlegm and wind in children is called ajagallikā. // 1 //
31.1ab Pustules caused by kapha and vāta are glossy, the same color [as the skin], and clustered; 31.1cd they are painless and resemble mung beans (mudga) in size.
31.1d They are painless and resemble mung beans.

Resembling barley, resembling barley, dense and attached to the flesh by those two [channels], mouthless, without pain, circular, containing a little pus, and thickly elevated—[these are the characteristics of alajī]. // 2 //
Resembling barley, shaped like barley, without openings, and circular like an *alajī*, with little pus, thick and elevated—
these five or six swellings are called *kacchapī*, being raised like the shell of a tortoise.
Above or all around the ear, there is a hard pustule accompanied by severe pain. (3)

31.3bv *Kacchapī* is characterized by a swelling shaped like a tortoise; *panasikā* resembles a lotus root (*śālūka*). A firm swelling with little pain arising at the joint of the jaw is called *pāṣāṇagardabha*, which results from those two [preceding conditions]. // 4 //
In young people, there appear painful, dense pustules shaped like the thorns of the silk-cotton tree (*śālmalī*), filled with fat; these two conditions cause the corruption of the face.

31.5dv And from those two [humors], the *mukha-dūṣaka* types are to be known as *padmakaṇṭaka*; by these, which arise from *kapha* and *vāta*, the body is covered with painless, white eruptions resembling the thorns of a lotus. // 6 //
Due to bile, there is a circular swelling resembling a ripe udumbara fruit;
it causes great burning and fever, and its mouth remains wide open. // 7 //
On the limbs and within the mouth, there appear dense pustules, the size of lentils, possessing the same color and name [as the disease], accompanied by burning sensations, fever, and pain. (8)
Then there are even more painful eruptions called visphoṭaka, which cause great agony;
they are pustules shaped like the pericarp of a lotus and covered with many small pustules. (9)
That [eruption], pierced by vāta and pitta, is called gardabhī; it is circular, extensive, elevated, and covered with reddish pustules. (10)
In regions generally near the armpits, due to pitta combined with wind, there arise small, dense pustules resembling parched grain. (11)
31.11–12. Subtle, dense, and resembling a net—such is the one great [fever] known as Gandhanāma.
When the limbs are overwhelmed by heat and sweat, there appear dense, painful pustules.
Those called *rājikā* have the color, shape, and size of a mustard seed;
they spread like erysipelas (*visarpa*) due to the humors, with pitta being predominant and the others diminished. (13)
Jālagaīrbha is characterized by swelling that is unripe (suppurating), thin, and copper-colored, and it causes fever;
in one suffering from fever, eruptions (sphoṭa) arise from the humors with an excess of pitta, which tear through the flesh.
In a fever patient, those [eruptions] that are as hard as flesh, tear the flesh, and arise in the armpits with a brilliance like fire are called Agni-rohiṇī;
they destroy life within five days, seven nights, or a fortnight.
A round, three-fold swelling above the collarbone is called *irivellikā*; one that is as hard as the tuber of the *vidārī* plant occurring in the armpits or groins is *vidārī*. (16)

A glandular swelling (granthi) formed by fat, wind, and phlegm, located in the tendons, flesh, or vessels, when burst, exudes a secretion resembling marrow, ghee, or honey; in that condition, the wind (anila) is predominant. (17)
Having dried the flesh, one should apply a sutured granulation;
then there arise foul-smelling, moist blood and impurities of various colors. (18)
31.18c–d One should recognize that as *śarkarārbuda* (gravel-like tumor) when it discharges foul-smelling, moist blood;
it accumulates on the palms and soles, at the joints, or above the collarbone. 31.19a–b It increases [in size] there.
They cause that [swelling] to drain away while it accumulates above the collarbone; like an anthill, a glandular swelling (granthi) gradually forms with many small openings,
rich in pain, burning, itching, and discharge— this is the Valmika type, arising from all three humors.

Due to the suppression of its natural impulse, the apāna wind, residing in the apāna, makes his internal and external passages narrow;
consequently, his feces [become difficult to pass].
The apāna wind, residing in the apāna, emerges with difficulty; this disease is known as ruddhaguda (obstructed anus).
It causes suppuration from pitta and vāta in the nails and flesh, accompanied by pain and fever.
One should know that [the disease] is *cipya*, as well as *akṣataroga* and *upanakha*. When the nail is black from injury, rough, and harsh, it is called *kunakha*. (24)

31.24 One should know that as *upanakha*; and from contact with foul mud, the spaces between the fingers become afflicted with itching and moisture—this they call *alasa*. Those [spots] resembling sesame seeds are called *tilakālaka*.
Black, painless, and superficial spots like mung beans; those very same [spots] when raised;
and white or black skin-pilings that are even higher than the maṣas. (26)
A lac-jewel (jatumaṇi) of that kind is naturally red;
however, a natural black or white circular mark is considered a flaw (lāñchana). // 27 //
31.27b–c. That [eruption] which is painful and bloody arises from vāta and pitta aggravated by grief, anger, and so forth;
it is a thin, darkish circular patch (maṇḍala) on the face called vyaṅga, while elsewhere on the body it is called nīlikā.
Due to Vāta, it is rough, rough to the touch, mottled, and dark-brown;
due to Pitta, it has copper-colored edges and a bluish center; and due to Kapha, it has white edges and is accompanied by itching.

From pitta it is copper-colored or blue; from kapha it has a white appearance and is itchy; from blood it is red at the edges, coppery in the center, and characterized by a stinging sensation. Driven by vāyu, the phlegm reaches the skin and dries up. (31.29cd–30)
31.30b–d. Then the face tingles, and subsequently the skin gradually becomes pale and insensate; accompanied by slight itching and no exudation, that is prasupti arising from prasupti.

31.31c–d Due to insufficient emesis and the suppression of pitta, śleṣman, and food, there arise circular patches with little itching and little moisture; however, when excessively provoked, they become numerous, intensely itchy, and reddish. 32.
When that *utkoṭha* is persistent, it is designated as *koṭha*.
Thus, these thirty-six minor diseases (*kṣudraroga*) have been described according to their classification. // 33 //
That is utkoṭha, which is a complication;
without understanding it, a physician may become confused in his treatment.
In the Uttarasthāna:
One should drain an unripened *ajagallikā* with leeches;
having fomented a *yavaprakhyā*, one should apply an ointment to dissolve it. // 1 //
With *dāru*, *kuṣṭha*, *manohvāla*, and so on, up to *pāṣāṇa* and *gardabha*, one should apply the procedure;
and once they have suppurated, one should treat them like ulcers, including those accompanied by *ajagallikā*. // 2 //
For a foul-smelling mouth, an ointment of *lodhra*, *kuṣṭhumburu*, and *vacā* should be applied;
or alternatively, fermented coconut water mixed with *vaṭa* sprouts. (3)
32.3 A paste of *lodhra*, *kuṣṭhumburu*, and *vacā* is applied for facial impurities (*mukha-dūṣikā*).
If there is no relief, emesis, nasal medication (*nasya*), and venesection on the forehead should be performed.
For *padma-kaṇṭaka*, one who has vomited using *nimba* water should take [a preparation] prepared with *nimba* water and *padmaka*.
One should drink ghee mixed with honey after applying an ointment of nimba and āragvadha.
One should treat the *vivṛta* and other types ending with *jālagaṇḍa*, as well as *serivellikā*, by applying an ointment of *nimba* and *āragvadha*.
One should treat *irivellikā* like *pitta-visarpa*; likewise, having rejected [the patient] as incurable, one should treat *agni-rohiṇī* in the same manner.

One should always administer fasting, bloodletting, drying therapies, and purification of the body, as well as the application of *dhātrī* and cooling plasters for one suffering from *jālaka-gardabha*. (6)

32.6b–c: One should employ drying therapies (virūkṣaṇa), purgation of the body (kāya-virecana), applications of *dhātrī* paste, and cooling treatments. Once blood has been removed, one should treat it like a phlegm-nodule (*śleṣma-granthi*).
One should perform the procedure for a fatty tumor (*medo-arbuda*), and especially so for a sugar-granule tumor (*śarkarā-arbuda*). // 7 //

One should avoid treating a *valmīka* (anthrax-like swelling) that is extensive, has many openings, is accompanied by swelling, and is located on a vital point (*marman*), as well as those occurring on the hands or feet; however, other types may be treated.
Furthermore, one should avoid the other [type of wound];

however, once pure blood has been removed from it, one should smear it with *paṭu*, *ārevata*, and *amṛta*, along with the roots of *śyāmā* and *kulatthikā*, *dantī*, meat-mince, and roasted grain flour (*saktu*). // 9 //
When cooked with *paṭola*, *āragvadha*, and *amṛtā*, it purifies all corrupted flesh and all [sinus] tracts;
subsequently, one should treat them properly with the scalpel, or with alkali, or with fire. // 10 //
Having excised it completely with a surgical instrument, one should cauterize the callus with oil;
the treatment for a constricted anus should be performed like that for an obstructed stone. 11.
Having extracted it entirely with a surgical instrument and having applied an astringent, one should treat the wound, which has overcome its heat through purification, by means of surgery.
In the same way, one should treat a diseased bad nail and likewise feet that are sluggish.

One should sprinkle [the area] with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) and smear it with kāsīsa, paṭolī, rocanā, sesame seeds, and nimba leaves; however, one should cauterize the black spots caused by sesame seeds (tilakālaka).
One should burn moles with a sun-crystal, with an alkaline solution, or with fire;
likewise, one should excise skin-warts, warts, and jaṭūmaṇi with a surgical instrument.
One should perform venesection on one of the three marks, etc., as is most convenient;
and one should apply a plaster made of the bark and sprouts of milk-exuding trees ground with milk. (15)
32.15–16ab. One should apply a plaster consisting of the three [substances] that cover the downward-facing [parts], or else arjuna-bark with mañjiṣṭhā and honey for the various skin lesions (vyaṅga);
or a plaster of fresh butter together with the soot produced from the hooves of a white horse.

32.16ab For freckles (*vyaṅga*), either the bark of the *arjuna* tree, or red sandalwood, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *kuṣṭha*, *lodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, the sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree, and lentils (*masūra*) destroy freckles and bestow beauty upon the face.
Two grains of cumin, black sesame seeds,
and mustard seeds ground together with milk will make the moon of the face free from freckles and blemishes.
Or dehusked lentils (*masūra*) ground with milk and mixed with ghee and honey;
or sharp *śālmali* thorns ground with milk. // 19 //
Either jujube pulp with jaggery, or a paste of rabbit blood mixed with honey, kept for seven days in a citron (mātuluṅga) vessel, or kuṣṭha combined with honey [should be used]. 20.
Alternatively, one may take kuṣṭha combined with madhuka, ground with goat’s milk;
or mausalī and jaṭā mixed with honey;
or cow’s bone combined with the root of musalī, along with clarified butter and honey.

Jambū leaves, mango sprouts, whey, the two types of turmeric, and fresh jaggery—this is a paste that restores the natural skin color; likewise, tinduka fruit ground with its own juice [is used for the same purpose]. (22)
Blue lotus, blue kuṣṭha, priyaṅgu, kālīyaka, and the marrow of the jujube fruit—this rubbing powder makes the face resemble a hundred-petaled lotus. (23)

With these same medicinal herbs ground together, one should prepare an ointment for anointing the face, which produces the appearance of a hundred-petaled lotus (*śatapattraka*). One should administer unctuous substances (*sneha*) appropriate to the specific disorder and season, combined with a decoction of *madhuka*.
One should cook barley, resin of the Sarja tree, Lodhra, Uśīra, Madana, honey, ghee, and jaggery in cow's urine until it reaches the consistency of a paste that adheres to a ladle. (25)
32.25b–c. Uśīra, sandalwood, and honey—this [mixture], when used as an ointment, quickly destroys *nīlikā*, *vyaṅga*, and *dūṣikā*.
It makes the face resemble a lotus and the feet like lotus petals. (32.26)
32.26b–c To cure *nīlikā*, *vyaṅga*, and skin discolorations, one should use saffron, *uśīra*, *kālīya*, lac, licorice, sandalwood,
tender shoots of the *nyagrodha* tree, *padmaka*, and lotus filaments. (27)

Having boiled one *pālika* measure each of blue lotus and madder in one *āḍhaka* of water until reduced to one-fourth, [one should prepare the ointment] with those [decoctions] and with one *karṣa* each of the following ground [drugs]: // 28 //
One *kuḍava* of oil should be cooked with lac, *pattaṅga*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, and saffron, along with twice as much goat’s milk. (29)

32.29cv When combined with double the amount of goat’s milk, this [oil], when practiced as nasal therapy (nasya), destroys blue patches, graying hair, freckles, wrinkles, moles, and eye-secretions; it promotes the growth of the face and improves the complexion. 30.
Mañjiṣṭhā, śabarodbhava, tubarikā, lākṣā, and the two types of haridrā. // 31a //
Nepalese yellow orpiment, saffron, gadā, gorocanā, and red ochre. // 31b //
Nepalese yellow orpiment, saffron, *gada*, *gorocanā*, red ochre, the leaf of the pale banyan tree, the two types of sandalwood, *kālīyaka*, and mercury.
Pattaṅga, the bark of kanaka, the seed born from the lotus, and likewise the filament. // 31d //

Siktha, tuttha, the padmakādi group, muscle fat, ghee, marrow, milk, and the water of milky trees—when prepared repeatedly in the fire, this destroys facial freckles, indigo-stains, and the like, and quickly bestows a moon-like luster upon the face. (32)
The fresh juice of *mārkava*, milk, and water are recommended for nasal administration (*nāvana*) in cases of numbness;
one should also apply the treatments prescribed for *vāta-kuṣṭha* and perform cauterization with fire.
32.33bv – These, ground with water, are for nasal administration (nāvana) in cases of *utkoṭha*.
For abdominal diseases caused by *kapha* and *pitta*, everything prescribed for the abdomen (*kauṣṭhika*) should be employed. // 33 //ab //
In the Uttarasthāna:

For one who has abstained from sexual intercourse with women and then suddenly engages in it again— whether with a woman whose vaginal passage is inhabited by morbid humors (*doṣa*), or is congested, impure, or filled with minute particles of dust— (1)

33.1 For one who has desisted from sexual intercourse, [there is no fault] in touching a woman of another species, an unwilling woman, an unapproachable woman, or one recently delivered; nor is there any fault in touching water that has been defiled, even at the conclusion of sexual acts. // 2 //

Desiring to increase their power, they administer sharp ointments and other treatments, and inflict injuries with fists, teeth, and nails, or by squeezing, like poison, or by causing the discharge of semen. (3)
33.3dv–Through the falling of owls like poison, the suppression of natural urges, and friction from long, excessively harsh touch,
the vitiated humors (doṣas) reach the secret region and produce twenty-three diseases. // 4 //
Through contact with rough textures and the like, or through contact with coarse grass and the like, they produce conditions such as *upadaṃśa* (venereal sores). Here, *upadaṃśa* is fivefold:
[arising] from each of the *doṣas* individually, from blood, and from all [the *doṣas*] combined; among these, that caused by *māruta* (vāta) is as follows: // 5 //
They produce appetizers and other such items. Here, the appetizer (avadāṃśa) is fivefold:
swelling of the penis, various types of pain, stiffness, cracking of the skin, a swelling resembling a ripe udumbara fruit, and fever caused by pitta. //6//
33.6ab Swelling of the penis with various pains occurs due to kapha; it is hard, unctuous, itchy, cold, and heavy.
Due to blood, there is the appearance of blackish vesicles, discharge of blood, and fever. // 7 //

In *sarvajā* (the type caused by all three doṣas), there is the presence of all symptoms, as well as swelling of the scrotum, intense pain, rapid suppuration, bursting, and the appearance of worms. // 8 //
33.8dv. Piercing, the appearance of worms, and that arising from blood are palliable; among these, that born of the *saṃnipāta* [of all three humors] leads to death.
These arise when the provoked *doṣas* take refuge in the secret parts, the blood, and the flesh. 9.
Itching fleshy nodules inside or outside the penis, or similar growths resembling an umbrella in the vagina that discharge slimy blood; (10)

Through neglect, they destroy the hemorrhoids; [they also cause] disorders of the penis, virility, and the female genitalia and menses, as well as pustules born of phlegm and blood, either externally or internally on the private parts. (11)
33.11b The penis, virility, the female organ, and the menses [are mentioned].
The *sarṣapikā* eruptions are known to be dense, the size and shape of mustard seeds.
They are numerous, elongated pustules that burst open in the middle. (12)
That avamantha, arising from kapha and blood, is accompanied by pain and horripilation;
kumbhīkā arises from raktapitta and appears like the fruit of the jambu tree, appearing suddenly.
One should recognize *alajī* as being like the fruit of the *jāmbava*, inauspicious, and arising from an excess of *pitta* and blood, similar to *meha*.
A *piṭikā* resembles a black gram or mung bean, and is covered with small pustules. (33.13–14)
33.14b–c: That which arises from blood and bile (rakta-pitta) and is most severe, resembling the pericarp of a lotus, should be known as *puṣkarikā*.
When [the area] is excessively squeezed by both hands, it becomes a *saṃvyūḍha-piṭikā*. 33.15d.

When the rectum is repeatedly pressed down and compressed by clothing due to the provocation of wind (vāta), it becomes uneven, hard, and distorted; this condition caused by wind is known as aṣṭhīlikā.
33.16ab That which is repeatedly crushed, that crushed object,
33.16b or [the swelling] arising from the frenum due to the provocation of Vāta by wind vitiated through excessive rubbing and so forth;
It subsides along with pain and burning, and in some cases, it undergoes suppuration. // 17 //
