In some cases, it does not suppurate;
that thickened, knotted skin hangs down below the glans penis. It is devoid of sensation, accompanied by phlegm, and characterized by itching and hardness.
That which is clumped together or knotted, or hangs down below the glans (maṇi), is called *vipralamba*. When the skin is poorly healed or split open, it is designated as *avapāṭikā*.
If the skin, vitiated by wind (vāta), becomes adhered to the glans and obstructs it; // 19 //
The skin [of the urethral opening] becomes painful and cracked; attached to the glans (maṇi), it obstructs that channel. Consequently, urine flows out with difficulty and without pain.
Furthermore, there is an obstruction of the dilation of the glans; this disease is known as Niruddhamani.
The *liṅga* that is filled with hair-like filaments (*śūka*) arising from phlegm is called *grathita*.
That which arises from blood vitiated by those filaments, characterized by a loss of sensitivity to touch, is named after that [condition]. (21)
That which is covered all over with minute-mouthed openings due to the provocation of wind and blood should be known as śataponaka.

Inflammation of the skin (tvak-pāka), caused by pitta and blood, is accompanied by fever and burning sensations. Inflammation of the flesh (māṃsa-pāka) arises from all [three] doshas; it involves all types of pain and causes the wasting away of the flesh. (23)
One should recognize that condition as *asṛg-arbuda* (blood-tumor) when the penis is afflicted by dark, eruptive pustules and carbuncles, accompanied by severe pain. (24)
The fleshy tumor (māṃsārbuda) has been described previously, as well as the abscess (vidradhi) born from the three doṣas;
in these conditions, the blackened flesh disintegrates on all sides. // 25 //

One should recognize those [lesions] as *tilakālaka* when they are matured by the combination of all three humors (*saṃnipāta*); likewise, one should identify *arbuda*, *pāka*, *vidradhi*, and *tilakālaka* as arising from the flesh. // 26 //
One should avoid these four [types of food] and quickly treat the remaining ones;
twenty complications arise from the female reproductive tract due to improper diet. (27)
Through sleeping on uneven limbs, excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse, corrupted menses, complications, defects of the seed, or by fate; // 28 //
Due to vitiated menstrual blood, the provoked Vayu in the vagina may cause pain, pricking, distension, numbness,
a sensation like the crawling of ants, stiffness, roughness, and a ringing sound. (33.28–29)
33.29c–30. One should recognize the flow of menses that is like the movement of ants—
frothy, reddish-brown, black, scanty, thin, and dry—
as well as a sense of sagging in the groin, flanks, and other areas, pain, and the gradual development of a gulma (abdominal tumor).

33.30cv When there is severe pain in the thighs, groins, sides, and so forth, and those various specific diseases arise, it is known as the complication called *vātikī*. That same condition, when accompanied by swelling due to excessive sexual intercourse, is called *aticaraṇā*.
He suffered various diseases peculiar to himself from excessive sexual intercourse with a very young woman; [the affliction] reached his back, calves, thighs, and groins.
When Vāyu causes pain and corrupts the womb, it is called Prākcaraṇā.
Due to the upward churning caused by excessive force, the wind (māruta) presses upon the womb;
she then painfully discharges frothy menstrual blood that has been turned upward.

Due to the forceful upward turning [of the fetus], it releases the birth canal; this complication is called *udāvarta*. But when the wind (*vāyu*) has turned upward and causes the release, this disorder is known as *jātighnī*.
Out of harshness, she kills each son as soon as he is born, for they arise from a corrupted menses.
This disorder, known as *udāvarta*,

occurs when the wind (*marut*) in a woman who has overeaten or who has remained in an uneven position during sexual intercourse is compressed by food and, becoming lodged in the channel of the vagina, causes it to become crooked.
That [disease] in which the mouth, including the teeth and flesh, is intensely painful is called *antar-mukhī*;
it occurs when the wind (*anila*) becomes aggravated in a mother who consumes food that increases *vāta*. (36)

The *vakra-mukhī* causes pain and makes the woman's vagina narrow-mouthed; the *sūcī-mukhī* does the same. Due to the suppression of urges during menstruation, the vitiated wind (*vāyu*) causes the retention of feces and urine. (33.36b–37)
It causes the drying up of the womb and is known as *śuṣkā*, accompanied by intense pain; after six or seven nights, the wind draws the semen from the uterus. (38)
She who vomits, whether with or without pain, is considered a *vāminī*.
This occurs when the womb is afflicted by *vāta* due to defects in the seed within the woman's conception. (39)
She who vomits, whether with pain or without pain, is considered *vāminī*. She who hates men and lacks breasts is designated as *ṣaṇḍhā* (impotent), and there is no remedy for her.
The vitiated wind, having become obstructed, pervades the vaginal opening, the mouth, and the uterine cavity. // 40 //
When it remains wide open or drooping like a wind-afflicted [wound], with its flesh destroyed, they call that "Great Vagina" (mahā-yoni), which is accompanied by great pain. (41)
Just as bile, vitiated by its own specific defects and having taken refuge in the womb, produces burning, suppuration, ulceration, a fetid odor, and fever. (42)

Accompanied by a foul odor and fever, with menstrual blood that is intensely hot and abundant, and dark blue, yellow, or black in color— this is the *paittikī* complication known as *raktayoni*, resulting from excessive discharge of blood. (33.42–43)
Kapha, aggravated by obstructive factors, causes a vagina that is painless, cold, itchy, pale, slimy, and characterized by a similar kind of discharge. (44)

That [menstrual disorder] which is caused by phlegm (kapha) is suppressed; that in which the menstrual flow (rajas) is diminished due to wind (vāta) and bile (pitta), accompanied by burning sensations, emaciation, and discoloration, is known as lohita-kṣaya (loss of blood). // 45 //
In that [condition], known as *lohita-kṣayā*,

which belongs to those of a bilious (*pittala*) constitution, the womb becomes vitiated by wind combined with bile due to the suppression of sneezing and belching during sexual intercourse with a man. (33.45–46)
It causes swelling, intolerance to touch, pain, and the discharge of blue, yellow, or bloody [urine]; it produces heaviness in the bladder and abdomen, diarrhea, and loss of appetite. // 47 //
That [menstrual flow], when excessively overflowing, causes pain in the hips and groins, piercing sensations, and fever;
it is pervaded by disorders of wind and phlegm, and flows white and slimy. (48)
The womb is known as *upaplutā* when it is flooded; it is called *viplutā* due to lack of cleansing.
When a creature has been born, it is *kaṇḍūlā*; and when there is excessive itching, it is *atiratipriyā*. (49)
Due to riding at an improper time, the wind, combined with phlegm and blood, produces a polypus (karṇikā) in the vagina that obstructs the passage of the menstrual flow. (50)
That *karṇinī* [type of obstruction], due to the three doshas located in the womb and the uterus, produces their respective complications; that is the *sāṃnipātikī* [obstruction]. (51)
Thus, a woman with a vaginal disease (yoni-gada) who does not receive the semen does not conceive a fetus and instead suffers from dreadful diseases. (52)
[It cures] disorders such as menorrhagia, hemorrhoids, and abdominal tumors, as well as afflictions caused by the wind and other [humors]. (52cd)

33.52. Furthermore, regarding afflictions from wind and other humors: in a case of newly arisen *upadaṃśa* (venereal disease), one should pierce the vein located in the middle of the penis in the section on the upper part of the body.
One should employ cooling treatments and purification, especially through purgation.

34.1b–c. When a *avadāṃśa* has recently arisen, an ointment made of sesame paste, ghee, and honey should be applied; but when it is suppurated and incised, one should apply the sprouts of *jambu*, mango, *sumana*, *nīpa*, and white *kāmbojikā*. (2)
One should boil in water the barks derived from the śallakī, badarī, bilva, palāśa, and tiniśa trees, as well as the barks of milky trees and the three myrobalans (triphalā).
That decoction is used for washing; oil cooked with it serves as a healing agent, prepared with *tuttha*, *gairika*, *lodhra*, *elā*, *manohvā*, and *rasāñjana*.
That decoction, when used for washing,
along with a fine paste made of *hareṇu*, flower-sulphate (*puṣpakāsīsa*), *saurāṣṭrī*, and the best salt (*lavaṇottama*) mixed with honey, removes the ulcers of venereal disease (*upadaṃśa*). //5//
34.5dv Triphalā burnt in a skull and mixed with ghee is an excellent healer for wounds caused by the ingestion of food;
this is the general treatment, while for each specific humor (doṣa), it should be applied as in the case of swelling.
One should strive diligently so that it does not undergo suppuration;
for when the ligaments, veins, and flesh have mostly become suppurated, the penis is likely to perish. (7)
For hemorrhoids that have been excised or cauterized, the treatment should be performed like that for an upadaṃśa (syphilis/soft chancre).
One should scarify the hemorrhoids with mustard seeds and dust them with fine astringent powders. // 8 //
34.8bv The procedure is like that for the *avadāṃśa* [pustule]. 34.8cv Having drawn out mustard seeds with those same fine instruments, one should prepare an oil for anointing to heal the ulcer.
This same procedure applies to the *avamanya* as well; in both cases, blood should be let. 9.

In the case of *kumbhīkā*, one should extract the blood while it is unripe; once it has ripened, after the ulcer has been cleansed, an ointment made of *tinduka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *lodhra* should be applied, along with healing oil.
This same sequence of treatment applies when the *alajī* has discharged blood;
however, in the case of the pustule known as *uttamā*, one should incise it and extract it with a hook.
One should treat [these conditions] with pastes and powders of decoctions mixed with honey;
the regimen prescribed for Pitta-visarpa is beneficial for Puṣkaravyūḍha as well. (12)

In cases of inflammation of the skin (tvakpāka) and loss of sensation, one should again sprinkle the crushed part with lukewarm Bala-oil and apply a poultice made of drugs belonging to the Madhura group.
In cases of *tvakpāka* (skin suppuration) or loss of sensation,
after bloodletting, one should treat *aṣṭhīlikā* like a *śleṣmagranthi* (kapha-glandular swelling).
Once the bleeding has ceased, one should anoint it with ghee, apply fomentation, and then administer poultices (*upanāha*).
Having fomented [the area] with very unctuous *śālvaṇa* and other poultices for either three nights or five nights,
one should thereafter further bring the unctuous skin back into place.
34.15 One should apply an unctuous leather poultice, pressing it gently over the penis; once it has entered, a lubricating poultice should be applied.
Furthermore, unctuous food is recommended here again and again for the penis. 16.
This very same procedure should be employed even in the case of *avapāṭī*;
one should insert a tube with openings at both ends that has been blocked with lac.
Once it has been obstructed by lac, one should insert a tube made of lac that has been boiled and smeared with oil into the channel and irrigate it with unctuous substances that remove displacement.
Every three days, one should insert a thicker tube and gradually increase its size.
If the opening of the channel cannot be established, the learned physician should incise it with a surgical instrument;
avoiding the seam (sevanī), he should then apply the procedure for fresh wounds.
34.19 In cases of non-healing, one should apply fomentation to the orifice of the sinus or to the constricted area; then, having scarified it, one should bandage it with oil-soaked,
warm poultices and smear it with decoctions mixed with honey using a *śatapona* instrument.

The treatment for a blood tumor (śoṇitārbuda) should be performed like that for a blood abscess (rakta-vidradhi); in all cases, one should apply the management of ulcers according to the specific stage of the condition. // 21 //
In cases of most vaginal disorders, treatment that overcomes Vāta is highly recommended;
this is especially so for disorders born of Vāta, such as oleation, sudation, and enemas. // 22 //
For the womb of women does not become corrupted except through wind;
therefore, having conquered that [wind], one should apply the remedy for the other disorder. (23)

Therefore, without first conquering that [dosha] and the others, one should not administer a medicine for the doshas; rather, one should have the patient drink Balā-taila, Miśraka-taila, or Sukumāra-taila.
Likewise, one should restore a displaced vagina that has been lubricated and fomented to its proper position. // 24 //
One should have her drink *balā*-oil; one should have her drink that *balā*-oil, or one should have her drink *balā*-oil.
One should bend the curved [womb] with the hand, and one should pierce it again if it is constricted.
One should cause that which has emerged to enter, and one should turn back that which is open. // 25 //
One should bend with the hand that which is crooked, and again expand that which is constricted;
for a womb that has deviated from its natural position is considered by physicians to be like a foreign body in women.
One should treat a woman with mild medicinal actions and procedures such as emetics.
34.26ab For the womb that has undergone displacement from its position is extremely purified in every respect; the remaining treatment is prescribed as follows:
enemas, massage, affusion, medicinal pastes, tampons, and the application of medicated oils. // 27 //

34.27–28ab. But for one who is completely purified, [the enema should be prepared] with *kāśmarya*, the three fruits (*triphalā*), *drākṣā*, *kāsamarda*, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and *dāruharidrā*),
*guḍūcī*, *sairyaka*, *abhīru*, *śukanāsā*, and *punarnavā*.
34.28cv One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with equal parts (*akṣa*) of *guḍūcī*, red ochre (*gairika*), *abhīru*, and *parūṣaka*.
When drunk, it destroys disorders of the womb and wind, and is supreme for bestowing pregnancy. 29.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with *parūṣaka* fruits equal in measure to *akṣa* seeds;
likewise, one *prastha* of ghee [should be cooked] with *akṣa* seeds,
along with *vacā*, *upakuñcikā*, *jīraka*, black pepper, *vṛṣaka*, and rock salt.
Combined with ajamodā, barley-alkali, sugar, and citraka. // 30 //

Having ground [these] and stirred them with clear wine (*prasannā*), one should eat them fried in ghee for the removal of pain in the vagina and flanks, heart disease, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and hemorrhoids. (31)

34.31–32. To alleviate the pain of abdominal tumors (gulma) and hemorrhoids (arśas), one should drink vṛṣaka, the roots of mātuluṅga, and madayantikā with alcoholic liquors and salt; likewise, one may take kṛṣṇā and upakuñcikā.

34.32 Milk boiled with vṛṣa, mātuluṅga, as well as kṛṣṇopakuñcikā, rāsnā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and vṛṣaka, removes colic; likewise, affusion with decoctions of guḍūcī, triphalā, and dantī [is recommended]. 34.33
A tampon prepared from oil cooked with nata, vārtākinī, kuṣṭha, saindhava, and amaradāru should be inserted into the vagina; it relieves pain. (34)

For uterine conditions of the Pitta type, cold treatments that conquer Pitta—such as pouring liquids, massages, and the application of tampons—should be employed, as well as ghees for the purpose of oleation. (35)

34.35–36ab. For Pitta-dominant (pittala) types of gynecological disorders, one should cook one āḍhaka of ghee with the juice obtained by crushing and pressing four *tulās* of the roots of *śatāvarī*, together with an equal amount of milk. 36ab.
With the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, śatāvarī, grapes, parūṣaka, and priyāla—each ground in portions of one akṣa—and combined with two parts each of balā and madhuka; // 37 //
When it has been prepared with liquorice, *ṛddhi*, and *balā*, and has cooled, one should add eight *palas* of honey, eight *palas* of long pepper (*pippalī*),
and ten *palas* of sugar; then one should lick a *picu* (one *karṣa*) of this mixture.
It destroys defects of the womb, blood, and semen; it is aphrodisiac and a supreme promoter of male progeny.
It cures wasting of the chest, consumption, hemorrhagic disorders, cough, dyspnea, and chlorosis. (39)

34.39 It destroys wasting due to injury, hemorrhagic disorders, jaundice, gout, erysipelas, and stiffness of the heart and head; it also cures epilepsy, facial paralysis, convulsions, intoxication, and insanity. 40.
It destroys epilepsy, emaciation, intoxication, and insanity. Likewise, milk and ghee prepared with the *jīvanīya* [herbs] bestows conception and is supremely beneficial for diseases born of *pitta*.
One should cook one āḍhaka each of ghee and oil in a decoction of two droṇas of balā, with four times as much milk, along with pippalī, kākanāsā, and sugar. (42)
With jīvantī, kṣīrakākolī, sthirā, vīrā, ṛddhi, and jīvaka; with payasyā, śrāvaṇī, mudgaparṇī, pīluparṇī, and māṣaparṇī. // 43 //
34.43bv–sthirā-vīrarddhi-jīrakaiḥ | 34.43bv–sthirā-vīrā-dvi-jīvakaiḥ | 34.43dv–pīlu-māṣākhukarṇibhiḥ | Having destroyed disorders of vāta and pitta through drinking this, it bestows conception.
And in the case of a *rakta-yoni* (menorrhagia), having observed the persistence [of the disorder] through blood-colored [discharges], // 44 //
34.44bv By drinking that, one brings about conception; one should administer blood-stabilizing medicine according to the manifestation of the [specific] doṣa. [The drugs are:
pāṭhā, the stones of the jambū and mango trees, śilodbheda, and rasāñjana. // 45 //
With mañjiṣṭhā, aguru, kaṭphala, musta, priyaṅgu, miśī, and kuṣṭha;
with kaṭvaṅga, kuṭaja, śābara, kakubha bark, madhuka, padmaka, and madhūka. // 45.1+1 //

Ghee cooked with mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, kaṭphala, kuṅkuma, bilva, ativiṣā, mākṣika, rasāñjana, and kiñjalka— these being ground together— and combined with twice as much goat’s milk, [is used for healing].
One should always employ Kalyāṇaka-sarpiḥ in uttaravastis for women; it promotes conception and overcomes disorders of the vaginal tract and pain. (45.1+3)
Ambaṣṭhā, the down of the śālmalī tree, samaṅgā, the bark of vatsaka, bāhlīka, bilva, ativiṣā, lodhra, toyada, and gairika; (46)
34.46b–47. *Samaṅgā*, the bark of *vatsaka*,
*śuṇṭhī*, *madhūka*, *mācīka*, red sandalwood (*rakta-candana*), *kaṭphala*, *kaṭvaṅga*, *vatsaka*, *anantā*, *dhātakī*, *madhuka*, and *arjuna*.
34.47a Ginger, licorice, and grapes; 34.47a Ginger, licorice, and grape-wine;
34.47a Ginger, licorice, and grape-wine;
34.47a Ginger, licorice, and grape-wine; 34.47a Ginger, madhūka, and grapes.
34.47dv–48. Having taken dhātakī, madhuka, and añjana under the Puṣya asterism and having ground them into a powder, one should drink it with honey and rice-water in cases of hemorrhoids,
diarrhea, and for one who passes blood in the stool.
Taken with honey and rice-water,
it destroys those disorders caused by *jantu* (parasites) in children,
as well as vaginal disorders and menstrual defects characterized by dark, white, reddish, or blackish blood.
34.49ab Whatever defects are caused by the teeth, the powder known as Puṣyānuga is beneficial and honored by Ātreya.
In cases of the female reproductive tract (yoni) being afflicted by phlegm (balāsa), every medicine that is dry and hot [is indicated]. 50.
With dhātakī, āmalakī leaves, srotoñjana, madhuka, and utpala; with jambū, the heartwood of mango, kāsīsa, lodhra, kaṭphala, and tinduka. // 51 //
One should cook [the powder] of *saurāṣṭrikā*, pomegranate bark, and unripe figs—each in the measure of an *akṣa*—in goat’s urine and twice as much milk. (52)
One should employ one prastha of that oil for massage, cotton-pads, and enemas; by means of it, [the vagina] that is swollen, elevated, stiff, slimy, or discharging [is cured]. (53)

34.53c–54. A vagina that is swollen, protruding, elevated, rigid, overflowing, or overwhelmed, as well as one accompanied by eruptions and pain, may be cured. One should habitually consume barley-based food, *abhayāriṣṭa*, *sīdhu* liquor, and oil.
34.54b–c. A condition characterized by cracking and pain may be cured by the administration of long pepper (*pippalī*), iron filings, and *pathyā* (chebulic myrobalan), combined with honey.
34.55. Green vitriol (*kāśīsa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), potassium carbonate (*kāṅkṣī*), copper, jambu-stone, and *dhātakī* [are also effective].
34.55c–d. A powder consisting of kāsīsa, triphalā, and kācchī, combined with honey, produces clarity when there is excessive sliminess (paicchilya).
[A powder] derived from palāśa, dhātakī, jambū, samaṅgā, moca, and sarja [is likewise used]. 34.56.
In cases of foul odor, sliminess, and discharge, an astringent powder is desired;
a decoction of the *āragvadhādi* group is recommended for sprinkling. (57)
34.57dv A decoction should be used for sprinkling on parts that are stiff and rough to induce softness; likewise,
the application of vesavāra, kṛsarā, and milk-rice (pāyasa) is beneficial.
For foul-smelling substances, there should be a decoction, or oil, or a paste, or a powder made from all types of fragrant materials; these serve to remove putrid odors. (59)
34.59dv For those with phlegm disorders, enemas that remove foul odors, consisting mostly of pungent substances along with urine, are beneficial;
for those with bile disorders, they should be combined with madhuka and milk; and for those with wind disorders, they should be combined with oil and sour substances.
The action arising from the conjunction [of the three humors] is common and beneficial;
thus, women conceive a fetus when their wombs are pure. // 61 //
In the case of a woman whose conception arises from a derangement of the humors (saṃnipāta), the following [remedy] produces a fetus: sandalwood, tagara, uśīra, tiktā, padma, ibhakesara,
the bark and fruit of kuṭaja, musta, the stones of jambu and mango, and rasāñjana.
34.61.1–2. Night (niśā) prepared with tiktā, padma, ibhakesara, padmaka, utpala, bilva, abda, and kaṭphala;
along with dhātakī, ativiṣā, māṃsī, pāṭhā, and mocarasa, [mixed] with water.
Madhūka, madhuka, anantā, śārivā, the bark of pomegranate, clay, lodhra, arjuna, śaileya, samaṅgā, and nāgara in equal parts. (61.1+3)
This powder, when drunk with excellent water, destroys blood-dysuria (lohita-meha) for those afflicted by fainting, thirst, and fever, as well as blood-diarrhea and urinary disorders. (61.1+4)
It cures menorrhagia in women and is supreme for stabilizing the fetus.
When the natural seed is not corrupted and the entry of the living being occurs, the sense organ of even a person purified by the fivefold karma [arises]. (62)
Having examined it according to the colors [of the humors], one should treat the vitiated condition with remedies that destroy those specific defects.
Mañjiṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, tagara, triphalā, śarkarā, and vacā [are used for this]. (63)
A woman who has bathed after her menses and desires a son should drink the juice of *śirīṣa* leaves along with its paste for six days, subsisting on milk alone.
Two types of niśā, madhuka, medā, dīpyaka, kaṭurohiṇī, payasyā, hiṅgu, kākolī, vājigandhā, and śatāvarī; // 64 //
34.64a–d: The two types of niśā, madhuka, medā, dīpyaka, kaṭurohiṇī,
payasyā, hiṅgu, kākolī, vājigandhā, and śatāvarī.
Having ground one akṣa part [of each], one should cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much milk;
this is recommended for all disorders of the female reproductive tract and the semen. (65)
Having ground [the herbs] in measures of one akṣa each, one should cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much milk;
this is recommended for all [the aforementioned diseases].

Known as *phalasarpis*, it bestows longevity, nourishment, purity, and fortune; it is the supreme rite for producing male offspring, which, when drunk during menstruation, leads to the birth of a son. (66)
It is honored by people who are dying and by pregnant women; it is supreme for children, destroying the influence of seizing spirits (grahas) and promoting bodily growth. (67)
While the ocean was being churned by the gods and the asuras for the sake of the nectar of immortality,
a man of terrifying appearance was born before the emergence of the amṛta. (1)
Possessing blazing splendor, four tusks, golden hair, and eyes like fire—
seeing him and the world despondent, he was therefore designated as "Poison" (Viṣa).
With green hair and fire-like eyes, he was therefore designated as "Poison" (viṣa).
Then, having abandoned his own deceptive form, he presided over both the stationary and moving worlds, having been addressed with the sound "Huṃ" by Brahmā. (3)
35.3ab The embodied form was uttered by Brahmā as the syllable *huṃ*; 35.3bc from that [came] the stationary and the moving;
35.3bc from that, the stationary and the moving; 35.3bc from that, the stationary and the moving; 35.3bc from that.
Having abandoned the stable and the moving, that which is deceptive in nature—
though manifest as firm— is the potent energy established within the roots.
Kālakūṭa, Indravatsākhyā, Śṛṅgī, Hālāhala, and so forth. // 4 //
In the fangs of snakes, spiders, and the like, there is terrible mobile poison;
thus, poison is said to be of two kinds—unartificial: namely, stationary and mobile. (5)
That which is known as artificial poison (gara) is prepared from various medicinal herbs;
it kills quickly by the power of its formulation, or after a long time, or even much longer.
Or it may cause swelling, anemia, abdominal enlargement, insanity, dysentery, and other such ailments;
for it is sharp, hot, dry, clear, pervasive, quick-acting, and light. (7)
It produces bad odors and other such qualities; it is spreading, subtle, with unmanifest taste, and irregular in its digestion.
It is the opposite of *ojas* (vital essence) and is endowed with qualities such as sharpness (*tīkṣṇa*) and so forth. // 8 //
35.8 It is expansive, subtle, unmanifest,
possessed of tastes that are contrary [to those of *ojas*], and undigestible; indeed, it is the opposite of *ojas*.
In persons where vāta and pitta predominate, poison takes away life instantly;
for once it has entered the body, it first vitiates the blood. (9)
Then, having equally affected the phlegm, bile, and wind along with their respective seats, it takes refuge in the heart and prepares to sever the body.
35.10b When the humors (doṣas) are equal, along with their locations (āśayas), [it is like] having companions; 35.10b when the humors are equal, like having allies;
35.10b when the humors are equal, like having allies; 35.10b when the humors are equal, along with their substrates (āśrayas); 35.10d it leads to the destruction of the body.
When a stable poison has been ingested, the following symptoms first arise:
blackish discoloration of the tongue, numbness, fainting, terror, exhaustion, and vomiting. (11)
In the first stage, the onset (vega) arises;
and when the second stage arises, there is trembling, perspiration, a burning sensation, and pain in the throat.
When the poison has reached the stomach (āmāśaya), it causes pain in the heart.
In the third stage, however, there is dryness of the palate and intense pain in the stomach; his eyes become weak, yellowish-green, and swollen. (13)

When it has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), the patient becomes discolored, greenish, and emaciated; there is piercing pain, hiccups, coughing, and rumbling in the intestines. In the fourth stage of the paroxysm, extreme heaviness of the head arises. (35.13–14)

35.14 When [the vāyu] has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), there is piercing pain (todo), hiccups, coughing, rumbling in the intestines, excessive salivation of phlegm, discoloration, and a splitting sensation in the joints; in the fifth stage, there is the provocation of all the doṣas and pain in the receptacle of digested food (pakvādhāna). 35.15.
In the sixth [month], there is the loss of consciousness and one suffers from severe diarrhea;
in the seventh, there will be a breaking pain in the shoulders, back, and waist, and death occurs.

During the first stage of poisoning, one should quickly administer an anti-toxin mixed with clarified butter and honey to the patient who has been made to vomit and is being sprinkled with cold water. (17)
35.17 In the first stage of poisoning, and likewise in the second, one should cause the patient to vomit and purge as previously described;
in the third stage, however, the administration of medicine, as well as nasal drops and collyrium, is beneficial.
In the fourth [day], one should administer a medicine combined with oil;
in the fifth, it is beneficial to give it joined with honey and a decoction of madhuka.
In the sixth [case], success is achieved as in the case of diarrhea; but in the seventh, one should place a "crow's foot" mark on the head and apply blood or flesh. 20.

35.20b–21. And in the seventh [chapter], the *avapīḍa* (pressed-out drops) consist of *kośātakī*, *agnika*, *pāṭhā*, *sūryavallī*, *amṛtā*, *abhayā*, *śelu*, *śirīṣa*, *kiṇihī*, the two types of *haridrā*, and *kṣaudra*.
35.21b–d: Sūryavallī, amṛtā, abhayā, the two types of haridrā, kṣaudrasāhvaya,
the two types of punarnavā, trikaṭuka, the two types of bṛhatī, śārivā, and balā—
[one should prepare] a gruel from the decoction of these [drugs], served cold with ghee and honey.

Between the bouts [of vomiting], one should administer punarnavā, the three pungents (tri-kaṭuka), the two types of bṛhatī, śārivā, and balā— a remedy that destroys all poisons— to the patient who has completed the therapeutic procedure;
likewise, [one may use] madhūka, madhuka, padmakeśara, and candana.
Añjana, tagara, kuṣṭha, haritāla, manaḥśilā, phalinī, the three pungents (trikaṭu), spṛkkā, nāgapuṣpa, and kesara. // 24 //
Hareṇu, madhuka, māṃsī, rocanā, kākamālikā, śrīveṣṭaka, sarjarasa, śatāhvā, kuṅkuma, and balā. // 25 //
35.25bv Rocanā and kālamālikā; 35.25bv Rocanā and kālamañjikā.
[One should take] tamālapattra, tālīśa, bhūrja, uśīra, and the two types of niśā.
A maiden who has fasted, bathed, and is dressed in white garments [should prepare these] with honey as a liquid medium. // 26 //
With *tamālapattra*, *tālīśa*, birch bark, *uśīra*, and the two types of *niśā*,
one who wears white garments, having honored the twice-born with these substances soaked in honey under the asterism Puṣya, should prepare this supreme remedy.
And at that time, the physician, with a self-restrained mind, should recite this mantra.
Having honored the twice-born under the Puṣya constellation, the physician then quickly [recited] the mantra:
"Homage to the Lion among Men, homage to Nārāyaṇa!
So that he may not recognize the defeat of Kṛṣṇa in battle. (35.27–28)
35.28dv By this word of truth—that Kṛṣṇa was defeated in battle—may my freedom from disease be accomplished!
Homage to the Mother of Vaiḍūrya! Hulu hulu! Protect me from all poisons! // 29 //
35.29dv *Hulu kulu, protect me from all poisons!
O Gaurī, Gāndhārī, Cāṇḍālī, Mātaṅgī, svāhā!* This is the second mantra for the flour mixture (*piṣṭa*). 30ab.
Gaurī, Gāndhārī, Caṇḍālī, Mātaṅgī, svāhā!
Harimāyī, svāhā!
35.30 Hāritamāyi svāhā! [This is effective] against all poisons, vetālas, grahas, magical spells, and evils;
and in times of fear from pestilence, disease, famine, war, and thunderbolts. 31.
When employed as a drink, nasal drop, collyrium, ointment, or by binding it as a talisman, this [remedy] named Candrodaya is the supreme means for pacification and the attainment of well-being. 32.
Peace and supreme well-being;
indeed, Vāsava slew Vṛtra while being smeared with this very [substance].
35.32+(1)bv Coated with this [antidote], or destroyed by anti-poisonous herbs, or dried up by forest fires, wind, and heat,
or naturally not endowed with [poisonous] qualities, poison comes to be known as *dūṣīviṣa* (latent or residual poison). // 33 //
Whether by its own nature or due to a lack of its own qualities,
it becomes what is known as *dūṣīviṣa* poison.
Due to the deficiency of vigor, this [disease] is difficult to discern; covered by phlegm, it persists for many years.
Afflicted by it, the patient has the color of broken excrement, suffers from vitiated blood disorders, and is tormented by thirst and loss of appetite. (34)
One becomes fainting, vomiting, stammering, and delirious, exhibiting the symptoms of *dūṣyodara*;
when located in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), it causes diseases of phlegm and wind, and when located in the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*), it causes diseases of wind and bile.
Such a person would become like a bird with its feathers destroyed and its wings clipped;
or else, remaining within the fluids and other constituents, it produces various disorders arising from the bodily elements. (36)

Corrupted by easterly winds, indigestion, cold clouds, daytime sleep, and unwholesome food, it vitiates the bodily tissues (dhātus); therefore, it is known as *dūṣīviṣa* (slow-acting poison). // 37 //
35.37c–d: Because it vitiates the bodily constituents (dhātus) that have already been vitiated, it is known as *dūṣīviṣa* (latent poison).
35.38: One afflicted by *dūṣīviṣa* should be well-fomented and purified through both emesis and purgation;
then, one should have them lick the anti-poison medicine called *Dūṣīviṣāri*, saturated with honey.
Long pepper, dhyāmaka, māṃsī, lodhra, cardamom, suvarcikā, kuṭannaṭa, nata, kuṣṭha, yaṣṭīmadhu, sandalwood, and red ochre. // 39 //
This [remedy] is known by the name Dūṣīviṣāri and is not to be used for any other [poison];
however, one who has been pierced by a poisoned arrow faints again and again.
He assumes a discolored appearance and quickly falls into despondency;
his body, as if covered by insects, experiences a tingling sensation. (41)
The joints of the hips, back, head, and shoulders become painful; it discharges black, vitiated blood, and is accompanied by thirst, fainting, fever, and a burning sensation. (42)
In an instant, it causes turbidity of vision, vomiting, labored breathing, and coughing;
the ulcer has reddish-yellow margins, a dark-brown center, and is extremely painful. (43)
The flesh swells and suppurates immediately upon being touched; it turns black, becomes moist, frequently sloughs off, and exudes a slimy discharge. // 44 //

One should quickly apply a covering over the heart of the patient, provided it has not been pierced in a vital spot; then, having extracted the foreign object, one should cauterize the wound with heated iron.
Alternatively, one should rub [the area] with the alkali of muṣkaka, śvetā, soma-bark, tāmravalli, śirīṣa, and gṛdhranakhi. (46)
One should apply a plaster made from the roots of śukanāsā, prativiṣā, and vyāghrī, and one should perform the appropriate medical treatment for that person afflicted by an insect bite. // 47 //
When the wound contains putrid flesh, the treatment is like that for *pitta*-visarpa.
Out of a desire for good fortune, women, impelled by passion, [apply it] to their husbands or to kings. (48)
35.48cd–49ab Driven by malice, those who dwell near the king offer him poison mixed with his food;
[poisons] consisting of the excrement of various living beings, incompatible herbs, and ashes.
35.49c–d. A combination of the various limbs of diverse living beings along with impurities and horns, when possessing little potency, is known as *gara*.
By it, one becomes pale, emaciated, and has weak digestion, afflicted by cough, dyspnea, and fever. 50.
35.50–51. Due to the diminished potency of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) and the upward movement of *vāyu*, one becomes intent on sleep and anxious thoughts;
afflicted with enlargement of the abdomen, liver, and spleen, he is dejected in speech, weak, and lazy.

35.51c–d: One suffering from urinary disorders, enlargement of the spleen or liver, diminished speech, weakness, lethargy, swelling, constant flatulence, and parched hands and feet is a consumptive patient.
In dreams, he sees jackals, cats, mongooses, serpents, and monkeys.
For the most part, one sees trees and reservoirs as withered; the fair-skinned person considers himself dark, and the dark-skinned person considers himself fair. (53)
One whose senses are impaired would see his ears, nose, and eyes distorted;
thus afflicted by these and many other terrible calamities. (54)
But one whose senses are impaired and afflicted by poison may meet with destruction immediately if left untreated; however,
one afflicted by poison who has vomited it out should eat that [same] food and drink what is wholesome.
One of pure heart, recollecting the procedure for the Sūtra-sthāna, should practice [this] by consuming a powder of gold and copper mixed with sugar and honey. (56)

Remembering the procedure prescribed in the Sūtrasthāna, this electuary pacifies even severe poison produced by any combination [of agents]: mūrvā, amṛtā, nata, kaṇā, paṭolī, cavya, and citraka. (35.56–57)
One whose digestive fire has been impaired by poison should drink vacā, mustā, and viḍaṅga with buttermilk, warm water, or whey, or else with sour meat-broth. (58)
One should drink the cold infusion (himaja) of pigeon meat, śaṭhī, and puṣkaramūla, processed with sour meat-broth;
this removes artificial poison, thirst, pain, cough, dyspnea, hiccups, and fever. (35.58–59)
35.59b–d: Puṣkarāhvā boiled and cooled, along with trikaṭu, the five salts, mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of haridrā,
sūkṣmailā, trivṛt, pattra, viḍaṅga, and indravāruṇī.
And one should place madhuka together with honey inside a cow's horn;
then, one should administer a dose of it with warm water before a meal. (59+2)
Poison that has been consumed undergoes digestion and, being rendered non-toxic, causes no harm;
likewise, lac, priyaṅgu, mañjiṣṭhā, along with mṛṇāla and hareṇukā [act similarly]. (59+3)
One should prepare a paste of yaṣṭyāhvā mixed with honey and the bile of a goat, place it inside a cow's horn, and bury it in the ground for seven nights. (59+4)
Having fashioned a gem there and set it in gold, one should wear it on the hand;
anything touched by it that possesses poison immediately becomes free of poison. (59+5)

When poison, one's constitution, the season, food, the humors (doṣas), and the affected tissues (dūṣyas) come together, it is designated as a "poisonous crisis" (viṣasaṃkaṭa); here, only one in a hundred survives. (60)
By hunger, thirst, heat, debility, anger, grief, fear, and fatigue; by indigestion, loose stools, and the increase of bile and wind. // 61 //
By the smelling of sesame, flowers, and fruits; by the vapors from the earth and the thundering of clouds;
by the sounds of elephants, mice, and musical instruments; and by the perils of poison. // 62 //

35.62b–63. In the rainy season, poison increases due to the thundering clouds that are like tears of the earth, and through the intoxication of the blue lotuses stirred by the eastern winds; furthermore, because its origin is water, it becomes as moist as molasses.
35.63 Because its origin is water, poison spreads during the rainy season; when the clouds have departed, Agastya destroys it.
Therefore, at the end of the rains, the poison becomes weak in potency. 64.
Thus, having carefully examined with the intellect the constitution, suitability, season, location, the onset of symptoms, and strength or weakness, one should perform the subsequent treatment.
One should pacify phlegmatic poison (ślaiṣmika-viṣa) with emetics that are hot, dry, and sharp; with medicinal pastes; and with foods that are astringent, pungent, and bitter. (66)

The Pitta-type [fever] should be treated with purgatives, and with very cold affusions and plasters, as well as with foods combined with ghee and possessing astringent, bitter, and sweet tastes. // 67 //
One should conquer disorders of the vāta nature with foods and poultices that are sweet, unctuous, sour, and salty,
combined with ghee, as well as with meat preparations.
35.68b–d — A laxative combined with unctuous, sour, and salty substances, as well as medicinal ointments and dietary regimens, is recommended;
however, among all poisons and in all conditions, nothing is equal to clarified butter (ghṛta). 69.
When vāta is predominant, there is some specific remedy available;
that which resides in kapha is curable without effort, while that which takes refuge in the seat of pitta is curable with effort. (70)

35.70 A phlegmatic fever (ślaiṣmika) is curable without effort; one located in the seat of bile (pittāśaya) is difficult to cure or incurable even with effort; and one that has reached the seat of wind (vātāśaya) is likewise difficult to cure or incurable. 70u.āb.
With lac, resin, ushira, mustard seeds, pattra, and valaka; with valli, arushkara, puri, and the flowers of the arjuna tree.
35.70 Incense made from *vāllaja*, lotus roots (*puṣkara*), and *purī* destroys all poisons, both stationary and mobile, within the dwelling chamber.
Therein, no poisonous insects, nor mongooses, nor reptiles shall remain.
Neither magical spells nor sorcery and the like can prevail where this incense is burned.
In the Uttarasthāna:
Serpents are, in brief, of three kinds—hooded (darvīkara), circular-spotted (maṇḍalin), and striped (rājīmant)—yet they are further divided into many varieties. // 1 //
They are not described in detail according to their specific origins as they are of no practical use;
[the tastes are] specifically dry and pungent, sour and hot, and sweet and cool. (2)
They are not mentioned because they are of no practical use;
for instance, the poison of hooded snakes and others aggravates the *vāta* and other humors respectively, as does [the state of] youth, middle age, and old age, or rain, cold, and heat. (3)
These Vyantara deities become fierce with poison during the transitions between seasons;
they carry the emblems of a wheel, a plow, an umbrella, a svastika, and a goad. // 4 //
The snakes that move swiftly are known as *darvīkaras*; those that are coiled and adorned with various circular spots are to be known as *maṇḍalins*. // 5 //
36.5b-v The *darvīkara* snakes are considered to be tall and slow-moving; they are marked with stripes,
variegated with glossy, multicolored lines that run both horizontally and vertically.
Those with stripes are striped; those with smooth, multi-colored stripes are the *gaudhera*, the offspring of the *godhā*.
The *gaudhera* is equal to the hooded snakes (*darvī-kara*) in its venom.
One should know that the four-legged snakes are intermediate between these [two groups], arising from their very intermixture.
The offspring of a lizard is the *gaudheya*;
their characteristics are indeed mixed, and they provoke the humors through their combined action (*saṃnipāta*).
[They bite] for the sake of food, out of fear, from the touch of a foot, or from excessive venom and anger. // 8 //
Because of their evil conduct, out of enmity, and by the instigation of gods, sages, and Yama, serpents bite; it is said that their venom increases in intensity for each subsequent one.
36.9ab Through wicked conduct, enmity, and the instigation of celestial seers and Yama,
having understood the assigned cause, one should apply the appropriate remedy.
36.9cd Because of his sinful nature, the *vyantara* remains lurking along the path.

Having understood the cause from the possessed person, one should recognize that when the path [of the poison] is blocked and remains stationary where only the moistening of saliva is visible on the body,
but no bite mark caused by fangs is seen, that should be designated as a "sting" (tuṇḍāhata). // 11 //
Only a mere mark is seen on the limbs;
however, there is no bite with fang-marks—
such a bite should be designated as one struck by the [insect's] snout.
One or two tooth-marks that are bloodless are called *vyālīḍha*;
two tooth-marks with blood are *vyālupta*; and three of those [tooth-marks] constitute [the next stage]. (12)
36.12d–13ab. Those three [wounds] are torn open;
from the cutting of the flesh, they carry blood without interruption. A "bitten" wound has four fang-marks; likewise, a "pressed-bitten" wound is similar.
In this regard, one should say that the first two types are free from poison, while the latter is incurable.
Poison cannot be expelled without reaching the blood; once it reaches it, it vitiates the body.
Even a minute amount of blood, once it has been reached, increases like oil mixed with water;
however, in the case of one who is fearful, the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated by the fear arising from contact with a snake. 15.
Even a minute amount of blood that has been reached [by the poison] increases like a drop of oil; sometimes it produces swelling, as if struck by the body of a serpent.
Or, in a dark place with a foul odor, one who has been pierced may experience this due to the suspicion of having been bitten by someone.
36.16cv For one pierced by [a poison] in a difficult terrain or in darkness, there may arise agitation from the poison, fever, vomiting, fainting, or even a burning sensation;
or there may be exhaustion, delusion, or diarrhea—this is called "suspicion-poison" (śaṅkā-viṣa). // 17 //

From the onset of poison there is fever and vomiting; from the excess of poison there is fever and vomiting. The bite site, accompanied by poison, throbbs and is afflicted with itching, swelling, and pain.
If it is knotted, it burns slightly; however, if it is reversed, it is without poison. // 18 //
36.18 In the first stage of the poison-induced bite of constrictors (darvīkṛta), the site of the bite throbbs; the blood becomes vitiated and turns dark-brown.
Due to that, a dark-brown discoloration appears on the face and other parts, and it feels as if insects are crawling over them.

In the second stage, the blood becomes vitiated and dark-brown; there is a dark-brown discoloration of the eyes, face, and other parts. In the third stage, there are glandular swellings (granthi) and heaviness in the head.
In the fourth stage, there is obstruction of vision, moistening of the bite site, spitting, and vomiting.
In the third [stage], there is heaviness of the head;
in the fourth, impairment of vision, swelling of the bitten area, spitting, vomiting, and loosening of the joints; and in the fifth, breaking pain in the joints.
In the sixth stage, however, there is burning, hiccups, pain in the heart, and heaviness of the limbs.
In the sixth [day], there is burning, hiccups, fainting, indigestion, and diarrhea; but upon reaching the semen in the seventh [day],
there is a breaking pain in the shoulders, back, and waist, and the cessation of all physical movements.

36.22b–c. Having reached the semen on the seventh day, the vitiated blood of one bitten by a *maṇḍalin* snake turns yellow; because of that, there is yellowness of the limbs and a burning sensation on the second day, followed by the appearance of swelling. 36.23.
In the third [stage], the blood becomes vitiated and yellow; there occurs a moistening of the bite site, along with perspiration and thirst.
In the fourth, fever arises and a burning sensation; in the fifth, it spreads through all the limbs.
36.24b–c. In one bitten by *rājila* snakes, perspiration and thirst arise, and the blood becomes vitiated and turns pale.
Because of that, there is paleness of the limbs and heaviness in the second stage. 36.25.
In the third stage, there is swelling at the bite site and discharge from the nose, eyes, and mouth;
in the fourth, heaviness of the head; and in the fifth, stiffness of the neck.
One should describe body aches, fever, and chills for the remaining two stages as previously stated;
one should administer treatment during the five stages of the poison's intensity, but not beyond that. (27)
In the remaining two cases, it should be as previously described.
[The women] are drenched by water, exhausted from lovemaking, frightened, or defeated by mongooses;
they are also afflicted by cold, wind, heat, disease, hunger, thirst, and fatigue.
Having quickly arrived from other lands and cast off the slough of poison, they roam the forest like kusha-grass, medicinal herbs, and thorns. (29)

In a region inhabited by divine beings, those snakes are considered to have little venom; likewise in cremation grounds, on funeral pyres, at shrines, and so forth, as well as on the fifth day, during the dark fortnight, and at the junctions of time.
36.30 One should know that a place inhabited by learned men [is auspicious],
as well as during the eighth and ninth lunar days, at the two twilights, at midnight, and during the day;
and under the constellations of Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Maghā, Āśleṣā, Viśākhā, and those in the east and southwest.

One should abandon [the victim] if bitten during the muhūrta called Nairṛta or if bitten in the vital spots (marmas). Immediately upon being bitten, [the victim's] face and eyes turn white and his hair falls out.
36.32cv As soon as one has been bitten, the victim—with copper-colored eyes, a stiff tongue, frequent fainting, and cold breath—does not survive.
Hiccup, labored breathing, vomiting, and coughing occur in the person bitten at that very moment. 33.
36.33b–d. One who breathes cold breaths does not live; one for whom heart pains arise simultaneously does not live;
one who vomits foam while unconscious, with feet, hands, and face turned dark-brown, [does not live].
Lassitude, breaking of the limbs, diarrhea, and looseness of the joints occur in one who has drunk poison, or who has been bitten by a venomous creature, or struck by a poisoned weapon. (35)
36.35 When the end of life has arrived, these symptoms occur: drooping of the nose and pain in the limbs.
Consciousness is not restored by sharp nasal medications, nor does blood flow from an incision.

When the destruction of life has arrived, for one who has been struck by the staff and has gone into the presence of Yama, no line [of treatment] exists; otherwise, however, the physician must act with haste, as if [dealing with] a burning house. (36.36) (37)

36.37b–38. He who protects his life-breaths residing in the throat goes to the presence of Yama; [otherwise], the poison would quickly bring about death. Having remained in the bite of the bitten creature for a hundred mātrās, the poison [spreads].
It proceeds toward the body, vitiating the elements such as blood;
in the meantime, the action of cutting off the bite and so forth [is performed]. (39)
36.39b–d. It vitiates the blood and other constituents, and quickly acts so that the poisonous vine does not take root in the body.
As soon as it has bitten, it should immediately bite that very eater of air (the snake). 40.
36.40 Having bitten that very wind-eater (snake), or a clod of earth, or the ground itself, with great haste,
one should then smear the bite with spittle or with earwax.
Having quickly cut [the bite] with haste,
one who knows mantras should bind a ligature four finger-breadths above the bite using linen or similar materials wrapped in a cord, while reciting proven mantras.
Poison is checked by binding, like water by the construction of a dam;
and the vessels, being compressed by the binding, do not carry the poison. (43)

36.43c–d: The veins do not carry the poison for him when they are constricted by binding. Having squeezed out the bite that is not located at a vital spot (marman) or a joint, one should extract it; thus, the onset of the poison does not arise, just as a sprout does not grow from the destruction of the seed. 36.44.
36.44ab One should extract the bite after squeezing it; 36.44cd the onset of the poison does not occur, except in the case of the *maṇḍalin* snakes due to their bilious nature (*pittala*).
Does fire merely reduce something to ashes immediately; what indeed is the harm in that?
Or rather, one should suck it up with the mouth full of clay, ashes, medicinal herbs, and cow dung. 46.

What indeed does fire not consume in an instant? In particular, when the *ariṣṭā* is hidden within the shade, one should repeatedly smear the fleshy part of the limb, along with the bite itself, with medicinal antidotes (*agada*). // 47 //
One should sprinkle [the patient] with water mixed with sandalwood and uśīra;
when the poison has spread, one should perform venesection—this is the supreme treatment. // 48 //
For when the blood is being extracted, the entire poison is removed;
the foul-smelling, poisonous blood crackles and pops when placed in fire. (49)
36.49c–d. One should observe that the blood is foul-smelling, toxic, and purified according to the specific humor (doṣa), as previously described;
when the veins are not visible, horn-leeches should be applied. 50.
And the blood that remains after flowing, having been liquefied by the heat of the poison, should be coagulated repeatedly with very cold applications of ointments and sprinklings. (51)

For when the poison has not yet spread, fainting, intoxication, and the melting of the heart occur due to its force; one should overcome these with cold applications until the bristling of the body hair occurs. (52)
36.52dv–53ab. One should fan the patient until the hair stands on end; once the blood has been discharged, the force of the poison is immediately pacified.
Because of its sharpness, the poison draws toward the heart; therefore, one must protect the heart.
One should drink ghee, or ghee mixed with honey, or a medicinal preparation (agada) saturated with ghee;
for if the heart is not protected, phlegm accumulates within it. (54)

36.54c–55. Once his heart has been protected, one should cause him to vomit by means of liquids that exclude sour gruel (kāñjika), horse-gram soup (kaulattha), oil, wine, and the like, provided he suffers from nausea, distress, or a sense of fullness in the chest.

And by means of emetics and anti-poisonous remedies, the poison does not pervade the body in this manner, due to the specific differences in the snake, the nature of the poison, its location, and its intensity. (56)
Having carefully and correctly examined [the situation], one should perform the specialized ritual:
the roots of *sindhuvāra*, and *śvetā* and *girikarṇikā*. (57)

36.57b–58. One should perform a specialized treatment for one bitten by a hooded (*darvīkara*) snake: drinking [antidotes], nasal drops (*nasya*) of honey with *pākala* [mustard], and for one bitten by a black cobra (*kṛṣṇasarpa*), one should apply [the paste] to the bite after the blood has been removed.
36.58b–d: A nasal medication (nasya) with honey for *pākala*, or a nasal medication with honey and *vālaka*; or [a nasal medication] with *cāraṭī* and *nākulī*, or with a sharp root-poison.
And the drink is ghee combined with honey, mañjiṣṭhā, and soot from a house. // 59 //
36.59c–60. For drinking, honey, mañjiṣṭhā, taṇḍulīyaka, kāśmarya, kiṇihī, girikarṇikā,
mātuluṅgī, sugar, and śelu are beneficial when used as a drink, nasal drops, or collyrium.
36.60cv The root-bark of *mātuluṅga*, *śelu*,
and *agada* [are effective] against the terrible poison of hooded snakes (*phaṇin*) as well as that of banded kraits (*rājīmat*).
Equal [in efficacy] are *sugandhā*, *mṛdvīkā*, the one called *śvetā*, and *gajadantikā*.
36.61c–d: Equal parts of *sugandhā*, *mṛdvīkā*, and that which is called white *gajamṛttikā* (or *gajavṛttikā*). Half a part each of *saurasa* leaf, *kapittha*, *bilva*, and pomegranate.
This antidote mixed with honey is especially beneficial against circular poison (maṇḍalī-viṣa). // 62 //
The five barks, varā, yaṣṭī, nāgapuṣpa, elavāluka, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, sugar, padmaka, and utpala are cooling. (63)
The *Himavat* formulation— consisting of the five barks (*pañcavalka*), *balā*, *yaṣṭī*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and *uśīra*, mixed with honey— destroys the poison of *maṇḍalī* snakes.
As an ointment, it destroys swelling, erysipelas, pustules, fever, and burning sensations.
One bitten by a maṇḍalī snake should drink kāśmarya, the sprouts of the vaṭa tree, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, sugar, mañjiṣṭhā, and madhuka. (65)
36.65–66ab. Kāśmarya, banyan shoots, bamboo bark, seeds of *bījakā*, kaṭukā, seeds of *pāṭalī*, ginger, seeds of *śirīṣa*, ativiṣā, *gāvedhuka* root, and *vacā*.
36.66bv – *pāṭalā* seed and *nāgara*; 36.66dv the root of *gavedhukā* and *vacā*; 36.66dv the root of *śrīveṣṭaka* and *vacā*:
this eight-ingredient [formula], ground with cow’s urine, destroys the poison born of the *gonasa* snake.
Kaṭukā, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, gṛhadhūma, and hareṇukā. // 67 //
Honey combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and tagara destroys the poison of those possessing stripes (rājimat).
One should bury the bite of a kāṇḍacitrā in the ground for two watches (yāma).
Having extracted and purified ghee, one should smear it with powdered medicinal herbs and clay;
then one should drink aged ghee sprinkled with the powder of Varā.
Having extracted and prepared the ghee, one should start by sprinkling it with the powder of *varā*.
Once the ghee has been digested, the patient, having undergone purgation, should eat barley-based food prepared with soup.
[The following ingredients are used: *karavīra*, *arka* flowers, roots of *lāṅgalikā*, and *kaṇā*.

When the medicine has been digested and the patient has been purged, one should eat [the following]: one should grind the roots of *lāṅgalikā* and *kaṇā*, together with *pāṭhā* and black pepper, with fermented gruel (*āranāla*). This is a universal remedy for those bitten by *vyantara* spirits. (36.70–71)
White pepper, processed for seven days with the natural juice of *śirīṣa* flowers, is beneficial when administered as a drink, nasal drops, or an ointment for those bitten by snakes. (72)

It is beneficial when used as a drink, an errhine, or a collyrium. Two palas each of nata and kuṣṭha, with four palas of ghee and honey—this drink provides relief even for those bitten by Takṣaka. (36.72–73)

36.73b–c: Four *pala* each of ghee and honey; 36.73d: furthermore, for those bitten by a *tārkṣaka* [serpent], or in the first stage of the onset of a *darvīkṛta* [venom], having bled the wound, one should quickly drink the antidote (*agada*) combined with honey and ghee.
In the second [stage], having induced emesis, one should drink the same medicine;
in the third, one should employ collyrium and nasal drops that remove poison.
On the fourth day, after emesis has been performed, one should administer anti-poisonous [medicines] and drink the previously mentioned gruel (yavāgū).
On the fifth and sixth days, the body should be repeatedly sprinkled with cold liquids.
One should administer a strong emetic and a gruel prepared with anti-poisonous drugs;
on the seventh day, one should apply a potent medicinal collyrium and nasal drops.
Then, having made a deep incision with a blade in the shape of a crow's foot on the head, one should place flesh along with blood, or else skin, into that [wound]. // 78 //
In the third paroxysm, having vomited, one should drink thin gruel; in the sixth, one should drink a non-pungent antidote or the group of drugs beginning with *padmaka*. (79)
36.79–80. On the third day, one should drink gruel (peyā) that has been vomited up.

When bitten by a *rājila* snake during the first stage of envenomation, one should apply a cold immersion bath; then, using a gourd (*alābu*), one should extract the blood and drink an antidote (*agada*) as previously described.
In the sixth stage, one should apply the most potent collyrium and the pressed-out extract (avapīḍa);
and for those stages not mentioned, the treatment prescribed for the Darvīkara [venom] should be employed.

One should not pierce a vein gently in those who are pregnant, nor in children or the elderly. [The following are used for scarification: realgar, orpiment, the two types of haritaki, vakra, the juice of śārdūla, and tiger-claw. (82)
In the case of pregnant women, children, and the elderly, one should not pierce a vein with a sharp instrument;
rather, a cold paste of manaḥśilā, niśā, tamāla, and kesara, drunk with rice-water, [is to be used].
This [mantra] destroys all poisons, just as the thunderbolt destroys the asuras. // 83 //
This destroys all poisons, just as the discus and thunderbolt destroy the asuras,
or as the thunderbolt of the wielder of the thunderbolt destroys the asuras.
[It consists of] the root of *bilva*, the flower of *surasā*, the fruit of *karañja*, *nata*, and *surāhva*.
The three fruits, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and the two types of turmeric, finely ground with the urine of a goat; // 84 //

The three fruits, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and the two types of niśā, when used as collyrium, for drinking, or as nasal drops, restore to health men afflicted by the venom of snakes, spiders, rats, scorpions, and the like, as well as by cholera, chronic poisoning, and fevers, and those tormented by malevolent spirits.
36.85–86. One should completely extract the poison from the bite using plasters and other treatments for afflicted men who have been overwhelmed by malevolent spirits;
otherwise, the remnant may lead to a recurrence of the paroxysms or result in *dūṣī-viṣa* (latent or chronic poison).

The remaining [symptoms] are like those of *dūṣī-viṣa*. For the remaining [cases], one should treat the aggravated *vāta* after the poison has been eliminated with oleation and other therapies, using *vāta*-alleviating measures while avoiding oil, wine, horse gram (*kulattha*), and sour substances. (36.86–87)
One should treat pitta with decoction enemas (kaṣāya-vasti) and oil enemas (sneha-vasti) that alleviate pitta-fever;
one should treat kapha with the group [of drugs] beginning with mārkava and with the group beginning with āragvadha mixed with honey.
Sugar, fragrant substances, grapes, milk, licorice, and honey;
drinking water purified with mantras, sprinkling [with it], and consoling or gladdening [the patient]. (89)
36.89 One should employ sugar, *vaigandhaka*, and grapes for one struck by a snake; likewise for one afflicted by the poison of a *śaṅkhinī* snake.
[One should also use] *karketana*, emerald, diamond, and elephant pearl. 90.
Vaiḍūrya, gardabha-maṇi, picuka, viṣa-mūṣikā, somarājī produced on the Himavat mountain, and punarnavā. // 91 //
One should wear the *vaiḍūrya*, the *gardabha* gem, the *picuka*, the *viṣadūṣikā*,
as well as the *droṇā*, the *mahādroṇā*, the *mānasī*, and the serpent-born gem;
one should also carry potent poisons for the purpose of neutralizing poison.
Likewise, one who carries an umbrella and holds a *jharjhara* drum in hand should walk about at night, especially near Droṇa and Mahādroṇa;
terrified by its shadow and sound, the serpents will flee.
Carrying an umbrella and holding a *jarjhara* drum in his hand, he should always wander about at night; for the serpents flee [at such a sight].
Water, guñjā fruit, and uśīra, ground with water as a collyrium for eyes afflicted by poison, is like Garuḍa himself; it is called Gāruḍa. (93+1)
In the Uttarasthāna:

Insects are of four kinds, produced from the feces, urine, semen, eggs, and putrefying carcasses of snakes themselves, and they are associated with the humors (doṣas) either individually or collectively. (1)
In one bitten by Vāyavya insects, the bite is characterized by intense pricking and pain;
in one bitten by Āgneya insects, there is little discharge, but it is accompanied by burning, redness, and spreading inflammation (visarpa). // 2 //
Resembling a ripe pīlu fruit or like a date (kharjūra), it is characterized by mild pain when kapha is predominant; it resembles a ripe udumbara fruit. // 3 //
That which is abundant with discharge and possesses all symptoms should be avoided in cases of the combined (sāṃnipātika) type;
its urges are like those of a snake, the swelling increases, and there is a foul-smelling discharge of blood.
The sannipātika type is to be avoided;
it is characterized by heaviness of the head and eyes, fainting, vertigo, dyspnea, and excessive pain.
In all types, there is swelling of the earlobe, fever, itching, and loss of appetite. // 5 //
37.5bv Dizziness, dyspnea, and intense pain [occur]. The poison of a scorpion is sharp; at first it burns like fire.
It quickly ascends upward, but subsequently it remains localized at the site of the sting. // 6 //
37.6dc Following the bite, the bite site remains; it is immediately very painful, dark-brown, pruritic, and as if it were bursting open.
These [symptoms] arise from the putrefaction of cow dung and the like, or from the putrefaction of poisoned bites and similar [contaminants]. // 7 //
And those born from the slough of snakes possess mild, moderate, or great venom;
they are mild, yellow, white, dark-brown, rough, variegated, or blackish-blue.
37.8dv Rough, variegated, and dark-blue; hairy, with many joints, and red with white bellies;
smoke-colored bellies and three-jointed; while those of middling quality are tawny and reddish-brown. // 9 //
The Piśaṅgas, Śabaras, Citras, and those with the luster of blood are highly venomous;
those with the luster of fire have two or one joint, and they have red, black, or white bellies. // 10 //
Bitten by them, his tongue swelled, his limbs became rigid, and he was afflicted with fever;
vomiting black blood from his mouth, he lost consciousness of the objects of the senses.
Perspiring, fainting, with a parched mouth, agitated and afflicted by pain, and with his flesh falling away, he generally gives up his life-breaths. (12)
The *ucciṭiṅga*, however, bites with its mouth, causing excessive pain;
it is curable, yet more so than a scorpion's sting, and it causes stiffness of the penis and horripilation. (13)
But the *ucciṭiṅga* is [poisoned] by the mouth; it is inferior to the *vṛścika*. It causes stiffness of the limbs, as if from sprinkling them with cold water at the site of the bite.
That very same [poison] is called *uṣṭradhūma*, and because it moves about at night, it is also known as *rātrika*.
37.14b–d. In the case of a bite, [the following are treated] as if with cold water:
insects in which vāta and pitta predominate, those of the ślaiṣmika type, the kaṇabha and the mouse;
and generally, scorpions along with the camel-insect (uṣṭradhūmaka), whose poison is characterized by an excess of vāta.

Whichever specific humor one should diagnose as having an excess of symptoms, for that very humor one should administer treatment with medicines possessing qualities opposite to those [symptoms]. // 16 //
37.16bv An excess of symptoms arises: pain in the heart, upward movement of wind (ūrdhvānila), stiffness, stretching of the vessels, pain in the bones and joints,
vertigo, twisting sensations, and a darkish discoloration of the limbs in the case of Vata-type poison.
In the Pittaja type, there is loss of consciousness, hot breath, burning in the heart, a bitter taste in the mouth, tearing of the flesh, and swelling that is red and yellow. (18)

In the Pitta-type [fever], one should recognize the poison as being red and yellow, accompanied by vomiting, anorexia, nausea, excessive salivation, distress, and catarrh; in the Kapha-type, it is characterized by coldness and sweetness in the mouth. (37.18–19)
For a Vātika ulcer, an ointment made of oil-cake (piṇyāka), anointing with oil, fomentation using tubes, grain-husks, and similar means, as well as nourishing treatments, are beneficial. (20)
One should arrest the pitta-type [hemorrhage] with very cold affusions and plasters;
one should conquer the kapha-type by means of scraping, excision, sudation, and emesis. (21)
For the three types of insects, a threefold treatment is beneficial; one should generally administer lukewarm fomentation, ointments, and affusions. (22)
37.22b–d: Beneficial treatments are of three kinds; one should apply them while they are lukewarm, except in cases of fainting, inflammation of the bite, or sloughing. 37.23:
Human hair, mustard seeds, yellow pigment, and aged molasses constitute a fumigation.
Kāśyapa declared that for every kind of venomous bite, one should employ the supreme antidote to poison and perform all purificatory rites. (24)

37.24b–c Kaśyapa said further: Those bitten by snakes or by insects and scorpions with fierce venom should be treated like those bitten by snakes. One should drink *trivṛt* in a quantity equal to that of *taṇḍulīyaka*, mixed with clarified butter. 37.25d–38.1a [The physician] should administer this for the purpose of purging. It is beneficial when combined with honey and sugar. It is effective against poison, fever, and abdominal distension. It is a remedy for all types of poisoning. It is a supreme medicine for those afflicted by poison. It is the best among all purgatives. It is a destroyer of all poisons. It is a great medicine for those suffering from poison. its color is indistinct, it is slightly mobile, and is accompanied by a mild itching and pain. (61)
In the second [stage], it appears like a needle-prick; at its edges it is elevated as if covered with small pustules,
with distinct coloration, depressed in the center, itchy, and resembling a glandular swelling.
In the second stage, it is excessively elevated at the edges and appears as if covered with pustules;

in the third stage, accompanied by fever and causing horripilation, it consists of red circles, resembles a shallow bowl, is characterized by intense pricking pain, and has secretions from the hair follicles.
In the fourth stage, a great swelling with discharge occurs in the pores of the skin, accompanied by fever, dyspnea, and vertigo;
in the fifth stage, it produces various disorders born from the provocation of the poison.
"In the sixth [day] it pervades the vital points (marmāṇi), and in the seventh it destroys life.
Based on this, one should distinguish between sharp, medium, and inferior poisons. (65)
On the sixth day, the poison reaches the vital points (*marmāṇi*); within twenty-one nights, it is entirely pacified.
Now, in the case of one bitten by a spider (*lūtā*), one should quickly excise the bite with a surgical instrument.
37.66dv One should extract the sting with a surgical instrument and cauterize it with *jāmbavauṣṭha* and other [remedies], but one should not cauterize a case where pitta is predominant.
[One should avoid cauterizing] a wound that is rough, has torn hair, or is located in a vital organ (*marman*), a joint, or similar sensitive areas.
One should not cut or burn a spreading bite;
rather, one should apply medicinal ointments mixed with honey and rock salt to the burnt area.
One should not cut [the vessel] nor cauterize it;
rather, one should subsequently sprinkle it with very cold decoctions derived from milk-exuding trees.
One should remove the blood from all sides using horns and the like, or even by means of venesection.
Then, cooling sprinklings and ointments should be applied with *bodhi*, *śleṣmātaka*, and *akṣa*; with *phalinī*, the two types of *niśā*, honey, and ghee; and with that which is called *padmaka*.
Then, cold sprinklings and ointments [should be applied],
made from *bodhi*, *śleṣmātaka*, and *akṣika* (or *akṣaja*), as well as from *phalinī*, the two types of *niśā*, and *śreṣṭhā*.
This universal remedy is effective against all types of spiders and insects without exception;
it is prepared with the two kinds of turmeric, pattaṅga, mañjiṣṭhā, nata, and kesarā. (71)
The variety called Campaka, containing honey and ghee, is superior to the previous one;
likewise is the one prepared with cow-dung juice, sugar, ghee, and honey. (72)
Similarly, [one may use] cow dung, apāmārga, manohvā, dārvī, dhyāmaka, gairika,
nata, elā, kuṣṭha, marica, yaṣṭyāhvā, ghee, and honey.
There is the mountain named A-gada-mandara, and likewise another called Gandha-mādana;
[these are adorned] with nata, lodhra, vacā, kaṭvī, pāṭhā, elā, pattra, and saffron.
Mañjiṣṭhā, śleṣmātaka, rajanī, suvahā, śirīṣa, pālindī, along with sindhuvāra, elā, candana, and kanaka, destroy poison. (74+1)
One should employ purificatory therapy for those with many morbid humors (doṣas) who are resistant to poison;
[the drugs used are] yaṣṭyāhva, madana, aṅkolla, jālinī, and sindhuvārikā. (75)

In cases of severe poisoning involving many *doṣas*, one should administer [the powder] of *jālinī* and *sindhuvārita* along with anti-poisonous drugs; having drunk this with *jyeṣṭha* water when *kapha* is predominant, one will quickly vomit up the poison.
Or the leaf, bark, root, and fruit of the śirīṣa tree, like the root of the vaṅkola. // 76 //
One should cause purgation with the root of *aṅkolla* as described for its fruit, or with *triphalā*, *nīlinī*, *trivṛt*, and other such drugs.
Once the burning sensation, swelling, and other symptoms have subsided, one should extract the *karṇikā* (the central plug) from the ulcer.
37.77b–v: With *phalinī*, *trivṛt* and others;
with safflower, cow-tusk, *svarṇakṣīrī*, and pigeon dung;
likewise with *trivṛt*, rock salt, and *dantī*—this is the extraction of the *karṇikā*. 78.
Safflower, the flower of *go-danta*, *svarṇakṣīrī*, pigeon dung,
and the root of *uttaravāruṇī* combined with bamboo scrapings— this is the supreme means for causing the falling of the ear-studs.
And likewise, rock salt, kuṣṭha, dantī, and kaṭukadaugdhika [are used]. // 79 //
At the time of the falling of the pericarp, one should nourish [the plant] with the root of *rāja-kośātakī*, or with yeast produced from churning, along with anti-poisonous substances. (80)
Or the dregs produced from churning, or the scum produced from churning;
one should nourish [the patient] with anti-poisonous substances and perform the entire function of oleation using ghee alone.
It is like oil for the increase of poison, or like grass for a fire.
One should increase the oil with poison, just as fire consumes grass and weeds. [The ingredients are:
hribera, vaikaṅkata, gopakanyā, mustā, śamī, candana, ṭuṇṭuka;
śaivāla, nīlotpala, vakra, yaṣṭī, tvak, nākulī, padmaka, and rāṭhamadhya.
Mustā, śamī, candana, tinduka,
rajanī, ghana, sarpalocanā, kaṇa, śuṇṭhī, kaṇamūla,
citraka, varuṇa, aguru, bilva, pāṭalī, picumanda, āmaya, śelu, and kesara. // 83 //
37.83–84. Varuṇa, aguru, bilva, pāṭalā, bilva, candana, nata, utpala, śuṇṭhī, pippalī, nicula, vetasa, kuṣṭha;
śukti, śāka, vara, pāṭali, bhārgī, sindhuvāra, karaghāṭa, and varāṅga.

37.84c–d: Oyster shell, *śābaraka*, *pāṭalī*, *bhārgī*, *sindhuvāra*, *karahāṭa*, and *varāṅga*— these excellent remedies, when applied as a drink, collyrium, snuff, ointment, or sprinkling, ward off bile, phlegm, wind, and spider-poison,
just as those established in virtuous conduct ward off evil destinies.

These [remedies] tear apart [the afflictions] as if they were evil destinies; these tear apart [the afflictions] as if they were wrong views; these ward off [the afflictions] as if they were wrong thoughts. Lodhra should be used, along with padmaka, lotus pollen, that which is called kālīya, and red sandalwood.
The kāntā flower, dugdhinīkā, lotus stalk, and spiders destroy [the fetus] through all their actions. // 86 //
In the Uttarasthāna:
Lālana, Capala, Hasira, Cikkira, Ajira, Kaṣāyadanta, Kulaka, Kokila, Kapila, and Asita. (1)
Hasira, cikrira, ajana; hasira, cikkira, ajara; hasira, cikila, ajira;
Aruṇa, Śabara, Śveta, Kapota, Palita, and Undura.
The chuchundara and the one called rasāla—these are the eighteen types of mice. // 2 //
38.2b The pigeon, the *palita*, the *unduru*; 38.2c the *chucchundara* called *balāsa*, the *chucchundara* [called] *rasālākṣa*;
38.2d and eighteen species of mice.
Wherever their semen falls, or where they touch with limbs smeared by semen, that body part becomes afflicted by blood, turning pale. (3)
Knots, swelling, urticaria, circular patches, vertigo, loss of appetite, cold fever, excessive pain, exhaustion, shivering, and a splitting sensation in the joints [occur]. // 4 //
38.4ab Knots, swelling, suppuration, horripilation, discharge, fainting, persistence for a long time,
vomiting of phlegm-associated rat-suckling young, and thirst [are the symptoms]. (5)

In the case of rat-poison associated with phlegm (śleṣman), characterized by excessive urination and vomiting of undigested matter, the rat-poison spreads throughout the body; it is difficult to treat and recurs again and again.
Fainting, swelling of the limbs, discoloration, moisture, loss of hearing, and fever. // 6 //
Heaviness of the head, salivation, vomiting of blood—these are the signs of incurability; as well as a swollen bladder, discolored lips, and being covered with nodules resembling rats.

One should avoid food that has the odor of a muskrat or is contaminated by a rat; for in a dog, the humors characterized by an excess of phlegm reside in the consciousness-carrying channels and affect the consciousness itself.
Stealing away [the vital essence], they cause an extremely terrible agitation of the bodily constituents (dhātus);
drooling, blind, and deaf, he runs about in every direction. (9)
With his tail, jaw, and shoulders drooping, suffering headache, and with his face bent down—
the one bitten by that [insect] falls asleep, and black blood flows from him.
Subsequently, pain in the heart and head, fever, stiffness, thirst, and fainting arise;
by this, other vipers that strike with their fangs should also be understood. (11)
Pain in the heart and head, fever, and stiffness, followed by thirst and the onset of fainting,
occur in one struck by the fang of a venomous serpent.
Jackals, mules, horses, bears, leopards, tigers, wolves, and the like [are the presiding deities];
itching, piercing pain, discoloration, numbness, moisture, fever, and vertigo [are the symptoms]. (12)
Burning sensation, redness, pain, suppuration, swelling, and the bursting of glandular knots; tearing of the bite site, eruptions, and circular patches with central protuberances. // 13 //
In all cases, the symptoms are present when there is poison, but they are the opposite when there is no poison;
however, one who has been bitten perishes by imitating the movements and cries of the creature that bit him.

And seeing that very same [reflection] suddenly in mirrors, water, and so forth, one who would be terrified of water even though not bitten by it [would be terrified] through the hearing of sounds, the touch of contact, and the sight of forms. (15)
38.15 One should also avoid that [person] known as "Water-Terror" who has been bitten by [the snake] with sounds, touches, or sights.
For one merely bitten by a rat, one should cauterize the bite with a reed.
Alternatively, by using a mirror [to inspect], there may be intense pain in the ear-canal;
one should then drain the bite if it is burnt, or if it has been incised, one should apply an ointment. // 17 //
38.17c–d: Having cauterized the bite, one should drain it; 38.17d: and having incised it, one should apply a plaster made of *śirīṣa*, *rajanī*, *vakra*, saffron, and *amṛtavallī*;
or with soot from a house (*agāradhūma*), *mañjiṣṭhā*, *rajanī*, and the best salt (*lavaṇottama*).
The ointment conquers the poison of rats and causes the *karṇikā* to fall away;
then, having washed it with acidic substances and subsequently with water, one should apply the ointment again. (19)
38.19d Furthermore, one should apply a paste made from *pālindī*, white *kaṭabhī*, the root of *bilva*, and *guḍūcī*;
or other drugs that destroy poison and swelling, or one should quickly perform venesection. 20.
38.20 Or one should quickly have a vein bled; emesis should be induced with decoctions of *nīlinī*, as well as those of *śukākhyā* and *aṅkolla*.
