[One may also use] the fruit of *kośātakī*, *śukākhyā*, and *jīmūtaka*. 38.21.

38.21 Having powdered kośavatī, that which is called śukā, and madana, one should drink them with curd and vomit the poison; or else, vacā, madana, jīmūta, and kuṣṭha, ground with urine [should be drunk]. 38.22.
It should be drunk according to the previous method; it removes all poison from rats.
A purgative consisting of a paste of trivṛt, nīlī, and triphalā is recommended. (23)
38.23c–d For purgation,
the heartwood of *śirīṣa* and its fruits are used; for head-purgation (errhines),
collyrium mixed with cow-dung juice and the fine powder of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) is employed.
38.24c–d: Cow-dung juice mixed with the fine powder of the three pungents (vyoṣa) is used as a collyrium. 38.25: Cow-dung juice combined with honey and kapittha is a beneficial electuary (avalehana).
Ghee prepared with the root of taṇḍulīyaka is beneficial when taken as a drink.

38.25b-v For use as a linctus (avalehana), honey should be combined with the two types of niśā, kaṭabhī, raktā, yaṣṭyāhvā, and amṛtā; or else, [the linctus] prepared with the root of āsphota, or indeed the "five kāpittha" formulation.
A decoction of sindhuvāra, nata, the roots of śigru and bilva, punarnavā, vacā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, and jīmūta, mixed with honey—[this is used for sprinkling]. (27)
One afflicted by *mūṣikā* (rat-bite) should drink *sindhuvāra*, *nata*, *śigru*, the root of *bilva*, and *punarnavā*, while eating rice with curd;
or alternatively, one should drink the seeds of *śarapuṅkhā* ground into a powder with buttermilk (*takra*).
Alternatively, a paste made from the root of *aṅkolla* ground with goat's urine, when employed for both drinking and as an external application, destroys all types of rat poison. (29)

38.29c–30. When combined for drinking or as an external application, one should drink the pulp of *kapittha*, *tilaka*, *tila*, and *aṅkolla* roots along with cow urine; or one may drink the flower-cluster of *tilaka* with cow milk.
One should drink the pulp of the *kapittha* fruit as a *tilaka*,
or drink the stalks of sesame and *aṅkola*, or else the flower-clusters of the *tilaka*.
Alternatively, one may drink the root of *sairyaka* with honey and rice-water;
or water placed inside a bitter gourd (*kaṭukālābu*) and left to soak overnight. (31)

Or one should drink water that has been left to stand overnight. The roots of *sindhuvāra*, cat-bone, poison, and *nata*, ground with water, constitute a medicinal preparation (*agada*) that destroys rat-poison when administered as a nasal drop and by other means. (38.31–32)
The remaining rat-poison becomes aggravated at the sight of clouds, or at times when there is an increase in the causes for the aggravation of the *doṣas*, according to their respective natures. (33)
38.33–34ab. Regarding the residual poison of a rat, all therapeutic measures should be applied there according to the specific condition;
likewise, those remedies specifically prescribed for each case, as well as those that remove *dūṣīviṣa* (latent or chronic poison), should be employed.
For a bite by a rabid dog, one should cauterize the wound with warm clarified butter and apply various anti-poisonous medicinal pastes; furthermore, one should drink aged ghee.
And for him, a quick purgative should be administered combined with the milky sap of the Arka plant;
three palas of water boiled with the roots of Aṅkolla and the other [plants], along with one pala of clarified butter. (36)
38.36–37. Or, one should drink white *punarnavā* together with the fruit of *dhattūra*, combined with the milky sap of *arka*;
or likewise, a mixture of sesame paste, oil, the milk of *rūpikā*, and jaggery.
White *punarnavā* as well,
the milk of *rūṣikā* with jaggery— this destroys the venom of a rabid dog, just as the wind scatters a dense mass of clouds.
One should perform the ritual bathing accompanied by mantras, medicinal herbs, and precious gems. // 38 //
Wounds inflicted by the claws or teeth of quadrupeds or bipeds swell and suppurate, accompanied by redness, fever, discharge, and pain. (39)

38.39dv–40. A plaster made of *somavalka*, *aśvakarṇa*, *gojihvā*, *haṃsapādikā*, the two types of *rajanī*, and *gairika* removes the poison from nails and teeth, as well as fever, discharge, and pain.
The Uttarasthāna [declares]:
Longevity, mindfulness, intelligence, health, youthfulness, magnificence of luster, complexion, and voice, and the arising of strength in the body and the sense faculties. // 1 //
Through the elixir (rasāyana), one attains perfection of speech, virility, and beauty;
for rasāyana is indeed the means for obtaining the excellence of the bodily constituents, such as rasa and the rest. // 2 //
39.2cv Indeed, this is the means for attaining the seven [qualities];

it should be applied by one who has conquered the self, during the first or middle stage of life, and who is affectionate, has undergone bloodletting, and is thoroughly purified in every respect. // 3 //
For when the body is impure, the practice of alchemy or aphrodisiacs is as fruitless as dyeing a soiled cloth. // 4 //
39.4dv Like dye on a cloth, [the result] is fruitless;

the sages know two types of application for elixirs (*rasāyana*): the primary is the "entering the hut" method (*kuṭīprāveśika*), and the other is the "exposure to wind and sun" method (*vātātapika*). // 5 //
In a pure place, having obtained the necessary materials, in a palace that is windless and free from fear,
in an auspicious region toward the north, one should construct a three-chambered house with fine windows.
In a windless, fearless, and righteous palace,
having obtained the necessary implements in the city, one should [construct it] in the auspicious northeastern direction,
in a place not overrun by smoke, heat, dust, serpents, women, fools, and the like.
One should have a well-cleaned hut prepared, equipped with ready medical supplies. // 7 //
Then, on an auspicious day, having honored those worthy of honor, he, being pure, should enter;
there, purified by cleansing rites, he becomes happy and regains his strength. (8)

A celibate student, endowed with fortitude, full of faith, and having conquered his senses, is devoted to the practice of generosity, ethical conduct, compassion, truthfulness, vows, and righteousness. // 9 //
Devoted to the recollection of the deities, moderate in sleep and wakefulness, taking medicine as his favorite, and possessing gentle speech, he should begin the elixir. (10)
One who loves medicine and speaks kindly should begin the rejuvenative therapy (*rasāyana*).
One should drink *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, rock salt (*saindhava*), ginger (*nāgara*), *vacā*, turmeric (*haridrā*), long pepper (*pippalī*), *vella*, and jaggery (*guḍa*) with warm water. (39.10cd–11)

A person who has first been lubricated and fomented is properly purged by that [medicine]; thereafter, for one whose body is purified and who has undergone the regimen of gradual dietary restoration (saṃsarjana), [the medicine is administered]. // 12 //
39.12ab A person who has first been lubricated and fomented is thereby properly purified.

39.12cd–13ab One should administer barley-gruel mixed with ghee for three nights, five nights, or seven nights, until purification is achieved; or alternatively, until the old feces have been eliminated.

Thus, one who knows what is wholesome for each individual should examine everything and administer a medicinal elixir for the prepared stomach, using whatever is deemed appropriate for that person. (14)
One thousand *pathyā* fruits, combined with three times as many *dhātrī* fruits, along with two hundred and fifty palas of the five groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*). (15)
Having boiled [the ingredients] in ten times the amount of water until the liquid remains at one-tenth its original volume,
one should then crush the Vijayā and Āmalaka fruits, removing their seeds.
Having strained that decoction, one should add one kuḍava each of cinnamon, cardamom, musta, turmeric, long pepper, agallochum, and sandalwood. (17)
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, kanaka, śaṅkhapuṣpī, vacā, plava, yaṣṭyāhvaya, and viḍaṅga—these, powdered together, should exceed one tula in weight. (18)

One should cook half a bhāra of sugar candy, three vessels of clarified butter, and two [vessels] of oil; when all that has been cooked over the fire and reached the consistency of a linctus (leha), [it is ready]. 19.
When the snow has melted, one should mix it with three hundred parts of honey;
then, having stirred it with a churning stick, one should place it in a vessel of ghee. (20)
That which does not obstruct the intake of food is known as the "single measure" (ekamātra).
In this case, sixty-day-old rice with milk is desired as the meal once [the previous meal] has been digested. // 21 //

39.21b–22. A single measure of this is prescribed for them; the Vaikhānasas, the Bālakhilyas, and others whose wealth is their austerity, having consumed this blessed elixir ordained by Brahmā, [attained their state].
The Vaikhānasas and Bālikhilyas became free from weariness, fatigue, wrinkles, gray hair, and disease; endowed with intelligence, memory, and strength, they possessed immeasurable lifespans.
One thousand *abhayā* and *āmalaka* fruits, free from blemish, combined with one thousand *pippalī*, should be dissolved in the lye of fresh *palāśa* leaves and placed in a vessel. (24)
Once the alkali has been consumed, one should add it after being dried in the shade and powdered, along with a quarter-part of sugar and four times as much honey and ghee. (25)
Once the decoction has been consumed,

one should place that jar of ghee in the ground and leave it for six months; then, having extracted it, one should consume it at dawn according to one's digestive capacity and always maintain a regular diet as usual.
Having buried [the preparation] and left it for six months, one should extract it, consume it at dawn according to one's strength,
and thus employ it; remaining free from disease and devoid of old age, one shall live for a hundred years.
He lives endowed with strength, physical vigor, a healthy body, memory, intelligence, and so forth, especially in an eminent manner. // 27 //
39.27–28. Thus, when the head of a healthy *ārdra-palāśa* tree has been cut off, that wound—
two cubits deep and located within— should be filled with fresh *āmalaka* fruits until no part remains to be used.

39.28 When the head has been cut off, it should be carved out from the root, wrapped with *darbha* grass, and smeared with lotus mud; then, having ignited it with wild cow-dung, one should apply fomentation (*sveda*) in a windless place. 29.
A person should eat those steamed āmalaka fruits to their satisfaction, combined with honey and ghee;
thereafter, one should drink boiled milk as much as desired and subsist on that alone for one month. (30)
In that regard, one must carefully avoid both things to be avoided and things to be touched; even cold water should not be touched with the hand.
Then, on the eleventh day after that has passed, his hair, teeth, and nails fall out.
39.31 He should not touch even cold water with his hand;
then, within just a few days, he becomes handsome, inexhaustible among women, and equal to an elephant in vigor.
Possessing distinguished intelligence, strength, wisdom, and courage, he lives for a thousand years.
The ten roots, balā, musta, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, utpala, the two parṇinīs, pippalī, śṛṅgī, medā, tāmalakī, and truṭī. // 33 //
Jīvantī, joṅgaka, drākṣā, pauṣkara, candana, śaṭhī, punarnavā, ṛddhi, kākolī, kākanāsā, and the two types of amṛtā. // 34 //
39.34–35. One pala each of punarnavā, the two types of kākolī, kākanāsā, amṛtāhvayā (guḍūcī), vidārī,
and the root of vṛṣa should be boiled together with five hundred fruits of dhātrī in one droṇa of water.
From that [decoction], having taken the juice remaining after one-fourth, as well as the bones and *āmalaka* fruits,
one should fry them with twelve *palas* of oil and clarified butter.
When that liquid has reached the consistency of the residue of boiled rice, one should cook it like a linctus (leha), adding half a *tulā* of sugar candy (*matsyaṇḍikā*).
Once it is cooked, add half as much oil, honey, and four *palas* of *tavakṣīrī*.
39.37cv When it has cooled, one should add half as much of the fat as honey, two palas of long pepper (pippalī), and a quarter-pala each of the four aromatics (caturjāta) and long pepper (kaṇā).
Then, staying in a private chamber and eating wholesome food, one should lick the dose of this electuary (avaleha). 38.

39.38bv Four parts of the *caturjāta* and half a part of *kaṇā*; 39.38dv Remaining in a small hut while eating wholesome food— this is the *cyavanaprāśa*, having consumed which the sage Cyavana [attained his youth].
Though worn out by old age, he remained a delight to the eyes of women. // 39 //
It dispels cough, dyspnea, fever, wasting, heart disease, and gout; it also removes disorders of the urine and semen, as well as hoarseness of voice. (40)
It promotes the growth of the limbs for children, the elderly, those who are wounded, those who are emaciated, and those who are thin. // 41ab //
Intelligence, memory, luster, freedom from disease, longevity, and the proper functioning of the vital winds. // 41cd //
When used according to the prescribed method, it produces exhilaration in women, as well as strength for the senses and for the digestive fire.
With madhuka, tālakṣīrī, pippalī, and sindhujanman;
with the various metals, gold, vacā, honey, and ghee. (42)
Equal parts of Triphalā combined with sugar constitute an elixir (rasāyana) that destroys all diseases and bestows intelligence, longevity, memory, and wisdom. (43)

39.43–44. Combined with sugar or mixed with silver, it is an elixir (*rasāyana*). One should administer the fresh juice of *maṇḍūkaparṇī* according to one's digestive fire, the powder of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* with milk, the juice of *guḍūcī* along with its roots and flowers, and the paste (*kalka*) of *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
These elixirs bestow longevity, destroy diseases, and increase strength, digestive fire, complexion, and voice; they are clarifying, and among them, *śaṅkhapuṣpī* is especially clarifying. (45)

Especially pure are *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *nalada*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *payasyā*, *madhuka*, *candana*, *sārivā*, *ugragandhā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the three pungents (*kaṭukatriya*), the two types of *haridrā*, *paṭola*, and salt; with these well-ground together— 39.45d–46.

Having consumed *śaṅkhapuṣpī* boiled with milk, seasoned with ghee, and mixed with a threefold amount of juice, even a dull-witted person will become eloquent, a retainer of what has been heard, possessed of inspired intelligence, and free from disease. (47)
One who retains what they have heard, possesses eloquence,
and is free from disease—
[such a person should take] ghee prepared with milk, along with pieces of gold and with the pastes of lotus stalks, lotus roots, filaments, petals, and seeds.
That place, renowned on earth as Pañcāravinda, was frequented by those whose manly strength and prowess had utterly failed. 48.
39.48 That ghee known as *pañcāravinda*, which possesses exalted potency, is prepared from the stalk, bulb, petal, and filament of the blue lotus; it is celebrated as a second [type of] ghee.
Ghee made from four blue water-lilies (*kuvalaya*) along with golden leaves is purifying even for cows, let alone for humans.
Brāhmī, vacā, rock salt (saindhava), śaṅkhapuṣpī, matsyākṣaka, brahmasuvarcalā, and indrī—these should each be three barley-corns; likewise, two barley-corns of gold and one of poison. 50.

One should take one pala of ghee at a time and, once it has been digested, consume a meal rich in ghee along with honey; by practicing this for a year, one gains superior intelligence, memory, and wisdom. (51)
Practicing this, endowed with superior intelligence, mindfulness, and appearance,
and having transcended old age, disease, drowsiness, laziness, fatigue, and exhaustion,
he lives for a full hundred years, radiant with glory, majesty, beauty, and luster.

39.52–53. Endowed with beauty, splendor, luster, and a noble form, one is especially freed from leprosy, vitiligo, abdominal tumors, poisons, fevers, insanity, artificial poisons, and stomach ailments; furthermore, by this [remedy], malevolent spells (kṛtyā) produced by Atharvan mantras and the like, as well as exceedingly powerful wind-disorders (vāta), are pacified.
At the onset of autumn, one should extract Nāgabalā during the Puṣya conjunction;
then, one should drink a handful of the powdered root with milk. (54)
Then, one should drink the root, measuring an *akṣa*, ground into powder with milk;
or one should lick it with honey and ghee, subsisting on milk and abstaining from solid food.
By practicing this for a year, one will live for a hundred years, endowed with strength. (39.54–55)

Gokṣuraka, including its roots, with its flower-heads, dried in the shade and well-powdered, should be thoroughly saturated with its own juice; then, one who drinks a supreme dose of it, equal to a handful (prasṛti), [attains the desired result]. // 56 //
39.56–57. He who drinks two *prasṛta* measures of this [milk] with milk itself, and eats *śāli* rice when it has been digested, shall— by the consumption of two *tulās*—
become capable, handsome, fortunate, long-lived for a hundred years, lustful, and like a bull standing in a herd of cows.
One who drinks the fresh root of Vārāhī with milk for a month, while abstaining from food for one month and subsisting on milk and rice for the other month, shall conquer old age. (58)
One should lick the fine powder of its rhizome, well-saturated with its own juice, mixed with ghee and honey; or one should drink the ghee prepared by cooking it with those same ingredients. // 59 //

39.59cv One should lick [the powder] combined with ghee and honey; likewise, one should take vidārī, atibalā, balā, madhuka, vāyasī, śreyasī, pathyā, dhātrī, sthirā, and amṛtā, combined with ghee and honey.
39.60–61 One should consume *jīvantī*, *śreyasī*, *maṇḍūkī*, *śaṅkhakusumā*, *vājigandhā*, and *śatāvarī*,
which bestow intelligence, wisdom, stability of youth, and strength.

A wise person should employ [these] which bestow intelligence, memory, youthfulness, stability, and strength; Citraka is to be known by its flowers as yellow, white, or black according to their respective types.
Thus, in successive stages, he becomes endowed with qualities through the prescribed method of elixir therapy.
Then, having dried the root in the shade and reduced it to powder for a month, the ascetic should lick it with clarified butter, or drink it with honey and clarified butter, or with milk. (63)
Or, by eating food prepared with water, one lives for a hundred years free from disease;
being wise, strong, handsome, well-built, and possessing a radiant digestive fire.

Licked with oil for a month, it destroys even the most difficult-to-overcome wind disorders (*vāta*); drunk with urine, it cures leucoderma and leprosy (*śvitra-kuṣṭha*); drunk with buttermilk (*takra*), it cures ailments arising in the anus. (65)
39.65b–v: It destroys even most severe disorders of Vata.
One should cause well-nourished bhallātaka fruits to be stored in a heap of grain;
having collected them in the summer, one should apply them in the winter to the body with sweet, unctuous, and cold substances.
Having processed those [drugs] again with sweet, unctuous, and cold substances,
one should boil them in water possessing eight qualities until eight parts remain; that decoction, mixed with milk, should be drunk while cold.
One should increase that decoction, reduced to one-eighth, daily by adding one *aruṣkara* fruit for three weeks; thereafter, one should add three fruits each day.
From that point, one should decrease them by forty [days] as in the case of the increase;
one should employ [the medicine] for a thousand [days] over seven weeks. (69)

39.69 Even for seven weeks, one who has restrained the self and subsists on ghee, milk, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice should likewise practice for three times that duration even after the formal application is concluded.
Even at the conclusion of the practice, one should perform the ritual;
he obtains unprecedented blessings and especially the brilliance of fire.
He becomes free from urinary disorders, worms, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and the defects of excessive fat.
One obtains the aforementioned blessings by means of a steaming vessel filled with crushed *bhallātaka* fruits that have been shattered and freed from their husks;
this vessel is placed inside a jar buried in the ground and smeared with black clay.
39.72b–73. One should fill [the vessel] with well-pulverized *bhallātaka* fruits and surround it on all sides; then one should cook it over a mild fire of cow dung.
When its own juice exudes, one should collect it on another day.
One should cook this with a gentle fire of cow-dung;

having consumed this expressed juice mixed with one-eighth part honey and double the amount of ghee, and restraining oneself according to the previously mentioned regimen, one obtains those very same benefits.
One should consume this fresh juice [of bhallātaka] after the mature fruits have been processed by cooking. Having taken one āḍhaka measure of these bhallātaka fruits,
one should rub them with fine particles of brick powder, wash them with water, and dry them with wind.
One should boil the withered parts in a water-pot until reduced to one-quarter, strain it through ghee, and let it cool;
then one should boil that decoction again together with a pot of milk until one-quarter remains. (76)

39.76bv When reduced to one-quarter, the remaining ghee is strained off; 39.76bv When reduced to one-quarter, the ghee is strained off once it has cooled; 39.76bv Reduced to one-quarter, it is removed and allowed to cool; 39.76cv That decoction should be boiled again;
39.76dv Together with a jar of milk, until it stands at one-quarter [of its original volume].
One should add an equal measure of cooked ghee to that, and mix it at will with sugar and powders;
once these have become a single mass through stirring with a whisk, it should be placed well-protected in grain for seven nights. (77)

39.77 One should employ a *prastha* of clarified butter cooked with that [mixture] in equal measure, mixed with sugar and the powders; one should employ it clear, mixed with sugar and the powders. Once these have become a single mass...

He who, having consumed that cooked essence of nectar at dawn by stirring it with a ladle, drinks water, milk, or broth as desired, becomes endowed with memory, intelligence, strength, wisdom, and the essence of goodness; fair as a mass of gold, he attains a long life. (78)

From three hundred palas of droṇa water boiled down to one āḍhaka, one should prepare a vessel of sesame oil containing one pala each of tiktā, the two types of viṣā, varā, girijanman, and tārkṣya; when properly processed, this is supreme for the eradication of all forms of kuṣṭha.
Having boiled three hundred *droṇas* of water with the wound-inducing [herbs], one should cook it with *tiktā*, the two types of *niśā*, *vacā*, *girijanma*,
and *tārkṣya*; or with *tiktā*, the two types of *niśā*, *varā*, *girijanma*, and *tārkṣya*.
With *tiktā*, the two types of *viṣā*, *vacā*, *girijanma*, and *tārkṣya* (39.79c),
together with *āmalaka*, *śukti*, the cream of curd (*dadhisara*), or oil (80a).
Together with jaggery, milk, ghee, or barley flour. // 80b //
With sesame, honey, meat-mince, or soup. // 80c //
It bestows physical beauty, cures skin diseases, is supremely purifying, and promotes longevity.
Bhallātaka fruits are sharp and, when digested, are like fire; yet, when administered according to the prescribed method, they become like nectar. (81)
39.81–82 When prepared according to the prescribed method,
there is no disease born of phlegm (kapha) and no kind of constipation that bhallātaka would not quickly destroy; it bestows the strength of the digestive fire.
It quickly bestows digestive power;
however, one should especially avoid exposure to wind and heat,
as well as horse-gram, curd, fermented gruel, oil massage, and the use of fire.
There are trees named Tubarakas growing on the shore of the western ocean, their foliage tossed by the wind stirred by the agitation of waves and billows. (84)
From them, one should take the well-ripened fruits at the onset of the rainy season;
having extracted the marrow from the fruits, dried it, and ground it into powder, [one should proceed].
Having extracted the marrow from the fruits and dried it,
one should grind it into a powder and press it in a vat like sesame seeds, or alternatively, boil it like safflower.
That oil, having been collected again, should be cooked until the water is completely evaporated.
That oil, mixed with ghee once again— that oil, having been thoroughly processed— that oil, having been collected once more,
should be removed from the heat and placed in a heap of dried cow-dung for about a fortnight.
Having been lubricated and fomented, and having had his impurities removed, he should then be lifted up from that [bed] after a fortnight.

Having extracted [the oil] from the [sesame] husks, one who exerts effort, having fasted for three meals, should drink a palmful of the purified oil in the morning on an auspicious day, using this mantra: (39.87–88)
O essence of wine, O you of great potency, purify all the elements!
Acyuta, whose hands hold the conch, discus, and mace, commands you. (89)
"O marrow-essence, O one of great potency, Acyuta commands you:
by that [command], his humors (doṣas) shall repeatedly move upward and downward. Therefore, in the evening, he should drink cold gruel (yavāgū) without fat or salt. (39.89–90)
The doshas are eliminated repeatedly; one should drink the oil for five days at a time, thus avoiding things that must be avoided.
Eating food with mung bean broth for a fortnight, one is liberated from all types of skin diseases.
39.91b–92. In this manner, one should avoid those things that are to be avoided.
Then, having properly prepared [the medicine] in three times the amount of khadira decoction and stored it as previously described, one should drink it for a month while remaining well-restrained.
Having anointed his body with that and consuming the prescribed food, one should quickly cure a man afflicted by leprosy by means of this application. (93)
With a broken voice and bloodshot eyes, his limbs were withered and infested with worms.
With broken voice and bloodshot eyes,
his limbs shattered and covered with worms.
If that same [milk] is drunk without the khadira, combined with ghee and honey, while consuming a diet of meat broth for a fortnight, it makes one live for two hundred years. (94)
If that same cooked meat broth is used as a nasal medication for fifty days,
it makes one possessed of a beautiful body, a retainer of what has been heard, and grants a lifespan of three hundred years.
Possessing a beautiful body, retaining his learning from the Vedas, free from wrinkles and gray hair, with steady memory, hair, and teeth.
Seeking the benefits of rejuvenation (*rasāyana*), one should administer five, eight, seven, or ten *pippalī* fruits with honey and clarified butter for one year. (96)
One should administer three *pippalī* fruits at a time before breakfast and after the meal for one month;
these *pippalīs* should have been processed with the alkali of *kiṃśuka* and fried in ghee.
39.97b–v: However, one desiring the qualities of *rasāyana* should consume [the powder] mixed with honey at the beginning of a meal.
For ten days, the dose should be increased by one *pippalī* daily, until on the tenth day one takes ten *pippalīs*.
39.98cv For ten days, one should increase [the dose] by ten [pippalīs] each day; 39.98dv One should increase the *daśapippalika* by one per day along with milk, and likewise decrease it again.
Once the medicine is digested, one should eat *ṣaṣṭika* rice with milk and ghee. 99.
This application of a thousand *pippalī* fruits is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
They should be ground into a paste and drunk by those with strong constitutions, or boiled and drunk by men of middling strength. (100)
For those of inferior strength, [the treatment] has been made cool after observing the defects and diseases. 100+(1)ab //

Having observed that the humors (doṣas) have been cooled and their strength diminished, one should administer [the medicine] in the same manner; specifically, one should administer two thousand [drops] with goat’s milk.
By these applications, long peppers (pippalī) cure cough, asthma, and throat obstruction. 101.
They destroy consumption, urinary disorders, malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, anemia, and irregular fevers; as well as swelling, vomiting, hiccups, splenic enlargement, and gout. (102)
One should smear an iron vessel with long pepper (*pippalī*) the size of half a *bilva* fruit at night;
in the morning, one should drink it with two handfuls of water, while eating, drinking, and acting as one desires for a year. (103)
Dry ginger, viḍaṅga, the three myrobalans, guḍūcī, yaṣṭīmadhu, haridrā, atibalā, balā, mustā, surāhvā, aguru, citraka, saugandhika, paṅkaja, and utpala flowers. (104)
39.104c–d. Mustā, śatāhvā, aguru, citraka, as well as the heartwood of dhava, aśvakarṇa, āsana, and bālapattra, should be used in the same manner as pippalī.
When each is separately smeared with iron filings, one shall live for a hundred years, free from disease and old age.

39.105b One should likewise employ the essences like long pepper (pippalī). 39.105c By means of the iron-ointment, one may live quite separately [from disease]. 39.105c By means of the iron-ointment, one may live quite separately [from disease].

And these elixirs (rasāyana), when combined with two handfuls of milk and applied as an iron ointment, produce an excellence of the previously mentioned qualities and a doubling of the lifespan. (106)

One who, eating in moderation and wholesome food, licks during autumn Somarājī processed with the juices of *āsana* and *khadira*, combined with honey, ghee, *śikhī*, *pathyā*, and iron powder, abandons the disorders resulting from the transformation of food (*pāriṇāmika-vikāra*), just as one abandons those arising from the nature of food itself. (107)
39.107b–108. He whose body is overwhelmed by severe leprosy (kuṣṭha) should eat *somarājī* according to the prescribed rule, combined with honey, ghee, medicinal herbs, and iron powder.
If he eats this *somarājī* for a year while accompanied by black sesame seeds, he will surpass [even the god] Soma in beauty of form.

Those who, having extracted the essence from well-prepared milk mixed with the powder of *soma*—the king of plants—from which the husks have been removed, lick it with honey, drink that very same buttermilk at the end. (109)
Those lepers, with their limbs falling away yet possessing newly grown fingers and noses, shone like trees that have sprouted fresh new shoots once more. (110)
39.110 For those suffering from leprosy with limbs being eaten away, whose bodies are scorched by cold, wind, and frost, whose bones are stiff, broken, crooked, or pained,
and who are afflicted by disorders of the wind (vāta), the procedure for garlic as a medicine shall now be described.
39.110+(1) For those whose bodies are scorched by cold winds,
whose bones are stiff, bent, crooked, and pained,
and for those afflicted by the wind-humor (vāta), this is the remedy.
Those drops of nectar which fell upon the ground from Rāhu’s throat when it was severed during his theft of the nectar attained the state of garlic.
Because he was born from the body of a Daitya, twice-born men do not eat him, for he was destroyed by the discus of Acyuta; yet,
as he was produced directly from the nectar of immortality, he is the foremost elixir.
One who has a predominance of phlegm (kapha) should consume garlic in the cold season or even in spring;
one afflicted by wind (vāta) may do so at the onset of the rainy season; or one may always consume it with the ease of summer.

39.113b–114. And in spring, one whose *kapha* is predominant— having been treated with oleation and purification, his body slender, his internal organs prepared with cold and sweet substances, and the courtyards of his attendants adorned with floral ear-ornaments and head-garlands— [should proceed].
At the end of spring, one should take the tubers of that plant grown in the Himalayas or the Śaka country,
remove their skins, and soak them at night with wine and other such liquors.
Having removed the bark at night, one should soak it with wine and other liquids; then,
having ground it with wine and other liquids, one should press its paste and its own juice through a clean cloth in the morning.
Combined with one-third part of well-fermented liquor. // 116 //
Or, having carefully considered what is appropriate, one may take an appropriate amount of liquor, or another [beverage], or buttermilk, or whey, or sour gruel at that very time. // 117 //

39.117 One should [prepare] the juice of liquor, or other substances, with oil, or with oil, ghee, muscle fat, marrow, milk, meat-broth, or individually with a decoction according to the disease, or even the juice alone. 118.
One should drink a mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa) each of milk, ghee, muscle fat, marrow,
and the juices of the meat of wild animals (dhanvamāṃsa), individually,
beforehand for the purification of the throat canal.
Furthermore, continuous fomentation is recommended during the stage of pain. // 119 //
In this condition, continuous sudation and the sudden sprinkling of cold water on the face are indicated during vomiting and fainting.
One should drink the remainder of the medicine once exhaustion has subsided and the *ojas* has regained its stability.
To prevent burning sensations, one should apply very cool ointments and wear garlands of pearls and camphor interspersed with water droplets.
One should wear a garland of pearls with water droplets,
or a garland of pearls and camphor;
a *kuḍava* is the maximum dose for this, while half of that is for camphor alone.
One should first practice taking one pala of ground marrow along with cooked rice.

When the previous meal has been digested, one should eat aged śāli rice—which is as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon—along with soups, milk, or the meat broths of animals that roam arid lands. 123.
In that case, when there is a continuous sensation of thirst, one should drink a single measure of wine mixed with water;
however, one who does not drink wine should drink sour gruel (āranāla), fruit-water, or *parisikthakā*.

39.124a In this case, one should drink only wine; 39.124b if thirst is increased, it should be taken mixed with water; 39.124b if there is an obstruction of thirst, it should be taken mixed with water;
39.124d fruit-water (phalāmbu) [is used for] *parisiñcikā*; 39.124d fruit-water (phalāmbu) [is used for] *parisitthikā*.
Sprinkled with fruit-water (39.124d), or that same paste mixed with an equal amount of ghee, stirred with a churning-stick in a vessel of ghee;
One may eat it after ten days have passed, or likewise together with animal fat.
Likewise, one may eat to one's heart's content various side dishes containing abundant garlic and asafoetida mixed with milk, or meat on a spit,
or *nimardaka* preparations combined with ghee and fermented vinegar, while consuming only light and meager food.
Or one may eat vimardakas mixed with ghee and sour gruel (śukta) as much as desired; eating light food,
one who is free from the affliction of pitta and blood but still covered by all other [dosic] veils [should proceed].
Or rather, in pure air, there exists no substance other than garlic. (127)

Garlic is certainly fatal for one who is free from pitta and blood disorders, yet is shrouded by all [other] coverings; for one who dislikes water, molasses, milk, meat, wine, and sour things; for one who lacks endurance; and for one with indigestion. (39.127–128)
39.128b For those who loathe meat, wine, and the like; 39.128c for one who does not wish to vomit, and in cases of indigestion;
39.128c–d and for those who are excessively dry or suffering from indigestion, one should administer a mild purgative at the end out of fear of provoking the *pitta*.
In this way, one fully enjoys the qualities of the elixir (rasāyana). // 129 //
That which, when mountains heated by the sun in summer vomit forth a liquid essence of the six metals such as gold that is like lac, is called *śilājatu*. (130)

All [substances] that are bitter and pungent, not excessively hot, and pungent in their post-digestive effect (pākataḥ), as well as those that are specifically scarifying (chedana), are highly recommended therein; among these, iron is especially praised. 131.
Shilājatu that smells like cow urine, is black, resembles guggulu resin, is free from gravel, is earthen, unctuous, not sour or astringent, and is soft and heavy, is the best. (132)
Recalling the suitability for those afflicted by disease, one should perform the infusion in an iron vessel;
first, it should be washed with pure water alone and dried, and thereafter it should be infused with decoctions. (133)

Having boiled the medicinal herbs for infusion together with an equal amount of *girija* (mica) in water eight times their weight, one should add the *girija* to that strained, warm decoction when it has been reduced to one-eighth.
Once it has reached a state of uniform consistency and is thoroughly dried, one should again throw it into the liquid;
in this manner, it should be saturated with its respective decoctions for seven turns. (135)

Then, for one who has been lubricated and purified, one should administer ghee prepared with bitter herbs for three days; likewise, one should administer [ghee] derived from the mountain (girija) for three days at a time.

39.136–137. Then, once the patient has been lubricated and purified, one should subsequently administer a suitable medicinal formulation with the soup of the three fruits (*triphalā*), *paṭolī*, and *madhuka*, taking into account the appropriate time.

Then, one should apply that which is suitable for yoga to him; indeed, one should employ that which is produced from stone (mercury), taking time into account. In this way, it becomes extremely beneficial for the body.
It suddenly produces all virtues and does not bring about misfortune. 138.

One karṣa, three karṣas, and seven karṣas for one week; half a pala, and one pala—these are considered, in sequence, the inferior, middling, and superior yogas of mercury produced from cinnabar. (139)
The term *saṃskṛta*, when applied to a consecrated body called *girijāhvaya* (named after the mountain-born goddess),
is joined either with copper, iron, silver, and gold, both individually or collectively.
One should stir it with milk to quickly obtain the fruit of an elixir (rāsa-āyana).
One should always avoid horse gram (kulattha), black nightshade (kākamācī), and pigeons. 141.

There is no disease on earth that can be cured which this stone-born [remedy] would not forcibly conquer when applied according to the rules at the appropriate time; furthermore, it bestows abundant vigor upon one who is already healthy. (142)

39.142b Even that which is born of stone, which one might not otherwise forcibly extract; 39.142d the *kuṭīpraveśa* (bed-chamber therapy) bestows abundant vigor upon the healthy man and is beneficial for those who possess leisure and attendants, like a necessary accessory.
But for those who act otherwise than this, the procedure is that of the Sun and the Maruts. // 143 //

39.143 Entering a hut is for those who are patient and whose [diseases] have been exhausted; the regimen of sun and air is for those who can endure wind and heat. Hereafter, the specific applications for those capable of enduring wind and heat will be described in detail.
These are pleasant modes of conduct which do not cause affliction even when the body perishes. // 144 //
Cold water, milk, honey, and ghee—each one individually, two at a time, three at a time, or all together—if drunk first, will preserve one's youth. (145)
By constantly eating two of each—molasses, honey, ginger, black pepper, or salt—one who follows this wholesome regimen shall live happily for a hundred years. (146)
For one who consumes harītakī after heating it in ghee and drinks that ghee, strength shall remain long in the body, just as a good deed performed once endures in a grateful person. (147)
If he eats this while drinking ghee, his body shall possess enduring strength,
just as grateful people remember a good deed performed even once.

For those men who eat wholesome food and lick the juice of *dhātrī*, honey, sugar, and ghee, the disorders of old age go to their destruction, like voluminous books that have been poorly grasped. (148)

For men who eat wholesome food and lick [this preparation], the powder of *dhātrī*, *kṛmighna*, *asana*, and heartwood, combined with oil, ghee, honey, and iron filings— by using this, a man’s youth and beauty shall remain undiminished. (39.148–149)

39.149dv The beauty of youth is exceedingly well-established; yet even that beauty of youth has perished. Iron filings produced from *vellabhava* and clarified butter mixed with honey have been kept for one year.
A strong man who licks [this preparation] from a small box fashioned from the essence of *bījaka* lives with black hair. // 150 //
39.150 Iron filings,
along with *vela*-derived [resin] and clarified butter, should be placed in a casket smeared with the essence of *bījaka* (39.150c), or prepared with the alkali of *sāmudgaka* (39.150c).
Those men who consume viḍaṅga, bhallātaka, and ginger combined with ghee and honey, cross over the river of old age, surging with the waves of disease, endowed with beauty. (151)
If men regularly consume triphalā that has been infused with khadirāsana decoction and saturated with ghee and honey, and they live free from disease, what is there to marvel at? (152)
If one lives free from old age by consuming *triphalā* combined with ghee and honey, what wonder is there in this?
[Likewise,] the juice of *bījaka*, which can be taken up with the fingers, along with sugar, honey, ghee, and *triphalā*.
Among men who practice virtue, even old age, though it has arrived, is surely turned back.
One should drink sugar, honey, ghee,
and the three myrobalans (triphalā), or one should drink half a pala of fresh *punarnavā* ground with milk for half a month.
Whether for two months, three times that, or a year, even when worn out, it shall become new again. // 154 //
They prescribe the same procedure for mūrvā, bṛhatī, aṃśumatī, and balā; for uśīra, pāṭhā, asana, and śārivā; and for kālānusārya, aguru, and candana, as well as for punarnavā. (155)
Those who consume ghee prepared with the paste and decoction of śatāvarī, combined with sugar, do not have their path of life snatched away by the thieves of disease. (156)
Yellow Ashwagandha, taken for half a month with milk, ghee, oil, or warm water, brings nourishment to the body of one who is emaciated, just as a good rain does for young crops. (157)
39.157b–d: Finely ground with ghee or oil, it is like a rain of water upon a young tree;
for those who consume a handful (*prakuñca*) of black sesame seeds every day, followed by a drink of cold water.
There is no small nourishment for the body, and the teeth remain firm until death. (158)

39.158b For one who eats [this] with the drinking of cold water, or who licks the powder of *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *āmalaka*, and *amṛtā* mixed with portions of ghee and honey, he becomes virile and firm, with the suffering of diseases pacified; having black hair, he lives for a hundred years. 159.
Licking it with ghee and honey,
or combining it with sesame seeds, *āmalaka* fruits, black *akṣa* fruits, or *harītakī* fruits, having crushed them together.
Those men who live like peacocks attain a delightful transformation. // 160 //
One who consumes stone, lac, honey, viḍaṅga, ghee, iron, abhayā, mercury, and tāpya will have the tissues of his weak body replenished within fifteen nights, just like the moon. (161)
Those who drink for one month every day the natural juice derived from *bhṛṅgarāja*, subsisting on milk, become endowed with strength and virility and attain a lifespan of a hundred years. (162)
39.162cd–163ab Even by using vacā for a month with milk, oil, or ghee, they attain a lifespan of a hundred years;
they become invincible in form to rākṣasas, wise, and possessed of pure and polished speech.
Even those who eat maṇḍūkaparṇī fried in ghee for a month while abstaining from other food live for a vast period of time, full of vigor and established in the excellence of youth and beauty. (164)
For one month, abstaining from other food, they should consume *maṇḍūkaparṇī* fried in ghee;
[this preparation] is made with fifty palas of *lāṅgalī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and iron.
In the fresh juice of Mārkava, one should prepare three hundred and sixty pills.

39.165b—from that which has been made into fifty palas; 39.165b—made into fifty palas. 39.165c—ground in the fresh juice of *mārkava*; 39.165c—having ground it in the fresh juice of *mārkava*. 39.165d—from three hundred pills.
One should eat half a pill that has been dried in the shade; subsequently, one should gradually consume the entire dose.
Having been purged, one should follow the regimen in sequence: thin gruel, thick gruel, soft porridge, meat broth, and boiled rice. (166)

One who has controlled their mind should eat half a pill made from [medicinal] powder dried in the shade, lubricated with ghee, for one month; after the month, they may act according to their own will in every respect.
However, undigested food must always be avoided with great effort. In this manner, one should employ this formulation for a year.

After one month, in every respect, he attains a state of self-willed activity; after a year, by thus employing this very yoga, even one afflicted with incurable diseases becomes free from illness. Even an old man shines forth, possessing powerful human effort.
One who possesses well-developed, broad limbs, ears, eyes, and so forth, lives for five hundred years like a youth. // 168 //
The gāyatrī, śikhī, śiṃśipā, āsana, śivā, vellā, akṣa, and kāruṣkara [trees]. // 169a //
Having ground *gāyatrī*, *śikhī*, *śiṃśipā*, *asana*, *śivā*, *vellā*, *akṣa*,
and *āruṣkara* and boiled them in water eighteen times [their weight], one should add pieces of sugar-candy.
Having ground [the ingredients] together with sugar and *ayomala*,
it is boiled in water increased eighteenfold;
or, having ground them, it is boiled in water increased sixteenfold.
One should cook it for three days in an iron vessel, stirring it with the rays of the sun.
One should cook it for three days in a vessel made of iron, stirring it with the rays of the sun;
thereafter, one should cook it over a mild fire until it stands at the consistency of a quarter-part [of its original mass], along with the iron fragments.

One part of clarified butter, one part of milk, two parts from the resin of *bhārgī*, three parts of *varā* [liquor], and four parts of *haiyaṅgavīna*—having combined these, one should prepare this in a black iron vessel. (170)

39.170b Two parts of *bhārgī* extract and three parts of *varā*; 39.170c and four parts of fresh butter (*haiyaṅgavīna*), combined separately with pure sugar-candy, white sugar, and honey, or this ghee may be used alone.
One acts according to one's own inclination in eating and drinking, not by practicing [the path] bit by bit. // 171 //
Then, with pure white sugar and honey, one should consume it in pala-measures;
by practicing this, the illustrious man becomes cleansed of sin, possessing the strength of a forest buffalo, the speed of a horse, and firm limbs.
With hair as dark as a bumblebee's body and a mouth fragrant with honey, he is attended by many women. // 172b //
With hair as dark as a bhr̥ṅga bee, a mouth fragrant with honey, attended by many women,
and enriched with eloquence, memory, and intellect, one becomes like a very skillful sacrificial fire through the consumption [of this] for just one month.
By consuming it for just one month, he becomes eloquent, intelligent, prosperous, and possesses a most skillful digestive fire;
he assumes the body of Narasiṃha, shining like gold heated by the flames of fire.
Diseases do not even touch the one who protects himself, just as the Asuras, terrified of the Man-Lion, did not touch the Man-Lion whose arms were blazing with the discus. 173.
39.173 One who, with self-restraint, eats fried bhr̥ṅga and pravāla stalks with ghee— his arms radiant like [the spokes of] a wheel—
and who, having a purified digestive tract, consumes milk processed with the essence of *asanā* as a supplement to his meal, [is freed from disease].
By consuming it for one month, he lives happily for three hundred years;
with his memory and senses unimpaired, he retains even that which is spoken but once.
39.175b–176. And he who employs this very oil according to this same procedure lives for two hundred years;
he obtains those very same benefits and his hair becomes black.

The elixirs that are feasible, productive of results, and suited to the respective ages have been described; other elixirs of great benefit, though involving hardships such as [the pursuit of] attainment and so forth, have not been proclaimed.

39.177cv Even other [remedies] of great power and other [remedies] of great benefit may arise as diseases due to a failure in the procedure for *rasāyana*; in such cases, their respective specific medicines should be administered, setting aside the *rasāyana* itself. 178.
One should know that a speaker of truth, free from anger, with senses directed inward, peaceful, and devoted to virtuous conduct, is an eternal elixir. 179.
He who, endowed with these qualities, practices the elixir (rasāyana),
being one whose self is withdrawn, attains long life and rejoices both in this world and in the next.
Endowed with these combined qualities, he is at peace in soul and long-lived;
his conduct follows the scriptures, those attending him know his mind, and his intellect is unerring regarding its objects— this is the complete elixir.
A man who indulges in the objects of the senses should constantly seek aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*);
for therein depend satisfaction, nourishment, and virtuous offspring. (1)
That which produces offspring and progeny, which provides immediate exhilaration, and by means of which a man, possessing the strength of a stallion, goes unhindered toward women. (2)
Whatever by which one increases becomes exceedingly dear to women; for that is indeed aphrodisiac, and it is the supreme strengthener of the body. (3)
40.3 We rejoice in celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which is supremely invigorating for the body, righteous, conducive to fame and long life, an elixir for both worlds, and absolutely pure. // 4 //
It brings merit, fame, and long life; it bestows happiness upon both worlds and brings benefit to both worlds—
for one who has little strength, who is oppressed by afflictions, and who is full of passion.
Vājīkaraṇa is taught for the purpose of protecting the body from decay. // 5 //
And for one of little merit who is oppressed by afflictions and mental disturbances, or for a sick person, or for one who is healthy and of vigorous youth and uses aphrodisiacs.
In all seasons, sexual intercourse day after day is not forbidden.
40.6 For those of advanced age,
as well as for those who are unctuous and pure, one should administer non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) along with unctuous enemas (anuvāsana),
combined with ghee, oil, meat broth, milk, sugar, and honey.
The knower of yoga should first employ [regimens] for those who consume milk, meat, and meat broth; thereafter, he should apply aphrodisiac formulations that bestow semen, progeny, and strength. (8)

40.8dv A tree that increases its sap and offspring, yet lacks luster, has putrid flowers, and is devoid of fruit— just as such a tree is solitary, possesses but a single branch, and is childless, so too is that man. // 9 //
With faltering gait and indistinct speech, covered in dust and with a mouth soiled by saliva, it brings delight to the heart. (10)
40.10 With what can offspring, which brings joy to the heart, be equaled in its sight, touch, and so forth?
How much more so that which increases fame, virtue, honor, prosperity, and the lineage? 11.
With whom could offspring be equal? How much more so one who increases fame, dharma, honor,
prosperity, and lineage?
When the body is purified, one should employ aphrodisiac formulations according to one's capacity, using the roots of *śara*, sugarcane, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *vidārī*, and *vīraṇa*. (12)

40.12 When the body is purified, one should [administer] according to one's capacity the roots of *kaṇṭakārī*, as well as *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *balā*, the two types of *medā*, the two types of *kākolī*, the two types of *śūrpaparṇī*, and *śatāvarī*.
Aśvagandhā, atibalā, ātmaguptā, punarnavā, vīrā, payasyā, jīvantī, ṛddhi, rāsnā, and trikaṇṭaka— (14).
One should cook three palas each of madhuka and śāliparṇī, along with one āḍhaka of masha beans, in two droṇas of water.

One should cook it with the decoction until one *āḍhaka* remains; then, having added one *āḍhaka* of ghee and one *āḍhaka* each of the juices of *vidārī*, *dhātrī*, and sugarcane, [one should boil it further]. (16)
One should add milk four times the quantity of ghee and throw in these powders: vīrā, svaguptā, the two kākolyas, yaṣṭīmadhu, the phalgu fruits, and pippalī. (17)

40.17–18. One should add *yaṣṭikā*, elephant pepper (*gajapippalī*), grapes, *vidārī*, dates, licorice (*madhuka*), and *śatāvarī*— once these have been boiled and strained— to one *prastha* each of the powder.
With one *kuḍava* each of sugar, *tugākṣīrī*, and long pepper (*pippalī*), and with half a *palā* each of black pepper (*marica*) and [the other two ingredients], separately. (19)
One should then eat one *pala* of finely ground cinnamon (*tvak*), cardamom (*elā*), and saffron (*kesara*), along with two *kuḍava*s of honey, every day while subsisting on meat broth and milk. (20)
With two *kuḍava* measures of honey, one who eats honey and milk every day mounts like a stallion and becomes as excited as a sparrow.
[This is] the powder of *vidārī*, *pippalī*, *śāli*, *priyālā*, and sugarcane.
One *kuḍava* each of the roots of *svaguptā* and honey, half a *tulā* of powdered sugar, and half a *prastha* of fresh ghee. // 22 //

Therefore, he who has a hundred women in his house should eat from this [preparation] only the size of a seed of the *akṣa* tree—namely, *ātmaguptā* fruits cooked in milk with wheat, served cold. (23)
40.23b–d. He who has a hundred beautiful women in his house, eating beans with ghee and honey while following the regimen of drinking the milk of a cow that has recently calved,
remains awake through the entire night without fatigue, exhausting his women.
One who eats sesame seeds mixed with sugar, which have been repeatedly soaked in milk prepared with goat testicles, may approach a hundred women as if they were virgins. (25)
Having repeatedly soaked sesame seeds and the powder of vidārī many times with its own juice,
one who licks it mixed with honey and ghee attains a hundred women.

A woman who, having licked ten *kṛṣṇa-dhātrī* fruits ground into powder and well-impregnated with their own juice, mixed with sugar, honey, and clarified butter, subsequently drinks milk, conceives. (40.26–27)
That man, even if eighty years old, rejoices like a youth, by taking the powder of black *dhātrī* fruit;
likewise, one who takes a *karṣa* of *madhuka* powder combined with ghee and honey [attains the same]. 40.27–28ab.

40.28 If one who suffers from constant seminal discharge should lick [a paste] consisting of equal parts of ghee and honey, taking milk as an after-drink, he shall become free from it; likewise, he who drinks the paste of *kulīraśṛṅgī* stirred with milk [shall be cured].
He who eats white sugar, ghee, milk, and rice, and who consumes *payasyā* prepared with milk along with honey and ghee, becomes virile toward women. (30)
One should drink the meat broth of a *bāṣkayaṇa* cow followed by milk; thus, one does not suffer from depletion.
One may also take the powdered seeds of *svayaṅguptā* and *ikṣuraka* mixed with sugar. (31)
After drinking [the juice], a man should drink *bāṣkayina* with warm milk; having drunk it, he becomes like a donkey.
One should likewise employ the powder of *uccaṭā* and *śatāvarī* in this same manner.
Having eaten moon-white curd-whey with sugar and sixty-day rice, well-cleaned upon a cloth, even an old man becomes like a youth. (33)
Having consumed thirty-three cubic centimeters (cc) of this well-prepared [mixture] on a cloth,
and drinking dog-thorn, sugarcane, black gram, *ātmaguptā* seeds, and *śatāvarī* with milk, even an old man may go to a hundred women.
40.34c–d Even when one's digestion is impaired, one should drink milk;
whatever is sweet, unctuous, nourishing, strength-increasing, and gladdening to the mind—all that is called aphrodisiac (vṛṣya). 40.35ab
Therefore, emboldened by such possessions, one should approach a woman, impelled by his own momentum and gladdened by the qualities of women. (36)
40.36b–c. One who has cultivated [the mind] may approach a woman;
the five objects of sense, which provide pleasure to all the faculties, are the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree of Dharma. 40.37. They are the five arrows of the one whose bow is flowers.
40.37 Even the arrows of the flower-bowed god, when taken one by one, are indeed highly desired and bring supreme joy and pleasure;
how much more so those which are established together in the body of a woman? 38.
How much more so, then, regarding women’s bodies, the mere name of which brings a festival to the heart, for those who behold her there is no prior satisfaction;
she has become a snare that captivates all the senses, consecrated by the vow of devoted service to her beloved. (39)
40.39 She whose sight brings a satisfaction never before attained, who is adorned with artistic grace, youth, and beauty; who is pure, modest, yet bold in private;
who speaks kindly and shares the same desires—such a woman is supremely aphrodisiac for a man.
40.40 Speaking pleasantly and with an even-minded nature, she should practice the entire range of erotic conduct prescribed in the *Kāmasūtra*,
provided it is irreproachable, consistent with the place, time, strength, and capacity [of the partners], and not contrary to the medical treatises or established conventions. // 41 //

40.41b–42. Female companions who are irreproachable and instructed in the *kāmaśāstra*, skilled in the application of ointments, fragrant powders, affusions, perfumes, garlands, variegated garments, and various ornaments; proficient in music, poetry, and storytelling; and who are of similar disposition and under her control.
40.42b–c: Various kinds of garlands, food, garments, and ornaments;
they were skilled in narrating tales of Gandharva maidens and the like.
A long pond situated within their own residence was filled with birds intoxicated by the honey of lotus pollen.
In the valleys of the mountain peaks with blue ridges, there are forests situated at the outskirts of the city. // 43 //
40.43a Long ponds situated within their own dwellings, 40.43b where birds are intoxicated by the honey of lotus pollen;
40.43c mountain peaks with dark ridges and slopes.

Various species of trees are pleasing to the sight; the warbling of the cuckoo is pleasing to the ear; ornaments according to the influence of the seasons are pleasing to the body; and the entire retinue is pleasing to the mind. // 44 //
40.44b The warbling of the cuckoo, pleasing to the ear; 40.44c Ornaments suited to the specific season that delight the body; betel, clear wine, a beloved woman, and the night adorned by the moon;
whatever else is desired by the mind and acts as an aphrodisiac—all that [is beneficial]. 45.

40.45b Lovely are the nights, adorned with the crescent of the moon; 40.45d for that honey is indeed an aphrodisiac for the mind, like the face of a beloved woman with its blue lotus. Like a dear friend is the lute with its sweet resonance;
and the bed, delightful to the mind with its heap of flowers, is like a flowering creeper with its sprouting shoots. // 46 //
40.46b The tinkling of her ornaments was like a dear woman speaking sweet words; 40.46c And the bed, made of gathered flowers, was enchanting.
Neither in her dwelling nor in her body was there any pain, nor even the slightest mental distress regarding her possessions.
These aphrodisiac formulations, when employed, fulfill every desire of love. // 47 //
In this place and body, there shall never be pain; nor shall there be even the slightest affliction of the mind regarding worldly objects.
For fever, one should take *mustā* and *parpaṭaka*; for thirst, water produced from a clod of earth heated by fire.
Parched grain (lāja) for vomiting; realgar (girija) for disorders arising from the bladder; and myrobalan (dhātrī) and turmeric (niśā) for urinary disorders (meha).
Iron is the best for *pāṇḍu* disease, while long pepper is best for fearlessness, wind, phlegm, and splenic disorders.
In the case of a wound, [the paste] should be made from *kṛmijā*; for poison, *śukataru*; and for fat-type wind disorders (*medo-'nila*), *guggulu*. // 48d //
Vṛṣa is for blood-bile (asṛpitta), kuṭaja for diarrhea, bhallātaka for hemorrhoids, and gold for poisons;
tārkṣya for obesity, kṛmighna for worms, and liquor, goat’s milk, or meat for consumption (śoṣa). 49.

40.49b–d. *Bhallātaka* is used for hemorrhoids and poisons; gold for eye diseases; *triphalā* and *guḍūcī* for the disease of wind-blood (*vātāsra*); buttermilk for malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*);
the heartwood of *khadira* is to be used for skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*); and the substance called "stone" (*śilāhvaya*) for all diseases.
Fresh ghee overcomes insanity; liquor overcomes grief; *brāhmī* overcomes epilepsy; milk overcomes loss of sleep; and *rasālā* overcomes catarrh. (51)
40.51b–v: *Brāhmī* [overcomes] grief, wine [causes] loss of memory; meat [causes] emaciation; garlic [causes] wind [disorders]; sweating [causes] stiffness of the limbs.
From the application of *guḍamañjarī* as a nasal drop (*nasya*), *khapura* relieves pain in the shoulders, upper arms, and forearms.
Camel urine and milk, rubbed with fresh butter and sugar, used as nasal drops (nasya) cure pain in the shoulders, shoulders-blades, and arms; they also destroy abdominal enlargement (udara).
Nasal therapy cures disorders of the head and acute abscesses (vidradhi), while bloodletting treats similar conditions.
Camel urine and milk destroy abdominal enlargement (udara). Nasal medication (nasya) cures disorders of the upper body;

nasal medication [applied] to the head cures disorders of the head; gargling (kavala) cures disorders born of the mouth; and nasal medication, collyrium (añjana), and eye-satiation (tarpaṇa) cure ocular pains.
For an elderly person, milk, ghee, cold water, wind, and shade alleviate fainting.

Nasal drops (nasya) and gargles (kavaḍa) for diseases of the mouth; nasal drops alone for diseases of the mouth; nasal drops and gargles for ailments arising in the mouth; wine with equal parts of fermented gruel (śukta) and fresh ginger (ārdraka) when the digestive fire is weak; and bathing after physical exertion.
For enduring suffering and maintaining steadfastness, the exercise of *gokṣura* is beneficial in cases of *kṛcchra*.

40.55a Equal parts of dry ginger and fresh ginger; 40.55b the drinking of wine for one with weak digestion or after physical exertion; 40.55c endurance of hardship for stability; 40.55c endurance of hardship for corpulence;
40.55d *nidigdhikā* for cough, and the root-fiber (*jaṭā*) of *puṣkara* for pain in the flanks.
Dhātrī is for stabilizing youth; triphalā and guggulu are for wounds.
40.56a A drink of *nidigdhikā* is for cough; 40.56b and *pauṣkara* is for pain in the flanks.
40.56c For the restoration of youth, [use] *dhātrī*; enemas [treat] disorders of *vāta*, purgation [treats] those arising from *pitta*, and emesis [treats] those born of *kapha*.
Honey overcomes phlegm, ghee overcomes bile, and oil overcomes wind.

Thus, that which has been declared as the foremost medicine for diseases, sufficient for their pacification, should be applied according to the requirements, taking into account the place, time, and strength [of the patient]. (58)

Having thus received this aphorism of meaning from Ātreya, Agniveśa—unsatiated by those elegant sayings, esteemed by Bheda and others, and bowing with devotion—asked this while still harboring doubts. (59)
40.59ab Thus, having received from Ātreya this subtle meaning through sacred tradition (āgama), he remained unsatiated with those elegant and well-spoken words.
O Blessed One, some who possess self-mastery are seen to be afflicted by disease, even though they are provided with wealth and attendants and follow the instructions of experienced physicians. (60)
Some have their vitality diminished by disease, while others are the opposite;
therefore, the fruit of distinguishing between the beneficial and the harmful is uncertain.
To the group of disciples headed by Agniveśa, who were wondering what this treatise teaches, Punarvasu explained its true nature in its entirety.

40.62cd–63ab I shall explain that reality in its entirety; however, medical treatment and non-medical treatment ought not to be considered equal. For even without treatment, those who attain health do so by a sixteenth part [of the effort required].
For all who are sinking in the mire of affliction, the physician’s mastery is a hand to hold; for all who are dying, there is no life other than medicine. 64.
40.64 There is no medicine for all [diseases] at once; indeed, not all diseases are cured without regard for a means, nor otherwise.
They are successful only when accomplished through a means, because that which lacks a cause cannot possess a cause.
40.65–66. Therefore, it is not the case that there is no cause [for death] when one possesses a cause;
thus, what was said—that death occurs despite medical treatment endowed with every excellence—is not so. For there is no such thing as a non-remedy for a remedy.
40.66 Even for one who possesses wisdom and is endowed with skillful means, no action ever fails due to a lack of means; yet,
even through adverse fate, this [sixteen-fold practice] never fails to succeed.
Even for one endowed with skillful means, success may fail due to adverse fate;
yet for whom has this sixteenfold [science]— including fire, water, and so forth— not been proven effective in such actions as inducing perspiration or causing paralysis?
Neither the milking nor the nourishing of *gavedhuka* grass yields milk for anyone. (68)
40.68c–d: For whom is there neither nourishment nor emaciation? 40.68d: For whom is there no certainty regarding the aphrodisiac power of milk, gavedhuka, black gram, or ātmaguptā?
For whom are the functions of feces and urine, as well as their expulsion, considered doubtful in the case of barley?

40.69ab For whom is there no certainty regarding virility through the use of black gram (*māṣa*), *ātmaguptā*, and other such substances? 40.69cd For whom does poison not undergo digestion when deprived of mantras and ritual procedures?
70. Who has attained health from *rohiṇikā* and similar ailments without the aid of wholesome diet (*pathya*)?
40.70 Who has ever attained the state of a Kalpa through wholesome practices?
Furthermore, untimely death is certain according to all established doctrines;
how else could it be averted even with great effort? (71)

Even sandalwood and the like, though traditionally established for use in burning and similar conditions, attain their proven efficacy only through the authority of the treatise; likewise, fasting and nourishing therapies are established for fever only by means of the scripture.
Having properly considered and applied this treatment, which is endowed with the four qualities of a physician, do not harbor doubt regarding the destruction of disease through medical therapy. (73)
Do not think that this [treatment], though complete with the four qualities of its four parts, is sufficient for the destruction of disease;
for it is the firm severing of the nooses of death at an unexpected moment. It is a protective thread for those terrified and afraid of illness, even though it is itself without a thread.
This very nectar is manifest and free from the world's weariness;
yet, when placed in an unworthy vessel, it instantly turns into the Hālāhala poison.
This nectar of the Vedas is directly free from all exertion in this world; yet it becomes like the *hālāhala* poison for those who,
though devoted solely to the scriptures, do not understand the true essence of the teachings.
One should avoid from afar quack physicians, as one would avoid the snares of Vaivasvata.

40.76–77. The physician should avoid those who are mere quacks; rather, he should seek out physicians of virtuous conduct, who are auspicious and endowed with scriptural knowledge, who have mastered their craft, who are auspicious, and who desire what is auspicious for their patients.
40.77bv [May there be] welfare for those who possess many scriptural traditions and are habituated to the scriptures;
40.77cv For those who have practiced the ritual actions, there is success— [a work] endowed with the qualities of a *tantra* and devoid of the faults of a *tantra*.
It stands pervading the entire science of medicine on all sides. // 78 //

Free from the defects of the tantras, it stands pervading all directions; it follows the thought of the Great Sage of vast and stainless wisdom, and it is characterized by the essential meaning gathered as deep as the great ocean. // 79 //
40.79ab Vast, stainless consciousness, 40.79cd as deep as the great ocean, 40.79cd following the thought of the Great Sage,
40.79d characterized by the meaning of the summary; 40.79d that which perceives the meaning of the summary.

From the churning of the great ocean of the eightfold science of medicine, that great mass of nectar known as the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha* was obtained; from that, this separate treatise has been proclaimed for the sake of the pleasure of those with limited effort, yielding no small fruit. (80)

40.80b That which is equal to the essence of the great nectar of the compendium of the eight branches (aṣṭāṅga-saṃgraha-mahāmṛta-sāra-tulyaḥ) 40.80d has been thus spoken as a separate treatise for the sake of bringing joy, because it is established by scripture and because its results are seen directly.
It should be employed like a mantra; it must not be subjected to critical analysis in any way whatsoever. 81.

Because this is pure by virtue of its scriptural authority, it should never be subjected to critical scrutiny: through recitation, comprehension, and practice, one certainly attains long life, health, dharma, wealth, happiness, and fame. (40.81–82)
40.82 Having attained long life and health, this physician— capable of comprehensive understanding through the study of this [work], skilled in his own practice, and unshakable—
shakes the efforts of others who have applied themselves to vast treatises; if that is so, it is no wonder.

40.83cv He who causes other extensive treatises to tremble—if he studies Caraka, then he is certainly an outsider even regarding the mere names of the diseases described by Suśruta and others. Now, what indeed can that wretched man do for the sick if he is devoid of Caraka and remains unmoistened by its methodology? 84 //

40.84b–d: For those whose diseases have been described— or even for those whose diseases have not been described— if he is excluded by the mere mention of their names, what indeed can that wretched man do here for the sick?

He who, due to the force of dogmatic attachment, does not apply himself even to well-spoken words because he is profoundly dull-witted—let such a person, tireless throughout his entire human lifespan, diligently study the primary medical treatises. (85)
Oil is beneficial for wind (vāta), ghee for bile (pitta), and honey for the pacification of phlegm (śleṣman); this is the sequence.
Whether it was spoken by Brahmā or by one born of Brahmā—who possesses the power to speak such distinctions regarding the speaker when there is no difference in the mantra? // 86 //
40.86 Whether this was spoken by Brahmā or by one born of Brahmā, or whether it is distinguished by the power of the substance due to the influence of the speaker—
therefore, casting aside envy, let impartiality be adopted. 87.
40.87 If, due to the influence of the author, you have affection for something composed by a sage, then setting aside Caraka and Suśruta,
why are Bheda and others not also recited? Therefore, one should accept whatever is well-spoken.

Whatever merit has been acquired by me through composing this "Heart," which is like the very heart of the ocean of the verbal essence of the entire Ayurveda, may from that arise supreme well-being for the world. (89)
